books.title: A Doll's House
books.author: Henrik Ibsen
books.setting: One room in the Helmers' flat in a Norwegian town, across Christmas Eve, Christmas Day and the evening after
books.lengthNote: Three acts in prose, all in the same room, with every decisive event of the past reported rather than shown
books.openingLine: Hide the Christmas tree carefully, Helen. Be sure the children do not see it until this evening, when it is dressed.
books.summary: Nora Helmer forged her dying father's signature to borrow money that saved her husband's life, and has been paying it back in secret for years out of the housekeeping. Over three days at Christmas the loan comes due socially rather than financially: the man who holds the bond wants a job, the letter reaches the letterbox, and Nora waits for her husband to do the thing she has always assumed he would do. He does not, and the play ends with the most consequential exit in modern theatre.
books.referenceStyle: act. The translation checked against runs as continuous prose dialogue without line numbers, so quotations are placed by act and by the moment in the action rather than by line.

sourceText.label: Standard Ebooks text of A Doll's House, in R. Farquharson Sharp's English translation
sourceText.note: Ibsen wrote in Danish-Norwegian; every English quotation here is a translator's wording. Sharp anglicises some of the money, so the Porter is paid in shillings where Ibsen's has krone. The text carries no line numbering, so references give the act.

structure.label: Act I
structure.title: Christmas Eve: a tree, a promotion and a bond
structure.summary: Nora comes home with parcels and is teased about spending. Mrs Linde arrives looking for work, and Nora tells her the secret she has kept for eight years. Krogstad, who lent the money and holds a bond with a forged signature on it, comes to ask for his job at the bank and makes plain what he will do if he loses it.

scenes.summary: The skylark and the squirrel, the macaroons hidden in a pocket, and a household about to have money for the first time.
Nora tells Mrs Linde that the journey to Italy was paid for by her, not by her father.
The lender explains what the forged signature is worth to him.
Helmer lectures on how a deceitful parent poisons a household, and Nora sends the children away.

structure.label: Act II
structure.title: Christmas Day: the tree stripped, the letterbox locked
structure.summary: The tree stands bare in the corner and the letter has not yet come. Nora tries to get Krogstad's dismissal reversed and fails on a point of Helmer's pride; Doctor Rank makes his declaration at the worst possible moment; and the letter goes into the box, which Helmer keeps the key to. Nora dances the tarantella to stop him opening it.

scenes.summary: The fancy-dress dress needs mending, and Mrs Linde begins asking questions about Doctor Rank.
Helmer refuses to keep Krogstad on, and the reason turns out to be that the man calls him by his Christian name.
The black cross, and a request Nora can no longer make once he has spoken.
Krogstad drops his letter in the box; Nora dances to hold her husband's attention for twenty-four hours.

structure.label: Act III
structure.title: After the ball: two shipwrecked people, and one door
structure.summary: Mrs Linde and Krogstad settle their own past in ten minutes and she stops him withdrawing the letter, on the grounds that the Helmers need the truth more than they need safety. Helmer reads it, calls his wife a hypocrite and a criminal, reads the second letter, declares himself saved, and finds that the crisis has gone the wrong way round.

scenes.summary: Two people who lost each other for money agree to join forces.
Helmer's fear for his own position, and his plan to keep up appearances.
The bond is returned, Helmer forgives, and Nora changes her dress.
The first serious conversation of the marriage, conducted sitting down, and the door below.

characters.name: Nora Helmer
characters.role: Torvald's wife, mother of three
characters.summary: She has run a secret business for eight years, copying documents at night behind a locked door and calling it fun, while playing the spendthrift child her husband finds charming. The play's argument is that the performance and the competence are the same woman, and that nobody in the house has ever been curious enough to notice.
characters.clue: She eats macaroons in secret, saved her husband's life with a forged signature, and dances a tarantella to stop a letter being read.

relationships.label: brought up by, and employer of

characters.name: Torvald Helmer
characters.role: A lawyer, newly appointed manager of the bank
characters.summary: He is not a villain and is barely even unkind; he is a man who has arranged his household as a compliment to himself and cannot imagine it any other way. His refusal to keep Krogstad on turns out to rest on the fact that the man uses his first name, and that detail is the whole diagnosis.
characters.clue: He calls his wife a lark and a squirrel, lectures her on the household effects of a deceitful mother, and cannot dismiss an employee for the reason he gives.

characters.name: Nils Krogstad
characters.role: A subordinate at the bank, and Nora's creditor
characters.summary: He committed one forgery, was never prosecuted and has been paying for it socially ever since, which makes him the play's best witness on how respectability actually works. He is threatening for two acts and then, given one thing he wants, becomes reasonable in a page.
characters.clue: He did once what Nora has done, and has spent years finding out what it costs afterwards.

characters.name: Mrs Linde
characters.role: Nora's old schoolfriend, a widow looking for work
characters.summary: She married for money to keep a mother and two brothers alive, was widowed with nothing, and is the only character in the play who has supported herself. Her decision to let the letter stand is the hinge of the last act, and she takes it for a reason she states plainly: this house has been living on concealment.
characters.clue: She gave up the man she loved to support her family, and now asks a favour that turns out to cost her friend everything.
traits: decisive at the wrong moment for Nora

characters.name: Doctor Rank
characters.role: The family's friend and daily visitor
characters.summary: He is dying of a disease he attributes to his father's manner of living, and he keeps the fact from Helmer because Helmer cannot bear ugliness. His declaration to Nora removes the one source of money she had left, and his exit is arranged by visiting card so that nobody has to watch.
characters.clue: He will send a card with a black cross on it when the end begins, and asks to be allowed to die out of sight.
traits: in love with his friend's wife

characters.name: Anne
characters.role: The children's nurse, formerly Nora's
characters.summary: She gave up her own child to take a position, which is the same transaction Nora is about to make and the play puts them side by side without comment. She has two short scenes and they carry the entire cost of the ending in advance.
characters.clue: She nursed the mistress of the house when she was small, and left her own daughter behind to do it.

relationships.label: nurse to, then to her children

themes.name: The doll, and the performance of a marriage
themes.canonicalName: The doll, and the performance of a marriage
themes.summary: Nora is addressed as a bird, a squirrel and a child for two and a half acts, and answers in the same register because it works. When she finally describes the arrangement, she does it as a line of descent: her father played with her, Torvald played with her, and she has been playing with her own children in exactly the same way.
themes.development: Pet names and a hidden bag of macaroons in Act I; a costume, a rehearsed dance and a husband as audience in Act II; and in Act III the word doll used by Nora herself, at a table, with the tarantella dress changed for ordinary clothes.

themes.name: Money, law and a woman's signature
themes.canonicalName: Money, law and a woman's signature
themes.summary: The plot depends on a legal fact rather than a moral one: Nora could not borrow without a man's name, so she wrote her dying father's. Krogstad's answer, that the law cares nothing about motives, is not cruelty but an accurate statement of the position, and the play lets it stand unrefuted.
themes.development: A secret debt repaid out of housekeeping in Act I, a bond in a letterbox in Act II, and in Act III a woman announcing that she will find out whether the law or she is right.

themes.name: Reputation and what a man will risk
themes.summary: Helmer's whole conduct is governed by how things look to the bank. He will not keep Krogstad because the man addresses him familiarly in front of the staff, and when the letter arrives his first thought is not for his wife but for whether he might be suspected of prompting her.
themes.development: A promotion in Act I, a refusal on a point of manners in Act II, and in Act III a proposal that the marriage continue in the eyes of the world while ceasing in every other respect.

themes.name: Duties to others and duties to oneself
themes.summary: The last fifteen minutes are an argument about the word duty, conducted at a table with both parties sitting down. Helmer names the duties of a wife and mother as though listing established facts; Nora accepts them as widely held opinions and says she must first find out whether they are true for her.
themes.development: Sacred duties asserted, other duties just as sacred claimed, and then the shortest and most disruptive line in the play: duties to myself.

themes.name: Inheritance, sickness and the sins of fathers
themes.summary: Helmer believes moral corruption passes from parent to child and says so at length in Act I, not knowing whose household he is describing. Rank's spinal disease is attributed to his father's amusements, so the play sets a medical inheritance beside a moral one and declines to separate them cleanly.
themes.development: A lawyer's theory of deceitful mothers in Act I, a dying man's account of his father in Act II, and a mother in Act III who concludes that she is unfit to bring up children until she has educated herself.

themes.name: Work, and who is allowed to do it
themes.summary: Every character is defined by employment: a new managership, a subordinate clerkship, a widow looking for a post, a nurse who left her own child to take one, and a wife whose earnings had to be hidden because she was not supposed to have any. Nora describes the copying she did at night as the happiest work she has known.
themes.development: Secret night work in Act I, a job asked for and refused in Act II, and in Act III a woman leaving with nothing and intending to find something to do.

techniques.name: Analytic structure
techniques.definition: A play whose decisive events all happened before the curtain rose and reach the audience as disclosure.
techniques.bookDefinition: A play whose decisive events all happened before the curtain rose and reach the audience as disclosure.
techniques.inThisBook: The forgery, the illness, the journey to Italy and the father's death are all in the past; the three acts are the process by which they come out, which is why so much of the play is people telling each other things.

techniques.name: The single room
techniques.definition: Confining every scene to one interior so that entrances and exits carry the pressure.
techniques.bookDefinition: Confining every scene to one interior so that entrances and exits carry the pressure.
techniques.inThisBook: Nothing can be escaped except by leaving, which is why the final door has the force it does; the same doors admit Krogstad, Rank and the letter.

techniques.name: Stage properties
techniques.definition: Objects that carry meaning and change state across the acts.
techniques.bookDefinition: Objects that carry meaning and change state across the acts.
techniques.inThisBook: The Christmas tree is dressed in Act I and stripped in Act II; the macaroons, the locked letterbox, the fancy-dress costume and the returned bond each mark a stage of the concealment.

techniques.name: Diminutive address
techniques.definition: Characterising a relationship through the names one person is allowed to use for another.
techniques.bookDefinition: Characterising a relationship through the names one person is allowed to use for another.
techniques.inThisBook: Lark, squirrel, skylark, spendthrift, little person: Helmer almost never uses his wife's name in the first two acts, and the moment he starts to she has stopped answering.

techniques.name: The set-piece dance
techniques.definition: A performance inside the play that the audience watches being performed.
techniques.bookDefinition: A performance inside the play that the audience watches being performed.
techniques.inThisBook: Nora rehearses the tarantella wildly to keep her husband from the letterbox; he corrects her steps, which tells us exactly what he thinks he is watching.

techniques.name: The parallel couple
techniques.definition: A second pairing whose arrangement comments on the first.
techniques.bookDefinition: A second pairing whose arrangement comments on the first.
techniques.inThisBook: Mrs Linde and Krogstad negotiate their future in one honest conversation, which is the thing the Helmers have never once managed, and they do it in the same room.

quotations.text: Is that my little lark twittering out there?
quotations.speaker: Helmer
quotations.context: His first words in the play, called from the study without coming out.
quotations.analysis: The first thing said to Nora is not her name, and it is a question about a noise rather than a person. Ibsen puts the whole marriage in the opening exchange: a man who addresses his wife as wildlife, from another room, and a woman who answers in the character he has named.

quotations.text: It was I who saved Torvald’s life.
quotations.speaker: Nora
quotations.context: Pulling Mrs Linde down beside her on the sofa, after being told she knows nothing of real trouble.
quotations.analysis: The emphasis is placed on the pronoun, and it is the first sentence in the play in which Nora is the subject of a serious verb. She has been treated as an expense for two scenes and now produces the one fact that would reverse the household's opinion of her, and immediately makes her friend promise to keep it.

quotations.text: The law cares nothing about motives.
quotations.speaker: Krogstad
quotations.context: Answering Nora's claim that saving a life must count for something.
quotations.analysis: Six words, and they are the play's legal position stated correctly by its least admired character. Ibsen gives the blackmailer the accurate account of how the statute works, so that Nora's outrage has nothing to push against except the law itself.

quotations.text: Then it must be a very foolish law.
quotations.speaker: Nora
quotations.context: Her immediate reply to Krogstad.
quotations.analysis: She dismisses the entire legal code in eight words and then changes the subject, which in Act I reads as childishness. The last act picks the same sentence up and turns it into a programme: she will go away and find out whether the law is right or she is.

quotations.text: Almost everyone who has gone to the bad early in life has had a deceitful mother.
quotations.speaker: Helmer
quotations.context: Explaining to Nora, minutes after Krogstad has left the house, why a dishonest parent ruins children.
quotations.analysis: He delivers it as professional experience and it lands on the woman standing in front of him, who has just been threatened over a forged signature. The scene ends with Nora refusing to let the children in, which is the first thing she decides entirely on her own.

quotations.text: He suffers from a diseased moral character, Mrs. Helmer; but even he began talking of its being highly important that he should live.
quotations.speaker: Doctor Rank
quotations.context: Explaining who else is waiting to see Helmer.
quotations.analysis: A dying physician diagnoses a man's ethics as a medical condition, and the sentence turns on the word but: even the morally diseased want to go on living. Ibsen is putting Rank's spine and Krogstad's reputation into the same vocabulary, which is the play's quiet joke about inheritance.

quotations.text: Do you suppose I am going to make myself ridiculous before my whole staff, to let people think that I am a man to be swayed by all sorts of outside influence?
quotations.speaker: Helmer
quotations.context: Refusing to reinstate Krogstad at his wife's request.
quotations.analysis: The reason he gives is not that Krogstad is dishonest but that reversing himself would look like being led by someone. A few lines later he admits the real objection is that the man calls him by his first name in front of the clerks, and a marriage is destroyed on that point of etiquette.

quotations.text: As soon as I am quite certain that the worst has come, I shall send you my card with a black cross on it, and then you will know that the loathsome end has begun.
quotations.speaker: Doctor Rank
quotations.context: Telling Nora how she will know that he is dying.
quotations.analysis: He arranges his own death as a piece of correspondence, so that nobody has to be present for it. The card with the black cross is the play's most economical stage property: it converts a man into a piece of paper in a letterbox, which is precisely what Krogstad's letter does to Nora.

quotations.text: How should you understand it? A wonderful thing is going to happen!
quotations.speaker: Nora
quotations.context: To Mrs Linde, who has asked what she is waiting for.
quotations.analysis: She never says what the wonderful thing is, and the refusal is not coyness: naming it would require her to admit she has been counting on her husband to sacrifice himself. The phrase recurs half a dozen times and means something different each time she uses it.

quotations.text: You should have let it alone; you must prevent nothing. After all, it is splendid to be waiting for a wonderful thing to happen.
quotations.speaker: Nora
quotations.context: On being told that Mrs Linde has written to Krogstad and will see him tomorrow.
quotations.analysis: She forbids the one intervention that might save her, because the catastrophe has become the test she wants her husband to pass. It is the clearest evidence that by Act II Nora is no longer trying to avoid discovery; she is waiting for it.

quotations.text: Two on the same piece of wreckage would stand a better chance than each on their own.
quotations.speaker: Mrs Linde
quotations.context: Proposing to Krogstad in the Helmers' sitting room while the dance goes on upstairs.
quotations.analysis: A proposal expressed as arithmetic, offered by a woman who has already once chosen security over love and does not pretend otherwise. This is the only negotiation in the play conducted by two people who tell each other the truth, and Ibsen stages it in the same room that has held eight years of concealment.

quotations.text: Helmer must know all about it. This unhappy secret must be disclosed; they must have a complete understanding between them, which is impossible with all this concealment and falsehood going on.
quotations.speaker: Mrs Linde
quotations.context: Stopping Krogstad from asking for his letter back.
quotations.analysis: She takes the decision that ends the marriage, and she takes it on a principle rather than out of malice: a household running on a secret is worse off than one facing a scandal. Everything Nora suffers in the last twenty minutes is set in motion by the only person in the play who has been supporting herself.

quotations.text: Now you have destroyed all my happiness. You have ruined all my future. It is horrible to think of! I am in the power of an unscrupulous man; he can do what he likes with me, ask anything he likes of me, give me any orders he pleases⁠—I dare not refuse. And I must sink to such miserable depths because of a thoughtless woman!
quotations.speaker: Helmer
quotations.context: Moments after reading Krogstad's letter.
quotations.analysis: Count the possessives: my happiness, my future, my house. The forgery was committed to keep him alive and his response is a list of his own losses, which is the exact information Nora has been waiting eight years to receive.

quotations.text: Yes, it is true! I am saved! Nora, I am saved!
quotations.speaker: Helmer
quotations.context: Opening the second letter, which encloses the bond.
quotations.analysis: He says it twice and both times in the first person singular, then adds her name as an afterthought rather than as a subject. Nora's question in reply, what about her, gets the answer that she is saved too, and the pronouns have already decided the end of the play.

quotations.text: He called me his doll-child, and he played with me just as I used to play with my dolls.
quotations.speaker: Nora
quotations.context: At the table, explaining how she came to have no opinions of her own.
quotations.analysis: The word the play is named for is used by Nora only in the last ten minutes, and she applies it first to her father. What she is describing is not cruelty but an inheritance of arrangements, which is why the speech is delivered flatly rather than as an accusation.

quotations.text: But our home has been nothing but a playroom. I have been your doll-wife, just as at home I was Papa’s doll-child; and here the children have been my dolls. I thought it great fun when you played with me, just as they thought it great fun when I played with them. That is what our marriage has been, Torvald.
quotations.speaker: Nora
quotations.context: Continuing the same speech, a few lines later.
quotations.analysis: Three generations are lined up in one sentence: she was played with, she was played with again, and she has been doing it to her own children. The charge is not that her husband was a tyrant but that nothing in the house was ever serious, and she includes herself in the indictment.

quotations.text: Before all else, you are a wife and a mother.
quotations.speaker: Helmer
quotations.context: Answering Nora's claim that she has duties to herself.
quotations.analysis: He states it as a definition rather than an argument, which is what makes it answerable. The phrase before all else is then taken from him word for word in Nora's reply, and the theft of the construction is the point at which she stops being managed.

quotations.text: Duties to myself.
quotations.speaker: Nora
quotations.context: Asked what duties could possibly outrank those to husband and children.
quotations.analysis: Three words, and they are the sentence that caused the play to be banned, rewritten and argued about across Europe. Ibsen places them as a flat answer to a rhetorical question, with no justification attached, so that the audience has to supply the argument or refuse it.

quotations.text: I don’t believe that any longer. I believe that before all else I am a reasonable human being, just as you are⁠—or, at all events, that I must try and become one. I know quite well, Torvald, that most people would think you right, and that views of that kind are to be found in books; but I can no longer content myself with what most people say, or with what is found in books. I must think over things for myself and get to understand them.
quotations.speaker: Nora
quotations.context: Rejecting the definition of herself as wife and mother first.
quotations.analysis: She does not claim that most people are wrong, only that she can no longer take their word or a book's for it. The demand is not for rights but for the chance to find out what she thinks, which is a smaller and much harder thing to refuse.

quotations.text: According to it a woman has no right to spare her old dying father, or to save her husband’s life. I can’t believe that.
quotations.speaker: Nora
quotations.context: Explaining what she has learned about the law since Krogstad explained it to her.
quotations.analysis: She has taken Krogstad's legal lesson from Act I and turned it into a test the law has to pass, not one she has to. The last four words do all the work: not a claim about what the law is, but a refusal to accept it, which is where the play leaves the question.

quotations.text: I would gladly work night and day for you, Nora⁠—bear sorrow and want for your sake. But no man would sacrifice his honour for the one he loves.
quotations.speaker: Helmer
quotations.context: Told that the wonderful thing she waited for was his taking the blame himself.
quotations.analysis: The first clause offers a lifetime of labour and the second withholds the one thing that was actually asked for, and he sees no contradiction between them. Honour is being described as a possession a man cannot spend, which is the same logic his household has applied to money all along.

quotations.text: It is a thing hundreds of thousands of women have done.
quotations.speaker: Nora
quotations.context: Her reply, immediately after Helmer says no man would sacrifice his honour for love.
quotations.analysis: The sentence answers a claim about human nature with a fact about how many people have already done it. It also enlarges the play in one line, taking a quarrel in a Norwegian sitting room and setting it against every household the audience has come from.

quotations.text: Ah, Torvald, the most wonderful thing of all would have to happen.
quotations.speaker: Nora
quotations.context: Asked whether they might ever be more than strangers.
quotations.analysis: The phrase has been running through the play attached to a rescue she expected from her husband, and here it is transferred to something neither of them can arrange: a change in both of them. She says two lines later that she no longer believes in wonderful things happening, which is what makes the ending a departure rather than an ultimatum.

quotations.text: The sound of a door shutting is heard from below.
quotations.speaker: Stage direction
quotations.context: The last line of the play, printed as a stage direction after Helmer's final half-sentence.
quotations.analysis: Ibsen gives the curtain to a noise offstage rather than to a speech, and to a door that the audience never sees. The sentence is passive and impersonal, which leaves Helmer alone on stage with a hope he has just voiced and a sound that answers it.

atAGlance.label: Published
atAGlance.note: As Et dukkehjem, in Copenhagen, in a first printing of 8,000 copies.

atAGlance.label: First performed
atAGlance.note: At the Royal Theatre, Copenhagen, with Betty Hennings as Nora.

atAGlance.label: English text here
atAGlance.note: His translation was published by J. M. Dent in Everyman's Library in 1910.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.note: The forgery, the illness, the father's death and the journey to Italy all happen before the curtain rises.

criticalViews.position: A play about the position of women
criticalViews.summary: The reading the play has carried since 1879, and the reason it was banned, rewritten and imitated: a wife discovers that the law, her marriage and her upbringing have all treated her as a minor, and leaves to find out what she thinks.
criticalViews.counter: Ibsen himself resisted being enrolled as a campaigner, and the play is at least as interested in Helmer's fear of his colleagues as in Nora's rights.

criticalViews.position: A play about being a self at all
criticalViews.summary: A broader reading takes the subject to be the duty of any person to become something other than what their household has made them, with Nora's sex as the circumstance that makes the demand visible rather than its cause.
criticalViews.counter: It risks making the legal details of the forgery decorative, when the plot depends entirely on what a married woman could and could not sign.

criticalViews.position: A technical revolution
criticalViews.summary: Criticism of the staging has emphasised what Ibsen did to the well-made play: an ordinary room, contemporary clothes, a plot made of paper and post, and a final act in which two people sit down and talk instead of embracing or dying.
criticalViews.counter: The machinery is still that of melodrama, with a blackmailer, a bond, a lost letter and a coincidence of old lovers, however soberly it is handled.

essayQuestions.question: How does Ibsen present the Helmers' marriage before the crisis breaks?
essayQuestions.focus: Language, pet names and performance in Acts I and II
plan: Open on the first exchange: a husband addressing a bird from another room and a wife answering in character.
Collect the vocabulary of ownership and smallness, and note how rarely Helmer uses his wife's name.
Set against it what Nora has actually been doing: night work, secret repayments and eight years of accounts.
Use the tarantella as the moment the performance becomes literal, with Helmer correcting the steps.
Conclude on Act III, where Nora describes the arrangement in her own words and the vocabulary stops working.

essayQuestions.question: 'Krogstad is right about the law and Nora is right about everything else.' Discuss.
essayQuestions.focus: Law, motive and the forgery
plan: Set out the legal facts: what Nora signed, why she could not sign her own name, and what the bond is worth.
Read Krogstad's statement about motives as an accurate account rather than a threat.
Trace Nora's answer from her dismissal of a foolish law in Act I to her decision in Act III to test it.
Consider Krogstad's own history as evidence of what the law does after it has finished with someone.
Weigh what the play settles and what it deliberately leaves to the audience.

essayQuestions.question: What is the function of Mrs Linde and Doctor Rank?
essayQuestions.focus: The parallel plot and the play's other lives
plan: Establish Mrs Linde's history: a marriage for money, a widowhood with nothing, and work as survival.
Examine her decision to let Krogstad's letter stand, and the principle she gives for it.
Set the Linde and Krogstad conversation beside any conversation the Helmers have before Act III.
Read Rank as the play's other inheritance, and his removal of Nora's last financial option.
Assess whether the subplots comment on the marriage, cause its collapse, or both.

essayQuestions.question: Is the ending of A Doll's House earned?
essayQuestions.focus: The last act, the argument about duty, and the door
plan: Describe what changes in the staging of the final act: ordinary clothes, a table, two chairs and a conversation.
Track the argument through the words sacred, duty and religion, and note who keeps redefining them.
Weigh the objection that Nora changes too fast against the evidence of her competence in Acts I and II.
Consider the children, whom she leaves, and her own reason for doing so.
Close on Ibsen's alternative German ending and what its existence shows about how the original was received.

discussionQuestions: Nora has run a secret loan for eight years without anyone noticing. Does the play's ending come out of nowhere, or has it been in front of us all along?
Helmer will not keep Krogstad because the man uses his first name in front of the staff. Is that a small thing or the whole diagnosis?
Mrs Linde stops Krogstad withdrawing the letter. Is she right to?
Nora leaves her children with the nurse who once left her own child to look after Nora. What is Ibsen doing by putting those two facts in the same play?
Ibsen wrote an alternative ending in which Nora stays. What is lost, exactly, and is anything gained?

timeline.label: Henrik Ibsen born at Skien
timeline.detail: His father's business failed when he was a boy, and money and social standing recur throughout his work.

timeline.label: Peer Gynt published
timeline.detail: The last of the great verse plays before Ibsen turned to contemporary prose drama.

timeline.label: Pillars of Society published
timeline.detail: The first of the modern prose plays, and the beginning of the sequence this play belongs to.

timeline.label: Et dukkehjem published in Copenhagen
timeline.detail: Published on 4 December in a first printing of 8,000 copies.

timeline.label: First performance at the Royal Theatre, Copenhagen
timeline.detail: On 21 December, with Betty Hennings as Nora.

timeline.label: Ibsen supplies an alternative ending for the German stage
timeline.detail: In it Nora does not leave; his letter of February 1880 explains that he wrote it himself only to stop somebody else doing it worse.

timeline.label: Ghosts published
timeline.detail: Often read as his reply to those who had wanted Nora to stay: a marriage nobody leaves, and what it costs.

timeline.label: First public British production
timeline.detail: At the Novelty Theatre, London, on 7 June, with Janet Achurch as Nora and Charles Charrington as Helmer, in William Archer's translation.

timeline.label: Ibsen returns to Norway
timeline.detail: After twenty-seven years living in Italy and Germany.

timeline.label: Ibsen dies in Kristiania
timeline.detail: By then his contemporary plays were established across Europe and had reshaped what a serious stage play could be about.

timeline.label: R. Farquharson Sharp's translation published
timeline.detail: Issued by J. M. Dent in Everyman's Library; it is the English text these quotations are checked against.

places.name: Skien, Norway
places.note: Ibsen's birthplace, and the town whose commercial collapse shaped his sense of respectability and debt.

places.name: Rome
places.note: Where Ibsen was living when he began the play; he spent twenty-seven years out of Norway.

places.name: Amalfi
places.note: Where he worked on the play through the summer of 1879, on the coast south of Naples.

places.name: Copenhagen
places.note: The Royal Theatre, where the play was first performed on 21 December 1879.

places.name: Kristiania (Oslo)
places.note: The Norwegian capital, and the city Ibsen returned to in 1891 and died in.

places.name: London
places.note: The Novelty Theatre, where the first public British production opened in June 1889 and started the English argument about Nora.

related.why: Written twenty years later on the other side of the Atlantic, and asking what a woman who leaves actually has to go to.
The same decade's argument about a woman judged by a law and a reputation that take no interest in her circumstances.
A marriage examined from the inside a generation later, with the choices Nora walks out to face already taken.
The economic case set out directly: money and a door that locks, which is more or less what Nora leaves to look for.
A wife managed for her own good by a husband who knows best, taken to its conclusion in a few thousand words.

books.title: A Midsummer Night's Dream
books.author: William Shakespeare
books.setting: Athens and a wood outside it, over four days and one very long night
books.lengthNote: Around 2,100 lines, with four separate companies of characters to keep in the air
books.openingLine: Now, fair Hippolyta, our nuptial hour Draws on apace
books.summary: A father asks the Duke of Athens to have his daughter killed if she will not marry the man he has chosen, and the comedy proceeds from there. Four young people run into a wood where a quarrelling fairy king and queen are already using a drug that makes the sleeper love whatever they see first, and a company of Athenian tradesmen are rehearsing a tragedy they cannot act. The play's interest is that magic does not invent the lovers' cruelty to one another; it only speeds it up.

sourceText.label: Globe/Moby text of A Midsummer Night's Dream
sourceText.note: Line numbers follow the traditional Globe numbering. Modern editions based on the 1600 quarto may differ by a line or two.

structure.label: Act I
structure.title: A law, a deadline and a cast list
structure.summary: Theseus is four days from marrying a woman he defeated in battle when Egeus arrives demanding the Athenian law that lets a father dispose of a daughter. Hermia is given a month to obey, die or enter a convent; she and Lysander agree to run, tell Helena, and Helena tells Demetrius. In a separate room six tradesmen are allocating parts in a play about a double suicide.

scenes.title: The law
scenes.summary: Egeus demands his right; Theseus upholds it; the lovers plan to escape and Helena betrays the plan.

scenes.title: The casting
scenes.summary: Quince hands out parts and Bottom offers to play all of them.

structure.label: Act II
structure.title: A quarrel that has spoiled the weather
structure.summary: Oberon and Titania have fallen out over a stolen Indian boy, and the dispute has stopped the seasons behaving. Oberon sends for a flower whose juice makes the sleeper dote on whatever they first see, intending it for his wife, and adds an instruction about the Athenian youth he has just watched treat a woman badly. Puck anoints the wrong Athenian.

scenes.title: The flower
scenes.summary: Oberon and Titania quarrel; Helena pursues Demetrius through the wood; Puck is sent for love-in-idleness.

scenes.title: The mistake
scenes.summary: Titania is drugged asleep; Puck finds Lysander and Hermia lying apart and anoints the wrong man.

structure.label: Act III
structure.title: Everything wrong at once
structure.summary: Bottom acquires an ass's head, his friends run, and the fairy queen wakes and falls in love with him. In the other half of the wood both men now love Helena, who is certain she is being mocked, and the two women who grew up together insult each other's height until the men go off to fight. Oberon has Puck fog the wood and put them all to sleep.

scenes.title: The ass's head
scenes.summary: The rehearsal is interrupted; Bottom is transformed and Titania wakes to adore him.

scenes.title: The quarrel
scenes.summary: Both men court Helena, the two women fall out, and Puck leads the rivals astray in the dark.

structure.label: Act IV
structure.title: Waking up, and not asking questions
structure.summary: Oberon has what he wanted, releases Titania and says nothing about how he got it. Theseus finds the four lovers asleep in the wood, overrules Egeus and adds them to his own wedding — while Demetrius, alone of the four, is still under the drug. Bottom wakes last, in the middle of the stage, trying to describe something he has no words for.

scenes.title: The waking
scenes.summary: Titania is released; the hunt finds the lovers; Theseus overrules the law; Bottom wakes and gropes for his dream.

scenes.title: Back in Athens
scenes.summary: The players mourn their lost leading man until he walks in with news of a wedding.

structure.label: Act V
structure.title: The worst play ever performed, and a blessing
structure.summary: Three couples watch Pyramus and Thisbe, a tragedy of forbidden love and mistaken death performed by men who explain the wall and apologise for the lion. The court heckles it; the play they are mocking is the story they have just escaped. The fairies then come indoors to bless the marriages, and Puck asks the audience to call the whole thing a dream.

scenes.title: Pyramus and Thisbe, and the epilogue
scenes.summary: The mechanicals perform; the court comments; Oberon and Titania bless the house; Puck asks for pardon.

characters.name: Theseus
characters.role: Duke of Athens
characters.summary: He begins by upholding a law that would kill a girl for choosing the wrong husband and ends by overruling it without explanation, having changed nothing about his beliefs in between. His great speech dismisses lovers, lunatics and poets as the same kind of unreliable witness, which is spoken in a play that has just shown the audience fairies.
characters.clue: He won his bride in battle, tells a girl her father made her as a seal makes an impression in wax, and does not believe a word of what the lovers report.

characters.name: Hippolyta
characters.role: Queen of the Amazons, betrothed to Theseus
characters.summary: She says very little and almost all of it disagrees with her future husband. When he explains away the lovers' night as imagination, she points out that four people telling the same story is evidence of something, which is the only argument in the play for believing the audience's own eyes.

characters.name: Egeus
characters.role: Hermia's father
characters.summary: He appears twice, asks for his daughter's death both times, and is then simply overruled and forgotten. Shakespeare gives the comedy's opening crisis to a man with no interior life at all, so that the law he invokes looks like a piece of machinery rather than a feeling.

characters.name: Hermia
characters.role: Egeus's daughter, in love with Lysander
characters.summary: Threatened with death in the first scene, she argues back in front of a duke and then leaves the city. In the wood she loses her certainty piece by piece — first her lover, then her oldest friend — and the play's harshest comedy is about her height, which is the one thing she cannot answer.
characters.clue: Ordered to marry a man she does not want or die, she runs; by dawn she is being called a bead, an acorn and a painted maypole by her closest friend.

characters.name: Lysander
characters.role: An Athenian in love with Hermia
characters.summary: He is Demetrius's equal in everything except the father's approval, which is the whole plot. Drugged, he turns on Hermia with a viciousness the spell does not really account for, and the play never gives him a line acknowledging what he said.

characters.name: Helena
characters.role: In love with Demetrius, who has abandoned her
characters.summary: She betrays her friend's escape plan in order to be thanked by a man who despises her, and knows exactly how little that is worth while she does it. Her offer to be treated like a dog is the most uncomfortable speech in the comedy, and when both men suddenly want her she assumes it is a joke at her expense.
characters.clue: She hands over her best friend's secret to a man who has just told her he is sick when he looks at her, and asks only to be beaten and followed like a spaniel.

characters.name: Demetrius
characters.role: Egeus's choice for Hermia
characters.summary: He courted Helena, dropped her, and threatens her with violence in the wood when she will not stop following him. He is the only one of the four never released from the drug: the comedy's final pairing rests on an enchantment nobody on stage mentions again.

relationships.label: abandoned, then restored to by magic

characters.name: Oberon
characters.role: King of the fairies
characters.summary: He wants a boy his wife is raising and drugs her into humiliation until she gives him up. The same night he also takes pity on a woman he has never met and tries to fix her love life, and the play makes no attempt to reconcile the two impulses in one character.
characters.clue: He watches everything from the edge of the stage, corrects one couple out of pity and destroys his wife's dignity to win an argument about a child.

characters.name: Titania
characters.role: Queen of the fairies
characters.summary: Her account of the ruined seasons makes the fairy quarrel a matter of flooded fields and human disease, which is a larger claim than any other character makes for themselves. She keeps the changeling boy out of loyalty to his dead mother, and loses him while drugged into loving a weaver with an ass's head.
characters.clue: She keeps a dead friend's child, blames the rotted corn and the drowned fields on her marriage, and wakes to find herself feeding apricots to a man with an ass's head.

characters.name: Puck
characters.role: Robin Goodfellow, Oberon's servant
characters.summary: He belongs to English village folklore rather than to Athens, and he is brought into the play as both an employee and a hazard: he does what he is told and enjoys what goes wrong with it. He is given the last word, and uses it to offer the audience a way out of everything they have seen.
characters.clue: He frightens village girls, curdles the milk, mistakes one Athenian for another, and finally asks the audience to pretend they were asleep.

characters.name: Nick Bottom
characters.role: A weaver, playing Pyramus
characters.summary: He wants to play every part in the play and is the only mortal who meets the fairies awake and is not frightened of them. He is also the only one who tries to describe the night afterwards, and the speech in which he fails — senses swapped over, words giving out — is the play's most serious statement about what has happened to everyone.
characters.clue: A weaver who offers to play the lion, the lady and the tyrant, is given an ass's head, and wakes up trying to say what his eye has heard.

themes.name: Love without reason
themes.summary: The play's working definition of love is that it cannot be argued with and cannot be trusted: Helena says it looks with the mind rather than the eyes, Bottom observes that reason and love keep little company, and a flower produces the same effect as a lifetime's devotion. What the drug does is not unnatural; it is only quicker.
themes.development: Stated as theory in 1.1, demonstrated on the lovers in Acts II and III, and left standing at the end with Demetrius still under the influence.

themes.name: Law, fathers and consent
themes.summary: Athens opens with a father asking a duke to enforce his right to kill his daughter, and the duke agreeing that this is the law. Nothing in the last act repeals it — Theseus simply stops applying it, which leaves the comedy's happy ending resting on a ruler's mood.
themes.development: Egeus makes his demand in 1.1 and repeats it in 4.1; Theseus overrules him without argument, and Egeus is given nothing further to say.

themes.name: Transformation
themes.summary: Everyone in the wood is altered and almost nobody notices at the time. The one visible change, Bottom's head, is the least distressing of them: it is the invisible changes — a man waking to loathe the woman he loved — that the play treats as frightening.
themes.development: Titania is drugged in 2.2, Lysander in the same scene, Bottom transformed in 3.1; three of the four are undone by 4.1 and the fourth is not.

themes.name: Night, sleep and the morning story
themes.summary: The play's settlement depends on everybody agreeing to call the night a dream. Theseus produces the sceptical account, Hippolyta doubts it, Bottom cannot fit his experience into words, and Puck finally offers the whole audience the same bargain.
themes.development: The lovers wake half-remembering in 4.1; Theseus explains it away in 5.1; the epilogue makes the explanation the audience's responsibility.

themes.name: Theatre about theatre
themes.summary: The mechanicals worry about the things real companies worry about — casting, props, whether the audience will be frightened, whether a boy can play a woman — and solve them by explaining everything aloud. Their failure demonstrates the conventions the surrounding play is relying on at that exact moment.
themes.development: Rehearsal in 1.2 and 3.1, performance in 5.1, and an epilogue that asks the same indulgence the mechanicals begged for in their prologue.

themes.name: Who is allowed to decide
themes.summary: Fathers, dukes and fairy kings all get what they want, and each of them frames it as correction rather than force. The play lets that pattern show by repeating it at three social levels within an hour of stage time.
themes.development: Egeus invokes the law, Theseus invokes his sword and his wedding, Oberon invokes a flower; the changeling boy changes hands offstage and is never mentioned again.

techniques.name: Verse registers
techniques.definition: Giving different groups of characters distinct metres and forms.
techniques.bookDefinition: Giving different groups of characters distinct metres and forms.
techniques.inThisBook: The court speaks blank verse, the lovers slide into rhymed couplets as they become more ridiculous, the fairies use a short trochaic line, and the mechanicals speak prose except when performing, where they are given deliberately terrible verse.

techniques.name: Play within a play
techniques.definition: A staged performance watched by characters who are themselves being watched.
techniques.bookDefinition: A staged performance watched by characters who are themselves being watched.
techniques.inThisBook: Pyramus and Thisbe is a tragedy of parental prohibition and mistaken death, performed for four people who have just escaped one. The court's mockery is aimed at conventions the audience has been accepting all evening.

techniques.name: Doubling
techniques.definition: One actor taking two parts, so that the audience sees a resemblance the text does not state.
techniques.bookDefinition: One actor taking two parts, so that the audience sees a resemblance the text does not state.
techniques.inThisBook: Theseus and Oberon, Hippolyta and Titania, and Philostrate and Puck have often been doubled since Peter Brook's 1970 production, which turns the fairy quarrel into the same marriage seen at night.

techniques.name: Bathos
techniques.definition: A sudden drop from the elevated to the ridiculous.
techniques.bookDefinition: A sudden drop from the elevated to the ridiculous.
techniques.inThisBook: It is the engine of the whole last act — 'the wall is down that parted their fathers' — and also of the wood, where a fairy queen's love speech is answered by a weaver talking about the difficulty of getting out of a wood.

techniques.name: The catalogue
techniques.definition: A list allowed to run on past the point of usefulness, so that the accumulation itself becomes the effect.
techniques.bookDefinition: A list used to build a world faster than description can.
techniques.inThisBook: Oberon's bank of wild thyme, oxlips, violets, woodbine, musk-roses and eglantine gives the wood a physical existence on a bare stage in six lines, and Titania's list of rotted corn and drowned fields does the same for the damage.

techniques.name: Epilogue
techniques.definition: A direct address to the audience after the story has closed.
techniques.bookDefinition: A direct address to the audience after the story has closed.
techniques.inThisBook: Puck offers the audience the same excuse the characters have used on themselves — that they were asleep and this was a dream — which makes accepting the comedy an act the spectators have to perform.

quotations.text: Now, fair Hippolyta, our nuptial hour Draws on apace; four happy days bring in Another moon: but, O, methinks, how slow This old moon wanes!
quotations.speaker: Theseus
quotations.context: The opening lines, four days before the wedding.
quotations.analysis: The play starts a clock and immediately complains about it, which is how the whole comedy will run: everything is dated to the moon. The image Theseus reaches for — an old woman withering away a young man's inheritance — puts impatience and money in the first speech of a play about who may marry whom.

quotations.text: Hippolyta, I woo'd thee with my sword, And won thy love, doing thee injuries; But I will wed thee in another key,
quotations.speaker: Theseus
quotations.context: To his bride, in the same opening speech.
quotations.analysis: He describes a conquest as a courtship without appearing to notice the difference, and 'doing thee injuries' is left in the sentence as a plain fact. 'In another key' is a musical term, so the change he promises is one of tone rather than of relation — which is precisely the question Oberon and Titania will act out in the wood.

quotations.text: I beg the ancient privilege of Athens, As she is mine, I may dispose of her: Which shall be either to this gentleman Or to her death, according to our law
quotations.speaker: Egeus
quotations.context: Asking the duke to enforce his right over his daughter.
quotations.analysis: 'Dispose of' is a term for property, and the alternatives offered are a husband or an execution, in that order and in the same sentence. Egeus is not presented as a monster: he is invoking something he calls ancient and the duke agrees it exists, which is what makes the first scene of a comedy cold.

quotations.text: To you your father should be as a god; One that composed your beauties, yea, and one To whom you are but as a form in wax By him imprinted and within his power To leave the figure or disfigure it.
quotations.speaker: Theseus
quotations.context: Advising Hermia to obey, before setting out her choices.
quotations.analysis: The image makes a daughter a seal impression rather than a person, and the pun on figure and disfigure lets destruction sound like a matter of craft. It is offered as kindly counsel, which is the point: the play's cruelty is spoken in the register of good sense.

quotations.text: The course of true love never did run smooth;
quotations.speaker: Lysander
quotations.context: Comforting Hermia after the duke's judgement.
quotations.analysis: The most quoted line in the play is a young man consoling his girlfriend by telling her that their situation is an old story, and he is about to list the ways love goes wrong as if reciting from a book. What follows is not comfort but a catalogue of obstacles, ending in the image of darkness swallowing light.

quotations.text: And ere a man hath power to say 'Behold!' The jaws of darkness do devour it up: So quick bright things come to confusion.
quotations.speaker: Lysander
quotations.context: The end of his list of the ways love is thwarted.
quotations.analysis: Three heavy monosyllables — jaws, darkness, devour — arrive in a comedy fifteen minutes old. 'Quick' means living as well as fast, so the line describes both a flash of lightning and a short life, and it is the closest this play comes to the tragedy the mechanicals will perform badly in the last act.

quotations.text: Love looks not with the eyes, but with the mind; And therefore is wing'd Cupid painted blind:
quotations.speaker: Helena
quotations.context: Alone, deciding to betray Hermia's escape plan to Demetrius.
quotations.analysis: She works out the play's theory of love before any magic has appeared, and then acts on it in the worst available way. The rhymed couplets she has slipped into mark the moment a character stops talking to other people and starts constructing an argument for herself.

quotations.text: Let me play the lion too: I will roar, that I will do any man's heart good to hear me;
quotations.speaker: Bottom
quotations.context: At the casting, having already asked to play Pyramus and Thisbe.
quotations.analysis: 'Too' is the joke: he has accepted the lead and wants the other parts as well, including the one with no words. Quince talks him out of it by explaining that a convincing lion would get the company hanged, which is the first of the play's several reminders that theatre in 1595 was a licensed activity.

quotations.text: Ill met by moonlight, proud Titania.
quotations.speaker: Oberon
quotations.context: The first meeting of the fairy king and queen in the play.
quotations.analysis: Six words establish that this marriage is in the middle of a long argument, and the greeting inverts a courtesy — well met — into its opposite. Everything the fairies do for the rest of the night is a move in a quarrel that began before the audience arrived.

quotations.text: And thorough this distemperature we see The seasons alter: hoary-headed frosts Far in the fresh lap of the crimson rose,
quotations.speaker: Titania
quotations.context: In the middle of her account of the damage the quarrel has done.
quotations.analysis: The speech puts flooded fields, rotted corn and human disease on the domestic argument's account, which is a far larger claim than any mortal in the play makes. It also dates the comedy for the first audience: the mid-1590s were years of ruined harvests and abnormal weather, and this is the play noticing.

quotations.text: Set your heart at rest: The fairy land buys not the child of me. His mother was a votaress of my order:
quotations.speaker: Titania
quotations.context: Refusing to hand over the changeling boy.
quotations.analysis: Her reason for keeping the child is not possessiveness but a promise to a dead friend, and the speech that follows is the warmest thing in the play — two women laughing on a beach at the shape of the sails. The boy himself never appears, and after Act IV nobody mentions him again.

quotations.text: It fell upon a little western flower, Before milk-white, now purple with love's wound, And maidens call it love-in-idleness.
quotations.speaker: Oberon
quotations.context: Describing how Cupid's arrow missed an imperial votaress and struck a flower.
quotations.analysis: The drug that drives the rest of the plot is given an origin story in three lines, and its colour is a wound. 'Love-in-idleness' is a real country name for the wild pansy, so the enchantment arrives dressed as folklore rather than as sorcery — which is how the play prefers its magic.

quotations.text: I'll put a girdle round about the earth In forty minutes.
quotations.speaker: Puck
quotations.context: Sent to fetch the flower from wherever it grows.
quotations.analysis: The boast fixes the scale of the wood: the errand crosses the world and takes less time than an act. It also quietly sets the play's clock against the audience's, since forty minutes is roughly how long the fairies are then offstage.

quotations.text: I am your spaniel; and, Demetrius, The more you beat me, I will fawn on you: Use me but as your spaniel, spurn me, strike me, Neglect me, lose me; only give me leave, Unworthy as I am, to follow you.
quotations.speaker: Helena
quotations.context: Pursuing Demetrius into the wood after he has told her to go away.
quotations.analysis: Four imperatives in a row, all of them asking to be hurt, and the one thing she requests is permission rather than affection. Oberon overhears this, which is why he intervenes — the play's only act of supernatural kindness is provoked by a woman debasing herself in front of a stranger.

quotations.text: Your wrongs do set a scandal on my sex: We cannot fight for love, as men may do; We should be wood and were not made to woo.
quotations.speaker: Helena
quotations.context: After Demetrius threatens to do her mischief in the wood.
quotations.analysis: She identifies the rule she is breaking and states the cost of breaking it in one couplet. 'Wood' puns on wooed and on the old word for mad, and also names the place she is standing in — three meanings in a monosyllable, all of them about a woman who has come to the wrong place to do the wrong thing.

quotations.text: reason and love keep little company together now-a-days; the more the pity that some honest neighbours will not make them friends.
quotations.speaker: Bottom
quotations.context: Replying to the fairy queen's declaration of love, while wearing an ass's head.
quotations.analysis: The play's thesis is delivered in prose by the only character who has not been given the drug, and he treats the failure of reason and love as a neighbourly dispute that a bit of mediation might settle. It is also a polite way of telling a queen that she is not making sense.

quotations.text: Lord, what fools these mortals be!
quotations.speaker: Puck
quotations.context: Watching the four lovers converge, having caused the confusion himself.
quotations.analysis: The line is usually quoted as detached wisdom; on stage it is an author admiring his own mistake. Puck has just proposed that they stay and watch, which makes the lovers' worst hour into an entertainment with two spectators — the same arrangement the audience is in.

quotations.text: So we grow together, Like to a double cherry, seeming parted, But yet an union in partition; Two lovely berries moulded on one stem;
quotations.speaker: Helena
quotations.context: Accusing Hermia of joining the men in mocking her.
quotations.analysis: The most tender description of friendship in the play is made in the course of ending one, and every image in it is of two things that cannot be separated. 'Union in partition' is a paradox held together only by the grammar, which is what the friendship has become by this point in the night.

quotations.text: O, when she's angry, she is keen and shrewd! She was a vixen when she went to school; And though she be but little, she is fierce.
quotations.speaker: Helena
quotations.context: Hiding behind the men as Hermia loses her temper.
quotations.analysis: The line most often printed on posters is an insult delivered while retreating, and the evidence for it is what Hermia was like at school — the two women have known each other since childhood and are now using that knowledge as ammunition. Hermia's reply picks out the only word that matters to her: 'Little' again.

quotations.text: My Oberon! what visions have I seen! Methought I was enamour'd of an ass.
quotations.speaker: Titania
quotations.context: Waking after Oberon has taken the changeling boy and released her.
quotations.analysis: She calls it a vision, he says nothing about what he did, and the boy is never mentioned again by either of them. Her next line — that her eyes now loathe his visage — is aimed at a man asleep three feet away, and the comedy depends on the audience finding that funny rather than looking at it too closely.

quotations.text: The eye of man hath not heard, the ear of man hath not seen, man's hand is not able to taste, his tongue to conceive, nor his heart to report, what my dream was.
quotations.speaker: Bottom
quotations.context: Alone on stage, waking after the others have gone.
quotations.analysis: The senses have been shuffled, which is exactly right for someone describing an experience the available vocabulary does not cover; the pattern is a garbled echo of St Paul on what the eye has not seen. The mangling is the meaning — this is the only character who admits that something happened which cannot be tidied into a morning story.

quotations.text: The lunatic, the lover and the poet Are of imagination all compact:
quotations.speaker: Theseus
quotations.context: Dismissing the lovers' account of the night before the entertainment begins.
quotations.analysis: 'All compact' means made entirely of, so the three are not compared but identified. The speech is the rational case against everything the audience has just watched, delivered by a character out of Greek myth in a play with fairies in it, and Hippolyta's reply — that all four tell the same story — is the only answer it gets.

quotations.text: And as imagination bodies forth The forms of things unknown, the poet's pen Turns them to shapes and gives to airy nothing A local habitation and a name.
quotations.speaker: Theseus
quotations.context: The continuation of the same speech.
quotations.analysis: He intends this as evidence that poets are unreliable, and produces the best description of writing in Shakespeare while doing it. 'A local habitation and a name' is what a stage gives a story — an address and a cast list — so the sceptic accidentally states the terms on which the theatre he is standing in operates.

quotations.text: The best in this kind are but shadows; and the worst are no worse, if imagination amend them.
quotations.speaker: Theseus
quotations.context: Answering Hippolyta's complaint that the mechanicals' play is the silliest stuff she ever heard.
quotations.analysis: The defence of bad acting is also a defence of all acting, and it is made by the man who has just explained that imagination is not to be trusted. Hippolyta's answer is the sharper one: then it must be your imagination and not theirs, which puts the work of the theatre squarely on the people watching.

quotations.text: If we shadows have offended, Think but this, and all is mended, That you have but slumber'd here While these visions did appear.
quotations.speaker: Puck
quotations.context: The epilogue, spoken after the fairies have blessed the house.
quotations.analysis: 'Shadows' is Theseus's word for actors four hundred lines earlier, so the epilogue picks up the court's own dismissal and turns it into an apology. The offer is the one the characters have already accepted about themselves — call it a dream — and the rhymed tetrameter is the fairies' metre, which means the excuse is being made by the people who caused the trouble.

atAGlance.label: Written
atAGlance.note: Usually placed close to Romeo and Juliet, whose plot the mechanicals accidentally perform as farce.

atAGlance.label: First printed
atAGlance.note: A quarto printed for Thomas Fisher, whose title page says the play had been publicly acted by the Lord Chamberlain's Men.

atAGlance.label: Sources
atAGlance.note: Ovid, Chaucer, English fairy lore and Shakespeare's own theatre, combined rather than adapted.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.note: Court, lovers, fairies and players, each with a different kind of verse.

criticalViews.position: A wedding play
criticalViews.summary: The oldest account reads the comedy as an entertainment for an aristocratic marriage, pointing to the three weddings, the blessing of the house and the compliment to a virgin queen in Oberon's speech about the imperial votaress.
criticalViews.counter: No record connects it to any particular wedding, and the 1600 title page advertises public performance; the theory explains the ending but not the cruelty of Act III.

criticalViews.position: A darker wood
criticalViews.summary: Criticism and production since the middle of the twentieth century have emphasised the coercion in the play: a father demanding a death sentence, a husband drugging his wife, a woman asking to be beaten, and an ending that leaves one man enchanted.
criticalViews.counter: Pushed far enough it makes the last act unplayable, and has to treat the mechanicals' comedy as an interruption rather than as the answer the play gives.

criticalViews.position: A play about theatre
criticalViews.summary: A third reading takes Pyramus and Thisbe as the centre: the comedy examines what an audience agrees to do, and the epilogue makes that agreement explicit.
criticalViews.counter: It can turn the lovers into a device and leave the fairy marriage — the one quarrel with consequences for crops and weather — as decoration.

essayQuestions.question: How does the wood change the people who enter it?
essayQuestions.focus: Transformation, law and the limits of magic
plan: Establish what Athens is: a city with a law that can kill a daughter, and a duke who enforces it in the first scene.
Show that the lovers' behaviour in the wood exaggerates what they already do — Helena betrays Hermia before any magic is used.
Read Bottom's transformation against Titania's: one is visible and harmless, the other invisible and humiliating.
Use 4.1 to ask what actually gets undone, and note that Demetrius is never released from the flower.
Conclude on the return to Athens: the law is not repealed, only set aside by a ruler in a good mood.

essayQuestions.question: Discuss the presentation of women in the play.
essayQuestions.focus: Consent, friendship and the cost of the happy ending
plan: Begin with Hippolyta, won by the sword, and Hermia, offered a husband or a death, both in the first two hundred lines.
Trace Helena's self-abasement in 2.1 and ask what the play does with it: Oberon's pity, and no other consequence.
Use the double-cherry speech in 3.2 to show a friendship of years destroyed in a single scene, and by whom.
Examine Titania's account of the votaress: the one female relationship in the play that is not a rivalry, and the one that is broken offstage.
Weigh the three marriages of Act V against the means by which each was arranged.

essayQuestions.question: What is the function of the mechanicals and their play?
essayQuestions.focus: Comedy, craft and theatrical convention
plan: Describe the rehearsal problems of 1.2 and 3.1 as real problems for a real company: casting, fright, the boy playing a woman.
Note that Pyramus and Thisbe is the plot of Romeo and Juliet and very nearly the plot of the lovers' night.
Show how their over-explaining — a man playing Wall, a man apologising for the lion — exposes the conventions the surrounding play relies on.
Read the court's heckling in 5.1 and Theseus's 'the best in this kind are but shadows' as a statement about all acting.
Close with Hippolyta's correction: the imagination that mends a bad play belongs to the audience, not the actors.

essayQuestions.question: 'The comedy ends by asking everyone to call the night a dream.' How satisfying is that ending?
essayQuestions.focus: Sleep, explanation and the epilogue
plan: Collect the waking scenes of 4.1 and note how little the lovers can retrieve and how readily they let it go.
Set Theseus's explanation of lunatic, lover and poet against Hippolyta's objection that four people agree.
Use Bottom's speech as the one refusal to tidy the experience into an account.
Consider what is left unresolved: the changeling boy, Egeus, Demetrius's enchantment.
Finish with Puck's epilogue, which offers the audience the same bargain the characters accepted, and decide whether taking it is a comfort or an evasion.

discussionQuestions: Demetrius is still under the spell at the end. Does that spoil the comedy, or is it the point of it?
Oberon drugs his wife into loving a man with an ass's head in order to win a custody dispute. Can the play be staged without that being cruel?
Helena asks to be treated like a dog. What is an audience supposed to feel during that speech?
The mechanicals perform the tragedy the lovers only just avoided. Why does Shakespeare put it at the end rather than the beginning?
Theseus says imagination cannot be trusted, in a play with fairies in it. Who wins that argument?

timeline.label: The play probably written
timeline.detail: Usually placed in the mid-1590s on stylistic grounds, close to Romeo and Juliet; no document fixes the year.

timeline.label: Francis Meres lists the play in Palladis Tamia
timeline.detail: The earliest external record that it existed, two years before it was printed.

timeline.label: First Quarto, printed for Thomas Fisher
timeline.detail: The title page says the play had been publicly acted by the Lord Chamberlain's Men. Most modern editions descend from this text.

timeline.label: Second Quarto, falsely dated 1600
timeline.detail: Set from Q1 and belonging to the group of reprints associated with Thomas Pavier.

timeline.label: First Folio
timeline.detail: Printed among the comedies, from the second quarto, with small changes including the substitution of Egeus for Philostrate in the last act.

timeline.label: Samuel Pepys sees the play and detests it
timeline.detail: His diary records one of the bluntest hostile verdicts in the play's reception history.

timeline.label: Mendelssohn composes the overture
timeline.detail: Written when he was seventeen, and still the music most audiences hear in their heads.

timeline.label: Madame Vestris stages the play at Covent Garden
timeline.detail: A production that helped establish the Victorian fairy-spectacle tradition.

timeline.label: Mendelssohn's incidental music
timeline.detail: Added sixteen years after the overture, and the source of the wedding march.

timeline.label: Reinhardt and Dieterle's Hollywood film
timeline.detail: With James Cagney as Bottom and Mickey Rooney as Puck: the play as a studio fantasy.

timeline.label: Britten's opera premieres at Aldeburgh
timeline.detail: The libretto begins in the wood rather than in Athens, shifting the balance from law to enchantment.

timeline.label: Peter Brook's white box production for the RSC
timeline.detail: Sally Jacobs's bare white set, trapezes and circus skills replaced painted foliage and changed how the play could look.

places.name: Athens
places.note: Theseus's city, where the law gives a father the right to dispose of his daughter.

places.name: Sparta
places.note: Named by Theseus and Hippolyta when they compare hunting dogs on the morning after.

places.name: Crete
places.note: Where Hippolyta once heard hounds bay a bear, in the same exchange.

places.name: Thessaly
places.note: The third of the hunting regions Theseus lists when boasting about his pack.

places.name: India
places.note: The changeling boy's country, and the spiced Indian air where Titania's votaress laughed at the sails.

places.name: Fleet Street, London
places.note: Thomas Fisher's shop at the sign of the White Hart, where the 1600 quarto was sold.

related.why: Written at about the same time, with the same plot of parental prohibition and mistaken death — played straight instead of as farce.
The other play of spirits, spells and interrupted entertainments, with the magic put to the business of government.
The other comedy in which leaving the city for a wood rearranges everybody's affections.
Desire misdirected without any magic at all, which makes a useful control on this play's flower.
The expanded Astor edition, with fuller textual, critical and performance material.

videos.note: A short animated guide to the tangled plots of lovers, fairies and mechanicals and to what the comedy says about love and imagination.

books.title: Adventures of Huckleberry Finn
books.author: Mark Twain
books.setting: The Mississippi valley, from a Missouri village down past Cairo into the slave states, some forty or fifty years before the book was written
books.lengthNote: Forty-three chapters, with a Notice and a note on dialect standing in front of the first sentence
books.openingLine: You don’t know about me without you have read a book by the name of The Adventures of Tom Sawyer; but that ain’t no matter.
books.summary: A boy escapes a father who beats him by faking his own murder, and finds on an island in the river a man who has run because he is about to be sold away from his wife and children. They float south on a raft, which takes them further into slave country with every mile. Twain gives the whole book to Huck's voice, so that everything cruel in the society comes to the reader through a narrator who has been taught to think it ordinary, and the novel's central act of conscience is one Huck believes will damn him.

sourceText.label: Standard Ebooks text of Adventures of Huckleberry Finn
sourceText.note: References give the chapter; the last is numbered in the text as 'Chapter the Last'. The novel repeatedly uses a racial slur that is not reproduced here.

structure.label: Chapters 1–7
structure.title: Widow, Pap and a faked murder
structure.summary: Huck is being civilised by the Widow Douglas and schooled by Miss Watson when his father reappears to claim him and the money the last book left him. Locked in a cabin across the river and beaten, he saws his way out, kills a pig, scatters the blood and hair, and arranges the scene so that the whole village will go looking for a body.

scenes.title: Civilising Huck
scenes.summary: Prayer, the good place and the bad place, and a boy who would rather go where the company is better.

scenes.title: The cabin
scenes.summary: Pap takes him across the river and keeps him locked in while he drinks.

scenes.title: The pig
scenes.summary: A murder is staged so convincingly that nobody will look for a runaway.

structure.label: Chapters 8–11
structure.title: Jackson's Island
structure.summary: Huck finds he is not alone on the island: Miss Watson's Jim has run because he overheard that he was to be sold down to New Orleans for eight hundred dollars. Two escapes become one journey, although only one of them is a crime. A flooded house drifts past with a dead man in it whom Jim will not let Huck look at.

scenes.title: The meeting
scenes.summary: Jim admits he has run off; Huck promises not to tell, and immediately feels the weight of the promise.

scenes.title: Judith Loftus
scenes.summary: Huck goes ashore in a dress, is caught out by the way he throws, and learns men are searching the island.

structure.label: Chapters 12–16
structure.title: The fog, and the men with the guns
structure.summary: A wrecked steamboat, a night of borrowed provisions, and then the two decisive scenes of the first half: a fog that separates them, after which Huck tries to persuade Jim the whole night was a dream, and a skiff carrying two men hunting runaways, whom Huck turns away with a story about smallpox. They pass Cairo in the dark without knowing it.

scenes.title: The fog
scenes.summary: Jim's grief at losing Huck is turned into a joke, and then answered.

scenes.title: The slave hunters
scenes.summary: Huck cannot give Jim up, decides he has done wrong, and cannot work out why doing right would feel any better.

structure.label: Chapters 17–18
structure.title: The Grangerfords
structure.summary: Separated from Jim, Huck is taken in by a family of unfailing courtesy who have been shooting their neighbours for thirty years over a lawsuit nobody can now explain. He is given a parlour with an elegy-writing dead daughter's paintings in it, watches two boys he likes killed at a woodpile, and goes back to the raft without describing what he saw.

scenes.title: The woodpile
scenes.summary: Buck is shot; Huck climbs a tree and afterwards says he will not tell everything that happened.

structure.label: Chapters 19–30
structure.title: The duke and the king
structure.summary: Two confidence men take over the raft and turn the journey into a tour of what small river towns will pay to see. A camp meeting is robbed, a drunk is shot dead in the street in front of a crowd that wants to lynch his killer and is talked out of it, Shakespeare is mangled for money, and finally the pair impersonate the brothers of a dead man to steal his daughters' inheritance.

scenes.title: Colonel Sherburn
scenes.summary: A man who has just committed murder faces down a mob by telling them what they are.

scenes.title: The Wilks girls
scenes.summary: Huck decides to steal the money back because Mary Jane's trust is more than he can go on taking.

structure.label: Chapters 31–32
structure.title: The letter, and what Huck does with it
structure.summary: The king sells Jim for forty dollars. Huck tries to pray, finds he cannot pray a lie, writes to Miss Watson to tell her where Jim is, and feels clean for the first time in his life. Then he sits thinking about the journey, looks at the paper, and decides. He arrives at the Phelps farm and is taken for somebody else entirely.

scenes.title: The decision
scenes.summary: A letter is written, held, and torn up, and the boy tearing it believes he has chosen damnation.

structure.label: Chapters 33–43
structure.title: Tom Sawyer's arrangements
structure.summary: Tom arrives, discovers that Jim is being held in a shed, and refuses to simply open the door. Six weeks of rope ladders, sawn bedposts, anonymous letters, rats and a grindstone follow, because the books say so. The escape ends with Tom shot in the leg, Jim giving up his own freedom to fetch a doctor, and the news that Miss Watson freed him in her will two months earlier.

scenes.title: The plan
scenes.summary: Tom rejects every practical method on the grounds that it is not in the authorities.

scenes.title: The doctor
scenes.summary: Jim comes out of hiding to help the boy who has been using him, knowing what it will cost.

scenes.title: The Territory
scenes.summary: Jim is told he has been free all along, Tom pays him forty dollars, and Huck decides to leave before anyone can adopt him.

characters.name: Huckleberry Finn
characters.role: Narrator; a thirteen-year-old runaway
characters.summary: He lies constantly, competently and mostly to protect other people, and he tells the reader the truth about everything he does not understand.
