His moral education happens entirely in the wrong vocabulary: every decent thing he does, he records as a sin, which is why the book can show a conscience working without ever letting him take credit for it.
characters.clue: He fakes his own murder with a pig's blood, invents a new name in every town, and thinks he is going to hell for the best thing he ever did.

relationships.label: travels with, betrays, apologises to, protects

characters.name: Jim
characters.role: An enslaved man, husband and father, running for his family
characters.summary: He runs because he has heard he is to be sold to New Orleans and separated from his wife and children, and everything he does afterwards is directed at getting them back. He is the most competent adult in the book — he reads the river, the weather and the people — and he is the one character permitted a scene of unguarded grief, about a daughter he once struck for disobedience she could not hear.
characters.clue: He is worth eight hundred dollars, and says so; he stands another man's night watch so the boy can sleep; and he gives up his own escape to fetch a doctor for the child who trapped him.

relationships.label: enslaved by, and freed in her will

characters.name: Tom Sawyer
characters.role: Huck's friend, and the author of the last ten chapters' plans
characters.summary: He has read the romances and intends to live by them, which is charming at the start of the book and unbearable at the end. He knows throughout the escape that Jim has already been freed, and keeps that fact to himself because the adventure requires a prisoner. The novel lets him be shot in the leg and does not otherwise punish him.
characters.clue: He will not let anyone simply unlock a door, because the authorities require a rope ladder, a journal in blood and a pet rattlesnake.
traits: careless of other people's time and skin

characters.name: Pap Finn
characters.role: Huck's father
characters.summary: A drunk who appears when he hears his son has money, sues for custody, and is granted it by a new judge who believes in the sanctity of the family. His rant about a well-dressed free Black college professor is the clearest statement in the book of what the racial system is actually for, and it is delivered by the least competent man in Missouri.
characters.clue: He has hair like a dead fish's belly, goes to law to get his son's money, and reckons a government that lets an educated free man vote is not worth belonging to.

characters.name: Miss Watson
characters.role: The Widow Douglas's sister, and Jim's owner
characters.summary: She teaches Huck to spell and to pray, promises him a heaven consisting of a harp, and is about to sell a man away from his family for eight hundred dollars. The novel never treats these as separate facts. Her deathbed manumission arrives too late to be generosity and too conveniently to be anything else.
characters.clue: She sets a boy to his spelling-book, tells him about the good place, and is at the same moment considering an offer from a New Orleans trader.

relationships.label: owns, and frees in her will

characters.name: The duke and the king
characters.role: Two confidence men who take over the raft
characters.summary: One claims to be a displaced duke, the other the lost dauphin of France, and the river towns keep paying. They are funny for ten chapters and then they sell a man for forty dollars, which is the book's coldest joke: the frauds finally deal in the one commodity the respectable characters deal in too.
characters.clue: One is a duke and the other a king, both by their own account, and their best-attended show is the one nobody is allowed to describe afterwards.

characters.name: Buck Grangerford
characters.role: A boy of Huck's age in a feuding family
characters.summary: He is delighted to have a friend his own age and cannot explain the war he is fighting: a lawsuit, thirty years ago, that somebody lost. He is killed within two chapters of meeting Huck, and the manner of his death is the one thing Huck refuses to write down in detail.
characters.clue: He asks a stranger a riddle, cannot say what his family's war is about, and is shot at a woodpile before the chapter ends.

characters.name: Colonel Sherburn
characters.role: A storekeeper who shoots a drunk in the street
characters.summary: He gives the town twenty-four hours' notice, kills Boggs in front of the man's daughter, and then stands on his own porch and tells the lynch mob exactly why it will not come up the steps. The speech is contemptuous, accurate and entirely unpunished, and the novel gives nobody a voice to answer it.
characters.clue: He shoots an unarmed drunk at the appointed hour, then faces down the crowd that comes for him with nothing but a shotgun and an opinion of them.

characters.name: Mary Jane Wilks
characters.role: The eldest of three orphaned sisters
characters.summary: She inherits, with her sisters, the estate the king and the duke have come for, and she is the person whose straightforward decency finally makes lying unendurable to Huck. She is also the one character who cries over a family of enslaved people being sold apart, which the novel notes and the town does not.
characters.clue: Her trust is what makes the boy give up a fraud he had every reason to let run, and she leaves a candle burning for him.
traits: capable of grief for other people

themes.name: Conscience against instruction
themes.summary: Huck's conscience is a machine his society built, and it works perfectly: it tells him that helping Jim is theft and a sin, and it makes him feel filthy for doing it. What the novel dramatises is not a boy discovering that slavery is wrong but a boy acting against everything he believes and calling the result wickedness.
themes.development: First felt as an itch in Chapter 16, argued out and abandoned at the end of the same chapter, and brought to a decision in Chapter 31 when he tears up the letter and takes the damnation with it.

themes.name: The river and the shore
themes.summary: The raft holds talk, food, work and the only sustained kindness in the book, and it is moving in the wrong direction the whole time. Twain will not allow the water to be a symbol of liberty: it is a road, a workplace and a commercial highway that carries two fugitives deeper into the country they are escaping.
themes.development: Established in the night passages of Chapters 12 and 19, undercut when they pass Cairo in the fog, and closed off entirely when the raft is boarded in Chapter 19 by two men who take it over.

themes.name: People as property
themes.summary: The novel's most chilling sentences are arithmetic. Jim is worth eight hundred dollars, and says so about himself; he is sold for forty by a man who wanted a drink; a reward of two hundred is advertised for his return. The system is shown through prices rather than through argument, which is why the book does not need a speech against it.
themes.development: Named in Chapter 8 when Jim explains why he ran, priced in Chapter 31, and finally made absurd in Chapter 43 when Tom pays him forty dollars for having been a prisoner.

themes.name: Performance and fraud
themes.summary: Almost every character is playing somebody else: Huck is a girl, an orphan, a servant and then Tom Sawyer; the duke and the king are royalty; Tom conducts an escape according to books. The river towns are taken in because they want the show, and the novel keeps asking who is left paying when the audience goes home.
themes.development: Comic from Chapter 19, turns ugly at the Wilks funeral, and becomes cruelty in the last ten chapters, when the performance is staged around a man who cannot leave.

themes.name: Respectability and violence
themes.summary: The Grangerfords are courteous, hospitable, church-going and murderous; the town that wants to lynch Sherburn is the same town that laughed at Boggs; the ladies who set Huck to his spelling own the man on the raft. Twain arranges the episodes so that the violence is always underwritten by good manners.
themes.development: From the family that takes their guns to church in Chapter 18, through Sherburn's speech in Chapter 22, to the tarred and feathered frauds in Chapter 33 that make even Huck sick.

themes.name: What books do to people
themes.summary: Tom's romances give the gang its oath, the caravan of Spaniards that turns out to be a Sunday-school picnic, and finally a six-week escape plan for a man who could walk out of an unlocked door. Set beside them are Emmeline Grangerford's mortuary verses and the Shakespeare the king butchers for money: reading is presented as a way of not seeing what is in front of you.
themes.development: Introduced as a joke in Chapter 3, echoed in the Grangerford parlour, and turned into the structural problem of the last section.

techniques.name: Vernacular first person
techniques.definition: Telling a whole novel in the unliterary speech of its narrator, including its grammar and its blind spots.
techniques.bookDefinition: Telling a whole novel in the unliterary speech of its narrator, including its grammar and its blind spots.
techniques.inThisBook: There is no adult voice anywhere in the book to explain what Huck has got wrong, so the reader has to make the judgement from inside a sentence that is not making it.

techniques.name: Written dialect
techniques.definition: Spelling and grammar used to mark where a speaker comes from, and what being heard that way costs them.
techniques.bookDefinition: Rendering different regional and social speech by respelling it on the page.
techniques.inThisBook: The Explanatory insists on seven distinct varieties, done by ear rather than guesswork, and the claim is a warning: the way a character talks is going to be treated as evidence about them.

techniques.name: Dramatic irony
techniques.definition: A narrator reporting something the reader understands better than he does.
techniques.bookDefinition: A narrator reporting something the reader understands better than he does.
techniques.inThisBook: Huck calls his decision to help Jim wickedness, and the whole moral force of the book depends on the reader disagreeing with the only voice available.

techniques.name: Episodic structure
techniques.definition: A journey narrative built from self-contained encounters rather than a single developing plot.
techniques.bookDefinition: A journey narrative built from self-contained encounters rather than a single developing plot.
techniques.inThisBook: Feud, camp meeting, murder, mob, Shakespeare, funeral fraud: each landing is a separate examination of a community, and the raft between them is where the book breathes.

techniques.name: Deadpan
techniques.definition: Delivering an outrage or an absurdity in the same flat tone as everything else.
techniques.bookDefinition: Delivering an outrage or an absurdity in the same flat tone as everything else.
techniques.inThisBook: Huck reports a shooting, a lynch mob and his own damnation in the same register he uses for catfish and corn-dodgers, and the flatness is what makes them land.

techniques.name: The framing notice
techniques.definition: Prefatory matter that instructs the reader how — or how not — to read what follows.
techniques.bookDefinition: Prefatory matter that instructs the reader how — or how not — to read what follows.
techniques.inThisBook: A Notice threatens prosecution, banishment and shooting for anyone who looks for motive, moral or plot; the joke is a dare, and the book has a moral, a motive and very little plot.

quotations.text: Persons attempting to find a motive in this narrative will be prosecuted; persons attempting to find a moral in it will be banished; persons attempting to find a plot in it will be shot.
quotations.context: The single sentence printed on its own page before the novel begins.
quotations.analysis: Three legal punishments escalate from prosecution to execution across one sentence, which is the same escalation the book's river towns run on. The joke is also a set of instructions: it is precisely the motive, the moral and the plot that readers have been arguing about ever since, and the notice knows it.

quotations.text: The shadings have not been done in a haphazard fashion, or by guesswork; but painstakingly, and with the trustworthy guidance and support of personal familiarity with these several forms of speech.
quotations.context: The note on dialect, printed immediately after the Notice.
quotations.analysis: Having just forbidden the reader to look for anything, Twain makes one claim in earnest, and it is about accuracy of ear. The effect is to put speech under warranty before the first chapter: how a character talks is going to be offered as evidence, so the reader is warned not to treat any voice in the book as neutral.

quotations.text: You don’t know about me without you have read a book by the name of The Adventures of Tom Sawyer; but that ain’t no matter. That book was made by Mr. Mark Twain, and he told the truth, mainly. There was things which he stretched, but mainly he told the truth.
quotations.context: The opening of the novel.
quotations.analysis: The narrator reviews his own author in the third sentence, and grades him: mainly truthful, some stretching. That sets the terms for everything after it — this book will be judged by whether it tells the truth rather than whether it is well made — and it establishes at once that Huck's honesty and Huck's accuracy are not the same thing.

quotations.text: She said it was wicked to say what I said; said she wouldn’t say it for the whole world; she was going to live so as to go to the good place. Well, I couldn’t see no advantage in going where she was going, so I made up my mind I wouldn’t try for it.
quotations.context: Miss Watson has told Huck about heaven and hell, and he has said he wishes he were in the second one.
quotations.analysis: He rejects salvation on grounds of company, which is a child's reason and also the book's whole ethical method: Huck decides everything by who is in the room. The same calculation will produce his decision in Chapter 31, where he chooses hell again, and for exactly the same reason.

quotations.text: “Well, I b’lieve you, Huck. I⁠—I run off.”
quotations.speaker: Jim
quotations.context: On Jackson's Island, after Huck has sworn not to tell.
quotations.analysis: The hesitation is printed into the line — the pronoun is said twice with a dash between — and it is the only time in the book Jim stammers. He is handing a white child the power to have him hunted, and the novel measures the size of that in two syllables and a piece of punctuation.

quotations.text: “Yes; en I’s rich now, come to look at it. I owns mysef, en I’s wuth eight hund’d dollars. I wisht I had de money, I wouldn’ want no mo’.”
quotations.speaker: Jim
quotations.context: Telling Huck about his speculations in livestock and the bank that failed.
quotations.analysis: He performs the entire logic of slavery in three clauses: the man is the property, so running makes him the owner of an asset worth eight hundred dollars that he cannot sell or spend. The joke is exact and the final wish — that he had the money instead of merely being it — is the most desolate sentence in the chapter.

quotations.text: En all you wuz thinkin’ ’bout wuz how you could make a fool uv ole Jim wid a lie. Dat truck dah is trash; en trash is what people is dat puts dirt on de head er dey fren’s en makes ’em ashamed.
quotations.speaker: Jim
quotations.context: After Huck, reunited in the fog, has tried to convince him that the whole terrifying night was a dream.
quotations.analysis: Jim turns the leaves and rubbish on the raft into a definition and then applies it to a person, so the rebuke is built out of what is physically in front of them. It is the only moment in the book where an adult states a moral principle plainly, and it comes from the man the law counts as property; Huck's apology follows, and he records it as the hardest thing he ever did.

quotations.text: Jim said it made him all over trembly and feverish to be so close to freedom. Well, I can tell you it made me all over trembly and feverish, too, to hear him, because I begun to get it through my head that he was most free⁠—and who was to blame for it? Why, me.
quotations.context: Watching for the lights of Cairo, where the Ohio would carry them into free states.
quotations.analysis: The same four words describe two opposite feelings, and the repetition is what makes the passage work: Huck can feel exactly what Jim feels and has been taught to file it as guilt. 'Who was to blame' treats another man's liberty as damage, which is the vocabulary the whole book is trying to get out of and never quite does.

quotations.text: Then I thought a minute, and says to myself, hold on; s’pose you’d a done right and give Jim up, would you felt better than what you do now? No, says I, I’d feel bad⁠—I’d feel just the same way I do now.
quotations.context: Alone on the raft after turning two slave hunters away with a story about smallpox in the family.
quotations.analysis: He tests his moral training empirically and it fails: the two courses of action produce the same feeling, so the rule cannot be doing any work. Huck's conclusion is that he may as well stop bothering about right and wrong altogether, which is the funniest and bleakest joke in the novel — the failure of a corrupt ethics leaves him with no ethics he can name.

quotations.text: a feud is this way: A man has a quarrel with another man, and kills him; then that other man’s brother kills him; then the other brothers, on both sides, goes for one another; then the cousins chip in⁠—and by and by everybody’s killed off, and there ain’t no more feud. But it’s kind of slow, and takes a long time.
quotations.speaker: Buck Grangerford
quotations.context: Explaining to Huck what his family has been doing for thirty years.
quotations.analysis: The definition is delivered as a process with a predictable end state, like a recipe, and the last sentence complains about the pace rather than the outcome. Buck cannot say what the quarrel was about — a lawsuit, somebody lost — and he will be killed within two chapters, which makes his tone the exact measure of how thoroughly the thing has been inherited.

quotations.text: Not a sound anywheres⁠—perfectly still⁠—just like the whole world was asleep, only sometimes the bullfrogs a-cluttering, maybe.
quotations.context: The opening of the dawn passage, a few pages before the duke and the king come aboard.
quotations.analysis: The sentence is built entirely out of negatives and qualifications, which is how Huck describes anything he loves: he will not commit to the silence without adding the frogs. This is the last unspoiled morning in the book — within four pages two men will climb onto the raft — and Twain gives it the most careful prose Huck ever produces.

quotations.text: It’s lovely to live on a raft. We had the sky up there, all speckled with stars, and we used to lay on our backs and look up at them, and discuss about whether they was made or only just happened.
quotations.context: Describing the nights before the two confidence men arrive.
quotations.analysis: Two people on a raft conduct a cosmological debate in the flattest possible terms — made, or only just happened — and neither of them wins. It is the only conversation in the book between equals, and Twain has placed it in the middle of the chapter that ends with the raft being taken over.

quotations.text: I was born and raised in the South, and I’ve lived in the North; so I know the average all around. The average man’s a coward.
quotations.speaker: Colonel Sherburn
quotations.context: On his own porch, facing the mob that has come to lynch him for shooting Boggs.
quotations.analysis: The speech works because it is true and because the man delivering it has just committed murder in front of a child. Twain gives the book's sharpest analysis of crowd cowardice to a killer and then gives nobody the reply, which leaves the reader holding an argument they cannot comfortably accept or refute.

quotations.text: “Well, that’s what I’m a-saying; all kings is mostly rapscallions, as fur as I can make out.”
quotations.speaker: Huckleberry Finn
quotations.context: On the raft, after Jim asks whether the two impostors are typical of royalty.
quotations.analysis: Huck defends the frauds by generalising them, and then runs through Henry the Eighth and half the English succession to prove it — which is his one piece of book learning and it is all wrong. The comedy conceals the point: the duke and the king are not a departure from how power behaves in this novel, they are a small provincial version of it.

quotations.text: Oh, Huck, I bust out a-cryin’ en grab her up in my arms, en say, ‘Oh, de po’ little thing! De Lord God Amighty fogive po’ ole Jim, kaze he never gwyne to fogive hisself as long’s he live!’ Oh, she was plumb deef en dumb, Huck, plumb deef en dumb⁠—en I’d ben a-treat’n her so!
quotations.speaker: Jim
quotations.context: Late at night on the raft, after Huck has woken to find him mourning for his wife and children.
quotations.analysis: The story is told as a piece of evidence against himself: he struck a four-year-old for disobedience she could not hear. Twain gives Jim a scene of self-accusation of exactly the kind he gives Huck, and the repetition of 'plumb deef en dumb' is the sound of a man still, years later, working out what happened.

quotations.text: “Good-bye. I’m going to do everything just as you’ve told me; and if I don’t ever see you again, I shan’t ever forget you and I’ll think of you a many and a many a time, and I’ll pray for you, too!”⁠—and she was gone.
quotations.speaker: Mary Jane Wilks
quotations.context: Leaving the house on Huck's instructions, so that the fraud can be exposed without her present.
quotations.analysis: She promises to pray for a boy who has spent three days lying to her, and Huck's reaction is to say that she could no more pray for Judas than for him. The novel gives him a person to protect for the first time since Jim, and the test matters because Jim is not there: it is the one decision he makes for somebody he has known for three days.

quotations.text: You can’t pray a lie⁠—I found that out.
quotations.context: Kneeling to pray for the strength to give Jim up, and finding the words will not come.
quotations.analysis: Five words and a discovery, reported in the past tense as though it were a fact about the world rather than about him. The sentence is the hinge of the book: Huck has established that he cannot deceive God, which leaves him nothing to hide behind when he sits down twenty lines later with the letter in his hand.

quotations.text: It was a close place. I took it up, and held it in my hand. I was a-trembling, because I’d got to decide, forever, betwixt two things, and I knowed it.
quotations.context: Holding the letter that would tell Miss Watson where Jim is.
quotations.analysis: Four short sentences, no subordination, and one adverb doing all the work: 'forever'. Huck understands the stakes exactly — he has just spent a page remembering Jim standing his watch and calling him honey — and the physical detail of the trembling hand is the only description in a passage otherwise made entirely of thought.

quotations.text: “All right, then, I’ll go to hell”⁠—and tore it up.
quotations.speaker: Huckleberry Finn
quotations.context: The decision, spoken aloud to himself on the raft.
quotations.analysis: The most moral act in American fiction is recorded as a sin by the person committing it, and the sentence gives two thirds of its length to the damnation and one clause to the deed. 'All right, then' is the tone of a boy conceding an argument he has lost, which is precisely what has happened: his conscience won, and he did the right thing anyway.

quotations.text: It was awful thoughts and awful words, but they was said. And I let them stay said; and never thought no more about reforming.
quotations.context: Immediately after tearing up the letter.
quotations.analysis: 'Let them stay said' treats speech as something that could have been withdrawn and deliberately was not, which is as close as Huck comes to claiming a decision. He then reclassifies himself as wicked by profession, and the novel lets the misdescription stand — there is nobody in the book qualified to correct him.

quotations.text: Well, it made me sick to see it; and I was sorry for them poor pitiful rascals, it seemed like I couldn’t ever feel any hardness against them any more in the world. It was a dreadful thing to see. Human beings can be awful cruel to one another.
quotations.context: Watching a mob carry the tarred and feathered duke and king through the town on a rail.
quotations.analysis: He pities two men who sold his friend for forty dollars, which is the clearest evidence in the book that his sympathy operates independently of desert. The final sentence is the only general statement Huck makes in the whole novel, and it is about the crowd rather than about the frauds.

quotations.text: it don’t make no difference whether you do right or wrong, a person’s conscience ain’t got no sense, and just goes for him anyway
quotations.context: Walking home after the mob has gone past, feeling to blame for something he did not do.
quotations.analysis: This is the finding of the experiment he ran in Chapter 16, now stated as a law. It also quietly protects the ending: a conscience that punishes indiscriminately is not a moral instrument at all, which is why Huck's decision on the raft has to be understood as made against his conscience rather than by it.

quotations.text: Well, den, is Jim gywne to say it? No, sah⁠—I doan’ budge a step out’n dis place ’dout a doctor, not if it’s forty year!
quotations.speaker: Jim
quotations.context: After Tom is shot in the leg during the escape, with the raft waiting and the river open.
quotations.analysis: He reasons it out first — would Tom leave a man to die? — and answers with the one thing he has that is entirely his own, which is his word. The choice costs him his liberty within the hour, and Twain places it in the middle of the section most often accused of throwing the novel's moral seriousness away.

quotations.text: But I reckon I got to light out for the Territory ahead of the rest, because Aunt Sally she’s going to adopt me and sivilize me, and I can’t stand it. I been there before.
quotations.context: The last sentences of the novel.
quotations.analysis: The book ends where it began, with a boy running from a woman who wants to improve him, and the circle is the point: nothing in four hundred pages has changed his position. 'I been there before' is the flattest possible last line, and the Territory he proposes to light out for is Indian land the United States is in the process of taking.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Chapter the Last

atAGlance.label: British first
atAGlance.note: Chatto & Windus, London, some weeks ahead of the American issue.

atAGlance.label: American first
atAGlance.note: Charles L. Webster & Company, New York — Twain's own firm, selling by subscription.

atAGlance.label: Written over
atAGlance.note: Begun in 1876, abandoned, taken up briefly in 1880 and finished in 1883.

atAGlance.label: Front matter
atAGlance.note: One forbids the reader to look for a moral; the other insists the dialects were done by ear and on purpose.

atAGlance.label: Narration
atAGlance.note: Huck's grammar is the book's instrument: everything the reader knows arrives through a boy who does not know it.

criticalViews.position: The book as America's central novel of conscience
criticalViews.summary: The reading that made its reputation: Huck's decision in Chapter 31 is an individual moral judgement made against every institution that formed him, and the vernacular voice is what makes it possible.
criticalViews.counter: It makes a white boy's conscience the measure of the book, when Jim's aims — freedom, safety, his family — are the ones the plot keeps deferring.

criticalViews.position: The book as a failure in its last ten chapters
criticalViews.summary: A long-standing objection, put most influentially in the twentieth century: the arrival of Tom Sawyer turns a man's captivity into a game and throws away what the river journey had earned.
criticalViews.counter: The evasion can also be read as the point — Huck does not graduate into a hero, and a culture's habits are shown reasserting themselves the moment there is company.

criticalViews.position: The book as a document of racist forms
criticalViews.summary: Criticism has examined how far the novel's minstrel inheritance shapes Jim — the superstition, the comic routines, the long stretches where he is asleep or tied up — and how that sits beside the scenes of grief and judgement it also gives him.
criticalViews.counter: The same scenes can be read as Twain exhibiting the stereotype in order to break it, and readers disagree over where exhibition ends and reproduction begins.

criticalViews.position: The book as a study of its own language
criticalViews.summary: A formal reading that takes the Explanatory seriously: the novel is an experiment in what a whole book narrated in unliterary American speech can do, and the moral effects follow from the grammar rather than the plot.
criticalViews.counter: It can float free of the fact that the language includes a slur used more than two hundred times, and of what that does to a reader now.

essayQuestions.question: How does Twain use Huck's narration to criticise the society Huck belongs to?
essayQuestions.focus: Vernacular voice, dramatic irony and the absence of an adult narrator
plan: Establish the method: there is no second voice in the novel to correct Huck, so every judgement must be made by the reader.
Use Chapter 1 to show the technique at low stakes — heaven rejected on grounds of company.
Work through Chapter 16, where Huck's conscience argues for betrayal and loses on entirely practical grounds.
Bring in Chapter 31, where the moral vocabulary is completely inverted and the reader has to find the right word.
Consider the limits: what does the method make it hard for the novel to say, and about whom?

essayQuestions.question: 'The raft is not freedom.' Discuss the presentation of the river.
essayQuestions.focus: Geography, direction and the shape of the journey
plan: Begin with the direction of travel: the current runs south, and every mile is deeper into slave country.
Use the Cairo fog in Chapters 15 and 16 as the structural hinge — the one exit is missed in the dark.
Set the dawn passage of Chapter 19 against the arrival of the duke and king in the same chapter.
Show how each landing restores money, property and violence to a journey that had briefly escaped them.
Conclude on the Phelps farm, where the river has delivered Jim to precisely the situation he ran from.

essayQuestions.question: How should a reader judge the last ten chapters?
essayQuestions.focus: Tom Sawyer, the evasion and what the ending does to the book
plan: State the objection plainly: Jim's captivity becomes a game, and Tom knows all along that he has been freed.
Weigh the case that the regression is deliberate — Huck follows Tom, as he has followed him since Chapter 2.
Use Chapter 40 to complicate both readings: Jim gives up his escape to fetch a doctor, and is chained again for it.
Consider who the ending punishes and who it does not, and what Tom's forty dollars is meant to settle.
Decide whether the last line — lighting out for the Territory — is an escape or a repetition.

essayQuestions.question: How does the novel present Jim?
essayQuestions.focus: Knowledge, family, comedy and the limits of the narrator's attention
plan: Start from what Jim wants, stated in Chapter 8: not an adventure but his wife and children.
Gather the evidence of competence — the weather, the river, the dead man in the house, the night watches.
Read Chapter 15 and Chapter 23 closely: the rebuke and the account of his deaf daughter are the two places he is given a full interior.
Set against these the scenes where the comedy is at his expense, and ask who the joke is arranged for.
Conclude on Chapter 40 and the ending, and on how much of Jim's own story the novel is willing to finish.

discussionQuestions: Huck describes the best thing he does as the worst thing he does. What does the novel gain by refusing to correct him?
Jim is the most capable adult on the raft. Why does the book so often arrange for him to be absent, asleep or hidden?
Colonel Sherburn's speech about cowardice is accurate, and he is a murderer. What is Twain doing by giving nobody the reply?
The Notice forbids the reader to look for a moral. Is that a joke, a defence, or an instruction?
Tom knows Jim is free and keeps it to himself for six weeks. Does the novel hold him responsible?
The book's language includes a slur used constantly. How should a reader, a classroom or an edition handle that?

timeline.label: Samuel Langhorne Clemens born in Florida, Missouri
timeline.detail: The family moved to Hannibal on the Mississippi four years later.

timeline.label: The Clemens family settles in Hannibal
timeline.detail: A river town in a slave state, and the model for St Petersburg in both Tom Sawyer and this book.

timeline.label: Clemens begins training as a Mississippi steamboat pilot
timeline.detail: Four years on the river gave him the geography, the vocabulary and eventually the pen name.

timeline.label: The Thirteenth Amendment abolishes slavery in the United States
timeline.detail: The novel is set roughly a generation earlier, but written and published well after emancipation, and in the middle of its reversal in the South.

timeline.label: The Adventures of Tom Sawyer is published, and Huck's manuscript is begun
timeline.detail: Twain wrote the first stretch at Quarry Farm near Elmira and then put it aside for years.

timeline.label: A brief return to the manuscript
timeline.detail: Work resumed and stalled again; the Grangerford and river material belongs to this uneven period.

timeline.label: Life on the Mississippi is published and the novel is finished
timeline.detail: A trip back down the river seems to have unlocked the second half, which was written quickly.

timeline.label: Chatto & Windus publish the British edition in December
timeline.detail: The London issue came out some weeks before the American one, partly to secure copyright.

timeline.label: Charles L. Webster & Company publish the American edition in February
timeline.detail: Twain's own subscription house, with illustrations by E. W. Kemble.

timeline.label: The Concord public library removes the book from its shelves
timeline.detail: The stated objections were to coarseness and bad grammar; Twain professed himself delighted by the sales it would bring.

timeline.label: Mark Twain dies at Redding, Connecticut
timeline.detail: By then the book was established, and the arguments about its last ten chapters had already begun.

places.name: Hannibal, Missouri
places.note: Twain's boyhood town on the west bank, and the original of the village Huck runs from.

places.name: Cairo, Illinois
places.note: The mouth of the Ohio, and the turning they miss in the fog — the one place the journey could have gone north.

places.name: St Louis, Missouri
places.note: The city downstream that the steamboats and the slave trade both run through.

places.name: New Orleans, Louisiana
places.note: The market Jim is to be sold into, and the direction the river carries them the whole way.

places.name: Elmira, New York
places.note: Quarry Farm, the hilltop study where the manuscript was begun in 1876 and finished in 1883.

places.name: Hartford, Connecticut
places.note: The house Twain was living in while the book was written and published by his own firm.

related.why: The earlier book Huck reviews in his first paragraph, and the source of the boy who takes over the last ten chapters.
The same river system and the same institution, described from inside it by a man who escaped and wrote his own account.
The novel that made slavery a subject for American fiction thirty years earlier, and against which Twain's method is a deliberate argument.
Twain returning to the same river towns a decade later, with fingerprints, a switched baby and no comedy at all.
The other great first-person account of a boy whose moral education runs directly against what his society taught him.

books.title: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes
books.author: Arthur Conan Doyle
books.setting: London and the home counties, with excursions to Herefordshire, Surrey and Hampshire
books.lengthNote: Twelve stories, each written to fill a single issue of a monthly magazine
books.openingLine: To Sherlock Holmes she is always the woman.
books.summary: Twelve cases written to a monthly deadline, and the book that taught detective fiction its shape: a client with a story they have already misread, a detective who reads the room instead, and a narrator who withholds. Doyle's London runs on railway timetables, newspaper advertisements and rented lodgings, and the crimes are mostly about money and respectability rather than murder. Four of the twelve end without an arrest.

sourceText.label: Standard Ebooks text of The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes
sourceText.note: Quotations are placed by story. Standard Ebooks prints 'The Redheaded League' where most editions print 'The Red-Headed League'; the stories are otherwise in their magazine order.

structure.label: A Scandal in Bohemia
structure.title: The one he loses
structure.summary: A king wants a photograph recovered; Holmes fakes a fire to make its owner reveal the hiding place, and Irene Adler, who has already recognised him in disguise, walks out of the country with it. The collection opens by showing the method working perfectly and still failing.

structure.label: The Red-Headed League
structure.title: An absurd job with a tunnel under it
structure.summary: A pawnbroker is paid handsomely to copy out an encyclopaedia because of the colour of his hair. The comedy of the premise is what stops the reader asking the only question that matters, which is what his assistant does in the cellar all day.

structure.label: A Case of Identity
structure.title: A fiancé who was never there
structure.summary: Mary Sutherland's suitor vanishes on the way to the altar. The solution turns on a typewriter's worn letters and on an income of a hundred a year, and Holmes finds that he can prove everything and prosecute nothing.

structure.label: The Boscombe Valley Mystery
structure.title: A dying man's words, misheard
structure.summary: A son is charged with his father's murder on the strength of an overheard cry. Holmes reads the ground instead of the testimony, and uncovers a history of blackmail carried from the Australian goldfields into an English estate.

structure.label: The Five Orange Pips
structure.title: The case that arrives too late
structure.summary: Seed pips posted from abroad precede three deaths in one family. Holmes identifies the organisation, works out the ship and its route, and the client is drowned before any of it can be used — the collection's one outright failure to protect.

structure.label: The Man with the Twisted Lip
structure.title: A respectable man and his other trade
structure.summary: A City gentleman disappears in an opium den above the river, and a hideous beggar is found in his rooms. The answer is an income: begging in the correct make-up pays better than journalism, and the two men are one.

structure.label: The Adventure of the Blue Carbuncle
structure.title: A hat, a goose and a stone
structure.summary: A battered hat and a Christmas goose lead Holmes through the poultry markets to a jewel worth a fortune. Having solved it, he opens the door and lets the thief run, on the grounds that the season and the man's terror have done the work of a court.

structure.label: The Adventure of the Speckled Band
structure.title: A locked room and a stepfather's estate
structure.summary: Helen Stoner's sister died two weeks before her wedding; Helen is now moved into the same bedroom, and is due to marry. The bell-rope that rings nothing and the ventilator that ventilates nothing point at a will, an income and a doctor with a menagerie.

structure.label: The Adventure of the Engineer's Thumb
structure.title: A night job with a hydraulic press
structure.summary: A young engineer is hired for an enormous fee to service machinery in the dark, discovers what it is really pressing, and escapes with a hand short of a thumb. It is the story in which Holmes arrives after everything and solves nothing in time.

structure.label: The Adventure of the Noble Bachelor
structure.title: A bride who leaves during the wedding breakfast
structure.summary: An aristocrat marries American money and the bride disappears before the meal. Holmes works it out from a discarded dress and a note written on a hotel bill, and the solution is a first husband rather than a crime.

structure.label: The Adventure of the Beryl Coronet
structure.title: A banker who accuses the wrong child
structure.summary: A coronet pledged as security for a loan is found broken in a son's hands. The father's certainty about which of the young people in his house is dishonest turns out to be the case's central error, and the physical evidence is a matter of what a piece of gold will and will not do.

structure.label: The Adventure of the Copper Beeches
structure.title: A governess asked to cut off her hair
structure.summary: Violet Hunter takes a post on conditions so strange she writes to Baker Street about them. She observes, records and reasons before Holmes reaches the house, and the collection ends with the countryside, not the city, named as the more dangerous place.

characters.name: Sherlock Holmes
characters.role: Consulting detective, 221B Baker Street
characters.summary: He works for interest rather than money, refuses cases that bore him, and treats the law as one option among several. The stories are careful to show his conclusions resting on specialist knowledge, correspondence, disguise and paid informants as much as on the famous glance at a sleeve.
characters.clue: He keeps his tobacco in a slipper, can tell a man's trade from his cuffs, and once let a thief run out of the door on Christmas because gaol would have finished him.

characters.name: Dr John Watson
characters.role: Army surgeon, friend, narrator
characters.summary: He decides what the reader is told and when, which makes him the collection's most important technical device. His admiration shapes every portrait of Holmes, and his bafflement is what keeps a chain of inference feeling like a story rather than a demonstration.
characters.clue: An army surgeon invalided home, newly married in the middle of the book, who turns his friend's demonstrations into the thing his friend claims to despise.

characters.name: Irene Adler
characters.role: Contralto, formerly of the Warsaw Imperial Opera
characters.summary: She recognises Holmes in disguise, follows him home in men's clothes to be certain, and leaves the country with the photograph and a better husband. Watson records that Holmes has kept her picture and stopped joking about the cleverness of women.
characters.clue: An opera singer who spots a disguised detective in the street, wishes him goodnight by name, and is on the boat train before he opens the hiding place.

characters.name: Mary Sutherland
characters.role: A typist with an income of her own
characters.summary: Her hundred a year from a New Zealand annuity is the whole engine of the plot, and she cannot see it because she has been taught to think of the money as her mother's. Holmes solves her case and then declines to tell her the answer.

characters.name: Helen Stoner
characters.role: Stepdaughter of Dr Grimesby Roylott, of Stoke Moran
characters.summary: She arrives at Baker Street before seven in the morning, shaking, with bruises on her wrist from the man she lives with. Her sister died two weeks before a wedding and she is about to be married herself, which is the arithmetic the case actually runs on.
characters.clue: She comes in grey, veiled and shivering, and says it is not the cold that is making her shake.
characters.firstAppearance: The Adventure of the Speckled Band

characters.name: Dr Grimesby Roylott
characters.role: Physician, formerly of Calcutta, of Stoke Moran
characters.summary: A doctor with a temper, a prison record and a will that pays him while his stepdaughters stay unmarried. Doyle makes him physically enormous and has him bend a poker in the sitting room, so that the eventual method — small, quiet and indirect — comes as a genuine surprise.
characters.firstAppearance: The Adventure of the Speckled Band

characters.name: Violet Hunter
characters.role: Governess at the Copper Beeches
characters.summary: She is asked to cut her hair, wear a particular blue dress and sit with her back to a window, and she does all three while keeping a record. By the time Holmes arrives she has found the locked wing, tested the length of the ladder and worked out roughly what is being concealed.
characters.clue: A governess who accepts a post with impossible conditions, sits where she is told, and quietly uses a hand-mirror to see what is behind her.
characters.firstAppearance: The Adventure of the Copper Beeches

characters.name: Neville St. Clair
characters.role: A gentleman of Lee, and the beggar Hugh Boone
characters.summary: A journalist who went out to research an article on begging, discovered how much better it paid than writing, and spent years changing his face in a room above an opium den. He is the collection's clearest statement that respectability is a costume with an income attached.
characters.firstAppearance: The Man with the Twisted Lip

characters.name: Jabez Wilson
characters.role: Pawnbroker, of Coburg Square
characters.summary: A slow, red-headed, thoroughly ordinary man who is paid four pounds a week to copy out an encyclopaedia and never wonders why. His complete lack of curiosity is the mechanism of the crime, and Doyle makes him likeable enough that the reader shares it.

characters.name: Inspector Lestrade
characters.role: Scotland Yard
characters.summary: He appears to be there to be wrong, but the stories are more careful than that: he brings official power Holmes does not have, makes arrests, and is generally right about who had the opportunity and wrong only about what it means.

themes.name: Seeing against looking
themes.summary: The collection's founding distinction is that everyone in it has the same evidence and only one person uses it. Holmes reads sleeves, boots, hats and mud, but the stories are honest that this is not enough on its own: he also writes letters, pays informants, consults reference books and puts on costumes.
themes.development: Stated flatly in the first story with the stair-count, tested when the method wins and loses in the same case, and handed to a client in the last story, where Violet Hunter does the observing herself.

themes.name: Justice and testimony
themes.summary: Holmes is not a policeman, and several stories end with him deciding that the law would produce the worse outcome. He releases a thief at Christmas, keeps a dead man's secret, tells a client nothing, and in one case can only tell a scoundrel to his face that nothing can touch him.
themes.development: The pattern hardens across the book: early cases end in explanation, later ones in a private verdict, until the reader has to weigh the detective's authority as well as admire his method.

themes.name: Respectability
themes.summary: What most clients are really protecting is a position: a photograph that would end a royal engagement, a son who must not be charged, a husband whose City friends must not learn where his money comes from. The crimes are frequently less shocking than the exposure they threaten.
themes.development: From a king's marriage in the first story to a banker's household name in the eleventh, the pressure is the same, and the last story moves it out of London to show that distance from neighbours makes it worse, not better.

themes.name: Class and money
themes.summary: Almost every case has a figure in pounds at its centre: four pounds a week for copying, a hundred a year from an annuity, seven hundred a year from begging, fifty thousand pounds against a coronet. Doyle's London is a place where an exact income explains a person's conduct more reliably than their character does.
themes.development: The money is comic in the early stories and lethal by the middle ones, where two wills and an annuity are motives for killing.

themes.name: Marriage as a market
themes.summary: Weddings in these stories are transactions with documents attached. A stepfather invents a fiancé to keep his stepdaughter's income at home; a doctor needs his stepdaughters unmarried; a peer marries American mining money; a bride walks out of her own wedding breakfast.
themes.development: The collection keeps returning to the moment just before or just after a marriage, which is when money moves and when someone therefore becomes dangerous.

themes.name: Disguise and the law
themes.summary: Faces are unreliable throughout: Holmes as a groom and as a clergyman, a stepfather in whiskers and tinted spectacles, a journalist in a beggar's greasepaint, a governess made to sit where her face cannot be seen. Identity in this book is something worn, and often something owned by somebody else.
themes.development: Disguise begins as Holmes's tool, becomes the criminal's method by the third story, and ends as a way of controlling other people's bodies at the Copper Beeches.

techniques.name: The chain of inference
techniques.definition: A conclusion presented as a series of small observations, each of which the reader is invited to check.
techniques.bookDefinition: A conclusion presented as a series of small observations, each of which the reader is invited to check.
techniques.inThisBook: Doyle's trick is to show the links only after the effect: Holmes states the conclusion, is challenged, and then walks the reader back through boots, cuffs and postmarks, so surprise and explanation arrive in that order.

techniques.name: Retrospective narration
techniques.definition: A narrator telling their own earlier life, with the distance between the two selves doing the judging.
techniques.bookDefinition: An account given after the event by a narrator who already knows how it ends.
techniques.inThisBook: Watson is writing these up from notes, sometimes years later, and says so. He therefore controls the order of disclosure completely — the reader learns what Holmes noticed at the moment Watson chooses to record it.

techniques.name: Disguise
techniques.definition: A character concealing their identity, so that the audience knows more than the people on stage do.
techniques.bookDefinition: A character adopting another identity in full view of the audience.
techniques.inThisBook: Holmes goes out as a drunken groom and comes back as a Nonconformist clergyman; the collection's two best-hidden criminals are also in make-up, which puts detective and quarry in the same trade.

techniques.name: Frame narrative
techniques.definition: A story told inside another story, so that every account reaches the reader through somebody with an interest in it.
techniques.bookDefinition: A story enclosed within another story, often several layers deep.
techniques.inThisBook: Most cases contain a long uninterrupted first-person account by the client, inside Watson's account, inside the collection — and the client's version is always the one with the mistake in it.

techniques.name: The misdirecting detail
techniques.definition: A conspicuous fact placed where the reader will take it for the important one.
techniques.bookDefinition: A conspicuous fact placed where the reader will take it for the important one.
techniques.inThisBook: The absurdity of the Red-Headed League occupies all the attention the cellar should be getting; a gypsy band, a dying man's last word and a hat left in the street work the same way.

techniques.name: Idiolect
techniques.definition: A speech habit belonging to one character alone, so that they can be recognised before they are named.
techniques.bookDefinition: Giving each character a distinct and consistent way of speaking.
techniques.inThisBook: Holmes talks in imperatives and epigrams, Watson in careful subordinate clauses, and the clients in the vocabulary of their trade — a pawnbroker, a banker and an engineer each describe the same city in different nouns.

quotations.text: To Sherlock Holmes she is always the woman.
quotations.speaker: Dr Watson
quotations.context: The first sentence of the collection.
quotations.analysis: The present tense is the surprising part: Watson is writing long afterwards and the habit still holds. Naming her by a definite article rather than a name turns a person into a category of one, and the sentence works as an announcement that the book will begin with the case its hero lost.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, 'A Scandal in Bohemia'

quotations.text: He was, I take it, the most perfect reasoning and observing machine that the world has seen, but as a lover he would have placed himself in a false position.
quotations.speaker: Dr Watson
quotations.context: Watson explaining what Irene Adler did and did not mean to Holmes.
quotations.analysis: 'I take it' is a hedge, and it is Watson's, not Doyle's: the narrator is offering an assessment he cannot verify about a man he lives with. The machine image will be contradicted within twenty pages by the same narrator noticing that Holmes has kept a photograph.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, 'A Scandal in Bohemia'

quotations.text: You see, but you do not observe. The distinction is clear.
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.context: Before the stair-counting demonstration, in the sitting room at Baker Street.
quotations.analysis: The two verbs are almost synonyms in ordinary use, and Holmes prises them apart to make an ability sound like a discipline anyone could acquire. It is also a piece of self-promotion aimed at the man who writes the accounts, which is how the phrase came to be repeated for a century.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, 'A Scandal in Bohemia'

quotations.text: It is a capital mistake to theorise before one has data. Insensibly one begins to twist facts to suit theories, instead of theories to suit facts.
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.context: Refusing to speculate about an anonymous note before reading it properly.
quotations.analysis: The second sentence is the useful one, and it describes an error of character rather than of method — 'insensibly' concedes that nobody notices themselves doing it. Doyle, trained as a doctor, is describing diagnosis, and the collection's guilty parties are usually people who decided early what a fact meant.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, 'A Scandal in Bohemia'

quotations.text: I am lost without my Boswell.
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.context: Stopping Watson from leaving as a client arrives.
quotations.analysis: He does not say he needs an assistant; he says he needs a biographer. The joke concedes the whole structure of the book — that Holmes's work only exists for us because a companion writes it up — and it flatters Watson at the exact moment Holmes wants him to stay.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, 'A Scandal in Bohemia'

quotations.text: And that was how a great scandal threatened to affect the kingdom of Bohemia, and how the best plans of Mr. Sherlock Holmes were beaten by a woman’s wit.
quotations.speaker: Dr Watson
quotations.context: The closing sentence of the first story.
quotations.analysis: Watson gives the defeat the cadence of a triumph, with the long balanced clauses of a case closed. Note what the sentence does not say: the photograph is still in Adler's keeping, and the only thing actually recovered is Holmes's opinion of women.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, 'A Scandal in Bohemia'

quotations.text: It is quite a three pipe problem, and I beg that you won’t speak to me for fifty minutes.
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.context: In the stalls at a concert, before the night's work at the bank.
quotations.analysis: Thinking is given a unit of measurement and a duration, which is a very Victorian way of describing genius — as a quantity of labour rather than a flash. The fifty minutes also buys Doyle a scene break, and the reader is kept outside the reasoning until the cellar.

quotations.text: My life is spent in one long effort to escape from the commonplaces of existence. These little problems help me to do so.
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.context: After the arrest, yawning, as the case ends.
quotations.analysis: The motive stated here is not justice, money or curiosity but boredom, and it is offered as the ordinary condition of his life rather than an affectation. 'Little problems' reduces a bank robbery and a ruined pawnbroker to a distraction, which is the coldest thing Holmes says in the collection.

quotations.text: Depend upon it, there is nothing so unnatural as the commonplace.
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.context: Arguing that ordinary life is stranger than anything a novelist would invent.
quotations.analysis: It inverts the usual defence of realism: the commonplace is not the safe ground but the anomaly. Placed at the head of the collection's least violent case — a stepfather in false whiskers protecting an annuity — the remark functions as a working instruction for reading the rest.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, 'A Case of Identity'

quotations.text: The law cannot, as you say, touch you
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.context: To James Windibank, having proved that he courted his own stepdaughter in disguise.
quotations.analysis: He concedes the legal point and then, in the same breath, tells Windibank that no man ever deserved punishment more, before reaching for a hunting crop. The story ends with the crime proved, the criminal untouchable and the victim never told — a combination Doyle repeats often enough that it cannot be an accident.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, 'A Case of Identity'

quotations.text: There is nothing more deceptive than an obvious fact
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.context: On the train to Herefordshire, discussing the case against young McCarthy.
quotations.analysis: The line sets up the story's mechanism exactly: a son quarrels with his father, the father is found dead, and everybody stops there. Doyle is describing how circumstantial cases are built, and the story that follows is really about the difference between what happened and what a jury would believe.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, 'The Boscombe Valley Mystery'

quotations.text: You know my method. It is founded upon the observation of trifles.
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.context: Explaining to Watson how he read the ground by the pool.
quotations.analysis: 'Founded upon' is a builder's phrase, and the claim is that the small things are the foundation rather than the ornament. The sentence is also a piece of brand management — Holmes speaks of his method as an established system, to a man whose published accounts are what established it.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, 'The Boscombe Valley Mystery'

quotations.text: None of those which come to me are. I am the last court of appeal.
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.context: Answering a client who says his case is no ordinary one.
quotations.analysis: He describes himself in the language of a legal hierarchy while standing entirely outside it, and the claim is about position rather than skill: people reach him when the institutions have already failed. The story then makes the boast unbearable, since this client is dead within hours.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, 'The Five Orange Pips'

quotations.text: It was only by trying begging as an amateur that I could get the facts upon which to base my articles.
quotations.speaker: Neville St. Clair
quotations.reference: The Man with the Twisted Lip
quotations.context: Explaining how a journalist came to spend years as a beggar in the City.
quotations.analysis: The word 'amateur' is the hinge: he begins as a professional writer imitating a beggar and ends as a professional beggar imitating a gentleman, and the change is measured only in income. Doyle lets the man tell it himself, so the reader gets the whole social argument in the voice of someone who would rather not be making it.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, 'The Man with the Twisted Lip'

quotations.text: My name is Sherlock Holmes. It is my business to know what other people don’t know.
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.reference: The Adventure of the Blue Carbuncle
quotations.context: To a salesman in the Covent Garden market, having just won a bet about geese.
quotations.analysis: Two flat declarative sentences, one giving a name and one giving a trade, as though the second followed from the first. 'Business' is doing a lot of work: knowledge is stock, and the scene he has just played out was a small commercial transaction conducted with a sovereign and a wager.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, 'The Adventure of the Blue Carbuncle'

quotations.text: I suppose that I am commuting a felony, but it is just possible that I am saving a soul.
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.reference: The Adventure of the Blue Carbuncle
quotations.context: After letting James Ryder run out of the door at Christmas.
quotations.analysis: He names his own offence accurately and in legal language, then sets a soul against it on the other side of a 'but'. The balance of the sentence is the whole of his private jurisdiction: a man with no warrant weighing a prosecution against a life, and telling only Watson.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, 'The Adventure of the Blue Carbuncle'

quotations.text: It is not cold which makes me shiver
quotations.speaker: Helen Stoner
quotations.reference: The Adventure of the Speckled Band
quotations.context: At Baker Street before seven in the morning, moved nearer the fire.
quotations.analysis: Holmes has offered a physical explanation and she corrects it, which is the first sign that this client can be relied on to report accurately. Doyle gets a whole atmosphere out of a denial: the word 'terror' is never needed because the body has already supplied it.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, 'The Adventure of the Speckled Band'

quotations.text: When a doctor does go wrong he is the first of criminals. He has nerve and he has knowledge.
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.reference: The Adventure of the Speckled Band
quotations.context: Discussing Dr Grimesby Roylott with Watson, himself a doctor.
quotations.analysis: The observation is made to a physician by a man whose own qualifications are the same two — nerve and knowledge — which places Holmes and Roylott uncomfortably close together. Doyle had been a practising doctor, and the remark reads as a professional's assessment of what his training would equip him to do.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, 'The Adventure of the Speckled Band'

quotations.text: Violence does, in truth, recoil upon the violent, and the schemer falls into the pit which he digs for another.
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.reference: The Adventure of the Speckled Band
quotations.context: Standing over Roylott's body with the snake still in the room.
quotations.analysis: He reaches for a proverb and a psalm at the one moment in the collection where he has actually caused a death, and the borrowed wisdom does the work of not saying so. Holmes admits privately afterwards that he is indirectly responsible and that it will not weigh heavily on him.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, 'The Adventure of the Speckled Band'

quotations.text: I have lost my thumb and I have lost a fifty-guinea fee, and what have I gained?
quotations.speaker: Victor Hatherley
quotations.reference: The Adventure of the Engineer's Thumb
quotations.context: On the train back to London, the house burnt and the gang gone.
quotations.analysis: He totals the case as a balance sheet and finds it in deficit, which is the only story in the collection to end that way. Holmes answers 'Experience', and the joke does not quite cover the fact that the detective arrived after everything and caught nobody.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, 'The Adventure of the Engineer’s Thumb'

quotations.text: It is very good of Lord St. Simon to honour my head by putting it on a level with his own
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.reference: The Adventure of the Noble Bachelor
quotations.context: After the departing aristocrat has said the case will need wiser heads than either of theirs.
quotations.analysis: The client intended a courtesy and has delivered an insult, and Holmes returns it by taking the words literally. It is the collection's sharpest joke about rank, made by a man who has solved the case before the peer finished stating it and who declines to be thanked for it.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, 'The Adventure of the Noble Bachelor'

quotations.text: No, the debt is not to me. You owe a very humble apology to that noble lad, your son, who has carried himself in this matter as I should be proud to see my own son do, should I ever chance to have one.
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.reference: The Adventure of the Beryl Coronet
quotations.context: To Alexander Holder, who has had his son arrested for the theft.
quotations.analysis: The case is solved by physical evidence but judged on character, and the judgement falls on the client rather than the thief. The closing clause is the one glimpse of a private life the collection allows Holmes, and he offers it as a measure of someone else's conduct rather than a confidence.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, 'The Adventure of the Beryl Coronet'

quotations.text: I can’t make bricks without clay.
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.reference: The Adventure of the Copper Beeches
quotations.context: Waiting for Violet Hunter's next letter, with nothing to work on.
quotations.analysis: He has just barked the same word three times, and the sentence that follows turns detection into a trade with raw materials and a supplier. The clay comes from a governess who is already inside the house, which makes her the working investigator of the story's first half.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, 'The Adventure of the Copper Beeches'

quotations.text: It is my belief, Watson, founded upon my experience, that the lowest and vilest alleys in London do not present a more dreadful record of sin than does the smiling and beautiful countryside.
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.reference: The Adventure of the Copper Beeches
quotations.context: Looking out of a train window at isolated houses in Hampshire.
quotations.analysis: The reason he gives is not moral but architectural: isolation, and the impunity it grants. It closes the collection by reversing the expected geography of Victorian crime fiction — the city is dangerous because it is crowded, the country because nobody is near enough to hear.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, 'The Adventure of the Copper Beeches'

atAGlance.label: Serialised
atAGlance.note: One story a month in The Strand Magazine, illustrated by Sidney Paget.

atAGlance.label: Collected
atAGlance.note: Published as a volume by George Newnes, in the magazine's own order.

atAGlance.label: Narrator
atAGlance.note: Every story is his written-up account, which means every solution reaches the reader second-hand.

atAGlance.label: Endings
atAGlance.note: Holmes lets the culprit go, or declines to involve the police, in several of the twelve.

criticalViews.position: The stories as the template for modern detective fiction
criticalViews.summary: The collection fixed a formula — eccentric amateur, admiring narrator, client interview, false solution, physical clue, explanatory speech — that most twentieth-century detective writing either follows or deliberately breaks.
criticalViews.counter: It risks treating Doyle as a machine for producing puzzles, when several of these stories have no crime, no arrest, or no solution that arrives in time.

criticalViews.position: Watson as the essential device
criticalViews.summary: Criticism has long argued that the interest lies in the narration rather than the deduction: the reader's pleasure depends on a narrator who possesses the clues without understanding them, and whose affection colours every description of Holmes.
criticalViews.counter: Pushed far, it makes Holmes a projection, which the stories resist — his impatience with Watson's storytelling is one of their running jokes.

criticalViews.position: The collection as social record
criticalViews.summary: Later readings attend to what the cases are about rather than how they are solved: annuities, wills, mortgages, professional respectability, the economics of begging, and the vulnerability of women who depend on male relatives for an income.
criticalViews.counter: Doyle is not a reformer, and the stories usually restore the arrangements they have exposed rather than question them.

essayQuestions.question: How important is Watson to the effect of the Holmes stories?
essayQuestions.focus: Narration, withholding and the reader's position
plan: Establish that every story is written up afterwards by a participant, and find the places where Watson admits to selecting.
Use the opening of 'A Scandal in Bohemia' to show how his admiration frames the portrait before any case begins.
Examine a demonstration scene — the stair count, the hat, the boots — and track exactly when the reader is given each fact.
Contrast with 'The Man with the Twisted Lip', where the client tells his own story and Watson steps back.
Conclude on the running joke that Holmes despises the stories his method depends on for its reputation.

essayQuestions.question: 'Holmes is a private authority answerable to nobody.' Discuss with reference to at least three stories.
essayQuestions.focus: Justice, law and the endings
plan: Count the outcomes: how many of the twelve end in arrest, and how many in a private decision.
Take 'The Blue Carbuncle' as the clearest case of mercy, and weigh the reasoning Holmes gives Watson for it.
Set against it 'A Case of Identity', where the law cannot act and Holmes also declines to tell the victim the truth.
Consider 'The Speckled Band', where his intervention causes a death he then judges in borrowed proverbs.
Decide whether the collection presents this authority as a solution to the law's failures or as a second problem.

essayQuestions.question: Examine the presentation of women in The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes.
essayQuestions.focus: Clients, incomes and independence
plan: Begin with Irene Adler, who is introduced as an exception and defeats the method by using it.
Set the dependent clients — Mary Sutherland, Helen Stoner — beside the income or will that puts them in danger.
Use Violet Hunter, who investigates before the detective arrives, as the strongest counter-example.
Weigh Watson's habit of describing women's appearance first and their reasoning second.
Ask whether the collection admires independence or merely finds it striking.

essayQuestions.question: What does Doyle's London contribute to these stories?
essayQuestions.focus: Setting, anonymity and the machinery of a modern city
plan: Gather the infrastructure the plots run on: trains, cabs, post, newspapers, banks, lodging houses.
Show how the same systems that let Holmes move fast let criminals disappear — the beggar, the typewriter, the advertisement.
Consider class geography: Coburg Square, Harley Street, Swandam Lane and Lee are different economies as well as different addresses.
Turn to the final story's claim that the isolated countryside is worse, and test it against the rural cases.
Conclude on what the city does to identity when nobody's neighbours know them.

discussionQuestions: The collection opens with the case Holmes loses. What does beginning there do to everything that follows?
Watson keeps saying Holmes is a machine, and keeps recording evidence that he is not. Whose view should we take?
Four of the twelve cases end without anybody being charged. Is Holmes dispensing justice or avoiding it?
Violet Hunter does most of the observing in the last story. Does that strengthen the method or undermine the detective?
Nearly every case has an exact sum of money at its centre. What kind of society is being described?

timeline.label: Arthur Conan Doyle born in Edinburgh
timeline.detail: Into an Irish Catholic family; he took his medical degree at Edinburgh University.

timeline.label: Doyle enters the Edinburgh medical school
timeline.detail: There he encountered Dr Joseph Bell, whose habit of diagnosing a patient's trade and travels from their appearance is the acknowledged model for Holmes's method.

timeline.label: A Study in Scarlet
timeline.detail: Holmes and Watson's first appearance, in Beeton's Christmas Annual, to very little notice.

timeline.label: The Sign of the Four
timeline.detail: The second novel, commissioned at a Lippincott's Magazine dinner in 1889 that also produced Wilde's The Picture of Dorian Gray.

timeline.label: The Strand begins the series in July
timeline.detail: 'A Scandal in Bohemia' appears with Sidney Paget's illustrations, and the magazine's circulation climbs with each number.

timeline.label: The twelve stories collected as a volume
timeline.detail: Published by George Newnes in October, in the order they had appeared.

timeline.label: Doyle kills Holmes at the Reichenbach Falls
timeline.detail: 'The Final Problem' closes the second series; readers cancelled subscriptions in numbers the magazine did not forget.

timeline.label: The Hound of the Baskervilles begins serialisation
timeline.detail: Set before the Falls, so that the detective could return without being resurrected.

timeline.label: Holmes brought back to life
timeline.detail: 'The Adventure of the Empty House' explains the Reichenbach disappearance and restarts the series.

timeline.label: The last Holmes story published
timeline.detail: The Case-Book closes a sequence of fifty-six short stories and four novels written across forty years.

timeline.label: Doyle dies at Crowborough
timeline.detail: By then better known to himself for his spiritualist writings than for the detective.

places.name: Baker Street, London
places.note: The consulting room every case passes through, and the fixed point the collection returns to twelve times.

places.name: Covent Garden
places.note: The poultry market where Holmes traces the goose that swallowed the blue carbuncle.

places.name: Upper Swandam Lane, by the Thames
places.note: The riverside district east of London Bridge where the opium den of 'The Man with the Twisted Lip' is placed.

places.name: Stoke Moran, Surrey
places.note: The Roylott house in 'The Speckled Band', set by Doyle on the western border of Surrey near Leatherhead.

places.name: Winchester, Hampshire
places.note: The city Holmes and Watson travel to in 'The Copper Beeches', looking out at the isolated houses that prompt his last speech.

places.name: Boscombe Valley, Herefordshire
places.note: The estate and pool of the Boscombe case, where the ground rather than the witnesses gives the answer.

related.why: The novel published a year earlier, where the same partnership is given room for a chase, a treasure and Watson's marriage.
The English detective novel Doyle inherited: a stolen jewel, multiple narrators and a professional detective who gets it wrong.
An earlier sensation novel built on the same Victorian fears — disputed identity, a woman's income, and documents that can be forged.
Published five years before these stories and set in the same fog: professional respectability with a second address behind it.
The decade's other bestseller about reading evidence — timetables, letters and phonograph cylinders assembled against something the law cannot charge.

books.title: Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland
books.author: Lewis Carroll
books.setting: A riverbank on a hot afternoon, and the underground country Alice reaches by falling down a rabbit-hole
books.lengthNote: Twelve chapters, around 27,000 words — roughly twice the length of the manuscript it grew from
books.openingLine: Alice was beginning to get very tired of sitting by her sister on the bank, and of having nothing to do
books.summary: A child follows a rabbit underground and spends an afternoon among creatures who each treat a private rule as though it were the law. Alice grows, shrinks, is asked who she is by a caterpillar, and is sentenced before she is tried. The comedy is exact rather than woolly: almost every joke turns on someone taking a word at its face value, and the book ends when Alice stops agreeing to the fiction that the court is a court.

sourceText.label: Standard Ebooks text of Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland
sourceText.note: A proofed transcription following Carroll’s revised wording. References give the chapter, which is the only division the book uses.

structure.label: Chapters I–II
structure.title: A fall, and a body that will not hold still
structure.summary: Boredom, not magic, starts the book: Alice follows the Rabbit because an afternoon with nothing in it has become unbearable. Underground she finds a door she cannot fit, a bottle and a cake that change her size, and a pool made of her own crying. The problem is never the garden; it is that she cannot keep one body long enough to reach it.

scenes.title: Down the Rabbit-Hole
scenes.summary: The Rabbit’s waistcoat-pocket watch is the one detail Alice cannot explain away, and she is down the hole before she has thought about getting out.

scenes.title: The Pool of Tears
scenes.summary: Nine feet high and then two feet high, Alice tries lessons and recitation as proof of identity and finds both have gone wrong.

structure.label: Chapters III–IV
structure.title: Committees, and a house that does not fit
structure.summary: The soaked company invents a procedure for drying off in which everyone runs, everyone stops when told, and everyone wins. Then the Rabbit mistakes Alice for a servant, sends her for gloves, and she grows until she fills his house and has to be attacked from outside. Authority in Wonderland begins as a clerical error.

scenes.title: A Caucus-Race and a Long Tale
scenes.summary: The Mouse’s dry history fails to dry anybody; the Dodo’s race distributes prizes without a result.

scenes.title: The Rabbit Sends in a Little Bill
scenes.summary: Alice is taken for Mary Ann, grows to fill a house, and Bill the Lizard is sent down the chimney.

structure.label: Chapters V–VI
structure.title: Who are you, and what is a baby
structure.summary: The Caterpillar asks the question the first four chapters have made unanswerable, and gives Alice a mushroom that puts size under her own control at last. In the Duchess’s kitchen violence is ordinary household business, and the baby Alice rescues turns into a pig. The Cheshire Cat then explains, reasonably, that everybody present is mad.

scenes.title: Advice from a Caterpillar
