scenes.summary: Alice recites ‘You are old, Father William’ wrongly and is told she is wrong; the mushroom becomes a tool rather than an accident.

scenes.title: Pig and Pepper
scenes.summary: Pepper, a flying frying-pan and a baby that becomes a pig; the Cat grins itself away and gives directions that depend on Alice not minding where she goes.

structure.label: Chapter VII
structure.title: A tea-party that cannot end
structure.summary: Time has stopped for the Hatter, so the party moves round the table instead of moving on. A riddle is asked and never answered, Alice is told she means the opposite of what she says, and the Dormouse tells a story about three sisters living in a treacle-well. It is the chapter in which conversation itself stops working.

scenes.title: A Mad Tea-Party
scenes.summary: No room at a table with room to spare; the raven and the writing-desk; the Hatter’s quarrel with Time; Alice walks out.

structure.label: Chapters VIII–X
structure.title: A queen who sentences instead of deciding
structure.summary: The garden is finally reached and turns out to be a croquet ground where the equipment is alive and the head gardeners are painting roses to cover a mistake. The Queen orders executions at the rate of about one a minute and nobody is ever executed. The Gryphon and the Mock Turtle then supply the book’s one sustained parody of school and sentiment.

scenes.title: The Queen’s Croquet-Ground
scenes.summary: Flamingo mallets and hedgehog balls; the Cat’s disembodied head raises the question of whether a head with no body can be beheaded.

scenes.title: The Mock Turtle’s Story
scenes.summary: The Duchess finds a moral in everything; the Mock Turtle grieves for a schooling built entirely of puns.

scenes.title: The Lobster Quadrille
scenes.summary: A dance, a recitation that goes wrong again, and Alice’s admission that she cannot go back to yesterday.

structure.label: Chapters XI–XII
structure.title: The trial, and the end of consent
structure.summary: Everything a court needs is present — judge, jury, witnesses, evidence, verdict — and every one of them is used in the wrong order. Alice grows through the proceedings as she loses patience with them, until she can call the court what it is made of. The waking on the bank does not cancel the dream; it returns the reader to a child who has learned to hear adult language differently.

scenes.title: Who Stole the Tarts?
scenes.summary: The Hatter gives evidence in terror, the jury writes down its own names in case it forgets them, and Alice begins to grow.

scenes.title: Alice’s Evidence
scenes.summary: A nonsense poem is read as proof, sentence is demanded before verdict, and Alice refuses the whole performance.

characters.name: Alice
characters.role: A child of about seven, underground for an afternoon
characters.summary: She is the only person in the book who revises her opinions. Alice tries school knowledge, polite introductions and recitation, notices each time that the method has failed, and keeps a running commentary on her own conduct that is often sharper than anything the creatures say to her.
characters.clue: She gives herself very good advice and seldom follows it, and she grows tall enough to stop being frightened of a court made of playing cards.

relationships.label: follows, and is mistaken for a servant by
sentenced by, and finally dismissive of

characters.name: The White Rabbit
characters.role: A courtier in a hurry
characters.summary: He is the only creature in Wonderland who is frightened of being late, and the fear turns out to be well founded once the Queen appears. Anxious upwards and imperious downwards, he sets the plot going and then spends it running errands for people more dangerous than himself.
characters.clue: Pink eyes, a waistcoat-pocket watch, white kid gloves, and a permanent terror of the Duchess and of being late.

characters.name: The Mouse
characters.role: The first creature Alice tries to talk to
characters.summary: He is offended twice over by Alice’s cat and her neighbour’s terrier before he can begin his history, which is then delivered as the driest paragraph of Norman constitutional record Carroll could find. His long tale is the book’s first joke about a word doing two jobs at once.

characters.name: The Caterpillar
characters.role: Three inches high, on a mushroom, with a hookah
characters.summary: He conducts the only real interrogation in the book, and he is entitled to it: a creature that will shortly liquefy into a butterfly has a professional interest in whether anybody stays themselves. His contempt is useful to Alice, because it forces her to say out loud that she cannot explain herself.
characters.clue: Three inches high, smoking on a mushroom, and unimpressed by a girl who says she is not herself today.

characters.name: The Cheshire Cat
characters.role: A cat that can arrive and leave in pieces
characters.summary: The only creature who is candid with Alice, and the only one who can leave a conversation gradually. His directions are logically impeccable and practically useless, which makes him the book’s clearest demonstration that valid reasoning and helpful reasoning are different things.
characters.clue: It can vanish slowly from the tail upwards, leaving a smile behind, and it tells Alice that everyone present is mad, itself included.

characters.name: The Duchess
characters.role: A peeress with a kitchen full of pepper
characters.summary: In her own house she shakes a baby, sings about beating it, and is under sentence of execution; released, she becomes affectionate and turns every remark Alice makes into a moral. The two performances are the same person, which is the point: her manners have no connection to her conduct.

characters.name: The Hatter
characters.role: Host of a tea-party that never moves on
characters.summary: He quarrelled with Time while performing at a concert and has been stuck at six o’clock ever since, which turns his rudeness into a kind of grievance. He asks a riddle he cannot answer, corrects Alice’s grammar while ignoring her meaning, and later gives evidence in court shaking too hard to stand.
characters.clue: He fell out with Time at a concert and has been stuck at tea ever since, and he asks a riddle to which he admits he has not the slightest idea of the answer.

characters.name: The Queen of Hearts
characters.role: Sovereign of the croquet ground and the court
characters.summary: She has one procedure for every difficulty, and it is beheading. Nothing she orders is ever carried out, because the King quietly pardons everybody, so her power is pure noise — which is exactly what makes it frightening until somebody notices.
characters.clue: Her answer to every difficulty is the same three words, and the King pardons everyone behind her back so that none of her sentences is ever carried out.

characters.name: The Mock Turtle
characters.role: A grieving former pupil of the sea
characters.summary: He exists because mock turtle soup was made of veal, so Carroll gives him a calf’s head and a permanent sob. His account of an education in Reeling, Writhing and the different branches of Arithmetic is the book’s most sustained joke about school, and it is delivered as genuine grief.

themes.name: Identity and size
themes.summary: Alice’s height changes eleven times, and each change is treated as a question about who she is rather than how tall she is. Carroll keeps the enquiry in a child’s terms — other girls she knows, lessons she can or cannot recite — so that the philosophical problem arrives without any philosophical vocabulary.
themes.development: Panic in Chapter II, cross-examination in Chapter V, deliberate use of the mushroom afterwards, and finally a growth in Chapter XII that is an act of judgement rather than an accident.

themes.name: Rules and authority
themes.summary: Every creature Alice meets treats a private rule as universal and expects her to know it already. The book is unusually precise about how authority sounds: the Dodo’s procedure, the Queen’s sentences, the Hatter’s corrections and the King’s courtroom all use the grammar of settled law over nothing at all.
themes.development: A race with no contest, then a game with living equipment, then a trial that reverses verdict and sentence — the forms grow more official as they grow emptier.

themes.name: Language taken literally
themes.summary: Wonderland’s creatures are excellent close readers and terrible listeners. They hear the word and not the sentence, so ‘I mean what I say’ and ‘I say what I mean’ become different propositions, a tale becomes a tail, and a lesson is what lessens from day to day.
themes.development: The Mouse’s tale sets the pattern; the tea-party makes it a method; the trial turns it into a way of convicting somebody.

themes.name: Manners and violence
themes.summary: Politeness in Wonderland is not the opposite of cruelty but its packaging. A baby is shaken in time to a lullaby, a cook throws fire-irons during a conversation, and executions are ordered between croquet strokes, always in the correct register.
themes.development: Domestic in the Duchess’s kitchen, ceremonial on the croquet ground, and judicial by the trial, with the violence growing more formal as it grows less real.

themes.name: Lessons and what is remembered
themes.summary: Alice keeps reaching for the schoolroom to prove she is still herself, and the schoolroom keeps letting her down: multiplication that will not reach twenty, geography with the capitals in the wrong countries, poems that come out as other poems. Learning by heart is shown to be exactly that — learning that is not knowledge.
themes.development: Recitation fails in Chapter II, fails again under the Caterpillar in Chapter V, and is mourned in the Mock Turtle’s account of his education.

themes.name: The dream and the waking
themes.summary: The frame is not a get-out. Carroll lets the dream be dangerous while it lasts and then hands it to Alice’s sister, who dreams it again knowingly, so the book ends by describing the act of rereading rather than dismissing what was read.
themes.development: The fall, the afternoon underground, and a waking in which the cards become leaves and the Queen’s shrieks become a shepherd boy’s voice.

techniques.name: Nonsense logic
techniques.definition: Reasoning that is formally valid but proceeds from premises nobody has agreed to.
techniques.bookDefinition: Reasoning that is formally valid but proceeds from premises nobody has agreed to.
techniques.inThisBook: The Cat’s proof that it is mad, and its directions to Alice, are both watertight; the trouble is entirely with the starting point.

techniques.name: Parody
techniques.definition: Reproducing the shape of a known text while emptying or reversing its content.
techniques.bookDefinition: Reproducing the shape of a known text while emptying or reversing its content.
techniques.inThisBook: Alice’s recitations deform improving verse into crocodiles and lobsters, and the joke works even for readers who no longer know the originals, because the failure is Alice’s memory rather than the poem.

techniques.name: Puns and literalism
techniques.definition: Treating a word’s other sense, or its plainest sense, as the one that was meant.
techniques.bookDefinition: Treating a word’s other sense, or its plainest sense, as the one that was meant.
techniques.inThisBook: A long tale becomes a long tail, a school tortoise taught us, and ‘take more’ is answered with the impossibility of taking more than nothing.

techniques.name: Free indirect thought
techniques.definition: Narration that carries a character’s own phrasing without announcing it as speech.
techniques.bookDefinition: Narration that carries a character’s own phrasing without announcing it as speech.
techniques.inThisBook: Alice’s judgements leak into the narrator’s sentences — the ‘poor little thing’ who sits down and cries is being pitied by the narrator and by herself at the same moment.

techniques.name: Dream frame
techniques.definition: A narrative enclosed by a falling asleep and a waking.
techniques.bookDefinition: A narrative enclosed by a falling asleep and a waking.
techniques.inThisBook: The frame is used to end the book rather than to explain it: the sister’s second dream repeats Wonderland deliberately, which is not what waking up from a nightmare normally does.

techniques.name: Comic repetition
techniques.definition: A phrase or event repeated until the repetition itself becomes the joke.
techniques.bookDefinition: A phrase or event repeated until the repetition itself becomes the joke.
techniques.inThisBook: ‘Down, down, down’, the Queen’s standing order for beheadings and the Dormouse’s treacle all work by recurrence rather than by any single funny line.

quotations.text: “and what is the use of a book,” thought Alice “without pictures or conversations?”
quotations.context: The second sentence of the book, as Alice looks over her sister’s shoulder.
quotations.analysis: Carroll puts a judgement about books at the front of a book, and the judgement is a child’s test of quality: pictures and conversations. What follows is made almost entirely of both, so the opening is a specification that the rest of the text meets exactly.

quotations.text: “Do cats eat bats? Do cats eat bats?” and sometimes, “Do bats eat cats?”
quotations.context: Falling down the rabbit-hole, growing sleepy.
quotations.analysis: The question reverses because Alice is going to sleep, and the reversal is the first sign that Wonderland runs on grammar rather than on events. She herself supplies the reason it does not matter which way round it is put — she cannot answer either — which is the exact logic the Hatter will later use against her.

quotations.text: “Curiouser and curiouser!” cried Alice (she was so much surprised, that for the moment she quite forgot how to speak good English)
quotations.context: Immediately after eating the cake, as she shoots up to nine feet.
quotations.analysis: Alice knows the comparative is wrong and says so in the same breath, so the nonsense is not outside language but one step past its usual limit. The doubling also gives the sentence an upward motion that matches what her body is doing, which is why no other word would serve.

quotations.text: But if I’m not the same, the next question is, Who in the world am I? Ah, that’s the great puzzle!
quotations.context: Alone in the hall, fanning herself with the Rabbit’s fan.
quotations.analysis: The reasoning is a syllogism: if I am not the same, then I am someone else, so which one? Alice tests it against the only evidence a child has — Ada’s ringlets, Mabel’s ignorance, the multiplication table — and the test fails on all three, which is why the chapter ends with her in a pool of her own tears.

quotations.text: “Speak English!” said the Eaglet. “I don’t know the meaning of half those long words, and, what’s more, I don’t believe you do either!”
quotations.context: Interrupting the Dodo’s proposal for a Caucus-race.
quotations.analysis: The Eaglet does what nobody else in the book will do: it demands that an official voice be translated. Carroll gives the demand to the smallest bird present and immediately undercuts it — the Eaglet hides a smile — so the challenge to pompous language is itself a piece of social manoeuvring.

quotations.text: At last the Dodo said, “everybody has won, and all must have prizes.”
quotations.context: Ending the Caucus-race, in which the runners began when they liked and stopped when the Dodo said so.
quotations.analysis: A result is announced for a contest that had no start, no course and no finish. The sentence is perfectly formed and entirely empty, and it is the first of several occasions on which Wonderland uses correct official phrasing to settle something that was never in dispute.

quotations.text: “Who are you?” said the Caterpillar.
quotations.context: The Caterpillar’s first words, spoken from the mushroom.
quotations.analysis: Four words, and the book has spent four chapters making them unanswerable. Coming from a creature about to dissolve into a chrysalis and re-form as something else, the question is also a professional one, which is why Alice’s complaint about changing size gets so little sympathy.

quotations.text: “I can’t explain myself, I’m afraid, sir,” said Alice, “because I’m not myself, you see.”
quotations.context: Answering the Caterpillar’s demand that she explain herself.
quotations.analysis: ‘Explain myself’ is a dead metaphor that Alice revives by taking it at full strength: to explain herself she would have to have a self to explain. The politeness of the phrasing — ‘I’m afraid, sir’ — keeps a genuinely frightening admission inside the manners of a well-brought-up child.

quotations.text: “Oh, you can’t help that,” said the Cat: “we’re all mad here. I’m mad. You’re mad.”
quotations.context: The Cheshire Cat, in a tree, after Alice objects that she does not want to go among mad people.
quotations.analysis: The Cat includes itself and Alice in the same sentence, which converts an insult into a description of the premises. It then offers a proof by comparison with a dog, and the proof is formally respectable: the only thing wrong with it is that the premises about dogs are invented.

quotations.text: “That depends a good deal on where you want to get to,” said the Cat.
quotations.context: Answering Alice’s request for directions from the fork in the wood.
quotations.analysis: The Cat gives the only genuinely sound advice in the book, and it is useless to Alice because she has no destination. The exchange quietly names the book’s method: nothing underground can be navigated by a traveller who has not decided what she wants.

quotations.text: “Well! I’ve often seen a cat without a grin,” thought Alice; “but a grin without a cat! It’s the most curious thing I ever saw in my life!”
quotations.context: Watching the Cat vanish slowly, ending with the smile.
quotations.analysis: Alice separates a property from the thing that has it and notices that the result is impossible rather than merely odd. Her method here is the book’s in miniature: she states the ordinary case first, then the departure from it, and treats the gap as evidence worth recording.

quotations.text: “No room! No room!” they cried out when they saw Alice coming. “There’s plenty of room!” said Alice indignantly
quotations.context: Arriving at the tea-party, where three creatures are crowded into one corner of a large table.
quotations.analysis: The lie is contradicted by the furniture in the same sentence, and Alice answers it with a fact rather than an argument. Carroll establishes in two lines that this table runs on assertion, which is why the riddle that follows is allowed to have no answer.

quotations.text: The Hatter opened his eyes very wide on hearing this; but all he said was, “Why is a raven like a writing-desk?”
quotations.context: The Hatter’s first remark to Alice, dropped into a conversation about hair-cutting.
quotations.analysis: A riddle is a contract: you ask, I try, you tell me. The Hatter breaks it at every stage, and when Alice asks for the answer he says he has not the slightest idea. The joke is not the raven; it is a form of words that keeps its shape after its purpose has been removed.

quotations.text: “I’ve had nothing yet,” Alice replied in an offended tone, “so I can’t take more.”
quotations.context: The March Hare has just invited her to take more tea.
quotations.analysis: Alice is right and is told she is wrong, and the correction — that you cannot take less than nothing — is true of arithmetic and false of tea. It is the clearest case in the book of a creature winning an argument by changing which system the words belong to.

quotations.text: the Queen was in a furious passion, and went stamping about, and shouting “Off with his head!” or “Off with her head!” about once in a minute.
quotations.context: During the croquet game, in which the hoops keep walking away.
quotations.analysis: Carroll gives the rate rather than the drama: about once a minute. Turning a death sentence into a statistic drains it of menace, and the reader learns before Alice does that these orders are noise — the King has been quietly pardoning everybody behind the Queen’s back.

quotations.text: “We called him Tortoise because he taught us,” said the Mock Turtle angrily: “really you are very dull!”
quotations.context: Explaining why the old Turtle who taught him was called Tortoise.
quotations.analysis: The pun is delivered angrily, as though Alice were the slow one, and that is what makes the scene work: in Wonderland the person who has to have the joke explained is always at fault. The Mock Turtle’s whole education runs on the same principle, which is why he mourns it.

quotations.text: ‘Take care of the sense, and the sounds will take care of themselves.’
quotations.context: One of the Duchess’s morals, delivered with her chin in Alice’s shoulder.
quotations.analysis: The Duchess has inverted the proverb about pounds and pence, and the inversion is a fair description of Carroll’s own practice: mind the meaning and the sound follows. Coming from a woman who finds a moral in everything and observes none of them, it is advice the book both offers and mistrusts.

quotations.text: “I could tell you my adventures⁠—beginning from this morning,” said Alice a little timidly: “but it’s no use going back to yesterday, because I was a different person then.”
quotations.context: Offering to tell the Gryphon and the Mock Turtle her adventures.
quotations.analysis: This is the same question the Caterpillar asked, answered at last — not by working out who she is, but by accepting that yesterday’s Alice is no longer available for comparison. Her timidity over saying it is the measure of how large the admission is.

quotations.text: “Begin at the beginning,” the King said gravely, “and go on till you come to the end: then stop.”
quotations.context: Instructing the White Rabbit to read the verses offered as evidence.
quotations.analysis: The King’s only contribution to jurisprudence is a rule about reading aloud, delivered gravely as though it settled something. It is also the book’s sole piece of usable advice, and Carroll gives it to the least competent person in the room.

quotations.text: “No, no!” said the Queen. “Sentence first⁠—verdict afterwards.”
quotations.context: The Queen’s response to the King’s call for the jury to consider its verdict.
quotations.analysis: Every element of due process is present in the trial and only the order has gone; the Queen’s correction is procedural rather than mad. Alice’s reply, that the idea is stuff and nonsense, is the first time she names the problem instead of arguing inside it.

quotations.text: “Who cares for you?” said Alice, (she had grown to her full size by this time.) “You’re nothing but a pack of cards!”
quotations.context: The end of the trial, with Alice grown back to her full size.
quotations.analysis: ‘Nothing but’ does the work: the court is reduced to the material it is made of. Alice had noticed as much in Chapter VIII and kept it to herself; saying it aloud is what ends the dream, because the cards have no power once nobody agrees to treat them as a court.

atAGlance.label: First told
atAGlance.note: On a boating excursion from Oxford with Robinson Duckworth and the three Liddell sisters.

atAGlance.label: Manuscript
atAGlance.note: Written out and illustrated by Carroll himself and given to Alice Liddell in November 1864.

atAGlance.label: First published
atAGlance.note: The 1865 printing was withdrawn after Tenniel objected to the reproduction of his pictures; the replacement is dated 1866.

atAGlance.label: Illustrator
atAGlance.note: Forty-two wood-engraved illustrations, made from Tenniel’s drawings by the Dalziel brothers.

criticalViews.position: A book about logic and language
criticalViews.summary: Carroll taught mathematics and wrote on logic, and this reading takes the creatures’ arguments seriously as arguments: most are valid, and the fault lies in the premises or in a shift between senses of a word.
criticalViews.counter: It can make Wonderland sound like a textbook, when a great deal of the book’s force is emotional — fear of being someone else, and the misery of being talked down to.

criticalViews.position: A child’s book that satirises adult institutions
criticalViews.summary: School, etiquette, committees, monarchy and the law all appear in forms a child can follow, and all fail their own tests. On this account Alice is learning to tell a rule that helps people live together from a rule that only protects whoever is shouting.
criticalViews.counter: Carroll disliked being told what his book meant, and a satirical target can usually be swapped for another without the scene changing at all.

criticalViews.position: A book made twice over
criticalViews.summary: Because the 1864 manuscript survives, Wonderland can be read against the shorter story Carroll first wrote out, and the most famous episodes — the tea-party, the Cheshire Cat, the Duchess’s kitchen — turn out to be additions made for a public rather than for one child.
criticalViews.counter: Treating the manuscript as the ‘real’ version mistakes a private gift for a draft; the two texts were made for different readers and do different work.

essayQuestions.question: How does Carroll use changes of size to explore who Alice is?
essayQuestions.focus: Identity, the body and the limits of self-knowledge
plan: Establish the pattern: eleven changes of height, each of them answered with a question about identity rather than about measurement.
Read Chapter II closely — Ada’s ringlets, Mabel’s ignorance, the multiplication table — as an attempt to prove identity from evidence.
Set the Caterpillar’s interrogation against that failure, and note that Alice’s answer is an admission rather than a solution.
Turn the argument at the mushroom: from Chapter V onwards size is a tool she uses, not an accident she suffers.
Close on Chapter XII, where growing large is an act of judgement about the court rather than a physical event.

essayQuestions.question: ‘Wonderland is not lawless; it is over-governed.’ Discuss.
essayQuestions.focus: Rules, procedure and authority
plan: Distinguish the two claims: disorder, or an excess of rules that nobody has agreed to.
Use the Caucus-race as the first case — a complete procedure with no contest inside it.
Read the croquet ground for the relation between ceremony and effect: sentences are passed about once a minute and nothing is carried out.
Examine the trial for order rather than content: judge, jury, evidence and verdict are all present and only the sequence has gone.
Decide what Alice’s final refusal shows — that authority here depends on the consent of everybody who agrees to be frightened.

essayQuestions.question: What does Carroll do with parody, and does it still work for a reader who does not know the originals?
essayQuestions.focus: Verse, recitation and memory
plan: Set out what is being parodied: improving verse of the kind children were made to learn by heart.
Show how the parodies are staged as failures of memory, not as literary jokes — Alice sets out to recite and something else comes out.
Compare the Mock Turtle’s account of his schooling, where the joke is on the curriculum rather than on any one poem.
Test the question directly: what survives for a reader with no original in mind, and what is lost.
Conclude on what recitation is for in the book — a proof of identity that keeps failing.

essayQuestions.question: How does the dream frame affect the way the book ends?
essayQuestions.focus: Structure, the waking and the sister’s second dream
plan: Describe the frame precisely: a drowsy afternoon, a fall, and a waking with leaves on the face.
Ask whether the dream is used to explain the impossibilities, and note how little of the book depends on their being explained.
Read the transformations at the waking — cards into leaves, shrieks into a shepherd boy — as a translation rather than a cancellation.
Examine the sister’s deliberate re-dreaming, and what it says about rereading a book you already know.
Weigh the ending against the fear the middle chapters generate: is the frame a comfort, or an admission that none was needed?

discussionQuestions: Alice is the only character in the book who changes her mind. Does that make her the heroine, or just the outsider?
The Queen orders constant executions and none takes place. Is she frightening?
Almost every creature corrects Alice’s English. Why does Carroll make rudeness so specifically grammatical?
The tea-party has no plot and no consequence. What would the book lose without it?
Tenniel’s pictures arrived with the first published text. Can the book now be read without them?

timeline.label: Charles Lutwidge Dodgson born at Daresbury in Cheshire
timeline.detail: The eldest son of a clergyman, and the third of eleven children.

timeline.label: Dodgson is appointed Mathematical Lecturer at Christ Church, Oxford
timeline.detail: He held the post for a quarter of a century and lived in college for the rest of his life.

timeline.label: The river excursion of 4 July
timeline.detail: Dodgson tells the first version of the story to the three Liddell sisters on a boat trip towards Godstow.

timeline.label: Alice’s Adventures Under Ground given to Alice Liddell
timeline.detail: Written out and illustrated by Dodgson himself; the published book more than doubles it.

timeline.label: The first printing is withdrawn
timeline.detail: Tenniel objected to the quality of the reproduction of his illustrations.

timeline.label: The replacement impression reaches readers
timeline.detail: Dated 1866, this is the effective first published edition.

timeline.label: Through the Looking-Glass appears
timeline.detail: Published in December and dated 1872, again with Tenniel’s illustrations.

timeline.label: The Nursery ‘Alice’
timeline.detail: Carroll’s own shortened version for very young children, with coloured plates.

timeline.label: The last substantial revision of the text
timeline.detail: New settings incorporate Carroll’s final corrections to the standard wording.

timeline.label: Carroll dies at Guildford
timeline.detail: He died in January at his sisters’ house, The Chestnuts.

timeline.label: The book comes out of copyright in Britain
timeline.detail: New illustrated editions follow at once, among them Arthur Rackham’s.

timeline.label: The Under Ground manuscript comes to the British Museum
timeline.detail: Bought by American subscribers and presented to Britain; it is now British Library Add MS 46700.

timeline.label: Disney’s animated Alice in Wonderland
timeline.detail: It folds material from Through the Looking-Glass into Wonderland and fixes the book’s popular image for a century.

places.name: Christ Church, Oxford
places.note: Dodgson’s college for the whole of his adult life, and the Liddells’ home in the Deanery.

places.name: Folly Bridge, Oxford
places.note: Where the boat was hired for the excursion of 4 July 1862.

places.name: Godstow
places.note: The upstream destination of that afternoon’s row, where the party took tea on the bank.

places.name: Daresbury, Cheshire
places.note: Carroll’s birthplace, and the county that supplies the Cheshire Cat’s grin.

places.name: Guildford
places.note: The Chestnuts, his sisters’ house, where he died in January 1898.

related.why: Another traveller who measures an impossible country deadpan, and another book that children were given after the satire had been trimmed off it.
Talking animals with settled manners — the opposite arrangement, where the creatures are courteous and the rules hold.
Children left to work out an adult world for themselves, without any of Wonderland’s licence to be rude back.
Another heroine who talks herself through trouble, and another book in which recitation is a test of who a child is.
Nonsense logic promoted to social weapon: characters who reason impeccably from premises they have just invented.

books.title: Anne of Green Gables
books.author: L. M. Montgomery
books.setting: Avonlea, a farming village on the north shore of Prince Edward Island, in the 1890s
books.lengthNote: Thirty-eight chapters, each one shaped like a complete episode
books.openingLine: Mrs. Rachel Lynde lived just where the Avonlea main road dipped down into a little hollow, fringed with alders and ladies’ eardrops and traversed by a brook that had its source away back in the woods of the old Cuthbert place.
books.summary: Two elderly unmarried siblings send to an orphan asylum for a boy to help on the farm and are sent a talkative eleven-year-old girl instead. What follows is not a story about a child charming everybody, but about the slow and often reluctant conversion of a household and a village: Marilla learns to say what she feels only when it is nearly too late, and Anne learns which of her gifts are worth keeping. Montgomery puts the comedy of a broken slate and a green-dyed head beside a bereavement and a narrowed future, and lets the second give the first its weight.

sourceText.label: Standard Ebooks text of Anne of Green Gables
sourceText.note: The thirty-eight chapters are numbered I to XXXVIII in the text and cited here by Arabic numeral. The base text is the 1908 first edition, with its American spelling and punctuation.

structure.label: Chapters 1–6
structure.title: The mistake, and the decision not to send her back
structure.summary: Mrs Rachel Lynde sees Matthew drive past in his good clothes and goes to find out why. At Bright River a small girl is waiting on a pile of shingles, and by the time Marilla has decided that the mistake must be corrected, the alternative — a hard-worked household at Mrs Blewett’s — has shown her what correcting it would mean.

structure.label: Chapters 7–12
structure.title: Bringing-up begun
structure.summary: Anne is taught to say her prayers, offends Mrs Rachel Lynde about her hair and freckles, and refuses to apologise until an apology can be performed with full dramatic satisfaction. Sunday school, a wreath of buttercups on a hat, and the vow of eternal friendship with Diana Barry all belong to this stretch.

structure.label: Chapters 13–18
structure.title: School, Diana and the boy with the slate
structure.summary: Anne confesses to a theft she did not commit in order to attend a picnic, breaks a slate over Gilbert Blythe’s head for calling her carrots, and accidentally makes Diana drunk on Marilla’s currant wine. The croup night at the Barrys’ ends the estrangement and establishes Anne as useful in an emergency.

structure.label: Chapters 19–23
structure.title: A run of catastrophes
structure.summary: The Haunted Wood terrifies its own inventor, the liniment cake ruins a minister’s tea, and a dare on Mr Barry’s kitchen roof ends with a sprained ankle. Each disaster is also an introduction: Aunt Josephine, Mrs Allan and a village that begins to take Anne’s part.

structure.label: Chapters 24–29
structure.title: Puffed sleeves, green hair and the lily maid
structure.summary: Miss Stacy arrives and changes what school can be; Matthew, after a lengthy campaign of embarrassment, buys a dress with puffed sleeves. Anne dyes her hair green, has it cut off, and nearly drowns playing Tennyson’s Elaine — and is pulled out of the water by Gilbert Blythe, whose apology she still will not accept.

structure.label: Chapters 30–36
structure.title: Queen’s, the pass list and the Avery
structure.summary: The Queen’s class is organised, Anne and Gilbert tie for first place on the entrance list, and a year in Charlottetown ends with the Avery scholarship and the prospect of a B.A. Marilla and Matthew are proud in their separate, largely silent ways, and Matthew says the one thing he has never said.

structure.label: Chapters 37–38
structure.title: The reaper, and the bend in the road
structure.summary: A bank fails, Matthew dies of the shock, and Marilla learns that her eyes will not stand much more use. Anne gives up the scholarship, takes the Avonlea school, and makes her peace with Gilbert at a gate; the novel ends with a road that no longer runs straight.

characters.name: Anne Shirley
characters.role: An eleven-year-old sent by mistake to Green Gables
characters.summary: She arrives with a carpet-bag, a vocabulary out of borrowed books and a history of minding other people’s babies, and her talk is the only property she has ever been allowed to keep. The novel is careful never to cure her of imagination, only to teach her when it clarifies a thing and when it hides one that needs attention.
characters.clue: She renames a pond, a road and an avenue on the drive from the station, refuses to answer to a name spelled without its last letter, and once walked a ridgepole on a dare.
traits: unable to leave a name unimproved

characters.name: Marilla Cuthbert
characters.role: Mistress of Green Gables
characters.summary: Practical, sarcastic and frightened of her own affections, she is the character the novel actually changes. Montgomery gives her the funniest dry lines and then, in the last two chapters, the admission that she has never found it easy to say anything out of her heart — which is why the saying of it lands so hard.
characters.clue: She keeps her brooch in a drawer and her feelings further back than that, and her first recorded reaction to a strange child in her kitchen is to ask where the boy is.

characters.name: Matthew Cuthbert
characters.role: Marilla’s brother, a farmer afraid of women
characters.summary: He is frightened of everyone except Anne and says almost nothing to anybody, which makes the four or five sentences he does say the emotional pivots of the book. His campaign to buy a dress with puffed sleeves is comedy; his remark about a dozen boys is the reason the last chapters work.
characters.clue: Shy to the point of illness with any woman but his sister, he drives to the station in his best clothes, cannot bring himself to correct a mistake, and later buys brown sugar by accident while trying to buy a dress.
traits: the first to take her side

characters.name: Diana Barry
characters.role: Anne’s bosom friend
characters.summary: Pretty, good-natured and entirely without imagination, she is the ordinary against which Anne is measured and the first person ever to want Anne’s company for its own sake. The friendship survives being forbidden, which is more than most of the novel’s adult relationships are asked to do.
characters.clue: She is the only other girl of the right age at the right end of Avonlea, she is made drunk on three tumblers of what she thinks is cordial, and her mother forbids the friendship for a season.

characters.name: Gilbert Blythe
characters.role: The best scholar in Avonlea school
characters.summary: He calls Anne carrots in Chapter 15 and spends the rest of the novel paying for it, first with a broken slate and then with five years of refused apologies. Montgomery keeps him mostly offstage, so that the rivalry works as a spur to Anne’s ambition rather than as a romance.
characters.clue: He pulls a girl out of the river after her leaky flat sinks, and she thanks him and then declines to forgive him for something he said when they were thirteen.

characters.name: Mrs Rachel Lynde
characters.role: Avonlea’s chief authority on everybody
characters.summary: She runs the Sewing Circle, the Church Aid Society and, in practice, the village’s opinion of itself, and the book opens by describing a brook that behaves itself as it passes her window. Her quarrel with Anne over red hair and freckles is the first test of whether Avonlea will treat a child as a character or a case.
characters.clue: Sixteen cotton-warp quilts, a kitchen window over the main road, and an opinion delivered to a strange child’s face about her skinniness, her freckles and her hair.

characters.name: Miss Stacy
characters.role: The new teacher at Avonlea school
characters.summary: She takes the pupils into the woods, gets up concerts, and organises the Queen’s class that gives Anne a route out of the village. She is the book’s picture of what a good teacher does — she does not tame ambition, she gives it an examination timetable.
characters.clue: Field days, recitations and physical culture arrive with her, and the Avonlea parents are not sure about any of it until the pass list appears in the paper.

characters.name: Miss Josephine Barry
characters.role: Diana’s wealthy great-aunt from Charlottetown
characters.summary: Two children jump into her bed in the dark and she becomes, improbably, one of Anne’s allies — the first adult outside Green Gables to be won by talk rather than by good behaviour. She provides the tea-parties, the concert tickets and the second home in town that the last chapters need.
characters.clue: Rich, easily offended and staying in the spare room, she is landed on in the dark by two girls racing for the spare-room bed.

themes.name: Being kept
themes.summary: Anne arrives as a clerical error and spends the first six chapters not knowing whether she will be sent back, and the novel never lets the reader forget the alternative: Mrs Blewett’s household, where a child would be a pair of hands. Belonging here is decided by adults in kitchens, and it has to be decided again each time Anne does something disastrous.
themes.development: A mistake in Chapter 3, a decision in Chapter 6, a conditional welcome for twenty chapters, and finally Marilla saying it aloud when the household has nothing else left.

themes.name: Imagination as resource and risk
themes.summary: Anne’s imagination is a way of living inside material limits: nothing else she owns can turn a pond into the Lake of Shining Waters. The book is unusual in insisting that the same faculty is dangerous — it produces the Haunted Wood she cannot walk through, the hair dye she believes in and the Elaine who nearly drowns.
themes.development: A defence against the asylum in the early chapters, a social gift by the middle of the book, and by Queen’s a thing she can switch off long enough to pass an examination.

themes.name: Names, and the right to choose them
themes.summary: Anne’s first act at Green Gables is to negotiate the spelling of her own name, and her second is to rename the neighbourhood. For a child whose clothes, placements and prospects have all been decided elsewhere, naming is the one power available, and Montgomery treats it as a serious claim rather than a whimsy.
themes.development: Cordelia and the e in Chapter 3, the Lake of Shining Waters and the White Way of Delight on the drive, and at the end the names have stuck: the village uses them too.

themes.name: Orphans, hired help and respectable farms
themes.summary: The novel is quietly exact about money and position: a boy from an asylum is labour, a girl is a liability, Mrs Blewett wants someone to mind her children, and the Cuthberts’ respectability is what makes Green Gables a different proposition. The bank failure in the last chapters shows how narrow that margin of respectability actually is.
themes.development: An asylum and a farm in Chapter 6, hand-me-down wincey dresses against puffed sleeves in Chapter 25, and a scholarship given up for a mortgage-free house in Chapter 38.

themes.name: School, scholarship and ambition
themes.summary: Ambition in this book is specific and measurable — a pass list in the paper, a First Class licence, the Avery scholarship, a B.A. — and it belongs to a girl in a farming village in the 1890s. Miss Stacy does not soften it; she organises it, and the rivalry with Gilbert is the engine.
themes.development: A broken slate in Chapter 15, a class organised in Chapter 30, a tie at the head of the pass list, and then an ambition that has to be recalculated rather than abandoned.

themes.name: Grief, and a future made smaller
themes.summary: The last two chapters withdraw almost everything the book has been building: Matthew dies, Marilla’s sight is failing, and the scholarship goes to somebody else. Montgomery refuses both the tragic ending and the consolation prize, and has Anne argue that a narrowed road is not a closed one.
themes.development: A bank failure and a death in Chapter 37, a decision in Chapter 38, and a last paragraph in which the horizon has come in and the happiness is described as quiet.

techniques.name: Free indirect style
techniques.definition: Third-person narration that slips into a character’s own idiom without announcing that it is doing so.
techniques.bookDefinition: Third-person narration that slips into a character’s own idiom without announcing that it is doing so.
techniques.inThisBook: The narration shifts into Marilla’s vocabulary at the moments she would never speak aloud — worrying about what Mrs Rachel will say, admitting to herself that the house has changed — which is how a character who says almost nothing becomes the book’s second centre.

techniques.name: Idiolect
techniques.definition: A speech habit belonging to one character alone, so that they can be recognised before they are named.
techniques.bookDefinition: Giving each character a distinct and consistent way of speaking.
techniques.inThisBook: Anne speaks in paragraphs, with subordinate clauses and italics; Matthew begins almost every sentence with ‘Well now’; Marilla answers in one flat line. A page of dialogue needs almost no attribution.

techniques.name: Narratorial irony
techniques.definition: Saying one thing in a form that invites the opposite judgement.
techniques.bookDefinition: A narrator whose tone quietly judges what it reports.
techniques.inThisBook: The first page describes a brook that grows well-conducted as it passes Mrs Rachel Lynde’s window — the village’s power over its inhabitants stated as a fact about hydrology before a single person has spoken.

techniques.name: Allusion
techniques.definition: Quotation or reference used to enlarge, or to puncture, the scene at hand.
techniques.bookDefinition: Quotation or reference used to enlarge, or to puncture, the scene at hand.
techniques.inThisBook: Anne stages Tennyson’s Elaine in a leaky flat and nearly drowns, recites ‘The Dog at His Master’s Grave’ at Sunday school, and closes the novel with a line of Browning — her reading is always trying to convert Avonlea into something more like a poem.

techniques.name: The comic set piece
techniques.definition: A self-contained episode built to a single effect and complete in itself, whether comic or ceremonial.
techniques.bookDefinition: A self-contained episode built to a single disaster, complete in one chapter.
techniques.inThisBook: The liniment cake, the currant wine, the dyed hair and the ridgepole each occupy a chapter, end in humiliation, and leave one permanent change behind — a new ally, a lesson, or a piece of Avonlea folklore.

techniques.name: The year as structure
techniques.definition: Organising narrative time by season and recurring village event rather than by plot.
techniques.bookDefinition: Organising narrative time by season and recurring village event rather than by plot.
techniques.inThisBook: Blossom, harvest, the Sunday-school picnic, the winter concert and the examination timetable mark the passage of five years; chapters end with weather as often as with incident.

quotations.text: not even a brook could run past Mrs. Rachel Lynde’s door without due regard for decency and decorum
quotations.context: The opening sentence of the novel, describing the hollow where Mrs Rachel lives.
quotations.analysis: A brook that is headlong and full of dark secrets in the woods becomes quiet and well-conducted when it reaches a particular window: the village’s disciplinary power is established as a fact of the landscape before any character speaks. The alliteration of ‘decency and decorum’ is Mrs Rachel’s own phrasing, lent to the narrator a paragraph before she is introduced.

quotations.text: I asked her to go into the ladies’ waiting room, but she informed me gravely that she preferred to stay outside. ‘There was more scope for imagination,’ she said. She’s a case, I should say.
quotations.speaker: The station master
quotations.context: Matthew arrives at Bright River to collect a boy and is told what is waiting for him.
quotations.analysis: Anne’s defining phrase reaches the reader at second hand, inside a railwayman’s report, with quotation marks around it as though it were evidence. ‘She’s a case’ is the verdict Avonlea will keep offering for thirty chapters, and the novel’s method is to let her phrase outlive the judgement.

quotations.text: I shall call it⁠—let me see⁠—the Lake of Shining Waters. Yes, that is the right name for it. I know because of the thrill.
quotations.speaker: Anne Shirley
quotations.context: On the drive from Bright River, renaming Barry’s pond.
quotations.analysis: The test she applies is physical rather than aesthetic: a name is right when it produces a thrill, which makes naming a kind of instrument reading. Note that she does this before she knows whether she is allowed to stay — the renaming of the district is done by a child who may be sent back on the morning train.

quotations.text: But if you call me Anne please call me Anne spelled with an e.
quotations.speaker: Anne Shirley
quotations.context: In the Green Gables kitchen, being interrogated by Marilla about the mistake.
quotations.analysis: The sentence concedes and demands in the same breath: she gives up Cordelia and instantly opens a second negotiation. A child with no say over where she sleeps is bargaining over orthography, which is the only territory available to her, and the request is granted — Marilla uses the formula back at her twice in the same scene.

quotations.text: When you hear a name pronounced can’t you always see it in your mind, just as if it was printed out? I can; and A-n-n looks dreadful, but A-n-n-e looks so much more distinguished.
quotations.speaker: Anne Shirley
quotations.context: Explaining to Marilla why the letter matters.
quotations.analysis: The explanation is an accurate description of synaesthetic reading, offered by a child to an adult who has never thought about it. It also quietly establishes the difference between the two of them: Marilla hears words, Anne sees them printed, and most of their misunderstandings for the next thirty chapters follow from that.

quotations.text: I can’t. I’m in the depths of despair. Can you eat when you are in the depths of despair?
quotations.speaker: Anne Shirley
quotations.context: Refusing supper on her first evening, having been told she is not wanted.
quotations.analysis: The phrase is borrowed from books and used with complete sincerity, and the question that follows is genuine — she is asking for information. Marilla’s flat reply, that she has never been in the depths of despair, sets the two registers of the novel against each other in three lines of dialogue.

quotations.text: “We might be some good to her,” said Matthew suddenly and unexpectedly.
quotations.speaker: Matthew Cuthbert
quotations.context: Marilla has been listing the reasons the child cannot possibly stay.
quotations.analysis: Seven words that decide the book, and the narrator flags their rarity rather than their content — ‘suddenly and unexpectedly’ is about Matthew speaking at all. The grammar also reverses the household’s assumption: they had applied for a boy who would be some good to them.

quotations.text: Suppose she wasn’t really going to stay here! She would imagine she was. There was scope for imagination here.
quotations.context: Anne’s first morning, kneeling at the east gable window.
quotations.analysis: Free indirect style puts the reader inside a decision being made in real time: the exclamation is Anne’s, and so is the flat sentence that answers it. Imagination is presented here as a deliberate act of management rather than a daydream — she will imagine that she is staying because the alternative is unbearable and no other resource exists.

quotations.text: A bosom friend⁠—an intimate friend, you know⁠—a really kindred spirit to whom I can confide my inmost soul.
quotations.speaker: Anne Shirley
quotations.context: Explaining to Marilla what she means when she says she wants a bosom friend.
quotations.analysis: The definition arrives in three stages, each one more literary than the last, and the escalation is the joke. But the sentence also names the novel’s scarcest commodity: Anne has had households, matrons and other people’s twins, and has never once had a person of her own choosing.

quotations.text: It would be so much easier to be good if one’s hair was a handsome auburn, don’t you think?
quotations.speaker: Anne Shirley
quotations.context: To Mrs Rachel Lynde, immediately after making her apology for the quarrel about her looks.
quotations.analysis: The apology has just been performed with theatrical relish, and this is the sentence that follows it: goodness treated as a matter of appearance, offered to the woman whose remark about her hair caused the quarrel. Montgomery lets Anne win Mrs Rachel over in the same speech in which she reveals she has learned nothing about vanity.

quotations.text: “Carrots! Carrots!”
quotations.speaker: Gilbert Blythe
quotations.context: In the schoolroom, after Gilbert has failed to make Anne look at him.
quotations.analysis: Two words, one line to itself, and five years of plot. The word is an insult about poverty as much as about colour — red hair is the one feature of herself Anne has never been able to reimagine — and it arrives from the only pupil in Avonlea who is her intellectual equal.

quotations.text: “There’s a great deal of difference between being called a crow and being called carrots,” said Anne with dignity. “Gilbert Blythe has hurt my feelings excruciatingly, Diana.”
quotations.speaker: Anne Shirley
quotations.context: Diana has pointed out that Charlie Sloane calls her a crow and she does not mind.
quotations.analysis: ‘With dignity’ is the narrator’s small betrayal of a girl who has just broken a slate over a boy’s head, and ‘excruciatingly’ is Anne restoring the scale of the injury by vocabulary alone. The distinction she is defending is real to her and invisible to everyone else, which is the shape of most of her quarrels.

quotations.text: “Marilla, isn’t it nice to think that tomorrow is a new day with no mistakes in it yet?”
quotations.speaker: Anne Shirley
quotations.context: The evening of the liniment cake, after the minister and his wife have gone home.
quotations.analysis: The consolation is offered to Marilla rather than claimed for herself, which is the first sign of the adult Anne. ‘Yet’ is the word that keeps the sentence honest: it concedes that tomorrow will also be filled with mistakes, and proposes only that they have not happened.

quotations.text: “I must do it. My honour is at stake,” said Anne solemnly. “I shall walk that ridgepole, Diana, or perish in the attempt. If I am killed you are to have my pearl bead ring.”
quotations.speaker: Anne Shirley
quotations.context: Josie Pye has dared her to walk the ridgepole of the Barrys’ kitchen roof.
quotations.analysis: The language of chivalric romance is applied to a dare from a girl she dislikes, and the will disposing of a pearl bead ring is the exact measure of what Anne owns. The narrator then notes drily that walking ridgepoles is not a thing in which imagination helps you out much — the book’s clearest statement of where the gift stops.

quotations.text: “Yes, it’s green,” moaned Anne. “I thought nothing could be as bad as red hair. But now I know it’s ten times worse to have green hair.
quotations.speaker: Anne Shirley
quotations.context: Confessing to Marilla after buying hair dye from a pedlar.
quotations.analysis: The comedy depends on a genuinely painful fact established twenty chapters earlier: the hair is the one thing about herself Anne has never been able to redescribe. Her consolation afterwards — that a wicked act should at least be wicked to some purpose — is the closest the novel comes to a theology of mistakes.

quotations.text: There are so many things in this room and all so splendid that there is no scope for imagination. That is one consolation when you are poor⁠—there are so many more things you can imagine about.
quotations.speaker: Anne Shirley
quotations.context: In Miss Barry’s spare room in Charlottetown, on the visit that follows the hotel concert.
quotations.analysis: The novel’s economics stated in two sentences, and by the person they apply to: imagination is described as a compensation for not having things. It is also a considerable piece of tact, delivered in a velvet-carpeted room belonging to a rich woman who is listening.

quotations.text: I’m not a bit changed⁠—not really. I’m only just pruned down and branched out.
quotations.speaker: Anne Shirley
quotations.context: Sitting on Marilla’s lap at Green Gables, home from Queen’s, after Marilla has said she seems grown up and different.
quotations.analysis: The metaphor is taken from the orchard outside the window, which is the register Marilla can actually hear — Anne has learned to translate. It also concedes more than it admits: pruning is a loss of growth carried out deliberately, and the last chapters will require exactly that.

quotations.text: “Well now, I’d rather have you than a dozen boys, Anne,” said Matthew patting her hand. “Just mind you that⁠—rather than a dozen boys.
quotations.speaker: Matthew Cuthbert
quotations.context: Walking back with the cows on the last evening of his life, after Anne has said she wishes she had been the boy they sent for.
quotations.analysis: The sentence answers the clerical error of Chapter 1 directly, and Matthew repeats it because he knows he is bad at saying things. Montgomery places it the evening before his death, so that the novel’s one explicit declaration of love is also the last thing he manages to do.

quotations.text: It’s never been easy for me to say things out of my heart, but at times like this it’s easier. I love you as dear as if you were my own flesh and blood and you’ve been my joy and comfort ever since you came to Green Gables.
quotations.speaker: Marilla Cuthbert
quotations.context: The night after Matthew’s funeral, hearing Anne crying in her room.
quotations.analysis: Marilla explains why she can speak before she speaks, which is characteristic: the confession is prefaced by an account of her own reticence. ‘As dear as if’ preserves the fact that Anne is not her flesh and blood, and the novel’s whole argument about who belongs to whom is settled on that conjunction.

quotations.text: When I left Queen’s my future seemed to stretch out before me like a straight road. I thought I could see along it for many a milestone. Now there is a bend in it. I don’t know what lies around the bend, but I’m going to believe that the best does.
quotations.speaker: Anne Shirley
quotations.context: Telling Marilla that she has given up the Avery scholarship and will teach at Carmody instead.
quotations.analysis: The image is the opposite of the one she began with: a road she cannot see along is now preferable to a road she can. Note the verb — ‘I’m going to believe’ — which makes optimism an act of will rather than a temperament, and quietly answers everyone who has called her a case.

quotations.text: God’s in his heaven, all’s right with the world,
quotations.speaker: Anne Shirley
quotations.context: The last line of the novel, whispered at the gable window.
quotations.analysis: The line is Browning’s, sung by a child in a play about a village that is not in fact all right, and Montgomery hands it to a girl whose horizons have just closed in. Quoting rather than asserting is the point: Anne ends the book borrowing somebody else’s certainty and choosing to mean it.

quotations.text: I think some kinds of sewing would be nice; but there’s no scope for imagination in patchwork.
quotations.speaker: Anne Shirley
quotations.context: Set to sew red and white diamonds by Marilla, who believes in useful work.
quotations.analysis: The phrase that began as a description of a railway platform has become a general test she applies to everything, from cookery to algebra. It is also a joke about the novel’s own form: a book made of small self-contained episodes stitched into a pattern is complaining about patchwork.

atAGlance.label: First published
atAGlance.note: L. C. Page and Company of Boston, after Montgomery signed with the firm in April 1907.

atAGlance.label: Written at
atAGlance.note: Montgomery began the novel in June 1905 in the house where her grandparents had brought her up.

atAGlance.label: The premise
atAGlance.note: An elderly couple apply to an orphanage for a boy and are sent a girl by mistake.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.note: Roughly five years, counted in seasons, concerts, examinations and mistakes.

criticalViews.position: A novel about Marilla
criticalViews.summary: One long-standing reading holds that the book’s real development belongs to the guardian rather than the child: Anne is much the same person in Chapter 38 as in Chapter 3, while Marilla moves from regarding a girl as useless to saying she loves her as dear as her own flesh and blood.
criticalViews.counter: It underrates what Anne gives up in the last chapter, which is a genuine loss and a genuine decision.

criticalViews.position: An orphan story with the economics left in
criticalViews.summary: Read beside the period’s home-child schemes, the opening is not sentimental at all: children were placed on farms as labour, and the novel’s first crisis is that the wrong kind of labour has arrived. Mrs Blewett is the book’s reminder of what the ordinary outcome looked like.
criticalViews.counter: The novel then declines to follow the economics, since Green Gables can afford a child who is not useful.

criticalViews.position: A book about imagination and its limits
criticalViews.summary: Criticism has often focused on how carefully Montgomery balances the gift against the damage: the same faculty that renames a pond produces the Haunted Wood, the hair dye and the sinking flat. Growing up in this novel means learning when to switch it off, not learning to do without it.
criticalViews.counter: The final chapters can be read as a loss of nerve, in which a girl’s ambition is disciplined into a smaller life and called contentment.

criticalViews.position: The Island as industry
criticalViews.summary: The novel’s afterlife has made Prince Edward Island a literary destination, with a preserved farmhouse and a tourist economy built on a fictional village. Discussion of the book now has to include what happens when a landscape is recognised chiefly through somebody’s imaginary names for it.
criticalViews.counter: Montgomery herself distinguished source from setting, and never claimed Avonlea was a map of Cavendish.

essayQuestions.question: Whose education does the novel actually describe?
essayQuestions.focus: Anne, Marilla and the direction of change
plan: Establish what Anne is like in Chapters 2 to 4 and test how much of it survives to Chapter 38.
Track Marilla instead: the decision in Chapter 6, the amethyst brooch, the silent pride at the pass list, the confession in Chapter 37.
Use free indirect style as evidence — the narration enters Marilla’s thoughts at exactly the points she refuses to speak.
Consider Matthew as the constant against which both are measured, and what his death forces each of them to say.
Conclude on the last chapter: who has given something up, and who has learned to say something.

essayQuestions.question: How does Montgomery use Anne’s imagination?
essayQuestions.focus: Naming, invention and the cost of both
plan: Begin with naming as the only power available to a child with no possessions: Cordelia, the e, the Lake of Shining Waters.
Show imagination working as protection in Chapter 4 — she will imagine she is staying — and as sociability with Diana.
Turn to the damage: the Haunted Wood she cannot walk through, the pedlar’s dye, the leaky flat and Elaine.
Examine the narrator’s dry line about ridgepoles, which states the limit explicitly.
End with the last two chapters, where imagination becomes a decision to believe something about a road she cannot see.

essayQuestions.question: ‘A comic novel that turns serious too late.’ How far do you agree?
essayQuestions.focus: Structure, episode and the final chapters
plan: Describe the episodic method: each chapter a complete disaster with a lesson attached.
Show how the comedy accumulates consequence — the liniment cake gains an ally, the dyed hair loses a plait, the slate makes a rival.
Read the bank failure and Matthew’s death as an intrusion of a different kind of plot, with money and health at stake.
Assess the last chapter’s refusals: no scholarship, no reversal, no rescue, and a career redefined at Carmody.
Decide whether the ending is a change of key or the point the earlier chapters were preparing for.

essayQuestions.question: What does the novel show about Avonlea as a community?
essayQuestions.focus: Neighbours, respectability and who decides
plan: Start with the first page: a brook, a window and a village that knows what everyone is sowing.
Use Mrs Rachel Lynde’s quarrel and reconciliation as the test case for how the village handles a newcomer.
Weigh the institutions the book records — Sunday school, the manse, the Debating Club, the concert, the pass list in the paper.
Consider Mrs Blewett and the asylum as the alternatives lying just outside Avonlea’s charity.
Conclude with Chapter 38, where the same neighbours who judged Anne are the reason she can stay.

discussionQuestions: Matthew says seven words in Chapter 3 and changes the course of the book. What does the novel gain by making its most decisive character almost silent?
Anne refuses Gilbert’s apology for five years. Is the novel on her side?
The book insists that imagination is both Anne’s salvation and the cause of most of her disasters. Can it be both?
Marilla can only say that she loves Anne once Matthew is dead. What does the novel suggest about how such households work?
Is giving up the Avery scholarship a sacrifice, a defeat, or a choice? Does the last page persuade you?

timeline.label: Lucy Maud Montgomery born at Clifton, Prince Edward Island
timeline.detail: The village now called New London, a few miles from Cavendish.

timeline.label: Her mother dies; she is sent to her grandparents at Cavendish
timeline.detail: The household of an elderly couple and a child not quite their own is the one the novel rearranges.

timeline.label: Montgomery begins the novel
timeline.detail: She started writing in June, after months of what she called spade work on character and incident.

timeline.label: Contract with L. C. Page and Company
timeline.detail: Signed on 22 April, with the Boston firm that would publish the book and its sequels.

timeline.label: Anne of Green Gables published
timeline.detail: The first edition appeared in June; Montgomery recorded receiving her copies on the 20th.

timeline.label: First translation
timeline.detail: A Swedish edition appeared within a year, the beginning of an international readership.

timeline.label: Montgomery marries and leaves the Island
timeline.detail: She moved to Ontario as a Presbyterian minister’s wife, and wrote most of the Anne books away from Cavendish.

timeline.label: First film version
timeline.detail: A silent adaptation, now lost, made a decade after publication.

timeline.label: A reset text
timeline.detail: L. C. Page issued a newly set and slightly altered edition, which is why the 1908 printing matters as a base text.

timeline.label: Montgomery dies in Toronto
timeline.detail: She was buried at Cavendish, within sight of the landscape the novel renames.

timeline.label: The Canadian television adaptation
timeline.detail: Kevin Sullivan’s version fixed the novel’s appearance for a generation of readers and made Prince Edward Island a destination.

books.title: Antony and Cleopatra
books.author: William Shakespeare
books.setting: The Roman world after Julius Caesar’s death: Alexandria, Rome, Misenum, Athens, Syria and the sea off Actium
books.lengthNote: Around 3,000 lines spread over forty-two scenes — more scenes than any other play in the Folio
books.openingLine: Nay, but this dotage of our general's O'erflows the measure
books.summary: A triumvir who governs a third of the known world will not leave Alexandria, and Rome sends messengers instead of armies. Shakespeare gives the story forty-two scenes and no settled vantage point: every judgement passed on Antony is passed by someone with an interest in it. After Actium the play stops being about who wins and becomes about who gets to describe the losers, and Cleopatra spends the last act taking that job away from Caesar.

sourceText.label: Globe/Moby text of Antony and Cleopatra
sourceText.note: Line numbers follow the traditional Globe numbering; modern editions divide some of the short battle scenes differently.

structure.label: Act I
structure.title: A general who will not come home
structure.summary: Rome watches Egypt through other people's eyes and does not like what it reports. Antony hears of his wife's death and of Pompey's fleet, decides to leave, and discovers that leaving Cleopatra is a scene she intends to direct. Caesar meanwhile sets out the charge sheet in private.

scenes.title: The measure overflowed
scenes.summary: Philo tells a fellow officer what to look for, and the lovers walk on and perform exactly it.

scenes.title: News from Rome
scenes.summary: A soothsayer reads the women's palms; Antony learns that Fulvia is dead and resolves to break his Egyptian fetters.

scenes.title: The parting
scenes.summary: Cleopatra stages illness, accusation and forgiveness in one scene and lets Antony go on her own terms.

scenes.title: Caesar's account
scenes.summary: Caesar itemises Antony's failings to Lepidus, then praises the soldier Antony once was when he needs him back.

scenes.title: Absence
scenes.summary: Cleopatra fills the time with opium, memory and messengers, and dismisses her younger self as salad days.

structure.label: Act II
structure.title: A marriage, a treaty and a drunken galley
structure.summary: The triumvirs patch their quarrel with Antony's marriage to Caesar's sister, and Enobarbus tells the Romans what they have just bargained against. Pompey is bought off at Misenum, and the peace is celebrated by three rulers of the world dancing on a boat while a pirate offers to cut the cable.

scenes.title: Pompey's reckoning
scenes.summary: Pompey counts on Antony staying in Egypt and hears at once that he is coming to Rome.

scenes.title: The bargain and the barge
scenes.summary: Antony agrees to marry Octavia; minutes later Enobarbus describes Cleopatra on the Cydnus to the men who arranged it.

scenes.title: The soothsayer
scenes.summary: Told that his guardian spirit is always beaten by Caesar's, Antony decides to go back to Egypt.

scenes.title: Marching orders
scenes.summary: Lepidus and the others arrange to meet at Mount Misenum.

scenes.title: The messenger struck
scenes.summary: Cleopatra hales the bringer of the marriage news up and down, then calls him back to describe Octavia.

scenes.title: Terms at Misenum
scenes.summary: Pompey accepts Sicily and Sardinia; Enobarbus and Menas measure each other in prose afterwards.

scenes.title: On the galley
scenes.summary: Menas offers to cut the cable and make Pompey lord of the world; Pompey wishes it had been done without asking.

structure.label: Act III
structure.title: Actium, and the ship that turned
structure.summary: The alliance dissolves in short scenes and reported news: Lepidus is deposed, Octavia is sent back, Antony insists on fighting at sea and then follows Cleopatra's fleeing sails. Defeat is immediately fought over as a story, and Enobarbus begins to calculate what loyalty to a falling man is worth.

scenes.title: Ventidius in Syria
scenes.summary: A subordinate wins a victory and explains why winning too well is bad for a career.

scenes.title: Octavia leaves Rome
scenes.summary: Enobarbus and Agrippa mock the triumvirs' tears while the marriage is sealed.

scenes.title: The report on Octavia
scenes.summary: Cleopatra cross-examines the messenger until Octavia is short, low-voiced and dull.

scenes.title: Athens
scenes.summary: Antony lists Caesar's slights; Octavia asks to mediate between husband and brother.

scenes.title: Lepidus removed
scenes.summary: Eros reports that the third triumvir has been used and then imprisoned.

scenes.title: Caesar's case
scenes.summary: Antony's public enthronement of Cleopatra and her children gives Rome its pretext; Octavia arrives without ceremony.

scenes.title: By sea
scenes.summary: Every soldier argues for land; Antony fights by sea because Caesar dares him to.

scenes.title: Caesar's orders
scenes.summary: Caesar tells Taurus not to engage on land until the sea is decided.

scenes.title: Antony's orders
scenes.summary: Antony sets his squadrons where he can see the battle.

scenes.title: The flight
scenes.summary: Enobarbus and Scarus watch Cleopatra's sixty ships turn and Antony's flagship follow.

scenes.title: Shame in Alexandria
scenes.summary: Antony tells his followers to take his treasure and go, then forgives Cleopatra in the same breath as blaming her.

scenes.title: The schoolmaster
scenes.summary: Antony's ambassador is a tutor; Caesar refuses his terms and sends Thidias to work on Cleopatra.

scenes.title: Thidias whipped
scenes.summary: Antony has Caesar's envoy flogged for kissing Cleopatra's hand, calls for another supper, and Enobarbus decides to leave.

structure.label: Act IV
structure.title: A victory, a desertion, and a death that will not come cleanly
structure.summary: Antony wins a day on land, and the music of a god leaving the city is heard under the stage the night before he loses the rest. Enobarbus dies of his own defection. Told a false report of Cleopatra's death, Antony asks Eros to kill him, botches the attempt himself, and is hauled up into the monument to die by degrees.

scenes.title: Caesar laughs
scenes.summary: Antony's challenge to single combat is dismissed as the noise of a man out of options.

scenes.title: The last supper
scenes.summary: Antony makes his servants weep by thanking them as though tonight were the end.

scenes.title: Music under the stage
scenes.summary: Soldiers on watch hear hautboys beneath them and take it for Hercules leaving Antony.

scenes.title: Arming
scenes.summary: Cleopatra helps buckle his armour and is told she is a better squire than she knows.

scenes.title: Enobarbus's chest
scenes.summary: Antony hears of the desertion and sends his treasure after him with a kind message.

scenes.title: Caesar's front line
scenes.summary: Caesar puts the deserters in the vanguard; Enobarbus receives the treasure and turns away to die.

scenes.title: A day on land
scenes.summary: Scarus fights with new wounds and Antony's forces drive Caesar back to camp.

scenes.title: Home in triumph
scenes.summary: Antony presents the wounded Scarus to Cleopatra and asks the city to make its armour ring.

scenes.title: The ditch
scenes.summary: Enobarbus asks the moon to witness his repentance and dies before the watch can speak to him.

scenes.title: Sea again
scenes.summary: Antony resolves to fight by water once more.

scenes.title: Caesar's instruction
scenes.summary: Caesar tells his army to hold the valleys while the fleets meet.

scenes.title: The fleet yields
scenes.summary: The Egyptian ships surrender without a fight and Antony calls Cleopatra a triple-turn'd whore.

scenes.title: The monument
scenes.summary: Cleopatra takes refuge and sends word that she is dead, to see what it does.

scenes.title: Eros
scenes.summary: Antony watches his shape dissolve like cloud, orders Eros to kill him, and falls on his own sword when Eros will not.

scenes.title: Hauled aloft
scenes.summary: The dying Antony is lifted to Cleopatra, gives advice she refuses to take, and she resolves on a Roman death.

structure.label: Act V
structure.title: Caesar's triumph, and the scene Cleopatra takes out of it
structure.summary: Caesar has won and needs Cleopatra alive to walk in Rome. The last act is a negotiation conducted by both sides in bad faith, until Cleopatra decides that a basket of figs is a better ending than a procession. She dies dressed for a coronation, and Caesar is left arranging the funeral of a story he did not write.

scenes.title: The news of Antony
scenes.summary: Caesar weeps for the rival he has just destroyed and immediately asks how to keep Cleopatra from suicide.

scenes.title: The monument
scenes.summary: Cleopatra is taken, lies to Caesar about her treasure, dreams Antony into a colossus and dies by the asp.

characters.name: Mark Antony
characters.role: Triumvir of Rome, general
characters.summary: A soldier whose reputation is largely made of other people's memories of him, and who keeps being asked to live up to a version of himself that is already historical. He is generous, careless and consistently late, and the play's tenderness towards him comes from watching a man lose the shape he is supposed to hold.
characters.clue: He rules a third of the world and answers a summons from it with a shrug; he dies asking for wine and permission to speak a little.

characters.name: Cleopatra
characters.role: Queen of Egypt
characters.summary: She is never off duty: every mood is real and also calculated, and the play declines to separate the two. Her political intelligence is usually discussed as caprice by Romans who cannot see that testing a messenger, staging a faint or refusing a triumph are all the same skill.
characters.clue: She beats the bringer of bad news, then asks him to describe her rival's height; at the end she dresses for a coronation to meet a snake.

characters.name: Octavius Caesar
characters.role: Triumvir, later sole ruler of Rome
characters.summary: Young, dry and entirely without appetite, he wins because he is the only person in the play who never mistakes a gesture for an achievement. Shakespeare gives him no soliloquy at all, so the audience is never invited inside a mind that runs the world.
characters.clue: He drinks reluctantly, weeps on cue for a dead rival, and wants the queen alive mainly so that she can walk behind his chariot.

characters.name: Domitius Enobarbus
characters.role: Antony's lieutenant and closest follower
characters.summary: He talks to the audience in prose, sees through everyone including himself, and produces the one speech in the play that makes Cleopatra indisputable. His defection is a reasoned decision that kills him, which is the play's sharpest comment on reason.
characters.clue: He tells Rome about a burnished barge, calculates that loyalty to a falling lord is folly, acts on the calculation and dies of it in a ditch.

characters.name: Octavia
characters.role: Caesar's sister, Antony's second wife
characters.summary: A treaty in human form, and the play knows it: she is praised for holy, cold and still conversation by men deciding what to do with her. Her few speeches are attempts to be a person in an arrangement that needs her not to be.
characters.clue: Her marriage is the whole of the peace, and when she asks to travel between her brother and her husband she is really asking not to be the reason for a war.

characters.name: Charmian
characters.role: Cleopatra's attendant
