characters.summary: She jokes with a soothsayer in the second scene and closes the queen's eyes in the last, and the play gives her the final judgement on Cleopatra's life. Straightening the crown on a dead woman's head before dying herself is the only stage direction the ending needs.
characters.clue: She asks a fortune-teller for a husband who cannot be angry, and ends by mending her mistress's crown and following her.

characters.name: Sextus Pompeius
characters.role: Commander of the fleet, the triumvirs' opponent at sea
characters.summary: He has the strongest navy and the weakest stomach for what winning would require. Offered the world by a pirate who only needs permission to cut a rope, he explains that the deed would have been honourable if he had not been told about it.
characters.clue: He is master of the sea and loses it by refusing an offer he would have accepted if nobody had asked him first.

characters.name: Lepidus
characters.role: The third triumvir
characters.summary: His function is to agree with whoever is speaking and to keep asking the others not to quarrel. He is carried drunk off Pompey's galley and deposed offstage a few scenes later, which is how the play measures the value of a share in power without the means to defend it.
characters.clue: A third of the world is his; he spends his best scene asking what sort of thing a crocodile is, and is carried off the boat asleep.

themes.name: Rome and Egypt
themes.summary: The play offers the opposition — discipline against appetite, measure against excess — in its first fourteen lines, and then spends five acts making it unusable. Rome is as theatrical as Alexandria; it has simply trained its performance to look like plain fact.
themes.development: Philo states the Roman case before Antony has spoken; by Act V Caesar is arranging a procession and Cleopatra is refusing a part in it, and both are staging.

themes.name: Measure and excess
themes.summary: Counting is the Roman virtue: ships, legions, kingdoms, the terms of a treaty. Antony and Cleopatra answer in a vocabulary of boundlessness — new heavens, melting empires, an autumn that grew the more by reaping — and the play will not say which language is lying.
themes.development: Antony refuses to have love reckoned in 1.1; Caesar ends by counting the pair into a single grave and a solemn show.

themes.name: Performance and self-presentation
themes.summary: Everyone here is managing an image: Cleopatra openly, Caesar invisibly, Antony badly. The most dangerous thing Cleopatra imagines in the last act is not death but a bad performance of herself by a squeaking boy actor in Rome.
themes.development: Play-acting is flirtation in Act I, propaganda in Act III, and by Act V the only remaining way of winning.

themes.name: News, messengers and report
themes.summary: Almost everything important arrives through somebody else's mouth: Fulvia's death, the marriage, Actium, Antony's suicide. The play is built so that events reach the stage already interpreted, and the interpreter always has something at stake.
themes.development: A messenger is beaten in 2.5, a messenger is whipped in 3.13, and in 4.13 Cleopatra sends a false report of her own death to see what it will do.

themes.name: Melting and dissolving identity
themes.summary: Antony's imagery is full of things losing their edges: Rome melting in Tiber, a cloud that was a horse becoming indistinct as water in water, a crown of the earth that melts at his death. The tragedy asks whether a self must keep one shape to be worth anything.
themes.development: The images begin as extravagance in Act I and become a description of his actual condition by 4.14, where he says outright that he cannot hold this visible shape.

themes.name: Loyalty and defection
themes.summary: The play is full of people deciding when to leave, and it refuses to make any of those decisions simple. Enobarbus's desertion is reasonable, Antony's response to it is generous, and the generosity is what makes the reasonable decision unbearable.
themes.development: Ventidius declines to win too much in 3.1, Enobarbus leaves in 3.13, the Egyptian fleet yields in 4.12, and Charmian follows her mistress in 5.2.

techniques.name: Hyperbole
techniques.definition: Deliberate overstatement, used not to deceive but to claim a scale ordinary language cannot reach.
techniques.bookDefinition: Deliberate overstatement, used not to deceive but to claim a scale ordinary language cannot reach.
techniques.inThisBook: Cleopatra's dream of an emperor whose legs bestrid the ocean is the play's largest overstatement and its most searching question: Dolabella says no such man existed, and she asks whether that settles anything.

techniques.name: Scene fragmentation
techniques.definition: Building an act from many brief scenes rather than a few long ones.
techniques.bookDefinition: Building an act from many brief scenes rather than a few long ones.
techniques.inThisBook: Act III changes place thirteen times, and the battle of Actium is split into four scenes of which none shows the fighting. Political space is made to feel unmanageable by the form itself.

techniques.name: The messenger scene
techniques.definition: A convention in which offstage events are reported to a listener who reacts in front of us.
techniques.bookDefinition: A convention in which offstage events are reported to a listener who reacts in front of us.
techniques.inThisBook: Shakespeare turns a convention into a subject: the messenger who is beaten in 2.5 and recalled in 3.3 shows that the listener, not the news, decides what the news means.

techniques.name: The commentator within the action
techniques.definition: A character who stands slightly outside events and interprets them, without being exempt from them.
techniques.bookDefinition: A character who stands slightly outside events and interprets them, without being exempt from them.
techniques.inThisBook: Enobarbus supplies the barge speech, the jokes and the running assessment of his own commander, and then discovers that commentary is not a safe place to stand.

techniques.name: Run-on verse
techniques.definition: Blank verse in which sense spills past the line-ending instead of resting on it.
techniques.bookDefinition: Blank verse in which sense spills past the line-ending instead of resting on it.
techniques.inThisBook: The late style is at its loosest here: sentences begin mid-line, break off, and restart, so that even the grandest speeches sound like someone thinking rather than declaring.

techniques.name: Elemental imagery
techniques.definition: Fire, air, earth and water used as a vocabulary for what a person is made of.
techniques.bookDefinition: Fire, air, earth and water used as a vocabulary for what a person is made of.
techniques.inThisBook: Cleopatra's 'I am fire and air' discards the two heavier elements at the moment of dying, having earlier called kingdoms clay through Antony's mouth.

quotations.text: Nay, but this dotage of our general's O'erflows the measure: those his goodly eyes, That o'er the files and musters of the war Have glow'd like plated Mars, now bend, now turn, The office and devotion of their view Upon a tawny front
quotations.speaker: Philo
quotations.context: The opening lines of the play, spoken to a fellow Roman officer just before Antony and Cleopatra walk on.
quotations.analysis: The audience is given the Roman verdict before it is given a single fact, and the verb does the work: measure is the Roman unit of everything, and Antony is accused of exceeding it. Note that the criticism is grammatically a compliment gone wrong — the eyes still glow, they have simply been redirected.

quotations.text: There's beggary in the love that can be reckon'd.
quotations.speaker: Mark Antony
quotations.context: Answering Cleopatra's opening challenge, 'If it be love indeed, tell me how much.'
quotations.analysis: Her question is a piece of accounting and his answer refuses the ledger, which sets the terms of the whole play. 'Reckon'd' carries both counting and being called to account, so the line quietly declines two different Roman demands in one word.

quotations.text: Let Rome in Tiber melt, and the wide arch Of the ranged empire fall! Here is my space.
quotations.speaker: Mark Antony
quotations.context: Refusing to hear the messengers from Rome in front of Cleopatra.
quotations.analysis: The first of the play's melting images arrives as bravado and returns in Act IV as diagnosis. 'Here is my space' is three monosyllables after a collapsing empire, and it is spoken by a man standing on a stage — the smallest possible claim, made in the largest possible terms.

quotations.text: he fishes, drinks, and wastes The lamps of night in revel; is not more man-like Than Cleopatra; nor the queen of Ptolemy More womanly than he
quotations.speaker: Octavius Caesar
quotations.context: Reading the dispatches from Alexandria aloud to Lepidus.
quotations.analysis: The charge is not laziness but exchange: Caesar's grievance is that the two of them have swapped a quality he believes is fixed. The sentence is arranged as a balance with Antony and Cleopatra on either side of it, so the syntax performs the crossing it complains of.

quotations.text: This common body, Like to a vagabond flag upon the stream, Goes to and back, lackeying the varying tide, To rot itself with motion.
quotations.speaker: Octavius Caesar
quotations.context: On hearing that Pompey is gaining support among the people.
quotations.analysis: Caesar's one extended image in the play is of the public as pondweed, and it tells you what kind of ruler he will be. 'Lackeying' turns the crowd into a servant running beside a horse, and 'rot itself with motion' denies that popular movement is even alive.

quotations.text: My salad days, When I was green in judgment: cold in blood, To say as I said then!
quotations.speaker: Cleopatra
quotations.context: Silencing Charmian, who has reminded her how she once praised Julius Caesar.
quotations.analysis: She rewrites her own past on the spot rather than lose an argument, and the phrase has been so thoroughly borrowed since that its edge is easy to miss: green is unripe, and cold in blood is an accusation of having been insufficiently alive. The revision is the performance.

quotations.text: The barge she sat in, like a burnish'd throne, Burn'd on the water: the poop was beaten gold; Purple the sails, and so perfumed that The winds were love-sick with them
quotations.speaker: Domitius Enobarbus
quotations.context: In Rome, to Agrippa and Maecenas, minutes after Antony has agreed to marry Octavia.
quotations.analysis: The placing is the argument: the treaty has just been signed and Enobarbus immediately tells the signatories what they have bargained against. Shakespeare keeps much of North's prose almost word for word but breaks it across the verse line, so that the sentence never rests where the metre does.

quotations.text: With divers-colour'd fans, whose wind did seem To glow the delicate cheeks which they did cool, And what they undid did.
quotations.speaker: Domitius Enobarbus
quotations.context: Continuing the description of Cleopatra on the river Cydnus.
quotations.analysis: Four words at the end of the sentence contradict themselves twice and remain perfectly grammatical. It is the play's whole method in miniature: the fans cool and heat at once, and Cleopatra is not a paradox to be resolved but a description that has to hold both halves.

quotations.text: Age cannot wither her, nor custom stale Her infinite variety: other women cloy The appetites they feed: but she makes hungry Where most she satisfies
quotations.speaker: Domitius Enobarbus
quotations.context: Answering Maecenas, who has just said that Antony must now leave her for good.
quotations.analysis: The claim is presented as a prediction about Antony's behaviour, not a compliment, which is why the Romans take it seriously. 'Custom' and 'cloy' are both words about repetition wearing things out, and the line's argument is that Cleopatra has found a way of not repeating herself.

quotations.text: Mine honesty and I begin to square.
quotations.speaker: Domitius Enobarbus
quotations.context: An aside, watching Cleopatra receive Caesar's messenger after Actium.
quotations.analysis: 'Square' means to quarrel, and the line splits a man from his own integrity as though they were two soldiers falling out. Everything Enobarbus says for the rest of the scene is an argument with himself conducted in the third person, and he loses it.

quotations.text: Egypt, thou knew'st too well My heart was to thy rudder tied by the strings, And thou shouldst tow me after
quotations.speaker: Mark Antony
quotations.context: In Alexandria after Actium, forgiving Cleopatra for the flight he chose to follow.
quotations.analysis: He calls her by the name of her country, which is what the Romans do, and then describes himself as cargo. The accusation and the excuse are the same sentence: she knew, therefore it is her doing, and he was towed, therefore it is not his.

quotations.text: That which is now a horse, even with a thought The rack dislimns, and makes it indistinct, As water is in water.
quotations.speaker: Mark Antony
quotations.context: To Eros, watching the evening clouds change shape before his last defeat.
quotations.analysis: 'Dislimns' — unpaints — is rare enough that Shakespeare may have made it, and it treats the sky as a canvas being wiped. The simile then refuses the comfort of a comparison: water in water is not like dissolution, it is the thing itself, and there is nothing left to see it against.

quotations.text: My good knave Eros, now thy captain is Even such a body: here I am Antony: Yet cannot hold this visible shape, my knave.
quotations.speaker: Mark Antony
quotations.context: Applying the cloud image to himself, moments before asking Eros to kill him.
quotations.analysis: 'Here I am Antony' ought to be the most certain statement a man can make, and the next line takes it back. The name has been public property since the first scene — Philo's, Caesar's, Cleopatra's — and Antony is the last person to lose his grip on it.

quotations.text: But let the world rank me in register A master-leaver and a fugitive
quotations.speaker: Domitius Enobarbus
quotations.context: Alone in a ditch by Caesar's camp, after Antony has sent his abandoned treasure after him.
quotations.analysis: A man who has spent the play writing other people's reputations asks for his own to be filed under two words. 'Register' is a clerk's word, and the request is for no mitigation at all — he has understood that the record is the only judgement there will be.

quotations.text: I am dying, Egypt, dying: Give me some wine, and let me speak a little.
quotations.speaker: Mark Antony
quotations.context: Hauled up into the monument, bleeding from his own sword.
quotations.analysis: He has already said the same half-line twenty-seven lines earlier, and repetition is how the scene measures time: the dying takes long enough that he has to announce it twice. The request is for wine and for permission — the most public man in the world asking to be allowed to finish a sentence.

quotations.text: The crown o' the earth doth melt. My lord! O, wither'd is the garland of the war, The soldier's pole is fall'n: young boys and girls Are level now with men; the odds is gone, And there is nothing left remarkable Beneath the visiting moon.
quotations.speaker: Cleopatra
quotations.context: The moment Antony dies in her arms at the top of the monument.
quotations.analysis: Grief is expressed as the collapse of every scale of difference: with the pole gone, children and men measure the same. 'The odds is gone' is flat and almost colloquial in the middle of the grandest lament in the play, and it is the line that tells you what she thinks she has lost — not a lover but a standard.

quotations.text: His legs bestrid the ocean: his rear'd arm Crested the world: his voice was propertied As all the tuned spheres
quotations.speaker: Cleopatra
quotations.context: Describing her dream of Antony to Dolabella, one of Caesar's officers.
quotations.analysis: She is making a colossus out of a man who died badly two scenes ago, and she asks Dolabella outright whether such a person could have existed. His honest no does not end the exchange: she answers that dreaming him is itself a kind of evidence, which is the play's last defence of the imagination against Roman fact.

quotations.text: He words me, girls, he words me, that I should not Be noble to myself
quotations.speaker: Cleopatra
quotations.context: The instant Caesar leaves, having promised her kind treatment.
quotations.analysis: Turning the noun into a verb is the whole judgement: Caesar's courtesy is a technique and she has seen the mechanism. Her word for suicide here is 'noble to myself', which converts a Roman virtue into something a queen can do alone and in private.

quotations.text: the quick comedians Extemporally will stage us, and present Our Alexandrian revels; Antony Shall be brought drunken forth, and I shall see Some squeaking Cleopatra boy my greatness I' the posture of a whore.
quotations.speaker: Cleopatra
quotations.context: Explaining to Iras what a Roman triumph would actually involve.
quotations.analysis: The line was first spoken by a boy actor playing Cleopatra, so the theatre is required to admit its own limits at the very moment she rejects them. What she fears is not death or captivity but a bad performance, and the fear is what drives her to write a better final scene.

quotations.text: Give me my robe, put on my crown; I have Immortal longings in me
quotations.speaker: Cleopatra
quotations.context: After the clown has delivered the basket of figs and wished her joy o' the worm.
quotations.analysis: She dresses for a coronation rather than a death, and the stage business is deliberate: robe and crown are the properties Caesar intended to parade. The word 'longings' keeps the appetite the Romans accused her of and attaches it to eternity instead of to supper.

quotations.text: I am fire and air; my other elements I give to baser life.
quotations.speaker: Cleopatra
quotations.context: Dressed and crowned, a few lines before the asp is applied.
quotations.analysis: Four elements were supposed to make a body; she discards earth and water and keeps the two that rise. It is also a direct answer to Antony's 'kingdoms are clay' in the first scene — the play's opening and closing images of substance are spoken by the two lovers about the same set of things.

quotations.text: Dost thou not see my baby at my breast, That sucks the nurse asleep?
quotations.speaker: Cleopatra
quotations.context: With the asp at her breast, as Charmian cries out.
quotations.analysis: The image makes her death an act of feeding, and the venom a child. Cleopatra's own children are barely mentioned in the play; here, at the last possible moment, she becomes a mother to the thing killing her, and asks a question rather than making a claim.

quotations.text: Now boast thee, death, in thy possession lies A lass unparallel'd. Downy windows, close;
quotations.speaker: Charmian
quotations.context: Closing the dead queen's eyes before applying an asp to herself.
quotations.analysis: After five acts of Egypt, empire and infinite variety, the summing-up word is 'lass' — the smallest, plainest, most domestic noun available. Charmian then straightens the crown, which is the only correction anyone in the play manages to make to how Cleopatra will be seen.

quotations.text: She shall be buried by her Antony: No grave upon the earth shall clip in it A pair so famous.
quotations.speaker: Octavius Caesar
quotations.context: The play's closing speech, after the guards find Cleopatra dead.
quotations.analysis: The winner's last act is to arrange the funeral of the people who beat him to it, and 'clip' — embrace — lets the grave do what Caesar prevented. He is already speaking of them as a story worth lamenting, which is exactly the outcome Cleopatra spent the act securing.

atAGlance.label: Written
atAGlance.note: Close in date to King Lear and Macbeth, and to Shakespeare’s other Plutarch play, Coriolanus.

atAGlance.label: First printed
atAGlance.note: No quarto survives. The play was entered in the Stationers’ Register in 1608, but the Folio is the only early text.

atAGlance.label: Chief source
atAGlance.note: In Thomas North’s English translation of 1579, which Shakespeare follows closely enough that whole phrases survive into the verse.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.note: Act III alone changes location thirteen times; several scenes are under twenty lines long.

criticalViews.position: A tragedy of the world well lost
criticalViews.summary: The reading that takes the lovers at their own valuation: the Roman world is small, the love is large, and Cleopatra's last act converts political defeat into something Caesar cannot touch.
criticalViews.counter: It has to look past Actium, the whipping of Thidias and the desertion of the Egyptian fleet, all of which the play insists on showing.

criticalViews.position: A political play about the making of an emperor
criticalViews.summary: On this account the subject is Caesar's patient assembly of sole rule, with Antony as the last obstacle and Egypt as the pretext; the love story is the material out of which a founding myth of empire is built.
criticalViews.counter: Shakespeare gives Caesar no soliloquy and the lovers almost all the poetry, which is a strange way to write a play about the winner.

criticalViews.position: A play about how reputation is manufactured
criticalViews.summary: Recent criticism has concentrated on report, rumour and messengers: nearly every major event reaches us through someone with an interest in how it is described, and the last act is an open contest over who narrates the dead.
criticalViews.counter: Pressed too far, it makes the play sound sceptical about everything, when Antony's physical death and Enobarbus's are given no gloss at all.

criticalViews.position: Cleopatra and the limits of the Roman categories
criticalViews.summary: Feminist and postcolonial readings have examined how consistently Rome describes Egypt in terms of appetite, softness and race, and how far the play endorses that vocabulary or exposes it as a governing tool.
criticalViews.counter: The play also gives Cleopatra the theatrical extravagance the Roman case predicts, so the critique and the caricature are made from the same material.

essayQuestions.question: How far does the play invite us to accept Rome's judgement of Egypt?
essayQuestions.focus: Rome, Egypt and the reliability of the speaker
plan: Start with the fact that Philo's verdict comes before any action: the audience is given a reading before it is given evidence.
Set Caesar's dispatch in 1.4 beside Enobarbus's barge speech in 2.2 and ask what each speaker needs his description to achieve.
Show how Roman self-presentation is also theatre, using the galley scene at Misenum and Caesar's management of Octavia.
Test the opposition against Act IV, where Antony's Roman death fails and Cleopatra's Egyptian one succeeds.
Conclude on 5.2: Caesar's final speech adopts the lovers' scale, which suggests the Roman categories have not held.

essayQuestions.question: Discuss Shakespeare's presentation of Cleopatra.
essayQuestions.focus: Performance, politics and the last act
plan: Begin with 2.5 and 3.3, where testing a messenger is shown to be a method rather than a mood.
Use Enobarbus in 2.2 to establish that her theatricality is recognised by Rome as a political force.
Examine Actium and its aftermath as the point where her judgement is most open to attack.
Read 5.2 as a scene she constructs: the false account of her treasure, the dream of Antony, the robe and crown.
Weigh two conclusions: a woman who finally achieves dignity, or one who has been managing her own image throughout.

essayQuestions.question: What does the play gain from being written in so many short scenes?
essayQuestions.focus: Structure, pace and political space
plan: Count the shape: forty-two scenes, thirteen of them in Act III, some under twenty lines.
Take Actium as the case study — four scenes, no fighting shown, the disaster delivered by witnesses.
Show how juxtaposition does the arguing: a Roman judgement is answered by the next Egyptian scene before the audience can settle it.
Consider the cost as well as the gain, including how little sustained interiority any character is allowed.
Close on the two long scenes that break the pattern, 2.2 and 5.2, and ask why those are the ones given room.

essayQuestions.question: 'The tragedy of Enobarbus.' How useful is that description of the play?
essayQuestions.focus: Loyalty, judgement and the cost of being right
plan: Establish his function: prose, asides, jokes and the running assessment of his own commander.
Trace his reasoning from 3.13, where honesty and he begin to square, to the decision itself.
Set Antony's response — sending the treasure after him — against the logic that produced the desertion.
Read 4.9 closely: he asks the world to record him in two words and offers no defence.
Decide whether his death is a sub-plot, a commentary on the main action, or the play's clearest verdict on measuring loyalty by prospects.

discussionQuestions: Almost every major event reaches us as a report. Does that make the play sceptical, or simply realistic about how politics works?
Caesar is given no soliloquy at all. What does Shakespeare gain by keeping the winner's mind closed to us?
Antony's death takes two scenes and goes wrong; Cleopatra's is quick and beautifully staged. What is the play saying by the contrast?
Cleopatra fears a squeaking boy actor more than she fears dying. What does that tell us about what she thinks is at stake?
Is Octavia a character or an instrument? Does the play notice the difference?

timeline.label: The battle of Actium
timeline.detail: Octavian's fleet defeats Antony and Cleopatra off the western coast of Greece. Shakespeare keeps the sea-fight offstage and stages the reaction to it instead.

timeline.label: The deaths of Antony and Cleopatra
timeline.detail: Alexandria falls to Octavian, and within the year both are dead. Plutarch's account of the manner of Cleopatra's death is the source Shakespeare follows most closely.

timeline.label: North's translation of Plutarch published
timeline.detail: Thomas North's English Plutarch, made from Amyot's French, gives Shakespeare both his narrative and some of his phrasing.

timeline.label: Mary Sidney's Antonius printed
timeline.detail: A translation of Robert Garnier's French tragedy, and part of an English fashion for closet drama about the Egyptian queen.

timeline.label: Samuel Daniel's Cleopatra published
timeline.detail: Written as a companion to Mary Sidney's play, and evidence that the subject was already established before Shakespeare took it up.

timeline.label: Julius Caesar first performed
timeline.detail: Antony's oration over the body belongs to the same Plutarchan material, seven or eight years earlier in Shakespeare's career.

timeline.label: Antony and Cleopatra most likely written
timeline.detail: Usually dated 1606–07, between King Lear and Coriolanus.

timeline.label: Entered in the Stationers' Register
timeline.detail: The entry records an intention to print that produced no surviving quarto.

timeline.label: First Folio
timeline.detail: The only early text, printed among the tragedies with no act or scene divisions of the kind modern editions supply.

timeline.label: Dryden's All for Love published
timeline.detail: A rewriting of the story in neoclassical form, keeping the unities Shakespeare ignores; it held the stage for well over a century.

places.name: Alexandria
places.note: Cleopatra's palace and the monument in which both lovers die.

places.name: Rome
places.note: Caesar's house, the triumvirs' quarrel and the marriage to Octavia.

places.name: Actium
places.note: The sea battle of Act III, fought offstage and reported by two officers watching from the shore.

places.name: Misenum
places.note: Where the triumvirs come to terms with Pompey and then get drunk on his galley.

places.name: Athens
places.note: Antony and Octavia's household, and the scene in which the treaty begins to fail.

places.name: Tarsus
places.note: On the river Cydnus, where Enobarbus places the barge and the first meeting.

related.why: The same Plutarch and the same Antony, seven years earlier and considerably more in control of a crowd.
Shakespeare's other late Roman play from North, and the opposite temperament: a man who cannot perform at all.
Written within a year or two, and the contrast is instructive: one tragedy of terrible speed, one of enormous distances.
The other play in which lovers die by their own hands in a monument, but at the beginning of a career and with none of the politics.
Rome and a queen again, in the late mode where the tragic material is allowed to turn out otherwise.

books.title: As You Like It
books.author: William Shakespeare
books.setting: A usurped French dukedom and the Forest of Arden, where the exiles have set up a court without a court's powers
books.lengthNote: Around 2,700 lines, a large part of them in prose
books.openingLine: As I remember, Adam, it was upon this fashion bequeathed me by will but poor a thousand crowns
books.summary: Two women leave a court where one of them is about to be killed, walk into a wood and stay there for three acts. Rosalind, in a young man's clothes, meets the man who is writing poems about her and offers to cure him of love by playing the part of herself. Almost nothing happens in Arden except talking, which is exactly the point: the play is about what people become when the machinery of rank stops holding them in place.

sourceText.label: Globe/Moby text of As You Like It
sourceText.note: Line numbers follow the traditional Globe numbering. Much of the play is prose, and prose line numbers vary widely between editions.

structure.label: Act I
structure.title: Two brothers, two dukes, and the road out
structure.summary: Orlando has been kept as a servant by the brother who was told to educate him, and wins a wrestling match he was meant to lose. Duke Frederick, who has already usurped his own brother, turns on Rosalind for being her father's daughter, and the two cousins leave together with the court fool and a plan involving a doublet and hose.

scenes.title: The orchard
scenes.summary: Orlando complains that his brother keeps him worse than the horses, and Oliver arranges for the wrestler to break his neck.

scenes.title: The wrestling
scenes.summary: Rosalind and Celia try to talk the challenger out of it, Orlando wins, and Rosalind gives him a chain and no explanation.

scenes.title: Banishment
scenes.summary: Frederick exiles Rosalind on ten days' notice; Celia decides to go too, and Rosalind decides to go as a man.

structure.label: Act II
structure.title: Arden, on arrival
structure.summary: The forest is introduced twice over: once by the old duke, who finds sermons in stones, and once by a cold, hungry fool who observes that he was better off at home. Orlando arrives starving with an old servant on his back, draws his sword on a banquet, and is fed. Jaques delivers the seven ages to a stage that immediately contradicts him.

scenes.title: Co-mates and brothers in exile
scenes.summary: Duke Senior praises the woods and then proposes to go and kill deer, which Jaques has already objected to on their behalf.

scenes.title: The search
scenes.summary: Frederick discovers his daughter gone and blames Orlando's brother for it.

scenes.title: Adam's savings
scenes.summary: The old servant warns Orlando that Oliver means to burn his lodging, and offers him his own life's wages.

scenes.title: Weary legs
scenes.summary: The travellers reach Arden exhausted, overhear a shepherd in love, and buy a cottage and a flock.

scenes.title: Under the greenwood tree
scenes.summary: Amiens sings; Jaques supplies a verse of his own calling everyone who came here an ass.

scenes.title: Adam faints
scenes.summary: Orlando carries the old man to shelter and goes to find food.

scenes.title: The seven ages
scenes.summary: Jaques reports his meeting with a motley fool and delivers the great set piece, just as Orlando carries Adam in.

structure.label: Act III
structure.title: Poems on trees, and a cure for love
structure.summary: Orlando covers the forest with bad verses, Touchstone improves them by parody, and Rosalind — safely male — offers to cure him by making him woo a Ganymede who will play Rosalind. Meanwhile Touchstone courts a goatherd, Corin explains what a shepherd actually does all day, and Phebe falls for the wrong person.

scenes.title: Frederick's ultimatum
scenes.summary: Oliver is stripped of his lands and sent to find his brother or lose everything.

scenes.title: The bad poems
scenes.summary: Touchstone parodies Orlando's verses, Corin and Touchstone debate court and country, and Ganymede proposes the cure.

scenes.title: Touchstone and Audrey
scenes.summary: The fool arranges a marriage under a bush with a hedge-priest and is talked out of it by Jaques.

scenes.title: Waiting for Orlando
scenes.summary: Rosalind is furious that a lover can be late; Corin offers a pageant of scorn to watch.

scenes.title: Phebe and Silvius
scenes.summary: Ganymede tells the shepherdess to take the offer she has, and she falls in love with him on the spot.

structure.label: Act IV
structure.title: The lessons
structure.summary: The centre of the play is two long conversations in which a woman pretending to be a man pretending to be herself teaches the man who loves her what love is likely to be like once it is domestic. Then a bloodied handkerchief arrives, the brother who came to kill Orlando has been rescued by him, and the disguise starts to cost something.

scenes.title: Come, woo me
scenes.summary: Rosalind disposes of dying for love, marries Orlando in a mock ceremony and promises to be jealous as a Barbary cock-pigeon.

scenes.title: The deer
scenes.summary: A hunting song, sung by the men who were criticised for hunting in 2.1.

scenes.title: The bloody napkin
scenes.summary: Oliver brings the handkerchief and the story of the lioness; Ganymede faints and then claims it was counterfeited.

structure.label: Act V
structure.title: Everything settled in one scene
structure.summary: Four couples, one god of marriage and a conversion offstage: the play gathers every thread at once and knows how implausible it is being. Jaques declines the dance, Duke Frederick meets a religious man on the edge of the wood and gives back a dukedom, and Rosalind steps out of the play to ask for applause in a woman's clothes and a boy actor's body.

scenes.title: William
scenes.summary: Touchstone frightens off a rival suitor with a list of ways to kill him.

scenes.title: And so am I for no woman
scenes.summary: Oliver and Celia fall in love at sight; four voices build a formal round on the same refrain.

scenes.title: It was a lover and his lass
scenes.summary: Two pages sing to Touchstone and Audrey, who thinks little of the tune.

scenes.title: Hymen
scenes.summary: Rosalind returns as herself, four marriages are made, news arrives of Frederick's conversion, and Jaques leaves for a cave.

characters.name: Rosalind
characters.role: Daughter of the banished duke; in the forest, Ganymede
characters.summary: She has more lines than any other woman in Shakespeare and uses most of them to conduct her own courtship from behind a disguise. The wit is not decoration: playing Ganymede playing Rosalind lets her ask Orlando the questions a betrothed woman could not, and hear the answers before she commits.
characters.clue: She takes a boy's name and a boar-spear, and then teaches the man who loves her to woo a version of herself she can correct as he goes.

characters.name: Orlando
characters.role: Youngest son of Sir Rowland de Boys
characters.summary: Kept unschooled by his brother and still, in his own account, unable to explain why. He is brave, courteous and a genuinely terrible poet, and the play is fond of him without pretending he is clever; his best moment is drawing a sword on strangers to get food for an old servant.
characters.clue: He wins a wrestling match he was supposed to lose, hangs his verses on every tree in the wood, and is taught to court his own fiancée by a boy he does not recognise.

characters.name: Celia
characters.role: Duke Frederick's daughter; in the forest, Aliena
characters.summary: She gives up a dukedom for a cousin without a moment's discussion, which is the most decisive act anyone performs in the play. As the disguise takes over she is edged out of the dialogue, and her dry interruptions in Acts III and IV are the closest the play comes to noticing the cost.
characters.clue: She is the usurper's daughter and leaves with the usurped one, buys a cottage under a false name, and falls in love in the time it takes to read a letter.

characters.name: Touchstone
characters.role: The court fool, who follows the cousins into exile
characters.summary: He is the first character to say plainly that the forest is cold and the food is poor, and he spends the play testing pastoral sentiment against what things actually cost. His marriage to Audrey is the one in the final scene that nobody pretends will last.
characters.clue: A touchstone tests gold; this one tests shepherds, courtiers and poets, and takes a goatherd for a wife because nobody else will.

characters.name: Jaques
characters.role: A lord attending the banished duke
characters.summary: He has attached himself to the exiles in order to have something to be sad about, and he is the only person in the play who is not in love, in service or in danger. The seven ages speech is superb and immediately disproved on stage by the entrance of an old man being carried by a young one.
characters.clue: He weeps for a wounded deer, envies a fool his coat, will not dance at the end, and leaves for a cave because converts are more interesting than brides.

characters.name: Duke Senior
characters.role: The banished duke, Rosalind's father
characters.summary: He runs a court in the woods with all the ceremony and none of the power, and his first speech is an argument that the cold is honest. Whether this is philosophy or a way of making exile bearable is a question the play leaves open, and Jaques is there to keep asking it.
characters.clue: He finds books in brooks and sermons in stones, and proposes a deer hunt four lines later.

characters.name: Duke Frederick
characters.role: The usurping duke, Celia's father
characters.summary: He banishes his niece because she is well liked, which is the only reason he gives and probably the true one. He never sets foot in Arden: the play sends him to its edge, has him meet a religious man, and converts him offstage in a single reported sentence.
characters.clue: He took his brother's dukedom, exiles a young woman for being popular, and gives everything back after a conversation nobody in the play witnesses.

characters.name: Oliver
characters.role: Orlando's eldest brother
characters.summary: He admits in his first scene that he hates his brother for being better liked and cannot say why. His rescue from a lioness and his conversion take place offstage and are reported by himself, which asks a good deal of an audience — and is exactly the kind of demand the last act keeps making.
characters.clue: He plots his brother's death by wrestler and by fire, and is saved by that brother from a snake and a lioness in the same morning.

characters.name: Corin
characters.role: An old shepherd
characters.summary: He is the one person in the forest who works there, and he answers a courtier's philosophical needling with a list of things he knows: rain wets, fire burns, good pasture makes fat sheep. His account of being a hired man on another's land keeps the pastoral honest.
characters.clue: He cannot offer hospitality because the flock is not his, and his philosophy is entirely made of things he has had to learn on a hillside.

characters.name: Phebe
characters.role: A shepherdess
characters.summary: She refuses Silvius in the language of a Petrarchan mistress and then falls for a boy who has just told her she is nothing special. Her instant love at the sight of Ganymede is the play's demonstration that the conventions it laughs at are also how people actually behave.
characters.clue: She has been told her eyes cannot kill, disproves nothing, and writes a love letter to a young man who is a woman.

themes.name: Pastoral, and the work in it
themes.canonicalName: Pastoral, and the work in it
themes.summary: The forest is introduced as freedom from flattery and immediately shown to contain cold, hunger and wage labour. Shakespeare keeps a real shepherd on stage throughout — one who does not own his flock and cannot offer hospitality — so that the idyll can never quite close over.
themes.development: Duke Senior's praise in 2.1 is answered within twenty lines by Touchstone's arrival, and again in 2.4 by Corin's explanation of who owns the sheep.

themes.name: Disguise and gender
themes.summary: Rosalind's doublet and hose are a practical measure that turns into a method: as Ganymede she can teach, tease and interrogate a man she is engaged to marry. The layering was doubled in the original playhouse, where a boy played a woman playing a young man playing a woman.
themes.development: Adopted for safety in 1.3, used as a tool in 3.2 and 4.1, and beginning to fail in 4.3, when she faints at the sight of blood and has to claim she counterfeited it.

themes.name: Love and its conventions
themes.summary: The play sets four courtships side by side — Rosalind and Orlando, Silvius and Phebe, Touchstone and Audrey, Oliver and Celia — and lets each expose the others. Rosalind's cure is a course in the difference between the poetry of love and the twenty years that follow it.
themes.development: Verses on trees in 3.2, a demolition of dying for love in 4.1, and a formal round in 5.2 in which four people say the same thing and mean four different things.

themes.name: Court and exile
themes.summary: Two brothers have usurped two other brothers, and both crimes are motivated by nothing more explicable than dislike of someone better liked. The forest is not an alternative political order; it is a place where people wait, and the play returns them all to the court it criticised.
themes.development: Usurpation stated in 1.1 and 1.2, a parallel court assembled in 2.1, and in 5.4 a restoration announced by a messenger rather than won.

themes.name: Time
themes.summary: There is no urgency in Arden at all, and the play makes that its subject: Touchstone's dial marks ripening and rotting in the same sentence, Rosalind lectures a stranger on how differently time moves for different people, and Jaques turns a life into seven scenes and an exit.
themes.development: A fool's dial in 2.7, the seven ages in the same scene, and Rosalind's divers paces in 3.2 — three separate accounts of time within one act of each other.

themes.name: Melancholy and folly
themes.summary: Jaques and Touchstone are the play's two professionals: one is paid to be foolish and is frequently wise, the other is sad by choice and frequently ridiculous. Between them they supply a running commentary that the lovers neither hear nor need.
themes.development: Jaques wants the fool's coat in 2.7, catalogues his own sadness in 4.1, and in 5.4 leaves the wedding for a cave.

techniques.name: Prose as a medium of thought
techniques.canonicalName: Prose as a medium of thought
techniques.definition: Unmetred speech used for argument, wit and social flexibility rather than for low comedy.
techniques.bookDefinition: Unmetred speech used for argument, wit and social flexibility rather than for low comedy.
techniques.inThisBook: Rosalind conducts the courtship almost entirely in prose while Orlando writes verse at her, and the play's intelligence is largely on the prose side of that divide.

techniques.name: Disguise and dramatic irony
techniques.definition: A concealed identity that lets the audience hear two conversations at once.
techniques.bookDefinition: A concealed identity that lets the audience hear two conversations at once.
techniques.inThisBook: Every exchange between Orlando and Ganymede is double: he is practising, she is being courted, and only the audience is in both scenes at the same time.

techniques.name: Song
techniques.definition: A sung passage standing outside the dialogue, free to say what the speaking characters cannot.
techniques.bookDefinition: Lyric set into the action, marking time or supplying a mood the dialogue withholds.
techniques.inThisBook: There are more songs here than in any other Shakespeare comedy, and Jaques attaches a mocking verse to one of them — the play will not let even its music go unexamined.

techniques.name: The formal set piece
techniques.definition: A self-contained episode built to a single effect and complete in itself, whether comic or ceremonial.
techniques.bookDefinition: A self-contained speech that pauses the action to survey a subject.
techniques.inThisBook: Duke Senior on adversity, Jaques on the seven ages and Rosalind on the paces of time are all detachable, and all are answered by the stage business around them.

techniques.name: Pastoral convention
techniques.definition: The inherited literary world of shepherds, scornful shepherdesses and lovesick swains.
techniques.bookDefinition: The inherited literary world of shepherds, scornful shepherdesses and lovesick swains.
techniques.inThisBook: Silvius and Phebe are the convention played straight, Corin is what a shepherd is actually like, and Touchstone stands between them totalling up the difference.

techniques.name: Metatheatre
techniques.definition: The play stepping outside itself to address the audience directly.
techniques.bookDefinition: The play stepping outside itself to address the audience directly.
techniques.inThisBook: Rosalind ends the play by noting that a lady epilogue is unusual and then offering to kiss the men in the audience if she were a woman — which, in 1599, she was not.

quotations.text: and--in my heart Lie there what hidden woman's fear there will-- We'll have a swashing and a martial outside, As many other mannish cowards have That do outface it with their semblances.
quotations.speaker: Rosalind
quotations.context: Planning the disguise with Celia, in the hour after her banishment.
quotations.analysis: She describes manhood as a costume other men are also wearing, which turns her disguise into a general observation rather than a deception. 'Outface it with their semblances' is a courtier's phrase about courtiers, and it arrives before she has entered the wood — the play's scepticism about performed identity is in place from the start.

quotations.text: I'll have no worse a name than Jove's own page; And therefore look you call me Ganymede.
quotations.speaker: Rosalind
quotations.context: Choosing a name for the disguise, immediately after Celia asks what to call her.
quotations.analysis: Ganymede is the boy Jove carried off, and by 1599 the name was ordinary slang for a young male favourite — so Rosalind picks the most charged alias available and the play never explains it. Celia's answering choice, Aliena, simply means the estranged one, which makes the pair a comment on each other.

quotations.text: Sweet are the uses of adversity, Which, like the toad, ugly and venomous, Wears yet a precious jewel in his head;
quotations.speaker: Duke Senior
quotations.context: His first speech, to the lords who have followed him into exile.
quotations.analysis: The toadstone was a piece of folklore that had been doubted for a century, so the consolation rests on an example the audience may not believe. That is characteristic of him: the speech is beautiful, sincere and delivered by a man who will propose killing deer for dinner six lines later.

quotations.text: And this our life exempt from public haunt Finds tongues in trees, books in the running brooks, Sermons in stones and good in every thing.
quotations.speaker: Duke Senior
quotations.context: The end of the same speech.
quotations.analysis: Each clause puts a court accomplishment into a natural object — speech, learning, preaching — so the forest is praised for being a better version of what he has lost. The last phrase, 'good in every thing', is exactly the kind of generalisation the rest of the play spends five acts testing.

quotations.text: Ay, now am I in Arden; the more fool I; when I was at home, I was in a better place: but travellers must be content.
quotations.speaker: Touchstone
quotations.context: The moment the three exiles arrive in the forest, exhausted.
quotations.analysis: This is the first thing said about Arden by somebody who has just walked there, and it flatly contradicts the speech the audience heard two scenes ago. 'Travellers must be content' is a proverb used as a shrug, and the prose rhythm — three short clauses and a resigned fourth — is the opposite of the duke's expansive verse.

quotations.text: And so, from hour to hour, we ripe and ripe, And then, from hour to hour, we rot and rot; And thereby hangs a tale.
quotations.speaker: Jaques
quotations.context: Quoting the fool he met in the forest, to the duke and his lords.
quotations.analysis: Jaques is reporting Touchstone, so the play's bleakest formulation reaches us at second hand from a professional joker. The repeated verbs make growth and decay the same mechanical process, and the tag at the end — 'thereby hangs a tale' — refuses to draw any moral at all.

quotations.text: All the world's a stage, And all the men and women merely players: They have their exits and their entrances; And one man in his time plays many parts, His acts being seven ages.
quotations.speaker: Jaques
quotations.context: Picking up the duke's remark that their misery is only one scene in a universal theatre.
quotations.analysis: The speech is not Jaques's idea: the duke has just used the theatre image and Jaques takes it off him and runs. 'Merely' means entirely, not slightly, and the seven parts that follow are all masculine and all solitary — there is no scene in his account in which two people are together.

quotations.text: Last scene of all, That ends this strange eventful history, Is second childishness and mere oblivion, Sans teeth, sans eyes, sans taste, sans everything.
quotations.speaker: Jaques
quotations.context: The end of the seven ages, as Orlando carries the starving Adam onto the stage.
quotations.analysis: The staging answers the speech: Jaques finishes describing old age as an empty room and an actual old man is carried in and fed. Four repetitions of 'sans' — a French word in an English line — strip the sentence down as they go, and 'everything' arrives where a noun should be.

quotations.text: Blow, blow, thou winter wind. Thou art not so unkind As man's ingratitude; Thy tooth is not so keen, Because thou art not seen, Although thy breath be rude.
quotations.speaker: Amiens
quotations.context: Sung at the duke's table while Orlando and Adam eat.
quotations.analysis: The song makes the argument of the whole forest in six lines: weather is cruel but impersonal, and therefore easier to bear than people. 'Because thou art not seen' is the hinge — the wind has no face to be hurt by, which is precisely what Orlando and Adam have just escaped from at home.

quotations.text: Truly, shepherd, in respect of itself, it is a good life, but in respect that it is a shepherd's life, it is naught. In respect that it is solitary, I like it very well; but in respect that it is private, it is a very vile life.
quotations.speaker: Touchstone
quotations.context: Answering Corin's polite question about how he likes the shepherd's life.
quotations.analysis: Six clauses, each cancelling the last, and the joke is that the form is a parody of scholastic argument aimed at a man who has never been to school. It also happens to be a fair description of pastoral itself — charming in the abstract, poor in the particular.

quotations.text: the property of rain is to wet and fire to burn; that good pasture makes fat sheep, and that a great cause of the night is lack of the sun
quotations.speaker: Corin
quotations.context: Asked by Touchstone whether he has any philosophy in him.
quotations.analysis: Every item is something he has had to know in order to keep animals alive, and the list is funny only if you assume knowledge should look like something else. Touchstone's reply — that a man who has never been at court is damned — is the play's sharpest joke at the expense of the courtly position it keeps testing.

quotations.text: Do you not know I am a woman? when I think, I must speak.
quotations.speaker: Rosalind
quotations.context: To Celia, while dressed as Ganymede and desperate for news of Orlando.
quotations.analysis: She is wearing a doublet and hose and claiming a woman's licence to talk, which is the disguise's whole comedy in one sentence. The line is also a conventional joke about women's speech, put in the mouth of the character who has more lines than any other woman Shakespeare wrote.

quotations.text: Love is merely a madness, and, I tell you, deserves as well a dark house and a whip as madmen do: and the reason why they are not so punished and cured is, that the lunacy is so ordinary that the whippers are in love too.
quotations.speaker: Rosalind
quotations.context: Setting up the offer to cure Orlando of his love.
quotations.analysis: The dark house and the whip were the real treatment for madness in 1599, so the joke has a cold floor under it. The turn comes in the last clause: the reason nobody is treated is that everybody, including the people who would do the whipping, has the disease — which makes love a condition of the whole society rather than a fault in a lover.

quotations.text: Dead Shepherd, now I find thy saw of might, 'Who ever loved that loved not at first sight?'
quotations.speaker: Phebe
quotations.context: Alone with Silvius, after Ganymede has told her to take the offer she has.
quotations.analysis: The quotation is Marlowe's, from Hero and Leander, and the 'dead shepherd' is Marlowe himself, killed six years before — the only such tribute in Shakespeare. Phebe uses a borrowed line to describe a feeling she is convinced is original, which is the play's method for handling love poetry throughout.

quotations.text: it is a melancholy of mine own, compounded of many simples, extracted from many objects, and indeed the sundry's contemplation of my travels
quotations.speaker: Jaques
quotations.context: Explaining to Rosalind why his sadness is not like anyone else's.
quotations.analysis: The vocabulary is a pharmacist's — simples, compounded, extracted — so he presents his own temperament as a recipe he has made up himself. Rosalind's reply prices it exactly: a traveller who has sold his lands to see other men's has rich eyes and poor hands.

quotations.text: But these are all lies: men have died from time to time and worms have eaten them, but not for love.
quotations.speaker: Rosalind
quotations.context: Ending a survey of Troilus and Leander, after Orlando has said he will die if refused.
quotations.analysis: She has just spent ten lines rewriting two famous love-deaths as a club to the head and an attack of cramp, and the summary sentence is flat, unornamented and final. The word 'worms' does the work: it puts the plain physical fact where the literature was, and it is spoken by someone who is very much in love.

quotations.text: men are April when they woo, December when they wed: maids are May when they are maids, but the sky changes when they are wives.
quotations.speaker: Rosalind
quotations.context: Answering Orlando's 'For ever and a day' during the mock marriage.
quotations.analysis: The warning is aimed at both parties, which is what makes it more than a joke about husbands. She then promises to be jealous as a cock-pigeon and to weep for nothing, so the prediction includes herself — she is letting him see the whole marriage before he agrees to it.

quotations.text: And so am I for no woman.
quotations.speaker: Rosalind
quotations.context: The fourth voice in a formal round in which Silvius, Phebe and Orlando each declare what love is made of.
quotations.analysis: Three lovers name the person they want and the fourth, who wants somebody present, has to answer with a negative. Repeated three times over twenty lines, the refrain turns the disguise into a liturgy, and Rosalind ends the sequence by comparing the whole performance to Irish wolves howling at the moon.

quotations.text: a poor virgin, sir, an ill-favoured thing, sir, but mine own; a poor humour of mine, sir, to take that that no man else will
quotations.speaker: Touchstone
quotations.context: Presenting Audrey to the duke among the couples about to be married.
quotations.analysis: Four uses of 'poor' in one sentence, and the woman is introduced as a bargain nobody else bid for. It is the only marriage in the last scene described in terms of what it costs, and Shakespeare puts it directly before Hymen arrives to bless the rest.

quotations.text: You to your former honour I bequeath; Your patience and your virtue well deserves it
quotations.speaker: Jaques
quotations.context: Leaving the wedding party to join the converted Duke Frederick.
quotations.analysis: He distributes futures to each couple in turn, like a man reading a will, and keeps nothing for himself. 'I am for other than for dancing measures,' he says a few lines later, and the play lets him go — a comedy that ends with one guest walking out is making a claim about what its settlement does not cover.

quotations.text: It is not the fashion to see the lady the epilogue; but it is no more unhandsome than to see the lord the prologue. If it be true that good wine needs no bush, 'tis true that a good play needs no epilogue
quotations.speaker: Rosalind
quotations.context: Alone on stage after the dance, speaking the epilogue.
quotations.analysis: A bush of ivy was the sign hung outside a tavern, so the proverb means that quality advertises itself — and she is standing there advertising. The epilogue's first move is to point out that a woman is not supposed to be doing this, which prepares the ground for the last joke about what she is underneath.

quotations.text: If I were a woman I would kiss as many of you as had beards that pleased me, complexions that liked me and breaths that I defied not
quotations.speaker: Rosalind
quotations.context: The last sentence but one of the play.
quotations.analysis: The conditional is the joke and the point: the actor speaking has been a woman for three hours and a boy all along, and the play chooses its final line to say so out loud. Having spent five acts arguing that identity is something performed, it closes by handing the evidence to the audience.

atAGlance.label: Written
atAGlance.note: The same year as Henry V and Julius Caesar, and the year the Globe opened on Bankside.

atAGlance.label: First printed
atAGlance.note: No quarto. The play was entered in the Stationers' Register in 1600 with a note staying publication.

atAGlance.label: Chief source
atAGlance.note: Thomas Lodge's prose romance of 1590, which supplies the plot; Touchstone, Jaques and Audrey are Shakespeare's additions.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.note: Every scene after 2.3 but two takes place in the forest, and the plot stops moving for most of Acts III and IV.

criticalViews.position: A pastoral that argues with pastoral
criticalViews.summary: The forest is offered as an alternative to the court and then furnished with cold, hunger, wage labour and an old shepherd who cannot afford hospitality. On this reading the play's real subject is the distance between the literary countryside and the economic one.
criticalViews.counter: It risks making the play sound sour, when Arden also plainly works: three of the four couples are made there and a usurper is converted on its edge.

criticalViews.position: A play about gender as performance
criticalViews.summary: Rosalind's layered disguise — and the boy actor beneath it — has made the play central to criticism interested in how far masculinity and femininity are things done rather than things possessed.
criticalViews.counter: The play still ends in four marriages presided over by a god, and Rosalind hands herself to a father and a husband in successive lines.

criticalViews.position: The comedy of talk
criticalViews.summary: Almost nothing happens in Acts III and IV; what the play offers instead is conversation, and criticism has long treated its structure as a deliberate suspension of plot in favour of argument, song and wit.
criticalViews.counter: The suspension is paid for in the last act, where two conversions and a lioness have to be reported rather than shown.

criticalViews.position: Jaques as the play's dissenting voice
criticalViews.summary: A long tradition reads Jaques as the character who keeps the comedy honest — the one who weeps for the deer, doubts the songs and refuses the dance.
criticalViews.counter: The play also treats him as a pose: Rosalind prices his travels in a sentence, and his great speech is contradicted by the stage as he finishes it.

essayQuestions.question: How does Shakespeare use the Forest of Arden?
essayQuestions.focus: Pastoral, labour and the limits of the green world
plan: Set Duke Senior's praise in 2.1 against Touchstone's arrival in 2.4 and read them as a deliberate pair.
Use Corin throughout as the play's control: he works there, he does not own the flock, and his philosophy is entirely practical.
Examine what the forest actually permits — disguise, argument, courtship — and what it does not change.
Consider the weather: the songs about ingratitude and winter wind are sung by people who are cold.
Conclude on the ending, which returns almost everybody to the court and sends the two dissenters into a cave and a religious life.

essayQuestions.question: Discuss the presentation of Rosalind.
essayQuestions.focus: Disguise, control and the epilogue
plan: Begin with 1.3: the disguise is adopted for safety and immediately theorised as something men also wear.
Show how Ganymede converts a passive position into an active one — she can question Orlando as no betrothed woman could.
Analyse the two great prose scenes, 3.2 and 4.1, as a syllabus on the difference between love poetry and marriage.
Use 4.3, where she faints at blood and has to claim she counterfeited it, as the point where the costume starts to cost.
Close on the epilogue and the boy actor, and ask what the play is claiming about identity as it lets the audience go.

essayQuestions.question: What does the play gain from Jaques and Touchstone, neither of whom is in Lodge?
essayQuestions.focus: Commentary, folly and the play's own scepticism
plan: Establish that both are Shakespeare's additions, and that neither is required by the plot.
Read 2.7 as their joint scene: Jaques envying the fool's licence and then taking a set piece for himself.
Set Touchstone's economic exactness against Jaques's cultivated sadness, and note who the play lets be right.
Examine the marriages: one refuses to take place, the other is presented as a poor bargain.
Decide whether they undermine the comedy or make its optimism worth having.

essayQuestions.question: 'A play in which nothing happens.' How far is that a fair description, and is it a criticism?
essayQuestions.focus: Structure, prose and the suspension of plot
plan: Chart the plot: it is all but finished by the end of Act II and does not resume until 4.3.
Show what fills the gap — courtship lessons, debates, songs, set pieces — and why prose is the medium for it.
Look at how much the last act has to do offstage: a lioness, two conversions, a restored dukedom.
Compare the play's use of time with Jaques's seven ages and Rosalind's divers paces: the form is about duration.
Argue a conclusion about what a comedy is for, if not for events.

discussionQuestions: Duke Senior says the woods are freer from peril than the court. Does the play agree with him?
Rosalind does far more of the courting than Orlando. Why does she keep the disguise on for so long after the danger has passed?
Celia gives up a dukedom in a single scene and then gradually stops speaking. What has happened to her?
Touchstone's marriage is the one nobody expects to last. Why does Shakespeare put it in the middle of the final celebration?
Duke Frederick is converted by a man we never meet, offstage, in one reported sentence. Is that a weakness or a joke?

timeline.label: Lodge's Rosalynde published
timeline.detail: The prose romance that supplies almost all of the plot, including the wrestling, the disguise and the shepherds.

timeline.label: Christopher Marlowe killed at Deptford
timeline.detail: Phebe's 'Dead Shepherd' in 3.5 is the play's direct salute to him, and the line she quotes is his.

timeline.label: Marlowe's Hero and Leander published
timeline.detail: The poem Phebe quotes, and the source of the play's one open tribute to another writer.

timeline.label: The Globe opens on Bankside
timeline.detail: The theatre for which the play was almost certainly written, and the setting of the joke behind 'All the world's a stage'.

timeline.label: As You Like It most likely written
timeline.detail: Usually dated to 1599 or early 1600, close to Henry V and Julius Caesar.

timeline.label: Entered in the Stationers' Register
timeline.detail: The entry orders publication to be stayed, and no quarto ever appeared.

timeline.label: First Folio
timeline.detail: The only early text, printed among the comedies.

timeline.label: Restored to the London stage
timeline.detail: After long neglect the play returned to the repertory at Drury Lane, and Rosalind became one of the great parts for an actress.

timeline.label: Paul Czinner's film
timeline.detail: With Elisabeth Bergner as Rosalind and Laurence Olivier as Orlando; the first sound film of the play.

timeline.label: All-male production at the National Theatre
timeline.detail: Directed by Clifford Williams, it revived the Elizabethan casting convention and reopened the argument about what the disguise means.

places.name: Forest of Arden, Warwickshire
places.note: The wooded country north of Stratford, and the English name behind the play's forest.

places.name: The Ardennes
places.note: Lodge sets his romance in France; the play keeps the French court and lets the two Ardens overlap.

places.name: Stratford-upon-Avon
places.note: Shakespeare's mother was Mary Arden, from a family of the Warwickshire woodland.

places.name: The Globe, Bankside
places.note: Opened in 1599, and the likely first home of the play and of the seven-ages speech.

places.name: Deptford
places.note: Where Marlowe, the play's dead shepherd, was killed in 1593.

related.why: The other great disguise comedy, written within a year or two, with a woman in men's clothes and a considerably colder ending.
The same period and the same interest in couples who argue their way towards each other in prose.
The earlier wood outside the city, where love is rearranged by magic rather than by conversation.
A later island of exiles, usurped dukes and restored dukedoms, with the forgiveness made much harder to give.
Shakespeare's other comedy of talk, where wit is the entire action and the ending refuses to complete the marriages.

books.title: The Call of the Wild
books.author: Jack London
books.setting: The Santa Clara Valley in California, then the Klondike trail from Dyea over the Chilkoot Pass to Dawson and beyond
books.written: 1902, after London’s winter in the Yukon
books.lengthNote: Seven chapters, about 32,000 words — short enough to be read at a sitting, and built to be
books.openingLine: Buck did not read the newspapers, or he would have known that trouble was brewing, not alone for himself, but for every tidewater dog, strong of muscle and with warm, long hair, from Puget Sound to San Diego.
books.summary: A gardener’s helper with gambling debts sells a judge’s dog to the Klondike trade, and Buck is carried north into a labour market that values him by the pound. London writes the change that follows as an education rather than a liberation: the club teaches law, the traces teach work, and every step towards the wolves is paid for in hunger, frostbite and the deaths of other dogs. The book is told from inside an animal that cannot explain itself, which is why its conclusions have to be shown in behaviour rather than argued.

sourceText.label: Standard Ebooks text of The Call of the Wild
sourceText.note: The seven chapters are numbered I to VII and carry titles in the text; they are cited here by Arabic numeral.

structure.label: Chapter 1
structure.title: Into the Primitive
structure.summary: Buck is stolen from Judge Miller’s estate, crated, starved, and beaten into submission by a man with a club. The chapter turns a domestic animal into freight, and the beating is presented as a lesson rather than an outrage: he learns that a man with a club is to be obeyed, and never forgets it.

structure.label: Chapter 2
structure.title: The Law of Club and Fang
structure.summary: Curly is killed in two minutes on the Dyea beach, and Buck understands the rule of the place before anyone states it. He learns to sleep under the snow, to steal food without being caught and to pull in harness, and London is careful to record each of these as a loss as well as a skill.

structure.label: Chapter 3
structure.title: The Dominant Primordial Beast
structure.summary: The rivalry with Spitz turns into open war over a nest in the snow, and Buck begins undermining the lead dog’s authority by protecting the shirkers. The rabbit hunt ends in the fight that kills Spitz, and Buck wins it with cunning rather than weight.

structure.label: Chapter 4
structure.title: Who Has Won to Mastership
structure.summary: Buck takes the lead by refusing any other place in the team and drives it harder than Spitz ever did. The record run to Skagway is followed by the death of Dave, who cannot bear to be taken out of the traces, and by the sale of the whole team to men who know nothing.

structure.label: Chapter 5
structure.title: The Toil of Trace and Trail
structure.summary: Hal, Charles and Mercedes load too much, feed too much, then feed nothing, and beat dogs that can no longer stand. The chapter is the book’s clearest statement that cruelty in the North is usually incompetence, and it ends with the ice giving way beneath the sled Buck has been cut out of.

structure.label: Chapter 6
structure.title: For the Love of a Man
structure.summary: John Thornton nurses Buck back to strength and receives the only love Buck has ever given. The thousand-pound wager at Dawson turns that love into a public spectacle, and Buck’s rescues of Thornton show devotion working as an instinct faster than obedience.

structure.label: Chapter 7
structure.title: The Sounding of the Call
structure.summary: In the unmapped East, Buck hunts a bull moose for days and runs with a timber wolf, returning to camp each time because Thornton is there. The Yeehats kill Thornton, Buck kills the Yeehats, and the last tie to man is cut by other men.

characters.name: Buck
characters.role: A St Bernard and Scotch shepherd cross, latterly a sled dog
characters.summary: He begins as a well-fed aristocrat on a Californian estate and ends at the head of a wolf pack, and London insists that nothing in between is sudden. Each stage is a piece of learning under pressure — the club, the snow nest, the stolen bacon, the fight with Spitz — so that the wildest thing he does is also the best-trained.
characters.clue: Stolen from a judge’s lawn and sold by the pound, this one learns to sleep under snow, steal without being seen and lead a team, and finishes as a story the Yeehats tell about a valley they will not enter.

characters.name: Spitz
characters.role: Lead dog of the mail team
characters.summary: A Spitzbergen dog with an experienced sense of where power lies and a habit of laughing with his tongue out as he kills. He is not a villain so much as an incumbent, and the book gives him the same qualities it admires in Buck, minus imagination.
characters.clue: A snow-white incumbent who runs out his scarlet tongue in a way he has of laughing, and who is beaten at last by a trick he cannot see coming twice.

characters.name: John Thornton
characters.role: A prospector with frozen feet, later Buck’s master
characters.summary: He is the only man in the book who treats dogs as company rather than plant, and the book rewards him with a devotion so absolute it becomes dangerous to him. His death is arranged so that Buck loses him to other men rather than to the wild, which keeps the ending from being a simple choice.
characters.clue: Left behind with frozen feet to mend, he cuts a dying dog out of the traces with two strokes of a knife and never afterwards has to give that dog an order twice.

characters.name: Perrault and François
characters.role: Government couriers driving the mail team
characters.summary: Hard employers who know ice, pace and dogs, and who are set in the book as a standard against which later owners fail. They work Buck to the edge of his strength and are the only handlers who never waste him, which the novel counts as a kind of decency.
characters.clue: A French-Canadian courier and his halfbreed driver, in a hurry with government despatches, who judge ice by looking at it and are proud of a record run.
traits: fair by the standards of the trail

characters.name: The man in the red sweater
characters.role: A dog-breaker in Seattle
characters.summary: He appears for one chapter, hits Buck until Buck stops rising, and is then described as almost fair. The book needs him to state its first principle in a form that cannot be argued with, and gives him no name, no history and no cruelty beyond the professional.
characters.clue: He greets each crated arrival with a hatchet and a club, breaks it, feeds it, and sells it on at three hundred dollars a head, government money.

characters.name: Hal and Charles
characters.role: Gold-rush newcomers who buy the team
characters.summary: A young man with a Colt’s revolver and a hunting-knife and a middle-aged one with watering eyes, neither of whom can pack a sled or count a ration. Their failure is arithmetical before it is moral, and London lets the arithmetic do the condemning.
characters.clue: One wears a revolver and a bowie knife on a belt that bristles with cartridges; the other sits down very slowly on a log; between them they buy fourteen dogs and food for far fewer.

characters.name: Mercedes
characters.role: Charles’s wife and Hal’s sister
characters.summary: She weeps over the dogs while riding on the sled they are dragging, and her kindness is one of the book’s most exact pieces of cruelty. London uses her to show that sentiment about animals and knowledge of them are different things, and that in the North the difference kills.
characters.clue: She pleads for the dogs, hides food for them, throws her arms round the neck of one of them, and then weighs one hundred and twenty pounds on the load they cannot move.

characters.name: Dave
characters.role: Wheel dog
characters.summary: A morose animal who cares about nothing except the sled behind him, and who fights to be put back in harness when he is dying of an internal injury. His death is the book’s clearest statement that work can be an identity rather than an imposition.
characters.clue: Taken out of the traces to rest, this one staggers alongside the team, bites its way back into place, and is finally granted the dignity of a shot in the timber.

characters.name: Curly
characters.role: A good-natured Newfoundland
characters.summary: She makes an advance towards a husky in the way a Southland dog would, and is dead two minutes later with forty dogs looking on. Her death is the whole of the book’s argument compressed into one page, and Buck remembers it for the rest of the novel.
characters.clue: Friendly in the manner of a warmer country, she goes down once on the Dyea beach and never gets up, and the manner of it comes back to a watching dog at night for years.

themes.name: Club, fang and the making of law
themes.canonicalName: Club, fang and the making of law
themes.summary: The book’s laws are not agreed but demonstrated: a club teaches obedience, a pack teaches that a dog who goes down does not get up, and a lead dog holds rank only while he can hold it. London never calls this justice, but he does call it law, and the distinction is the novel’s hardest idea.
themes.development: Stated in the beating of Chapter 1, named in the title of Chapter 2, tested in the fight with Spitz, and finally turned against human beings in Chapter 7, where Buck kills men and feels pride rather than guilt.

themes.name: Trace, trail and the day’s haul
themes.summary: Everything in the North is measured in loads, miles and rations, and the novel keeps the figures in front of the reader: sixty miles in a day, a pound and a half of dried salmon, a thousand pounds of flour frozen to the snow. Buck's education is a working life, and the book's admiration for competence is as strong as its interest in instinct.
themes.development: Buck first finds that he does not despise the harness; Dave dies rather than leave it; and in Chapter 6 the same strength is put to a wager, which is work turned into entertainment.

themes.name: Owners, and what a dog is worth
themes.canonicalName: Owners, and what a dog is worth
themes.summary: Buck passes through the hands of a judge, a gardener’s helper, a saloon keeper, a dog-breaker, two couriers, a Scotch halfbreed, three incompetents and finally a man who does not think of him as property at all. Each transfer has a price attached, and the novel’s last move is to remove him from the market entirely.
themes.development: Theft in California, three hundred dollars in Seattle, a government sale at Skagway, a hopeless purchase at Dawson, and then Thornton, whose claim is never written down and who is killed by other men before it can be tested.

themes.name: Adaptation and the fit
themes.summary: London’s naturalism is practical rather than theoretical: the dog who learns to steal survives, the dog who keeps his Southland manners dies on the beach, and morality is treated as a luxury good that the climate cannot support. The book presents this as observation, and its confidence is one of the things modern readers argue with.
themes.development: Curly's death sets the terms, the first theft marks Buck as fit, and by Chapter 7 he is described as a creature in full flower — the same vocabulary applied to a killer rather than a survivor.

themes.name: The call, and ancestral memory
themes.summary: Beside the trail material runs a stranger book, in which Buck dreams of a hairy man beside a fire and hears something in the forest that has no object. London gives this the language of inheritance rather than of longing, so that going wild reads as recall rather than escape.
themes.development: First a half-memory by the campfire, then the wolf brother in Chapter 7, then a period of alternation in which the call and Thornton hold him equally, and finally the pack.

themes.name: Love for one man
themes.summary: The bond with Thornton is the only relationship in the novel that is not a transaction, and it is written as a physical habit — the hand taken in the jaws, the head rested on a knee, the watch kept from a distance.
