It is also the last thing standing between Buck and the forest, which is why the book has to kill it.
themes.development: Rescue in Chapter 5, convalescence and games in Chapter 6, the rapids and the wager, and then a pool in a mining camp from which no trace leads away.

techniques.name: The animal point of view
techniques.definition: Narration tied to the perceptions of a creature that cannot use language, so that thought has to be shown as sensation, memory and behaviour.
techniques.bookDefinition: Narration tied to the perceptions of a creature that cannot use language, so that thought has to be shown as sensation, memory and behaviour.
techniques.inThisBook: Buck understands the sale of a team as money passing between men, and the narrator regularly marks the limit — 'Not that Buck reasoned it out' — to keep him an animal while granting him an inner life.

techniques.name: The North as pressure
techniques.definition: Place and weather made to press on the people living in them, rather than serving as scenery.
techniques.bookDefinition: Using terrain, weather and scale to exert force on the characters rather than to decorate them.
techniques.inThisBook: Sixty below, thin fall ice, the Chilcoot Divide and a trail that has to be broken with webbed shoes are not scenery: they set the ration, the pace and the odds on any given dog living out the month.

techniques.name: Grand diction for animal experience
techniques.definition: Deliberately heightened, Latinate vocabulary applied to creatures and events that would ordinarily be described plainly.
techniques.bookDefinition: Deliberately heightened, Latinate vocabulary applied to creatures and events that would ordinarily be described plainly.
techniques.inThisBook: 'The dominant primordial beast', 'the articulate travail of existence', 'the inexorable elimination of the superfluous' — London writes a dog fight in the language of evolutionary science and epic at once.

techniques.name: The returning phrase
techniques.definition: A phrase brought back at intervals, so that its meaning shifts with what has happened since.
techniques.bookDefinition: A phrase repeated at intervals so that its meaning changes with each context.
techniques.inThisBook: 'The law of club and fang' arrives as a description of savages, becomes an excuse for theft, then a rule Buck enforces, and finally the standard he breaks by killing men.

techniques.name: Dialect
techniques.definition: Spelling and grammar used to mark where a speaker comes from, and what being heard that way costs them.
techniques.bookDefinition: Regional speech written phonetically.
techniques.inThisBook: François is given a thick phonetic French-Canadian English — 'Dat Buck two devils' — which sets the drivers' speech apart from a narrator who has the whole vocabulary of Victorian science at his disposal.

techniques.name: Objects that carry the argument
techniques.definition: An object the narrative keeps returning to until it stands for the argument rather than illustrating it.
techniques.bookDefinition: Things in the narrative that carry a meaning the characters half-register.
techniques.inThisBook: The club, the traces, the thousand-pound sled and the moosehide sack of gold are all ordinary equipment, and each one measures exactly how much of Buck belongs to somebody.

quotations.text: Buck did not read the newspapers, or he would have known that trouble was brewing, not alone for himself, but for every tidewater dog, strong of muscle and with warm, long hair, from Puget Sound to San Diego.
quotations.context: The novel’s opening sentence.
quotations.analysis: The joke about newspapers grants Buck ignorance rather than stupidity, and the sentence then does the reading for him: the danger is a market, described by geography and by coat length. Before the story starts, the reader has been told that what happens to Buck happens to a class of animals, which is why the book keeps count of other dogs.

quotations.text: He was beaten (he knew that); but he was not broken.
quotations.context: After the man in the red sweater has clubbed Buck to the ground for the last time.
quotations.analysis: The bracket is the sentence’s whole method: knowledge is separated from feeling and filed away, which is how Buck will meet everything from here on. Note the passive verbs — things are done to him in this chapter, and the first active thing he does with the lesson is remember it.

quotations.text: That club was a revelation. It was his introduction to the reign of primitive law, and he met the introduction halfway.
quotations.context: Buck, still unable to stand, watching the man who has beaten him.
quotations.analysis: 'Revelation', 'reign' and 'introduction' are the vocabulary of religion and of polite society, applied to a beating with a stick. 'Halfway' is the disturbing word: the novel is claiming that Buck consents to the arrangement, and that the consent is what makes him fit for the North.

quotations.text: They were savages, all of them, who knew no law but the law of club and fang.
quotations.context: Buck’s first day on the Dyea beach.
quotations.analysis: The sentence puts dogs and men in a single category, which is the book’s recurring move and the source of most of the trouble modern readers have with it. It also gives the chapter its title before any incident has proved the point — the proof arrives thirty lines later, when Curly goes down.

quotations.text: It marked, further, the decay or going to pieces of his moral nature, a vain thing and a handicap in the ruthless struggle for existence.
quotations.context: After Buck steals a chunk of bacon from Perrault’s supplies — the first theft of his life.
quotations.analysis: Two appraisals sit in one sentence: 'decay' and 'going to pieces' condemn the change, while 'a vain thing and a handicap' approves of it. The double vocabulary is the naturalist position in miniature, and the novel never resolves it — it simply stops using moral words once Buck has stopped needing them.

quotations.text: Not that Buck reasoned it out. He was fit, that was all, and unconsciously he accommodated himself to the new mode of life.
quotations.context: Immediately after the narrator has explained the theft in the language of Southland law and Northland necessity.
quotations.analysis: The narrator withdraws the argument he has just made from the character who prompted it, which is how London keeps a thinking dog from becoming a talking one. 'Fit' is doing technical work here: it belongs to the vocabulary of natural selection, not of praise.

quotations.text: The dominant primordial beast was strong in Buck, and under the fierce conditions of trail life it grew and grew. Yet it was a secret growth.
quotations.context: The opening of the chapter that ends with Spitz’s death.
quotations.analysis: The grammar makes the beast the subject and Buck the location, which is the book’s way of describing character as something inherited rather than chosen. 'Secret' matters for the plot: Buck spends the chapter avoiding fights precisely because he intends to win the only one that counts.

quotations.text: There is an ecstasy that marks the summit of life, and beyond which life cannot rise.
quotations.context: Buck leading the pack after a snowshoe rabbit in the moonlight.
quotations.analysis: The narrator steps away from the dog entirely here and makes a claim about artists and soldiers before returning to Buck, which is how the hunt is raised to the level of a general law. It is also the closest the novel comes to admitting that the wild is being sold to the reader as a pleasure.

quotations.text: There was no hope for him. Buck was inexorable. Mercy was a thing reserved for gentler climes.
quotations.context: Spitz on three legs, with the circle of huskies waiting to close in.
quotations.analysis: Three short sentences in place of the long periodic ones that surround them: the prose contracts at exactly the moment the killing begins. 'Climes' turns mercy into a matter of latitude rather than character, which excuses Buck and indicts the whole geography instead.

quotations.text: He fought by instinct, but he could fight by head as well.
quotations.context: The decisive moment of the fight with Spitz, as Buck breaks his forelegs one after the other.
quotations.analysis: The novel has spent two chapters arguing that instinct is what survives, and then awards the fight to calculation. Whatever the narrator says about primordial beasts, Buck wins because he does the same feint twice and the other dog cannot adapt.

quotations.text: For the pride of trace and trail was his, and, sick unto death, he could not bear that another dog should do his work.
quotations.context: Dave, dying of an internal injury, fighting to be put back in the harness he has been taken out of to rest.
quotations.analysis: 'Sick unto death' is biblical diction spent on a sled dog, and the effect is to take his preference seriously rather than to make it pathetic. The scene also states the book’s most unexpected proposition: that the harness can be an identity, so that removing it is the injury.

quotations.text: “Undreamed of!” cried Mercedes, throwing up her hands in dainty dismay. “However in the world could I manage without a tent?”
quotations.speaker: Mercedes
quotations.context: A bystander at Dawson has suggested that the party travel without a tent.
quotations.analysis: Her objection is grammatically about management and actually about self-image, and the book lets the word 'dainty' do the damage. The line belongs to the drawing room, which is the point: everything the three newcomers say is imported, and the North charges them freight on it.

quotations.text: And so it went, the inexorable elimination of the superfluous.
quotations.context: Mercedes’s clothes-bags being emptied onto the snow as the load is cut down.
quotations.analysis: The phrase is lifted from evolutionary argument and applied to luggage, and the comedy of that is exact: the same principle will shortly be applied to the dogs and then to the people. London rarely tells the reader a system is at work; here he names one and lets it run through three paragraphs of packing.

quotations.text: Love, genuine passionate love, was his for the first time.
quotations.context: Buck convalescing in John Thornton’s camp after being cut out of Hal’s traces.
quotations.analysis: The sentence is placed after a page of games and roughhousing rather than before it, so the claim is made to rest on evidence. It also quietly disposes of the Santa Clara Valley: the judge’s household gave Buck dignity, partnership and stewardship, and the book counts none of that as love.

quotations.text: “As you love me, Buck. As you love me,” was what he whispered.
quotations.speaker: John Thornton
quotations.context: Before Buck attempts to start a thousand-pound load frozen to the snow at Dawson.
quotations.analysis: Thornton does not give a command, and the repetition turns the wager into a request between equals. The sentence is also a confession that he has staked another creature’s body on a bar-room boast, which the crowd’s cheering afterwards does nothing to settle.

quotations.text: “Pooh! pooh!” said John Thornton; “Buck can start a thousand pounds.”
quotations.speaker: John Thornton
quotations.context: In the Eldorado Saloon, among men arguing about what their dogs can pull.
quotations.analysis: The boast is made in the grammar of the saloon, and the narrative immediately records that Thornton did not know whether it was true and had no money to back it. What follows is the one episode in the novel where Buck’s strength is converted directly into cash, and it is the humans who arrange the sale.

quotations.text: And closely akin to the visions of the hairy man was the call still sounding in the depths of the forest.
quotations.context: In camp during the long summer in the unmapped country east of Dawson.
quotations.analysis: The call is introduced as a relative of the dreams rather than as a voice, which keeps it inside Buck’s nervous system and out of the supernatural. Note that it has no content: London never says what it asks for, only that Buck goes looking for it as though it were a tangible thing.

quotations.text: He was a killer, a thing that preyed, living on the things that lived, unaided, alone, by virtue of his own strength and prowess, surviving triumphantly in a hostile environment where only the strong survived.
quotations.context: After Buck has hunted and killed a great bull moose over four days.
quotations.analysis: The clauses pile up without a main verb after the first, so the sentence performs the swelling pride it describes. 'A thing that preyed' also removes the personal pronoun for a moment: the book’s most individual dog is being described, briefly, as a category of animal.

quotations.text: He had killed man, the noblest game of all, and he had killed in the face of the law of club and fang.
quotations.context: Buck among the bodies of the Yeehats, after Thornton’s death.
quotations.analysis: The phrase 'the law of club and fang' has travelled a long way: it began as a description of what men and dogs on the beach knew, and is now the thing Buck has successfully broken. 'Game' is the cruellest word in the book — it places human beings in the category of animals hunted for sport, exactly reversing the trade that opened the story.

quotations.text: John Thornton was dead. The last tie was broken. Man and the claims of man no longer bound him.
quotations.context: By the pool in the ruined camp, as the wolf pack comes down the valley under a full moon.
quotations.analysis: Three flat statements, the shortest sentences in the chapter, and all of them about other people’s claims rather than Buck’s desires. The novel has been careful never to let him choose the wild over Thornton: the tie is cut by the Yeehats, so the ending is a release rather than a preference.

quotations.text: But more remarkable than this, the Yeehats tell of a Ghost Dog that runs at the head of the pack.
quotations.context: The closing pages, years after the events of the story.
quotations.analysis: The narration hands the ending over to the people Buck has been killing, so that the last account of him is hearsay from his victims. It is also the moment the book stops being naturalism: a dog whose every action has been explained by environment and inheritance leaves the record as a legend.

quotations.text: he may be seen running at the head of the pack through the pale moonlight or glimmering borealis, leaping gigantic above his fellows, his great throat a-bellow as he sings a song of the younger world, which is the song of the pack.
quotations.context: The last sentence of the novel.
quotations.analysis: The song was introduced in Chapter 3 as the huskies’ nightly wail, 'the pleading of life' pitched in a minor key; here the same phrase returns with Buck leading it. The tense has also changed to habitual present, which lifts him out of the story’s chronology and into something that keeps happening.

quotations.text: Old longings nomadic leap, Chafing at custom’s chain; Again from its brumal sleep Wakens the ferine strain.
quotations.context: The verse epigraph printed before the first chapter, from John Myers O’Hara’s poem ‘Atavism’.
quotations.analysis: Four lines that give the whole plot away and supply its vocabulary: longing, custom, sleep and strain. 'Brumal' and 'ferine' are dictionary words for winter and wildness, and their stiffness is useful — the book will argue that what wakes in Buck is a technical inheritance rather than a romantic urge.

atAGlance.label: First published
atAGlance.note: Serialised in five instalments in The Saturday Evening Post before Macmillan issued the book.

atAGlance.label: Written from
atAGlance.note: London went north in 1897 and came back with almost no gold and the whole of his Northland material.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.note: Three of them are named for a law, a beast and a toil; only the last is named for the call.

atAGlance.label: Point of view
atAGlance.note: Buck is given memory, calculation and dream, but never speech and never a human sentence of his own.

criticalViews.position: The book as naturalism
criticalViews.summary: The standard reading takes London at his word: heredity and environment do the work, morality is a local luxury, and Buck’s progress is a demonstration that the fit survive. The novel supplies its own technical vocabulary for this, from adaptation to the elimination of the superfluous.
criticalViews.counter: The fight with Spitz is won by a feint rather than by strength, and Dave dies for something that looks very like pride, so the machinery keeps producing characters.

criticalViews.position: The book as a labour story
criticalViews.summary: Read from the harness rather than the forest, the novel is about work: ownership, rations, overloading, the difference between a hard employer and an ignorant one, and a body that is bought and sold by weight. London had been a labourer and an oyster pirate before he was a writer, and the trail sections are written by someone who has costed a day’s work.
criticalViews.counter: It has to explain away the ending, in which the worker does not organise or escape but leaves the species.

criticalViews.position: The book’s evolutionary language and its politics
criticalViews.summary: Criticism since the later twentieth century has examined how readily the novel moves between dogs, 'savages' and named peoples, and how its talk of breed and strain belongs to a period vocabulary of racial hierarchy. The Yeehats in the final chapter are the clearest test case.
criticalViews.counter: The same vocabulary is used of white gold-seekers, who are eliminated by the North with no more ceremony than anybody else.

criticalViews.position: The question of the animal mind
criticalViews.summary: London was accused of granting his animals reasoning they could not have, and he answered that Buck acts on association and inference rather than thought. The dispute is still the most useful way into the book’s narrative method, because it asks exactly what a sentence like 'Not that Buck reasoned it out' is doing.
criticalViews.counter: The dream of the hairy man beside a fire is inheritance, not inference, and no account of animal psychology explains it.

essayQuestions.question: Is Buck’s change a liberation or a training?
essayQuestions.focus: Instinct, learning and the shape of the plot
plan: Start with the club in Chapter 1: the first thing that happens to Buck is instruction, and he is said to meet it halfway.
Trace the skills in Chapter 2 — the snow nest, the stolen bacon, the harness — and note that each is described as both a gain and a loss.
Use the fight with Spitz to complicate the instinct case: the decisive move is a repeated feint, and the narrator calls it imagination.
Weigh the dreams of the hairy man and the call, which are inherited rather than learned, and which use a different vocabulary.
Close on the last chapter: the tie to Thornton is cut by the Yeehats, so the wild is something Buck is released into rather than something he chooses.

essayQuestions.question: How does London use human beings in a novel about a dog?
essayQuestions.focus: Owners, handlers and the moral scale of the book
plan: Set out the sequence of owners as a series of transactions, from Manuel’s gambling debts to the Government sale at Skagway.
Contrast Perrault and François with Hal, Charles and Mercedes: competence against sentiment, and what each costs the dogs.
Examine Mercedes closely — her pity for the team and her hundred and twenty pounds on the sled — as the book’s definition of useless kindness.
Read Thornton as the exception who proves the rule, since his claim on Buck is the only one never expressed in money.
Conclude with the Yeehats and the killing of men, and ask what the novel has done to the category of the human by that point.

essayQuestions.question: Discuss London’s narrative voice and the problem of telling a story from inside an animal.
essayQuestions.focus: Focalisation, diction and the limits the narrator sets
plan: Identify the two registers: plain trail reporting with figures and distances, and heightened evolutionary diction.
Collect the narrator’s corrections — 'Not that Buck reasoned it out' — and ask what work they do for a reader who has just been given Buck’s reasoning.
Show how sensation replaces speech: the smell of fat earth, the frost in the fur, the feel of a hand on the head.
Consider the moments the narrator leaves Buck entirely, such as the passage on ecstasy, and what is gained and lost there.
End with the final chapter's change of tense and source, where Buck becomes a story told by the Yeehats.

essayQuestions.question: ‘A book about work, not about wilderness.’ How far do you agree?
essayQuestions.focus: Labour, ownership and the economics of the trail
plan: Gather the novel’s measurements: rations, loads, mileage, sixty below, a thousand pounds of flour frozen to the runners.
Use Dave’s death to show work as an identity rather than an imposition, and Buck’s first day in harness as consent to it.
Read the wager at Dawson as the moment labour becomes spectacle and a dog’s strength is paid for in gold dust.
Set against this the three chapters of dream, call and hunting, which use no economic language at all.
Decide whether the ending cancels the working book or completes it by removing Buck from the market.

discussionQuestions: The man in the red sweater is described as fair by the standards of his trade. Does the novel agree with him?
Mercedes is the only character who consistently pities the dogs, and she does them the most harm. What is the book arguing?
Why does London kill John Thornton rather than let Buck leave him?
Buck kills men and feels pride. Is the reader meant to share it, resist it, or simply observe it?
The last page hands the story to the Yeehats. What changes when a naturalist novel ends in legend?

timeline.label: Jack London born in San Francisco
timeline.detail: Born John Griffith Chaney; he took the surname of his stepfather, John London.

timeline.label: Gold found on a tributary of the Klondike
timeline.detail: The strike that emptied the Pacific ports of strong dogs the following summer.

timeline.label: London travels north to the Klondike
timeline.detail: He went in over the Chilkoot route in the first season of the stampede and wintered in the Yukon.

timeline.label: London returns to California
timeline.detail: He came back with almost no gold and with the material for the Northland stories that made his name.

timeline.label: The Call of the Wild serialised and published
timeline.detail: Five instalments in The Saturday Evening Post, then the Macmillan book, in a green pictorial binding with colour plates.

timeline.label: The argument about animal minds reaches the magazines
timeline.detail: Naturalists began attacking popular animal stories for granting their subjects human reasoning — a charge London would later answer directly.

timeline.label: White Fang published
timeline.detail: London called it a companion piece, reversing the journey: a wild dog brought into domestication.

timeline.label: London dies at Glen Ellen, California
timeline.detail: He was forty, and one of the first American writers to have made a large income from fiction alone.

timeline.label: First feature film adaptation
timeline.detail: Produced by Hal Roach and directed by Fred Jackman, beginning a century of screen versions.

timeline.label: William A. Wellman’s film with Clark Gable
timeline.detail: The studio version enlarges Thornton and adds a romance, a pattern most later adaptations follow.

timeline.label: Chris Sanders’s film with a digital Buck
timeline.detail: The animal is computer-generated throughout, which changes what a performance by Buck can be.

places.name: Santa Clara Valley, California
places.note: Judge Miller’s place, with its cement swimming tank and its Mexican hairless — the sun-kissed Southland Buck is stolen from.

places.name: Seattle
places.note: Where the crate is opened with a hatchet and the man in the red sweater sells dogs on at three hundred dollars a head.

places.name: Dyea, Alaska
places.note: The beach where Curly is killed within hours of landing; the town itself was abandoned within a few years of the rush.

places.name: Chilkoot Pass
places.note: The climb the team makes on its first day out, and the reason strong dogs were worth stealing in California.

places.name: Lake Laberge
places.note: Lake Le Barge in the novel, where Buck first fights Spitz over a nest dug in the snow.

places.name: Dawson City
places.note: The end of the mail run, the saloon where the thousand-pound wager is made, and the last town before the unmapped East.

related.why: London’s deliberate counterpart, running the journey the other way: a wild-born dog brought into a house.
The same American naturalism applied to a boy under fire, with instinct and cowardice measured just as coldly.
Crane’s men in an indifferent sea, where survival is again a matter of conditions rather than deserving.
The other great American book about an animal, and about what men need it to mean.
Published five years later and the opposite experiment: animals given speech, manners and houses rather than instinct.

books.title: Coriolanus
books.author: William Shakespeare
books.setting: Rome in the first years of the Republic, with the Volscian towns of Corioli and Antium
books.lengthNote: Around 3,750 lines in the Globe text, among the longest of the tragedies
books.openingLine: Before we proceed any further, hear me speak.
books.summary: A city short of grain makes a soldier its hero and then asks him to stand in the marketplace, show his scars and ask for votes. He can take a walled town almost single-handed and cannot say a civil sentence to a citizen, so Rome banishes him and he brings the enemy back to its gates. The play gives the crowd real arguments, gives the hero none worth having, and then hands the ending to his mother.

sourceText.label: Globe/Moby text of Coriolanus
sourceText.note: Line numbers follow the traditional Globe numbering. The only early text is the First Folio, which carries unusually detailed stage directions.

structure.label: Act I
structure.title: A grain riot, and a war that solves it
structure.summary: Citizens with clubs come out over the price of corn and are answered with a fable about a belly. Marcius insults them, the senate grants them tribunes anyway, and then a Volscian war conveniently arrives. He takes Corioli almost alone, is renamed for the city he captured, and refuses his share of the spoils.

scenes.title: Corn at our own price
scenes.summary: The citizens rise over grain; Menenius tells the fable of the belly; Marcius arrives and calls them scabs.

scenes.title: Corioli
scenes.summary: Aufidius learns that Rome knows his plans and says he wants Marcius in the field.

scenes.title: The women at home
scenes.summary: Volumnia rejoices in her son's wounds; Virgilia will not leave the house until he returns.

scenes.title: The gates
scenes.summary: Marcius curses his own retreating soldiers and is shut inside the town alone.

scenes.title: Inside the walls
scenes.summary: Romans loot while Marcius, still bleeding, goes to find Cominius.

scenes.title: Make you a sword of me
scenes.summary: He asks for volunteers and is taken up in the arms of the whole army.

scenes.title: A garrison left
scenes.summary: Lartius secures Corioli and follows to the field.

scenes.title: Marcius and Aufidius
scenes.summary: The two meet in single combat and are parted by Volscian soldiers.

scenes.title: The name
scenes.summary: He refuses the tenth of the spoils, is hailed Coriolanus, and forgets the name of a poor host he wanted pardoned.

scenes.title: Aufidius vows
scenes.summary: Beaten five times, Aufidius says he will have Marcius by any means, honourable or not.

structure.label: Act II
structure.title: The gown of humility
structure.summary: Rome welcomes him back with a noise that frightens the tribunes, and the senate offers the consulship. Custom requires him to stand in the Forum in a plain gown, show his wounds and ask each citizen for a voice. He gets the votes by sneering through the ceremony, and the tribunes go to work on the men who gave them.

scenes.title: The return
scenes.summary: Menenius baits the tribunes; Volumnia counts her son's wounds before he arrives.

scenes.title: The Capitol
scenes.summary: Cominius reports his deeds while Coriolanus walks out rather than hear them praised.

scenes.title: The Forum
scenes.summary: He asks for voices, receives them, and the tribunes persuade the citizens to take them back.

structure.label: Act III
structure.title: Banished
structure.summary: Told his election is revoked, he says in public what the patricians say in private: that giving the people a share in power will destroy the state. The tribunes call it treason and stage a trial. Volumnia persuades him to go and apologise; he lasts a few lines before the word 'traitor' undoes the performance, and Rome expels him.

scenes.title: The street
scenes.summary: Coriolanus argues for abolishing the tribunate and is nearly seized on the spot.

scenes.title: His mother's instruction
scenes.summary: Volumnia teaches him how to perform humility; he agrees to try.

scenes.title: The Forum again
scenes.summary: Provoked by the charge of treason, he curses the city and banishes it from himself.

structure.label: Act IV
structure.title: A world elsewhere
structure.summary: He parts from his family at the gate with unexpected gentleness, and walks to Antium in disguise to offer his throat to his oldest enemy. Aufidius embraces him, gives him half the army, and then watches his own officers begin to prefer the newcomer. The Volscian force moves on Rome and the tribunes discover what they have arranged.

scenes.title: The parting
scenes.summary: He comforts his mother and wife at the city gate and leaves alone.

scenes.title: Anger's my meat
scenes.summary: Volumnia meets the tribunes in the street and curses them with an appetite of her own.

scenes.title: A road
scenes.summary: A Roman spy and a Volscian exchange news of the banishment and the mobilisation.

scenes.title: Antium
scenes.summary: Disguised outside Aufidius's house, he reflects on how quickly friends turn enemies.

scenes.title: The offer
scenes.summary: He names himself, offers his throat, and is given half the Volscian command.

scenes.title: Rome hears
scenes.summary: The tribunes are congratulating themselves on a quiet city when the news arrives.

scenes.title: Aufidius reconsiders
scenes.summary: His lieutenant reports that the soldiers now follow Coriolanus; Aufidius begins to plan.

structure.label: Act V
structure.title: The silence, and what follows it
structure.summary: Cominius and Menenius are sent to plead and are turned away. Then his mother, wife and son come, and Volumnia argues, kneels and finally stops. He takes her hand and says nothing for as long as the scene will hold, then grants the peace and tells her what it will cost him. Aufidius kills him in Corioli, over a name.

scenes.title: Menenius is persuaded to go
scenes.summary: Cominius reports that Coriolanus would not answer to his own name.

scenes.title: The sentry
scenes.summary: Menenius is refused at the guard post and sent back to Rome.

scenes.title: The embassy of women
scenes.summary: Volumnia, Virgilia and Young Marcius kneel; he holds her hand, silent, and yields.

scenes.title: Rome waits
scenes.summary: Menenius describes a man grown from grub to dragon; the city hears the news and goes out to meet Volumnia.

scenes.title: The mother welcomed
scenes.summary: Rome honours the women as its deliverers.

scenes.title: Corioli
scenes.summary: Aufidius calls him boy and traitor; the conspirators kill him, and then carry the body out with honour.

characters.name: Caius Marcius Coriolanus
characters.role: A Roman patrician and general, named for the city he captured
characters.summary: He is superb at the one thing Rome no longer principally needs and incapable of the thing it now requires. His refusal to display his wounds or ask for votes is usually read as pride, but it is also a refusal to let his body be turned into an argument, which is the only consistent principle he has.
characters.clue: He takes a walled town almost single-handed, and cannot get through a five-minute conversation with the men whose votes he needs.
traits: unable to be flattered or to flatter

relationships.label: son of
relationships.note: She made him, tells him so, and uses the fact twice.

characters.name: Volumnia
characters.role: Coriolanus's mother
characters.summary: She built him: she says she sent him to a cruel war when he was still a boy and would rather have eleven sons die nobly than one live idly. She is also the best politician in the play, and the one person who understands that the Forum requires acting — which is why her final speech works and destroys him at the same time.
characters.clue: She would rather see her son's forehead bleeding than a trophy gilded, and she teaches him to bow to a crowd she despises as thoroughly as he does.
traits: victorious at a price she names

characters.name: Virgilia
characters.role: Coriolanus's wife
characters.summary: She is the play's other kind of attachment: where Volumnia counts wounds, Virgilia refuses to leave the house until her husband is home and cannot bear the word blood. Her husband calls her his gracious silence, and in 5.3 she speaks eleven words that reach him before any of his mother's rhetoric does.
characters.clue: She will not cross her own threshold while her husband is at the war, and her tears succeed where an argument has not.

characters.name: Menenius Agrippa
characters.role: A patrician, and Coriolanus's oldest friend in Rome
characters.summary: He handles the crowd with jokes and a fable about the belly, which is the most sophisticated piece of political management in the play and also a way of telling hungry men that the distribution is natural. His confidence that the general will listen to him is the play's cruellest small humiliation.
characters.clue: He answers a riot about the price of grain with a story about the stomach and the other parts of the body.

characters.name: Tullus Aufidius
characters.role: General of the Volscians
characters.summary: He is the only man in the play who values Coriolanus at his own valuation, which is why exile takes him to Antium rather than anywhere else. The embrace in 4.5 is in the language of a wedding night, and by 4.7 he is already calculating how to be rid of a guest who has taken his army's affection.
characters.clue: He dreams of his enemy, welcomes him into his house with more warmth than he showed his bride, and has him stabbed in a public place.

characters.name: Sicinius Velutus
characters.role: A tribune of the people
characters.summary: He reads a crowd the way a general reads ground, and knows that the surest way to defeat a candidate is to let him speak. His question in 3.1 — what is the city but the people? — is the clearest statement of republican principle anyone makes, and he makes it while managing a prosecution.
characters.clue: He asks what a city is if not its people, and then coaches those people on exactly when to shout.
traits: principled and manipulative in the same breath

characters.name: Junius Brutus
characters.role: A tribune of the people
characters.summary: The quieter half of the pair, and the one who does the detailed work: rehearsing the citizens on what they should have said, choosing the moment to say the word traitor. He is right that a consul who wants to abolish the tribunate is a danger to the people who elected him.
characters.clue: He tells the citizens what they ought to have replied in the Forum, then sends them back to unsay their votes.

characters.name: Cominius
characters.role: Consul and general of the Roman army
characters.summary: He gives the long report of Marcius's deeds at the Capitol, which is the only place in the play where the hero's worth is set out at length by someone who was there. In Act V he comes back from the Volscian camp with the detail that says everything: the man would not answer to his own name.
characters.clue: He praises a soldier who walks out rather than hear it, and returns from an embassy to report that the man no longer answers to any name at all.

characters.name: The Citizens of Rome
characters.role: The plebeians, who riot, vote and banish
characters.summary: Shakespeare gives them numbered voices with different opinions, so they argue with each other before anyone argues with them. They are mocked for changing their minds, and the play is careful to show exactly who worked on them each time they did.
characters.clue: They come on with clubs over the price of corn, grant a man their voices in the Forum, and take them back before the scene is over.

themes.name: Hunger and the distribution of grain
themes.canonicalName: Hunger and the distribution of grain
themes.summary: The play opens with men who want corn at their own price, not with an abstraction about liberty, and it never lets the political argument float free of that. Menenius answers a material complaint with a story about the body's parts working together, which is a good fable and a bad answer, and the play says so by keeping the citizens hungry.
themes.development: The riot in 1.1 is settled by the grant of tribunes; the corn arrives from Greece by 3.1, where Coriolanus objects that it was given free to men who did not earn it.

themes.name: Voices and consent
themes.summary: The word 'voices' means votes, and Coriolanus repeats it until it stops meaning anything, which is precisely his problem with it: he hears noise where the constitution hears consent. Rome's new arrangement requires the powerful to ask, and he would rather starve than crave the hire he thinks he has already earned.
themes.development: He collects voices in 2.3 with open contempt, the tribunes teach the citizens to withdraw them, and by 3.3 the same voices are a cry of curs that he claims to banish.

themes.name: The body and the body politic
themes.canonicalName: The body and the body politic
themes.summary: Rome is described as a body from the first scene, and the metaphor is never allowed to stay comfortable: a belly that hoards, a great toe that leads a rebellion, wounds that must be shown in public, scars counted by a mother at home. What the state wants from Coriolanus is his body as evidence, and that is the one thing he will not surrender.
themes.development: Menenius's fable in 1.1 is answered by the demand for wounds in 2.3, and by Volumnia in 5.3 asking him to tread on the womb that bore him.

themes.name: Mother and son
themes.summary: Volumnia states plainly that she made her son what he is, and the play offers no competing account of where his valour came from. The tragedy is not that he disobeys her but that he obeys twice: once in 3.2, when she teaches him to act, and once in 5.3, when the acting has to stop.
themes.development: She counts his wounds in 2.1, coaches him in 3.2, and in 5.3 wins the argument and, by his own statement, kills him with it.

themes.name: Names and what they cost
themes.summary: He is given a new name for a city he took and has to be told what it is; he then discovers that the name is a possession which can be used against him. By Act V he will not answer to it, and in the last scene he is killed for insisting on it in front of the men he took it from.
themes.development: He is hailed Coriolanus in 1.9, cannot recall the name of the man he wanted saved, refuses his own name in 5.1, and dies reciting the deed it commemorates in 5.6.

themes.name: Public performance and integrity
themes.summary: The gown of humility is a costume, the Forum is a stage, and everyone except Coriolanus can see that this is not a scandal but the ordinary condition of public life. His refusal to act looks like the play's only honesty, until his mother points out that he has been playing a part called 'the man I am' all along.
themes.development: He cannot perform in 2.3, agrees to try in 3.2 and fails within twenty lines in 3.3; in 5.3 he says he has forgotten his part like a dull actor, and that is when he becomes human.

techniques.name: The political fable
techniques.definition: A story told to a crowd in order to settle an argument by analogy.
techniques.bookDefinition: A story told to a crowd in order to settle an argument by analogy.
techniques.inThisBook: Menenius's belly and its rebellious members is lifted from the historical tradition, and Shakespeare stages the citizens interrupting it, so the audience sees the device being used and resisted at the same time.

techniques.name: Crowd scenes
techniques.definition: Staging a group as a set of distinct voices rather than a single mass.
techniques.bookDefinition: Staging a group as a set of distinct voices rather than a single mass.
techniques.inThisBook: The citizens are numbered, disagree with each other, and reason out loud before they act, which makes the patricians' contempt for them a claim the play can test.

techniques.name: Animal imagery
techniques.definition: Comparisons that place people on a scale from vermin to predators.
techniques.bookDefinition: Comparisons that place people on a scale from vermin to predators.
techniques.inThisBook: Curs, scabs, geese, hares, a lamb that baes like a bear, a grub that becomes a butterfly and a man who becomes a dragon: the insults define the political sides before the arguments do.

techniques.name: Imagery of the body
techniques.definition: The state described as anatomy, and anatomy treated as evidence.
techniques.bookDefinition: The state described as anatomy, and anatomy treated as evidence.
techniques.inThisBook: Wounds are counted, displayed, refused and finally invoked in 5.3, so the same body that took Corioli becomes the disputed ground of the political plot.

techniques.name: The significant stage direction
techniques.definition: A moment of action written into the text with no words attached to it.
techniques.bookDefinition: A moment of action written into the text with no words attached to it.
techniques.inThisBook: 'He holds her by the hand, silent' is the most famous direction in Shakespeare, and it gives the turning point of the tragedy to a pause rather than a speech.

techniques.name: Heroic hyperbole
techniques.definition: Deliberate overstatement, used not to deceive but to claim a scale ordinary language cannot reach.
techniques.bookDefinition: Description inflated past the plausible in order to make a man into a monument.
techniques.inThisBook: Cominius reports a soldier who entered a city alone and came out painted with blood; the play keeps the language of epic while showing us the ordinary politics it cannot survive.

quotations.text: Before we proceed any further, hear me speak.
quotations.speaker: First Citizen
quotations.context: The opening line of the play, spoken by a citizen carrying a club.
quotations.analysis: No Shakespearean tragedy begins with a commoner claiming the floor, and the claim is procedural: he is asking for order before an action, not for pity. The whole play is contained in the request, because the one thing Coriolanus will never grant the citizens is the right to be heard before anything proceeds.

quotations.text: There was a time when all the body's members Rebell'd against the belly, thus accused it: That only like a gulf it did remain I' the midst o' the body, idle and unactive, Still cupboarding the viand, never bearing Like labour with the rest,
quotations.speaker: Menenius
quotations.context: Talking a crowd of hungry men out of a riot over the price of corn.
quotations.analysis: The fable answers a complaint about hoarding by conceding the hoarding and calling it digestion. Its rhetorical trick is the opening 'There was a time', which shifts the argument out of this year's harvest into a fable where the belly's case has already been settled — and the citizens interrupt him twice to say so.

quotations.text: What's the matter, you dissentious rogues, That, rubbing the poor itch of your opinion, Make yourselves scabs?
quotations.speaker: Caius Marcius
quotations.context: His entrance, immediately after Menenius has spent a hundred lines calming the crowd.
quotations.analysis: His first words undo the fable in three lines: where Menenius made the citizens limbs of a body, he makes them a skin disease on it. 'Opinion' is treated as an itch, which is to say a physical irritation with no content, and that is precisely his view of the vote he will later have to ask for.

quotations.text: He that will give good words to thee will flatter Beneath abhorring.
quotations.speaker: Caius Marcius
quotations.context: Answering a citizen who says they have always had his good word.
quotations.analysis: He treats courtesy to an inferior as a form of lying, which is consistent and politically fatal in equal measure. The line also explains why he cannot be bought: a man who regards flattery as beneath contempt has no currency to spend in a republic that runs on it.

quotations.text: Marcius, I had rather had eleven die nobly for their country than one voluptuously surfeit out of action.
quotations.speaker: Volumnia
quotations.context: In the house, sewing with Virgilia, on the subject of sons.
quotations.analysis: The arithmetic is the shock: eleven is not a figure of speech but a rate of exchange she has evidently worked out. 'Surfeit' plants the play's other appetite — the city outside is rioting over food — so her contempt for a well-fed son runs on the same imagery as the grain crisis.

quotations.text: it more becomes a man Than gilt his trophy: the breasts of Hecuba, When she did suckle Hector, look'd not lovelier Than Hector's forehead when it spit forth blood At Grecian sword, contemning.
quotations.speaker: Volumnia
quotations.context: Virgilia has just cried out at the thought of her husband's bloody brow.
quotations.analysis: The comparison sets a nursing mother against a wounded son and decides for the wound, which tells us exactly what kind of feeding Volumnia believes in. The verb 'spit' does the work: blood is given an agency and a contempt of its own, as though the forehead were answering the Greek sword back.

quotations.text: O, me alone! make you a sword of me? If these shows be not outward, which of you But is four Volsces?
quotations.speaker: Caius Marcius
quotations.context: The soldiers take him up in their arms and throw their caps in the air.
quotations.analysis: It is the one moment where a crowd loves him and he is delighted by it, which shows that his difficulty is not with numbers of people but with what those people are entitled to ask. Being made into a weapon is the only public use of his body that he can accept.

quotations.text: Nature teaches beasts to know their friends.
quotations.speaker: Sicinius
quotations.context: Sparring with Menenius in a public place while Rome waits for the victorious army.
quotations.analysis: Menenius answers by asking who the wolf loves, and the exchange turns into a small contest over who gets to use the animal metaphors. It is worth noticing that the tribunes are given the wit to hold their own here: the play does not write them as fools, only as men with an interest.

quotations.text: Bid them wash their faces And keep their teeth clean.
quotations.speaker: Coriolanus
quotations.context: Asked what he shall say to the citizens who are coming to give him their voices.
quotations.analysis: Standing in the gown of humility, he answers a question about political speech with a note about hygiene, and the joke is directed at the audience rather than at anyone on stage. The contempt is specifically for their mouths — the parts that are about to give him what he needs.

quotations.text: Most sweet voices! Better it is to die, better to starve, Than crave the hire which first we do deserve.
quotations.speaker: Coriolanus
quotations.context: Alone in the Forum, between groups of citizens.
quotations.analysis: The sarcasm of the first phrase gives way to a rhymed couplet, and the rhyme makes it a maxim he has clearly held for a long time. 'Starve' is a reckless word to choose in this city in this month, and the citizens who riot over corn in Act I are exactly the men whose hire he is refusing to crave.

quotations.text: What custom wills, in all things should we do't, The dust on antique time would lie unswept, And mountainous error be too highly heapt For truth to o'er-peer.
quotations.speaker: Coriolanus
quotations.context: Still in the Forum, arguing himself out of completing the ceremony.
quotations.analysis: It is a genuinely radical argument — that custom preserves error — and it is being used to avoid asking poor men for their votes. The play repeatedly gives him positions that would be admirable in another mouth, which is what makes him a tragic figure rather than a snob.

quotations.text: For the mutable, rank-scented many, let them Regard me as I do not flatter, and Therein behold themselves:
quotations.speaker: Coriolanus
quotations.context: In the street, after being told his election is revoked.
quotations.analysis: He offers his own refusal to flatter as a mirror in which the people may see their own inconstancy, which is an argument and an insult in the same sentence. 'Mutable' is the charge the play half sustains: the citizens do change their minds, and we have just watched two men talk them into it.

quotations.text: What is the city but the people?
quotations.speaker: Sicinius
quotations.context: In the street riot, as the tribunes move to arrest Coriolanus.
quotations.analysis: The citizens answer 'The people are the city', and the echo turns a rhetorical question into something closer to a chant. It is the most quotable line of political theory in the play, and Shakespeare gives it to a man in the middle of organising a lynching — which is not a refutation, only a complication.

quotations.text: Why did you wish me milder? would you have me False to my nature? Rather say I play The man I am.
quotations.speaker: Coriolanus
quotations.context: His mother has just told him he should have dissembled until he had the office.
quotations.analysis: He means 'play' as an accusation and it turns into a confession: the verb concedes that even being oneself is a performance. From this point the play measures him not by whether he acts but by which part he is willing to take, and in 5.3 he will use the language of the theatre again, as a man who has forgotten his lines.

quotations.text: Action is eloquence, and the eyes of the ignorant More learned than the ears--waving thy head, Which often, thus, correcting thy stout heart,
quotations.speaker: Volumnia
quotations.context: Teaching her son how to stand and what to do with his hands in front of the people.
quotations.analysis: She is giving him a lesson in stagecraft, complete with a demonstration of the gesture, and the phrase 'the eyes of the ignorant' shows she shares his contempt entirely. The difference between mother and son is not principle but competence: she can do the thing they both despise.

quotations.text: You common cry of curs! whose breath I hate As reek o' the rotten fens, whose loves I prize As the dead carcasses of unburied men That do corrupt my air, I banish you;
quotations.speaker: Coriolanus
quotations.context: Immediately after the tribunes pronounce his banishment in the Forum.
quotations.analysis: Everything he hates is airborne — breath, reek, corrupted air — which is the same sense in which their votes are only noise to him. Reversing the sentence is magnificent and changes nothing: a man can banish a city only from himself, and the city goes on without him for two more acts.

quotations.text: There is a world elsewhere.
quotations.speaker: Coriolanus
quotations.context: His exit line from Rome.
quotations.analysis: Five words to close an act, and the only thing in the speech that turns out to be true: there is a world elsewhere, and it is Antium, and it kills him. The plainness after twenty lines of curses is what makes it land — he stops performing for exactly one line.

quotations.text: Anger's my meat; I sup upon myself, And so shall starve with feeding.
quotations.speaker: Volumnia
quotations.context: In the street, having just cursed the tribunes who banished her son.
quotations.analysis: The play's food imagery finally reaches the patrician household: where the citizens wanted corn, she eats her own rage and expects to die of the diet. It is also an exact description of what she does to her son in 5.3, where feeding on him and destroying him are the same act.

quotations.text: One fire drives out one fire; one nail, one nail; Rights by rights falter, strengths by strengths do fail.
quotations.speaker: Aufidius
quotations.context: Alone with his lieutenant, having learned that the Volscian soldiers now prefer Coriolanus.
quotations.analysis: Two proverbs and a rhymed couplet, and the effect is of a man consoling himself with common sense while deciding on a murder. The symmetry of the second line — rights against rights, strengths against strengths — makes assassination sound like a law of physics rather than a choice.

quotations.text: let the Volsces Plough Rome and harrow Italy: I'll never Be such a gosling to obey instinct, but stand, As if a man were author of himself And knew no other kin.
quotations.speaker: Coriolanus
quotations.context: Watching his mother, wife and son approach his tent, and steeling himself.
quotations.analysis: 'As if' gives him away before the sentence ends: he knows the self-authorship is a fiction he is choosing to act out. Four scenes after a mother's teaching failed to make him bow to a crowd, he is using her own vocabulary of performance to try to resist her.

quotations.text: Like a dull actor now, I have forgot my part, and I am out, Even to a full disgrace.
quotations.speaker: Coriolanus
quotations.context: Virgilia has spoken three words to him and he cannot continue.
quotations.analysis: The man who refused to act in the Forum now describes his own collapse as a failure of acting, and 'out' is the technical term for an actor who has dried. His wife does it with a greeting; his mother will need fifty lines and a kneeling child.

quotations.text: Trust to't, thou shalt not--on thy mother's womb, That brought thee to this world.
quotations.speaker: Volumnia
quotations.context: Telling him he will not reach Rome except over her body.
quotations.analysis: She makes her own body the gate of the city, which completes the play's long argument that Rome is an anatomy. Virgilia and the boy each add a line immediately afterwards, so the threat arrives as a family in sequence rather than as one woman's rhetoric.

quotations.text: O mother, mother! What have you done? Behold, the heavens do ope, The gods look down, and this unnatural scene They laugh at.
quotations.speaker: Coriolanus
quotations.context: Breaking the silence after holding his mother's hand without speaking.
quotations.analysis: The Folio's direction — he holds her by the hand, silent — gives the turn of the tragedy to a pause, and this is what comes out of it: not a decision but a question addressed to the person who made him. 'Unnatural' is the word the play has used for a son marching on his birthplace, and he now applies it to the scene of his surrender.

quotations.text: You have won a happy victory to Rome; But, for your son,--believe it, O, believe it, Most dangerously you have with him prevail'd, If not most mortal to him.
quotations.speaker: Coriolanus
quotations.context: Granting the peace his mother has come to ask for.
quotations.analysis: He states the cost accurately and in the same breath as the concession, which is why the scene is not a redemption. The repeated 'believe it' is the only time in the play he begs anyone to listen, and it is addressed to the one person who has never needed persuading of anything.

quotations.text: There is differency between a grub and a butterfly; yet your butterfly was a grub. This Marcius is grown from man to dragon: he has wings; he's more than a creeping thing.
quotations.speaker: Menenius
quotations.context: Back in Rome, telling Sicinius there is no hope of mercy.
quotations.analysis: Menenius has spent the play making people into parts of a body, and now he makes his friend into a different species altogether. The animal ladder that began with curs and scabs in 1.1 ends with a dragon, and the man himself is by this point absent from every scene that discusses him.

quotations.text: Name not the god, thou boy of tears!
quotations.speaker: Aufidius
quotations.context: In Corioli, in front of the Volscian lords, as Coriolanus swears by Mars.
quotations.analysis: Aufidius has watched him for five acts and knows the one word that will work: not traitor, which is a political charge, but boy, which is a charge about his mother. The insult is accurate, which is why it destroys him — he yielded to a woman and he knows Aufidius watched him do it.

quotations.text: Cut me to pieces, Volsces; men and lads, Stain all your edges on me. Boy! false hound! If you have writ your annals true, 'tis there, That, like an eagle in a dove-cote, I Flutter'd your Volscians in Corioli: Alone I did it. Boy!
quotations.speaker: Coriolanus
quotations.context: His last speech, to the citizens of the city he sacked.
quotations.analysis: He answers an insult about his mother by reciting the deed that gave him his name, in the city that gave it, to the survivors of it. 'Alone I did it' is the claim the play has been quietly disputing since 1.6, when an entire army picked him up and carried him — and it is the last thing he says before the conspirators move.

quotations.text: My rage is gone; And I am struck with sorrow. Take him up. Help, three o' the chiefest soldiers; I'll be one.
quotations.speaker: Aufidius
quotations.context: Standing over the body, moments after standing on it.
quotations.analysis: The reversal takes four words, and the practical instruction that follows is what makes it convincing: he stops speaking about himself and starts organising a stretcher party. Shakespeare gives the killer the last rites rather than the family, so the play's final act of tenderness comes from the enemy and not from Rome.

atAGlance.label: Written
atAGlance.note: Shakespeare's last Roman play, and probably his last tragedy.

atAGlance.label: First printed
atAGlance.note: Folio only. Its stage directions are fuller than usual, which is why the silence in 5.3 carries so much weight.

atAGlance.label: Chief source
atAGlance.note: Whole speeches are lifted from the Life of Caius Martius Coriolanus and turned into verse with minimal alteration.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.note: Act I alone has ten, most of them short: the battle for Corioli is cut like a sequence of dispatches.

criticalViews.position: A tragedy of pride
criticalViews.summary: The traditional reading takes Coriolanus at his own valuation and finds the fault in him: an aristocratic contempt so complete that it cannot survive contact with ordinary politics.
criticalViews.counter: It has to ignore how much of what he says about flattery and custom the play allows to be true, and how carefully the tribunes' manipulation is staged.

criticalViews.position: A political play about class
criticalViews.summary: Since the nineteenth century the play has been read as Shakespeare's most direct treatment of the conflict between rich and poor, with the grain riot as its foundation and the tribunes as a genuine constitutional innovation.
criticalViews.counter: Productions in this vein have been claimed by the left and the right with equal confidence, which suggests the text does not settle the argument it stages.

criticalViews.position: A play about a mother and a son
criticalViews.summary: Psychological criticism has concentrated on Volumnia, on a valour she describes as her own creation, and on a hero whose entire public identity collapses the moment his family kneel in front of him.
criticalViews.counter: Read too narrowly, it turns a play with numbered citizens and a working senate into a family drama with a war in the background.

essayQuestions.question: Does the play take the citizens seriously?
essayQuestions.focus: Crowd, class and the grain riot
plan: Begin with 1.1: the demand is specific — corn at their own price — and one of the citizens is allowed to answer Menenius back.
Examine the belly fable as rhetoric: what it concedes, what it evades, and how the crowd receives it.
Show the citizens in 2.3 reasoning about whether they owe him their voices, and then being told what they should have said.
Weigh the mockery of their inconstancy in 2.3 and 4.6 against the evidence of who is steering them each time.
Conclude on whether the play mocks a mob or shows a new political class being formed and immediately managed.

essayQuestions.question: What happens in the silence of 5.3?
essayQuestions.focus: Volumnia's plea and the play's turning point
plan: Set up the scene: two embassies have already failed, and Coriolanus has just declared he will act as if a man were author of himself.
Track the sequence of interruptions — Virgilia's greeting, the boy, the kneeling — and note that he calls himself a dull actor before his mother's long speech begins.
Read Volumnia's argument closely, especially the moment she makes her own body the gate of Rome.
Treat the Folio direction, 'He holds her by the hand, silent', as text: what does an audience watch during it?
Judge whether the yielding is a recovery of humanity, a final obedience, or both at once, using his own statement of the cost.

essayQuestions.question: How does the play use the body?
essayQuestions.focus: Wounds, the belly and the body politic
plan: Start with Menenius's fable and the state imagined as an anatomy with a hoarding centre.
Follow the wounds: Volumnia counting them in 2.1, Rome demanding to see them in 2.3, and what the refusal to display them actually claims.
Consider the food imagery running alongside — famine, surfeit, anger eaten in 4.2.
Bring in the animal ladder, from scabs and curs to the dragon in 5.4, as the body politic seen from above.
End on 5.3, where a mother's womb becomes the last piece of ground between an army and a city.

essayQuestions.question: Is Aufidius a rival, a lover or an executioner?
essayQuestions.focus: Enmity, admiration and the last scene
plan: Set out the pattern of Act I: beaten five times, and vowing in 1.10 to have him by any means, honourable or not.
Read the welcome at Antium in 4.5 for its language, which borrows freely from marriage and dreaming.
Use 4.7 to show admiration turning into arithmetic once the soldiers begin to prefer the newcomer.
Examine the choice of insult in 5.6 — boy, not traitor — and what it reveals about how closely he has been watching.
Finish with 'My rage is gone', and ask what it means that the play gives its last tenderness to the killer.

discussionQuestions: The citizens are given numbers, arguments and changes of mind. Does that make them a mob or a parliament?
Coriolanus will not show his wounds. Is that integrity, shame, or a refusal to let his body be used as evidence?
Volumnia saves Rome and destroys her son in the same speech. Which does the play think she came to do?
The turning point of the tragedy is a stage direction rather than a line. What does that ask of an actor?
Aufidius kills him for using the name Rome gave him. Who does the name belong to by the end?

timeline.label: North's translation of Plutarch's Lives
timeline.detail: Thomas North's English version of Amyot's French Plutarch, and the source Shakespeare follows most closely of any he ever used.

timeline.label: North's Plutarch reissued
timeline.detail: A second edition kept the Lives in print and in circulation through Shakespeare's Roman plays.

timeline.label: Julius Caesar
timeline.detail: The first of the plays taken from North, and the one that establishes Shakespeare's method of turning Plutarch's prose into verse.

timeline.label: Antony and Cleopatra
timeline.detail: Usually dated to 1606 or 1607, and the immediate predecessor of this play in the Roman sequence.

timeline.label: The Midland Revolt
timeline.detail: Risings against enclosure and grain shortage across the midland counties, often linked by scholars to the corn riot with which this play opens.

timeline.label: The play is written
timeline.detail: Generally dated around this year, which makes it Shakespeare's last tragedy.

timeline.label: The King's Men take the Blackfriars
timeline.detail: An indoor playhouse with a smaller, closer audience — a room in which a long silence between two actors can be made to work.

timeline.label: Plague closes the London playhouses
timeline.detail: A closure that ran on well into the following year and disrupted the company's plans for the new theatre.

timeline.label: The First Folio
timeline.detail: The play is printed first among the tragedies, from a manuscript whose stage directions are unusually full.

places.name: Rome
places.note: The Forum, the Capitol and the street: almost every political scene in the play.

places.name: Antium
places.note: Modern Anzio, where Coriolanus arrives in disguise and offers Aufidius his throat. Corioli's own site is not securely known.

places.name: Chaeronea
places.note: Plutarch's home town in Boeotia; his Life of Caius Martius gave the play its plot and much of its wording.

places.name: Northampton
places.note: At the centre of the 1607 midland risings over enclosure and the price of corn, a year or so before the play was written.

places.name: Blackfriars, London
places.note: The indoor playhouse the King's Men took on in 1608, well suited to a tragedy whose turning point is a silence.

related.why: The other Roman play built on North's Plutarch, and the other crowd that can be turned round inside a single scene.
Written immediately before, and the opposite case: a soldier undone by appetite rather than by an inability to ask for anything.
The nearest companion piece — a man who leaves his city in fury and takes an enemy's money to punish it.
The earlier tragedy of a man who cannot perform the words a public occasion requires, and loses everything in the first scene for it.
Shakespeare's first Rome, and a useful measure of how far the political writing had travelled by 1608.

books.title: Doctor Faustus
books.author: Christopher Marlowe
books.setting: Wittenberg, spelt 'Wertenberg' in the 1604 text, with excursions to Rome, the Emperor's court and the Duke of Vanholt's
books.lengthNote: About 1,500 lines in the 1604 text, roughly half the length of Hamlet; the 1616 version is some 600 lines longer
books.openingLine: Not marching now in fields of Thrasymene.
books.summary: A Wittenberg scholar who has run through logic, medicine, law and divinity signs his soul to Lucifer in exchange for twenty-four years with Mephistopheles at his command. He asks for omnipotence and gets a travelling show: a box on the Pope's ear, grapes in January, a pair of horns on a heckler. The play's real action is the repentance that is offered in nearly every scene and never taken, and its last hour is the first time Faustus counts time honestly.
books.referenceStyle: Prologue, Chorus 2, Chorus 3, Scene 1 to Scene 14 and Epilogue. The 1604 quarto has no act or scene divisions and the source text prints it continuously without line numbers, so scenes are counted in the quarto's own order

sourceText.label: Project Gutenberg text of the 1604 quarto (the A-text), edited by Alexander Dyce
sourceText.note: This is the shorter of the two early versions, keeping Dyce's spellings 'Mephistophilis' and 'Wertenberg'. It is not divided into acts or scenes. The scene numbers used here begin a new scene wherever the stage clears, and at the two places where editors usually start one although it does not: at 'When I behold the heavens' (Scene 6) and at the Horse-courser's entrance (Scene 11). The Helen speech therefore falls in Scene 13 and the last hour in Scene 14. Editions that follow the 1616 text, or that arrange the play in five acts, number differently.

structure.label: Prologue, Scenes 1–2
structure.title: Learning is declared too small
structure.summary: The Chorus promises neither war nor love, only the form of one scholar's fortunes. Faustus sits in his study and dismisses each university discipline in turn because none of them can make him more than a man, then sends for two magicians. His colleagues already fear the worst.

scenes.title: The waxen wings
scenes.summary: The Chorus gives Faustus's birth, his doctorate and his fall in advance, as Icarus.

scenes.title: The study
scenes.summary: Faustus rejects logic, medicine, law and divinity, hears the two Angels, and is promised the world by Valdes and Cornelius.

scenes.title: Two scholars and a servant
scenes.summary: Wagner chops logic with two scholars, who guess where Faustus is dining and go to tell the Rector.

structure.label: Scenes 3–5
structure.title: A warning becomes a contract
structure.summary: Faustus conjures and Mephistopheles comes, though not, he explains, because he was summoned. The devil describes hell truthfully and begs Faustus to stop asking; Faustus lectures him on manly fortitude and offers his soul. After a comic scene in which Wagner hires a servant on the same terms, the deed is written in blood that tries not to flow.

scenes.title: The conjuring
scenes.summary: Mephistopheles appears, is sent back to change into a friar, and tells Faustus that this is hell.

scenes.title: Wagner and the Clown
scenes.summary: Wagner binds a hungry clown to seven years' service with two devils and a handful of coins.

scenes.title: The deed of gift
scenes.summary: The blood congeals, 'Homo, fuge' appears on Faustus's arm, the contract is read aloud, and his first request, a wife, is refused.

structure.label: Scene 6, Chorus 2, Scene 7
structure.title: Questions become spectacles
structure.summary: Faustus wavers, and each time he wavers he is given something to look at. When he asks who made the world Mephistopheles will not answer; when he calls on Christ, Lucifer arrives in person with the Seven Deadly Sins as a pastime. The Chorus sends him round the heavens in a dragon-drawn chariot and sets him down in Rome to snatch the Pope's dinner.

scenes.title: The Seven Deadly Sins
scenes.summary: An astronomy lesson ends at the question of creation; Lucifer answers Faustus's prayer with a parade.

scenes.title: Olympus' top
scenes.summary: A chorus speech reports the journey through the sky and announces Rome.

scenes.title: The Pope's banquet
scenes.summary: Invisible, Faustus steals dishes, boxes the Pope's ear and is cursed with bell, book and candle.

structure.label: Chorus 3, Scenes 8–12
structure.title: Empire becomes entertainment
structure.summary: The man who was going to wall Germany with brass becomes a court entertainer with a famous name. Ostlers steal one of his books and conjure with it well enough to fetch Mephistopheles from Constantinople. Faustus shows the Emperor a likeness of Alexander, cheats a horse-dealer of forty dollars and fetches grapes for a pregnant duchess, while the years run out between scenes.

scenes.title: Fame
scenes.summary: The Chorus reports Faustus's return home and his invitation to the court of Charles V.

scenes.title: Robin's book
scenes.summary: Robin the ostler plans to use a stolen conjuring book on the maids of the parish.

scenes.title: The goblet
scenes.summary: Robin and Ralph gull a vintner, summon Mephistopheles by accident and are turned into an ape and a dog.

scenes.title: The Emperor
scenes.summary: Faustus raises spirits in the shapes of Alexander and his paramour and plants horns on a sceptical knight.

scenes.title: The Horse-courser
scenes.summary: A horse sold for forty dollars turns to hay in the water; Faustus, asleep, loses a false leg to the buyer.

scenes.title: Grapes in January
scenes.summary: At the Duke of Vanholt's, Faustus sends a spirit to the other side of the world for a dish of grapes.

structure.label: Scenes 13–14, Epilogue
structure.title: Time becomes the antagonist
structure.summary: An Old Man makes the last human appeal and very nearly succeeds. Mephistopheles answers with a threat, Faustus renews the bond in blood and asks for Helen to put repentance out of his mind. The scholars leave him to pray next door, the clock strikes eleven, and twenty-four years are paid for in fifty-odd lines.

scenes.title: Helen and the Old Man
scenes.summary: Helen crosses the stage for the scholars, the Old Man pleads, the bond is renewed, and Faustus takes Helen as his paramour.

scenes.title: One bare hour
scenes.summary: Faustus confesses to the scholars, then faces eleven, half past and midnight alone.

scenes.title: The burned laurel
scenes.summary: The Chorus draws the moral: wonder at unlawful things, and do not practise them.

characters.name: Doctor Faustus
characters.role: Doctor of divinity at Wittenberg; conjuror; party to the bond
characters.summary: A man of low birth who has reached the top of his university and found the view disappointing. He is a brilliant talker and a careless reader, quick to quote half a verse of scripture and build a philosophy on it. What he wants changes from scene to scene, which is part of the point: a god's power in Scene 1, a wife in Scene 5, a nap in Scene 11. He addresses himself by name throughout, as though Faustus were someone he was managing.
characters.clue: He quotes 'the reward of sin is death' and stops reading before the half of the verse that would have saved him.

relationships.label: believes he commands
relationships.note: The contract says Mephistopheles is his servant. Every refusal, threat and distraction in the play runs the other way.

relationships.label: is almost turned by, then asks devils to torment
master of, and leaves his goods to

characters.name: Mephistopheles
characters.role: A devil, servant to Lucifer, bound to Faustus for twenty-four years
characters.summary: Spelt 'Mephistophilis' in the 1604 text. He is the most honest speaker in the play: he says plainly that conjuring did not compel him, that he is in hell as he stands there, and that the loss of heaven is a torment he would rather not discuss. Faustus takes none of it in. Once the deed is signed the candour hardens into management, and by Scene 13 he is handing Faustus a dagger and threatening to tear him in pieces.
characters.clue: Asked how he comes to be out of hell, he answers that he is not out of it.

relationships.label: servant to
relationships.note: He cannot follow Faustus without Lucifer's leave, and says so at their first meeting.

characters.name: Lucifer
characters.role: Prince of devils; the other party to the contract
characters.summary: He appears once in the 1604 text, at the exact moment Faustus calls on Christ to save his soul, and treats the prayer as a breach of contract. His method is a lawyer's and then a showman's: first the reminder of what was promised, then the Seven Deadly Sins to take Faustus's mind off it.
characters.clue: He arrives in answer to a prayer addressed to somebody else.

characters.name: The Good Angel
characters.role: A voice from the morality plays, urging repentance
characters.summary: Always enters with the Evil Angel and usually speaks first. The advice is short and practical: put the book down, read the scriptures, think of heaven. In Scene 6 the Good Angel gives the play's most important line of doctrine, that it is never too late if Faustus can repent, and the whole argument turns on that 'can'.
characters.clue: Says it is never too late, on one condition.

characters.name: The Evil Angel
characters.role: The opposing voice, urging Faustus on
characters.summary: Where the Good Angel offers heaven, the Evil Angel offers honour, wealth and the rule of the elements, and when those stop working offers fear instead: repent and devils will tear you in pieces. The Evil Angel generally gets the last word in each exchange, and Faustus's next speech generally picks it up.
characters.clue: Tells Faustus he is a spirit now, and that God cannot pity him.

characters.name: The Old Man
characters.role: An unnamed believer who makes the last appeal
characters.summary: He has no history and no stake in the matter, which is what makes him persuasive. He sees an angel over Faustus's head with a vial of grace and talks him out of suicide. Faustus repays him by asking Mephistopheles to torture him. The devils can hurt his body and nothing else, and he leaves the stage for God as Faustus leaves it for Helen.
characters.clue: Mephistopheles admits he cannot touch this man's soul.

relationships.label: is what Faustus might have been

characters.name: Wagner
characters.role: Faustus's servant and student
characters.summary: A sharp boy who has picked up his master's manner without his learning. He defeats two scholars with mock logic, hires a clown with borrowed devils, and in Scene 13 notices, puzzled, that a man who has just made his will is carousing with students. He inherits everything.
characters.clue: He binds a servant for seven years with the help of two devils called Baliol and Belcher.

characters.name: Valdes and Cornelius
characters.role: Two German magicians, Faustus's tutors in the art
characters.summary: They appear in one scene, promise spirits like lions and argosies from Venice, lend the books and the method, and are never seen again. Their disappearance is pointed: they know the art well enough to teach it and have evidently never signed anything themselves.
characters.clue: Infamous through the world, according to the scholars, and absent from the play after dinner.

characters.name: The Scholars
characters.role: Faustus's university colleagues
characters.summary: They frame the play. In Scene 2 they fear he has fallen into a damned art and go for help; in Scene 13 they ask, innocently, to see the most beautiful woman who ever lived; in Scene 14 they tell him to look up to heaven, and go next door to pray. They are the ordinary, decent, companionable life he says he wishes he had kept.
characters.clue: One of them offers to stay with Faustus through the last night and is talked out of it.

characters.name: Robin and Ralph
characters.role: An ostler and his friend
characters.summary: Robin steals one of Faustus's conjuring books and means to use it for drink and for Nan Spit the kitchen-maid. The joke is that it works: his gibberish fetches Mephistopheles all the way from Constantinople. Their ambitions are Faustus's with the poetry taken out, and their punishment, to be an ape and a dog, delights them.
characters.clue: He cannot read, by his friend's account, and conjures a devil anyway.

relationships.label: steals a book from, and repeats the career of

characters.name: Helen of Troy
characters.role: A silent figure brought by Mephistopheles
characters.summary: She crosses the stage twice and says nothing. Faustus has already told the Emperor that he cannot raise true bodies, only spirits that resemble them, so the play has explained what she is before she enters. She is requested as a cure for thoughts of repentance, and she works.
characters.clue: The most praised character in the play has no lines.

characters.name: The Chorus
characters.role: Speaker of the prologue, two linking speeches and the epilogue
