characters.summary: The Chorus tells the ending before the beginning and the moral after the end, and its tone is cooler than anything in between. It praises the scholar, names the fault as self-conceit, and closes by recommending that the wise wonder at unlawful things from a distance. How far the play agrees with its own Chorus is the oldest argument about it.
characters.clue: Announces that the play will not be about war or love.

themes.name: Knowledge and its limits
themes.summary: Faustus is not punished for curiosity. He is shown abandoning it. The opening soliloquy measures every discipline by what it can do for him, and once he has a devil to question he settles for answers Wagner could give. The one question that matters, who made the world, is the one Mephistopheles refuses, and Faustus lets it drop.
themes.development: From the survey of the faculties in Scene 1, through the 'freshmen's suppositions' of the astronomy lesson in Scene 6, to the wish in Scene 14 that he had never seen Wittenberg or read a book.

themes.name: Ambition
themes.summary: The Prologue gives the pattern in one image: waxen wings that mount above their reach. What the play adds is the anticlimax. Faustus plans to be emperor of the world and ends up performing for one, and the distance between the programme of Scene 1 and the grapes of Scene 12 is Marlowe's harshest comment on what the bargain bought.
themes.development: The plans are largest before the contract is signed. Afterwards nobody mentions walling Germany with brass again, Faustus least of all.

themes.name: Appetite and habit
themes.summary: Faustus names his own god early: 'thine own appetite'. Each time conscience stirs, something pleasant is put in front of him, and he takes it. The play is unusually exact about how a free choice becomes a habit and a habit becomes a hardened heart, until he can say 'I cannot repent' and mean it as a description rather than an excuse.
themes.development: Devils with crowns in Scene 5, the Sins in Scene 6, a quiet sleep in Scene 11, Helen in Scene 13: each is asked for or accepted at a moment of doubt.

themes.name: Despair and repentance
themes.summary: In the theology the play works with, despair is the conviction that one's sin is too great to be forgiven, and it is itself the sin that cannot be forgiven because it refuses the remedy. Faustus is told by an Angel, an Old Man and three scholars that mercy is available, and answers each time that it is not available to him. Whether he is right is what the play leaves open.
themes.development: 'Despair in God' is a resolution in Scene 5 and a condition by Scene 13, where 'I do repent; and yet I do despair' puts both in one line.

themes.name: Grace, sin and the Reformation argument
themes.summary: The play is set in Luther's university and written for an audience taught that salvation is God's gift rather than man's achievement. That makes Faustus's case genuinely hard. If he cannot repent, is that because he will not, or because grace has been withheld? The 1604 text keeps both answers alive and gives the Evil Angel the bleaker one.
themes.development: The half-quoted verses of Scene 1 start the argument; 'Christ cannot save thy soul, for he is just' in Scene 6 is its darkest moment; the blood in the firmament in Scene 14 reopens it with minutes to go.

themes.name: Time
themes.summary: Twenty-four years pass in a few hundred lines of clowning and court visits, and the final hour takes fifty-seven lines of verse with a clock striking through it. Marlowe makes the audience feel how the years were wasted by wasting them in front of us, and then makes a single hour unbearable by counting it.
themes.development: First mentioned as a contractual term in Scene 3, felt as 'the restless course that time doth run' in Scene 11, and turned into sound in Scene 14.

themes.name: Power, service and who commands whom
themes.summary: The deed of gift makes Mephistopheles the servant and Faustus the master, and the play shows that arrangement to be a fiction from the first meeting, when the devil explains he came of his own accord. Faustus's requests are refused whenever they matter. The comic scenes repeat the pattern downwards: Wagner hires a clown, Robin summons a devil, and nobody who gives orders in this play is in charge.
themes.development: 'How pliant is this Mephistophilis' in Scene 3; 'Thou traitor, Faustus, I arrest thy soul' in Scene 13.

techniques.name: Soliloquy
techniques.definition: A character alone on stage, thinking aloud to the audience.
techniques.bookDefinition: A character alone on stage, thinking aloud to the audience.
techniques.inThisBook: The play opens and closes on long solo speeches, and they mirror each other: a man alone with books deciding he has time for everything, and the same man alone with a clock. The first is orderly and wrong; the last is broken and clear-sighted.

techniques.name: Blank verse
techniques.definition: Unrhymed iambic pentameter, in which the sentence and the line are free to disagree.
techniques.bookDefinition: Unrhymed iambic pentameter, in which the sentence and the line are free to disagree.
techniques.inThisBook: Marlowe's line is end-stopped and cumulative, each verse a complete boast: 'I'll have them', 'I'll have them', 'I'll have them'. In the final speech the same metre is made to stumble, with short lines, a line of Latin, and outcries that will not scan.

techniques.name: The Chorus
techniques.definition: A narrator who addresses the audience directly between the acts.
techniques.bookDefinition: A speaker outside the action who introduces, links and judges it.
techniques.inThisBook: Four speeches fix the play's moral frame and cover its gaps in time. Because the Chorus gives the verdict before the evidence, the audience watches knowing the end, and attention moves from what will happen to why nothing prevents it.

techniques.name: Allegory
techniques.definition: Abstractions given bodies and names so an argument can be seen.
techniques.bookDefinition: Abstractions given bodies and names so an argument can be seen.
techniques.inThisBook: The Good and Evil Angels and the parade of Sins come from the older morality drama, where a representative man is fought over. Marlowe keeps the machinery and changes the man: Faustus has a name, a degree and a city, and the Angels may be heard as his own divided mind.

techniques.name: Parody subplot
techniques.definition: A low plot that repeats the main plot's action in a debased form.
techniques.bookDefinition: A low plot that repeats the main plot's action in a debased form.
techniques.inThisBook: Wagner binds the Clown for seven years straight after Faustus offers himself for twenty-four; Robin wants a stolen book for wine and a kitchen-maid. The comic scenes are not relief. They state, without the verse, what Faustus's ambitions come to.

techniques.name: Scriptural argument
techniques.definition: Quoting or contesting scripture as a way of settling a dispute.
techniques.bookDefinition: Quoting or contesting scripture as a way of settling a dispute.
techniques.inThisBook: Faustus reads half of Romans 6:23 and half of 1 John 1:8–9, leaving out the gift of eternal life and the promise of forgiveness that complete them. 'Consummatum est', Christ's last words in John's gospel, is what he says on signing the deed.

techniques.name: Allusion
techniques.definition: A deliberate reference to another text, used to borrow its argument.
techniques.bookDefinition: A deliberate reference to another text, used to borrow its argument.
techniques.inThisBook: Icarus in the Prologue, Paris and Semele in the Helen speech, and a line from Ovid's Amores in the last hour, where a lover's plea for the night to go slowly is spoken by a man waiting for devils. The classical references are beautiful and every one of them ends in a fall or a fire.

techniques.name: Third-person self-address
techniques.definition: A speaker who habitually refers to himself by name, as though to someone else.
techniques.bookDefinition: A speaker who habitually refers to himself by name, as though to someone else.
techniques.inThisBook: 'Settle thy studies, Faustus'; 'What art thou, Faustus, but a man condemn'd to die?' He gives himself orders, encouragement and sentence in the second and third person, which splits the self that acts from the self that watches, and lets him talk about damnation as something that is happening to Faustus.

quotations.text: His waxen wings did mount above his reach, And, melting, heavens conspir'd his overthrow
quotations.speaker: Chorus
quotations.context: The Chorus sums up Faustus's career before he has appeared.
quotations.analysis: Icarus was warned, flew too high and fell, which seems a tidy moral until the verb arrives. 'Conspir'd' makes heaven an active party to the overthrow, not a spectator of it, and that one word plants the question the play never settles: whether Faustus falls or is dropped.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg text of the 1604 quarto, Prologue

quotations.text: Yet art thou still but Faustus, and a man.
quotations.speaker: Faustus
quotations.context: Faustus has just listed his medical triumphs, whole cities saved from plague.
quotations.analysis: The complaint is not that medicine fails but that success leaves him what he was. 'But' and 'and a man' treat being human as a rank he has been stuck at. It is the play's first use of his name as a reproach, and the ambition it announces is less for knowledge than for a change of species.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg text of the 1604 quarto, Scene 1

quotations.text: The reward of sin is death: that's hard.
quotations.speaker: Faustus
quotations.context: Reading from Jerome's Bible, Faustus translates the Latin he has just quoted.
quotations.analysis: The verse he is reading goes on to say that the gift of God is eternal life. He stops at the half that suits his mood and delivers a verdict on the whole of divinity in two colloquial words. A doctor of theology would know the rest, so the misreading is either wilful or the first sign of a mind already closing.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg text of the 1604 quarto, Scene 1

quotations.text: But his dominion that exceeds in this, Stretcheth as far as doth the mind of man; A sound magician is a mighty god
quotations.speaker: Faustus
quotations.context: Faustus compares the magician's reach with that of emperors and kings, who are obeyed only in their own provinces.
quotations.analysis: The limit he sets on the magician's empire is 'the mind of man', which sounds boundless and is in fact the boundary he has just complained of. 'Sound' is a scholar's word, used of arguments and doctrine, and here it is attached to the one study his university would call unsound.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg text of the 1604 quarto, Scene 1

quotations.text: I'll have them fly to India for gold, Ransack the ocean for orient pearl, And search all corners of the new-found world For pleasant fruits and princely delicates
quotations.speaker: Faustus
quotations.context: After the Angels leave, Faustus imagines what his spirits will fetch him.
quotations.analysis: The speech begins by promising to resolve 'all ambiguities' and within four lines has become a shopping list. The verbs are a conqueror's, 'ransack' and 'search', but the objects are gold, pearl and fruit. When the play finally shows a spirit sent across the world, it comes back with grapes.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg text of the 1604 quarto, Scene 1

quotations.text: O, Faustus, lay that damned book aside, And gaze not on it, lest it tempt thy soul
quotations.speaker: Good Angel
quotations.context: The Angels' first entrance, while Faustus waits for Valdes and Cornelius.
quotations.analysis: The danger is located in looking. 'Gaze' makes the book a spectacle rather than a text, and the rest of the play bears that out: Faustus is managed by being given things to watch. The line also sets book against book, since the Angel's next words tell him to read the scriptures instead.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg text of the 1604 quarto, Scene 1

quotations.text: For, when we hear one rack the name of God, Abjure the Scriptures and his Saviour Christ, We fly, in hope to get his glorious soul
quotations.speaker: Mephistopheles
quotations.context: Faustus asks whether his conjuring raised Mephistopheles. The answer is that it did so only incidentally.
quotations.analysis: The spell did nothing; the blasphemy did. Faustus has just congratulated himself as 'conjuror laureat', and the devil removes the ground of the boast in three lines without Faustus appearing to notice. 'Glorious' is the striking word: the hunter values the soul more highly than its owner does.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg text of the 1604 quarto, Scene 3

quotations.text: Why, this is hell, nor am I out of it
quotations.speaker: Mephistopheles
quotations.context: Faustus has asked how a damned spirit comes to be standing in Wittenberg, outside hell.
quotations.analysis: Ten monosyllables replace the hell of fire and pitchforks with a state of loss carried everywhere. The line is spoken to a man standing in the same spot, so 'this' takes in Faustus's study too. He has asked for a location and been given a definition, and he responds by changing the subject to his own fortitude.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg text of the 1604 quarto, Scene 3

quotations.text: O, Faustus, leave these frivolous demands, Which strike a terror to my fainting soul!
quotations.speaker: Mephistopheles
quotations.context: Mephistopheles has described being deprived of everlasting bliss.
quotations.analysis: The tempter asks his victim to stop. It is the oddest moment in the scene and the most persuasive warning Faustus ever receives, because it comes from the only witness with direct experience and nothing to gain by it. Faustus's reply is to tell a devil to learn courage from him.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg text of the 1604 quarto, Scene 3

quotations.text: Had I as many souls as there be stars, I'd give them all for Mephistophilis.
quotations.speaker: Faustus
quotations.context: Alone after Mephistopheles has gone to carry his offer to Lucifer.
quotations.analysis: The hyperbole works by multiplying the one thing he has only one of. It is also a lover's sentence, given for a person rather than for power, and the play keeps that note: he cuts his arm 'for love of thee'. What he wants from the bargain, at this moment, is company.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg text of the 1604 quarto, Scene 3

quotations.text: he would give his soul to the devil for a shoulder of mutton, though it were blood-raw.
quotations.speaker: Wagner
quotations.context: Wagner sizes up the ragged Clown he intends to hire.
quotations.analysis: The scene follows directly on Faustus's offer, and the Clown's answer sharpens the comparison: at that price he would want it well roasted, with good sauce. A starving man haggles over his soul more carefully than the doctor of divinity has just done, and in prose that makes the terms sound like what they are.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg text of the 1604 quarto, Scene 4

quotations.text: The god thou serv'st is thine own appetite
quotations.speaker: Faustus
quotations.context: Waiting at midnight for Lucifer's answer, Faustus hears a voice telling him to turn to God again, and argues himself out of it.
quotations.analysis: He says it to harden himself, and it is the most accurate sentence he speaks about his own case. The idol is not Lucifer or Belzebub but wanting. The grammar gives him away as well: a man who calls himself 'thou' can diagnose the fault and still treat it as somebody else's.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg text of the 1604 quarto, Scene 5

quotations.text: My blood congeals, and I can write no more.
quotations.speaker: Faustus
quotations.context: Faustus has stabbed his arm and begun to write the deed of gift.
quotations.analysis: His body objects before his mind does. The blood that will not flow for Lucifer is answered in the last scene by blood he cannot reach, streaming in the sky. Here the remedy is a pan of coals fetched from below, and he reads the omen correctly for one line before deciding his soul is his own to give.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg text of the 1604 quarto, Scene 5

quotations.text: Consummatum est; this bill is ended, And Faustus hath bequeath'd his soul to Lucifer.
quotations.speaker: Faustus
quotations.context: The blood flows again and the deed is finished.
quotations.analysis: 'It is finished' are Christ's last words on the cross in John's gospel, spoken as a debt is paid for others. Faustus uses them to close a sale. The blasphemy is so exact that it is hard to believe a theologian commits it by accident, and the legal diction, 'bill' and 'bequeath'd', belongs to the profession he despised in Scene 1.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg text of the 1604 quarto, Scene 5

quotations.text: Hell hath no limits, nor is circumscrib'd In one self place; for where we are is hell
quotations.speaker: Mephistopheles
quotations.context: Faustus's first question under the new contract: where is hell?
quotations.analysis: Faustus wanted dominion without limits and is told which kingdom actually has none. 'Circumscrib'd' picks up the circle he drew to conjure in: he thought he was enclosing a spirit and has stepped inside something with no edge. His reply is that he thinks hell's a fable, said to a devil in his own study.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg text of the 1604 quarto, Scene 5

quotations.text: My heart's so harden'd, I cannot repent: Scarce can I name salvation, faith, or heaven, But fearful echoes thunder in mine ears
quotations.speaker: Faustus
quotations.context: The Angels have just left; the Evil Angel's last words were that Faustus never shall repent.
quotations.analysis: The hardened heart is Pharaoh's in Exodus, where the text says both that Pharaoh hardened it and that God did. Marlowe leaves the verb passive, so the question of who did the hardening stays open. The speech then shows the mechanism at work: despair offers him knives and halters, and pleasure, in the shape of Homer singing, talks him round.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg text of the 1604 quarto, Scene 6

quotations.text: Never too late, if Faustus can repent.
quotations.speaker: Good Angel
quotations.context: Faustus asks 'Is't not too late?' and the Evil Angel answers first: 'Too late.'
quotations.analysis: The line everyone quotes for its comfort has a condition in the middle of it. Later versions of the play print 'will' here; the 1604 text's 'can' allows that he might not be able to, and turns a promise into a question about grace. The Angel speaks of him in the third person, as he does himself.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg text of the 1604 quarto, Scene 6

quotations.text: Christ cannot save thy soul, for he is just: There's none but I have interest in the same.
quotations.speaker: Lucifer
quotations.context: Faustus has cried out to Christ his Saviour. Lucifer, Belzebub and Mephistopheles enter at once.
quotations.analysis: Lucifer argues from justice and leaves mercy out, exactly as Faustus left out the second half of his verses in Scene 1. 'Interest' is a lender's word: the soul is a property with a claim on it. The fact that Lucifer needs to come in person suggests the prayer was more dangerous to him than he admits.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg text of the 1604 quarto, Scene 6

quotations.text: I cannot read, and therefore wish all books were burnt.
quotations.speaker: Envy
quotations.context: The fourth of the Seven Deadly Sins introduces itself to Faustus.
quotations.analysis: A throwaway joke in the parade that the last line of the tragedy turns serious. The most learned man in Germany will end by offering to burn his books too, and the echo puts him, at the finish, in the position of the sin that hates what it cannot use. Faustus watches the show as a spectator; several of the Sins are portraits.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg text of the 1604 quarto, Scene 6

quotations.text: How! bell, book, and candle,--candle, book, and bell,-- Forward and backward, to curse Faustus to hell!
quotations.speaker: Faustus
quotations.context: In Rome, invisible, Faustus has boxed the Pope's ear and learns he will be excommunicated.
quotations.analysis: 'Forward and backward' is the phrase he used in Scene 3 for Jehovah's name anagrammatised in his conjuring circle. The ritual of cursing and the ritual of conjuring are made to sound alike, which flatters a Protestant audience and also removes any comfort: he laughs at a curse that the play means literally. The verse has shrunk to a jingle.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg text of the 1604 quarto, Scene 7

quotations.text: But such spirits as can lively resemble Alexander and his paramour shall appear before your grace
quotations.speaker: Faustus
quotations.context: The Emperor has asked to see Alexander the Great. Faustus explains what he can and cannot do.
quotations.analysis: An honest disclaimer, in courtly prose, from the man who was going to raise the dead and be a god. Magic can supply likenesses and nothing more. The Emperor forgets this within a minute and takes the spirits for 'true substantial bodies'; Faustus forgets it three scenes later, when the likeness is Helen and the one deceived is himself.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg text of the 1604 quarto, Scene 10

quotations.text: Tush, Christ did call the thief upon the Cross; Then rest thee, Faustus, quiet in conceit.
quotations.speaker: Faustus
quotations.context: Between two halves of the horse-dealer farce, Faustus admits his time is nearly out, and settles down to sleep in his chair.
quotations.analysis: The penitent thief was the standard proof that repentance is possible at the last moment. Faustus uses it as a sedative. 'Tush' and 'quiet in conceit' show him turning a doctrine of mercy into permission to postpone, and the play's cruellest stage direction follows: he sleeps, and a cheated customer pulls his leg off.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg text of the 1604 quarto, Scene 11

quotations.text: I see an angel hovers o'er thy head, And, with a vial full of precious grace, Offers to pour the same into thy soul: Then call for mercy, and avoid despair.
quotations.speaker: Old Man
quotations.context: Mephistopheles has handed Faustus a dagger. The Old Man stops him.
quotations.analysis: The Good Angel has not been seen since Scene 6; now an angel is reported by a human witness and the offer is described as present tense and specific. If the Old Man is to be believed, grace is available in the last act, which makes what follows a refusal. His final clause names the enemy as despair, not the devil.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg text of the 1604 quarto, Scene 13

quotations.text: I do repent; and yet I do despair: Hell strives with grace for conquest in my breast
quotations.speaker: Faustus
quotations.context: The Old Man has left Faustus alone to think about his sins.
quotations.analysis: The line is built as a balance, the same verb form on either side of a semicolon, and that is the trouble with it. Repentance and despair cannot both be true at once in the play's theology, since despair denies what repentance asks for. He describes the contest in his breast as a spectator would, and Mephistopheles settles it with a threat in the next speech.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg text of the 1604 quarto, Scene 13

quotations.text: Was this the face that launch'd a thousand ships.
quotations.speaker: Faustus
quotations.context: Helen re-enters, brought by Mephistopheles at Faustus's request to drive out thoughts of repentance. The sentence runs on to the burning of Troy.
quotations.analysis: The most famous compliment in English drama is a question, and its measure of beauty is a fleet of warships. 'Was this' carries a faint note of surprise, as if the scholar were checking the legend against the exhibit. He has told the Emperor that such figures are spirits in borrowed shapes, and he greets this one as the woman herself.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg text of the 1604 quarto, Scene 13

quotations.text: Her lips suck forth my soul: see, where it flies!-- Come, Helen, come, give me my soul again.
quotations.speaker: Faustus
quotations.context: Faustus has asked Helen to make him immortal with a kiss, and kisses her.
quotations.analysis: The souls of lovers passing in a kiss was an old poetic conceit. Spoken by a man whose soul is contracted to the power that sent this figure, it becomes a literal report, and he delivers it with delight. Asking for the soul back as a game, from a spirit, a few lines after refusing to ask for it from God, is the scene's whole argument.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg text of the 1604 quarto, Scene 13

quotations.text: I will be Paris, and for love of thee, Instead of Troy, shall Wertenberg be sack'd
quotations.speaker: Faustus
quotations.context: Faustus imagines himself as Helen's lover and champion.
quotations.analysis: The scholar casts himself in the story he used to teach, and offers his own university town as the city to be burned. It is said as gallantry. Every comparison in the speech, Paris, Semele, Arethusa, is a mortal ruined by contact with something greater, and the speaker never notices what his examples have in common.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg text of the 1604 quarto, Scene 13

quotations.text: His faith is great; I cannot touch his soul; But what I may afflict his body with I will attempt, which is but little worth.
quotations.speaker: Mephistopheles
quotations.context: Faustus has asked Mephistopheles to torment the Old Man with the greatest torments hell affords.
quotations.analysis: A devil states the limits of his own power, and they are narrow. Against faith he can manage only bodily harm, which he himself rates as worth little. The admission makes nonsense of the threat that has governed Faustus since Scene 6, that repentance will get him torn in pieces, and Faustus is standing there when it is made.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg text of the 1604 quarto, Scene 13

quotations.text: the serpent that tempted Eve may be saved, but not Faustus.
quotations.speaker: Faustus
quotations.context: A scholar has reminded Faustus that God's mercies are infinite.
quotations.analysis: This is pride wearing the clothes of humility. To claim the one sin too large for infinite mercy is to claim, still, to be exceptional, and the man who wanted to be more than a man now insists on being worse than the devil. The scene is in prose, the only time Faustus speaks plainly to friends, and the plainness makes the claim more shocking.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg text of the 1604 quarto, Scene 14

quotations.text: Stand still, you ever-moving spheres of heaven, That time may cease, and midnight never come
quotations.speaker: Faustus
quotations.context: The clock has struck eleven and Faustus is alone.
quotations.analysis: He opens the last speech in the imperative, the mood of a conjuror, and addresses the same spheres he once questioned Mephistopheles about. Nothing obeys. 'Ever-moving' concedes the defeat inside the command. The speech goes on asking for less and less: a year, a month, a week, a natural day.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg text of the 1604 quarto, Scene 14

quotations.text: O, I'll leap up to my God!--Who pulls me down?-- See, see, where Christ's blood streams in the firmament! One drop would save my soul, half a drop: ah, my Christ!
quotations.speaker: Faustus
quotations.context: Midway through the final soliloquy, before the half-hour strikes.
quotations.analysis: The verse breaks into cries and the long second line overruns its metre. His own blood congealed when he tried to sign; this blood streams, and he bargains for it in fractions, a drop and then half a drop, still thinking in prices. 'Who pulls me down?' has no stage direction to answer it, and whether the hand is a devil's or his own is left to the actor.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg text of the 1604 quarto, Scene 14

quotations.text: Ugly hell, gape not! come not, Lucifer! I'll burn my books!--Ah, Mephistophilis!
quotations.speaker: Faustus
quotations.context: Midnight has struck and the devils have entered. These are Faustus's last words.
quotations.analysis: The final offer is the first one the Good Angel asked for, that he lay the book aside, made twenty-four years late and addressed to the wrong party. It is a bargain, not a prayer. The last word is the devil's name, and 'Ah' can be played as terror, reproach or recognition of the only companion he has had.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg text of the 1604 quarto, Scene 14

quotations.text: Cut is the branch that might have grown full straight, And burned is Apollo's laurel-bough, That sometime grew within this learned man.
quotations.speaker: Chorus
quotations.context: The Chorus returns after the devils have taken Faustus away.
quotations.analysis: Both main verbs are passive and come first, so the loss is felt before its subject. 'Might have grown' grants that the outcome was not fixed, which sits awkwardly with a Prologue in which the heavens conspired. The laurel is Apollo's, the prize of poets and scholars, and the Chorus mourns the learning even while warning against where it led.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg text of the 1604 quarto, Epilogue

atAGlance.label: Written
atAGlance.note: Nothing fixes the date. The English Faust book Marlowe used survives in an edition of 1592, which may not have been the first.

atAGlance.label: First printed
atAGlance.note: Eleven years after Marlowe's death. A longer and different version followed in 1616.

atAGlance.label: Two texts
atAGlance.note: The Astor edition and every reference here follow the 1604 text. The 1616 version adds papal politics, a revenge plot for the horned knight and devils watching the final scene from above.

atAGlance.label: The bargain
atAGlance.note: One year for each hour of a day, which is how the last scene spends them.

atAGlance.label: First Faustus
atAGlance.note: The leading actor of the Admiral's Men, who also created Tamburlaine and Barabas.

atAGlance.label: Source
atAGlance.note: A translation, signed only 'P. F.', of the German Historia von D. Johann Fausten of 1587.

criticalViews.position: An orthodox warning
criticalViews.summary: On this reading the Chorus speaks for the play. Faustus is a gifted man ruined by pride, the means of rescue are put in front of him repeatedly, and he declines them with his eyes open. The comic scenes and the shrinking of his ambitions show what sin does to a mind, and the ending is just. The structure of Angels, Sins and last-minute appeal comes from the morality play because the moral is the same.
criticalViews.counter: It has to explain away the Prologue's 'heavens conspir'd', the Good Angel's 'if Faustus can', and the fact that the verse gives Faustus's longing a grandeur the Chorus's verdict never matches. A play that only wanted to warn would not make the sinner its best poet.

criticalViews.position: A Renaissance overreacher
criticalViews.summary: Here Faustus is the tragic hero of a new age, a self-made scholar who refuses the limits an old order sets on what a man may know and be, and is destroyed for it. The sympathy of the play is with the aspiring mind of Scene 1, and the terror of the ending is an indictment of the cosmos that requires it. Marlowe's own reputation for dangerous opinions is usually called in support.
criticalViews.counter: The play gives this Faustus very little to do. He asks few real questions, accepts evasive answers, and spends his power on pranks. If he is a hero of the intellect, the middle of the play is a strange way to honour him, and the author's biography is not evidence about a character.

criticalViews.position: A tragedy of predestination
criticalViews.summary: A third view sets the play inside the Calvinist teaching of Elizabethan England, in which God has chosen the saved and the damned in advance and the reprobate cannot truly repent. Faustus's hardened heart, his inability to weep or lift his hands, and the devils who arrive at each prayer then look less like his choices than like the symptoms of a sentence already passed. The horror is theological: he may be right that mercy is not for him.
criticalViews.counter: The Old Man sees grace offered in the present tense, and Mephistopheles admits he has no power over a faithful soul. Characters inside the fiction, with no reason to lie, say the door is open. The text supports the fear of reprobation without ever confirming it.

essayQuestions.question: Is Faustus damned by his own choice, or was he never free to choose otherwise?
essayQuestions.focus: Free will, grace and the hardened heart
plan: Begin with the two verbs that frame the problem: the heavens that 'conspir'd' in the Prologue and the branch that 'might have grown full straight' in the Epilogue. The Chorus itself gives both answers.
Set out the case for choice from Scenes 1 to 5: the half-read verses, the ignored warning of Mephistopheles, the congealing blood and 'Homo, fuge', each a chance taken knowingly.
Turn to Scene 6 for the case against: 'My heart's so harden'd, I cannot repent', the Good Angel's conditional 'can', and Lucifer arriving in answer to a prayer to Christ.

Use Scene 13 as the test. The Old Man reports grace on offer and Mephistopheles admits he cannot touch a faithful soul; Faustus renews the bond because he is threatened with pain, which is a choice made in fear but still made.
Conclude that the 1604 text is built to keep the question open, and that Faustus's own certainty that he cannot be forgiven is the one position the play marks as a sin.

essayQuestions.question: 'The comic scenes are the play's sharpest commentary on its hero.' How far do you agree?
essayQuestions.focus: Structure, parody and the middle of the play
plan: Acknowledge the old complaint that Scenes 4 and 7 to 12 are padding, possibly not all Marlowe's, and then argue from what they do instead of who wrote them.
Pair Scene 4 with Scene 3: a soul for a shoulder of mutton, a seven-year bond enforced by devils, straight after Faustus offers twenty-four years. The Clown bargains harder.
Pair Robin's stolen book in Scenes 8 and 9 with the books Faustus is given in Scene 5. Both men want sex and drink from magic; only one of them says so.

Show that Faustus's own scenes descend into the same register. The Emperor, the Horse-courser and the grapes are prose, not verse, and his soliloquy in Scene 11 is wedged into a farce about a false leg.
Weigh the limit of the claim: the comedy diagnoses the waste, but it cannot produce the feeling of Scene 14. The sharpest commentary and the deepest are different things.

essayQuestions.question: Discuss the presentation of Mephistopheles and his relationship with Faustus.
essayQuestions.focus: Service, honesty and control
plan: Start with the first exchange in Scene 3, where every assumption Faustus makes is corrected: the spell did not raise him, he serves Lucifer, and he is in hell as he speaks.
Analyse 'Why, this is hell' and 'leave these frivolous demands' as testimony from a witness, and note that the tempter's most effective move is to tell the truth to a man who will not hear it.
Trace the change once the deed is signed: the refused wife, the refused answer about creation, the dagger and 'I arrest thy soul'. Candour gives way to management and then to force.
Consider the language of affection on Faustus's side, 'sweet Mephistophilis', 'for love of thee', and what it suggests about what he wanted from the bargain.
End on the last line of the part: 'Ah, Mephistophilis!' Set out at least two ways of speaking it and what each implies about who has been master.

essayQuestions.question: How does Marlowe use time in Doctor Faustus?
essayQuestions.focus: Dramatic time, the Chorus and the final soliloquy
plan: Establish the contract's arithmetic, twenty-four years for a soul, and show how the Choruses and the short middle scenes let those years vanish almost unnoticed.
Read the brief soliloquy in Scene 11, 'the restless course that time doth run', as the first moment Faustus feels time passing, and note that he answers it by going to sleep.
Examine Scene 14 in detail: the striking clock as a stage effect, the shrinking requests from a year to a day, and the Ovidian line that asks the horses of the night to run slowly.
Show how the verse enacts the pressure, with short lines, exclamations and an hour of stage time compressed into under sixty lines, so the audience experiences time as speeding up.
Conclude that the play's proportions are its argument: the years are spent carelessly in front of us so that the hour can be counted.

discussionQuestions: Mephistopheles tells Faustus the truth about hell before the contract is signed. Why does the play make the devil the most honest character on stage?
Faustus quotes two verses of scripture in his first speech and stops each one halfway. Is this a scholar's mistake, a deliberate choice, or something the play wants us to be unable to decide?
The Good Angel says 'if Faustus can repent'; later versions of the play print 'will'. How much changes with one word?
What, exactly, does Faustus get for his soul? Make a list from the text and compare it with what he says he will do in Scene 1.
Helen never speaks. What would be lost, or given away, if she did?
Does the Epilogue's advice, to wonder at unlawful things without practising them, match the experience of watching the play?

timeline.label: Luther's ninety-five theses at Wittenberg
timeline.detail: The university where Marlowe sets his play became the centre of the Reformation, and of its arguments about grace, faith and the freedom of the will.

timeline.label: A German magician called Faust dies, c. 1540
timeline.detail: A wandering astrologer and conjuror of that name is mentioned in several sixteenth-century German records. Almost nothing about him is certain, and the legend grew after his death.

timeline.label: Christopher Marlowe born in Canterbury
timeline.detail: The son of a shoemaker, baptised in February, two months before Shakespeare.

timeline.label: The fire-ship at Antwerp
timeline.detail: During the Prince of Parma's siege, an explosive ship wrecked his bridge across the Scheldt. Faustus wants 'stranger engines' than 'the fiery keel at Antwerp's bridge', which dates the speech after this event.

timeline.label: The German Faust book printed at Frankfurt
timeline.detail: The Historia von D. Johann Fausten, published by Johann Spies, gathered the legends into one cautionary life. In the same year Marlowe took his Cambridge MA and Tamburlaine reached the London stage.

timeline.label: Earliest surviving edition of the English Faust book
timeline.detail: The translation by 'P. F.' is Marlowe's direct source, down to the grapes and the horse-dealer. An earlier printing may have existed, which is one reason the play cannot be dated firmly.

timeline.label: Marlowe killed at Deptford
timeline.detail: Stabbed on 30 May, aged twenty-nine, days after being called before the Privy Council. None of his plays except Tamburlaine had yet been printed.

timeline.label: First recorded performances
timeline.detail: Philip Henslowe's diary lists the play in the Admiral's Men's repertory at the Rose from the autumn of this year. It was already an old play by then.

timeline.label: Henslowe pays for additions
timeline.detail: William Birde and Samuel Rowley received four pounds for 'adicyones in doctor fostes'. Whether their work survives in the 1616 text is still debated.

timeline.label: The A-text printed
timeline.detail: The first quarto, the shorter version, and the one followed here.

timeline.label: The B-text printed
timeline.detail: A longer version with new comic and papal scenes, a softened vocabulary of oaths, and a title page showing Faustus in his conjuring circle.

timeline.label: Goethe's Faust, Part One
timeline.detail: Goethe's scholar is saved in the end. The contrast with Marlowe's has shaped how both are read.

timeline.label: Alexander Dyce's edition of Marlowe
timeline.detail: Dyce printed the 1604 and 1616 texts separately instead of blending them. His text of the 1604 quarto is the one used for every quotation here.

timeline.label: Thomas Mann's Doktor Faustus
timeline.detail: The pact retold as the life of a German composer, written in exile during and after the Second World War.

places.name: Wittenberg
places.note: Faustus's university and Luther's. The 1604 text spells it 'Wertenberg', and Faustus offers to have it sacked for Helen.

places.name: Stadtroda, Thuringia
places.note: The 'town call'd Rhodes' of the Prologue is Roda, as this town was then known, where the Faust book says he was born to parents 'base of stock'.

places.name: Rome
places.note: Mephistopheles gives a guidebook tour of the seven hills and the Ponte Angelo before the visit shrinks to stealing the Pope's dinner.

places.name: Trier
places.note: The first stop on the aerial tour of Scene 7, 'environ'd round with airy mountain-tops'.

places.name: Naples
places.note: Where Faustus sees 'learned Maro's golden tomb'. Medieval legend made Virgil a magician, so one conjuror visits another.

places.name: Anhalt
places.note: The play's 'Vanholt' is usually identified with this small German principality, a day's ride from Wittenberg. The Duchess gets her grapes here.

places.name: Canterbury
places.note: Marlowe's birthplace. He went from the King's School to Cambridge on a scholarship intended for future clergymen.

places.name: The Rose, Bankside
places.note: Henslowe's playhouse, where the Admiral's Men played Faustus with Edward Alleyn in the part.

related.why: A phrase-by-phrase reading of the Helen speech, in which every image of beauty turns out to be on fire.
Milton's Satan carries his hell within him wherever he flies, which is Mephistopheles's answer in Scene 3 expanded into an epic.
Another man given a prediction by dark powers who hears every warning clearly, and a last act that counts down in the same way.
Shakespeare's magician also rules through a serving spirit and also promises to give up his book, but does it voluntarily and in time.
A later student at a German university who wants forbidden knowledge and cannot bear to look at what it gets him.
Wilde's version of the pact: a soul traded without a contract or a devil, and the same slide from grand appetite to squalor.
Jacobean tragedy a generation on, where a Cardinal ends his life puzzling over a question about hell.

books.title: The Picture of Dorian Gray
books.author: Oscar Wilde
books.setting: London, from a Mayfair studio to the docks, over roughly eighteen years
books.lengthNote: A preface and twenty chapters, of which one contains almost no action at all
books.openingLine: The studio was filled with the rich odour of roses, and when the light summer wind stirred amidst the trees of the garden, there came through the open door the heavy scent of the lilac, or the more delicate perfume of the pink-flowering thorn.
books.summary: A painter finishes the best thing he will ever do, a clever man says something careless about youth in front of the sitter, and the sitter wishes the picture could age instead of him. Wilde then spends twenty chapters watching what a person becomes when consequences are stored somewhere else. The talk is the pleasure of the book and also its subject: almost every disaster in it starts with a remark made to be admired.
books.referenceStyle: chapter, with the 1891 opening cited as Preface

sourceText.label: Standard Ebooks text of The Picture of Dorian Gray — Wilde’s revised 1891 edition
sourceText.note: Wilde’s only novel exists in two authorial forms. This is the twenty-chapter book of 1891 with its preface, not the thirteen-chapter version printed in Lippincott’s Monthly Magazine in 1890.

structure.label: Chapters I-II
structure.title: A portrait, a conversation and a wish
structure.summary: Basil Hallward will not exhibit his best painting because he has put too much of himself into it. Lord Henry meets the sitter anyway and spends an afternoon in a garden explaining that youth is the only thing worth having. By the end of the second chapter Dorian has wished the picture would take the years instead, and Basil’s studio has produced two things it cannot control.

scenes.summary: Basil explains to Lord Henry why the portrait can never be shown; Dorian is announced.
The sermon in the garden, the finished picture, the wish, and Basil offering to destroy the canvas.

structure.label: Chapters III-VIII
structure.title: An actress who stops being able to act
structure.summary: Dorian falls in love with a girl who plays Juliet in a shabby theatre off the Euston Road, and loves her for the parts rather than the person. When love makes her performance sincere and therefore bad, he tells her so in front of her mother and leaves. She kills herself that night, and the mouth of the portrait has changed by morning.

scenes.summary: Lord Henry’s inquiries into Dorian’s parentage; the engagement announced over tea.
The Vanes at home: a mother acting grief, a brother leaving for Australia and a sworn threat.
Sibyl plays badly because she has stopped pretending; Dorian’s speech in the dressing room; a cruel line added to the painted mouth.
The news of her death arrives with the morning post, and Lord Henry converts it into an aesthetic experience over lunch.

structure.label: Chapters IX-XI
structure.title: The picture goes upstairs and eighteen years go past
structure.summary: Dorian has the canvas carried to the disused schoolroom at the top of the house, locks it in and keeps the key. A yellow-bound French novel arrives from Lord Henry, and the narrative loosens into years of collecting — perfumes, jewels, embroideries, portraits of ancestors — with rumours accumulating in the gaps between paragraphs.

scenes.summary: Basil calls to console him, is refused a sight of the portrait, and is refused a drawing of Sibyl.
The frame-maker’s men carry the picture upstairs; the book in the yellow paper cover arrives.
Eighteen years of study, fashion, ritual and rumour, told almost entirely as inventory.

structure.label: Chapters XII-XIV
structure.title: The painter asks to see his own work
structure.summary: Basil comes on the eve of his thirty-eighth birthday to repeat the rumours to his face and to ask him to deny them. Dorian takes him up to the schoolroom instead, shows him the thing he made, and stabs him behind the ear. The next morning a chemist he once knew is blackmailed into destroying the body.

scenes.summary: A meeting in the fog at Grosvenor Square; Basil lists the friends Dorian has ruined.
The lamp held up to the portrait, the prayer, and the knife on the chest behind the door.
A forged note, Alan Campbell’s arrival, and five hours in a locked room with nitric acid.

structure.label: Chapters XV-XVIII
structure.title: A sailor with a long memory, and a shot in a beech wood
structure.summary: Dorian goes from a dinner party to an opium den near the docks, where a woman calls him Prince Charming and Sibyl’s brother hears it. James Vane holds a pistol to his head, is talked out of it by a face that looks twenty, and follows him to the country. A beater’s accident removes the threat and leaves Dorian more frightened than before.

scenes.summary: Lady Narborough’s dinner, then Blue Gate Fields; the woman’s name for him nearly kills him.
Selby Royal, an argument about naming things, and a face at the conservatory window.
Three days indoors, a shooting party, and a body brought in from the covert.

structure.label: Chapters XIX-XX
structure.title: An attempt at goodness, and a knife
structure.summary: Dorian tells Lord Henry he intends to reform and offers a spared country girl as evidence; Lord Henry laughs and denies that a book can poison anybody. Alone that night, Dorian looks for a change in the picture, finds only cunning added to the face, and attacks the canvas with the knife that killed Basil.

scenes.summary: The last conversation: confession offered as a story and refused as impossible.
A walk home, a mirror broken, the portrait unchanged, and a cry heard by the servants.

characters.name: Dorian Gray
characters.role: A young man of fortune with an unusually beautiful face
characters.summary: He is nineteen, orphaned, rich and almost characterless when the book starts, which is exactly why Lord Henry can write on him. What he acquires over eighteen years is not wickedness so much as the habit of treating other people as experiences, and the one thing the novel never lets him have is a consequence he can see.
characters.clue: He is nineteen when a painter finishes him and a lord explains him, and eighteen years later he still looks it.

characters.name: Lord Henry Wotton
characters.role: A titled talker with no occupation
characters.summary: He supplies the theory, takes none of the risk, and is the only major character alive and unmarked at the end. His paradoxes are designed to be quoted rather than acted on, and the novel’s quiet joke is that the one person who lives by them is the one person Lord Henry never expected to be listened to by.
characters.clue: He never does anything in the whole book except talk, and everything that happens in it can be traced to something he said in a garden.

characters.name: Basil Hallward
characters.role: The painter of the portrait
characters.summary: He refuses to exhibit the picture because it shows the feeling of the man who made it rather than the face of the man who sat for it, which is the most honest statement about art in the book. His worship is genuine and useless: he is the only person who tries to ask Dorian a direct moral question, and he is killed for it.
characters.clue: He paints the best thing he will ever do and will not show it to anyone, because it is a portrait of his own feeling rather than of a face.

characters.name: Sibyl Vane
characters.role: An actress at a small theatre off the Euston Road
characters.summary: She plays Juliet, Rosalind and Imogen for a shilling audience, and Dorian loves the succession of heroines rather than the girl performing them. When real feeling makes her a bad actress she becomes worthless to him, and the novel’s sharpest irony is that her sincerity is what he punishes.
characters.clue: She is loved for playing Juliet and Rosalind, and abandoned the night she stops being able to pretend.

characters.name: James Vane
characters.role: Sibyl’s brother, a sailor
characters.summary: He leaves for Australia swearing to kill the gentleman if anything happens to his sister, and returns years later as the one force in the novel that cannot be talked round. He is beaten by the same thing that has protected Dorian throughout — a face too young to belong to the man he is looking for.
characters.clue: He swears an oath on a dreary road before sailing, and comes back eighteen years later to find that the man he wants still looks like a boy.

characters.name: Alan Campbell
characters.role: A chemist, once an intimate friend
characters.summary: He arrives certain that nothing will make him help and leaves having agreed, after Dorian writes a single sentence on a piece of paper. Wilde never says what the sentence contains, and the blank is the most efficient thing in the novel: a reader is handed the mechanics of blackmail without a word of its content.
characters.clue: A scientist who swears he will do nothing, reads one written line, and spends five hours upstairs with a set of chemicals.

characters.name: The portrait
characters.role: Basil’s canvas, kept behind a locked door
characters.summary: It changes first at the mouth, then the hands, then the whole visage, and Dorian visits it the way other people visit a conscience. It is the only character in the novel that keeps an accurate record, and the last two pages establish that it was also the only one telling the truth about what he looked like.
characters.clue: It hangs behind a locked schoolroom door under a Venetian cloth, and it is the only honest record of a man in the whole book.

themes.name: Beauty and surface
themes.summary: The preface announces that those who go beneath the surface do so at their peril, and the plot then buries the truth under a cloth in a locked room. Everyone in the novel makes moral judgements from faces, and everyone is wrong. The book is not an argument that appearances deceive; it is an argument that people would rather they did.
themes.development: A face admired in a studio, a mouth that changes overnight, a murder prevented by looking twenty, and a body identified only by its rings.

themes.name: Influence
themes.summary: Lord Henry claims that all influence is immoral because it stops a person being themselves, and immediately sets about influencing a nineteen-year-old. The novel takes him seriously enough to test the claim: Dorian’s whole life afterwards is an echo of somebody else’s music, which is the objection Lord Henry himself raised.
themes.development: A sermon in a garden in Chapter II, a book sent as a present in Chapter X, and a final conversation in which the teacher denies that anything he said could have had an effect.

themes.name: Art and morality
themes.summary: The preface insists that a book cannot be moral or immoral and that art has no ethical sympathies. The plot then hands Dorian a novel that changes his life and a painting that keeps his moral accounts. Wilde builds a story whose events contradict its own opening statement, and never resolves the disagreement.
themes.development: Aphorisms in the preface, a yellow book in Chapter X, a man poisoned by it in Chapter XI, and Lord Henry’s flat denial in Chapter XIX that such a thing is possible.

themes.name: The double life
themes.summary: Dorian goes from a Mayfair dinner to a den near the docks in the same evening and is received in both. The doubling is spatial as much as moral — a house with a locked upper room, a city with a respectable west and an unwatched east — and he describes the arrangement itself as a pleasure.
themes.development: A locked schoolroom in Chapter X, the calm demeanour noted in Chapter XV, and a country house where the hunted man is a guest with a headache.

themes.name: Youth and time
themes.summary: Lord Henry’s opening speech is about the shortness of youth, and Dorian’s wish is a refusal to be billed for time passing. What the novel shows is that the time still happens: eighteen years go by in one chapter of catalogues, and the man who stopped ageing has also stopped accumulating a life.
themes.development: A warning in a garden, a wish beside an easel, an inventory in Chapter XI, and a dead man of fifty found in evening dress.

themes.name: Conscience and confession
themes.summary: Dorian keeps trying to confess and keeps being prevented — by Lord Henry’s amusement, by Basil’s death, by his own vanity about how the story will sound. The portrait offers him an exact account of himself at any hour, which is what a conscience is, and he responds by locking it upstairs and visiting when the mood takes him.
themes.development: A prayer in front of the canvas in Chapter XIII, a confession offered as gossip in Chapter XIX, and a last look for improvement that finds only cunning.

techniques.name: Epigram and paradox
techniques.definition: A short balanced sentence that sounds like settled wisdom and usually turns a received idea inside out.
techniques.bookDefinition: A short, polished statement that inverts an expected idea in order to be memorable.
techniques.inThisBook: Lord Henry speaks almost entirely in them, and the novel’s method is to let a line that works brilliantly in a drawing room be acted on by somebody who takes it literally.

techniques.name: The portrait as symbol
techniques.definition: An object made to carry the meaning that characters cannot state directly.
techniques.bookDefinition: An object made to carry the meaning that characters cannot state directly.
techniques.inThisBook: The canvas keeps the record: cruelty at the mouth, blood on the hands, cunning in the eyes. It is a conscience with a frame, and it is the only thing in the book Dorian cannot argue with.

techniques.name: The Faustian pact
techniques.definition: A bargain in which something is granted at a price the taker does not fully understand.
techniques.bookDefinition: A bargain in which something is granted at a price the taker does not fully understand.
techniques.inThisBook: Wilde gives no devil, no contract and no witness — only a wish said aloud in a studio, which is granted and then never explained by anybody.

techniques.name: Catalogue
techniques.definition: A list allowed to run on past the point of usefulness, so that the accumulation itself becomes the effect.
techniques.bookDefinition: A long list of objects or names used in place of narrative.
techniques.inThisBook: Chapter XI replaces eighteen years with embroideries, jewels, church vestments and Dorian’s ancestors. The absence of scenes is the point: a life spent collecting leaves nothing that can be told as a story.

techniques.name: Free indirect style
techniques.definition: Third-person narration that slips into a character’s own vocabulary and self-justification.
techniques.bookDefinition: Third-person narration that slips into a character’s own vocabulary and self-justification.
techniques.inThisBook: The prose keeps taking Dorian’s side from inside his head, so that a reader has to notice for themselves when the language of exquisite sensation is describing something squalid.

techniques.name: Aestheticist description
techniques.definition: Dense, sensuous writing about surfaces, colours, scents and materials.
techniques.bookDefinition: Dense, sensuous writing about surfaces, colours, scents and materials.
techniques.inThisBook: The novel opens on roses, lilac and thorn before a person is mentioned, and it returns to perfumes and fabrics whenever the moral pressure rises — the style itself is a way of looking away.

quotations.text: There is no such thing as a moral or an immoral book. Books are well written, or badly written. That is all.
quotations.context: From the preface Wilde added in 1891, after the reviews of the magazine version.
quotations.analysis: This is a reply to specific attacks, printed as if it were a general principle. Set it against Chapter XI, where a book poisons the hero, and against Lord Henry’s denial in Chapter XIX that such a thing could happen: the preface and the plot are arguing with each other on the same pages.

quotations.text: All art is at once surface and symbol. Those who go beneath the surface do so at their peril. Those who read the symbol do so at their peril.
quotations.context: The preface’s last substantial pair of statements before the closing line.
quotations.analysis: The two sentences are identical in shape and cancel each other, which leaves a reader with no safe position from which to interpret. It is also a plot summary: this is a book in which a surface and a symbol are separated from each other, and everyone who looks under the cloth comes off badly.

quotations.text: All art is quite useless.
quotations.context: The final line of the preface, standing alone.
quotations.analysis: Useless here means unable to be put to work, which was the aesthetic movement’s defence against a century that wanted everything to improve somebody. The book that follows is about a work of art doing a job — keeping accounts — and destroying the man it belongs to.

quotations.text: I know you will laugh at me,” he replied, “but I really can’t exhibit it. I have put too much of myself into it.
quotations.speaker: Basil Hallward
quotations.context: Basil explaining why the finished portrait will never be shown.
quotations.analysis: He thinks he is confessing to bad art and he is confessing to love. The line also sets the novel’s central proposition before any magic happens: a portrait can contain a person who is not the sitter, which is what makes the later transfer feel less like a spell than a completion.

quotations.text: But beauty, real beauty, ends where an intellectual expression begins.
quotations.speaker: Lord Henry Wotton
quotations.context: Lord Henry, in the studio, before he has met Dorian.
quotations.analysis: It is said as a joke about clever men’s faces and it is the rule Dorian will live by: to remain beautiful is to remain unmarked by thought. The novel then arranges for a face that never records a thought and a canvas that records every one, and lets the reader decide which is the man.

quotations.text: I have grown to love secrecy. It seems to be the one thing that can make modern life mysterious or marvellous to us. The commonest thing is delightful if one only hides it.
quotations.speaker: Basil Hallward
quotations.context: Basil explaining why he has never told anyone Dorian’s name.
quotations.analysis: The novel’s great theme is stated in the first chapter by the man who will be murdered for wanting things brought into the open. Concealment is presented here as a refinement of pleasure rather than a moral failure, which is the exact argument Dorian will later use about a locked room at the top of a house.

quotations.text: There is no such thing as a good influence, Mr. Gray. All influence is immoral⁠—immoral from the scientific point of view.
quotations.speaker: Lord Henry Wotton
quotations.context: The opening of the speech in the garden, minutes after being introduced.
quotations.analysis: He is establishing his authority by disclaiming it, which is the oldest move a persuader has. From the scientific point of view is decoration — there is no science in the sentence — and the whole novel is the experiment that follows from a man announcing that influence is impossible and then applying it for an hour.

quotations.text: The aim of life is self-development. To realize one’s nature perfectly⁠—that is what each of us is here for.
quotations.speaker: Lord Henry Wotton
quotations.context: The same speech, a few sentences on.
quotations.analysis: It is genuinely liberating and completely unsupervised: a doctrine with no account at all of other people. Wilde gives it to a man who will never test it, and then hands the testing to somebody with money, beauty and eighteen years, which is as close as the novel comes to an argument against its own best lines.

quotations.text: The only way to get rid of a temptation is to yield to it.
quotations.speaker: Lord Henry Wotton
quotations.context: Part of the garden speech, arguing that resistance is what makes desire monstrous.
quotations.analysis: The reasoning around it is medical rather than moral — the body sins once and has done with its sin — and that is the trick. A sentence built to sound like a cure for obsession is in fact a licence, and the novel spends twenty chapters showing that yielding does not get rid of anything.

quotations.text: Nothing can cure the soul but the senses, just as nothing can cure the senses but the soul.
quotations.speaker: Lord Henry Wotton
quotations.context: Said quietly, with a hand on Dorian’s shoulder, in the garden.
quotations.analysis: Dorian repeats this line to himself sixteen chapters later on the way to an opium den, and Wilde prints it twice in that scene to make sure the reader hears where it has ended up. A balanced, harmless-sounding chiasmus becomes a man’s excuse for buying oblivion the night after a murder.

quotations.text: If it were I who was to be always young, and the picture that was to grow old! For that⁠—for that⁠—I would give everything! Yes, there is nothing in the whole world I would not give! I would give my soul for that!
quotations.speaker: Dorian Gray
quotations.context: In front of the finished portrait, after Lord Henry’s speech in the garden.
quotations.analysis: There is no devil, no contract and no witness who understands what has happened: the most consequential sentence in the novel is a tantrum in front of a canvas. Wilde keeps the machinery invisible for the rest of the book, so that a reader can never quite decide whether anything supernatural has occurred or whether Dorian is simply right about himself.

quotations.text: It is the real Dorian Gray⁠—that is all.
quotations.speaker: Lord Henry Wotton
quotations.context: Dismissing Dorian’s outburst as merely the young man showing his true character.
quotations.analysis: He means it as a shrug about temperament, and it turns out to be a literal description of the object on the easel. This is the novel’s method in one line: a piece of drawing-room cleverness is quietly promoted into a fact, and nobody in the room notices it happen.

quotations.text: Harry! Sibyl Vane is sacred!
quotations.speaker: Dorian Gray
quotations.context: Answering Lord Henry’s amused questions about when he will be paying for her.
quotations.analysis: The exclamation marks are the only ones Dorian earns in the whole book, and three chapters later he tells the same girl she has killed his love. Sacred belongs to the vocabulary of worship rather than of affection, which is the flaw: he has cast her as a shrine, and shrines are not allowed to have a bad night.

quotations.text: Yes, Dorian, you will always be fond of me. I represent to you all the sins you have never had the courage to commit.
quotations.speaker: Lord Henry Wotton
quotations.context: At dinner, hours before Sibyl’s performance.
quotations.analysis: He is boasting about being a spectator, and he has the relation exactly backwards — Dorian will commit the sins and Lord Henry will hear about them as anecdotes. The line reads as flirtation on the night it is spoken and as an epitaph by Chapter XX, when the one man who acted is dead and the one who talked is unchanged.

quotations.text: you have killed my love. You used to stir my imagination. Now you don’t even stir my curiosity. You simply produce no effect.
quotations.speaker: Dorian Gray
quotations.context: In the dressing room, after Sibyl has acted Juliet badly for the first time.
quotations.analysis: The three sentences descend from love to imagination to curiosity to effect, ending in the language of a critic rather than a lover. She has just told him that she can no longer act because she has discovered what love is; he replies by explaining that she was only ever a performance he enjoyed.

quotations.text: It was a poisonous book. The heavy odour of incense seemed to cling about its pages and to trouble the brain.
quotations.context: Dorian reads the yellow-backed French novel Lord Henry has sent him.
quotations.analysis: The narration takes Dorian’s side of the argument the preface has just refused: a book here is an atmosphere you breathe rather than a set of propositions you weigh. Wilde never names the novel, which leaves it as a pure idea of a dangerous book — and keeps the preface’s denial technically intact.

quotations.text: Dorian Gray had been poisoned by a book.
quotations.context: In the middle of a paragraph about Renaissance methods of murder.
quotations.analysis: It arrives at the end of a list of poisoned helmets, gloves and pomanders, so the book is filed as one more elegant instrument. Seven words flatly contradict the preface, and the novel simply lets both stand — which is either Wilde’s carelessness or the point of publishing the preface at all.

quotations.text: It is the face of my soul.
quotations.speaker: Dorian Gray
quotations.context: Holding the lamp up to the portrait for Basil, minutes before the murder.
quotations.analysis: He has been asked to deny the rumours and instead produces a physical exhibit, which is a confession made in the only terms he still understands. Basil’s response is to suggest that they pray, and Dorian’s is to reach for a knife — the novel refuses him the one moment in which saying the true thing might have changed anything.

quotations.text: Each of us has heaven and hell in him, Basil
quotations.speaker: Dorian Gray
quotations.context: In the schoolroom, when Basil urges him to pray.
quotations.analysis: It is said with a wild gesture of despair and it is the most ordinary piece of theology in the novel — the one thing Dorian says that Lord Henry could not have taught him. Within a page he has stabbed the man he said it to, which is the book’s way of showing that knowing the doctrine is not the same as having a conscience.

quotations.text: What was that loathsome red dew that gleamed, wet and glistening, on one of the hands, as though the canvas had sweated blood?
quotations.context: The morning after the murder, looking at the portrait before Alan Campbell arrives.
quotations.analysis: Dew is a word for something clean, and the sentence spends three modifiers being beautiful before it says blood. This is the aestheticist prose doing its usual job of looking away, and the detail it will not name outright is the one that has moved from the body downstairs onto a painted hand.

quotations.text: He himself could not help wondering at the calm of his demeanour, and for a moment felt keenly the terrible pleasure of a double life.
quotations.context: At Lady Narborough’s dinner table, the evening after the body has been destroyed.
quotations.analysis: Terrible pleasure is not remorse; it is connoisseurship applied to his own situation. The novel has him admire his own composure from the outside, which is what the portrait does for him structurally — and it explains why he keeps the thing rather than burning it.

quotations.text: The soul is a terrible reality. It can be bought, and sold, and bartered away. It can be poisoned, or made perfect.
quotations.speaker: Dorian Gray
quotations.context: The last conversation with Lord Henry, who has just called the soul a fashionable myth.
quotations.analysis: The pupil corrects the teacher, using the commercial verbs Lord Henry taught him, and Lord Henry laughs. This is the only time anyone in the novel states the plot as a fact to somebody who could still act on it, and it is received as a good remark and nothing else.

quotations.text: You are the type of what the age is searching for, and what it is afraid it has found.
quotations.speaker: Lord Henry Wotton
quotations.context: Praising Dorian for having produced nothing but himself.
quotations.analysis: Afraid it has found is the sharpest thing Lord Henry says, and he says it without noticing. He has spent the novel recommending a life made entirely of sensation, and here he admits that the age which wants such a life is also frightened of the person who actually lives one.

quotations.text: As it had killed the painter, so it would kill the painter’s work, and all that that meant. It would kill the past, and when that was dead, he would be free.
quotations.context: Picking up the knife in front of the portrait on the last night.
quotations.analysis: The reasoning is stated as free indirect thought, so the reader gets Dorian’s logic without a narrator to correct it, and the logic is good — except that he has never worked out which of the two of them is the painting. Kill the past is the wish from Chapter II repeated in the language of a man who has run out of other ideas.

quotations.text: Lying on the floor was a dead man, in evening dress, with a knife in his heart. He was withered, wrinkled, and loathsome of visage. It was not till they had examined the rings that they recognized who it was.
quotations.context: The servants break into the locked room; the last sentences of the novel.
quotations.analysis: The book ends with an identification made from jewellery, because the face — the thing everyone in twenty chapters has judged him by — is no longer evidence of anything. Evening dress is the detail that finishes it: the accounts are settled at last, and he is still dressed for dinner.

atAGlance.label: First published
atAGlance.note: In Lippincott’s Monthly Magazine, in thirteen chapters, and attacked in the press within days.

atAGlance.label: Revised
atAGlance.note: Wilde added six chapters, softened some passages, sharpened others, and put a preface of aphorisms in front of the whole thing.

atAGlance.label: Text used here
atAGlance.note: Twenty chapters and a preface, published in London by Ward, Lock and Co.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.note: Chapter XI covers eighteen years and contains scarcely a scene — a catalogue of jewels, embroideries and ancestors standing in for a life.

criticalViews.position: A Gothic fable with a moral
criticalViews.summary: The oldest reading, and the one Wilde himself offered when defending the book: every excess is punished, and the ending delivers exactly the judgement a Victorian reader would want.
criticalViews.counter: The punishment arrives only in the last two pages, after eighteen years of unbroken pleasure, and Lord Henry, whose ideas they were, is never touched at all.

criticalViews.position: A manifesto for aestheticism, and a test of it
criticalViews.summary: The preface states the case for art without ethical sympathies; the novel then puts that case into the hands of a man with money and a beautiful face. It can be read as Wilde arguing with his own position at full strength on both sides.
criticalViews.counter: A reader can reasonably say the argument is rigged, since the aesthetic life is represented almost entirely by furnishings and dinner parties.

criticalViews.position: A book about coded desire
criticalViews.summary: Basil’s confession that he has put too much of himself into the picture, the unspecified ruin of a series of young men, and Wilde’s own revisions between 1890 and 1891 have made this the dominant modern reading. The 1891 text is measurably more cautious than the magazine version.
criticalViews.counter: The novel’s own vagueness about what Dorian does can carry many meanings, and reducing it to one risks flattening the social range of the rumours Basil actually lists.

criticalViews.position: A novel about celebrity and surface
criticalViews.summary: Dorian’s fame rests on nothing but how he looks; his influence spreads through imitation of his clothes and manner; and he is finally identified by his rings. Read this way, the book is about a person who is entirely an image and knows it.
criticalViews.counter: It underplays the portrait, which is the one thing in the novel insisting that there is an inside for the surface to conceal.

essayQuestions.question: Who is responsible for what Dorian becomes?
essayQuestions.focus: Influence, agency and Lord Henry’s position
plan: Begin with Lord Henry’s own claim that all influence is immoral, and what he does immediately afterwards.
Use Chapter II to show a nineteen-year-old with no formed character being given one in an afternoon.
Turn the argument at Sibyl’s death, which is Dorian’s decision and Lord Henry’s interpretation.
Weigh the yellow book against Lord Henry’s denial in Chapter XIX that a book can affect anybody.
Close on the last chapter, where the attempt at reform fails because Dorian is still performing for an audience.

essayQuestions.question: How does the portrait work as a symbol?
essayQuestions.focus: The canvas, conscience and what the novel makes visible
plan: Establish Basil’s claim in Chapter I that the picture contains the painter rather than the sitter.
Trace the changes in order — mouth, then hands, then the whole visage — and what each one follows.
Read Chapter XIII as the only confession in the book, made by exhibit rather than in words.
Consider the room: a schoolroom, locked, at the top of the house, visited when the mood takes him.
Conclude with the reversal of the last page and what it implies about where the man was all along.

essayQuestions.question: ’The preface and the plot contradict each other.’ Discuss.
essayQuestions.focus: Art, morality and the 1891 revisions
plan: Set out the preface’s claims: no moral or immoral books, no ethical sympathies, all art quite useless.
Put beside them the yellow book in Chapters X and XI, and the flat sentence that Dorian was poisoned by it.
Consider the circumstances: the preface was written in answer to reviews of the 1890 version.
Test whether the contradiction is a failure or a deliberate refusal to settle.
Decide what the ending implies, given that it delivers precisely the moral judgement the preface disowns.

essayQuestions.question: What is the effect of Chapter XI?
essayQuestions.focus: Structure, catalogue and the passing of eighteen years
plan: Describe what the chapter contains: perfumes, music, jewels, embroideries, vestments, ancestors, and almost no events.
Ask what is achieved by spending a chapter on objects at the point where a life should be narrated.
Connect the inventory to Dorian’s habit of treating people as experiences to be collected.
Note where the rumours are placed — between the lists, unattributed and never confirmed.
Weigh the cost: many readers find the chapter inert, and the second half has to work harder because of it.

discussionQuestions: Lord Henry never does anything, and is the only major character unharmed at the end. Is that a failure of justice or the point?
Sibyl becomes a bad actress because she has started to feel something real. What is Wilde saying about art and sincerity?
Wilde never tells us what is in the yellow book, or what Dorian writes on the paper that makes Alan Campbell comply. What do those blanks achieve?
Dorian’s last act is meant to be a reform. Is there any point in the novel where reform was genuinely available to him?
Would you print the preface if you were editing the novel today, knowing it was written in answer to hostile reviews?

timeline.label: Oscar Wilde is born in Dublin
timeline.detail: Son of a surgeon and of the poet who wrote as Speranza.

timeline.label: Walter Pater’s Studies in the History of the Renaissance
timeline.detail: Its conclusion — to burn always with a hard, gem-like flame — is the argument Lord Henry repeats in a garden with the ethics removed.

timeline.label: Huysmans publishes A rebours
timeline.detail: The decadent French novel usually identified with the yellow-backed book Lord Henry sends; Wilde declined to confirm it.

timeline.label: The novel appears in Lippincott’s Monthly Magazine
timeline.detail: Thirteen chapters, printed in the July issue, and denounced in several London papers as a book for outlawed noblemen.

timeline.label: The revised book edition
timeline.detail: Published by Ward, Lock and Co. with six new chapters, a preface of aphorisms, and the James Vane plot added to give the second half a pursuer.

timeline.label: Intentions and Lord Arthur Savile’s Crime also appear
timeline.detail: Wilde’s most productive year as a prose writer, immediately before he turned to the stage.

timeline.label: The Importance of Being Earnest opens at the St James’s Theatre
timeline.detail: In February, with Wilde at the height of his fame and three months from the first trial.

timeline.label: The novel is used as evidence in court
timeline.detail: Passages were read out and Wilde was cross-examined on them during the libel action he brought against the Marquess of Queensberry.

timeline.label: De Profundis is written in Reading Gaol
timeline.detail: A long letter to Lord Alfred Douglas, and Wilde’s own account of a life lived for sensation.

timeline.label: Wilde dies in Paris
timeline.detail: At the Hôtel d’Alsace, aged forty-six, three years after his release.

timeline.label: Albert Lewin’s film for MGM
