timeline.detail: Shot in black and white with the portrait revealed in colour — the best-known of many attempts to show what Wilde only describes.

places.name: Grosvenor Square, Mayfair
places.note: Dorian’s house, with the locked schoolroom at the top of it.

places.name: Curzon Street
places.note: Lord Henry’s address, where he is nearly always at home at five o’clock.

places.name: Euston Road
places.note: The Vanes’ shabby lodgings, and the theatre district where Sibyl plays Juliet for a shilling audience.

places.name: Covent Garden
places.note: Where Dorian walks at dawn after leaving Sibyl, among carts of lilies.

places.name: Blue Gate Fields, Shadwell
places.note: The docks district of the opium dens, where a woman calls him Prince Charming and Sibyl’s brother hears it.

places.name: Paris
places.note: Basil’s destination on the night he is killed, and the city of the yellow book and of Wilde’s last years.

related.why: The same decade’s other story of a respectable Londoner with a second life and a locked room, and the same refusal to specify the pleasures.
Wilde four years later, using the double life for comedy instead — Bunbury is the same arrangement with nothing at stake.
Published six years afterwards, and the other 1890s novel in which a beautiful surface conceals something that must be dealt with in a sealed room.
The earlier study of a maker destroyed by what he has brought into being, and of a creation that outlives its creator.
James’s novella of the same period, built on the same principle that what is never named is more disturbing than what is described.

books.title: Dracula
books.author: Bram Stoker
books.setting: Transylvania, Whitby, Purfleet, Hampstead and London, then the Danube and the Borgo Pass
books.lengthNote: Twenty-seven chapters and a closing note, with no narrator outside the documents
books.openingLine: 3 May. Bistritz.—Left Munich at 8:35 p.m., on 1st May, arriving at Vienna early next morning; should have arrived at 6:46, but train was an hour late.
books.summary: A solicitor’s clerk goes to Transylvania to complete a property purchase and finds his client is not leaving the country alone. Stoker tells the whole thing in journals, letters, telegrams, ships’ logs, newspaper cuttings and phonograph cylinders, so the reader assembles the danger months before the characters manage to compare notes. The hunt is finally won by filing: Mina types the papers into order, and the order shows them where he has gone.
books.referenceStyle: chapter, with the closing section given as Note

sourceText.label: Standard Ebooks text of Dracula
sourceText.note: Chapters are numbered but untitled in the original; the closing section is headed Note. Stoker’s characters date their entries by day and month and never give a year.

structure.label: Chapters I-IV
structure.title: A business trip that turns into an imprisonment
structure.summary: Harker records meals, train times and local customs with a clerk’s precision, and keeps recording them as the food becomes strange, the peasants press crucifixes on him and his host turns out to cast no reflection. The documentary habit is what makes the horror land: nothing is asserted, everything is minuted.

scenes.summary: The journey through Bistritz and the Borgo Pass; Dracula’s welcome at the threshold; the shaving mirror.
The Count’s history of his race, the crawling descent of the wall, and the three women in the unused room.
Fifty boxes of earth, the letters Harker is forced to post-date, and his climb down to escape.

structure.label: Chapters V-VIII
structure.title: Letters between two women, and a ship that arrives steering itself
structure.summary: The novel switches to Lucy and Mina’s correspondence, three proposals of marriage in one day, and a seaside holiday. Then a storm drives an empty Russian schooner onto the sands at Whitby with its dead captain lashed to the wheel, and a large dog leaps ashore. Lucy starts walking in her sleep.

scenes.summary: Lucy’s three proposals, Seward’s phonograph diary, Renfield’s ledger of flies and spiders, and the Whitby churchyard.
The cutting from the Dailygraph and the Demeter’s log, kept until the last crewman is gone.
Lucy found on the seat above the harbour with two small punctures; Mina is called to Budapest to marry Jonathan.

structure.label: Chapters IX-XIII
structure.title: Four transfusions and a funeral that does not hold
structure.summary: Seward cannot account for anaemia without blood loss and sends for his old teacher. Van Helsing knows at once, treats with garlic and transfusion, and is defeated four times by a household that keeps tidying the flowers away. Lucy dies, is buried, and children on Hampstead Heath begin coming home with small wounds.

scenes.summary: Van Helsing arrives; the first transfusions; the garlic that a well-meaning mother removes from the room.
The wolf Bersicker, Mrs Westenra’s death, and Lucy’s last change of voice at the moment of dying.
The funeral, the newspaper reports of the bloofer lady, and Van Helsing’s proposal to open the tomb.

structure.label: Chapters XIV-XVIII
structure.title: Mina types the papers, and a scattered case becomes one story
structure.summary: The novel’s real turning point is clerical. Mina transcribes Jonathan’s shorthand, copies Seward’s cylinders, and puts every document into one chronological sequence, at which point five people can finally see what the reader has seen since Whitby. Lucy is dealt with in her tomb, and the group agrees to hunt.

scenes.summary: Mina’s transcription; Van Helsing reads Jonathan’s journal; the tomb is found empty and then occupied.
The woman in the churchyard, the child she carries, and what is done at the tomb by daylight.
The papers are brought together at Purfleet; Van Helsing sets out what a vampire can and cannot do.

structure.label: Chapters XIX-XXIII
structure.title: Fifty boxes, one asylum window, and the price of leaving Mina out
structure.summary: The men decide to protect Mina by excluding her from the work, and the decision is what exposes her. Renfield is beaten to death for refusing an invitation; upstairs, the group breaks in on a scene that Seward describes and Mina afterwards has to live with. She is marked on the forehead by the communion wafer.

scenes.summary: Carfax is sterilised box by box; Mina is kept from the meetings and begins to sleep heavily.
Renfield’s confession and death; the scene in the Harkers’ bedroom; the burn on Mina’s forehead.
Piccadilly, the last box, and Dracula’s promise that his revenge has only started.

structure.label: Chapters XXIV-XXVII and the Note
structure.title: A chase by timetable, and a record nobody could produce in court
structure.summary: Mina’s hypnotic trances give the group a compass and her own condition gives them a clock. They work out the route by shipping schedules and river maps, split into parties, and reach the castle road as the sun goes down. The closing note, written seven years later, admits that not one of the papers is an original.

scenes.summary: Mina is hypnotised at dawn and dusk; the party divides for Varna and then Galatz.
The river journey, the horse-borne pursuit, and Van Helsing and Mina crossing the last miles alone.
The three women dealt with at the castle, the fight at the gate, Quincey’s death, and a postscript about proof.

characters.name: Count Dracula
characters.role: A Transylvanian boyar, and a purchaser of London property
characters.summary: He appears in person in perhaps a dozen scenes and is offstage for most of the book, which is why he works. He is a historian of his own family, a careful reader of Bradshaw and the Law List, and his invasion of England is carried out by conveyancing, shipping agents and carters.
characters.clue: He studies English from books until his accent is perfect, buys a ruined estate by post, and packs fifty boxes of his own soil for the journey.

characters.name: Jonathan Harker
characters.role: Newly qualified solicitor, the novel’s first narrator
characters.summary: He goes east to complete a purchase and keeps taking notes after the notes stop being professional — recipes, train times, then the fact that his host has no reflection. His shorthand journal is the document everything else is later measured against, and for four months nobody believes a word of it, including him.
characters.clue: He asks the waiter for a paprika recipe to send home, and carries on making entries in the same notebook while climbing down a castle wall.

characters.name: Mina Harker
characters.role: Assistant schoolmistress, then the hunt’s archivist
characters.summary: She learns shorthand and typewriting to be useful to her husband and ends up as the only person who can see the whole case, because she is the one who puts it in order. The men then decide to protect her by leaving her out, and every disaster in the second half follows from that decision.
characters.clue: She practises stenography to help her fiancé, and it is her chronological typescript, not anyone’s courage, that shows five men where the enemy has gone.

characters.name: Lucy Westenra
characters.role: Mina’s friend, engaged to Arthur Holmwood
characters.summary: She receives three proposals in one day and asks in a letter why a girl cannot marry three men. The novel then spends five chapters draining her, killing her, burying her and killing her again, and the second death is carried out by the man she was going to marry with the other two watching.
characters.clue: Three men propose to her on the same day, and all three of them give her their blood before the year is out.

relationships.label: proposed to by, and patient of

characters.name: Professor Abraham Van Helsing
characters.role: Dutch physician, lawyer and philosopher, Seward’s old teacher
characters.summary: He arrives with a diagnosis he refuses to state, which is both a medical judgement and a narrative device. His English is wrong in a consistent and characterised way, and his argument against his own profession — that science wants to explain everything and dismisses whatever it cannot — is the book’s defence of its own plot.
characters.clue: A Dutch doctor with several degrees and shaky English, who treats a wasting illness with garlic flowers and will not say why until he has been proved right.

characters.name: Dr John Seward
characters.role: Head of the asylum next to Carfax
characters.summary: He dictates his diary onto wax cylinders, which is both the most modern thing in the novel and the reason his account cannot be searched until Mina types it out. He is a careful clinician who keeps a man in a cell while failing entirely to hear what the man is telling him.
characters.clue: He records his private grief on phonograph cylinders, and does not notice that the lunatic in his care is announcing the neighbour’s arrival.

characters.name: R. M. Renfield
characters.role: A patient at Seward’s asylum
characters.summary: He eats flies, then feeds them to spiders, then the spiders to sparrows, and keeps a ledger of the lives he has accumulated. He is the only person in England who knows Dracula has arrived, and he is the only person nobody thinks to ask. He dies for refusing to let his master in a second time.
characters.clue: He keeps an account book of the flies, spiders and birds he has eaten, and is beaten to death for changing his mind about an invitation.

characters.name: Quincey Morris
characters.role: A Texan, one of Lucy’s three suitors
characters.summary: He talks in a stage American that even the other characters notice, proposes to Lucy with a speech about prairie fires, and is the only member of the party who reacts to a wolf in the grounds by buying Winchesters. He dies at the castle gate and the last child born to the group carries his name.
characters.clue: The one American in the party, who answers a supernatural threat by buying rifles, and whose name is given to the child born on the anniversary of his death.

themes.name: Blood and contagion
themes.summary: Blood in this novel is property, inheritance and infection at once. Dracula lectures Harker on the blood of his race before anyone has been bitten; Lucy receives blood from four men in one week; and the final horror at the Harkers’ bedside is a forced exchange rather than a theft. Nothing here stays inside one body.
themes.development: A boast about ancestry in Chapter III, a transfusion ward in Chapters IX to XII, and a scene in Chapter XXI that the novel’s own narrator can barely bring himself to write down.

themes.name: Modernity against the old world
themes.summary: Stoker arms his hunters with the newest equipment available in 1897: shorthand, a typewriter, a phonograph, telegrams, blood transfusion, Kodak photographs and railway timetables. The joke is that none of it detects anything. What finally works is the oldest office skill in the book, which is putting papers in date order.
themes.development: Harker’s shorthand in Chapter I, Seward’s cylinders in Chapter V, and Mina’s typescript in Chapter XIV, which converts a pile of private records into a usable case.

themes.name: Arrival and invasion
themes.summary: The threat enters England legally. A solicitor conveys the property, a shipping firm moves the cargo, and a carter delivers the boxes to Purfleet for a fee. Late-Victorian anxieties about what might come in through the docks are given a shape that is less an army than a change of address.
themes.development: A purchase completed in Chapter II, a ship that reaches Whitby in Chapter VII, and a chase in the last four chapters that simply reverses the route.

themes.name: Women, desire and protection
themes.summary: The novel separates its two women and treats them very differently. Lucy’s appetite is punished in a tomb; Mina is useful and is therefore shielded from the work, which is exactly how she is reached. The men’s protectiveness is presented as chivalry and shown, repeatedly, to be the tactical error that costs most.
themes.development: Lucy’s question about marrying three men, the three women in the castle, and the decision in Chapter XVIII to keep Mina out of the council.

themes.name: Faith, science and what counts as knowledge
themes.canonicalName: Faith, science and what counts as knowledge
themes.summary: Seward can only see a case of anaemia because anaemia is what his training allows. Van Helsing’s method is to keep an open mind past the point where his profession would close it, and to use a communion wafer and a garlic flower as instruments. The book sets belief and evidence against each other and then makes them cooperate.
themes.development: Lanyon-like scepticism in Chapters IX to XII, Van Helsing’s lecture on the limits of science in Chapter XIV, and his formal statement of the case in Chapter XVIII.

themes.name: Records, proof and the closing doubt
themes.canonicalName: Records, proof and the closing doubt
themes.summary: Everything the reader knows arrives as a document, and the last page points out that not one of those documents is an original. Seven years after the events the survivors hold a bundle of typescript that would convince nobody, and the novel’s final gesture is to refuse to ask for belief at all.
themes.development: Harker’s fear in Chapter IV that his journal will never be read, Mina’s transcriptions in the middle chapters, and the admission in the Note that there is hardly one authentic document among them.

techniques.name: Documentary form
techniques.definition: A narrative assembled entirely from papers, recordings and cuttings, with no outside narrator.
techniques.bookDefinition: A narrative assembled entirely from papers, recordings and cuttings, with no outside narrator.
techniques.inThisBook: Journals, letters, telegrams, a ship’s log, a newspaper cutting, phonograph cylinders and a memorandum. Even the moment of the Count’s death is somebody’s diary entry written afterwards.

techniques.name: Multiple narrators
techniques.definition: Several first-person accounts, each limited to what that writer knew at the time.
techniques.bookDefinition: Several first-person accounts, each limited to what that writer knew at the time.
techniques.inThisBook: Seven or eight hands write this novel, and their ignorance is the plot: Harker knows what the Demeter was carrying and cannot tell Seward, who is treating the result.

techniques.name: Dramatic irony
techniques.definition: The reader knowing more than the characters, because of how the material is arranged.
techniques.bookDefinition: The reader knowing more than the characters, because of how the material is arranged.
techniques.inThisBook: Stoker prints the Demeter’s log immediately before Lucy’s sleepwalking, so a reader watches a diagnosis being missed for five chapters by people with all the information in separate drawers.

techniques.name: Idiolect
techniques.definition: A speech habit belonging to one character alone, so that they can be recognised before they are named.
techniques.bookDefinition: Giving each character a distinct and consistent way of speaking.
techniques.inThisBook: Van Helsing’s broken syntax, Quincey’s Texan idiom, the Whitby fishermen’s Yorkshire and Renfield’s ledger-keeping precision make the documents identifiable before a heading names them.

techniques.name: Gothic setting
techniques.definition: Landscape and architecture used to generate dread and to trap characters.
techniques.bookDefinition: Landscape and architecture used to generate dread and to trap characters.
techniques.inThisBook: Stoker puts the castle in the first quarter and then relocates the Gothic to a ruined Essex estate, a Hampstead tomb and a Piccadilly house with the dust sheets still on.

techniques.name: Inventory and catalogue
techniques.definition: A list allowed to run on past the point of usefulness, so that the accumulation itself becomes the effect.
techniques.bookDefinition: Lists of objects, dates and quantities used to make the impossible feel administrative.
techniques.inThisBook: Fifty boxes counted and recounted, sailing dates, train timetables, Renfield’s tally of flies: the horror is tracked by arithmetic, and arithmetic is what eventually finds it.

quotations.text: Welcome to my house! Enter freely and of your own will!
quotations.speaker: Count Dracula
quotations.context: The Count greets Harker at the castle door, standing perfectly still.
quotations.analysis: It sounds like hospitality and it is a legal condition: the folklore rule that a vampire must be invited is being satisfied in advance, and Harker signs up to it by walking through the door. The Count makes no move to meet him, which the text notes twice — the crossing has to be the guest’s own act.

quotations.text: Listen to them⁠—the children of the night. What music they make!
quotations.speaker: Count Dracula
quotations.context: Wolves howling outside the castle during Harker’s first supper.
quotations.analysis: The possessive is doing quiet work — them, not the wolves — and the Count is watching his guest’s face to see whether the phrase registers. What follows is an apology for the tastes of a hunter, which is the second time in a page he has explained himself in terms that only make sense later.

quotations.text: I am all in a sea of wonders. I doubt; I fear; I think strange things, which I dare not confess to my own soul.
quotations.speaker: Jonathan Harker
quotations.context: A journal entry written in the castle, before he understands he is a prisoner.
quotations.analysis: Three clauses, each shorter than the last, in a journal that has so far been full of train times and paprika. The diary is the only person he can talk to, and the last clause admits that he is censoring even that — the document the entire novel rests on is being written by a man who dare not write everything down.

quotations.text: We are in Transylvania; and Transylvania is not England. Our ways are not your ways, and there shall be to you many strange things.
quotations.speaker: Count Dracula
quotations.context: Explaining away one of the household’s peculiarities to his guest.
quotations.analysis: He is telling the truth and using it as cover, which is his usual method. The sentence also states the book’s geography as a rule, so that the second half — in which the ways of Transylvania are unloaded at Whitby by a shipping agent — reads as a violation of terms the Count himself set out.

quotations.text: Blood is too precious a thing in these days of dishonourable peace; and the glories of the great races are as a tale that is told.
quotations.speaker: Count Dracula
quotations.context: The end of the Count’s long account of his family’s wars.
quotations.analysis: He has spent several pages using blood to mean lineage, and here he prices it. The double sense is set up before a single drop is taken, so that every later transfusion carries an argument about descent as well as a medical procedure. A tale that is told is from the Psalms, and he means it as a complaint about being finished.

quotations.text: This man belongs to me! Beware how you meddle with him, or you’ll have to deal with me.
quotations.speaker: Count Dracula
quotations.context: Driving the three women away from Harker in the disused room.
quotations.analysis: Harker has been lying still with his eyes almost shut, waiting, and his own journal admits to a wicked longing. The Count’s intervention is a rescue and a claim of ownership in the same sentence, and the vocabulary is commercial — belongs, deal — which is how he handles everything, including the Essex property.

quotations.text: The last I saw of Count Dracula was his kissing his hand to me; with a red light of triumph in his eyes, and with a smile that Judas in hell might be proud of.
quotations.speaker: Jonathan Harker
quotations.context: Harker watches the Count leave the castle, having been made to write letters dated weeks in advance.
quotations.analysis: The triumph is over paperwork: the Count has just obtained three post-dated letters that will keep anyone from looking for Harker until long after he is dead. Stoker gives the villain his most theatrical exit in the novel at the exact moment his weapon is a set of forged dates.

quotations.text: God and the Blessed Virgin and the saints help a poor ignorant soul trying to do his duty.
quotations.speaker: The captain of the Demeter
quotations.context: The last entry in the ship’s log, found lashed to the wheel with the captain’s body.
quotations.analysis: The log is the purest example of the novel’s method: a form designed for positions, weather and watches, kept up by a man whose crew is vanishing one at a time. He records the facts he is permitted to record and can name nothing else, and the empty ship reaches Whitby carrying both its cargo and an official document that proves something happened without being able to say what.

quotations.text: The blood is the life! The blood is the life!
quotations.speaker: R. M. Renfield
quotations.context: Renfield, having cut Seward’s wrist and licked the floor, is taken away by the attendants.
quotations.analysis: He is quoting Deuteronomy, and Seward files it as a symptom. Every element of the diagnosis the doctors need is in this room — an appetite for blood, a servant who responds to a master, a man who knows the neighbouring house is occupied — and it is all written down under the heading of a case note.

quotations.text: There are darknesses in life, and there are lights; you are one of the lights.
quotations.speaker: Professor Van Helsing
quotations.context: Van Helsing to Mina, after reading her transcription of Jonathan’s journal.
quotations.analysis: He says it to the person who has just done the filing, not to anyone who has done anything brave, and it is worth setting beside the decision four chapters later to keep her out of the council. The novel praises Mina in the language of light and then removes her from the room where the work is done.

quotations.text: I shall get my typewriter this very hour and begin transcribing. Then we shall be ready for other eyes if required.
quotations.speaker: Mina Harker
quotations.context: Mina resolves to type out Jonathan’s shorthand journal.
quotations.analysis: This is the sentence on which the second half of the novel turns, and it is about office equipment. Ready for other eyes is the whole problem stated in five words: private records held by separate people cannot be compared, and a hunt that has failed for three hundred pages becomes possible the moment somebody makes copies.

quotations.text: Ah, it is the fault of our science that it wants to explain all; and if it explain not, then it says there is nothing to explain.
quotations.speaker: Professor Van Helsing
quotations.context: Rebuking Seward for refusing to believe what he has seen.
quotations.analysis: The broken grammar makes the argument sound folkloric, but it is a precise objection: a method that treats the unexplained as the non-existent will always return the answer it started with. Stoker gives his most modern characters the newest instruments in the world and then has the oldest man in the room point out that instruments only find what they are built to find.

quotations.text: the consensus of their excuses is that they had been with a “bloofer lady.”
quotations.context: A Westminster Gazette cutting about children going missing on Hampstead Heath.
quotations.analysis: The newspaper reports the phrase as a childish fashion and prints it in inverted commas to keep its distance. Bloofer is a small child’s attempt at beautiful, so the most frightening development in the novel reaches the reader as a piece of quaint local colour in a light news column — which is exactly how it reaches the characters.

quotations.text: She seemed like a nightmare of Lucy as she lay there; the pointed teeth, the bloodstained, voluptuous mouth⁠—which it made one shudder to see⁠—the whole carnal and unspiritual appearance, seeming like a devilish mockery of Lucy’s sweet purity.
quotations.speaker: Dr John Seward
quotations.context: In the Westenra tomb, before Arthur drives the stake.
quotations.analysis: Seward’s vocabulary gives the game away: voluptuous and carnal are not clinical terms, and the man writing is one of the suitors she refused. The novel keeps describing the changed Lucy in the language of unacceptable desire rather than of predation, which is why so much criticism has fixed on this scene.

quotations.text: you would in time, when you had died, have become nosferatu, as they call it in Eastern Europe, and would all time make more of those Un-Deads that so have fill us with horror.
quotations.speaker: Professor Van Helsing
quotations.context: Explaining to Arthur why Lucy’s kiss would have destroyed him.
quotations.analysis: The condition is described as an inheritance that spreads rather than as a curse on an individual, and the reasoning is epidemiological: one case makes more cases, indefinitely. Van Helsing borrows a foreign word to name it because English medicine has none, which is the novel’s argument about the limits of a vocabulary in one sentence.

quotations.text: There are such beings as vampires; some of us have evidence that they exist.
quotations.speaker: Professor Van Helsing
quotations.context: Opening the formal briefing at the asylum, with all the papers in order.
quotations.analysis: He states it as a finding rather than a revelation, and the second clause does the work: not belief, evidence, and some of us, meaning the people in this room who have read the typescript. The supernatural is admitted to the novel by the same procedure a court would use.

quotations.text: We have on our side power of combination⁠—a power denied to the vampire kind; we have sources of science; we are free to act and think; and the hours of the day and the night are ours equally.
quotations.speaker: Professor Van Helsing
quotations.context: Setting out the group’s advantages before the hunt begins.
quotations.analysis: Combination is a late-Victorian word for organised collective action, and it names the thing the novel actually values: not courage but committee work, shared papers and a division of labour. The Count is enormously strong and entirely alone, and the book’s proposition is that the second fact beats the first.

quotations.text: Unclean! Unclean! Even the Almighty shuns my polluted flesh! I must bear this mark of shame upon my forehead until the Judgment Day.
quotations.speaker: Mina Harker
quotations.context: After the communion wafer burns her forehead.
quotations.analysis: The cry is from Leviticus, where it is what a leper is required to shout to warn others off, and Mina applies it to herself before anyone else can. The novel has her take up the vocabulary of ritual pollution for something done to her while she was drugged and held down, and nobody in the room corrects her.

quotations.text: My revenge is just begun! I spread it over centuries, and time is on my side.
quotations.speaker: Count Dracula
quotations.context: Cornered in the Piccadilly house, before escaping through the back.
quotations.analysis: It is the only speech he makes to the whole group, and the boast is about duration rather than strength. Everything the hunters have — telegrams, timetables, a chartered launch — is built for speed, and he answers with centuries. The last four chapters are the novel testing which of the two is right.

quotations.text: Now God be thanked that all has not been in vain! See! the snow is not more stainless than her forehead!
quotations.speaker: Professor Van Helsing
quotations.context: At the moment the Count crumbles, with Mina watching.
quotations.analysis: The victory is announced as a fact about a woman’s complexion. Van Helsing checks Mina’s forehead before he checks anything else, and the novel closes its plot by restoring her to a state of visible purity — which tells a reader a good deal about what was thought to have been lost.

quotations.text: We were struck with the fact, that in all the mass of material of which the record is composed, there is hardly one authentic document; nothing but a mass of typewriting
quotations.speaker: Jonathan Harker
quotations.context: Seven years later, taking the papers out of the safe.
quotations.analysis: The book’s last move is to withdraw its own evidence. Mina’s typing saved their lives by making the records comparable, and it destroyed them as proof by leaving no originals — the same act did both. A novel that has spent six hundred pages insisting on documentation ends by admitting it has none.

quotations.text: We want no proofs; we ask none to believe us!
quotations.speaker: Professor Van Helsing
quotations.context: The last speech in the novel, with the Harkers’ son on his knee.
quotations.analysis: He turns a fatal evidential weakness into a refusal, and then changes the subject to the boy’s mother. It is a generous ending and an evasive one, and it leaves the reader holding a book that has just declined to argue for its own truth.

atAGlance.label: First published
atAGlance.note: In London by Archibald Constable and Company, in yellow cloth with red lettering.

atAGlance.label: Form
atAGlance.note: Journals in shorthand, letters, telegrams, a ship’s log, newspaper cuttings, a phonograph diary and a memorandum — no outside narrator at any point.

atAGlance.label: Research
atAGlance.note: Stoker’s working papers show the name and the Transylvanian setting arriving late, over an existing plan.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.value: Twenty-seven chapters and a closing note
atAGlance.note: Roughly four in the castle, ten in England, and the rest a chase back the way Harker came.

criticalViews.position: A novel about invasion and the foreign
criticalViews.summary: The most established modern reading takes the Count’s careful, legal arrival — a purchase, a shipment, a change of address — as a late-Victorian anxiety about what might enter a confident empire through its own ports and offices.
criticalViews.counter: It can make the book tidier than it is. The Count’s most effective allies are English professionals doing their jobs properly, and the novel is at least as interested in them.

criticalViews.position: A novel about women and desire
criticalViews.summary: Criticism has long contrasted Lucy, whose appetite is punished in a tomb by the men who wanted her, with Mina, who is useful and is therefore shielded. The vocabulary Seward reaches for in the tomb scene is not medical, and the book’s own language keeps admitting it.
criticalViews.counter: Mina is also the most capable person in the novel, and the plot’s turning point is her clerical work rather than anyone’s heroism, which complicates any simple account of Stoker’s women.

criticalViews.position: A novel about information
criticalViews.summary: On this reading the subject is how a scattered group turns private records into shared knowledge. Nothing supernatural is defeated until the papers are copied and dated, and the closing note’s admission that no original survives is the book’s real last twist.
criticalViews.counter: The approach can leave the horror out. The scenes readers remember are in a tomb and a bedroom, not in a typing room.

criticalViews.position: The Count as a figure who barely appears
criticalViews.summary: Dracula speaks in only a handful of scenes and is absent from the middle of his own novel. Much of his power comes from being reconstructed out of other people’s documents, which is also why every adaptation has had to invent him.
criticalViews.counter: The absence may be a limitation rather than a design: Stoker’s notes show a good deal of material planned for the Count that never reached the page.

essayQuestions.question: What does Stoker gain by telling the whole novel in documents?
essayQuestions.focus: Form, dramatic irony and the closing note
plan: Establish the range: shorthand journal, letters, telegrams, a ship’s log, cuttings, phonograph cylinders and a memorandum.
Show how the arrangement creates irony — the Demeter’s log printed before anyone in England can read it.
Use Mina’s transcription in Chapter XIV as the hinge on which the plot turns.
Consider what the form costs: the Count can only be seen through people who fear or misunderstand him.
Close on the Note, where the survivors admit that not one of the papers is authentic.

essayQuestions.question: How does the novel treat Lucy and Mina differently, and why?
essayQuestions.focus: Women, desire and protection
plan: Begin with Lucy’s letter about three proposals, and the novel’s response to the question she asks in it.
Trace the medical treatment of Lucy as a body acted on by four men in a week.
Read the tomb scene for its vocabulary rather than its events.
Set against it Mina’s usefulness, and the Chapter XVIII decision to exclude her from the council.
Ask whether the ending restores Mina or simply certifies her, and on whose authority.

essayQuestions.question: ’The most modern people in the novel are the least effective.’ Discuss.
essayQuestions.focus: Science, technology and Van Helsing’s method
plan: Inventory the modern equipment: shorthand, typewriter, phonograph, telegrams, transfusion, timetables.
Show Seward’s clinical training producing a diagnosis that cannot include the evidence.
Use Van Helsing’s objection in Chapter XIV about what science does with the unexplained.
Note that the decisive tools are in the end organisational rather than scientific.
Weigh the ending: the Count is destroyed by knives in the open air, after weeks of paperwork.

essayQuestions.question: How does Stoker create dread without showing very much?
essayQuestions.focus: Setting, absence and the Count’s brief appearances
plan: Count the scenes in which Dracula is actually present, and note how few they are.
Examine the castle chapters for the technique of accumulating small impossibilities in a factual register.
Use the Demeter’s log as the clearest case of horror generated by an official document’s limits.
Follow the Gothic as it moves from a castle to an Essex estate, a Hampstead tomb and a Piccadilly drawing room.
Conclude with the effect on adaptation: everything visual about the Count has had to come from outside the book.

discussionQuestions: Renfield tells the truth for several chapters and nobody listens. What would it have cost Seward to take him seriously?
Mina is excluded from the council in order to protect her, and the exclusion is what exposes her. Is the novel aware of this?
Dracula appears in very few scenes. Does that make him more frightening or simply thinner?
The last page says the papers would convince nobody. Why end a documentary novel by discrediting its own documents?
Almost every screen Dracula comes from the 1924 play rather than the book. What does the novel look like if you forget the cloak?

timeline.label: Polidori’s The Vampyre is published
timeline.detail: Begun during the same 1816 Geneva summer as Frankenstein, and the story that made the vampire an aristocrat rather than a peasant revenant.

timeline.label: Bram Stoker is born in Dublin
timeline.detail: He was bedridden until about the age of seven, and later became an athlete at Trinity College.

timeline.label: Sheridan Le Fanu’s Carmilla appears in In a Glass Darkly
timeline.detail: A fellow Dubliner’s vampire novella, and the closest predecessor to Stoker’s handling of desire and illness.

timeline.label: Stoker becomes business manager of the Lyceum Theatre
timeline.detail: Twenty-seven years working for Henry Irving, whose stage presence is often heard behind the Count’s manners.

timeline.label: Stoker begins his working notes
timeline.detail: The surviving papers show a planned vampire novel taking shape before the name Dracula or the Transylvanian setting arrives.

timeline.label: A summer at Whitby
timeline.detail: The harbour, the abbey steps, the churchyard seat and the Russian schooner story all reached the novel from this visit.

timeline.label: Dracula published by Archibald Constable and Company
timeline.detail: A staged reading was given at the Lyceum in the same year, chiefly to secure the dramatic copyright.

timeline.label: Stoker dies in London
timeline.detail: He had written a dozen other novels, none of which is much read.

timeline.label: Murnau’s Nosferatu
timeline.detail: An unauthorised adaptation with the names changed; Stoker’s widow sued, and the court ordered the negatives destroyed.

timeline.label: Hamilton Deane’s authorised stage version opens
timeline.detail: At the Grand Theatre, Derby; the evening dress and the cloak with a standing collar are the play’s inventions, not the novel’s.

timeline.label: Universal’s Dracula with Bela Lugosi
timeline.detail: Adapted from the stage version rather than the book, and the reason most readers arrive expecting a very different Count.

places.name: Bistritz
places.note: Where Harker sleeps before the last stage, and where the landlady presses a crucifix on him.

places.name: The Borgo Pass
places.note: The road where the Count’s calèche takes over from the public coach, exactly at midnight.

places.name: Whitby
places.note: The harbour the Demeter runs into, and the churchyard seat where Lucy is found.

places.name: Purfleet
places.note: Carfax, the estate bought by post, with Seward’s asylum on the other side of the wall.

places.name: Hampstead
places.note: The Westenra tomb, and the Heath where children come home with small wounds.

places.name: Galatz
places.note: Where the box is transferred to a river launch, and the chase becomes a matter of maps and timetables.

related.why: The other late-Victorian horror assembled from professional documents, and the other one in which respectable men decline to ask the obvious question.
The earlier novel built from letters and nested testimony, and the earlier monster who is described only by the people who fear him.
Collins’s method of narration by successive witnesses, which Stoker takes over almost intact and makes frightening.
The same documentary structure applied to a theft, and the source of the idea that each narrator should give evidence only within their own knowledge.
Published six years earlier, and the other 1890s novel about something in a locked room that must not be seen.

books.title: Ethan Frome
books.author: Edith Wharton
books.setting: Starkfield, a declining Massachusetts hill village, across one winter and twenty-four years later
books.written: Out of an earlier French exercise, Hiver, written while Wharton was living in Paris
books.lengthNote: A prologue, nine short chapters and an epilogue — under two hundred pages
books.openingLine: I had the story, bit by bit, from various people, and, as generally happens in such cases, each time it was a different story.
books.summary: An engineer stranded by a strike in a New England village becomes curious about a lame, silent man at the post office, and assembles the reason from what the neighbours will tell him. What he arrives at is a winter twenty-four years earlier, a farm that cannot be sold, a wife with symptoms and a young cousin with nowhere else to go. The cruelty of the book is not the accident at the end but what the accident fails to end.
books.referenceStyle: chapter — the framing narrative is unnumbered and is referenced here as Prologue and Epilogue

sourceText.label: Standard Ebooks text of Ethan Frome
sourceText.note: Chapters are numbered I to IX, with Wharton's unnumbered opening and closing sections given here as Prologue and Epilogue. The phonetic Starkfield speech is reproduced as printed.

structure.label: Prologue
structure.title: A visiting engineer collects a village's version
structure.summary: Held in Starkfield by a carpenters' strike, the narrator notices a ruined man at the post office and starts asking. Harmon Gow supplies the accident, Mrs Ned Hale supplies a reticence, and a snowstorm finally puts him inside the Frome kitchen — at which point the book goes back twenty-four years.

structure.label: Chapters I–III
structure.title: Waiting outside the dance
structure.summary: Ethan stands in the cold watching Mattie Silver dance with Denis Eady, and walks her home the long way past the graveyard. Zeena is awake when they get in, and by the third chapter she has announced a trip to Bettsbridge to see a new doctor.

structure.label: Chapters IV–V
structure.title: An evening alone, and the cat breaks the dish
structure.summary: With Zeena away, Ethan and Mattie have supper in a kitchen that briefly feels like a different life. The cat knocks Zeena's red glass pickle-dish off the table, and Ethan puts the pieces back on the shelf intending to buy glue in the morning.

structure.label: Chapters VI–VII
structure.title: Complications, a hired girl, and the broken dish found
structure.summary: Zeena comes back with a diagnosis and a hired girl already engaged, which means Mattie must leave in the morning. Ethan has no money and no argument, and when the pieces of the dish are discovered the quarrel stops being about anybody's health.

structure.label: Chapters VIII–IX
structure.title: No money, no letter, and the elm at the bottom of the hill
structure.summary: Ethan drafts a letter he cannot send, goes to Andrew Hale for an advance he does not get, and drives Mattie to the station by way of the sledding hill. She asks him not to leave her, and then asks him for something else.

structure.label: Epilogue
structure.title: The kitchen, twenty-four years on
structure.summary: The narrator is shown into the room the three of them share, and the two women in it are not arranged as anyone would have predicted. Mrs Hale afterwards says the thing nobody in Starkfield has said aloud for a quarter of a century.

characters.name: Ethan Frome
characters.role: A farmer and sawmill owner, twenty-eight in the reconstructed winter
characters.summary: He studied engineering for a year at Worcester and came back to nurse first his father, then his mother, then the wife he married because the silence after his mother's funeral was unbearable. Every exit is costed in the book and none of them clears: he cannot sell the farm, cannot raise fifty dollars, and cannot leave without abandoning a sick woman.
characters.clue: A lame man with a red gash across his forehead who drives into the village every day at noon for a newspaper he never opens.

characters.name: Zenobia (Zeena) Frome
characters.role: Ethan's wife, seven years older than him
characters.summary: She came to nurse his mother and stayed as his wife, and her illness — never diagnosed by the book — is the only authority a woman in her position has. Wharton gives her almost no interior life and a great deal of power, and the epilogue reverses the two so completely that the reader has to reconsider everything said about her.
characters.clue: She goes to a new doctor in a neighbouring town and comes home with a word that outranks trouble, and a hired girl already engaged.

characters.name: Mattie Silver
characters.role: Zeena's young cousin, working in the house for her keep
characters.summary: Her father's failure left her with fifty dollars and no training; shop work and stenography both broke her health, so she is at the Fromes because there is nowhere else. She is not a great beauty or a great mind — the novel is careful about that — she is simply the only warm thing in the house.
characters.clue: She hangs a ribbon at her neck, uses the good dish for one supper, and asks at the top of a hill to be steered at a tree.

characters.name: The engineer
characters.role: An unnamed visitor sent to Corbury Junction on a job
characters.summary: He is never named and never explains his own life, and he states at the outset that the story came to him in pieces that did not agree. The central chapters are his construction, not testimony, which means every judgement the reader makes about Zeena arrives through a stranger who spent one night in the house.

characters.name: Harmon Gow
characters.role: Former driver of the Bettsbridge stage
characters.summary: He knew the families along the route before the trolley and the railway came, and he supplies the narrator with the accident, the dates and the single sentence that the whole reconstruction is built on. His information stops exactly where the village's sympathy stops.

characters.name: Mrs Ned Hale
characters.role: The narrator's landlady, formerly Ruth Varnum
characters.summary: She was the first person into the house after the accident and has said almost nothing about it since. Her reticence is what gives the epilogue its force: when she finally speaks she delivers the harshest verdict in the book, and immediately apologises for it.

characters.name: Andrew Hale
characters.role: A builder, Ethan's chief customer
characters.summary: He pays for lumber three months after delivery and is himself short of money because he is fitting out a house for his son's marriage. His refusal of an advance is delivered kindly and is the exact point at which every remaining exit closes.

characters.name: Denis Eady
characters.role: The grocer's son, with his father's horses to drive
characters.summary: He has money, a cutter and no obligations, which makes him the version of Ethan's life that was available to somebody else. He offers Mattie a lift home from the dance and is refused, and afterwards he functions mainly as the future the Fromes cannot compete with.

themes.name: Class and money
themes.summary: The book gives exact figures and lets them do the work of fate: fifty dollars asked for and refused, lumber paid for three months in arrears, a mortgage that cannot be cleared, a girl with no saleable skill. Wharton's tragedy is not a matter of temperament but of a household that cannot raise the fare out.
themes.development: The poverty is scenery in the early chapters and machinery by Chapter VIII, where the plan to run away collapses not on conscience but on the price of the tickets.

themes.name: Duty and the sick wife
themes.summary: Ethan is held by illness rather than affection: first his father's, then his mother's, then Zeena's, in an unbroken sequence of people who need nursing. The novel refuses to say whether Zeena is ill or has discovered that illness is the one form of authority open to her, and that refusal is the point.
themes.development: Marriage is presented as the consequence of a funeral, and the epilogue completes the pattern by putting the invalid on her feet to nurse the girl she sent away.

themes.name: What is never said
themes.summary: Almost nothing in this book is spoken at the moment it matters. Ethan rehearses sentences he does not deliver, writes a letter he does not send, and says goodbye without saying anything; Mrs Ned Hale keeps her verdict for twenty-four years. Wharton makes the unspoken sentence a physical event, with a place in the scene.
themes.development: The narrator names the silence in the prologue as something frozen; by Chapter IX the two people involved can only reach each other by doing rather than speaking.

themes.name: Winter as a material fact
themes.summary: Cold in this book is not atmosphere but economics: it decides what work can be done, which roads are passable, how long a journey to the station takes and what a farm can earn. The village's phrase for a man ruined by staying — too many winters — is a piece of local economics rather than a metaphor.
themes.development: The narrator experiences one winter and finds it merely severe; the reconstruction shows what twenty-eight of them do, and the epilogue confines all three survivors to a single heated kitchen.

themes.name: Love as damage
themes.summary: The feeling between Ethan and Mattie is made of very small things — a ribbon, a chair moved, a shared supper — and the novel is precise about how little it would have taken to satisfy it and how completely that little is unavailable. What it produces is not liberation but an attempt at joint suicide that leaves both alive.
themes.development: It begins as company in Chapter I, becomes a domestic fantasy over one supper, and by the top of the sledding hill has turned into the conviction that there is no version of being together except not surviving.

themes.name: Isolation
themes.summary: Starkfield is described as a place where the clever leave and the rest are snowed in, and the Frome farm stands a mile beyond even that. The house has had a wing pulled down, which the narrator reads as the look of a body with a limb missing, and the epilogue shuts three people into one room with nobody to overhear them.
themes.development: Geographic at first, then social — nobody visits — and finally absolute, when the only stranger to enter the kitchen in years is a man waiting out a storm.

techniques.name: Frame narrative
techniques.definition: A story told inside another story, so that every account reaches the reader through somebody with an interest in it.
techniques.bookDefinition: A story enclosed within another story, often several layers deep.
techniques.inThisBook: The prologue and epilogue belong to an outsider who admits his sources contradicted each other; the nine chapters between them are his reconstruction, given with a confidence about Ethan's private thoughts that no informant could have supplied.

techniques.name: Landscape as pressure
techniques.definition: Place and weather made to press on the people living in them, rather than serving as scenery.
techniques.bookDefinition: Using terrain, weather and scale to exert force on the characters rather than to decorate them.
techniques.inThisBook: The hill, the snow, the distance to Corbury Flats and the elm at the bottom of the run are all load-bearing: each of them limits what a character is physically able to do next.

techniques.name: Dialect
techniques.definition: Spelling and grammar used to mark where a speaker comes from, and what being heard that way costs them.
techniques.bookDefinition: Regional speech written phonetically.
techniques.inThisBook: The villagers' speech is set down as it sounds — 'wust kind', ''cept', 'ha' died' — while the narrator's prose stays formal, so the gap between the observer and the observed is audible on every page he quotes.

techniques.name: Objects and omens
techniques.definition: An object the narrative keeps returning to until it stands for the argument rather than illustrating it.
techniques.bookDefinition: Things in the narrative that carry a meaning the characters half-register.
techniques.inThisBook: A wedding-present pickle-dish taken down for one supper and broken by a cat carries the whole marriage; so do a hanging ribbon, a dead cucumber-vine and a gravestone with the wrong first name on it.

techniques.name: The gap in the telling
techniques.definition: What the narrative declines to show, placed where the reader will notice the gap and fill it.
techniques.bookDefinition: Leaving out the part of a story the reader most expects to be shown.
techniques.inThisBook: The novel jumps from a sled aimed at an elm to a kitchen twenty-four years later without narrating the crash, the injuries or the decisions afterwards, so the reader reconstructs the worst of it from a woman's shape in a chair.

techniques.name: Understatement
techniques.definition: Reporting extreme events in language deliberately too mild for them.
techniques.bookDefinition: Reporting extreme events in language deliberately too mild for them.
techniques.inThisBook: The village calls a catastrophe a smash-up, a driver says Ethan will likely touch a hundred, and the book's cruellest judgement is delivered by a kindly landlady who then worries she has spoken out of turn.

quotations.text: I had the story, bit by bit, from various people, and, as generally happens in such cases, each time it was a different story.
quotations.speaker: The narrator
quotations.context: The opening sentence of the book.
quotations.analysis: The first sentence of a tragedy is a warning about evidence. 'Bit by bit' concedes that the pieces arrived separately, and the last clause concedes that they contradicted each other — so everything the reader is about to be shown in close-up third person has been assembled by a man who has just told us his materials do not agree.

quotations.text: He’s looked that way ever since he had his smash-up; and that’s twenty-four years ago come next February
quotations.speaker: Harmon Gow
quotations.context: The first explanation the narrator is offered for Frome's appearance.
quotations.analysis: The village's word for the event is a word for a cart overturning, and the sentence dates it with the precision people use for a wedding or a death. The whole book is contained in the gap between the mildness of 'smash-up' and the fact that somebody has been counting the Februaries.

quotations.text: He looks as if he was dead and in hell now!
quotations.speaker: Harmon Gow
quotations.context: Answering his own remark that Frome will probably live to a hundred.
quotations.analysis: Gow has just said the Fromes are tough and will last, and he immediately spoils the compliment. Putting hell in the present tense makes the rest of the book an explanation rather than a mystery: the reader now knows the outcome and is waiting only to be told what it cost.

quotations.text: Guess he’s been in Starkfield too many winters. Most of the smart ones get away.
quotations.speaker: Harmon Gow
quotations.context: The sentence the narrator says he built all his later inferences around.
quotations.analysis: Two flat statements which between them contain a theory of the whole district: that staying is what does the damage, and that staying is what the less able do. The narrator quotes it twice, and the second quotation is his admission that a reconstruction of twenty-four years has been grown from one man's offhand remark.

quotations.text: it seemed to produce no change except that of retarding still more the sluggish pulse of Starkfield
quotations.speaker: The narrator
quotations.context: The effect of a spell of bright clear cold on the village.
quotations.analysis: The village is given a pulse, which makes the winter a condition rather than a season and the place a patient rather than a location. It is the first of the book's many transfers of medical language away from Zeena, who is the only person in it with a diagnosis.

quotations.text: He seemed a part of the mute melancholy landscape, an incarnation of its frozen woe, with all that was warm and sentient in him fast bound below the surface; but there was nothing unfriendly in his silence.
quotations.speaker: The narrator
quotations.context: After several winter drives to the Junction in Frome's sleigh, in near-silence.
quotations.analysis: The man is absorbed into the scenery and then, in the last clause, quietly handed back his humanity. 'Fast bound below the surface' describes ice over water, and the reconstruction that follows is an attempt to get at what is under it — an attempt the narrator has already told us is guesswork.

quotations.text: We’ll always go on living here together, and some day she’ll lie there beside me.
quotations.speaker: Ethan Frome
quotations.context: Walking Mattie home past the Frome graves, which had always oppressed him.
quotations.analysis: This is the novel's love scene, and it consists of a man imagining a shared grave. The graves that used to stand for everything he could not escape have been converted, in one sentence, into a promise — which tells the reader exactly how narrow the available happiness is.

quotations.text: There was in him a slumbering spark of sociability which the long Starkfield winters had not yet extinguished.
quotations.context: Ethan driving to the village in unusually good spirits, with Zeena away.
quotations.analysis: 'Not yet' is the word that turns a kind sentence into a threatening one. The metaphor is a fire going out slowly in a cold house, and the chapter that contains it is the only one in which Ethan whistles, sings and behaves like a man of twenty-eight.

quotations.text: There the silence had deepened about him year by year.
quotations.context: The history of the farm after his father's accident and his mother's decline.
quotations.analysis: Silence is given a depth and a rate of increase, like snow or debt. The sentence also supplies the motive for the marriage twenty pages before the book states it: Ethan asks Zeena to stay because she has been speaking in a house where nobody spoke.

quotations.text: Sacred to the memory of Ethan Frome and Endurance his wife, who dwelled together in peace for fifty years.
quotations.context: An ancestor's headstone on the knoll, which had interested him as a boy because it bore his name.
quotations.analysis: The wife's name is a virtue and the epitaph is a sentence about duration rather than affection — fifty years, in peace, together. Wharton then has Ethan wonder whether the same words will be written over him and Zeena, and the epilogue answers the question without needing a stone.

quotations.text: backed into the pickle-dish, which fell to the floor with a crash
quotations.context: The cat, startled off the table during the supper Ethan and Mattie have alone.
quotations.analysis: The agent of the disaster is a cat, which lets Wharton destroy the marriage's most valued object without giving anybody the blame or the satisfaction. The dish was a wedding present never used; taking it down for one meal is the only extravagance in the book, and it is punished within the hour.

quotations.text: I’ve got complications
quotations.speaker: Zeena Frome
quotations.context: Reporting the new Bettsbridge doctor's verdict, on her return.
quotations.analysis: Three words, delivered with the air of somebody singled out for a great fate. In a village where everybody has troubles, the word is a promotion, and Wharton has Zeena win the only argument that matters by producing a noun her husband cannot contradict.

quotations.text: To have them was in itself a distinction, though it was also, in most cases, a death-warrant.
quotations.context: The narrator explaining what the word means in that part of the country.
quotations.analysis: The sentence balances social promotion against a death sentence on either side of a comma, and the phrase 'in most cases' quietly leaves room for the ones who live for decades. It is the book's one moment of open irony about Zeena, and it is also the book's refusal to say whether she is ill.

quotations.text: The doctor says it’ll be my death if I go on slaving the way I’ve had to.
quotations.speaker: Zeena Frome
quotations.context: Justifying the hired girl she has already engaged, which means Mattie must go.
quotations.analysis: The medical authority is quoted rather than present, and the word 'slaving' recasts a household in which somebody else does the work. The sentence is unanswerable by design: to argue with it is to be a man who would rather keep a girl than keep his wife alive.

quotations.text: now you’ve took from me the one I cared for most of all
quotations.speaker: Zeena Frome
quotations.context: Holding the pieces of the red glass pickle-dish.
quotations.analysis: She is grieving over crockery, and the phrasing is that of a woman mourning a person — which is the nearest the novel lets her come to saying what she knows about her husband and her cousin. She then stops in a spasm of sobs and hardens again, and the marriage never discusses any of it.

quotations.text: He was a prisoner for life, and now his one ray of light was to be extinguished.
quotations.context: After the failure to raise fifty dollars from Andrew Hale.
quotations.analysis: The sentence arrives immediately after a page of arithmetic — the price of tickets, the mortgage, the three months' credit — so the prison metaphor is being cashed against a ledger rather than a mood. Wharton is precise that the walls are financial, and that the door was shut by a kind man who was also short of money.

quotations.text: Right into the big elm. You said you could. So ’t we’d never have to leave each other any more.
quotations.speaker: Mattie Silver
quotations.context: At the top of the coast, after one run down, her lips against his ear.
quotations.analysis: She proposes it, not him, and she does so by quoting his own boast back at him. The reasoning in the last clause is a child's — this is the only way of not being separated — and the flat construction, with no word for death anywhere in it, is what makes the moment unbearable.

quotations.text: But suddenly his wife’s face, with twisted monstrous lineaments, thrust itself between him and his goal
quotations.context: The second run down the hill, with the elm ahead.
quotations.analysis: Zeena appears at the last possible instant as a hallucination and physically deflects the sled, so the crash that follows is neither a clean death nor a clean escape. Wharton has the marriage intervene in the accident itself, which is why the survivors end up in one kitchen rather than two graves.

quotations.text: A slatternly calico wrapper hung from her shoulders and the wisps of her thin grey hair were drawn away from a high forehead and fastened at the back by a broken comb.
quotations.context: The narrator's first sight of the woman who gets up to prepare the meal in the Frome kitchen.
quotations.analysis: The description is given before the name, so the reader spends a paragraph deciding which of the two women this is and gets it wrong. The broken comb is the detail that does the work: everything in the room has been mended once and is now simply being used broken.

quotations.text: And I say, if she’d ha’ died, Ethan might ha’ lived
quotations.speaker: Mrs Ned Hale
quotations.context: The impulse of complete avowal that seizes her after twenty-four years of reticence.
quotations.analysis: She has already said her minister was shocked by the same sentence, and she repeats it anyway, in dialect, with 'I say' at the front to mark that she knows what she is doing. It converts the accident from a tragedy into a failed mercy, which is a far harder thing for the reader to hold.

quotations.text: I don’t see’s there’s much difference between the Fromes up at the farm and the Fromes down in the graveyard; ’cept that down there they’re all quiet, and the women have got to hold their tongues.
quotations.speaker: Mrs Ned Hale
quotations.context: The last words of the book.
quotations.analysis: The joke is that the dead are quieter, and the sting is in what it concedes about the living: the kitchen is a grave with the arguing left in. Ending a novel about a man who could not speak on a line about women who cannot stop is Wharton's final adjustment to who, in Starkfield, has actually been silenced.

atAGlance.label: First published
atAGlance.note: By Charles Scribner's Sons, after serialisation in Scribner's Magazine.

atAGlance.label: Written first in French
atAGlance.note: A composition exercise Wharton wrote while living in Paris supplied the situation and the setting.

atAGlance.label: Time span
atAGlance.note: The distance between the winter the narrator reconstructs and the kitchen he finally walks into.

atAGlance.label: Narration
atAGlance.note: Everything between the prologue and the epilogue is what the engineer has made of other people's fragments.

criticalViews.position: A tragedy of economics rather than character
criticalViews.summary: On this reading the novel's subject is a household that cannot raise money: the unsellable farm, the three months' credit, the fifty dollars refused. Every emotional development is preceded by a financial one, and the ending is what happens when no exit can be paid for.
criticalViews.counter: It underrates how much of the trap Ethan builds himself — he has a letter written and abandons it before the money question is settled.

criticalViews.position: The frame as the novel's real subject
criticalViews.summary: Wharton gives an outsider nine chapters of confident access to a silent man's mind, having first told us his sources disagreed. Read this way the book is about how a village's reticence gets turned into a story, and about who is entitled to narrate a marriage.
criticalViews.counter: The reconstruction is so sustained and so intimate that most readers forget the frame entirely until the epilogue reopens it.

criticalViews.position: Zeena as the novel's misread figure
criticalViews.summary: Later criticism has argued that the one character denied an interior life is the one with the least power — a woman whose only available authority is illness, judged throughout by a narrator who met her once, and who is then found nursing the rival she dismissed.
criticalViews.counter: The epilogue's reversal may be less a rehabilitation than a final cruelty: all three are kept alive in one room precisely so that nobody is released.

criticalViews.position: New England realism against the pastoral
criticalViews.summary: Wharton said she was writing against the prettified rural New England of earlier fiction, and the novel's bareness — no charm, no folk wisdom, no redemptive nature — is a deliberate correction.
criticalViews.counter: The severity is itself a style, and the book's symmetry and symbolism are as shaped as anything it was reacting against.

essayQuestions.question: How far is the tragedy of Ethan Frome caused by poverty?
essayQuestions.focus: Money, obligation and the closing of every exit
plan: Collect the figures the novel is precise about: the mortgage, the unsold farm, three months' credit, fifty dollars, Mattie's fifty from her father.
Show how the plan to leave collapses in Chapter VIII on the price of the journey rather than on conscience.
Weigh the competing cause: duty to a sick wife, and the sequence of invalids that began with Ethan's father.
Consider Mattie's position separately — her health broken by paid work, and no household but this one.
Decide whether the book presents poverty as the cause or as the thing that makes character irreversible.

essayQuestions.question: What does the framing narrator contribute to the novel?
essayQuestions.focus: Reconstruction, reliability and the limits of testimony
plan: Begin with the first sentence and its admission that the accounts did not agree.
Establish what the narrator could actually have learned, and from whom — Harmon Gow, Mrs Hale, one night in the kitchen.
Set that against the intimacy of the central chapters, which report Ethan's unspoken thoughts.
Examine the epilogue's reopening of the frame and the effect of hearing Mrs Hale's verdict in her own words.
Judge whether the frame undermines the story it introduces or gives it its authority.

essayQuestions.question: Discuss Wharton's presentation of Zeena.
essayQuestions.focus: Illness, power and the novel's silences
plan: Note that the reader never enters her mind, and ask who is responsible for that — Wharton, or the narrator she invented.
Trace the sequence by which illness becomes authority: the doctor at Bettsbridge, the word complications, the hired girl already engaged.
Read the pickle-dish scene as the only place her feeling reaches the surface, and consider what it is really about.
Use the epilogue, where she is on her feet and doing the nursing, to test every earlier judgement.
Conclude on whether the novel condemns her, pities her, or declines to decide.

essayQuestions.question: 'The most important thing in Ethan Frome is what the book does not narrate.' Discuss.
essayQuestions.focus: Silence, ellipsis and the gap before the epilogue
plan: List the unspoken: the unsent letter, the goodbye that is not said, Mrs Hale's twenty-four years of reticence.
Analyse the jump from the sled to the kitchen, and what the reader is required to construct across it.
Show how objects — a dish, a ribbon, a gravestone — carry the conversations the characters never have.
Consider the effect of putting the book's harshest statement in the mouth of its most reticent character, at the very end.
Assess what would be lost if the crash and its aftermath were narrated in full.

discussionQuestions: The narrator admits his sources contradicted each other. How much of the story should we believe?
Mattie proposes the crash, not Ethan. Does that change how you read her?
Zeena never gets a point of view. Is that Wharton's judgement on her, or the narrator's limitation?
The novel gives exact sums of money throughout. What would be different if it did not?
Mrs Hale says it would have been better if Mattie had died. Is the book agreeing with her?

timeline.label: Edith Newbold Jones born in New York
timeline.detail: Into the old moneyed society she would spend a career anatomising.

timeline.label: Marriage to Edward Robbins Wharton
timeline.detail: A match that became increasingly unhappy and ended in divorce in 1913.

timeline.label: The Mount completed at Lenox, Massachusetts
timeline.detail: Wharton designed the house and gardens herself and lived in the Berkshire hill country this book is set in.

timeline.label: A coasting accident at Lenox
timeline.detail: A documented sledding accident in the town, often connected with the novel's ending, though Wharton did not identify it as her source.

timeline.label: The House of Mirth
timeline.detail: The novel that made her reputation, and the first of her studies of a woman destroyed by an economy she is not allowed to work in.

timeline.label: Ethan Frome published
timeline.detail: By Charles Scribner's Sons, after appearing in Scribner's Magazine.

timeline.label: The Custom of the Country
timeline.detail: Published two years later, and as ruthless about money in drawing rooms as this book is about money on a hill farm.

timeline.label: The Age of Innocence
timeline.detail: Written after the war, from France, looking back at the New York of her childhood.

timeline.label: Wharton awarded the Pulitzer Prize for fiction
timeline.detail: The first woman to receive it, for The Age of Innocence.

timeline.label: Wharton dies in France
timeline.detail: At Saint-Brice-sous-Forêt, north of Paris, where she had lived for years.

places.name: Lenox, Massachusetts
places.note: Where Wharton built The Mount and learned the Berkshire winters that Starkfield is made from.

places.name: Pittsfield, Massachusetts
places.note: The nearest real town of any size to Wharton's Berkshire country, and the model for the errands the Fromes take to Bettsbridge.

places.name: Mount Greylock
places.note: The highest point in Massachusetts, in the hill country whose isolated farms Wharton took her setting from.

places.name: Paris
places.note: Where Wharton was living when she wrote the French exercise, Hiver, that supplied the situation of this book.

places.name: New York
places.note: The city of Scribner's Magazine, which serialised the novella, and the society Wharton usually wrote about instead.

related.why: Another short American novel about a marriage that offers no exit, published a decade earlier and equally unwilling to console.
The New England that Wharton was writing against and out of: small, watchful, and organised around what cannot be said.
A frame narrator piecing together a passion from other people's accounts, in a landscape that does half the work.
Rural poverty treated as a mechanism rather than a backdrop, with the same refusal to let a good character escape it.
Published fourteen years later, and also concerned with a life closed off by other people's care and the difference between surviving and living.

books.title: Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus
books.author: Mary Shelley
books.setting: Geneva, Ingolstadt, the Alps, the Orkneys and the Arctic ice, in the previous century
books.lengthNote: Four letters and twenty-four chapters, told by three narrators nested inside one another
books.openingLine: You will rejoice to hear that no disaster has accompanied the commencement of an enterprise which you have regarded with such evil forebodings.
books.summary: A student in Ingolstadt works out how to animate dead matter, succeeds, looks at what he has made and runs out of the room. The being he abandons teaches itself to speak and read, is driven off by everyone who sees it, and comes back to demand a companion. Shelley builds the whole argument as a set of nested testimonies, so that neither maker nor made ever gets to tell the story alone.
books.referenceStyle: chapter, with the outer frame given as Letter I to Letter IV

sourceText.label: Standard Ebooks text of Frankenstein — Mary Shelley’s revised 1831 edition
sourceText.note: The text checked here is the one-volume 1831 revision, not the anonymous 1818 first edition. It can be identified from the inside: it carries Shelley’s 1831 introduction about the summer at Geneva, it runs as twenty-four continuous chapters rather than three volumes, and Elizabeth Lavenza arrives as an orphan taken in by the Frankensteins rather than as Victor’s cousin.

structure.label: Letters I-IV
structure.title: An explorer writes home and finds a better story than his own
structure.summary: Robert Walton, sailing north in search of a passage and a friend, writes to a sister who never answers. Ice closes around the ship, a huge figure crosses it on a sledge, and the next day the crew pulls aboard a starving European who has been chasing him. Everything that follows is inside a letter.

scenes.summary: Walton, at St Petersburgh, describes an expedition he expects to make him famous.
At Archangel he complains that he has no friend, and no one to correct him.
A short, confident note sent from open sea.
The ship is frozen in; the sledge is sighted; Victor Frankenstein comes aboard and begins to talk.

structure.label: Chapters I-V
structure.title: A Geneva childhood, a university, and one night in November
structure.summary: Victor describes an upbringing so protected that his own account can find nothing in it to blame. At Ingolstadt he moves from discredited alchemists to modern chemistry, works alone for two years, and animates the thing he has assembled. The success lasts one sentence; the horror begins in the next.

scenes.summary: The Frankenstein household, Elizabeth’s arrival, and a boy’s reading in Agrippa and Paracelsus.
His mother dies; at Ingolstadt, Waldman’s lecture redirects him towards modern chemistry.
Two years in charnel houses and dissecting rooms; he breaks off his account to warn Walton.
The creature opens its eye; Victor flees, falls ill, and is nursed by Clerval.

structure.label: Chapters VI-X
structure.title: A child is killed and a servant is hanged for it
structure.summary: News from Geneva: William is dead. Victor sees the creature by lightning on the way home and says nothing while Justine Moritz is tried, persuaded to confess and executed. This is the section that makes the novel a moral problem rather than a horror story, because Victor’s silence costs a life and he presents it as suffering.

scenes.summary: Clerval’s friendship, then the letter announcing William’s murder; a figure seen in a storm near Plainpalais.
Justine’s trial and execution; Victor keeps what he knows to himself.
Grief-stricken travel in the Alps; on the Mer de Glace the creature approaches and asks to be heard.

structure.label: Chapters XI-XVI
structure.title: The being’s own account of learning to be a person
structure.summary: For six chapters the novel hands its voice to the thing it has been calling a wretch. It describes sensation before language, a year of watching the De Lacey family through a chink, an education gathered from Volney, Milton and Goethe, and the moment Felix beats it out of the cottage. It has been benevolent and is becoming something else.

scenes.summary: First sensations, fire, hunger, flight from villages, and the hovel beside the De Lacey cottage.
Safie’s arrival gives the creature language lessons by proxy, and the De Laceys’ own history.
Three books, and Victor’s laboratory journal; the blind old man listens until his family returns.
The cottage is abandoned; the creature saves a girl and is shot for it, then meets William.

structure.label: Chapters XVII-XXIII
structure.title: A promise made in Chamounix and broken in the Orkneys
structure.summary: The creature asks for one thing: a female of its own kind, and exile. Victor agrees, travels to England and Scotland, and tears the half-made companion apart with the creature watching at the window. The threat that follows is answered by a wedding, which is exactly what the threat was designed to produce.

scenes.summary: The bargain is struck; Victor delays for months, then leaves for England with Clerval.
London, Oxford, Scotland, and a hut on a remote Orkney island.
The second creature is destroyed; the creature promises to be with him on his wedding night.
Clerval is found strangled and Victor is charged; acquitted, he marries Elizabeth, who dies that night.

structure.label: Chapter XXIV and Walton’s close
structure.title: Two ruined men and an argument that will not close
structure.summary: Victor chases the creature north until the ice stops both of them, and dies on Walton’s ship still recommending ambition in the same breath as warning against it. The creature comes aboard to grieve over him, tells Walton what the pursuit cost on its side, and leaves. Nobody is left to settle who was right.

scenes.summary: The pursuit across Russia and the ice; Victor’s last speech to Walton’s mutinous crew.
Victor dies; the creature is found weeping over the body and speaks for itself one last time.

characters.name: Victor Frankenstein
characters.role: Genevese student of natural philosophy
characters.summary: He gives two years to the problem of animating dead matter and about ten seconds to the question of what he will do afterwards.
