scenes.summary: Wasps, apples, a monkey, a dwarf and the maids of honour: the body is the subject of the middle chapters.

scenes.title: Gunpowder refused
scenes.summary: Gulliver offers the recipe for artillery as a gift and is refused with horror; an eagle carries his box out to sea and he is picked up by an English ship.

structure.label: Part III
structure.title: Laputa and after: learning without use
structure.summary: The loosest and most various of the voyages: a flying island whose philosophers must be struck with bladders to attend to anything, a ruined country improved into famine by its academy, a governor who can raise the dead, and the Struldbrugs, who are immortal but not young. Reason is not attacked here; reason detached from ordinary life is.

scenes.title: The flying island
scenes.summary: Pirates, then Laputa: music, mathematics, terror of comets, and a king who suppresses rebellion by lowering the island onto the town.

scenes.title: The Academy of Lagado
scenes.summary: Munodi’s prosperous estate is a scandal to his neighbours; the projectors extract sunbeams from cucumbers and build houses from the roof down.

scenes.title: Glubbdubdrib
scenes.summary: The dead are summoned and modern history is corrected; the honours of the last century turn out to have been bought.

scenes.title: Luggnagg and the Struldbrugs
scenes.summary: Gulliver plans a glorious immortal life, then meets people who have had one for two hundred years.

structure.label: Part IV
structure.title: Houyhnhnmland: a creature that cannot lie
structure.summary: Set ashore by his own mutinous crew, Gulliver finds rational horses and filthy human animals, and spends the voyage explaining England to a master who has no word for falsehood. The account convinces him: he learns to speak in whinnies, is expelled by an assembly that cannot see why a Yahoo should be kept, and comes home unable to be in a room with his family.

scenes.title: Arrival
scenes.summary: Mutiny, the shore, the Yahoos, and the slow acquisition of a language with no term for saying the thing which is not.

scenes.title: England described
scenes.summary: War, law, money, medicine and ministers, set out plainly and heard by someone with no reason to make allowances.

scenes.title: A happy life
scenes.summary: Houyhnhnm virtue, education and marriage; Gulliver keeps house, imitates their gait and voice, and calls these the happiest years of his life.

scenes.title: Expulsion and return
scenes.summary: The assembly exhorts his master to send him away; Don Pedro’s kindness is unbearable, and Gulliver ends among horses in his own stable.

characters.name: Lemuel Gulliver
characters.role: Ship’s surgeon, then captain, and the book’s narrator
characters.summary: A competent, incurious man who measures everything and understands almost nothing, and whose plainness is what makes the satire work. He is not a fixed point the reader can stand on: each voyage adjusts what he admires, and by the fourth he is arguing for the extinction of his own species.
characters.clue: He records latitudes, cargoes and the exact height of everything he meets, learns each new language quickly, and comes home at last preferring the conversation of his horses.

characters.name: The Emperor of Lilliput
characters.role: Sovereign of a country six inches high
characters.summary: Taller than his courtiers by the breadth of a fingernail, and described in the vocabulary of universal monarchy. He is generous while Gulliver is useful and merciful in the technical sense afterwards: the sentence of blinding is presented at court as an act of clemency.
characters.clue: He is almost the breadth of a nail taller than any of his court, describes himself as the delight and terror of the universe, and calls it mercy when he only orders your eyes put out.

characters.name: The King of Brobdingnag
characters.role: A ruler who asks questions and waits for the answers
characters.summary: Swift’s one straightforwardly admirable figure, and a deliberately limited one: he is learned, he keeps a small army, and he cannot conceive of a state secret worth a massacre. His verdict on English history is delivered after several audiences of careful notes, which is what makes it hard to dismiss.
characters.clue: He questions his six-inch guest about England over several sittings, takes notes, and concludes that the natives of that island are the most pernicious little vermin nature ever suffered to crawl.

characters.name: Glumdalclitch
characters.role: The farmer’s daughter, nine years old and forty feet tall
characters.summary: She names him, sews his clothes, makes him a box to travel in and is the only person in four voyages who loves him. Swift lets her stand outside the satire entirely, which is why her grief when the eagle takes the box is the one uncomplicated feeling in the book.

characters.name: Lord Munodi
characters.role: A nobleman of Balnibarbi with a working estate
characters.summary: His fields are full, his house stands up and his neighbours despise him for it, because his methods are the old ones. Munodi is the measure that makes the Academy funny rather than merely grotesque: the country has not failed for want of ingenuity but because ingenuity has been given authority over farming.

characters.name: The Struldbrugs
characters.role: The immortals of Luggnagg
characters.summary: Born with a spot over the eyebrow, they never die and they also never stop ageing. Swift uses them to separate two wishes that are usually confused, and the chapter’s real cruelty is that Gulliver delivers his rapturous plan for an immortal life before he is taken to see any of them.
characters.clue: A red circular spot over the left eyebrow marks them at birth; at eighty they are declared legally dead, and they go on for centuries after that.

characters.name: Gulliver’s Houyhnhnm master
characters.role: The horse who teaches him the language and hears his account of England
characters.summary: Patient, literal and entirely without a concept of deception, he has to be given a new word — the thing which is not — before Gulliver can describe a lawsuit. His difficulty in believing the account is the engine of Part IV: everything sounds worse when explained to someone who cannot supply the usual excuses.
characters.clue: He has no word for lying and must be taught one before his guest can describe a European law court.

characters.name: The Yahoos
characters.role: The human animals of Houyhnhnmland
characters.summary: Filthy, greedy, tribal and recognisably human, they are the satire’s hardest device because Gulliver accepts the identification completely and the book does not obviously stop him. They hoard coloured stones they cannot use, which is the one detail that makes the resemblance impossible to argue with.

characters.name: Don Pedro de Mendez
characters.role: The Portuguese captain who takes Gulliver home
characters.summary: He clothes a raving man, gives him his own cabin, refuses payment and asks nothing in return, and Gulliver can barely stand to breathe near him. Swift plants an entirely good human being in the last chapters, and lets his narrator fail to notice, which is the strongest evidence that Part IV is not simply Gulliver’s opinion.

themes.name: Scale and perspective
themes.summary: Size is an argument rather than a spectacle. At twelve to one Gulliver finds Lilliputian politics comic; at one to twelve he finds Brobdingnagian skin disgusting and English politics indefensible. The same facts about Europe are funny in Part I and monstrous in Part II, and only the vantage point has moved.
themes.development: Giant, then miniature, then a tourist at the ordinary human scale in Part III, and finally an animal being classified by someone else in Part IV.

themes.name: Pride
themes.summary: Swift identified pride as the target of the whole book, and it is the last word of the last chapter. What is attacked is not achievement but the claim to be a reasoning creature, which the Houyhnhnms replace with the more modest description: an animal capable of reason on occasion.
themes.development: National pride in Part I, personal vanity in Part II, intellectual pride in Part III, and species pride in Part IV, where Gulliver catches it himself in the act of despising Yahoos.

themes.name: Reason and its uses
themes.summary: The Laputans calculate beautifully and cannot build a house that stands; the Academy improves agriculture into famine; the Houyhnhnms are perfectly rational and would exterminate the Yahoos by a vote. Reason detached from use, and reason detached from mercy, are both examined and neither is spared.
themes.development: Munodi’s working farm sets the standard in Part III; the general assembly in Part IV shows what the standard costs when applied without feeling.

themes.name: Party, office and faction
themes.summary: High heels and low, big ends and little: Swift reduces confessional and party conflict to distinctions with no content and then counts the dead. Office in Lilliput is won by jumping over a stick, which is a joke about preferment, and the joke is that it explains a great deal.
themes.development: Local and topical in Part I, generalised into a European history of war in Part II, and restated to a creature with no politics at all in Part IV, Chapter V.

themes.name: Travel, discovery and possession
themes.summary: Gulliver measures, classifies and reports every people he meets, which is exactly what the voyage literature of the period did. The last chapter turns the habit inside out by explaining how a new country is normally taken, and then exempting his own discoveries on the grounds that they are not worth the trouble.
themes.development: The Lilliputian inventory of his pockets in Part I is the first survey; his refusal to help enslave Blefuscu is the first refusal; Part IV, Chapter XII states the case plainly.

themes.name: Bodies and disgust
themes.summary: Swift will not let the reader forget that a human being is a body that eats, sweats and smells. Gulliver’s excretions are a practical problem in Lilliput, the giant nurses are unbearable at close range, and in Part IV the smell of his own wife drives him into the stable.
themes.development: Comic in Part I, magnified and clinical in Part II, and finally moralised in Part IV, where disgust at the body becomes disgust at the species.

techniques.name: Mock travel writing
techniques.definition: Borrowing the apparatus of factual voyage literature — dates, bearings, cargoes, vocabularies — for an invented country.
techniques.bookDefinition: Borrowing the apparatus of factual voyage literature — dates, bearings, cargoes, vocabularies — for an invented country.
techniques.inThisBook: Each voyage opens with a ship, a date and a latitude, and the first edition carried maps; the fiction is guaranteed by exactly the machinery that guaranteed Dampier.

techniques.name: Deadpan narration
techniques.definition: Delivering an outrage or an absurdity in the same flat tone as everything else.
techniques.bookDefinition: Reporting the outrageous in the tone reserved for the ordinary, leaving the reader to supply the judgement.
techniques.inThisBook: Gulliver describes the sentence of blinding as a favour and the gunpowder refusal as a failure of nerve in the king, and in both cases says nothing the reader can agree with.

techniques.name: Making the familiar strange
techniques.definition: Describing a known thing from outside, in terms that do not name it.
techniques.bookDefinition: Describing a known thing from outside, in terms that do not name it.
techniques.inThisBook: A pocket watch becomes an engine that makes a noise like a water-mill and is filed as a possible god; a law court becomes a procedure for proving the thing which is not.

techniques.name: Satirical escalation
techniques.definition: Arranging a sequence so that each part is harder to laugh off than the last.
techniques.bookDefinition: Arranging a sequence so that each part is harder to laugh off than the last.
techniques.inThisBook: Rope-dancers, then gunpowder, then the Academy, then a reasoned proposal to exterminate a species: the structure is a slope rather than four independent jokes.

techniques.name: The false document
techniques.definition: Prefaces, letters and publisher’s notes that stand outside the narrative and vouch for it.
techniques.bookDefinition: Prefaces, letters and publisher’s notes that stand outside the narrative and vouch for it.
techniques.inThisBook: Sympson certifies Gulliver’s truthfulness, and Gulliver then attacks Sympson for corrupting the text — the guarantee and the complaint cancel each other before Chapter I.

techniques.name: Exact measurement
techniques.definition: Precise numbers used where a vague impression would do.
techniques.bookDefinition: Precise numbers used where a vague impression would do.
techniques.inThisBook: Six inches, a twelfth, 1,728 Lilliputian meals, the compass of a silver threepence: the arithmetic is consistent throughout and is what makes the impossible countries feel surveyed rather than dreamed.

quotations.text: I do, in the next place, complain of my own great want of judgment, in being prevailed upon by the entreaties and false reasoning of you and some others, very much against my own opinion, to suffer my travels to be published.
quotations.reference: A Letter from Captain Gulliver to His Cousin Sympson
quotations.context: The prefatory letter added for Faulkner’s edition, written years after the voyages.
quotations.analysis: The book opens by regretting its own publication. Swift builds a paratext that quarrels with itself — a publisher vouching for the text, an author disowning it — so that a reader who wants to know what is authoritative here has nowhere to stand before the first voyage begins.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, A Letter from Captain Gulliver to His Cousin Sympson

quotations.text: they shouted for joy, and danced upon my breast, repeating several times as they did at first, “Hekinah degul.”
quotations.context: After Gulliver has drunk two hogsheads of Lilliputian wine while pegged to the ground.
quotations.analysis: The foreign words are left untranslated, so the reader is put exactly where Gulliver is: watching a ceremony and guessing at its meaning. Swift also gets the scale into the verb — they dance on his chest — which makes the wonder physical before it is political.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Part I, Chapter I

quotations.text: we conjecture it is either some unknown animal, or the god that he worships; but we are more inclined to the latter opinion
quotations.context: From the official inventory two Lilliputian officers make of Gulliver’s pockets.
quotations.analysis: The officers reason correctly from what they can observe: the object is consulted before every action, so it governs him. Swift’s joke about a nation that worships the clock is delivered entirely inside a customs document, and the form of the passage — a numbered search of a man’s body — is as pointed as its content.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Part I, Chapter II

quotations.text: It is allowed on all hands, that the primitive way of breaking eggs, before we eat them, was upon the larger end
quotations.context: Reldresal explaining the origin of the war with Blefuscu.
quotations.analysis: The phrase ‘allowed on all hands’ is the vocabulary of settled doctrine applied to breakfast. Swift then supplies casualty figures — eleven thousand deaths rather than submit — so the scene works by keeping the cause trivial while the consequences stay at full historical size.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Part I, Chapter IV

quotations.text: his majesty has determined to make use only of low heels in the administration of the government
quotations.context: The same conversation, on the two parties of the empire.
quotations.analysis: Party is reduced to footwear and the reduction changes nothing about how the politics behaves: patronage follows the heel height, and the heir hedges by wearing one of each and walking with a hobble. The satire is not that the difference is small but that a small difference is enough.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Part I, Chapter IV

quotations.text: They look upon fraud as a greater crime than theft, and therefore seldom fail to punish it with death
quotations.context: Gulliver’s account of Lilliputian laws, which he reports with approval.
quotations.analysis: This chapter is the one place where Lilliput is used as a model rather than a joke, and the reasoning given is commercial: honesty has no defence against fraud, so credit collapses without it. Swift puts his own convictions into the mouth of a ridiculous state, which stops the book being read as simple contempt.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Part I, Chapter VI

quotations.text: I cannot but conclude the bulk of your natives to be the most pernicious race of little odious vermin that nature ever suffered to crawl upon the surface of the earth.”
quotations.context: The king’s conclusion after several audiences on the history and constitution of England.
quotations.analysis: The sentence is built to sound judicial: he has recapitulated, compared question with answer, and only then delivers. Swift makes the verdict physically intimate — the king is stroking Gulliver as he says it — so that contempt and gentleness arrive in the same gesture.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Part II, Chapter VI

quotations.text: The king was struck with horror at the description I had given of those terrible engines, and the proposal I had made.
quotations.context: After Gulliver has offered the king the secret of gunpowder as a proof of his usefulness.
quotations.analysis: The reversal is complete and Gulliver misses it entirely: he files the refusal under the king’s narrow principles and nice scruples. Swift lets the reader hold two readings of the same scene at once, and the gap between them is where the satire lives.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Part II, Chapter VII

quotations.text: whoever could make two ears of corn, or two blades of grass, to grow upon a spot of ground where only one grew before, would deserve better of mankind, and do more essential service to his country, than the whole race of politicians put together.”
quotations.context: Gulliver reporting the king’s opinion of what constitutes useful knowledge.
quotations.analysis: The standard offered here is the one the whole book measures learning against, and it is agricultural rather than philosophical: does it feed anybody? Part III is built to fail this test, which is why the Academy of Lagado is placed a hundred pages after this sentence rather than before it.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Part II, Chapter VII

quotations.text: he proceeds to the last remedy, by letting the island drop directly upon their heads, which makes a universal destruction both of houses and men.
quotations.context: The means by which the king of Laputa suppresses a rebellious town below.
quotations.analysis: The flying island is a machine for occupation: it blocks the sun and rain first, and only crushes as a last resort. Swift gives the tactic a bureaucratic sequence of escalating measures, and the chapter then explains why the king hesitates — his own estates are down there, and the island’s bottom might crack.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Part III, Chapter III

quotations.text: He has been eight years upon a project for extracting sunbeams out of cucumbers, which were to be put in phials hermetically sealed, and let out to warm the air in raw inclement summers.
quotations.context: The first projector Gulliver meets in the grand academy of Lagado.
quotations.analysis: The project is not absurd in principle — it is a scheme to store summer heat — and that is what makes it dangerous: the man is eight years in and asking for funds. Swift attacks not curiosity but the institution that pays for eight years of it while the country outside has stopped growing food.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Part III, Chapter V

quotations.text: Perjury, oppression, subornation, fraud, pandarism, and the like infirmities, were among the most excusable arts they had to mention; and for these I gave, as it was reasonable, great allowance.
quotations.context: In Glubbdubdrib, where the governor can summon the dead and question them.
quotations.analysis: The list is arranged as a descent and then stopped short, so the reader waits for what could possibly be worse. Swift’s device here is historiographical rather than fantastic: the dead are called up not for spectacle but to correct the record that the living have written about them.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Part III, Chapter VIII

quotations.text: “Happy nation, where every child hath at least a chance for being immortal! Happy people, who enjoy so many living examples of ancient virtue, and have masters ready to instruct them in the wisdom of all former ages!
quotations.context: Gulliver’s reaction on first hearing that some Luggnaggians never die, before he has met one.
quotations.analysis: Swift makes him deliver the whole eloquent programme — wealth, learning, a record of the ages — and only then takes him to see the Struldbrugs. The chapter separates two things the wish for immortality usually keeps welded together, and Gulliver has already committed himself in public before the distinction arrives.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Part III, Chapter X

quotations.text: They were the most mortifying sight I ever beheld; and the women more horrible than the men.
quotations.context: Meeting five or six Struldbrugs of various ages at Luggnagg.
quotations.analysis: The correction is flat and brief after the rapture, and the second clause — that the women are worse — is the period’s ordinary misogyny surfacing in a passage about the horror of not dying. Swift’s satire and Swift’s prejudices are in the same sentence, and an honest reading has to hold both.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Part III, Chapter X

quotations.text: “that the use of speech was to make us understand one another, and to receive information of facts; now, if anyone said the thing which was not, these ends were defeated, because I cannot properly be said to understand him
quotations.context: The Houyhnhnm master working out what Gulliver can mean by a lie.
quotations.analysis: The argument is a definition rather than a moral: if speech exists to convey facts, a false sentence is not wicked but void, and leaves the hearer worse informed than silence. It takes the master some difficulty to grasp the concept at all, and Gulliver needs it before he can explain a single English institution.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Part IV, Chapter IV

quotations.text: in recounting the numbers of those who have been killed in battle, I cannot but think you have said the thing which is not.”
quotations.context: The master’s response to Gulliver’s account of European wars and their casualties.
quotations.analysis: The Houyhnhnm phrase for lying is used, for once, against Gulliver, and it is used because the truth is too large to be credible. Swift gets the sharpest effect available to satire here: the honest report of Europe is indistinguishable, to a reasonable listener, from an invention.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Part IV, Chapter V

quotations.text: I enjoyed perfect health of body, and tranquillity of mind; I did not feel the treachery or inconstancy of a friend, nor the injuries of a secret or open enemy.
quotations.context: Gulliver’s account of his settled life among the Houyhnhnms.
quotations.analysis: The happiness is described entirely by subtraction — no treachery, no enemy, no bribes, no informers — so the paragraph is a catalogue of England with the sign reversed. He is at his most contented exactly where he has nobody of his own kind to be content with.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Part IV, Chapter X

quotations.text: wherein I have not been so studious of ornament as of truth.
quotations.context: The opening of the last chapter, addressed to the reader.
quotations.analysis: The claim to plainness is the oldest guarantee in travel writing and Swift has spent four voyages making it worthless. Gulliver closes the account with the same promise Sympson opened it with, and by now the reader has seen what his plain reporting can be made to carry.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Part IV, Chapter XII

quotations.text: principal design was to inform, and not to amuse thee.
quotations.context: The same paragraph, on his purpose in publishing.
quotations.analysis: Six words that a great many readers have ignored for three centuries, since the book’s afterlife has been mostly in nurseries. Set beside the letter to Sympson, where Gulliver complains that nobody has reformed in six months, the sentence is already an admission of failure.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Part IV, Chapter XII

quotations.text: when I behold a lump of deformity and diseases, both in body and mind, smitten with pride, it immediately breaks all the measures of my patience
quotations.context: The final paragraph of the book, on what he can and cannot tolerate in his own species.
quotations.analysis: He will forgive humanity its natural vices and not its pride, which is precisely the vice he is displaying while he says so, and Swift has him admit as much a few lines earlier. The book ends by catching its narrator in the fault the book exists to attack.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Part IV, Chapter XII

atAGlance.label: First published
atAGlance.note: By Benjamin Motte in London, in two volumes, with Lemuel Gulliver named as the author.

atAGlance.label: Attributed author
atAGlance.note: Swift’s name appears nowhere in the first edition, and the title imitates the factual confidence of voyage literature.

atAGlance.label: Corrected edition
atAGlance.note: George Faulkner’s Dublin edition prints the book in Swift’s collected works and adds Gulliver’s complaint that the text had been altered.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.note: Lilliput, Brobdingnag, the flying island and its neighbours, and the country of the Houyhnhnms.

criticalViews.position: A topical political satire
criticalViews.summary: Read against the Whig ministry, the South Sea Bubble and Anglo-Irish politics, much of Part I maps onto identifiable quarrels, and the high heels and egg ends onto identifiable parties and churches.
criticalViews.counter: The mapping stops working after Part I, and a satire that needed footnotes to be funny would not have survived in nurseries for three hundred years.

criticalViews.position: A general satire on human pride
criticalViews.summary: Swift himself described the design as vexing the world rather than diverting it, and this reading takes the four voyages as one escalating argument against the definition of man as a rational animal.
criticalViews.counter: It tends to treat Gulliver as a mouthpiece, when the last chapters make him ridiculous — a man who cannot sit at table with his wife but can talk to his horses for four hours a day.

criticalViews.position: The Part IV problem
criticalViews.summary: Everything turns on how far Swift stands behind the Houyhnhnms. They are chaste, rational and serene, and they also debate the extermination of a species by show of hands; Don Pedro is kind, and Gulliver cannot bear him.
criticalViews.counter: Making the Houyhnhnms simply a trap risks the opposite error, since the book gives them the only society in which its narrator is ever happy.

essayQuestions.question: How does Swift use changes of scale to make his satire work?
essayQuestions.focus: Perspective, proportion and judgement
plan: Set out the arithmetic: a ratio of twelve to one in each direction, kept consistent down to meals and clothing.
Use Part I to show scale producing comedy — court politics observed from above looks like ceremony without weight.
Reverse it with Part II: the same English institutions, described upwards, become a case for the prosecution.
Note what happens in Parts III and IV, where Gulliver is at ordinary human size and the disorientation is moral rather than physical.
Conclude on the reader’s position: the book never supplies a scale from which humanity looks reasonable.

essayQuestions.question: ‘Swift attacks not reason but reason without use.’ Discuss with reference to Part III.
essayQuestions.focus: The Academy, Munodi and the Struldbrugs
plan: Distinguish the two charges, and note that Swift wrote for readers who admired the new science.
Examine the Laputans: mathematics and music at the expense of houses that stand and clothes that fit.
Set Munodi’s working estate against the improved countryside around it as the chapter’s explicit control.
Read the Academy projects for the pattern — each is rational in aim and ruinous in cost.
Close with the Struldbrugs, where the failure is not technical but a failure to ask what the wish was for.

essayQuestions.question: Is Gulliver a reliable narrator? Does the question matter?
essayQuestions.focus: Voice, irony and the reader’s work
plan: Define the problem: Gulliver is accurate about facts and unreliable about their meaning.
Use the gunpowder scene, where his report of the king’s horror is filed under the king’s narrowness.
Take the prefatory documents as evidence that Swift undermines his narrator before the voyages begin.
Test the hardest case: how far Part IV endorses the Houyhnhnms, using Don Pedro as the counterweight.
Decide what the irony asks of a reader, and whether a satire that gives no reliable position can still teach anything.

essayQuestions.question: How does Gulliver’s Travels treat empire and the describing of other peoples?
essayQuestions.focus: Travel writing, possession and the last chapter
plan: Begin with form: the book imitates the voyage literature that supplied Europe with its picture of the world.
Read the inventory of Gulliver’s pockets as a survey performed on him rather than by him.
Use his refusal to help reduce Blefuscu to a province, and the terms in which the refusal is received.
Examine Part IV, Chapter XII, where he sets out how a country is normally taken and then exempts his own discoveries.
Weigh the irony against its limits: the Yahoos are described in the language contemporary travellers used for peoples they despised.

discussionQuestions: Swift published the book under Gulliver’s name and then had Gulliver attack the publisher. What does that arrangement do to a reader before Chapter I?
The King of Brobdingnag is the book’s nearest thing to a moral standard. Is he a good ruler, or only a shocked one?
The Houyhnhnms vote on whether to exterminate the Yahoos. Does that single detail change how Part IV should be read?
Don Pedro de Mendez is kind, patient and generous, and Gulliver cannot bear him. Why does Swift put him there?
For three centuries this has been sold as a children’s book about little people. What has to be removed to make that possible?

timeline.label: Jonathan Swift born in Dublin
timeline.detail: Educated at Kilkenny and Trinity College, Dublin, and later secretary to Sir William Temple.

timeline.label: Gulliver sails for the South Sea
timeline.detail: The fictional first voyage is dated 4 May 1699 — the book gives dates for every departure.

timeline.label: A Tale of a Tub and The Battle of the Books published
timeline.detail: Swift’s first sustained attack on false learning and modern authorship, and an anonymous one.

timeline.label: Swift installed as Dean of St Patrick’s, Dublin
timeline.detail: The post he held for the rest of his life, and the source of the name by which Ireland knew him.

timeline.label: The Drapier’s Letters
timeline.detail: Swift’s campaign against Wood’s halfpence, written in the voice of a Dublin cloth merchant — another invented plain-speaking narrator.

timeline.label: Travels into Several Remote Nations of the World published
timeline.detail: Benjamin Motte issues it in two volumes on 28 October, with Lemuel Gulliver on the title page.

timeline.label: Keys, sequels and imitations appear
timeline.detail: Explanatory ‘keys’, spurious continuations and parodies follow within months of publication.

timeline.label: A Modest Proposal
timeline.detail: The same deadpan applied to Irish famine, by a narrator whose arithmetic is as careful as Gulliver’s.

timeline.label: Faulkner’s Dublin edition
timeline.detail: The Travels appear in volume III of Swift’s collected works, with the letter to Sympson added.

timeline.label: Swift dies in Dublin
timeline.detail: He left the bulk of his estate to found a hospital for the mentally ill.

timeline.label: Fleischer Studios’ animated Gulliver’s Travels
timeline.detail: One of the best-known screen versions, and a clear case of the book surviving as Lilliput alone.

timeline.label: A television version attempts all four voyages
timeline.detail: Unusually among adaptations, it keeps Part IV and Gulliver’s damaged return.

places.name: Nottinghamshire
places.note: Gulliver’s father’s small estate, and the county he retires to at the end.

places.name: Emanuel College, Cambridge
places.note: Where Gulliver was sent at fourteen before being apprenticed to a London surgeon.

places.name: Leyden
places.note: Where he studied physic for two years and seven months, the standard training for a ship’s surgeon.

places.name: Bristol
places.note: The port from which the Antelope sails for the South Sea in 1699.

places.name: Nangasac
places.note: Nagasaki, the one real country Gulliver visits, reached from Luggnagg in Part III.

places.name: Amsterdam
places.note: His route home from Japan, and the port whose Dutch traders he treats with a marked and pointed hostility.

related.why: The other great English fiction dressed as a factual voyage, published seven years earlier and taken seriously as fact by many first readers.
The ancestor of the form: a traveller’s report of a rationally ordered commonwealth, delivered with the same straight face.
Political satire that makes its argument through animals, and that also has to be read twice by anybody who first met it as a story.
An earlier first-person report from the colonies that claims documentary authority for what it saw.
Another impossible country described with deadpan precision, and another book whose harder edges were trimmed away by its popularity.

books.title: Hamlet
books.author: William Shakespeare
books.setting: Elsinore, the Danish royal castle, with journeys to Paris, Wittenberg and England reported rather than shown
books.lengthNote: The longest play in the canon; no surviving early text has ever been performed uncut as a matter of routine
books.openingLine: Who's there?
books.summary: A prince comes home to a court that has already buried his father and married his mother, and a ghost tells him the new king is the murderer. What follows is not a hunt but an investigation: Hamlet has to decide what would count as proof of something no witness saw, and every answer he reaches arrives late or costs a life he did not mean to spend.

sourceText.label: Globe/Moby text of Hamlet
sourceText.note: Line numbers follow the traditional Globe numbering of a conflated text. The three early witnesses — Q1, Q2 and the Folio — differ, and modern editions number accordingly.

structure.label: Act I
structure.title: A dead king speaks before the living one is questioned
structure.summary: The Ghost walks twice before Hamlet is told about it, so the audience knows Denmark is disturbed before it meets the man who will be blamed for disturbing it. Claudius disposes of mourning, marriage and a foreign war in a single speech; by the end of the act Hamlet has a murder accusation from a source he cannot classify, and a plan to behave strangely on purpose.

scenes.title: The watch
scenes.summary: Sentries and Horatio see the Ghost and connect it to Denmark's rearmament against Fortinbras.

scenes.title: The court
scenes.summary: Claudius performs state business fluently; Hamlet refuses the performance, and hears that his father has been seen.

scenes.title: Advice and prohibition
scenes.summary: Laertes leaves for Paris with a lecture from Polonius, who then forbids Ophelia to see Hamlet.

scenes.title: The platform
scenes.summary: Hamlet meets the Ghost in the cold and follows it against his friends' advice.

scenes.title: The Ghost's account
scenes.summary: Poison in the ear, a command to revenge, an exemption for Gertrude, and an oath of silence.

structure.label: Act II
structure.title: The court turns observation into policy
structure.summary: Polonius sends a man to France to spread lies about his own son in order to hear the truth about him, which is the method of the whole court in miniature. Rosencrantz and Guildenstern are hired to do the same to Hamlet. The act ends with Hamlet inventing a better version of the same technique: a play staged to be watched by one man.

scenes.title: Reynaldo and the report
scenes.summary: Polonius teaches an informer to invent small vices; Ophelia describes Hamlet's silent visit.

scenes.title: Friends, ambassadors, players
scenes.summary: The schoolfellows are recruited, the Norwegian crisis is settled offstage, and the players give Hamlet an idea.

structure.label: Act III
structure.title: A play catches a king; a sword misses one
structure.summary: Two scenes of arranged watching sit either side of the Mousetrap. Claudius reacts, which Hamlet reads as proof, and then kneels to pray, which Hamlet reads as a bad moment to kill him. Within a hundred lines Hamlet does kill, through a curtain, without looking, and the man behind it is Ophelia's father.

scenes.title: The nunnery scene
scenes.summary: Hamlet's most famous soliloquy is spoken into a trap, and Ophelia is the bait he then turns on.

scenes.title: The Mousetrap
scenes.summary: Advice to the players, then a murder play; Claudius rises and calls for light.

scenes.title: The prayer
scenes.summary: Claudius finds he cannot repent; Hamlet postpones the killing on theological grounds.

scenes.title: The closet
scenes.summary: Polonius dies behind the arras, and the Ghost returns to a room where only Hamlet can see it.

structure.label: Act IV
structure.title: Grief is converted into political weapons
structure.summary: Hamlet is exported. In his absence the play shows what happens to the people he has damaged: Ophelia goes mad and drowns, Laertes comes home with a mob behind him, and Claudius spends one long scene turning a young man's grief into a poisoned foil. The act runs on offstage events reported by letters and messengers.

scenes.title: The report
scenes.summary: Gertrude tells Claudius of the killing and describes her son as mad.

scenes.title: The sponge
scenes.summary: Hamlet refuses to say where the body is and tells Rosencrantz what a courtier is for.

scenes.title: Supper of worms
scenes.summary: Claudius, working in public calm, sends Hamlet to England with a sealed order for his death.

scenes.title: The army crossing
scenes.summary: Fortinbras marches for a worthless patch of Poland; Hamlet measures himself against it.

scenes.title: Ophelia's songs
scenes.summary: Madness set to old tunes and flowers, then Laertes at the door with an armed crowd.

scenes.title: Pirates
scenes.summary: Horatio receives the letter that returns Hamlet to Denmark by accident.

scenes.title: The plot
scenes.summary: Claudius arranges the unbated sword and the poisoned cup; Gertrude reports the drowning.

structure.label: Act V
structure.title: Death becomes ordinary work, then arrives
structure.summary: A man who digs graves for a living sings at it, and Hamlet finally talks about death without metaphor, holding the skull of somebody he knew. The duel is a rigged fencing match that goes wrong in every direction at once; four people die of a plot designed to kill one, and the last Danish voice in the play gives the throne to a Norwegian.

scenes.title: The graveyard
scenes.summary: Gravediggers argue law and precedence; Yorick's skull; a funeral turns into a fight in the grave.

scenes.title: The duel
scenes.summary: Hamlet tells how he rewrote the commission, accepts the match, and the poison finds everyone.

characters.name: Hamlet
characters.role: Prince of Denmark, son of the murdered king
characters.summary: A student called home into a job he has no evidence for and no appetite for. His delay is usually described as a flaw, but the play keeps showing him doing the work of proof: testing the Ghost, staging the play, reading the commission. What he cannot do is act while he is still thinking, and the two things almost never stop at the same time.
characters.clue: He wears black at a wedding, talks to a skull, and stages a play in order to watch one man's face.
traits: unable to act and think at once

relationships.label: kills the father of, then fights

characters.name: Claudius
characters.role: King of Denmark, the dead king's brother
characters.summary: The most competent politician in the play and the only character who tells the audience outright that he is guilty. He settles a foreign crisis by letter, manages a rebellion by talking to it, and never once mishandles a room — which is what makes the prayer scene devastating, because it is the single thing he cannot negotiate.
characters.clue: He opens with a speech that makes a funeral and a wedding sound like one piece of administration, and later cannot pray.

characters.name: Gertrude
characters.role: Queen of Denmark
characters.summary: She is given very few lines in which to be anything other than the subject of other people's speeches about her. The play never says whether she knew about the murder, and the closet scene is the one place where she is asked directly and answers in a way that settles nothing. Her clearest moment is the speech describing Ophelia's drowning.
characters.clue: Her marriage is the scandal the play opens on, and her longest speech is a description of a drowning she did not witness.

relationships.label: hoped to have as a daughter-in-law

characters.name: Ophelia
characters.role: Polonius's daughter
characters.summary: Every scene she appears in before her madness has been arranged by a man: her father tells her what to feel, her brother tells her what to fear, and she is placed in a corridor with a book to be watched. When she loses her reason she is finally allowed to speak first and at length, and the court cannot stop her singing.
characters.clue: Told to return a suitor's letters, she is later the only person at court who can say anything she likes, and does it in songs and flowers.

characters.name: Polonius
characters.role: Counsellor to the king
characters.summary: A man who mistakes talking for thinking and surveillance for care. His famous advice to Laertes is a string of maxims delivered by somebody who immediately sends a spy after him. He dies because he is hiding in a room where he has no business, which is the only end the play could reasonably give him.
characters.clue: He gives his son a lecture of proverbs and then hires a man to slander him abroad; he dies behind a curtain.

characters.name: Laertes
characters.role: Polonius's son
characters.summary: He does in one scene what Hamlet cannot do in four acts: hears of his father's death, raises a mob and breaks into the palace. The play uses him to show that speed is not the same as justice — he is willing to cut throats in a church, and Claudius steers him within minutes of his arrival.
characters.clue: He storms the castle with a crowd at his back and is talked into poisoning a fencing sword instead.

characters.name: Horatio
characters.role: Hamlet's fellow student
characters.summary: The only person in Elsinore who wants nothing from Hamlet, and therefore the only one told the truth. He is a sceptic in the first scene who has to concede that the Ghost is real, and a survivor in the last who is ordered to stay alive and tell the story — a job the play leaves him doing after the lights go down.
characters.clue: He doubts the ghost, watches the king's face on Hamlet's behalf, and is talked out of drinking the poison so that someone can report what happened.

characters.name: The Ghost
characters.role: The spirit of the dead King Hamlet
characters.summary: It comes in armour, refuses to speak to anyone but its son, and gives an account of its own murder that no living witness can confirm. The play deliberately leaves its status open: a soul in purgatory, a devil exploiting grief, or a projection. Everything Hamlet does from Act II onwards is an attempt to work out which.
characters.clue: Armed from head to foot, it walks the same cold hour twice before it will say what happened in the orchard.

characters.name: Rosencrantz and Guildenstern
characters.role: Hamlet's schoolfellows, hired by the king
characters.summary: They are summoned by name, given a task neither of them quite admits to, and are never separated by the text into two distinguishable people. Their function is to show that friendship at this court is a form of employment; their deaths are reported in a single line by a messenger who has no idea who they were.
characters.clue: Two old friends sent for by the king, who cannot play a recorder but agree to play a prince.

characters.name: Fortinbras
characters.role: Prince of Norway
characters.summary: He is talked about for four acts and appears for a few minutes, which is exactly the point: he is the other son of a dead king, and he is busy. Hamlet watches his army march past to fight over ground not worth farming, and the play then hands Denmark to him because everyone with a better claim is dead on the floor.
characters.clue: A soldier who never meets the prince he is compared with, and who walks in at the end to find the throne empty.

themes.name: Revenge and delay
themes.summary: The play takes a genre in which a son is told to kill and asks what would have to be true before killing were justified. Hamlet's problem is not nerve — he stabs through a curtain without hesitating — but the standard of proof. The Ghost is testimony, not evidence, and no court in Denmark is going to hear it.
themes.development: Commanded in 1.5, doubted through Act II, tested in 3.2, deferred in 3.3, and finally performed in 5.2 by a man who is already dying and no longer choosing.

themes.name: Seeming and performance
themes.summary: Hamlet's first substantial line rejects the word 'seems', and he spends the rest of the play acting: a feigned madness, a play staged as an experiment, a rewritten commission sealed with a stolen signet. Claudius is doing the same thing from the other side of the throne, and only the audience gets to see both scripts.
themes.development: Set out in 1.2, adopted as policy in 1.5, professionalised in 3.2, and abandoned in Act V, where Hamlet stops performing and starts reporting.

themes.name: Watching and being watched
themes.summary: Almost no private conversation in this play is actually private. Reynaldo is sent to spy on Laertes, Ophelia is used as bait, Polonius hides twice, Rosencrantz and Guildenstern are briefed, and the king watches a play while being watched watching it. Elsinore does not punish dissent; it listens to it.
themes.development: A habit in Act II, a policy in Act III, and lethal in 3.4, where the listener behind the curtain is killed for listening.

themes.name: Death and the body
themes.summary: The play is unusually interested in what happens to bodies: poison in an ear, a corpse dragged to a lobby, a king going on progress through the guts of a beggar, a skull with earth in its jaw. Hamlet's metaphysics stay unresolved, but his physiology is exact, and the graveyard is where the two finally meet.
themes.development: Abstract in the soliloquies of Acts I and III; literal from 3.4 onwards, and entirely material by 5.1, where death is a trade with tools and songs.

themes.name: Madness, real and performed
themes.summary: Hamlet announces in advance that he will pretend, which ought to settle the question and does not: the pretence gives him licence to say things that are far too accurate to be mad and far too wild to be safe. Ophelia's madness is not announced, not strategic and not interpretable, and the court's response to it is to keep watching.
themes.development: Declared in 1.5, diagnosed by Polonius in Act II, weaponised in 3.1, and set beside the real thing in 4.5.

themes.name: Memory and record
themes.summary: The Ghost's actual demand is 'Remember me', and Hamlet answers by treating his mind as a notebook to be wiped and rewritten. The play is full of records: tables, letters, commissions, songs, an old jester remembered by a skull. Its last act of business is arranging for the story to be told correctly.
themes.development: A vow in 1.5, a joke about writing it down moments later, and a formal commission to Horatio in 5.2 — the play ends by appointing its own narrator.

techniques.name: Soliloquy
techniques.definition: A character alone on stage, thinking aloud to the audience.
techniques.bookDefinition: A character alone on stage, thinking aloud to the audience.
techniques.inThisBook: Hamlet has seven, and they do different jobs: self-disgust in 1.2, self-accusation in 2.2, abstract argument in 3.1, and in 4.4 a comparison with an army he can see from where he stands.

techniques.name: Metatheatre
techniques.definition: A play that draws attention to its own nature as performance.
techniques.bookDefinition: A play that draws attention to its own nature as performance.
techniques.inThisBook: A troupe of actors is hired, given a lecture on acting, and used to conduct an experiment on a spectator — inside a theatre, watched by spectators.

techniques.name: Foils
techniques.definition: A character constructed to throw another's choices into relief by making different ones.
techniques.bookDefinition: A character constructed to throw another's choices into relief by making different ones.
techniques.inThisBook: Laertes and Fortinbras are both sons of dead fathers who act at once. The play puts one in Act IV and the other in Act V so that Hamlet's hesitation is measured twice.

techniques.name: Prose against verse
techniques.definition: Shifting between metrical speech and prose to mark status, sanity or intimacy.
techniques.bookDefinition: Shifting between metrical speech and prose to mark status, sanity or intimacy.
techniques.inThisBook: Hamlet drops into prose with the players, the spies and the gravediggers, and rises into verse when he is alone; Ophelia's madness arrives as prose broken by snatches of song.

techniques.name: Disease and rot
techniques.definition: A sustained figurative field that describes a political situation as a body's illness.
techniques.bookDefinition: A sustained figurative field that describes a political situation as a body's illness.
techniques.inThisBook: Denmark is rotten, an unweeded garden, an ulcer with a skin over it; the murder itself is a poison poured into a body, so the metaphor and the plot share a mechanism.

techniques.name: Hendiadys
techniques.definition: Joining two nouns with 'and' where grammar would expect one noun modifying another.
techniques.bookDefinition: Joining two nouns with 'and' where grammar would expect one noun modifying another.
techniques.inThisBook: 'The book and volume of my brain' and 'the expectancy and rose of the fair state' are typical: the figure doubles a thought instead of completing it, and the play's language keeps hesitating in the same way its hero does.

quotations.text: Seems, madam! nay it is; I know not 'seems.'
quotations.speaker: Hamlet
quotations.context: His first extended speech, answering Gertrude's question about why his grief looks so particular.
quotations.analysis: He objects to a verb, which tells you what kind of hero this is going to be. The irony is scheduled three scenes later, when he decides to put on an appearance deliberately, and the play never lets him have the word back.

quotations.text: O, that this too too solid flesh would melt Thaw and resolve itself into a dew!
quotations.speaker: Hamlet
quotations.context: The first soliloquy, immediately after the court has left the stage.
quotations.analysis: Three verbs of dissolving in a row, each one weaker than the last, so the wish loses force as it is spoken. Nothing here is about revenge or a ghost: the speech happens before he knows anything, which means the despair is prior to the plot rather than caused by it.

quotations.text: Frailty, thy name is woman!
quotations.speaker: Hamlet
quotations.context: In the same soliloquy, on his mother's remarriage.
quotations.analysis: He generalises from one woman to half the species in five words, and the grammar does the work: an abstract noun is addressed directly, then given a name. The line is quoted as if it were the play's verdict, but it is spoken by a man who has just told us he cannot bear to think about it.

quotations.text: This above all: to thine ownself be true, And it must follow, as the night the day, Thou canst not then be false to any man.
quotations.speaker: Lord Polonius
quotations.context: The end of a long farewell lecture to Laertes, who is trying to catch a ship.
quotations.analysis: The most quoted piece of wisdom in the play belongs to its most tiresome speaker, and he contradicts it within a scene by sending Reynaldo to lie about Laertes abroad. Read in context it is advice about self-interest rather than integrity, which is why the court repeats it and nobody follows it.

quotations.text: Something is rotten in the state of Denmark.
quotations.speaker: Marcellus
quotations.context: Watching Hamlet follow the Ghost away along the platform.
quotations.analysis: It is given to a minor soldier, not to the prince, which matters: the corruption is visible from the guard post before anyone at court admits it. 'Something' is doing a great deal of work — nobody on stage yet knows what, and the audience has not been told either.

quotations.text: My tables,--meet it is I set it down, That one may smile, and smile, and be a villain;
quotations.speaker: Hamlet
quotations.context: Alone, minutes after the Ghost has gone.
quotations.analysis: He has just been told his uncle is a murderer and his response is to reach for a notebook. Writing it down converts unbearable testimony into a manageable proposition, and the stage direction that follows — he actually writes — makes the intellectual habit physical.

quotations.text: There are more things in heaven and earth, Horatio, Than are dreamt of in your philosophy.
quotations.speaker: Hamlet
quotations.context: To Horatio, who has just been asked to swear on the sword while the Ghost calls from under the stage.
quotations.analysis: It is usually quoted as mysticism; in position it is an argument with a sceptic who has already seen the ghost and is still reasoning. Note the address: Hamlet uses his friend's name to make the rebuke personal, and the line's authority depends on a spirit shouting from beneath the floorboards.

quotations.text: How strange or odd soe'er I bear myself, As I perchance hereafter shall think meet To put an antic disposition on,
quotations.speaker: Hamlet
quotations.context: Swearing his friends to secrecy about anything they may see him do.
quotations.analysis: The madness is announced in advance, under oath, as a wardrobe decision — 'put on' is the verb used for clothes. That advance notice is what keeps the question alive for four acts: everything strange Hamlet does afterwards has been pre-authorised, so nothing he does can settle the matter.

quotations.text: Though this be madness, yet there is method in 't.
quotations.speaker: Lord Polonius
quotations.context: An aside during the conversation about words, words, words.
quotations.analysis: Polonius is right and cannot use it. He detects the design under the nonsense and then draws the wrong conclusion about what the design is for, which is the court's characteristic failure: good observation, bad inference. The line is spoken aside, so the audience is invited to grade his reading against theirs.

quotations.text: Denmark's a prison.
quotations.speaker: Hamlet
quotations.context: To Rosencrantz and Guildenstern, moments after working out that they were sent for.
quotations.analysis: Three words of prose, offered as a flat statement of fact to two men who have just been hired as warders without quite realising it. The exchange that follows turns it into a philosophical game about thinking making it so, which is exactly how Hamlet avoids being pinned down by people fishing for symptoms.

quotations.text: What a piece of work is a man! how noble in reason! how infinite in faculty!
quotations.speaker: Hamlet
quotations.context: Explaining to the schoolfellows why he has lost all his mirth.
quotations.analysis: A textbook humanist celebration of mankind, delivered in prose to two informers, and finished a few lines later with dust. He is performing an orthodoxy in order to demonstrate that he no longer holds it — the praise is a set-up for the dismissal.

quotations.text: O, what a rogue and peasant slave am I!
quotations.speaker: Hamlet
quotations.context: Alone after the First Player's speech about Hecuba.
quotations.analysis: The trigger is not the murder but a professional actor crying about a woman dead for centuries. Hamlet's self-disgust is comparative and aesthetic: somebody else produced a convincing performance of grief and he has not, which is a strange thing to punish yourself for and a precise clue to what he thinks feeling is.

quotations.text: the play 's the thing Wherein I'll catch the conscience of the king.
quotations.speaker: Hamlet
quotations.context: The couplet that ends Act II, having just admitted the Ghost may be a devil.
quotations.analysis: It is the only plan in the play arrived at by argument, and it is a piece of experimental design: a stimulus, a subject, an observer. The rhyme gives it the confidence of a conclusion, and the flaw is buried in the verb — a conscience caught is a reaction, not a confession.

quotations.text: To be, or not to be, that is the question, Whether 'tis nobler in the mind to suffer The slings and arrows of outrageous fortune, Or to take arms against a sea of troubles, And by opposing end them?
quotations.speaker: Hamlet
quotations.context: Spoken while Claudius and Polonius are hidden, having placed Ophelia in his path.
quotations.analysis: The speech contains no first-person pronoun and names nobody: it is written as a general problem in ethics, not a private confession. That is worth noticing because two men are listening for symptoms and hear philosophy instead — the most intimate speech in the play is also the most carefully depersonalised.

quotations.text: Thus conscience does make cowards of us all; And thus the native hue of resolution Is sicklied o'er with the pale cast of thought,
quotations.speaker: Hamlet
quotations.context: The close of the same soliloquy, before he sees Ophelia.
quotations.analysis: 'Conscience' here means consciousness as much as moral scruple, and the metaphor is a complexion: thought spreads over resolve like an illness over a face. It is the play's own diagnosis of its hero, offered by the hero, which is one reason the diagnosis has never quite been improved on.

quotations.text: O, what a noble mind is here o'erthrown!
quotations.speaker: Ophelia
quotations.context: Alone on stage after Hamlet's exit, before the watchers come out.
quotations.analysis: She is the only character who mourns Hamlet as a loss rather than assessing him as a problem, and she does it in a formal lament built from three-part lists — eye, tongue, sword. The speech also establishes what he was like before the play began, information the audience has no other way of getting.

quotations.text: The lady protests too much, methinks.
quotations.speaker: Queen Gertrude
quotations.context: Watching the Player Queen swear she will never remarry.
quotations.analysis: Asked to judge a play about a widow's promise, Gertrude gives a critic's verdict on the acting rather than a wife's answer to the charge. Whether that is composure or blindness is the closest the play comes to telling us what she knows, and it declines to decide.

quotations.text: O, my offence is rank it smells to heaven;
quotations.speaker: King Claudius
quotations.context: Alone, trying to pray, immediately after the play has broken up.
quotations.analysis: This is the moment the audience stops needing the Ghost: the confession comes from the murderer, unprompted, with nobody listening. Shakespeare gives the proof to the theatre and withholds it from Hamlet, who walks in forty lines later and sees only a man at his devotions.

quotations.text: My words fly up, my thoughts remain below: Words without thoughts never to heaven go.
quotations.speaker: King Claudius
quotations.context: Rising from his knees, seconds after Hamlet has left without killing him.
quotations.analysis: The couplet is a joke at Hamlet's expense that Hamlet never hears: he spared a man whose prayer was not working. The chiastic arrangement of words and thoughts — up, below, words, thoughts — makes the failure sound like a law of physics rather than a moral judgement.

quotations.text: How all occasions do inform against me, And spur my dull revenge!
quotations.speaker: Hamlet
quotations.context: On a plain in Denmark, watching Fortinbras's army march towards Poland.
quotations.analysis: 'Inform against' is legal language for turning informer, so Hamlet describes the world as a witness giving evidence against him. It is his last soliloquy, and the resolution it reaches is immediately undercut by the fact that he is being escorted onto a ship to England as he speaks it.

quotations.text: Alas, poor Yorick! I knew him, Horatio: a fellow of infinite jest, of most excellent fancy:
quotations.speaker: Hamlet
quotations.context: In the churchyard, holding a skull the gravedigger has identified.
quotations.analysis: It is the first death in the play he can speak about without a theory, and the reason is that he has a name and a memory to attach to the bone. The scene is in prose, and the joking goes on around him: the play's most affecting moment about mortality is set in a workplace where corpses are routine.

quotations.text: There's a divinity that shapes our ends, Rough-hew them how we will,
quotations.speaker: Hamlet
quotations.context: Telling Horatio how he found and rewrote the sealed commission on board ship.
quotations.analysis: He credits providence in the middle of an account of his own forgery, seal and all. The Hamlet of Act V explains his actions after he has taken them rather than before, and the change in tense is the change in the man: less deliberation, more report.

quotations.text: the readiness is all: since no man has aught of what he leaves, what is't to leave betimes?
quotations.speaker: Hamlet
quotations.context: To Horatio, who has offered to call off the fencing match.
quotations.analysis: Set this against 'To be, or not to be': the same question about dying, answered now in prose, in one sentence, with no metaphors. He has stopped arguing, and the calm is not peace but a kind of exhaustion that the plot immediately exploits.

quotations.text: Which have solicited. The rest is silence.
quotations.speaker: Hamlet
quotations.context: Dying, having given his vote for the succession and told Horatio to report the circumstances.
quotations.analysis: His last act is administrative: a vote, a request for an accurate account, and then nothing. 'The rest' means both what remains to be said and what remains of him, and the man who could not stop talking hands the talking over and stops.

atAGlance.label: Written
atAGlance.note: Close in date to Julius Caesar, which the play itself remembers when Polonius says he once played Caesar.

atAGlance.label: First printed
atAGlance.note: The short First Quarto. A longer Second Quarto followed in 1604/5, and the Folio text in 1623.

atAGlance.label: Three early texts
atAGlance.note: Each preserves material the others lack, so no edition can print all of Hamlet without choosing.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.note: Two of the five acts pass before Hamlet takes any action against Claudius at all.

criticalViews.position: Hamlet as a problem of character
criticalViews.summary: The reading that dominated the nineteenth century and shaped most since: the play is the study of a particular temperament, and the delay is explained by something in the man — reflectiveness, melancholy, a will paralysed by thought.
criticalViews.counter: It has to treat Elsinore as scenery. A court that hires spies, opens letters and stages entrapments gives Hamlet practical reasons for caution that have nothing to do with temperament.

criticalViews.position: Hamlet as a play about proof
criticalViews.summary: On this account the delay is rational. The only evidence is a ghost of uncertain origin; Hamlet designs a test, gets a reaction rather than a confession, and has to decide what a reaction is worth.
criticalViews.counter: It struggles with 3.4, where he kills a concealed listener without checking who it is — a man careful about evidence has just behaved as carelessly as possible.

criticalViews.position: Hamlet as three plays, not one
criticalViews.summary: Because Q1, Q2 and the Folio differ substantially, textual criticism since the late twentieth century has argued that editors who conflate them produce a play no early audience ever saw.
criticalViews.counter: Readers and actors still need a text to work from, and the conflated tradition has shaped four centuries of performance, which is itself a fact about the play.

essayQuestions.question: Is Hamlet's delay a failure of character or a problem of evidence?
essayQuestions.focus: Revenge, proof and the status of the Ghost
plan: Establish what Hamlet actually has at the end of Act I: unverifiable testimony from a spirit whose nature he says he cannot classify.
Trace the design of the Mousetrap in 2.2 and 3.2 as an experiment, and ask precisely what Claudius's reaction proves.
Turn the argument at 3.3: the refusal to kill a praying man is a theological calculation, not hesitation — and the audience knows the prayer failed.
Test the counter-case with 3.4, where he stabs a concealed listener without identifying him.
Close on Act V, where the killing finally happens under conditions Hamlet did not arrange and cannot control.

essayQuestions.question: How does Shakespeare use watching and being watched in Hamlet?
essayQuestions.focus: Surveillance, privacy and the court
plan: Open with Reynaldo in 2.1: the court's method stated in its purest form, applied by a father to his own son.
Map the arranged scenes — 3.1 with two men concealed, 3.2 with the whole court watching a king watch a play, 3.4 with a listener behind the arras.
Show how Hamlet adopts the method rather than rejecting it: the play, the rewritten commission, the friends he tests.
Consider what the play makes private: the soliloquies, Claudius's prayer, and the fact that the audience is always the extra watcher.
Decide whether the arrival of Fortinbras ends the surveillance or simply changes who is doing it.

essayQuestions.question: Discuss the presentation of Ophelia and Gertrude.
essayQuestions.focus: Constraint, silence and what the play declines to tell us
plan: Count what each is allowed to say, and note how much of it is answering a question put by a man.
Read 1.3 and 3.1 as a sequence in which Ophelia is instructed, positioned and then abused for being where she was told to stand.
Examine 4.5: madness as the first occasion on which she speaks first, at length, and without being interrupted.
Weigh Gertrude's silences — her refusal to answer directly in 3.4, and the strangely detailed drowning speech in 4.7.
Assess two readings: a play that exposes the constraints on these women, or one that shares them.

essayQuestions.question: 'Hamlet is a play about acting.' Discuss.
essayQuestions.focus: Performance, theatre and the antic disposition
plan: Begin with 1.2, where Hamlet rejects 'seems', and 1.5, where he schedules a performance of madness.
Use the players in 2.2: a professional weeping for Hecuba shames a son who cannot produce feeling on demand.
Take the advice to the players in 3.2 as the play's own theory of acting, then watch it applied to an audience of one.
Set Claudius beside Hamlet as a rival performer whose public manner never slips until he is alone in 3.3.
Conclude with Act V, where Hamlet stops performing, and ask what he loses and gains by it.

discussionQuestions: The Ghost's account of the murder has no other witness. What would it take for Hamlet to know it is true?
Hamlet announces his madness before he performs it. Does that settle the question of whether any of it is real?
Is Claudius a good king? Consider how he handles Norway, the rebellion and the succession.
Why does Shakespeare keep Hamlet offstage for so much of Act IV?
Horatio is told to stay alive and report what happened. Do you trust the account he would give?

timeline.label: Saxo Grammaticus writes the Amleth story into the Gesta Danorum
timeline.detail: Composed around the turn of the thirteenth century: feigned madness, a murdered father and a dangerous uncle are all already there.

timeline.label: Belleforest retells Amleth in the Histoires tragiques
timeline.detail: The French version that carried the Danish story into sixteenth-century print and, in some form, to Shakespeare.

timeline.label: The Globe opens on Bankside
timeline.detail: The playhouse the Lord Chamberlain's Men built for themselves, and the theatre Hamlet was written for.

timeline.label: Hamlet most likely completed
timeline.detail: Usually dated to about 1599-1601, close to Julius Caesar and Twelfth Night.

timeline.label: Entered in the Stationers' Register by James Roberts
timeline.detail: The entry precedes the first printing by a year.

timeline.label: The First Quarto printed
timeline.detail: Published by Nicholas Ling and John Trundle. Much shorter than the later texts, and differently ordered in places.

timeline.label: The Second Quarto printed
timeline.detail: Printed by James Roberts for Nicholas Ling, and advertised as enlarged; the longest of the early versions.

timeline.label: The First Folio text
timeline.detail: Prints material the Second Quarto lacks and omits material it has, so the two are witnesses rather than drafts.

timeline.label: Thomas Betterton plays Hamlet after the theatres reopen
timeline.detail: The beginning of the long tradition in which the part is treated as the measure of an actor.

timeline.label: Sarah Bernhardt plays Hamlet
timeline.detail: A reminder that the role has never been securely fixed to one kind of body or voice.

timeline.label: Laurence Olivier's film
timeline.detail: Heavily cut, and the first Shakespeare film to win the Academy Award for Best Picture.

timeline.label: Kenneth Branagh films a full-text Hamlet
timeline.detail: A four-hour screen version that keeps the material most productions have to lose.

places.name: Kronborg Castle, Helsingør
places.note: The fortress on the sound that gave Shakespeare his Elsinore, guarding the narrowest crossing into the Baltic.

places.name: The Øresund
places.note: The strait the battlements overlook, and the water Hamlet is shipped across towards England.

places.name: Wittenberg
places.note: The university Hamlet and Horatio come from, and which Claudius will not let him return to.

places.name: Paris
places.note: Where Laertes goes, and where Reynaldo is sent to spread useful slander about him.

places.name: London
places.note: England, where the sealed commission sends Hamlet to die — and where the play was first performed.

related.why: The opposite case: a tragedy of soliloquy in which the hero acts far too quickly and thinks about it afterwards.
Written within a few years, and equally concerned with what happens when a court stops being able to tell truth from performance.
The play Hamlet remembers when Polonius says he once played Caesar, and another study of a political killing argued out in advance.
The next of the great tragedies, and the clearest contrast: a hero destroyed by accepting evidence too quickly.
The expanded Astor edition, with fuller textual, critical and performance material on the three early texts.

videos.title: Why should you read "Hamlet"? - Iseult Gillespie
videos.note: A short animated overview of the story and of why Hamlet's hesitation has kept audiences arguing for four centuries.

videos.title: To be, or not to be, that is the question | Hamlet's Soliloquy | Hamlet (2018) | Shakespeare's Globe
videos.note: Michelle Terry performs the most famous soliloquy on the Globe stage, a chance to hear the speech spoken directly to an audience in daylight as it first was.

videos.title: Hamlet: A Character Study
videos.note: Actor Rory Kinnear and director Nicholas Hytner explain the key aspects of Hamlet's character as they understood it for the National Theatre production.

books.title: Henry IV, Part 1
books.author: William Shakespeare
books.setting: England and Wales in 1402 and 1403, from the Boar's-Head in Eastcheap to the field at Shrewsbury
books.lengthNote: Around 3,000 lines, with the Eastcheap scenes carrying an unusually large body of prose for a history play
books.openingLine: So shaken as we are, so wan with care, Find we a time for frighted peace to pant,
books.summary: A king who took the crown from Richard II cannot get out of England to atone for it, because the men who helped him take it now want paying. His heir is drinking in Eastcheap with a fat knight who thinks honour is a word, while the son of the rebel earls is winning the reputation the prince should have. The play cuts between court, tavern and rebel camp until all three arrive on the same field, and lets Hal settle the account in person.

sourceText.label: Globe/Moby text of Henry IV, Part 1
sourceText.note: Line numbers follow the traditional Globe numbering, which counts prose lines as printed. Modern editions vary.

structure.label: Act I
structure.title: Three plots introduced, and a prince who has already decided
structure.summary: The king postpones his crusade because Wales and Scotland are both in flames, and envies Northumberland the son he has. Hal robs a coach with Falstaff and then tells the audience, alone, that the whole tavern life is a calculated eclipse. Hotspur refuses to hand over his prisoners and the Percys begin to plan.

scenes.title: The crusade deferred
scenes.summary: News from Wales and Northumberland cancels the king's journey to Jerusalem before it starts.

scenes.title: Eastcheap
scenes.summary: Falstaff and Hal trade insults, Poins proposes the Gadshill trick, and Hal explains his plan to nobody but us.

scenes.title: The prisoners
scenes.summary: Hotspur's account of the popinjay on the battlefield does not save him; Worcester turns a quarrel into a conspiracy.

structure.label: Act II
structure.title: A robbery, a robbery of the robbers, and a rehearsal
structure.summary: Carriers, chamberlains and thieves fill the road to Gadshill, and the practical joke goes exactly as Poins designed it. Back at the tavern Falstaff's lie grows from two men to eleven while the audience counts, and then the two of them take turns playing the king so that Hal can hear his own reckoning read out in advance.

scenes.title: The inn yard at Rochester
scenes.summary: Carriers complain about fleas and the price of oats; Gadshill arranges his intelligence.

scenes.title: The highway
scenes.summary: Falstaff robs the travellers and is robbed in turn by Hal and Poins in disguise.

scenes.title: Warkworth
scenes.summary: Hotspur reads a letter of refusal aloud and refuses to tell his wife where he is going.

scenes.title: The Boar's-Head
scenes.summary: Francis is baited, the buckram men multiply, the sheriff knocks, and Falstaff is banished in play.

structure.label: Act III
structure.title: Two fathers, two interviews
structure.summary: At Bangor the rebels divide England on a map and quarrel about the course of a river, and Glendower and Hotspur cannot be in a room together for ten lines. In London the king tells his son that a crown is kept by being rarely seen, and compares him — to his face — with Richard II. Hal promises to redeem everything on Percy's head.

scenes.title: The map
scenes.summary: Mortimer, Glendower, Worcester and Hotspur carve up the kingdom and argue over a bend in the Trent.

scenes.title: The interview
scenes.summary: Henry accuses Hal of being the new Richard; Hal answers with a promise and gets a command.

scenes.title: The reckoning
scenes.summary: Falstaff quarrels with the Hostess over a picked pocket and is given a charge of foot.

structure.label: Act IV
structure.title: The rebellion thins out
structure.summary: Northumberland is sick, Glendower cannot raise his men in time, and Hotspur decides that fighting without them will look better anyway. Falstaff marches a company of scarecrows he has recruited for the bribes, and admits it. The king offers terms that Worcester decides not to repeat.

scenes.title: The rebel camp
scenes.summary: Two allies fail to arrive, and Hotspur converts each absence into an argument for attacking.

scenes.title: The road near Coventry
scenes.summary: Falstaff explains, to the audience, how he sold the men who could afford to buy their way out.

scenes.title: Terms offered
scenes.summary: Blunt brings the king's offer of pardon; Hotspur recites the Percys' grievances back to the beginning.

scenes.title: York
scenes.summary: The Archbishop sends letters, expecting the rebellion to fail and the reprisals to reach him.

structure.label: Act V
structure.title: Shrewsbury
structure.summary: Worcester suppresses the king's pardon, so the battle happens on a lie. Decoy kings are killed across the field while the real one is saved by his son. Hal kills Hotspur, speaks over him with unexpected tenderness, and then watches Falstaff claim the body and the credit.

scenes.title: The catechism
scenes.summary: Hal offers single combat, the king offers pardon, and Falstaff, left alone, takes honour apart word by word.

scenes.title: The suppressed offer
scenes.summary: Worcester keeps the pardon from Hotspur, who hears instead how handsomely the prince praised him.

scenes.title: Counterfeit kings
scenes.summary: Blunt dies dressed as the king; Falstaff offers Hal a bottle of sack instead of a pistol.

scenes.title: Two stars
scenes.summary: Hal saves his father, kills Hotspur, and finds Falstaff playing dead and then claiming the kill.

scenes.title: After
scenes.summary: Worcester is sent to execution, Douglas is freed, and the king divides his armies for the campaigns still to come.

characters.name: Prince Hal
characters.role: Henry, Prince of Wales, the king's eldest son
characters.summary: He tells the audience his whole strategy in his first scene alone, which leaves the play free to spend four acts on the question of whether a man can perform disgrace for years without being changed by it. He is funnier than Falstaff intends him to be and colder than the tavern realises.
characters.clue: He explains his entire plan in a soliloquy before the audience has had time to like him, then goes back to drinking for two more acts.

relationships.label: companion, straight man and eventual judge of
relationships.note: Every scene between them rehearses the rejection that closes Part 2.

characters.name: Sir John Falstaff
characters.role: A knight, and the prince's tavern companion
