books.title: Macbeth
books.author: William Shakespeare
books.setting: Eleventh-century Scotland, with one scene at the English court
books.lengthNote: Around 2,100 lines — the shortest of the major tragedies
books.openingLine: When shall we three meet again In thunder, lightning, or in rain?
books.summary: Three witches greet a victorious general with a prophecy that he will be king. Within a day he has murdered the king who trusts him, and the rest of the play watches him kill to keep a crown that gives him nothing. It is Shakespeare's fastest tragedy, and the speed is the argument: Macbeth is never allowed the time to become a different kind of man.

sourceText.label: Globe/Moby text of Macbeth
sourceText.note: Line numbers follow the traditional Globe numbering. Modern editions vary by a line or two.

structure.label: Act I
structure.title: A prophecy, and a decision made in the dark
structure.summary: Macbeth and Banquo meet the witches on the heath and hear that Macbeth will be thane of Cawdor and king. When the first title arrives within minutes, the second stops being an absurdity. Lady Macbeth reads his letter, judges him too decent to take the nearest way, and has the murder arranged before he reaches the door.

scenes.title: Thunder
scenes.summary: Three witches agree to meet Macbeth on the heath.

scenes.title: The report
scenes.summary: A wounded sergeant describes Macbeth carving his way through a rebel army.

scenes.title: The prophecy
scenes.summary: The witches hail Macbeth as Glamis, Cawdor and king hereafter, and tell Banquo he will father kings.

scenes.title: Malcolm named heir
scenes.summary: Duncan thanks Macbeth and then names his own son Prince of Cumberland, putting a step in Macbeth's way.

scenes.title: The letter
scenes.summary: Lady Macbeth reads Macbeth's letter and calls on the spirits to strip her of pity.

scenes.title: The welcome
scenes.summary: Duncan arrives at Inverness and praises the sweetness of the air.

scenes.title: The argument
scenes.summary: Macbeth decides against the murder; his wife changes his mind in under fifty lines.

structure.label: Act II
structure.title: The murder, and the noise that follows it
structure.summary: Macbeth sees a dagger that is not there, kills Duncan offstage, and comes back unable to say 'Amen'. The knocking at the gate, the Porter's drunken joke about hell, and the discovery of the body turn a private act into a public emergency. Malcolm and Donalbain run, which conveniently makes them suspects.

scenes.title: The dagger
scenes.summary: Banquo confesses uneasy dreams; alone, Macbeth follows a dagger he cannot grasp.

scenes.title: After
scenes.summary: Macbeth returns with the grooms' daggers, hearing a voice cry sleep no more.

scenes.title: The knocking
scenes.summary: The Porter plays hell's gatekeeper; Macduff discovers the body and Macbeth kills the grooms.

scenes.title: Unnatural signs
scenes.summary: Ross and an Old Man report horses eating each other; Macbeth goes to Scone to be crowned.

structure.label: Act III
structure.title: Killing to keep what killing won
structure.summary: Banquo suspects and says nothing. Macbeth, who now fears the second half of the prophecy more than the first, hires murderers without telling his wife. Fleance escapes, the ghost sits in Macbeth's chair at the banquet, and the marriage that planned the first murder comes apart over the third.

scenes.title: Banquo's suspicion
scenes.summary: Banquo weighs what Macbeth has gained; Macbeth hires two murderers.

scenes.title: Scorpions
scenes.summary: Macbeth keeps his wife ignorant of the plan for the first time.

scenes.title: The ambush
scenes.summary: Banquo is killed and Fleance escapes into the dark.

scenes.title: The banquet
scenes.summary: Banquo's ghost takes Macbeth's seat and the state dinner collapses.

scenes.title: Hecate
scenes.summary: Hecate rebukes the witches — a scene most scholars think was added later.

scenes.title: Rumour
scenes.summary: Lennox speaks in careful irony; Macduff has gone to England.

structure.label: Act IV
structure.title: Apparitions, and a household murdered
structure.summary: Macbeth demands more prophecy and is given three riddles that sound like safety. He orders the killing of Macduff's wife and children, an act with no strategic purpose at all. In England, Malcolm tests Macduff by pretending to be worse than the tyrant, and the news from home arrives.

scenes.title: The apparitions
scenes.summary: Beware Macduff; none of woman born shall harm Macbeth; he is safe till Birnam wood moves.

scenes.title: Fife
scenes.summary: Lady Macduff and her son are murdered on stage.

scenes.title: The English court
scenes.summary: Malcolm tests Macduff's loyalty; Ross brings the news from Fife.

structure.label: Act V
structure.title: The riddles come true, and mean nothing
structure.summary: Lady Macbeth washes hands that are clean. Macbeth, told of her death, can find no more feeling in it than a line about tomorrow. Birnam wood moves because the army carries it; the man not of woman born was delivered by caesarean section. Every guarantee holds and every one betrays him.

scenes.title: Sleepwalking
scenes.summary: A doctor and gentlewoman watch Lady Macbeth relive the murders in her sleep.

scenes.title: The march
scenes.summary: The Scottish lords join Malcolm's army near Birnam.

scenes.title: The yellow leaf
scenes.summary: Macbeth clings to the apparitions and asks the doctor to cure his wife's mind.

scenes.title: Branches
scenes.summary: Malcolm orders each soldier to cut a bough for cover.

scenes.title: Tomorrow
scenes.summary: The queen is dead; a messenger reports that the wood is moving.

scenes.title: The assault
scenes.summary: The army throws down its screen of branches.

scenes.title: Young Siward
scenes.summary: Macbeth kills a man he cannot fear and begins to look for Macduff.

scenes.title: The end
scenes.summary: Macduff reveals his birth, kills Macbeth, and Malcolm is hailed king.

characters.name: Macbeth
characters.role: Thane of Glamis, then Cawdor, then king of Scotland
characters.summary: A soldier praised for a savagery the state approves of, who discovers that the same nerve is unbearable when he uses it for himself. He imagines every murder in full before he commits it and feels every consequence afterwards, which is why the play is a tragedy rather than a case study.
characters.clue: A soldier whose imagination is his conscience: he sees the dagger before he uses it and hears the voice that will not let him sleep afterwards.

relationships.label: married to
relationships.note: Partners in the first murder, strangers by the third.

characters.name: Lady Macbeth
characters.role: Macbeth's wife, later queen
characters.summary: She reads her husband accurately in a single speech and organises the murder he cannot organise himself. Her strength is a performance she has to summon, and once the crown is won she has no further part to play, which is where the sleepwalking begins.
characters.clue: She calls on spirits to unsex her, tells her husband to look like the innocent flower, and later cannot get a spot off a clean hand.

characters.name: Banquo
characters.role: A general, father of Fleance
characters.summary: He hears the same prophecy and does nothing with it, which makes him the play's control experiment. His silence after Duncan's death is not innocence either: he suspects Macbeth of foul play and keeps quiet because the prophecy also promised something to him.

characters.name: Duncan
characters.role: King of Scotland
characters.summary: Generous, trusting and a poor judge of faces — he says as much about the last thane of Cawdor moments before promoting the next traitor. Shakespeare makes him gentler than the historical king so that the murder costs the audience something.

characters.name: Macduff
characters.role: Thane of Fife
characters.summary: He discovers the body, refuses the coronation, and leaves for England without warning his household — a decision the play does not let him off. His grief in 4.3 is the one moment where a man is allowed to feel a loss fully before acting on it.

characters.name: Malcolm
characters.role: Duncan's elder son, Prince of Cumberland
characters.summary: Named heir in 1.4, which is the political fact that makes the prophecy inconvenient. He flees, learns caution, and tests Macduff with a portrait of himself as a worse tyrant than Macbeth — a scene that shows a king being manufactured rather than born.

characters.name: The Weird Sisters
characters.role: Three witches
characters.summary: They tell the truth in a form designed to be misheard. Nothing they say compels anybody to do anything, which is the difficulty: the play never settles whether they cause the future or merely describe it accurately enough to be dangerous.

characters.name: Lady Macduff
characters.role: Macduff's wife
characters.summary: She gets one scene, and uses it to say the thing nobody else will: that a man who leaves his wife and children unguarded has behaved like a traitor to them, whatever his politics. She is killed on stage, which is rare in Shakespeare and deliberate here.

characters.name: Fleance
characters.role: Banquo's son
characters.summary: He speaks eleven words and then escapes into the dark, and the whole second half of the play runs on that escape. James VI and I's line claimed descent from Banquo, so Fleance running offstage is also the future sitting in the audience.

themes.name: Ambition
themes.summary: The play is careful to show that ambition is not the same as wanting power. Macbeth has power already and is praised for it; what the witches give him is a way of picturing more, and the picture will not leave him alone. Shakespeare gives the desire a body — a spur, a leap, a fall — and no destination.
themes.development: Suggested in 1.3, argued over in 1.7, and by 3.4 it has become momentum rather than choice: he is so far in blood that going back is as tedious as going on.

themes.name: Guilt and conscience
themes.summary: Guilt in this play is physical. It stops a man saying 'Amen', it will not wash off, it takes a seat at dinner, and it eventually walks the corridors at night with a candle. Nobody is punished for the murders by the state; they are punished by their own nervous systems.
themes.development: Macbeth's imagination runs ahead of his conscience in Acts I and II, and his wife's runs behind hers — she is unshaken at the murder and destroyed by it five acts later.

themes.name: Kingship and the state
themes.summary: Scotland is described as a body: bleeding, sick, needing a physician. Malcolm's list of the king-becoming graces in 4.3 sets out what Macbeth is not, and the play's interest is less in who deserves the crown than in what happens to a country when its head is afraid.
themes.development: Duncan's Scotland rewards loyalty in public; Macbeth's rewards silence; Malcolm's begins with a promise of order that the audience has been given reason to doubt.

themes.name: Fate, prophecy and equivocation
themes.summary: Every prophecy in the play is true and every one misleads. The apparitions promise safety in terms that are technically exact and practically worthless, which is the same trick the Jesuit doctrine of equivocation was accused of in the Gunpowder Plot trials of 1606.
themes.development: First a prediction, then a riddle, then a trapdoor: Birnam wood does move, and the man not of woman born does exist.

themes.name: Appearance and reality
themes.summary: The play opens by declaring that fair is foul, and then spends five acts proving it operationally: a welcoming castle, a loyal host, an innocent flower, a safe prophecy. Reading the play is largely a matter of watching characters fail to read each other.
themes.development: Duncan cannot find the mind's construction in the face; by Act IV Malcolm will not trust a face at all, and tests Macduff with a false one of his own.

themes.name: Manhood and gender
themes.summary: 'When you durst do it, then you were a man' is an argument, not an insult, and it works. The play keeps asking what manhood is supposed to license: Macduff's answer in 4.3 — that he must also feel the loss as a man — is offered as a correction to everything Macbeth has been told.
themes.development: Lady Macbeth asks to be unsexed in 1.5; Macbeth asks his wife to bring forth men-children only in 1.7; Macduff refuses the equation in 4.3.

techniques.name: Equivocation
techniques.definition: Saying something literally true in a form designed to be understood wrongly.
techniques.bookDefinition: Saying something literally true in a form designed to be understood wrongly.
techniques.inThisBook: The witches' apparitions and the Porter's joke about the equivocator who could not equivocate to heaven belong to the same 1606 argument about oaths and mental reservation.

techniques.name: Blood imagery
techniques.definition: A repeated image used to bind separate scenes into one idea.
techniques.bookDefinition: A repeated image used to bind separate scenes into one idea.
techniques.inThisBook: Blood arrives as heroism in 1.2, becomes a stain in 2.2, a debt in 3.4 and a hallucination in 5.1 without ever leaving the stage.

techniques.name: Soliloquy
techniques.definition: A character alone on stage, thinking aloud to the audience.
techniques.bookDefinition: A character alone on stage, thinking aloud to the audience.
techniques.inThisBook: Macbeth's soliloquies are where the murders actually happen; by Act V they have thinned to a report on how little he feels.

techniques.name: Antithesis
techniques.definition: Balancing opposed terms against each other inside one line.
techniques.bookDefinition: Balancing opposed terms against each other inside one line.
techniques.inThisBook: 'Fair is foul, and foul is fair' sets the pattern, and the play keeps pairing terms that should exclude each other — lost and won, innocent flower and serpent.

techniques.name: Dramatic irony
techniques.definition: The audience knows something a character on stage does not.
techniques.bookDefinition: The audience knows something a character on stage does not.
techniques.inThisBook: Duncan praising the sweetness of the air at Inverness is the clearest case: the audience has just heard what is waiting inside.

techniques.name: Disordered nature
techniques.definition: Weather and animal behaviour made to answer human action.
techniques.bookDefinition: Weather and animal behaviour made to answer human action.
techniques.inThisBook: Horses eat each other, an owl kills a falcon and darkness strangles the day after Duncan's murder: the killing of a king is reported as a fault in the world.

quotations.text: Fair is foul, and foul is fair: Hover through the fog and filthy air.
quotations.speaker: The Witches
quotations.context: The closing couplet of the first scene, spoken by all three witches together.
quotations.analysis: Twelve lines into the play, the audience is handed its instructions: nothing here will be safely readable. The chiasmus turns two opposed words into a closed loop, and the shift into rhymed trochaic tetrameter sets the witches apart from every other voice in the play before they have done anything at all.

quotations.text: All hail, Macbeth, thou shalt be king hereafter!
quotations.speaker: Third Witch
quotations.context: The third of three greetings on the heath, after Glamis and Cawdor.
quotations.analysis: The sentence does not contain an instruction, a condition or a route. It is the flat future tense that does the damage: Macbeth is told what will be, and spends the play converting a prediction into a plan while believing he is only keeping an appointment.

quotations.text: It is too full o' the milk of human kindness To catch the nearest way.
quotations.speaker: Lady Macbeth
quotations.context: Reading Macbeth's letter about the prophecy, alone.
quotations.analysis: She diagnoses him in a single image, and the image is not an insult — it grants him a nature she considers a practical obstacle. 'The nearest way' is the whole murder rendered as a route on a map, which is exactly the kind of euphemism the couple will need for the next two acts.

quotations.text: Come, you spirits That tend on mortal thoughts, unsex me here, And fill me from the crown to the toe top-full Of direst cruelty!
quotations.speaker: Lady Macbeth
quotations.context: Alone, after learning that Duncan will arrive that night.
quotations.analysis: The cruelty she wants has to be sent for, which tells the audience she does not already possess it. 'Crown to the toe' puts the crown on her body as well as on Duncan's head, and the request to be unsexed treats womanhood as a set of feelings — pity, remorse, the milk she later names — that would get in the way.

quotations.text: Look like the innocent flower, But be the serpent under't.
quotations.speaker: Lady Macbeth
quotations.context: Instructing Macbeth as Duncan approaches the castle.
quotations.analysis: The advice is a compressed piece of stage direction: a face to wear and a thing to be. It also answers Duncan's complaint sixty lines earlier that there is no art to find the mind's construction in the face — the play has just supplied the art, and given it to the other side.

quotations.text: If it were done when 'tis done, then 'twere well It were done quickly.
quotations.speaker: Macbeth
quotations.context: Alone, leaving the banquet at which Duncan is his guest.
quotations.analysis: Four uses of 'done' in twelve words, and not one of them names the act. The line is thinking in circles because the speaker will not let the word 'murder' into it, and the soliloquy goes on to reject the plan entirely on grounds of consequence rather than conscience.

quotations.text: I have no spur To prick the sides of my intent, but only Vaulting ambition, which o'erleaps itself And falls on the other.
quotations.speaker: Macbeth
quotations.context: The end of the soliloquy in which he decides not to kill Duncan.
quotations.analysis: He can find no reason for the murder except the wanting of it, and he says so as though that settled the matter. The rider who over-leaps the saddle is a comic image for a catastrophic one, and the sentence breaks off before it lands — the falling is left to the rest of the play.

quotations.text: Is this a dagger which I see before me, The handle toward my hand?
quotations.speaker: Macbeth
quotations.context: Alone at night, moving towards Duncan's chamber.
quotations.analysis: The dagger is offered to him handle first, as a servant would offer it — the hallucination is helpfully arranging the murder. He asks a question rather than making a claim, and keeps asking: the speech is a man conducting an experiment on his own mind and losing.

quotations.text: Methought I heard a voice cry 'Sleep no more! Macbeth does murder sleep'.
quotations.speaker: Macbeth
quotations.context: Immediately after the murder, still holding the daggers.
quotations.analysis: He reports the sentence rather than owning it, and the voice uses his name as though he were already a story being told about someone else. Sleep is the first of the ordinary things the murder takes away, and the play keeps the receipt: Lady Macbeth will be walking in her sleep three acts later.

quotations.text: Will all great Neptune's ocean wash this blood Clean from my hand? No, this my hand will rather The multitudinous seas in incarnadine, Making the green one red.
quotations.speaker: Macbeth
quotations.context: Looking at his hands after Duncan's murder.
quotations.analysis: The scale inverts inside four lines: an ocean cannot clean one hand, so the hand stains the ocean. 'Incarnadine' and 'multitudinous' are Latinate and enormous; 'making the green one red' is four monosyllables and a colour. Shakespeare gives the man the grand version and then the plain one, and the plain one is worse.

quotations.text: O, full of scorpions is my mind, dear wife!
quotations.speaker: Macbeth
quotations.context: Speaking to Lady Macbeth while concealing the plan to kill Banquo.
quotations.analysis: The endearment and the scorpions arrive in the same breath, and he tells her about the state of his mind precisely in order to avoid telling her its contents. This is the scene where the marriage stops being a partnership: from here he acts and she is informed afterwards, if at all.

quotations.text: It will have blood; they say, blood will have blood.
quotations.speaker: Macbeth
quotations.context: After the guests have been sent away from the ruined banquet.
quotations.analysis: He quotes a proverb, which is the closest he now comes to a moral framework: murder is described as a creature with an appetite of its own. The grammar has no agent in it anywhere, and that is the point — by Act III he has stopped experiencing his killings as things he decides to do.

quotations.text: Macbeth shall never vanquish'd be until Great Birnam wood to high Dunsinane hill Shall come against him.
quotations.speaker: Third Apparition
quotations.context: The third apparition, a crowned child holding a tree.
quotations.analysis: The prophecy hands him an impossibility and he accepts the gift without examining the wrapping — a child holding a branch has already shown him how the wood will move. Equivocation works here not by lying but by offering a picture the listener would rather keep.

quotations.text: Give sorrow words: the grief that does not speak Whispers the o'er-fraught heart and bids it break.
quotations.speaker: Malcolm
quotations.context: To Macduff, on hearing that his wife and children are dead.
quotations.analysis: The one piece of straightforwardly good advice in the play, and it is about language. Set it against Macbeth, who has spent four acts refusing to name what he is doing; the play's cure for grief is the opposite of the habit that produced it.

quotations.text: Out, damned spot! out, I say!
quotations.speaker: Lady Macbeth
quotations.context: Sleepwalking, watched by a doctor and her gentlewoman.
quotations.analysis: She told her husband in 2.2 that a little water clears us of this deed, and she is now scrubbing a hand that has nothing on it. The speech is in prose, which for a queen at this point in a tragedy is itself a diagnosis, and it is broken into fragments that move between all three murders at once.

quotations.text: My way of life Is fall'n into the sear, the yellow leaf; And that which should accompany old age, As honour, love, obedience, troops of friends, I must not look to have.
quotations.speaker: Macbeth
quotations.context: Alone at Dunsinane as the English army approaches.
quotations.analysis: He itemises exactly what he has lost, in order, and the list is entirely made of relationships. It is the most accurate self-assessment anyone makes in the play, and it changes nothing — a few lines later he is shouting at a servant about the colour of his face.

quotations.text: To-morrow, and to-morrow, and to-morrow, Creeps in this petty pace from day to day To the last syllable of recorded time.
quotations.speaker: Macbeth
quotations.context: On being told that the queen is dead.
quotations.analysis: Asked to feel something about his wife's death, he produces a theory of time instead. The repetition flattens the future into a queue, and 'syllable' quietly turns all of history into something merely said aloud — which sets up the walking shadow and the poor player five lines later.

quotations.text: Life's but a walking shadow, a poor player That struts and frets his hour upon the stage And then is heard no more.
quotations.speaker: Macbeth
quotations.context: The continuation of the same speech.
quotations.analysis: The metaphor is aimed at the actor saying it, in a theatre, to people who will go home in an hour. It is the bleakest thing in the play and also the most theatrically self-aware: the man who wanted to be remembered as king describes existence as a performance nobody will recall.

quotations.text: Macduff was from his mother's womb Untimely ripp'd.
quotations.speaker: Macduff
quotations.context: In single combat with Macbeth, answering the claim that no man of woman born can harm him.
quotations.analysis: The last guarantee fails on a technicality, and the technicality is a birth. Macbeth's response — that the word has 'cow'd my better part of man' — admits the whole trick: he had been fighting on the strength of a sentence rather than an army.

quotations.text: Our fears do make us traitors.
quotations.speaker: Lady Macduff
quotations.context: To Ross, on learning that her husband has fled to England.
quotations.analysis: Six words that convict Macduff of the thing the whole play is about — acting on fear and calling it strategy. She is defending nobody, least of all herself, and the scene that follows makes her the only character permitted to be simply right.

quotations.text: More needs she the divine than the physician.
quotations.speaker: Doctor
quotations.context: After watching Lady Macbeth sleepwalk.
quotations.analysis: Medicine hands the case over: what is wrong with her is not a condition. The line pairs with Macbeth's demand two scenes later that the same doctor pluck a rooted sorrow from the memory, and with Scotland itself, repeatedly described as a patient nobody can treat.

quotations.text: Stars, hide your fires; Let not light see my black and deep desires.
quotations.speaker: Macbeth
quotations.context: Aside, immediately after Duncan names Malcolm his heir.
quotations.analysis: The first thing he does after the obstacle appears is ask the universe to look away. Light and dark run through the whole play as a moral lighting rig, and here Macbeth is operating it himself — he wants not to be seen, including by himself.

atAGlance.label: Written
atAGlance.note: Soon after the Gunpowder Plot trials, and three years into James VI and I's English reign.

atAGlance.label: First printed
atAGlance.note: No quarto survives. The First Folio is the only early text.

atAGlance.label: Chief source
atAGlance.note: Shakespeare compresses decades of Scottish history into a matter of months.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.note: Two of the five acts are over before the murder is half an hour old on stage.

criticalViews.position: Macbeth as a study in conscience
criticalViews.summary: The oldest and still the most common reading: the play's interest is psychological, and its subject is a man who knows exactly what he is doing at every stage and does it anyway.
criticalViews.counter: It can make the witches decorative, when the play gives them the first and last word on what Macbeth becomes.

criticalViews.position: Macbeth as a Jacobean political play
criticalViews.summary: Read alongside the Gunpowder Plot, Daemonologie and the Stuart claim of descent from Banquo, the play looks less like a tragedy of character and more like an argument about legitimate rule addressed to a particular king.
criticalViews.counter: The flattery reading struggles with Act IV: a play written to please James spends a long scene teaching an audience to distrust the man who will be king.

criticalViews.position: The play as a study of manhood
criticalViews.summary: Criticism since the 1980s has focused on how consistently violence is licensed by the word 'man' — in Lady Macbeth's taunt, in Macbeth's answer to the murderers, and in Macduff's refusal of the equation in 4.3.
criticalViews.counter: Lady Macbeth's collapse can then be read as the play retreating into a conventional punishment for a woman who overreached.

essayQuestions.question: How far is Macbeth responsible for his own downfall?
essayQuestions.focus: Fate, choice and the limits of prophecy
plan: Open with the fact that nothing the witches say is an instruction: the prophecy is in the future tense, not the imperative.
Use 1.3 and 1.7 to show Macbeth reasoning his way to a decision and then reversing it under pressure from his wife.
Turn the argument at Act III: Banquo's murder is planned without prophecy, without his wife, and without hesitation.
Test the counter-case with 4.1 — the apparitions do not compel Fife, and the play offers no motive for it at all.
Close on 5.5: the man who blamed nobody reduces his own life to a story told by an idiot.

essayQuestions.question: Discuss the presentation of Lady Macbeth.
essayQuestions.focus: Gender, power and collapse
plan: Begin with 1.5: she has to send for cruelty, which means she does not start with it.
Read her control of 1.7 as rhetorical rather than temperamental — the argument she wins is about the meaning of the word 'man'.
Mark the hinge at 3.2, where Macbeth stops telling her things, and note how little she says at the banquet by comparison.
Use 5.1 to show the same material returning as prose, fragments and a clean hand that will not come clean.
Weigh two readings: a psychological collapse, or a play that gives a woman power and then takes it back.

essayQuestions.question: How does Shakespeare use the supernatural in Macbeth?
essayQuestions.focus: Prophecy, equivocation and staging
plan: Set out what the supernatural actually does: it predicts, it never commands, and it is always accurate.
Compare Banquo's response to the same prophecy as a control on Macbeth's.
Examine the apparitions in 4.1 as equivocation in the strict 1606 sense, alongside the Porter in 2.3.
Consider the dagger and the ghost, which may be supernatural or may be symptoms, and which the play refuses to settle.
Conclude with staging: a production that makes the witches literal and one that makes them internal produce two different plays.

essayQuestions.question: 'A play about the health of a country, not the guilt of a man.' Discuss.
essayQuestions.focus: Kingship, the state and Act IV Scene 3
plan: Gather the imagery of Scotland as a body: bleeding, sick, in need of a physician.
Set Duncan's public rewards against Macbeth's rule by informer and Lennox's careful irony in 3.6.
Use Malcolm's list of the king-becoming graces in 4.3 as the play's explicit standard.
Test the statement against 5.1 and 5.5, which are as private as the play gets.
Decide whether the ending restores order or simply installs a more careful politician.

discussionQuestions: The witches never tell Macbeth to do anything. Does that make them innocent?
Why does Shakespeare kill Lady Macduff and her son on stage, when almost every other death happens offstage?
Macbeth hears of his wife's death and talks about time. Is that grief, or the absence of it?
Malcolm pretends to be worse than Macbeth in order to test Macduff. What does the scene suggest about the skills a king needs?
The play is the shortest of the major tragedies. What would be lost if it were longer?

timeline.label: The historical Macbeth becomes king of Alba
timeline.detail: He ruled for seventeen years, a reign Shakespeare compresses to a few violent months.

timeline.label: The historical Macbeth is killed at Lumphanan
timeline.detail: Not at Dunsinane, and not by Macduff.

timeline.label: Holinshed's Chronicles reissued
timeline.detail: Shakespeare's chief source for the Scottish material, including the meeting with the three weird sisters.

timeline.label: James VI publishes Daemonologie
timeline.detail: The future king of England writes a dialogue on witchcraft six years before inheriting the English throne.

timeline.label: James VI of Scotland becomes James I of England

books.title: Measure for Measure
books.author: William Shakespeare
books.setting: Vienna: a palace, a nunnery, a brothel, a prison and a city gate
books.lengthNote: Around 2,800 lines, with the prison and brothel scenes largely in prose
books.openingLine: Of government the properties to unfold, Would seem in me to affect speech and discourse;
books.summary: A duke who has let the sexual laws lapse for years hands Vienna to a deputy known for severity, then stays behind disguised as a friar to watch what happens. Angelo condemns a man for getting his betrothed with child, and then offers the man's sister his life in exchange for her body. The comedy machinery — a substitution in bed, a substituted head, a public hearing — arrives on time and saves everyone it is supposed to save, and the play still ends with a marriage proposal that nobody on stage answers.

sourceText.label: Globe/Moby text of Measure for Measure
sourceText.note: Line numbers follow the traditional Globe numbering. The only early text is the First Folio of 1623, and modern editions vary by a line or two.

structure.label: Act I
structure.title: A government handed over, and a law switched back on
structure.summary: The Duke gives Angelo his authority in a scene of strange, clotted syntax, and announces a journey to Poland he does not take. Within hours a dormant statute has a man under sentence of death for fornication, and his sister is fetched out of a convent before she has taken her vows.

scenes.title: The commission
scenes.summary: The Duke deputes Angelo, with Escalus as his second, and leaves without explanation.

scenes.title: Vienna hears the news
scenes.summary: Lucio and the bawds learn that the brothels in the suburbs are to be pulled down; Claudio is led to prison.

scenes.title: The friar's cell
scenes.summary: The Duke admits he let the laws sleep for fourteen years and explains why he wants someone else to wake them.

scenes.title: The nunnery
scenes.summary: Isabella asks for a stricter rule; Lucio arrives and sends her to plead for her brother's life.

structure.label: Act II
structure.title: Two pleas, and a bargain
structure.summary: Escalus argues for mercy and gets nowhere. Isabella argues better, and gets somewhere worse: Angelo discovers desire at exactly the moment he is being praised for having none. The second interview drops the metaphors and states the price.

scenes.title: The law and the constable
scenes.summary: Angelo refuses Escalus's appeal, then leaves him to a bawdy case that no court could untangle.

scenes.title: The first interview
scenes.summary: Isabella pleads for Claudio; Angelo refuses, tells her to come again, and is left horrified by his own appetite.

scenes.title: The prison
scenes.summary: The disguised Duke hears Juliet's confession and asks whether she repents the act or the shame.

scenes.title: The offer
scenes.summary: Angelo names his terms, threatens to outweigh her word with his reputation, and gives her until tomorrow.

structure.label: Act III
structure.title: A brother asks, a sister refuses, a friar has a plan
structure.summary: The Duke, in his friar's habit, prepares Claudio for death with a long argument that life is not worth keeping, and Claudio agrees until the alternative is named. Isabella's refusal is absolute and her brother's collapse is immediate. Out of that wreck the Duke improvises the bed trick, and the play's verse gives way to plotting.

scenes.title: Be absolute for death
scenes.summary: The Duke's consolation, Claudio's terror, Isabella's fury, and the first mention of Mariana.

scenes.title: The street before the prison
scenes.summary: Pompey is arrested, Lucio slanders the absent Duke to his face, and the Duke is left alone with a rhymed verdict on Angelo.

structure.label: Act IV
structure.title: Substitutions
structure.summary: A woman takes another woman's place in the dark and the law is satisfied by a technicality it was never told about. Angelo breaks his side of the bargain anyway and orders the execution brought forward, so a second substitution is needed; a condemned man refuses to be hanged, and a prisoner who has died of fever supplies the head.

scenes.title: The moated grange
scenes.summary: A song for Mariana, and Isabella's account of the garden gate, the keys and the appointed hour.

scenes.title: The warrant
scenes.summary: Angelo's message demands Claudio's head by four; the Duke persuades the Provost to disobey.

scenes.title: Barnardine will not die
scenes.summary: A drunk prisoner declines to be executed, and Ragozine's death of a fever provides a head instead.

scenes.title: Angelo alone
scenes.summary: He cannot understand the Duke's instructions, and admits he would not now undo the deed if he could.

scenes.title: Letters
scenes.summary: The Duke, out of disguise, sets his return in motion.

scenes.title: Instructions
scenes.summary: Isabella is told to accuse herself of what never happened, and does not know why.

structure.label: Act V
structure.title: The hearing at the city gate
structure.summary: The Duke returns in his own person and judges a case in which he has already been every witness. He lets Isabella be called mad, lets Mariana be dismissed, and reveals himself only after Angelo has condemned himself twice. Four marriages are ordered, two of them as punishments, and the last question of the play is put to a woman who does not reply.

scenes.title: The city gate
scenes.summary: Accusation, disbelief, the friar unhooded, Angelo's sentence, Mariana's plea, Isabella's kneeling, Claudio alive, and a proposal.

characters.name: Duke Vincentio
characters.role: Duke of Vienna, disguised for most of the play as Friar Lodowick
characters.summary: He owns the problem and delegates the correction, which he admits privately is a way of avoiding the odium of enforcing laws he let sleep. As a friar he is everywhere, hearing confessions he has no right to hear and arranging the outcome scene by scene, and the play keeps him charming enough that his manipulations take a while to feel like manipulations.
characters.clue: He announces a journey to Poland, borrows a friar's habit instead, and spends the rest of the play eavesdropping on the government he gave away.

relationships.label: deputes and then tries
relationships.note: He suspects the outcome before he leaves; 1.3 says as much.

characters.name: Angelo
characters.role: The Duke's deputy
characters.summary: He is not a hypocrite when the play begins; he is a man with no experience of his own appetite, and he says so with something close to wonder the first time it appears. What makes him dangerous is not lust but the discovery that his reputation will carry any accusation he chooses to deny.
characters.clue: His blood is called snow-broth in Act I, and by Act II he is asking himself whether the tempter or the tempted sins most.
traits: willing to use his own name as a weapon

characters.name: Isabella
characters.role: A novice of the order of Saint Clare, Claudio's sister
characters.summary: She enters asking for a stricter rule than the convent offers and is immediately handed the most worldly argument in the play. Her rhetoric is the best in it — she wins every exchange with Angelo on the merits — and the same absolutism that makes her unanswerable on mercy makes her merciless to her brother twenty minutes later.
characters.clue: She asks the nuns for a stricter rule, out-argues a deputy on the nature of mercy, and calls her own brother a beast for wanting to live.

characters.name: Claudio
characters.role: A young gentleman under sentence of death
characters.summary: His offence is getting his own betrothed with child before the contract was made public, which is why the sentence looks less like justice than like a demonstration. He accepts death for about forty lines, and the speech in which he stops accepting it is the most frightened writing in Shakespeare about what being dead might be.
characters.clue: He is condemned for a child conceived with the woman he was already contracted to marry, and he changes his mind about dying the moment a way out is named.

characters.name: Lucio
characters.role: A gentleman, and Claudio's friend
characters.summary: He fetches Isabella, coaches her through the first interview and keeps the plot moving whenever it stalls, which makes his punishment at the end feel wildly out of proportion. He is also the only character who tells the disguised Duke what Vienna actually thinks of him, and the Duke never forgives it.
characters.clue: He is the one who tells a novice to go and plead, stands at her elbow whispering that she is doing well, and is later sentenced to marry a punk.

characters.name: Escalus
characters.role: An ancient lord, second in the commission
characters.summary: He is the play's picture of what ordinary good government looks like: he argues for Claudio, loses, and then spends a whole scene patiently failing to get a coherent account of a case out of a constable and a bawd. His reward for consistency is to be the last man in Vienna to learn what has been going on.
characters.clue: He observes that some rise by sin and some by virtue fall, and is still trying to run an orderly courtroom while a constable mangles every word he uses.

characters.name: Mariana
characters.role: Betrothed to Angelo, living at the moated grange
characters.summary: She was abandoned when her dowry was lost at sea and has been waiting ever since, which the play presents without comment as a normal consequence of a marriage market. Her plea for the man who wronged her is the moral turn of the last scene, and she makes it by asking Isabella — of all people — to kneel with her.
characters.clue: She lives alone at a moated grange with a boy to sing to her, and asks to keep the husband everyone else wants executed.

relationships.label: betrothed to, and married at the end
substitute for, and then suppliant to

characters.name: Pompey Bum
characters.role: A tapster and bawd, later assistant to the executioner
characters.summary: He asks whether the state intends to geld and splay all the youth of the city, which is the sharpest question anyone puts to the new policy. Moving him from brothel to scaffold is the play's bluntest joke: the trade is the same, and the second one is legal.
characters.clue: He argues that his trade is lawful if the law will allow it, and ends the play learning to cut heads off instead.

characters.name: Barnardine
characters.role: A prisoner of nine years, condemned for murder
characters.summary: He is guilty, he is due to die, and he simply declines, which stops the whole machinery of the plot until a corpse can be found elsewhere. He is the one person in Vienna over whom neither the law nor the Duke has any purchase at all, and at the end he is pardoned without asking.
characters.clue: Drunk, unrepentant and nine years in gaol, he refuses to be executed on the grounds that he is not in the mood.

themes.name: Justice, mercy and measure
themes.summary: The title is a rule of equivalence from the Sermon on the Mount, and the play spends five acts testing whether human courts can operate it. Angelo applies the statute exactly and produces monstrosity; the Duke suspends it entirely and produces a city where liberty plucks justice by the nose. Neither extreme is offered as the answer.
themes.development: Escalus pleads proportion in 2.1, Isabella pleads mercy in 2.2, and in 5.1 the Duke pronounces an eye-for-an-eye sentence he has already arranged not to carry out.

themes.name: Authority and substitution
themes.summary: Everyone in the play stands in for someone else: a deputy for a duke, a friar for a deputy's judge, a woman for another woman, a dead man's head for a living man's. The play's political question is what happens to power when it is lent out, and whether the lender can ever really put it down.
themes.development: Angelo receives the commission in 1.1, exceeds it by 2.4, and in 5.1 is tried by the man whose authority he was using.

themes.name: Desire and the law made against it
themes.summary: Vienna's statute treats sex as a matter of licensing, and the play answers by showing desire arriving where it was least expected, in a man who had built an identity on not having any. Angelo's horror is genuine; what he does with it is the crime.
themes.development: Lucio calls his blood snow-broth in 1.4; by 2.2 Angelo is asking who sins most, and by 4.4 he admits he would not undo the deed even if he could.

themes.name: Reputation and who gets believed
themes.summary: Angelo's most chilling line is not a threat of force but a statement of fact about testimony: his unsoiled name will outweigh her accusation, and he is right. The last act is built to prove him right for as long as possible, with Isabella dismissed as mad in front of a crowd before the truth is allowed out.
themes.development: The threat is made in 2.4 and executed in 5.1, where both women are publicly disbelieved by a judge who knows exactly what happened.

themes.name: Chastity, the body and exchange
themes.summary: Bodies in this play are currency: a maidenhead against a life, a marriage against a dowry lost at sea, a head against a head. Isabella's refusal is usually discussed as a moral choice, but the play frames it as a refusal to accept a rate of exchange that everyone around her treats as normal.
themes.development: The offer is made in 2.4, refused in 3.1, and then quietly satisfied in 4.1 by a substitution that pays the price with somebody else's body.

themes.name: Silence and consent
themes.summary: The play's loudest moment is a gap in the text. Isabella has more lines than almost anyone up to Act V, argues her way through two interviews with a judge, and then receives a proposal of marriage and says nothing — twice. Whatever a production does with that silence becomes its reading of the whole play.
themes.development: She kneels for Angelo's life without being asked in 5.1, and then answers neither of the Duke's proposals; the Folio gives her no more words after her plea for Mariana.

techniques.name: The disguised ruler
techniques.definition: A character concealing their identity, so that the audience knows more than the people on stage do.
techniques.bookDefinition: A governor who moves among his own subjects unrecognised.
techniques.inThisBook: The habit lets the Duke hear confessions, coach witnesses and edit the evidence, so the device that usually produces comic knowledge here produces a judge who has tampered with his own case.

techniques.name: The bed trick
techniques.definition: A substitution in the dark, in which one woman takes another's assignation.
techniques.bookDefinition: A substitution in the dark, in which one woman takes another's assignation.
techniques.inThisBook: Because Mariana was already contracted to Angelo, the trick makes his sin technically lawful and hers technically a marriage, which is the play at its most legally exact and least comfortable.

techniques.name: Shifts of register
techniques.definition: Moving between verse and prose to change the standing of a scene.
techniques.bookDefinition: Moving between verse and prose to change the standing of a scene.
techniques.inThisBook: The great moral arguments are in verse and the cases that actually come to court — Elbow, Froth, Pompey — are in prose, so the law is heard twice, once as philosophy and once as a shambles.

techniques.name: Imagery of coin and seal
techniques.definition: Metaphors drawn from minting, weighing, stamping and testing metal.
techniques.bookDefinition: Metaphors drawn from minting, weighing, stamping and testing metal.
techniques.inThisBook: Angelo is a name stamped on metal, virtues are coins that must go forth to be worth anything, and the bargain in 2.4 is transacted in the language of false coining.

techniques.name: Soliloquy
techniques.definition: A character alone on stage, thinking aloud to the audience.
techniques.bookDefinition: A character alone on stage, thinking aloud to the audience.
techniques.inThisBook: Angelo gets the play's best ones and uses them to discover himself in real time; Isabella is given none, which is one reason her decisions are so fiercely argued over.

techniques.name: Dramatic irony
techniques.definition: The audience knows something a character on stage does not.
techniques.bookDefinition: The audience knows something a character on stage does not.
techniques.inThisBook: For three acts the audience watches people confess to, plead with and slander a friar they do not know is the duke, and in 5.1 that accumulated knowledge is used to make the audience complicit in a public humiliation.

quotations.text: Spirits are not finely touch'd But to fine issues, nor Nature never lends The smallest scruple of her excellence But, like a thrifty goddess, she determines Herself the glory of a creditor,
quotations.speaker: Duke Vincentio
quotations.context: Handing the commission to Angelo in the first scene.
quotations.analysis: Virtue is described as a loan advanced on interest, and the metaphor governs the rest of the play: nothing in Vienna is given, everything is lent, weighed or repaid. The Duke is also, in the same breath, telling Angelo that a reputation which is never spent is worthless — advice he is about to enforce experimentally.

quotations.text: Mortality and mercy in Vienna Live in thy tongue and heart: old Escalus, Though first in question, is thy secondary.
quotations.speaker: Duke Vincentio
quotations.context: The formal transfer of power, with Escalus standing by.
quotations.analysis: Two abstractions are located in two organs, and the split is exact: death is something Angelo will say and mercy something he would have to feel. The last clause is the quiet cruelty — the older and better judge is demoted in the same sentence that gives the younger man the power of life.

quotations.text: so our decrees, Dead to infliction, to themselves are dead; And liberty plucks justice by the nose; The baby beats the nurse, and quite athwart Goes all decorum.
quotations.speaker: Duke Vincentio
quotations.context: Explaining to Friar Thomas why he has let the laws lapse and why he will not enforce them himself.
quotations.analysis: This is the Duke's own confession of negligence, and it is made to a priest rather than to the city. The two images are of insolence rather than crime — a nose pulled, a nurse slapped — which suggests the danger he fears is to the dignity of the law rather than to anybody's safety.

quotations.text: a man whose blood Is very snow-broth; one who never feels The wanton stings and motions of the sense, But doth rebate and blunt his natural edge With profits of the mind, study and fast.
quotations.speaker: Lucio
quotations.context: Lucio describing the new deputy to Isabella at the nunnery.
quotations.analysis: Melted snow is water that was once solid, so even the insult concedes that something has been made cold rather than being cold by nature. Lucio is usually unreliable; here he is exactly right about the diagnosis and exactly wrong about the prognosis, which is the play's method with him throughout.

quotations.text: Our doubts are traitors And make us lose the good we oft might win By fearing to attempt.
quotations.speaker: Lucio
quotations.context: Pushing a reluctant Isabella to go and plead for her brother.
quotations.analysis: The line is quoted as encouragement so often that its context is worth keeping: it is a rake persuading a novice to leave her convent and go and bargain with a man for a life. 'Attempt' carried a sexual sense in this period, and the play will make that second meaning explicit within one act.

quotations.text: We must not make a scarecrow of the law, Setting it up to fear the birds of prey, And let it keep one shape, till custom make it Their perch and not their terror.
quotations.speaker: Angelo
quotations.context: The first words of his administration, refusing Escalus's plea for Claudio.
quotations.analysis: It is the best defence of enforcement anybody makes, and it is made with an image of birds settling comfortably on the thing meant to frighten them. Notice that Angelo's argument is about the law's appearance rather than its justice: he is worried about being laughed at, which is the same anxiety the Duke admitted in 1.3.

quotations.text: Some rise by sin, and some by virtue fall: Some run from brakes of ice, and answer none: And some condemned for a fault alone.
quotations.speaker: Escalus
quotations.context: Alone, after failing to save Claudio.
quotations.analysis: Three lines of rhyme dropped into a prose-heavy scene, marking a moment of private judgement in a public office. The chiasmus balances rising and falling so evenly that it refuses to blame anyone, which is precisely the temper Angelo has just overruled.

quotations.text: Condemn the fault and not the actor of it? Why, every fault's condemn'd ere it be done: Mine were the very cipher of a function, To fine the faults whose fine stands in record, And let go by the actor.
quotations.speaker: Angelo
quotations.context: Answering Isabella's opening argument in the first interview.
quotations.analysis: He is right, and the rightness is the problem: a law that punishes acts and not persons is not a law at all. 'Cipher' means a zero, so he pictures his own office as a nothing — and by the end of the scene he will have become exactly the actor he refuses to distinguish from the fault.

quotations.text: And mercy then will breathe within your lips, Like man new made.
quotations.speaker: Isabella
quotations.context: The climax of her first appeal: if he were in Claudio's place and Claudio in his.
quotations.analysis: The image is of God breathing life into Adam, so showing mercy is presented not as a kindness but as the moment a man becomes human at all. It is also the most physical thing she has said to him, and the speech that follows it is the one in which he begins to notice her voice.

quotations.text: O, it is excellent To have a giant's strength; but it is tyrannous To use it like a giant.
quotations.speaker: Isabella
quotations.context: Pressing the argument after Angelo tells her that her brother dies tomorrow.
quotations.analysis: The sentence concedes the power before objecting to its use, which is why it works on a man who will not hear his authority questioned. It also states the play's political thesis in fifteen words: nothing here is wrong with the law itself, only with the scale at which a person chooses to apply it.

quotations.text: but man, proud man, Drest in a little brief authority, Most ignorant of what he's most assured, His glassy essence, like an angry ape, Plays such fantastic tricks before high heaven As make the angels weep;
quotations.speaker: Isabella
quotations.context: Contrasting divine thunder with the noise a magistrate makes.
quotations.analysis: 'Glassy essence' means both mirror-like and breakable, so the soul is at once a reflecting surface and something easily smashed. She is describing authority in general and has no idea she is describing the man in front of her; the audience, having heard him for a scene and a half, does.

quotations.text: What's this, what's this? Is this her fault or mine? The tempter or the tempted, who sins most? Ha! Not she: nor doth she tempt: but it is I
quotations.speaker: Angelo
quotations.context: Alone on stage the moment Isabella leaves.
quotations.analysis: The question is asked and answered inside four lines, and he gets it right: she does not tempt, and the fault is his. The play never lets him plead ignorance afterwards, which is why what he does in 2.4 is a decision rather than a fall.

quotations.text: Thieves for their robbery have authority When judges steal themselves.
quotations.speaker: Angelo
quotations.context: Still alone, working out what his desire will cost the city.
quotations.analysis: He sees the whole constitutional consequence before he commits the offence: a corrupt bench licenses every crime beneath it. The line is also the play's answer to its own title, since a judge who steals has set the measure by which he must be measured.

quotations.text: Blood, thou art blood: Let's write good angel on the devil's horn: 'Tis not the devil's crest.
quotations.speaker: Angelo
quotations.context: Waiting for Isabella's second visit, having found he cannot pray.
quotations.analysis: The tautology is the point: after a scene of argument he arrives at a fact that admits no argument. The heraldic image turns his own name into a label that can be written on the wrong animal, and 'good angel' is one letter away from the name he signs on warrants.

quotations.text: I do arrest your words. Be that you are, That is, a woman; if you be more, you're none; If you be one, as you are well express'd By all external warrants, show it now, By putting on the destined livery.
quotations.speaker: Angelo
quotations.context: Isabella has just said that women are frail; Angelo takes the admission literally.
quotations.analysis: He uses the vocabulary of his office to conduct a seduction — arrest, warrants, livery — so the extortion is phrased entirely in legal terms. The trap is grammatical: she conceded a general frailty, and he converts it into a personal obligation with the word 'now'.

quotations.text: Who will believe thee, Isabel? My unsoil'd name, the austereness of my life, My vouch against you, and my place i' the state, Will so your accusation overweigh, That you shall stifle in your own report
quotations.speaker: Angelo
quotations.context: Isabella threatens to tell the world what he is.
quotations.analysis: He does not deny that she could prove it; he explains that proof is not what decides such cases. 'Overweigh' returns the play to its scales, and in Act V the Duke will stage a hearing designed to demonstrate, at length and in public, that Angelo's calculation was accurate.

quotations.text: Then, Isabel, live chaste, and, brother, die: More than our brother is our chastity.
quotations.speaker: Isabella
quotations.context: Alone at the end of Act II, having refused Angelo's terms.
quotations.analysis: The decision is taken in a rhymed couplet, the form Shakespeare uses to close a scene and settle a question, so the verse itself insists that there is nothing left to discuss. She addresses herself and her absent brother in the same line, which is as close as the play comes to showing her weigh the two.

quotations.text: Be absolute for death; either death or life Shall thereby be the sweeter. Reason thus with life: If I do lose thee, I do lose a thing That none but fools would keep:
quotations.speaker: Duke Vincentio
quotations.context: The disguised Duke preparing Claudio for execution.
quotations.analysis: It is a consolation built entirely out of contempt for living, and it persuades Claudio for about a hundred lines. The Duke knows at this point that he intends to save him, which makes the whole speech an exercise conducted on a man under sentence for the benefit of the man delivering it.

quotations.text: Ay, but to die, and go we know not where; To lie in cold obstruction and to rot; This sensible warm motion to become A kneaded clod; and the delighted spirit To bathe in fiery floods, or to reside
quotations.speaker: Claudio
quotations.context: Two words after agreeing that death is a fearful thing and shamed life a hateful one.
quotations.analysis: The fear is entirely physical until the fourth line, and the shift from 'warm motion' to 'kneaded clod' is the whole argument: what terrifies him is not punishment but the loss of temperature and movement. The speech begins with 'Ay, but' — a man conceding the philosophy and then finding it does not reach.

quotations.text: Sweet sister, let me live: What sin you do to save a brother's life, Nature dispenses with the deed so far That it becomes a virtue.
quotations.speaker: Claudio
quotations.context: Asking Isabella to accept Angelo's bargain.
quotations.analysis: He does not ask her to sin for him; he argues that in these circumstances it would not be a sin, which is exactly the reasoning Angelo used on her an act earlier. Hearing her brother speak in the deputy's voice is what produces the violence of her reply.

quotations.text: O you beast! O faithless coward! O dishonest wretch! Wilt thou be made a man out of my vice? Is't not a kind of incest, to take life From thine own sister's shame?
quotations.speaker: Isabella
quotations.context: Her immediate answer to Claudio's plea.
quotations.analysis: Three vocatives in a line and a half, each one shorter in patience than the last, and then a legal-sounding question that is not really a question. 'Made a man' is the cruellest phrase: she tells him that buying his life at this price would cost him his manhood as surely as it would cost her her chastity.

quotations.text: O, what may man within him hide, Though angel on the outward side!
quotations.speaker: Duke Vincentio
quotations.context: Alone at the end of Act III, in rhymed tetrameter.
quotations.analysis: The metre changes to the short, chanting line Shakespeare gives to choruses and spirits, which lifts the Duke out of the action and into the position of a commentator on it. The pun on Angelo's name has been waiting since the first scene, and it is sprung only once the plot to trap him is already in motion.

quotations.text: Take, O, take those lips away, That so sweetly were forsworn; And those eyes, the break of day, Lights that do mislead the morn:
quotations.speaker: A boy, singing
quotations.context: The song at Mariana's moated grange, which she breaks off when the friar arrives.
quotations.analysis: The only song in the play is given to the one character with nothing to do but wait, and she apologises for it immediately. Its subject is a broken oath, which is Angelo's offence against her five years before the plot begins, so the scene of the bed trick opens by reminding us who was wronged first.

quotations.text: I swear I will not die to-day for any man's persuasion.
quotations.speaker: Barnardine
quotations.context: Dragged out of his cell to be executed so that his head can be sent to Angelo.
quotations.analysis: A guilty man defeats the entire apparatus of the plot by declining to co-operate with it, and the Duke has no answer except to look for a different corpse. It is the one point in the play where authority, disguised or not, is simply told no and has to go away.

quotations.text: 'An Angelo for Claudio, death for death!' Haste still pays haste, and leisure answers leisure; Like doth quit like, and MEASURE still FOR MEASURE.
quotations.speaker: Duke Vincentio
quotations.context: Sentencing Angelo at the city gate, after the marriage to Mariana.
quotations.analysis: The title arrives as a judicial formula in the mouth of a judge who has already prevented the death he is avenging. Everything in the line is balanced — haste against haste, like against like — and the balance is a performance, since Claudio is alive behind the scenes and the Duke knows it.

quotations.text: Let him not die. My brother had but justice, In that he did the thing for which he died: For Angelo, His act did not o'ertake his bad intent, And must be buried but as an intent
quotations.speaker: Isabella
quotations.context: Kneeling beside Mariana to beg for the life of the man she believes killed her brother.
quotations.analysis: She saves Angelo on a technicality of intention, not on a plea for mercy — the argument is that nothing actually happened, which she believes to be true. It is also the first time she concedes that Claudio's sentence was lawful, so her forgiveness of Angelo is bought at the price of agreeing that her brother deserved to die.

quotations.text: If he be like your brother, for his sake Is he pardon'd; and, for your lovely sake, Give me your hand and say you will be mine.
quotations.speaker: Duke Vincentio
quotations.context: Claudio has just been unmuffled and restored; the proposal follows within three lines.
quotations.analysis: A pardon and a proposal are delivered in the same sentence, with the grammar making the second conditional on the goodwill created by the first. The Folio gives Isabella no reply here or at the second asking forty lines later, and every production has to decide what a woman does with a hand held out in front of a crowd.

atAGlance.label: Written
atAGlance.note: The first year of James I's English reign, and the first full season after a long plague closure.

atAGlance.label: First recorded performance
atAGlance.note: Played at court during the Christmas season.

atAGlance.label: First printed
atAGlance.note: No quarto survives; the First Folio is the only early text, and some of its oddities are still argued over.

atAGlance.label: Chief sources
atAGlance.note: The Epitia story in Cinthio's Hecatommithi and George Whetstone's play Promos and Cassandra, in both of which the heroine yields.

criticalViews.position: A Christian allegory of justice and mercy
criticalViews.summary: An older tradition reads the Duke as a figure of providence, the title as a text from the Sermon on the Mount, and the ending as a deliberate demonstration that strict law must give way to grace.
criticalViews.counter: It requires the Duke's methods to be above scrutiny, and the play goes out of its way to show him lying to a condemned man and to a grieving sister.

criticalViews.position: A problem play about power and coercion
criticalViews.summary: Twentieth-century criticism took the discomfort as the subject rather than a flaw: an unresolvable case about consent, the abuse of office, and whether any authority in the play is exercised cleanly.
criticalViews.counter: Read only for its problems, the play can lose its comedy, and Pompey, Elbow and Barnardine are not incidental to it.

criticalViews.position: A Jacobean play about a particular kind of ruler
criticalViews.summary: Historicist readings set the disguised duke beside contemporary arguments about how a prince should show himself, govern through deputies and temper law with clemency.
criticalViews.counter: The parallel can flatter the Duke, since the play gives Lucio several hundred lines of unflattering gossip about him and never quite refutes them.

essayQuestions.question: Is the Duke a good governor?
essayQuestions.focus: Authority, delegation and manipulation
plan: Start with his own account in 1.3: fourteen years of unenforced law, and an explicit wish to avoid being the one who enforces it.
Examine the friar's habit as a working method — confessions heard without right, evidence arranged, Claudio told he will die when the Duke means to save him.
Weigh what the disguise achieves against what it costs: Mariana is rescued, Isabella is deceived for two whole acts.
Read 5.1 as a piece of theatre he has scripted, and ask who it is for.
Close on the proposal, and on whether a governor who arranges his own marriage as the last item of a public hearing has understood anything he has seen.

essayQuestions.question: How does the play present Isabella's refusal?
essayQuestions.focus: Chastity, argument and the absence of soliloquy
plan: Establish what she is actually being asked for in 2.4, and in what terms Angelo phrases it.
Show her winning the argument on mercy in 2.2 and losing control of the situation for reasons that have nothing to do with the argument.
Set the couplet at the end of 2.4 beside her attack on Claudio in 3.1 and consider the difference between resolve and cruelty.
Note that she is never given a soliloquy, so the audience is denied the access it has to Angelo.
Test a modern reading against a Jacobean one: what does the play assume its audience already believes about a novice's vow?

essayQuestions.question: What is gained and lost by the bed trick?
essayQuestions.focus: Plot machinery and moral consequence
plan: Explain the legal position: Mariana's prior contract makes the encounter arguably a consummated marriage rather than a crime.
Show what it saves — Isabella's vow, Claudio's life, Mariana's standing — and at whose expense.
Consider Angelo's position: he believes he has done the thing he is later condemned for, and 4.4 shows he does not repent it.
Compare the second substitution, Ragozine's head, and what the doubling of the device suggests about the plot's own methods.
Ask whether a device that resolves the plot without changing anybody's intentions can resolve the play.

essayQuestions.question: Why does the play end in silence?
essayQuestions.focus: The last scene, its marriages and its gaps
plan: Count the marriages ordered in 5.1 and note which are rewards and which are punishments.
Track Isabella's lines through the scene, from the accusation to her plea for Angelo, and mark where they stop.
Set the Duke's two proposals side by side and note that neither receives a spoken answer in the Folio.
Bring in Barnardine, pardoned without repenting, and Lucio, punished more heavily than the man who extorted a woman.
Conclude by judging whether the silences are a fault in an unfinished text or the play's last and hardest statement.

discussionQuestions: Angelo tells Isabella that nobody will believe her, and the last act proves him right for as long as the Duke allows. Why stage the disbelief at all?
Claudio is condemned for a child conceived with the woman he was contracted to marry. Does the play think the law is wrong, or only the sentence?
Barnardine simply refuses to be executed, and it works. What is he doing in the play?
Mariana asks Isabella to kneel with her, and Isabella does. Is that forgiveness, or exhaustion?
Lucio ends the play punished more severely, in his own estimation, than Angelo. Is the joke on him, or on the Duke?

timeline.label: Cinthio's Hecatommithi
timeline.detail: The collection containing the Epitia story, in which the sister yields to the magistrate and the brother is executed anyway.

timeline.label: George Whetstone's Promos and Cassandra
timeline.detail: A two-part English play on the same material, and Shakespeare's nearest model in his own language.

timeline.label: James VI's Basilikon Doron
timeline.detail: The king's own book of advice on rule, reprinted in London in 1603; its arguments about how a prince should hold himself were fresh when this play was written.

timeline.label: James VI of Scotland becomes James I of England
timeline.detail: A new ruler with known views on justice, clemency and the private conduct of magistrates.

timeline.label: Plague closes the London playhouses
timeline.detail: A long closure that pushed the King's Men out to the provinces and back to court performance.

timeline.label: The play is written
timeline.detail: Usually dated to this year, alongside Othello and the other so-called problem plays.

timeline.label: First recorded performance at court
timeline.detail: Played on 26 December during the Christmas season, before James I.

timeline.label: The Act to Restrain Abuses of Players
timeline.detail: Oaths and holy names were legislated off the public stage, one reason Folio texts of the period can differ from what was first spoken.

timeline.label: The First Folio
timeline.detail: The only early text of the play, printed among the comedies.

timeline.label: Davenant's The Law Against Lovers
timeline.detail: A Restoration adaptation that grafted Beatrice and Benedick onto this plot and gave the ending the romance the original withholds.

places.name: Vienna
places.note: The play's setting: palace, nunnery, prison and city gate, imagined rather than observed.

places.name: Whitehall, London
places.note: The royal palace where the first recorded performance was given at Christmas 1604.

places.name: Bankside, Southwark
places.note: The Globe's own neighbourhood of theatres, brothels and prisons, which the play's Vienna resembles more than any Austrian city.

places.name: Ferrara
places.note: The city of Cinthio, the Italian writer whose story of a corrupt magistrate lies behind the plot.

places.name: Warsaw
places.note: Poland is where the Duke announces he is going and where he never goes.

related.why: Written within a year or so, and equally concerned with how easily a good name outweighs a true accusation.
The other play built on a bed trick, and the other comedy that ends with a marriage the text refuses to make comfortable.
A courtroom in which mercy is argued for at length and then administered in a way that leaves the audience uneasy.
The preceding tragedy of a ruler who watches from behind a disguise of his own and stages a scene to catch a conscience.
Written a year or two later, and the fullest version of this play's question about what authority looks like from below.

books.title: Moby-Dick
books.author: Herman Melville
books.setting: New Bedford and Nantucket, then the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific whaling grounds, in the 1840s
books.lengthNote: One hundred and thirty-five chapters and an epilogue, with two compilations of quotation and word-history standing in front of the narrative
books.openingLine: Call me Ishmael.
books.summary: A schoolmaster with no money and a grim November in his soul signs on to a Nantucket whaler and finds that the captain has turned a commercial voyage into a hunt for the white whale that took his leg. Melville keeps interrupting the chase with sermons, stage directions, dictionary entries and a whole natural history of the animal, so that the book acquires the shape of Ishmael's mind rather than Ahab's. Everyone aboard dies except the man telling the story, and he survives on a coffin.

sourceText.label: Standard Ebooks text of Moby-Dick
sourceText.note: References give the chapter. The text follows the American edition, which carries the epilogue the London issue left out.

structure.label: Chapters 1–22
structure.title: New Bedford, Nantucket, and a bargain made in bed
structure.summary: Ishmael goes to sea to keep himself from stepping into the street and knocking people's hats off. He shares a bed with a tattooed harpooneer, hears Father Mapple preach on Jonah from a pulpit shaped like a ship's bow, and signs articles with two Quaker owners who haggle over his lay while Ahab stays below, unseen.

scenes.title: Loomings
scenes.summary: Ishmael explains why water draws landsmen to the ends of piers, and why he ships as a sailor rather than a passenger.

scenes.title: The Spouter-Inn
scenes.summary: A night of terror at sharing a bed with a cannibal ends in the calmest sleep Ishmael has had.

scenes.title: The Sermon
scenes.summary: Father Mapple makes Jonah a story about flight, punishment and obedience, and preaches it to men about to sail.

scenes.title: The Ship
scenes.summary: Peleg and Bildad bargain over Ishmael's share of the profits and let slip that the captain is not himself.

structure.label: Chapters 23–40
structure.title: The oath that changes the voyage
structure.summary: The Pequod clears the harbour on Christmas Day with the captain invisible. When Ahab finally appears he nails a gold doubloon to the mast, tells the crew what the voyage is actually for, and has them drink to the death of the white whale. Starbuck objects once, on the record, and is overruled by a speech.

scenes.title: Knights and Squires
scenes.summary: Starbuck is introduced as a man whose courage is an instrument rather than a temperament.

scenes.title: The Quarter-Deck
scenes.summary: Ahab nails up the doubloon, names the whale, and turns a business voyage into a private war.

scenes.title: Sunset
scenes.summary: Alone in the cabin, Ahab describes his own will as rolling stock on rails it cannot leave.

scenes.title: Midnight, Forecastle
scenes.summary: The crew sings and quarrels in a scene printed as a play, with stage directions and no narrator.

structure.label: Chapters 41–47
structure.title: What the whale is, and what white means
structure.summary: The narrative stops to explain the enemy. Ishmael gathers the rumours that make Moby Dick ubiquitous and immortal, sets out Ahab's transfer of every grievance onto one animal, and then devotes a whole chapter to the colour white, which he cannot make mean anything and cannot make mean nothing.

scenes.title: Moby Dick
scenes.summary: The whale's reputation is assembled out of sailors' talk, and Ahab's monomania is dated to the loss of his leg.

scenes.title: The Whiteness of the Whale
scenes.summary: Ishmael tries to explain why the colour frightens him and produces a chapter about the failure of symbols.

scenes.title: The Chart
scenes.summary: Ahab plots currents and seasons to predict where one animal will be in an ocean.

structure.label: Chapters 48–92
structure.title: The industry underneath the hunt
structure.summary: Boats are lowered, whales are killed, and the book becomes an account of work: the line coiled in tubs where one snag will take a man overboard, the cutting-in, the head hoisted against the rail, the blubber rendered down. Gams with other ships bring news, and each captain Ahab meets refuses or fails to give him what he wants.

scenes.title: The Line
scenes.summary: The whale-line is described as a thing that sits in loops around every man in the boat.

scenes.title: The Grand Armada
scenes.summary: Inside a panicked herd the boats drift into a calm centre where whales are nursing their young.

scenes.title: Fast-Fish and Loose-Fish
scenes.summary: A rule of whaling property is extended, without comment, to nations, colonies and human beings.

structure.label: Chapters 93–110
structure.title: Pip overboard, the try-works alight, the coin read aloud
structure.summary: The cabin boy jumps from a boat and is left in the open sea long enough to lose his reason, which the book treats as a form of sight. Ishmael squeezes sperm until he loves everyone aboard, warns himself against staring into the try-works fire at night, and watches every officer in turn read the doubloon and find himself in it.

scenes.title: The Castaway
scenes.summary: Pip is abandoned in the water; the ship recovers a body and the crew decides the mind is gone.

scenes.title: A Squeeze of the Hand
scenes.summary: Working sperm back to liquid produces the most unguarded happiness in the book.

scenes.title: The Try-Works
scenes.summary: The ship rendering blubber at night looks like something sailing out of hell, and Ishmael nearly steers it onto a course by staring.

scenes.title: The Doubloon
scenes.summary: Ahab, Starbuck, Stubb, Flask, the Manxman, Queequeg, Fedallah and Pip each interpret the same coin.

structure.label: Chapters 111–132
structure.title: Compass, quadrant, coffin, calm
structure.summary: Ahab smashes the quadrant, remagnetises the compass needles after a typhoon, and refuses the Rachel's captain a day's search for his own lost son. The carpenter turns Queequeg's coffin into a life-buoy. In one clear morning Ahab asks Starbuck to let him look into a human eye, and then orders him to stay aboard.

scenes.title: The Candles
scenes.summary: St Elmo's fire burns at the mastheads and Ahab addresses the lightning as a personal acquaintance.

scenes.title: The Pequod Meets the Rachel
scenes.summary: A captain begs help searching for his missing boat and his son; Ahab refuses and sails on.

scenes.title: The Symphony
scenes.summary: Ahab weeps into the sea, wonders what is commanding him, and sends Starbuck away.

structure.label: Chapters 133–135 and the Epilogue
structure.title: Three days, and one man left
structure.summary: The whale is raised at last and fought for three days. It stoves the boats, drowns Fedallah in the lines, and finally runs at the ship itself and sinks it. Ahab goes down fastened to his own harpoon rope. Ishmael, thrown clear on the first day of the chase, floats out of the vortex on the coffin.

scenes.title: The Chase — Third Day
scenes.summary: The Pequod is holed and sinks with the sky-hawk nailed to her mast; Ahab is carried off by his own line.

scenes.title: Epilogue
scenes.summary: The narrator explains how he alone survived, and which ship picked him up.

characters.name: Ishmael
characters.role: Narrator, foremast hand, sole survivor
characters.summary: He signs on as an ordinary sailor and then takes over the book, interrupting the voyage to explain whale anatomy, quote Sir Thomas Browne and stage a scene as drama. His curiosity is what saves him from Ahab's kind of attention: he keeps wanting to know what things are, rather than what they mean about him.
