books.title: Paradise Lost
books.author: John Milton
books.setting: Hell, Chaos, Heaven and the garden of Eden, in the days around the Fall
books.written: Composed largely in the 1650s and early 1660s, by dictation
books.lengthNote: Over ten thousand lines of unrhymed iambic pentameter, arranged in twelve books
books.openingLine: Of Man’s first disobedience, and the fruit Of that forbidden Tree, whose mortal taste Brought death into the world, and all our woe
books.summary: A blind republican, on the losing side of a revolution, writes an epic about the first defeat. Milton gives the rebel angel the best speeches and then spends twelve books showing what those speeches cost, and the crisis of the poem is not a battle but a conversation between a husband and a wife about whether to work apart for a morning. It ends with two people walking into an unmapped world, holding hands.
books.referenceStyle: book — the source text carries no line numbers, so quotations are placed by book alone

sourceText.label: Standard Ebooks text of Paradise Lost
sourceText.note: The text used for checking runs one verse line to a line but prints no line numbers, so references here stop at the book. Line numbers in printed editions follow the twelve-book arrangement of 1674.

structure.label: Book I
structure.title: Defeat reorganised as policy
structure.summary: The fallen angels come to on a burning lake, and Satan turns the worst news imaginable into a programme. The roll-call of the devils doubles as a catalogue of the gods later worshipped on earth, and Pandemonium rises out of the ground in the time it takes to describe it.

structure.label: Book II
structure.title: The debate, the gates, and the flight through Chaos
structure.summary: Hell holds a policy meeting with four speakers and a fixed outcome, since Beelzebub is arguing Satan's case for him. Satan then leaves alone, meets his own daughter and grandson keeping the gate, and beats his way up through Chaos towards the new world.

structure.label: Book III
structure.title: Heaven answers the charge before it is made
structure.summary: God sees Satan coming and states, in advance, that man will fall and that the fall will be man's own doing. The Son volunteers to pay for it. The book opens with the poem's most personal passage, an address to light by a man who cannot see it.

structure.label: Book IV
structure.title: Eden watched by an enemy who cannot look away
structure.summary: Satan reaches the garden and finds that he has brought Hell with him. What follows is mostly domestic: two people gardening, talking, going to bed, while the intruder squats beside them taking notes and the angelic guard finally moves him on.

structure.label: Book V
structure.title: An angel to dinner, and the first refusal
structure.summary: Eve wakes from a dream she did not choose, and Raphael arrives to eat fruit and explain the terms. His history of the revolt gives the poem Abdiel, the one angel who hears Satan's argument through and walks out of the meeting.

structure.label: Book VI
structure.title: Three days of war that settle nothing
structure.summary: Angels fight, invent artillery, throw hills at each other and cannot be killed, which is precisely the point: the war is unwinnable until the Son ends it alone in a single afternoon. Force is shown to be the least interesting power in the poem.

structure.label: Book VII
structure.title: Creation described to a man who was not there
structure.summary: Raphael answers Adam's question about how the world began. Milton's six days are noisy, crowded and physical, full of animals shouldering their way out of the ground, and the whole account is framed as speech accommodated to a listener who could not otherwise follow it.

structure.label: Book VIII
structure.title: Adam's own story, and a warning about wanting more
structure.summary: Adam asks about astronomy and is told to be lowly wise. He then describes his first minutes of consciousness, his argument with God about loneliness, and his response to Eve — at which Raphael frowns and delivers the poem's least comfortable piece of marital advice.

structure.label: Book IX
structure.title: The morning apart, and the fruit
structure.summary: The crisis is a disagreement about how to spend a working day. Eve wants a virtue that has been tested; Adam yields rather than command her; the serpent finds her alone and argues her into eating, and Adam eats knowing exactly what he is doing. The book ends in mutual accusation.

structure.label: Book X
structure.title: Judgement, and the road built from Hell
structure.summary: The Son comes down to sentence them and stays to clothe them. Sin and Death pave a highway from Hell to earth, Satan returns to an ovation that turns into hissing, and Eve — who is blamed for everything — is the first to propose that they stop blaming each other.

structure.label: Book XI
structure.title: The future shown as a series of deathbeds
structure.summary: Michael takes Adam up a hill and shows him what his choice has produced: the first murder, a lazar-house of diseases, war, and a flood. Adam learns history the way a man learns of a bereavement, one instance at a time.

structure.label: Book XII
structure.title: History finished, and the gate behind them
structure.summary: Michael switches from vision to narration and carries the story to the Incarnation and beyond. Adam is offered a paradise that cannot be lost because it is internal, and the poem closes on two figures walking away with the whole world to choose from.

characters.name: Satan
characters.role: Leader of the rebel angels, formerly Lucifer
characters.summary: The most persuasive speaker in English poetry and the one the poem most wants you to distrust. He is magnificent in Books I and II, cannot stop talking to himself in Book IV, and by Book IX has agreed to be squeezed into a snake — a career the poem records as a steady shrinking.
characters.clue: He calls the worst place in creation his own possession, decides that his mind can furnish it, and ends the poem in the body of an animal.

characters.name: Eve
characters.role: The first woman
characters.summary: She is given the poem's best argument — that an untested virtue is not virtue at all — and the poem never answers it, only shows what happens next. She also speaks its tenderest lines and makes the first move towards reconciliation after the Fall, while Adam is still composing his complaint.
characters.clue: She proposes that they work apart for one morning, wins the argument, and the world changes before lunch.

characters.name: Adam
characters.role: The first man
characters.summary: He is told the whole truth in advance by an archangel and falls anyway, not from ignorance but from an unwillingness to live without her. Milton is careful about this: Adam is not deceived, which makes his eating the more deliberate act and the harder one to condemn cleanly.
characters.clue: Warned in person, at length, by an angel over dinner, he still swallows the fruit within seconds of learning what she has done.

characters.name: God the Father
characters.role: Creator, and the poem's defendant
characters.summary: Milton puts him on the stand in Book III and has him argue his own case: the angels and man were made free, freedom that cannot fail is not freedom, and therefore the blame is not his. Readers have found the voice cold ever since, which may be the price of making an argument rather than an atmosphere.

characters.name: The Son
characters.role: The Father's agent in war, creation, judgement and mercy
characters.summary: He does everything in the poem that actually takes effect: he ends the war alone, speaks the world into being, passes sentence in Eden and then kneels down to clothe the people he has sentenced. Where Satan announces, the Son acts and says very little about it.

characters.name: Raphael
characters.role: The affable archangel, sent to warn Adam
characters.summary: He comes to lunch and stays for four books, explaining the revolt, the war and the creation in terms a person without experience of either could hold. His honesty has limits he admits to, and his parting advice — be lowly wise — is the one instruction Adam and Eve both fail to keep.
traits: candid about what he cannot say

characters.name: Michael
characters.role: The archangel who carries out the eviction
characters.summary: He leads the loyal host in the war and returns in the last two books as the poem's historian, showing Adam the future in pictures until the pictures become unbearable and he switches to plain narration. He is the one who names the paradise within.

characters.name: Abdiel
characters.role: A seraph among the rebel legions
characters.summary: Milton invents him. He hears out Satan's case for independence, answers it in public, and then walks the whole night back through an army that despises him. For a poet who had defended a beheaded king's executioners and then watched the monarchy return, the figure of the lone dissenter was not an abstraction.
characters.clue: One angel out of an entire rebel legion says no, argues the point, and walks out alone through a jeering camp.

characters.name: Beelzebub
characters.role: Satan's second, and the voice of the winning motion
characters.summary: He speaks last in the debate in Hell and proposes the plan Satan wants, which the assembly then adopts as its own idea. The manoeuvre is the most recognisable piece of politics in the poem: the leader does not have to argue for his policy if the right subordinate does.

characters.name: Sin and Death
characters.role: The keepers of Hell's gate
characters.summary: Half allegory and half family, they are Satan's daughter and his son by her, and they guard the door he needs opened. Once the Fall has happened they build a bridge from Hell to earth, which turns a moral idea into a piece of civil engineering.

themes.name: Freedom, foreknowledge and fault
themes.summary: The poem's stated purpose is to justify the ways of God to men, and its argument is entirely about liberty: obedience that could not have been withheld would prove nothing, so the possibility of the Fall is the price of everything good in Eden. God knows what will happen and insists this is not the same as causing it.
themes.development: Set out as doctrine in Book III, dramatised as a marital argument in Book IX, and left with Adam in Book XII as a choice about how to live in a world where the worst has already happened.

themes.name: Persuasion as a weapon
themes.summary: Almost every turn of the plot is a speech that works. Satan raises an army with one, carries a parliament with another through a proxy, and takes Eden with a third; the loyal side answers with Abdiel's rebuttal and Raphael's patient exposition. Milton, who wrote pamphlets for a revolution, knew how much damage a good argument can do.
themes.development: From public oratory in Books I and II, to private flattery in Book IX, to the quieter persuasion of Michael's history, which changes Adam without once raising its voice.

themes.name: Rule and service
themes.summary: Satan frames the whole conflict as a choice between reigning and serving, and the poem spends twelve books dismantling the opposition. Service in Heaven turns out to be a form of activity and delight; Satan's reign is a monarchy of one over a wasteland, maintained by speeches to people who have no alternative.
themes.development: Announced in Book I as a preference, tested in the Hell debate, and answered in Book VI, where the Son's single-handed victory shows what authority looks like when it does not need to be asserted.

themes.name: Manhood and gender
themes.summary: The poem states a hierarchy plainly and then writes scenes that strain against it. Eve is described as made for Adam, and it is Eve who produces the argument nobody refutes, who eats first, and who ends the quarrel after the Fall. Milton's hierarchy is doctrine; his drama keeps handing the initiative to the wrong person.
themes.development: Declared in Book IV, accepted by Eve in her own voice, contested in the separation scene of Book IX, and quietly reversed at the end of Book X.

themes.name: Knowledge and its limits
themes.summary: The forbidden tree is a tree of knowledge, and the poem is full of people asking questions they are told not to press: Adam on astronomy, Eve on what the fruit might do, Satan on whether he was created at all. Raphael's answer is not that curiosity is wicked but that some knowledge has no use to the person wanting it.
themes.development: Raphael's warning in Book VIII is repeated in the serpent's temptation as its exact inversion — knowledge offered as promotion — and settled in Book XII, where what Adam needs turns out to be practice rather than information.

themes.name: Loss, exile and what can be carried out
themes.summary: Everyone in the poem has been thrown out of somewhere. The angels lose Heaven, Adam and Eve lose the garden, and Milton — blind, out of favour, on the wrong side of a restored monarchy — writes the loss from the inside. What the ending offers is not the place back but a portable version of it.
themes.development: Hell in Book I is exile as rage; Book IV is exile as homesickness watching other people's happiness; Book XII makes it a journey with a direction, undertaken hand in hand.

techniques.name: Blank verse
techniques.definition: Unrhymed iambic pentameter, in which the sentence and the line are free to disagree.
techniques.bookDefinition: Unrhymed iambic pentameter, in which the sentence and the line are free to disagree.
techniques.inThisBook: Milton's sentences habitually run past the line-ending, so the verse arrives at its main verb late and the reader holds several clauses in suspense — the opening sentence takes sixteen lines to reach its imperative, 'Sing'.

techniques.name: Beginning in the middle
techniques.definition: Opening an epic after the decisive events, and supplying the earlier history later through a character's narration.
techniques.bookDefinition: Opening an epic after the decisive events, and supplying the earlier history later through a character's narration.
techniques.inThisBook: The war in Heaven has been over for nine days when the poem starts. Books V to VIII are Raphael filling in the past, which turns exposition into a warning delivered to the two people it concerns.

techniques.name: Epic simile
techniques.definition: An extended comparison that leaves the narrative for several lines and acquires a life of its own.
techniques.bookDefinition: An extended comparison that leaves the narrative for several lines and acquires a life of its own.
techniques.inThisBook: The fallen angels lie thick as autumn leaves in Vallombrosa; Satan's shield is the moon seen through Galileo's glass. The comparisons keep reaching for the ordinary world, which is the only one the reader has.

techniques.name: Invocation
techniques.definition: A direct address to a muse or a source of inspiration, placed at the head of a book.
techniques.bookDefinition: A direct address to a muse or a source of inspiration, placed at the head of a book.
techniques.inThisBook: Four of them punctuate the poem, and they are where Milton speaks in his own person — most openly at the start of Book III, where the address to light becomes an account of blindness.

techniques.name: Catalogue
techniques.definition: A list allowed to run on past the point of usefulness, so that the accumulation itself becomes the effect.
techniques.bookDefinition: A long list of objects or names used in place of narrative.
techniques.inThisBook: The roll-call of devils in Book I names them by the gods they will later become in Canaan, Egypt and Greece, so that the list of the defeated is simultaneously a history of idolatry to come.

techniques.name: Allegory
techniques.definition: Figures who are named for what they mean, moving through a narrative alongside literal characters.
techniques.bookDefinition: Figures who are named for what they mean, moving through a narrative alongside literal characters.
techniques.inThisBook: Sin and Death are abstractions with a family tree, and Milton lets them do physical work — keeping a gate, building a road — so that the machinery of the idea is visible in a poem otherwise committed to persons.

quotations.text: Of Man’s first disobedience, and the fruit Of that forbidden Tree, whose mortal taste Brought death into the world, and all our woe, With loss of Eden, till one greater Man Restore us, and regain the blissful seat
quotations.context: The opening of the poem, before the invocation names its muse.
quotations.analysis: The sentence withholds its verb for sixteen lines: everything here is object, and the reader is left holding disobedience, fruit, death, woe and Eden with nothing yet to do with them. Placing the remedy inside the first sentence, before the crime has been narrated, also tells you the poem is not a suspense plot.

quotations.text: That to the highth of this great argument I may assert the Eternal Providence, And justify the ways of God to men.
quotations.context: The close of the invocation to the heavenly muse.
quotations.analysis: 'Argument' means both the poem's subject and a case put to a court, and Milton takes the second sense seriously enough to have God testify in Book III. 'Justify' is a legal verb: he is not proposing to praise God but to answer a charge, which is a startling thing to promise in a poem's first thirty lines.

quotations.text: yet from those flames No light, but rather darkness visible Served only to discover sights of woe
quotations.context: Satan's first sight of Hell, as far as angels can see.
quotations.analysis: The phrase is a contradiction that works as a description: flames that illuminate nothing except how much there is to dread. Milton needs light in Hell so that the fallen can see each other and their situation, and needs it to be useless, so he invents a category of darkness that performs the office of light.

quotations.text: What though the field be lost? All is not lost; the unconquerable will, And study of revenge, immortal hate, And courage never to submit or yield:
quotations.context: Satan's first speech to Beelzebub on the burning lake.
quotations.analysis: Read the list rather than the tone: an unconquerable will, a course of study in revenge, and hate described as immortal. Three of the four items are heroic virtues and one is simply a refusal to stop, and the speech works on the reader exactly as it works on the legions — by sounding like resolve before it can be inspected as a programme.

quotations.text: The mind is its own place, and in itself Can make a Heaven of Hell, a Hell of Heaven.
quotations.context: Satan taking possession of Hell on landing.
quotations.analysis: The claim is refuted by the speaker himself three books later, when he finds that the mind being its own place is precisely the trouble. The symmetry of the line invites agreement before the sense has been checked: it is the kind of sentence that survives detached from its speaker, which is how it usually travels.

quotations.text: Better to reign in Hell, than serve in Heaven.
quotations.context: The conclusion of Satan's speech on first surveying his new kingdom.
quotations.analysis: The line presents a choice that was never on offer — nobody asked him to choose between ruling and serving — and its balance disguises the fact that one half is imaginary. It also sets the terms the rest of the poem will dismantle, since service in Heaven is shown to involve conversation, work and food, and reigning in Hell turns out to mean addressing an audience with nowhere else to go.

quotations.text: Awake, arise, or be for ever fallen!
quotations.context: Satan rousing the legions lying stunned on the lake.
quotations.analysis: Three imperatives and a threat, all in one line of monosyllables after hundreds of lines of elaborate syntax — the sudden plainness is the point. 'Fallen' does double work as a military disgrace and as their actual physical position, and the whole sentence can be shouted, which is what it is for.

quotations.text: Long is the way And hard, that out of Hell leads up to light;
quotations.speaker: Satan
quotations.context: Satan addressing the assembly before volunteering for the journey alone.
quotations.analysis: He is describing a route through Chaos and stating, without noticing, the moral condition of everyone listening. The line is also a piece of management: by making the errand sound impossible he ensures nobody else offers to share it, and the sole risk becomes sole credit.

quotations.text: The one seemed woman to the waist, and fair, But ended foul in many a scaly fold Voluminous and vast, a serpent armed With mortal sting.
quotations.context: The first description of Sin, seated at the gates of Hell.
quotations.analysis: Milton gives the allegory a joint: fair above, foul below, with the change of substance happening at the waist. The serpent's shape arrives here, long before Eden, so that when Satan enters a real snake in Book IX he is putting on something already in the family.

quotations.text: Chaos umpire sits, And by decision more embroils the fray By which he reigns; next him, high arbiter, Chance governs all.
quotations.context: The description of the abyss Satan must cross.
quotations.analysis: Both officials named here are supposed to settle disputes, and both make them worse: the umpire's rulings increase the brawl he presides over. Milton is describing a region without providence, and he does it by borrowing the vocabulary of courts and games and showing it failing.

quotations.text: Hail, holy Light, offspring of Heaven first-born!
quotations.context: The invocation opening Book III, as the poem leaves Hell for Heaven.
quotations.analysis: A blind man greets the one thing he cannot have, and the greeting is a formal salutation rather than a lament. The passage that follows turns the poem's structure into biography: he has just come up out of darkness in the narrative, and has not come up out of it at all.

quotations.text: I made him just and right, Sufficient to have stood, though free to fall.
quotations.speaker: God the Father
quotations.context: God, seeing Satan approach the new world, states in advance where the fault will lie.
quotations.analysis: The whole defence is balanced on one line, and on the difference between 'sufficient' and 'certain'. Had man been made unable to fall, the standing would have been mechanical; the poem's God would rather be accused of cruelty than build a creature whose obedience proves nothing.

quotations.text: Freely they stood who stood, and fell who fell.
quotations.speaker: God the Father
quotations.context: Extending the same argument from man to the angels.
quotations.analysis: Nine words, eight of them monosyllables, and the same adverb governing both halves — the freedom is identical on either side of the outcome. The chiasmus makes standing and falling grammatically equal, which is exactly the claim: nothing in the arrangement favoured one result over the other.

quotations.text: Which way I fly is Hell; myself am Hell; And, in the lowest deep, a lower deep Still threatening to devour me opens wide,
quotations.speaker: Satan
quotations.context: Alone on Mount Niphates, in sight of Eden, before entering the garden.
quotations.analysis: This is the answer to his own boast in Book I: the mind being its own place is the trap, not the escape. The geometry is the frightening part — a lowest deep that keeps opening a lower one means there is no floor, and Milton gives the idea in four monosyllables before the sentence stops.

quotations.text: So farewell hope, and with hope farewell fear, Farewell remorse! All good to me is lost; Evil, be thou my good:
quotations.speaker: Satan
quotations.context: The conclusion of the soliloquy on Niphates, where he considers repentance and rejects it.
quotations.analysis: He gives up fear in the same breath as hope, which is an accurate account of what despair buys. The last clause is an address, not a statement: he is conscripting evil the way a poet conscripts a muse, and the sentence has the shape of a prayer with the object swapped.

quotations.text: For contemplation he and valour formed, For softness she and sweet attractive grace; He for God only, she for God in him.
quotations.context: The narrator's first description of Adam and Eve, seen through Satan's eyes.
quotations.analysis: The doctrine is stated in the most memorable line available, with the parallel structure doing the work of proof. It is worth noticing who is looking: the description is placed inside Satan's field of view, and the poem's own drama spends five more books quietly declining to behave as the line prescribes.

quotations.text: My author and disposer, what thou bidd’st Unargued I obey; so God ordains: God is thy law, thou mine: to know no more Is woman’s happiest knowledge, and her praise.
quotations.speaker: Eve
quotations.context: Eve answering Adam at the end of their first day in the poem.
quotations.analysis: She states the hierarchy more absolutely than Adam ever does, and she states it in an argument — the speech is fluent, ordered and rhetorically confident, which is not what unargued obedience sounds like. Five books later she will open a debate on exactly this question and win it.

quotations.text: With thee conversing I forget all time, All seasons and their change: all please alike.
quotations.speaker: Eve
quotations.context: Eve to Adam in the garden at evening.
quotations.analysis: The love poem she then speaks is built as a list of everything she likes and a repeat of the same list with the word 'without' inserted, so that the structure itself performs the point. Here at its head, 'conversing' carries its older sense of living with as well as talking to, and it is talk that the Fall will first spoil.

quotations.text: Abashed the Devil stood, And felt how awful goodness is, and saw Virtue in her shape how lovely
quotations.context: Satan, discovered in the garden, faced down by the young angel Zephon.
quotations.analysis: The verb comes first and the subject second, so the shame arrives before the person it belongs to. 'Awful' still means awe-producing here, and the moment matters because it is the one place where Satan is shown recognising good as attractive rather than as an obstacle — and then walking on.

quotations.text: So spake the Seraph Abdiel, faithful found; Among the faithless, faithful only he;
quotations.context: After Abdiel has answered Satan's argument in front of the assembled rebel host.
quotations.analysis: The repetition works like a count: faithful, faithless, faithful, with the tally narrowing to 'only he'. Milton, writing after the Restoration had made his own politics unspeakable, gives his invented character the one action available to a defeated dissenter — to say so out loud and then leave.

quotations.text: ‘Let there be light!’ said God; and forthwith light Ethereal, first of things, quintessence pure, Sprung from the Deep
quotations.speaker: Raphael
quotations.context: Raphael's account of the first day of creation.
quotations.analysis: The quoted command takes half a line and the consequence begins in the same line, so the syntax enacts the speed of the thing described. Milton then cannot leave it alone and spends three clauses classifying the light, which is the characteristic movement of this book: a scriptural sentence followed by a poet unable to stop looking at it.

quotations.text: Heaven is for thee too high To know what passes there; be lowly wise; Think only what concerns thee and thy being;
quotations.speaker: Raphael
quotations.context: Raphael closing down Adam's questions about the motion of the heavens.
quotations.analysis: 'Lowly wise' is not an instruction to be ignorant but to be wise about the right things, and the test of it is that the angel has just spent three books answering questions. The serpent will offer Adam's wife the exact opposite bargain — knowledge as promotion — and the phrasing of this warning is what makes the offer recognisable.

quotations.text: And what is faith, love, virtue, unassayed Alone, without exterior help sustained?
quotations.speaker: Eve
quotations.context: Eve arguing that she and Adam should work in separate parts of the garden.
quotations.analysis: This is Milton's own position, put in the mouth of the character about to be ruined by acting on it: he had argued in print that a virtue never exposed to its opposite is worth nothing. The poem does not refute her. It simply lets the argument be correct and the morning be a disaster.

quotations.text: Go; for thy stay, not free, absents thee more; Go in thy native innocence, rely On what thou hast of virtue, summon all; For God towards thee hath done his part; do thine.
quotations.speaker: Adam
quotations.context: Adam conceding the argument and letting Eve go alone.
quotations.analysis: He gives way on the same principle he is worried about: keeping her by command would make her presence worthless. The last four words are the whole theology of the poem compressed into a domestic exchange, and they are said by a man who has just lost an argument he was right to be having.

quotations.text: So saying, her rash hand in evil hour Forth reaching to the fruit, she plucked, she eat. Earth felt the wound, and Nature from her seat, Sighing through all her works, gave signs of woe
quotations.context: The Fall itself, at the end of the serpent's argument.
quotations.analysis: Two monosyllabic verbs, side by side without a conjunction, take up less room than the adjective attached to her hand — the act is smaller than everything around it. Then the sentence widens instantly to the whole planet, and the disproportion between the gesture and the consequence is the effect Milton has been building for nine books.

quotations.text: he scrupled not to eat, Against his better knowledge, not deceived, But fondly overcome with female charm.
quotations.context: Adam eating the fruit Eve brings him.
quotations.analysis: The clauses are arranged to remove every excuse in turn: not ignorant, not tricked, simply unwilling to be left. 'Fondly' means foolishly, and the line is the poem's coldest, because it denies Adam the dignity of a mistake and gives him a motive most readers recognise.

quotations.text: Nor love thy life, nor hate; but what thou livest Live well; how long or short, permit to Heaven.
quotations.speaker: Michael
quotations.context: Michael answering Adam, after the vision of the lazar-house of diseases.
quotations.analysis: Adam has just asked how to meet death and been shown every way it arrives. The answer refuses both available postures, clinging and despair, and puts the emphasis on an adverb: the question is not the length of the life but the manner of it, which is the first piece of advice in the poem that applies to a reader.

quotations.text: then wilt thou not be loth To leave this Paradise, but shalt possess A Paradise within thee, happier far.
quotations.speaker: Michael
quotations.context: Michael's summary of what Adam is to add to his knowledge before leaving.
quotations.analysis: The offer is comparative — happier far — which is a startling thing to say to a man being evicted from the best place there has ever been. The list that leads up to it is all practice rather than information: faith, virtue, patience, temperance, love. Paradise becomes something done, not somewhere lived.

quotations.text: The world was all before them, where to choose Their place of rest, and Providence their guide. They, hand in hand, with wandering steps and slow, Through Eden took their solitary way.
quotations.context: The last four lines of the poem.
quotations.analysis: Every phrase pulls two ways at once: a whole world to choose from and nowhere in particular to go; guided, and wandering; hand in hand, and solitary. Milton refuses either a triumph or a lament, and the final rhythm — slow, with a caesura in each of the last two lines — makes the reader walk out at their pace.

atAGlance.label: First published
atAGlance.note: In ten books, from a London still rebuilding after the Fire.

atAGlance.label: Second edition
atAGlance.note: Books VII and X were each divided in two, giving the twelve books now standard, and the year Milton died.

atAGlance.label: Verse
atAGlance.note: Milton added a note defending the absence of rhyme, which he called no necessary adjunct of a poem.

atAGlance.label: Composition
atAGlance.note: Milton had been entirely blind since about 1652; the poem was spoken to whoever was at hand to write.

criticalViews.position: The Romantic reading: Satan as the poem's true energy
criticalViews.summary: From the 1790s onwards, readers have argued that Milton writes at full power in Hell and at half power in Heaven, and that the sympathy the poem generates for its rebel is not fully under its author's control.
criticalViews.counter: It requires ignoring the poem's shape. Satan's speeches get shorter and his form smaller as the work proceeds, and Books XI and XII belong to somebody else entirely.

criticalViews.position: The theological reading: a poem about free will
criticalViews.summary: On this account the epic is doing exactly what it says in line twenty-six — mounting a defence of divine justice by insisting that creatures who could not have failed would prove nothing, and that the Fall therefore belongs to the people who chose it.
criticalViews.counter: A defence conducted by the defendant, in speeches many readers find chilly, may win the argument and lose the case.

criticalViews.position: The political reading: a defeated republican writing after the Restoration
criticalViews.summary: Milton wrote for a revolution, served its government, and finished the poem under the monarchy it had killed. Read this way, the questions of who deserves to rule, what service means and how a lone dissenter behaves are not decoration.
criticalViews.counter: The parallels do not line up neatly: the poem's rebel against a monarch is Satan, which makes any simple mapping of Milton's politics onto the plot collapse at once.

criticalViews.position: Feminist readings of Eden
criticalViews.summary: Criticism since the 1970s has examined the gap between the hierarchy the poem asserts and the initiative it repeatedly gives to Eve — the strongest argument in Book IX is hers, and so is the first step towards reconciliation in Book X.
criticalViews.counter: The poem also gives her the fall, and states the subordination in its own narrating voice rather than leaving it to a character.

essayQuestions.question: Does Paradise Lost succeed in justifying the ways of God to men?
essayQuestions.focus: Free will, foreknowledge and the poem's stated purpose
plan: Take the promise literally: 'justify' is a legal verb, so establish what charge is being answered.
Set out God's own defence in Book III — created sufficient to have stood, though free to fall — and note that it is put as argument, not assertion.
Test it on the angels, where Abdiel in Book V shows that the rebellion was refusable by somebody standing in the same room.
Turn to Book IX, where the doctrine becomes a domestic argument and Adam concedes on exactly the principle God has stated.
Weigh the cost: a case won in Book III may still be lost in tone, and decide whether Books XI and XII repair that or confirm it.

essayQuestions.question: How far is Satan the hero of Paradise Lost?
essayQuestions.focus: Rhetoric, structure and the reader's sympathy
plan: Begin with what the speeches actually promise: unconquerable will, a study of revenge, and a reign that nobody offered as an alternative to service.
Trace the diminishing shape — soliloquy on Niphates in Book IV, the toad and the mist, the serpent in Book IX, the hissing in Book X.
Distinguish the reader's experience of the verse from the poem's judgement, and consider whether Milton means the seduction to happen to us.
Use Abdiel as the control: a character given the same information who does the opposite.
Conclude on structure — the last two books remove Satan entirely, which is an argument in itself.

essayQuestions.question: Discuss Milton's presentation of Eve.
essayQuestions.focus: Hierarchy, argument and the poem's internal contradictions
plan: Start with the narrator's own statement of hierarchy in Book IV and note who is looking when it is made.
Read her speech of obedience as a rhetorical performance, fluent and shapely, and ask what that does to the word 'unargued'.
Give full weight to the separation scene: the argument about untested virtue is Milton's own published position.
Follow the aftermath in Book X, where she proposes reconciliation and Adam is still assigning blame.
Decide whether the poem contains a contradiction or dramatises one deliberately.

essayQuestions.question: What does the ending of Paradise Lost offer its readers?
essayQuestions.focus: Exile, consolation and the last four lines
plan: Establish what Michael has actually shown Adam in Books XI and XII, and how the method changes from vision to narration.
Examine the paradise within: a comparative claim, happier far, made to somebody being evicted.
Read the closing lines phrase by phrase, noting how each carries its own contradiction.
Set the ending against Book I, where exile produced rage, and measure the distance travelled.
Consider what a reader in 1667 London — plague, fire, a restored monarchy — would hear in a consolation of this kind.

discussionQuestions: Satan's finest speeches are in the first two books and he never sounds that way again. Is the decline a judgement, or a loss of interest?
Eve argues that virtue untested is not virtue. Does the poem ever answer her, or only show the consequences?
Adam is explicitly not deceived. Does that make his fall worse than hers, or more forgivable?
Raphael tells Adam to be lowly wise after answering questions for three books. Where is the line meant to fall?
The poem ends with the whole world available and two people walking slowly. Is that a consolation or a sentence?

timeline.label: John Milton born in Bread Street, London
timeline.detail: The son of a scrivener and composer, in a household that could afford tutors and music.

timeline.label: Milton travels in Italy
timeline.detail: He later wrote of having visited the aged Galileo, then a prisoner of the Inquisition; Galileo's telescope appears in the poem.

timeline.label: Areopagitica published
timeline.detail: His argument against pre-publication licensing turns on the claim that a virtue never tested is no virtue — the position Eve takes in Book IX.

timeline.label: Charles I executed; Milton defends the regicide in print
timeline.detail: The Tenure of Kings and Magistrates appears within weeks, and Milton is appointed Secretary for Foreign Tongues to the Council of State.

timeline.label: Milton is completely blind
timeline.detail: From this point everything he writes is dictated, including the whole of the epic.

timeline.label: The Restoration
timeline.detail: Milton goes into hiding, is arrested and released; his defences of the regicide are burnt by the hangman.

timeline.label: Plague drives Milton out of London
timeline.detail: He took a cottage at Chalfont St Giles in Buckinghamshire, where work on the poem continued.

timeline.label: Paradise Lost published in ten books
timeline.detail: Printed in London the year after the Great Fire, with a contract paying Milton five pounds down.

timeline.label: Paradise Regained and Samson Agonistes published together
timeline.detail: The brief epic of the temptation in the wilderness, and a tragedy about a blind man among his enemies.

timeline.label: The twelve-book second edition; Milton dies
timeline.detail: Books VII and X were each split in two and a few lines added. Milton died in November and was buried at St Giles-without-Cripplegate.

timeline.label: Tonson's illustrated folio
timeline.detail: The first grand edition, published by subscription, which established the poem as a national monument rather than a recent book.

timeline.label: Blake begins The Marriage of Heaven and Hell
timeline.detail: The first of the Romantic readings that take Milton's Satan as the poem's real energy — a reading the poem's structure was built to resist.

places.name: Mount Sinai
places.note: Oreb, or of Sinai: the mountain named in the opening invocation as where the shepherd Moses was first inspired.

places.name: Jerusalem
places.note: Zion hill and Siloa's brook, offered in the invocation as the alternative source of the poet's inspiration.

places.name: Mount Helicon
places.note: The Aonian mount of the Greek muses, which Milton announces at the outset that he intends to fly above.

places.name: Vallombrosa
places.note: The Tuscan valley whose autumn leaves supply the simile for the fallen angels lying on the lake in Book I.

places.name: Chalfont St Giles
places.note: The Buckinghamshire village where Milton took a cottage during the plague of 1665, with the poem near completion.

places.name: St Giles-without-Cripplegate, London
places.note: The church where Milton was buried in November 1674, months after the twelve-book edition appeared.

related.why: The epic Milton measured himself against most closely, down to the arming, the councils and the visit to the underworld.
The war poem behind the war in Heaven, and the source of the catalogue and the extended simile.
An earlier English study of a magnificent speaker arguing himself out of repentance, seventy years before Satan does it on Niphates.
Shelley takes her epigraph from Book X, and her creature reads Paradise Lost and identifies with both Adam and Satan.
A later English poem about a single act with cosmic consequences, and a penitent who must tell the story afterwards.

books.title: Pride and Prejudice
books.author: Jane Austen
books.setting: Hertfordshire, Kent, London and Derbyshire, in the years of the militia camps
books.lengthNote: Sixty-one chapters, first issued in three volumes
books.openingLine: It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife.
books.summary: A family of five daughters, an estate entailed away from all of them, and a neighbourhood that treats every new arrival as an opportunity. Elizabeth Bennet is the best reader of character in the book and gets the two most important readings wrong, and Austen builds the plot so that correcting them costs her something. The comedy never lets go of the arithmetic underneath it: who has money, who will inherit, and who can afford to refuse.

sourceText.label: Standard Ebooks text of Pride and Prejudice
sourceText.note: Chapters are numbered continuously from 1 to 61, as in the Standard Ebooks text; first editions divide the same chapters across three volumes.

structure.label: Chapters 1–12
structure.title: Netherfield taken, and everybody measured
structure.summary: A single man with four or five thousand a year moves into the neighbourhood and the Bennets begin calculating. The Meryton assembly fixes Darcy’s reputation in one overheard sentence, and Jane’s convenient illness keeps Elizabeth at Netherfield long enough for the two of them to start sparring in earnest.

structure.label: Chapters 13–23
structure.title: The heir, the officer and the practical marriage
structure.summary: Mr Collins arrives to inspect the estate he will inherit and the cousin he intends to marry; Wickham arrives with a grievance that flatters Elizabeth’s judgement. Within three days Collins is refused, Charlotte Lucas accepts him, and the Bingleys leave for London taking Jane’s prospects with them.

structure.label: Chapters 24–34
structure.title: Hunsford, Rosings and a proposal nobody wanted
structure.summary: Elizabeth visits Charlotte’s parsonage and sees what a comfortable home actually costs. Lady Catherine presides, Colonel Fitzwilliam lets slip that Darcy separated Bingley from Jane, and Darcy proposes in terms that make refusing him easy and enjoyable.

structure.label: Chapters 35–42
structure.title: The letter, and a second reading
structure.summary: Darcy hands over a letter and walks away, and the novel changes direction without a single event taking place. Elizabeth reads it twice, reconstructs Wickham from the beginning, and arrives at the only self-accusation in the book that is not comic.

structure.label: Chapters 43–50
structure.title: Pemberley, and the news from Brighton
structure.summary: A house, a housekeeper and a set of grounds supply the evidence about Darcy that conversation could not. Then Lydia runs off with Wickham, and the family’s standing, which has been a joke for forty chapters, becomes something that can actually be destroyed.

structure.label: Chapters 51–61
structure.title: What the settlement cost, and who paid it
structure.summary: Lydia returns married and unembarrassed, and the reader learns before Elizabeth does who bought the marriage. Lady Catherine’s attempt to extract a promise produces the opposite of the one she wants, and the last chapters distribute incomes as carefully as affections.

characters.name: Elizabeth Bennet
characters.role: Second of the five Bennet daughters
characters.summary: Quick, funny and justly confident in her own judgement, which is exactly why the novel arranges for her to be wrong about the two men she is most certain of. Her wit is a form of courage in a household where nobody else will say anything true.
characters.clue: She refuses two proposals, walks three miles through mud to nurse her sister, and only discovers her own vanity by reading a letter twice.

relationships.label: closest friend, and a test of her principles

characters.name: Fitzwilliam Darcy
characters.role: Owner of Pemberley in Derbyshire
characters.summary: Ten thousand a year and no talent for a room full of strangers. Austen gives him the novel’s worst opening sentence and then spends fifty chapters showing that his conduct has always been better than his manner, which is not quite the same as saying he was right.
characters.clue: He insults a woman within her hearing at a country dance, proposes to her against his own better judgement, and later pays a blackguard to marry her sister without telling anyone.

characters.name: Jane Bennet
characters.role: The eldest Bennet daughter
characters.summary: Her determination to think well of everybody is presented as a moral achievement and a practical disaster: it makes her unreadable to Bingley, unreadable to Darcy, and defenceless against Caroline Bingley. The novel likes her and does not recommend her method.
characters.clue: She catches cold riding to dinner in the rain because her mother wanted her to stay the night, and forgives everyone involved.

characters.name: Charles Bingley
characters.role: Tenant of Netherfield Park
characters.summary: Amiable, rich and so willing to be guided that his friend can detach him from the woman he loves with a few words about her family. He is the novel’s evidence that good nature without judgement is a kind of weakness.
characters.clue: He takes a house for the shooting, falls in love at the first assembly, and is talked out of it by a friend and a sister in a single winter.

characters.name: George Wickham
characters.role: Lieutenant in the militia
characters.summary: He tells Elizabeth a story about Darcy within an hour of meeting her, and she believes it because it is well told and because she wants to. His charm is a working method rather than a temperament, and the militia’s presence in Meryton is what gives it a market.
characters.clue: The steward’s son who was left a living in a will, sold it for ready money, and then complained for the rest of the book that he had been robbed of it.

relationships.label: elopes with, and is paid to marry
slanders and is bought off by

characters.name: Mr Collins
characters.role: Clergyman of Hunsford, heir to Longbourn
characters.summary: He proposes to two women in three days and is not embarrassed by either outcome, because the proposal was never about a person. Everything he says is addressed upwards to his patroness, even when he is standing in somebody else’s parlour insulting their daughter.
characters.clue: He offers his hand as a favour to the family he will dispossess, and numbers his reasons for marrying like items in a sermon.

characters.name: Charlotte Lucas
characters.role: Elizabeth’s friend, later Mrs Collins
characters.summary: Twenty-seven, without fortune, and the only character who states the terms of the marriage market out loud without either joking or complaining. Her parsonage is arranged so that she sees as little of her husband as the house allows, which is the closest the novel comes to a verdict on the bargain.
characters.clue: She accepts in three days the man her closest friend refused, and explains that she asks only a comfortable home.

characters.name: Lydia Bennet
characters.role: The youngest Bennet daughter
characters.summary: Fifteen, unsupervised and encouraged, she does exactly what her upbringing has trained her to do, and the novel is careful to spread the blame across her mother’s indulgence and her father’s amused neglect. Her elopement is the one plot event that could not be undone by an explanation.
characters.clue: She is delighted to be married before her elder sisters and cannot understand why the family is not delighted too.

characters.name: Mr Bennet
characters.role: Master of Longbourn
characters.summary: He retreats to his library and treats his family as a source of entertainment, and the novel charges him for it: the daughter he never bothered to check runs away, and his best line about making sport for our neighbours is spoken just before he finds out what that costs.
characters.clue: He tells his least favourite daughter that one parent will refuse to see her again whichever way she answers a proposal.

characters.name: Lady Catherine de Bourgh
characters.role: Of Rosings Park, Darcy’s aunt
characters.summary: She gives orders about other people’s carriages, shelves and marriages with the same confidence, and is the only character who states the class objection to the match in plain words. Her one decisive action in the plot is the one that brings the marriage about.
characters.clue: She drives to a small Hertfordshire village to demand a promise, and is told that she has no right to ask for one.

characters.name: Mrs Bennet
characters.role: Mistress of Longbourn
characters.summary: Ridiculous and not wrong. Her single subject is getting five daughters married before her husband dies, and the entail means that the alternative is genuine poverty, so the novel laughs at her method rather than her motive.
characters.clue: Her nerves are her oldest companions, and she can turn a wet evening into an engagement if the house is far enough from home.

themes.name: First impressions and judgement
themes.summary: The discarded title is still the working one. Almost every character forms a verdict in a single evening and then spends the book defending it, and Austen makes the reader do the same thing so that the correction lands on both at once.
themes.development: Fixed at the Meryton assembly, hardened by Wickham’s story, dismantled by a letter in Chapter 35, and formally re-examined at Pemberley.

themes.name: Marriage and money
themes.summary: Every attachment in the novel is quoted with a figure attached, from Bingley’s four or five thousand a year to the hundred a year Mr Bennet is asked to promise for Lydia. Austen does not treat this as vulgar; she treats it as the arithmetic within which affection has to operate.
themes.development: Stated as a joke in the first sentence, argued seriously by Charlotte in Chapter 22, and paid in cash by Darcy in the last volume.

themes.name: Rank and connection
themes.summary: The obstacle between Elizabeth and Darcy is not money on her side but relations on hers: an uncle in trade, an aunt in Cheapside, a mother who cannot be taken anywhere. The novel dismantles the objection by making the Gardiners the most sensible adults in it.
themes.development: Voiced by Caroline Bingley, formalised by Darcy’s first proposal, and shouted by Lady Catherine in the last volume after it has stopped being true for anyone the reader trusts.

themes.name: Entail and female security
themes.summary: Longbourn passes to Mr Collins, so five daughters must find husbands or find lodgings. The legal fact sits under every comic scene, and it is why Charlotte’s calculation is a calculation rather than a failure of feeling.
themes.development: Explained early and never forgotten: it makes Mrs Bennet’s campaign rational, Collins’s proposal a favour in his own eyes, and Lydia’s ruin a threat to four other women.

themes.name: Reputation and family conduct
themes.summary: Character in this novel is public property. A sister’s elopement is treated as a defect in every other sister, and Mary’s moralising about a woman’s irretrievable ruin is contemptible and, within the world of the book, accurate about the consequences.
themes.development: From the embarrassment of the Netherfield ball, through Darcy’s letter about Jane’s family, to the Brighton crisis where reputation becomes something that must be bought back.

themes.name: Self-knowledge
themes.summary: Both leading characters have to revise not an opinion but a habit of mind. Elizabeth discovers that she was flattered into belief; Darcy discovers that being brought up on good principles is not the same as being taught to apply them.
themes.development: Elizabeth’s reckoning comes in Chapter 36, Darcy’s is reported in Chapter 58, and the novel makes the two confessions echo each other’s grammar.

techniques.name: Free indirect style
techniques.definition: Narration that takes on a character’s vocabulary and assumptions without marking them as quotation.
techniques.bookDefinition: Narration that takes on a character’s vocabulary and assumptions without marking them as quotation.
techniques.inThisBook: The narrative sits so close to Elizabeth that her errors arrive as facts; the reader distrusts Darcy on her evidence and has to re-read the first half after the letter.

techniques.name: Irony
techniques.definition: Saying one thing in a form that invites the opposite judgement.
techniques.bookDefinition: Saying one thing in a form that invites the opposite judgement.
techniques.inThisBook: The famous first sentence states a truth nobody in the book holds and everybody acts on: it is the mothers, not the single men, who are in want of anything.

techniques.name: Letters
techniques.definition: Written documents inserted into a narrative as evidence and as plot.
techniques.bookDefinition: Written documents inserted into a narrative as evidence and as plot.
techniques.inThisBook: Darcy’s letter is the structural hinge, and Austen distinguishes her characters by their prose: Collins pompous, Jane over-careful, Lydia unpunctuated and untroubled.

techniques.name: Dialogue as exposure
techniques.definition: Letting characters convict themselves in their own speech rather than describing their faults.
techniques.bookDefinition: Letting characters convict themselves in their own speech rather than describing their faults.
techniques.inThisBook: Mr Collins numbers his reasons for marrying and Lady Catherine interrogates a stranger about her sisters’ accomplishments; neither needs a word of narrative comment.

techniques.name: Epigram
techniques.definition: A short balanced sentence that sounds like settled wisdom and usually turns a received idea inside out.
techniques.bookDefinition: A generalisation compressed into a single balanced sentence.
techniques.inThisBook: Characters reach for maxims when they are least reliable — Mary on vanity and pride, Charlotte on happiness in marriage, Mary again on a woman’s ruin.

techniques.name: Parallel courtships
techniques.definition: Running several versions of the same situation so that each comments on the others.
techniques.bookDefinition: Running several versions of the same situation so that each comments on the others.
techniques.inThisBook: Five marriages are set side by side — Jane’s, Charlotte’s, Lydia’s, Elizabeth’s and the Bennets’ own — so that the reader can see what each one was bought with.

quotations.text: It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife.
quotations.context: The opening sentence of the novel.
quotations.analysis: The sentence claims to report a consensus and names nobody who holds it; the passive construction hides the mothers who are the actual subject. Read strictly it is also false in the book that follows, where the single men are in want of nothing and the women are in want of an income.

quotations.text: You mistake me, my dear. I have a high respect for your nerves. They are my old friends. I have heard you mention them with consideration these twenty years at least.
quotations.speaker: Mr Bennet
quotations.context: Answering his wife’s complaint that he has no compassion on her nerves.
quotations.analysis: The joke depends on treating an ailment as an acquaintance, and it establishes the marriage in a line: he has been amusing himself at her expense for two decades and has changed nothing. Twenty years is also the age of the eldest daughter, which quietly dates the arrangement.

quotations.text: She is tolerable; but not handsome enough to tempt me; and I am in no humour at present to give consequence to young ladies who are slighted by other men.
quotations.speaker: Mr Darcy
quotations.context: At the Meryton assembly, refusing Bingley’s suggestion that he dance with Elizabeth, who is sitting close enough to hear.
quotations.analysis: Eight words decide the first half of the book. The grammar is the insult: she is graded, then found insufficient for a purpose, with no verb that admits she is a person in the room. Elizabeth’s response is to repeat it as a comic story, which is how a wound is kept fresh.

quotations.text: I could easily forgive his pride, if he had not mortified mine.
quotations.speaker: Elizabeth Bennet
quotations.context: Discussing Darcy’s behaviour at the assembly with Charlotte Lucas and her family.
quotations.analysis: She names the mechanism of her own prejudice and does not notice she has done it. The two pronouns are balanced against each other across the comma, which is the shape the whole novel will take: two kinds of pride meeting and neither able to see the other’s.

quotations.text: Vanity and pride are different things, though the words are often used synonymously. A person may be proud without being vain. Pride relates more to our opinion of ourselves, vanity to what we would have others think of us.
quotations.speaker: Mary Bennet
quotations.context: Mary offering the company the benefit of her reading.
quotations.analysis: The distinction is sound and the novel uses it: Darcy is proud and Wickham is vain, and the difference is exactly the one Mary draws. Austen’s joke is that the book’s dullest speaker supplies its most useful definition, and nobody in the room listens.

quotations.text: My good opinion once lost is lost forever.
quotations.speaker: Mr Darcy
quotations.context: At Netherfield, admitting to a resentful temper during an evening of sparring with Elizabeth.
quotations.analysis: He says this as a confession of a fault and plainly regards it as a standard. The novel then spends fifty chapters disproving it about him, since his good opinion of Elizabeth survives her refusal and her family; the line is a self-portrait that has stopped being accurate.

quotations.text: That will do extremely well, child. You have delighted us long enough. Let the other young ladies have time to exhibit.
quotations.speaker: Mr Bennet
quotations.context: Stopping Mary’s second song at the Netherfield ball.
quotations.analysis: A father humiliates a daughter in public and the sentence is constructed so that the cruelty travels inside a compliment. It is the clearest instance of the habit Elizabeth will later have to judge: her father’s wit is aimed at his own children and costs him nothing.

quotations.text: My reasons for marrying are, first, that I think it a right thing for every clergyman in easy circumstances (like myself) to set the example of matrimony in his parish.
quotations.speaker: Mr Collins
quotations.context: Proposing to Elizabeth, having secured her mother’s permission but not her attention.
quotations.analysis: He begins a proposal with an enumerated list and the first item is professional example. The woman is not in the sentence at all; she appears later, as the third reason, on the recommendation of somebody else. Austen lets the syntax do the whole characterisation.

quotations.text: An unhappy alternative is before you, Elizabeth. From this day you must be a stranger to one of your parents. Your mother will never see you again if you do not marry Mr. Collins, and I will never see you again if you do.
quotations.speaker: Mr Bennet
quotations.context: Called in by Mrs Bennet to force Elizabeth to accept Collins.
quotations.analysis: He supports his daughter by pretending not to, which lets him defeat his wife and stay amusing at the same time. The sentence is perfectly balanced around the two parents, and the balance is the point: Elizabeth’s rescue arrives as a joke, and the same detachment will let Lydia go to Brighton.

quotations.text: I am not romantic you know. I never was. I ask only a comfortable home; and considering Mr. Collins’s character, connections, and situation in life, I am convinced that my chance of happiness with him is as fair, as most people can boast on entering the marriage state.
quotations.speaker: Charlotte Lucas
quotations.context: Telling Elizabeth that she has accepted Mr Collins.
quotations.analysis: She asks only for a house and states her odds like an actuary, and the novel never corrects her arithmetic. Set against the first sentence of the book, this is the same proposition with the irony taken out, spoken by the person whom the marriage market has priced most accurately.

quotations.text: In vain have I struggled. It will not do. My feelings will not be repressed. You must allow me to tell you how ardently I admire and love you.
quotations.speaker: Mr Darcy
quotations.context: The first proposal, at the Hunsford parsonage, while Elizabeth is re-reading Jane’s letters.
quotations.analysis: Four short sentences, three of them about his own resistance, and the declaration arrives only in the fourth. ‘Struggled’ and ‘repressed’ treat his feeling as an enemy position, so that by the time he reaches ‘admire and love’ he has already told her what the offer costs him.

quotations.text: I had not known you a month before I felt that you were the last man in the world whom I could ever be prevailed on to marry.
quotations.speaker: Elizabeth Bennet
quotations.context: Refusing Darcy, after he has asked why he is rejected with so little civility.
quotations.analysis: The superlative is a hostage to fortune and Austen collects on it twenty-six chapters later. Note the precision of ‘a month’: she dates her verdict exactly, which is what makes it possible for the novel to show her the evidence she had not yet seen.

quotations.text: Be not alarmed, Madam, on receiving this letter, by the apprehension of its containing any repetition of those sentiments, or renewal of those offers, which were last night so disgusting to you.
quotations.speaker: Mr Darcy
quotations.context: The opening of the letter handed to Elizabeth in the park at Rosings.
quotations.analysis: He hands over the one form of speech she cannot interrupt, and opens by disclaiming any renewal of the offer, which is how he makes the document readable. From here the novel’s evidence arrives in writing, and its turning point involves no event at all — only a second reading.

quotations.text: But vanity, not love, has been my folly. Pleased with the preference of one, and offended by the neglect of the other, on the very beginning of our acquaintance, I have courted prepossession and ignorance, and driven reason away, where either were concerned. Till this moment, I never knew myself.
quotations.speaker: Elizabeth Bennet
quotations.context: Alone, having read Darcy’s letter twice and reconstructed everything Wickham told her.
quotations.analysis: She does not accuse herself of loving the wrong man but of a fault in method: she was pleased by one and slighted by the other, and let that do her thinking. ‘Vanity, not love, has been my folly’ applies Mary’s distinction from Chapter 5 to herself, thirty chapters after it was laughed at.

quotations.text: I have never had a cross word from him in my life, and I have known him ever since he was four years old.
quotations.speaker: Mrs Reynolds
quotations.context: The Pemberley housekeeper showing the house to Elizabeth and the Gardiners.
quotations.analysis: The testimony that changes Elizabeth’s mind comes from a servant with twenty years of observation and no reason to flatter a stranger. Austen makes the evidence economic rather than romantic: landlord and master are job titles, and Darcy is being assessed on how he treats people who cannot answer back.

quotations.text: In what an amiable light does this place him!
quotations.speaker: Elizabeth Bennet
quotations.context: Standing in the Pemberley gallery, hearing the housekeeper describe Darcy’s care of his sister.
quotations.analysis: ‘This place’ is doing double duty: the phrase means this circumstance, and she is standing in the house itself. The estate is functioning as evidence — grounds, portraits, accounts of conduct over years — where conversation had produced only impressions.

quotations.text: Unhappy as the event must be for Lydia, we may draw from it this useful lesson; that loss of virtue in a female is irretrievable⁠—that one false step involves her in endless ruin⁠—that her reputation is no less brittle than it is beautiful⁠—and that she cannot be too much guarded in her behaviour towards the undeserving of the other sex.
quotations.speaker: Mary Bennet
quotations.context: To Elizabeth, while the family waits for news of Lydia.
quotations.analysis: The consolation is monstrous and the description is correct, which is the difficulty the novel will not dissolve. ‘Brittle’ and ‘beautiful’ are yoked by alliteration into a single property that a woman owns and can break, and nothing in the plot disproves the account — only Darcy’s money limits the damage.

quotations.text: Are the shades of Pemberley to be thus polluted?
quotations.speaker: Lady Catherine de Bourgh
quotations.context: In the Longbourn shrubbery, demanding that Elizabeth promise never to accept Darcy.
quotations.analysis: The objection has left the realm of income and become almost sacramental: a house has shades, and a marriage would defile them. It is the class argument in its purest and least answerable form, and the novel answers it by having the interview itself convince Darcy to propose again.

quotations.text: I am only resolved to act in that manner which will, in my own opinion, constitute my happiness, without reference to you, or to any person so wholly unconnected with me.
quotations.speaker: Elizabeth Bennet
quotations.context: Refusing Lady Catherine the promise she has come for.
quotations.analysis: She claims the right to define her own happiness and denies her interrogator any standing at all, and she does it in the flattest, least witty sentence she speaks in the book. The wit is dropped because this is not a duel; it is a jurisdictional claim.

quotations.text: For what do we live but to make sport for our neighbours, and laugh at them in our turn?
quotations.speaker: Mr Bennet
quotations.context: Reading Mr Collins’s letter aloud to Elizabeth, who cannot enjoy it.
quotations.analysis: It is the closest thing he has to a philosophy, and the novel has just finished showing what it costs: the daughter he did not watch has been retrieved with somebody else’s money. The rhetorical question assumes an answer that the last hundred pages have withdrawn.

quotations.text: I have been a selfish being all my life, in practice, though not in principle. As a child I was taught what was right, but I was not taught to correct my temper.
quotations.speaker: Mr Darcy
quotations.context: Walking with Elizabeth after the second proposal has been accepted.
quotations.analysis: The distinction between practice and principle is the same one Elizabeth reached in Chapter 36, and Austen gives the two confessions a matching shape so that the marriage is founded on a shared diagnosis. He blames an upbringing and does not use it as an excuse, which is the difference between him and Wickham.

quotations.text: I am the happiest creature in the world. Perhaps other people have said so before, but not one with such justice. I am happier even than Jane; she only smiles, I laugh.
quotations.speaker: Elizabeth Bennet
quotations.context: Writing to Mrs Gardiner, who had been at Pemberley with her.
quotations.analysis: She claims a superlative and then immediately audits it, which is exactly how she has argued all book. The comparison with Jane is not vanity but accuracy about temperament: the sister who thinks well of everyone smiles, and the one who has had to revise her judgements laughs.

atAGlance.label: First published
atAGlance.note: Thomas Egerton, London, in three volumes, credited to the author of Sense and Sensibility.

atAGlance.label: Earlier title
atAGlance.note: The 1796–97 draft; the discarded title names the novel’s central test more plainly than the published one.

atAGlance.label: Copyright
atAGlance.note: Austen sold the copyright to Egerton for £110 rather than publishing on commission, and so earned nothing from later editions.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.note: The first proposal falls almost exactly at the centre of the book, and everything after it is re-reading.

criticalViews.position: A comedy of moral education
criticalViews.summary: The oldest reading takes the novel at the word of its discarded title: two people form wrong first impressions, gather better evidence, and are rewarded with each other. On this account the book’s subject is the discipline of judgement.
criticalViews.counter: It has to explain away how much of the reward is material, and why the plot is settled by Darcy’s chequebook rather than by anybody’s improved understanding.

criticalViews.position: An economic novel about women without money
criticalViews.summary: Criticism attentive to the entail reads the courtships as a survey of what is available to genteel women with no income: Charlotte’s bargain, Lydia’s disaster and Elizabeth’s luck are three outcomes of one predicament.
criticalViews.counter: Pressed hard it can make Elizabeth’s refusals look like bad economics rather than integrity, and it struggles with how funny the book is.

criticalViews.position: A study in narrative point of view
criticalViews.summary: Formalist and stylistic criticism has focused on Austen’s free indirect style, arguing that the novel’s real achievement is the reader’s induced error: we misjudge Darcy because we are reading through Elizabeth without being told so.
criticalViews.counter: The technique is not applied evenly — several chapters step away from Elizabeth entirely — so the effect may owe as much to withheld information as to style.

essayQuestions.question: How does Austen present the relationship between marriage and money?
essayQuestions.focus: Entail, income and the price of refusal
plan: Start with the entail as a legal fact, not a theme: Longbourn passes to Collins, and five daughters must therefore marry or be dependent.
Read the first sentence as a joke whose real subject is the mothers, then set Charlotte’s speech in Chapter 22 beside it as the same proposition without irony.
Compare the three completed bargains — Charlotte’s comfort, Lydia’s rescue, Elizabeth’s Pemberley — and note what each one cost and who paid.
Test the romantic reading against Chapter 47: Lydia’s ruin is averted by money, and the novel says so plainly.
Conclude on whether the ending endorses the system it has mocked, or simply gives one heroine an exemption from it.

essayQuestions.question: ‘The novel is about learning to read people.’ Discuss.
essayQuestions.focus: Judgement, evidence and revision
plan: Establish the pattern of instant verdicts: the assembly in Chapter 3, Wickham’s history in Chapter 16, Mrs Bennet on Bingley’s income.
Show how Austen implicates the reader through free indirect style, so that Elizabeth’s misreadings arrive as narrative fact.
Make Chapter 35 the hinge: the evidence is written, it can be re-read, and nothing happens except a change of mind.
Use Pemberley in Chapter 43 to argue that the novel trusts long testimony and property over conversation and charm.
Weigh the counter-case: Jane reads everybody generously and is wrong about nobody’s character, only about their conduct.

essayQuestions.question: Examine Austen’s presentation of Mr Bennet.
essayQuestions.focus: Wit, detachment and paternal failure
plan: Open with the twenty-year joke about his wife’s nerves: the marriage as a settled comic arrangement.
Show the wit turned on his own children in Chapter 18, and on Elizabeth’s proposal crisis in Chapter 20, where it happens to help.
Trace the cost: Lydia goes to Brighton because refusing would have been tiresome, and the library is his habitual answer to every demand.
Read his line about making sport for our neighbours in Chapter 57 against the crisis that has just been paid for by Darcy.
Decide whether the novel forgives him, and what his brief self-reproach after Lydia’s flight is worth.

essayQuestions.question: How far does Pride and Prejudice challenge the class system it describes?
essayQuestions.focus: Rank, connection and the Gardiners
plan: Separate money from rank: the Bennets are gentry without capital, the Gardiners have capital without rank, and Darcy has both.
Track the objection as it hardens: Caroline Bingley’s sneers, Darcy’s first proposal, Lady Catherine’s shades of Pemberley.
Use the Gardiners as the novel’s counter-argument — the tradesman’s family are the most sensible adults in the book and the ones Darcy treats best.
Note the limits: no character crosses a class line without a fortune arriving to make it respectable, and Wickham’s rise is punished.
Conclude on the ending’s arithmetic, where affection is settled alongside incomes in the same sentences.

discussionQuestions: Charlotte Lucas asks only for a comfortable home. Does the novel think she is wrong?
Elizabeth changes her mind about Darcy after seeing his house. Is that a shallow reason or a sound one?
Mr Bennet is the funniest character in the book and arguably the most culpable. Can both be true at once?
Lydia’s elopement is settled with money and never with an apology. What does the novel want us to feel about that?
The book was first called First Impressions. Which title describes it better, and what does the change cost?

timeline.label: Jane Austen born at Steventon
timeline.detail: The seventh child of a Hampshire rector, in a household that read aloud and wrote for each other.

timeline.label: First Impressions drafted
timeline.detail: Written in 1796–97, in Austen’s early twenties. No manuscript of this version survives.

timeline.label: The manuscript is offered to Thomas Cadell
timeline.detail: Austen’s father wrote to the London publisher, who declined without asking to see it. The novel waited more than a decade.

timeline.label: Sense and Sensibility published
timeline.detail: Austen’s first published novel, issued anonymously, made a second Austen title commercially plausible.

timeline.label: Pride and Prejudice published
timeline.detail: Thomas Egerton issued it in three volumes on 28 January, credited to the author of Sense and Sensibility. A second edition followed the same year.

timeline.label: Mansfield Park published
timeline.detail: The first of Austen’s novels written entirely after she had become a published author.

timeline.label: Emma published
timeline.detail: Issued by John Murray with an 1816 date on the title page.

timeline.label: Austen dies at Winchester
timeline.detail: She was forty-one. Her name had still not appeared on a title page.

timeline.label: Northanger Abbey and Persuasion published together
timeline.detail: Issued in the last days of 1817 with 1818 on the title page, and carrying the biographical notice by her brother Henry that named her at last.

timeline.label: Richard Bentley reprints the novels
timeline.detail: Austen enters the cheap standard-novel market, and stays in print from this point on.

timeline.label: The Peacock edition
timeline.detail: George Allen publishes Hugh Thomson’s illustrated edition, whose gilt peacock binding became the novel’s most recognisable object.

timeline.label: MGM’s Pride and Prejudice
timeline.detail: Directed by Robert Z. Leonard, with Greer Garson and Laurence Olivier, and costumed with cheerful disregard for the Regency.

timeline.label: BBC serial adapted by Andrew Davies
timeline.detail: Jennifer Ehle and Colin Firth in six episodes; the version against which most later screen Darcys are measured.

timeline.label: Joe Wright’s film
timeline.detail: Keira Knightley and Matthew Macfadyen, in a version that puts mud, livestock and noise back into Longbourn.

places.name: Hertfordshire
places.note: Longbourn, Meryton and Netherfield: a neighbourhood of twenty-four families, small enough that one new tenant changes everything.

places.name: Gracechurch Street, London
places.note: The Gardiners’ house, within sight of their own warehouses — the address that Caroline Bingley finds fatal and the novel finds respectable.

places.name: Kent
places.note: Hunsford parsonage and Rosings Park, where Charlotte’s bargain and Darcy’s first proposal are both inspected at close range.

places.name: Derbyshire
places.note: Pemberley and the village of Lambton, reached on a tour that Elizabeth undertakes only because the Lakes proved too far.

places.name: Brighton
places.note: The militia’s summer quarters, and the town Lydia is allowed to visit because refusing would have caused a scene.

places.name: Newcastle upon Tyne
places.note: Where Wickham’s new regiment is quartered after the marriage: far north, and paid for by Darcy.

related.why: Austen’s first published novel, and the same marriage market seen from the side of women who have already lost their income.
Another governess-adjacent heroine who refuses a proposal on principle, written thirty years later and with the comedy removed.
A hero who has to discover that his own judgement was bought for him, and that the money came from a source he despised.
The marriage market as farce, with the interrogation about income and connections played at full volume.
The opposite settlement of the same questions about property, rank and who may marry whom.

videos.note: A lecture on the novel's social world, its irony and the economics of marriage that drive the plot.

videos.title: Liberals, Conservatives, and Pride and Prejudice, Part 2: Crash Course Literature 412
videos.note: The second part considers the politics of the novel and whether Austen is defending or questioning the society she describes.

videos.note: A short animated introduction to Austen's satire and narrative voice across her novels, with Pride and Prejudice as a principal example.

books.title: The Red Badge of Courage
books.author: Stephen Crane
books.setting: An unnamed Civil War battlefield in Virginia, over roughly two days
