books.lengthNote: Twenty-four short chapters covering about forty-eight hours
books.openingLine: The cold passed reluctantly from the earth, and the retiring fogs revealed an army stretched out on the hills, resting.
books.summary: A farm boy enlists expecting Greek battles and finds a muddy camp full of rumour. When the fighting comes he holds, then runs, then wanders among the wounded until another fleeing soldier cracks his skull with a rifle butt — an injury his regiment reads as evidence of courage. Crane, who was born six years after the war ended and had never seen a battle, wrote the whole thing from inside one frightened private's head and never names the battle, the cause or, for most of the book, the private.

sourceText.label: Standard Ebooks text of The Red Badge of Courage
sourceText.note: This is the 1895 Appleton book text, which is shorter than Crane's surviving manuscript. Editions based on the manuscript restore a good deal of Henry's self-justifying reasoning and change the balance of the ending.

structure.label: Chapters I–III
structure.title: Rumour, and a private question
structure.summary: The regiment has been camped for months and lives on contradictory reports of a coming move. Henry Fleming, who enlisted against his mother's advice and expecting something Homeric, discovers that the only question that interests him is whether he will run, and that he cannot answer it by reasoning or by watching other men.

scenes.title: The tall soldier's rumour
scenes.summary: A washed shirt brings news of a march; Henry remembers enlisting, and his mother peeling potatoes instead of making a speech.

scenes.title: Comparisons
scenes.summary: He tries to find another man as frightened as he is, and concludes that he is alone in it.

scenes.title: The march
scenes.summary: Knapsacks are thrown away along the road, and Henry realises the regiment cannot be left.

structure.label: Chapters IV–VI
structure.title: He holds, and then he runs
structure.summary: The first assault comes and Henry fires with everybody else, absorbed into the line and briefly free of himself. When a second wave arrives and men on either side begin to go, he goes too — fast, before any argument has taken place in him — and looks back to find that the regiment held.

scenes.title: The line holds
scenes.summary: Henry loses his separate self in the regiment and discovers that courage can be produced by a crowd.

scenes.title: The second charge
scenes.summary: He runs like an insane sprinter, and learns from an officer's shouting that the position was not lost.

structure.label: Chapters VII–XII
structure.title: The forest, the wounded column, the blow
structure.summary: Alone in the woods, Henry builds a case for his own wisdom out of a squirrel and a quiet glade, and then walks into a chapel of pine boughs containing a corpse. He joins a column of wounded men, watches Jim Conklin die, abandons the tattered soldier, and is finally struck on the head by a panicking man from another regiment.

scenes.title: Nature's evidence
scenes.summary: A squirrel runs from a thrown pine cone, which Henry takes as a law; the dead man in the chapel is the reply.

scenes.title: Jim Conklin
scenes.summary: The procession of the wounded, the tattered man's questions, and the tall soldier's death in a field.

scenes.title: The wound
scenes.summary: Henry deserts the tattered soldier, hopes privately for a defeat that would vindicate him, and is clubbed with a rifle in the retreat.

structure.label: Chapters XIII–XVIII
structure.title: Read as a hero
structure.summary: A cheerful stranger walks him back to his own fires, where the regiment assumes his head wound is a graze from a bullet and Wilson nurses him. Henry keeps the account, discovers that the loud soldier has quietly become a serious man, and recovers his swagger in time to overhear a general describe the regiment as mule drivers.

scenes.title: The bandage
scenes.summary: Wilson binds his head and gives up his blanket; nobody asks how the wound was made.

scenes.title: The packet of letters
scenes.summary: Henry holds Wilson's envelope of last words over him, and then fights like a wild man while the regiment watches.

scenes.title: Mule drivers
scenes.summary: Two officers discuss the regiment as an expendable unit within earshot of two of its men.

structure.label: Chapters XIX–XXIV
structure.title: The flag, and the story he settles on
structure.summary: Henry takes the colours from a dying sergeant and carries them through two charges, is called a war devil by men who watched him, and hears the same officer who insulted the regiment praise him by name. In the last chapter he assembles all of it, including the tattered soldier, into an account of himself he can live with.

scenes.title: The colours
scenes.summary: He seizes the flag, the charge falls short, and the regiment is jeered and then defended.

scenes.title: The fence
scenes.summary: A stand under fire, a captured flag, and four prisoners.

scenes.title: The account
scenes.summary: Marching away in the rain, Henry reviews his deeds, flinches at the memory of the tattered man, and decides he is a man.

characters.name: Henry Fleming
characters.role: A private in the 304th New York, called 'the youth' for most of the book
characters.summary: He enlisted for a war he had read about and finds one made of smoke, rumour and other men's faces. Everything that happens to him happens twice: once as an event and again, shortly afterwards, as a version of the event in which he comes off better, and Crane keeps both on the page.
characters.clue: He ran from his first real fight, was knocked senseless by a man from his own side, and let his regiment believe a bullet had done it.
traits: eventually brave, on terms he chooses

relationships.label: friend, rival and keeper of a secret

characters.name: Jim Conklin
characters.role: The tall soldier
characters.summary: He starts the novel by carrying a rumour through the camp on the strength of a washed shirt, and he ends it in a field, refusing help and looking for a place to fall down. Crane gives him the one death in the book described in full, and no consoling language whatever.
characters.clue: He brought the camp its first news of the march, and later walked away from the column to die standing, shaking off every hand that reached for him.

characters.name: Wilson
characters.role: The loud soldier
characters.summary: He begins by announcing his own courage and handing Henry a packet of letters for his family, and comes back from the first day quiet, useful and no longer interested in being watched. He is the novel's evidence that a man can change without narrating the change to himself.
characters.clue: He gave away a packet of last letters before the first battle, survived, and had to ask for it back from a man who had been enjoying the power of holding it.

relationships.label: nurses, and is held to ransom by

characters.name: The tattered soldier
characters.role: A wounded man in the column
characters.summary: He is friendly, badly hurt, losing his grip, and he keeps asking Henry the one question Henry cannot answer: where are you hit. Henry leaves him wandering in a field, and the memory is the only thing in the last chapter that the new self-account cannot absorb.
characters.clue: Shot twice and admiring everyone, he asked a stranger a brotherly question about his wound and was walked away from and left in a field.

characters.name: Henry's mother
characters.role: A farm widow in New York State
characters.summary: She refuses to give her son the send-off he has imagined, keeps peeling potatoes while he announces his enlistment, and tells him to watch out and to remember that he is nothing special in an army of thousands. Her advice is the most accurate assessment of his situation in the novel.
characters.clue: She would not make a speech about her son's country; she gave him socks, blackberry jam and the information that he was one man among many.

characters.name: Lieutenant Hasbrouck
characters.role: The regiment's officer
characters.summary: He swears at his men, drags them forward by the collar, and is the first person to see Henry fight. He is also the one who passes Henry's name upward, which is how a private's private crisis becomes a matter of official record.
characters.clue: He cursed his company along like a fishwife and then told a colonel the names of the two men who carried the colours.

characters.name: The 304th New York
characters.role: Henry's regiment, treated throughout as a single creature
characters.summary: Crane describes it as a box, a machine, a worm and a dragon, and gives it moods of its own that run ahead of any individual's decision. It is the thing that makes Henry brave in Chapter V and the thing he cannot escape in Chapter III, and a general disposes of it in a sentence as the unit he can best spare.
characters.clue: It is called a box, a machine and a worm, it can be brave before any man in it has decided to be, and a general sacrifices it because it fights like a lot of mule drivers.

themes.name: What courage is evidence of
themes.summary: Henry wants a fact about himself that can be established once and then relied on, and the novel refuses to supply one. Courage in these chapters is produced by crowds, by rage at an insult, by fear of being seen, and it never becomes a property a man can own between engagements.
themes.development: The unanswerable question of Chapters I–II, the borrowed courage of the first stand, the flight, and the final charges made in a temper about the words 'mule drivers'.

themes.name: The story he tells about himself
themes.summary: Every action Henry takes is followed by a version of it in which he acted rightly, and Crane keeps the narration close enough to make the versions persuasive. The book's real subject is not whether he is brave but how quickly a mind can manufacture the account it needs.
themes.development: The squirrel as proof in Chapter VII, the private hope for a defeat in Chapter XI, the wound accepted as a battle scar, and the settled narrative of Chapter XXIV with the tattered man still in it.

themes.name: Manhood and gender
themes.summary: Henry's fear is not of dying but of being seen to be the kind of man who runs, and the last line of the book awards him the title he has been chasing. The one woman in the novel declines to supply the heroic language he wants, and his mother's flat advice keeps returning to correct the story.
themes.development: The refused send-off in Chapter I, the shame of the unwounded man among the wounded in Chapter IX, the epithet 'war devil' in Chapter XVII, and the three words that close Chapter XXIV.

themes.name: The regiment as a body
themes.summary: Individual nerve counts for less in this novel than the state of the thing a man is standing in. The regiment is described in the vocabulary of animals and machinery, it acquires moods before its members do, and a general can decide to spend it in one line of dialogue overheard by two of its privates.
themes.development: The moving box of Chapter III, the welded common personality of Chapter V, the mule-driver conversation of Chapter XVIII, and the collective rage that carries the last charges.

themes.name: Nature's indifference
themes.summary: Henry keeps asking the landscape for a verdict and it keeps declining to give one. He reads a fleeing squirrel as a law of self-preservation and walks straight into a chapel of trees with a rotting corpse in it, and the sun goes on standing in the sky like a pasted wafer over the death of his friend.
themes.development: The religion of peace in Chapter VII, the dead man among the pines, the red sun over Jim Conklin's body, and the sunlight in the last paragraph that refuses to mean anything in particular.

themes.name: War without an overview
themes.summary: No battle is named, no campaign explained, no cause argued. What the private knows is smoke, noise, shouted contradictions and the men within a few yards of him, and the novel's method is to refuse the reader any information Henry does not have.
themes.development: Rumour in Chapter I, the local and partial fighting of Chapters IV–VI, the wandering of Chapters VII–XII, and the absence at the end of any statement about who won.

techniques.name: Free indirect style
techniques.definition: Third-person narration that takes on the vocabulary and bias of the character it follows.
techniques.bookDefinition: Third-person narration that takes on the vocabulary and bias of the character it follows.
techniques.inThisBook: The prose adopts Henry's reasoning without endorsing it, so that his case for running is made in his own inflated terms while the sentences quietly leave room for the reader to decline it.

techniques.name: Colour as feeling
techniques.definition: Colour used to register emotional and physical states rather than to describe appearance.
techniques.bookDefinition: Colour used to register emotional and physical states rather than to describe appearance.
techniques.inThisBook: Red eyes across the river, the red sickness of battle, the red badge itself, a blue demonstration, a corpse's uniform faded to green: colour arrives before information does, which is how the book keeps the reader at the private's eye level.

techniques.name: Animal imagery
techniques.definition: Men and formations described as creatures.
techniques.bookDefinition: Men and formations described as creatures.
techniques.inThisBook: Dragons advance, the army is a worm, war is a red animal and a blood-swollen god, and men develop teeth and claws when cornered — the effect is to remove heroism from the vocabulary altogether.

techniques.name: Irony
techniques.definition: Saying one thing in a form that invites the opposite judgement.
techniques.bookDefinition: Saying one thing in a form that invites the opposite judgement.
techniques.inThisBook: The wound that certifies Henry's courage is given to him by a terrified man on his own side, and the regiment's finest hour is arranged by a general who chose it as the unit he could best spare.

techniques.name: Naming by epithet
techniques.definition: Characters identified by a single visible attribute instead of a name.
techniques.bookDefinition: Characters identified by a single visible attribute instead of a name.
techniques.inThisBook: The youth, the tall soldier, the loud soldier, the tattered man: the labels are how an army sees its own people, and Crane withholds Henry's name for most of the book so that the reader inherits that view.

techniques.name: Simile
techniques.definition: An explicit comparison, usually brief, doing the work of a longer description.
techniques.bookDefinition: An explicit comparison, usually brief, doing the work of a longer description.
techniques.inThisBook: The most famous sentence in the book is a five-word comparison — the sun pasted in the sky like a wafer — placed alone as a paragraph immediately after a death, and refusing to say anything more.

quotations.text: The cold passed reluctantly from the earth, and the retiring fogs revealed an army stretched out on the hills, resting.
quotations.context: The first sentence of the novel.
quotations.analysis: The two active verbs belong to the weather, and the army is merely revealed by it, lying still. Before a single man has spoken, the grammar has established the arrangement the book will keep: the natural world does things, and the soldiers are things it does them to.

quotations.text: He had grown to regard himself merely as a part of a vast blue demonstration.
quotations.context: After months of drill and no fighting.
quotations.analysis: A war is reduced to a colour and a gesture, as though the Union army were a piece of political theatre he has been hired to stand in. 'Merely' is Henry's word, not Crane's, and it registers the disappointment of a boy who enlisted for something with names in it.

quotations.text: He was a mental outcast.
quotations.context: After failing to find any other man visibly wrestling with the same fear.
quotations.analysis: Four words on their own, and the isolation is entirely self-generated: he has been reading other men's faces and finding nothing, which proves only that they are doing the same thing he is. The novel's first joke is that everyone in the regiment believes himself the only coward in it.

quotations.text: And there were iron laws of tradition and law on four sides. He was in a moving box.
quotations.context: On realising that he cannot simply leave the regiment on the march.
quotations.analysis: The image turns a body of comrades into a container with walls, and the repetition of 'law' inside one clause makes the enclosure sound legal rather than social. It also sets up the chapters ahead: when he does escape the box, he finds that there is nowhere outside it to be.

quotations.text: He suddenly lost concern for himself, and forgot to look at a menacing fate. He became not a man but a member.
quotations.context: During the first assault, firing with the rest of the line.
quotations.analysis: Courage arrives here as a loss rather than an achievement — of self-consciousness, and then of separate selfhood. The pun on 'member' is doing real work: he is briefly a limb of something larger, which is exactly the condition he cannot reproduce when he is alone in Chapter VI.

quotations.text: He felt that he was a fine fellow. He saw himself even with those ideals which he had considered as far beyond him.
quotations.context: Immediately after surviving the first charge, and minutes before the second.
quotations.analysis: The verbs are all of perception — felt, saw — because nothing has been established except a sensation. Crane places this self-congratulation directly before the flight so that the reader watches an identity get assembled and demolished inside a single short chapter.

quotations.text: To the youth it was an onslaught of redoubtable dragons.
quotations.context: As the second attack comes on and the men around him begin to break.
quotations.analysis: The phrase 'to the youth' is the hinge: Crane marks the image as Henry's own, so the dragons are a boy's reading matter arriving on a battlefield. He will use the same creatures later to congratulate himself on having met them, which is how the novel measures what he has learned.

quotations.text: He had fled, he told himself, because annihilation approached.
quotations.context: Alone in the woods, constructing a defence of his flight.
quotations.analysis: 'He told himself' is the whole technique in three words: the sentence reports a proposition without adopting it. The Latinate 'annihilation' is several registers above anything Henry says out loud, which marks the reasoning as a performance for an audience of one.

quotations.text: There was the law, he said. Nature had given him a sign.
quotations.context: After throwing a pine cone at a squirrel, which runs away.
quotations.analysis: He has conducted an experiment designed to produce the result he wanted and calls the result a law. Crane lets the reasoning stand for a page and then walks him into a dead man's face, which is nature's other sign and is not addressed to him at all.

quotations.text: It was the religion of peace. It would die if its timid eyes were compelled to see blood. He conceived Nature to be a woman with a deep aversion to tragedy.
quotations.context: Walking deeper into the woods, away from the sound of the guns.
quotations.analysis: 'He conceived' marks the whole proposition as Henry's invention, and the gendering of Nature as a squeamish woman is the sentimental nineteenth-century picture the book exists to dismantle. Three sentences later he pushes aside the green boughs and finds the corpse.

quotations.text: The corpse was dressed in a uniform that had once been blue, but was now faded to a melancholy shade of green.
quotations.context: In the clearing of pine boughs that Henry has just described as a chapel.
quotations.analysis: A Union uniform has decayed into the colour of the forest, so the man has been absorbed by the landscape rather than commemorated by it. Crane spends the rest of the paragraph on ants moving across the face: the detail is clinical, and the only emotion in the sentence has been transferred onto a colour.

quotations.text: Where yeh hit, ol’ boy?
quotations.speaker: The tattered soldier
quotations.context: In the column of wounded men, asked in what Crane calls a brotherly tone.
quotations.analysis: It is the friendliest sentence in the novel and the one Henry cannot bear, because among these men the wound is the credential and he has none. The question is asked twice more in the next chapters, and it is what finally drives him to leave a badly hurt man alone in a field.

quotations.text: He wished that he, too, had a wound, a red badge of courage.
quotations.context: Walking among men whose injuries he has begun to envy.
quotations.analysis: The title phrase appears once, in Henry's mind, as a wish — which makes the whole book the story of a metaphor he goes looking for and then receives by accident. A badge is worn to be read by others, so what he wants is not courage but the sign of it.

quotations.text: The red sun was pasted in the sky like a wafer.
quotations.context: The final sentence of the chapter, immediately after Jim Conklin's death.
quotations.analysis: The comparison is flat, domestic and slightly absurd, and it stands alone as a paragraph where a novel of 1895 would normally place a reflection. Whether the wafer is a communion host or a seal on an envelope has been argued for a century; either way the sky is doing nothing, and the refusal to say more is the point.

quotations.text: He felt that he was regarding a procession of chosen beings.
quotations.context: Watching a column of troops move up towards the fighting.
quotations.analysis: Men marching into danger become a religious procession because he is looking at them from outside, and the novel is careful that this is a matter of position rather than of merit. A few pages later he privately hopes the army will be beaten, so that his flight will look like foresight.

quotations.text: He adroitly and fiercely swung his rifle. It crushed upon the youth’s head. The man ran on.
quotations.context: In a retreating crowd, after Henry grabs at a man to ask what has happened.
quotations.analysis: Three short sentences, no adjective of feeling, and the assailant is gone before the second one ends. This is the wound the regiment will read as evidence of courage, delivered by a panicking Union soldier to a man who has run away — the novel's central irony arrives in nineteen words and is never commented on.

quotations.text: He had been out among the dragons, he said, and he assured himself that they were not so hideous as he had imagined them.
quotations.context: The morning after his return to the regiment, with his head bandaged.
quotations.analysis: Two verbs of self-address in one sentence — he said, he assured himself — and the dragons are the same ones he ran from in Chapter VI. The revision is complete: an experience he did not have is now a qualification, and the reader is shown the machinery rather than told about it.

quotations.text: It was not well to drive men into final corners; at those moments they could all develop teeth and claws.
quotations.context: Henry's state of mind before the fighting in which the regiment is told to hold.
quotations.analysis: The proposition is offered as general wisdom and is in fact a threat made by a frightened man to nobody in particular. Crane has been describing armies as animals since Chapter II, and here the imagery finally arrives inside Henry's own account of himself.

quotations.text: they now looked upon him as a war devil.
quotations.context: After Henry keeps firing at an enemy that has already withdrawn.
quotations.analysis: The reputation is made by men watching him rather than by anything he decided, and the thing they watched was him failing to notice that the fighting had stopped. Courage in this novel is consistently a reading made by other people of behaviour that had some quite different cause.

quotations.text: They fight like a lot ’a mule drivers. I can spare them best of any.
quotations.speaker: An officer
quotations.context: Two officers on horseback, discussing which regiment to send in, within hearing of Henry and Wilson.
quotations.analysis: The regiment's finest hour is arranged in a sentence about expendability, and the two men who overhear it go back and say nothing. Everything Henry does in the last six chapters is fuelled by an insult, which means the novel's climax of courage has an entirely petty engine.

quotations.text: It was a woman, red and white, hating and loving, that called him with the voice of his hopes.
quotations.context: As Henry takes the regimental colours from a dying sergeant.
quotations.analysis: The flag is given the only romantic attachment in the novel, and it is granted invulnerability precisely because Henry needs something in the field that cannot be killed. Note that the colours are described by their colours: the book's whole palette turns up in one object a man can carry.

quotations.text: He found that he could look back upon the brass and bombast of his earlier gospels and see them truly.
quotations.context: Marching away from the field in the rain, reviewing everything that has happened.
quotations.analysis: He congratulates himself on having seen through his own self-congratulation, which is the same operation one level up. The novel's difficulty is concentrated here: nothing in the sentence is false, and nothing in it is evidence, since the man assessing the account is the man who wrote it.

quotations.text: He had been to touch the great death, and found that, after all, it was but the great death. He was a man.
quotations.context: The settled conclusion of his review of himself.
quotations.analysis: The repetition of 'the great death' drains the phrase between its first appearance and its second, which is either maturity or the deflation of a boy's word. Then four monosyllables award him the title he wanted in Chapter I, and the book declines to say whether the award is deserved.

quotations.text: Over the river a golden ray of sun came through the hosts of leaden rain clouds.
quotations.context: The last sentence of the novel.
quotations.analysis: It is the shape of a consoling ending without the content of one: a ray of sun, a river, and no statement about what any of it means. 'Hosts' is the only word carrying any military weight, and it belongs to the clouds — the weather keeps the vocabulary of armies, and the armies have marched off the page.

atAGlance.label: Serial
atAGlance.note: A shortened version went out through newspaper syndication before any publisher would take the book.

atAGlance.label: First book edition
atAGlance.note: D. Appleton and Company, New York. Crane was twenty-three and instantly famous.

atAGlance.label: The battle
atAGlance.note: The circumstances have long been associated with Chancellorsville in May 1863, but no place, date or commander is given in the text.

atAGlance.label: Names
atAGlance.value: The youth, the tall soldier, the loud soldier
atAGlance.note: Crane withholds most personal names for chapters at a time, and the epithets are how the army sees its own men.

criticalViews.position: The novel as impressionism
criticalViews.summary: The oldest account of Crane's method treats the book as painting rather than reporting: colour before information, fragments of sensation, a battlefield assembled from what one pair of eyes can register in smoke.
criticalViews.counter: Read only as technique, the book's moral argument disappears — and the argument about self-deception is conducted in sentences, not in colours.

criticalViews.position: A naturalist novel
criticalViews.summary: On this reading Henry is a specimen: an organism acted on by crowd, terrain and instinct, in a universe with nothing to say about him, and courage is simply what the machinery produces under certain loads.
criticalViews.counter: The book keeps giving Henry choices he is capable of assessing — the tattered soldier is the clearest — and it is hard to convict a man of nothing while the novel is so plainly convicting him.

criticalViews.position: Growth, or a better story
criticalViews.summary: The last chapter can be read as genuine maturity or as the final and most sophisticated act of self-justification in the book; a century of criticism has divided on the question, and the text supports both readings without settling either.
criticalViews.counter: The strongest evidence against simple growth is the tattered man, whose memory Henry has to push away in the same paragraphs where he declares himself free of shame.

criticalViews.position: Which Red Badge
criticalViews.summary: The 1895 Appleton book is shorter than Crane's manuscript, and editions built from the manuscript restore passages of Henry's reasoning and alter the weight of the ending. The question of which text to read is therefore also a question about how ironic the book is.
criticalViews.counter: The Appleton text is the one that was read for a century and made the novel's reputation, which is an argument for treating it as the book rather than as a mutilation of one.

essayQuestions.question: How does Crane use point of view to make the reader distrust Henry Fleming?
essayQuestions.focus: Free indirect style and irony
plan: Establish the technique: third-person narration that borrows Henry's diction, with markers such as 'he told himself' and 'he conceived'.
Work through the squirrel episode in Chapter VII, where an experiment is designed to produce its own conclusion.
Contrast the inflated vocabulary of Henry's self-defence with the flat reporting of the rifle blow in Chapter XII.
Consider how the reader is denied any information Henry lacks, and what that costs and gains.
Apply the whole method to Chapter XXIV, and decide whether the final assessment can be trusted.

essayQuestions.question: 'The wound is the novel's central irony.' Discuss.
essayQuestions.focus: Evidence, signs and reputation
plan: Set out what Henry wants in Chapter IX: not courage but a visible mark that certifies it.
Describe how the wound is actually received, and from whom.
Trace the regiment's misreading and Wilson's care in Chapters XIII–XIV.
Weigh the later fighting: does a false credential make the subsequent bravery false?
Conclude on what the book suggests about all reputations, including the ones it calls deserved.

essayQuestions.question: What part does nature play in the novel?
essayQuestions.focus: Landscape, indifference and the refusal of meaning
plan: Begin with the opening sentence, where the weather acts and the army is acted on.
Set the squirrel and the 'religion of peace' against the corpse in the pine chapel.
Analyse the wafer simile as a refusal of the consolation the moment calls for.
Note where nature is described as female or sympathetic, and whose language that is.
Close on the last sentence, and whether its golden ray means anything at all.

essayQuestions.question: How far is courage in this novel a property of individuals?
essayQuestions.focus: The regiment, the crowd and the insult
plan: Use Chapter III's moving box and Chapter V's common personality to show courage arriving collectively.
Show the flight in Chapter VI beginning with other men's movement rather than with a decision.
Examine the mule-driver conversation as the actual cause of the final charges.
Consider Wilson, who changes quietly and never narrates it, as a control on Henry.
Decide what is left of individual courage once the crowd, the insult and the accident are subtracted.

discussionQuestions: Crane never names the battle, the cause or the year. What does the novel gain by withholding all of it?
Henry is 'the youth' for most of the book. What changes when a character is described rather than named?
The tattered soldier is the only thing the last chapter cannot absorb. Why does Crane leave him there?
Wilson changes without ever explaining himself to anyone. Is he the novel's answer to Henry, or simply a quieter version of him?
Crane had never seen a battle when he wrote this. Does that matter to what the book is doing?

timeline.label: The American Civil War begins
timeline.detail: The war Crane's novel is set in, and which he was born too late to see.

timeline.label: The Battle of Chancellorsville
timeline.detail: Fought in Virginia in early May: confused fighting in woodland, and a Union defeat. Long associated with the novel, though Crane never names it.

timeline.label: The war ends
timeline.detail: Veterans' reminiscences, many of them published in magazines Crane read, became a large part of American periodical writing.

timeline.label: Stephen Crane born in Newark, New Jersey
timeline.detail: The fourteenth child of a Methodist minister, and six years too late for the war he made his name on.

timeline.label: Maggie: A Girl of the Streets
timeline.detail: Crane's first novel, printed at his own expense and largely unsold.

timeline.label: A shortened version syndicated in newspapers
timeline.detail: The story reached its first readers cut down for the press, before any publisher would take the full book.

timeline.label: Published by D. Appleton and Company
timeline.detail: The book made Crane famous in his early twenties, in Britain as well as in America.

timeline.label: Shipwrecked off the Florida coast
timeline.detail: The sinking of the Commodore, on a gun-running voyage to Cuba, produced 'The Open Boat'.

timeline.label: War correspondent in Cuba
timeline.detail: Reporting the Spanish-American War finally gave him the experience readers had assumed lay behind the novel.

timeline.label: Crane dies at Badenweiler
timeline.detail: Of tuberculosis, in a German sanatorium, aged twenty-eight.

timeline.label: John Huston's film
timeline.detail: With Audie Murphy, one of the most decorated American soldiers of the Second World War, as Henry; the studio cut it heavily before release.

places.name: Chancellorsville, Virginia
places.note: The battle of May 1863 most often matched to the novel's circumstances, though the text names nothing.

places.name: Fredericksburg, Virginia
places.note: The town on the Rappahannock beside which the armies of the novel's sort of campaign were camped through the winter.

places.name: Newark, New Jersey
places.note: Crane's birthplace, 1871.

places.name: New York
places.note: Where D. Appleton and Company published the book in 1895, and where Crane had been living as a struggling reporter.

places.name: Badenweiler, Germany
places.note: The spa town where Crane died of tuberculosis in 1900, five years after the novel appeared.

related.why: The other great American naturalist short novel: instinct, environment and a creature reshaped by pressure rather than by decision.
A comparable New England compression — few characters, a short span, and a landscape that refuses to comfort anybody.
American prose on a vastly larger scale, and the earlier version of the question about how much a man can know of what he is inside.
The novel that put the argument behind this war in front of a mass readership, forty years before Crane's private stopped caring why he was fighting.
Another American book built entirely out of one young narrator's limited view, published a decade earlier.

books.title: Richard II
books.author: William Shakespeare
books.setting: England and Wales, 1398 to 1400, from the lists at Coventry to a cell at Pomfret
books.lengthNote: Around 2,800 lines, and not one of them in prose
books.openingLine: Old John of Gaunt, time-honour'd Lancaster, Hast thou, according to thy oath and band, Brought hither Henry Hereford thy bold son?
books.summary: A king who believes the crown was fixed on him by God seizes his cousin's inheritance to pay for a war in Ireland, and finds that the cousin comes home for the land and stays for the throne. Bolingbroke wins without a battle; Richard loses without a defeat. The play is written entirely in verse, so the man who cannot hold a kingdom can still out-speak everyone in it, and the deposition turns into an argument about what words a king is made of.

sourceText.label: Globe/Moby text of Richard II
sourceText.note: Line numbers follow the traditional Globe numbering. Modern editions vary by a line or two, and quarto and Folio witnesses differ over the deposition passage in 4.1.

structure.label: Act I
structure.title: A quarrel the king will not let anyone finish
structure.summary: Bolingbroke accuses Mowbray of treason and of Gloucester's murder, a charge that leads back towards Richard himself. Richard first orders trial by combat and then stops it mid-ceremony, banishing both men. The interruption saves him from a verdict and costs him the only two men who could have given one.

scenes.title: The accusation
scenes.summary: Bolingbroke and Mowbray throw down their gages before the king, who fails to reconcile them.

scenes.title: Gloucester's widow
scenes.summary: The Duchess asks Gaunt for revenge; he answers that the quarrel is God's, because the king ordered the murder.

scenes.title: The lists at Coventry
scenes.summary: Richard halts the combat at the trumpet and banishes Mowbray for life and Bolingbroke for ten years, then six.

scenes.title: Farming the realm
scenes.summary: Alone with his favourites, Richard mocks Bolingbroke's popularity and decides to lease out England to fund the Irish wars.

structure.label: Act II
structure.title: An inheritance seized, and an army landed
structure.summary: Gaunt dies telling Richard that a king who rents out his country is a landlord. Richard confiscates the Lancastrian estate on the spot, which converts a private grievance into a constitutional one: he has broken the law of inheritance that his own title rests on. Before he reaches Ireland, Bolingbroke has landed at Ravenspurgh.

scenes.title: Ely House
scenes.summary: Gaunt's dying speech on England; Richard seizes his lands, and York warns him what that means.

scenes.title: The Queen's foreboding
scenes.summary: The Queen feels a grief with no cause yet; news arrives that Bolingbroke has landed with a growing following.

scenes.title: Gloucestershire
scenes.summary: Bolingbroke gathers support and tells York he has come only for his own inheritance.

scenes.title: The Welsh camp disperses
scenes.summary: Salisbury watches the Welsh troops leave on a rumour that the king is dead.

structure.label: Act III
structure.title: The descent from the walls
structure.summary: Richard lands from Ireland, greets the soil of his kingdom, and then loses the country in three scenes of bad news. At Flint Castle he comes down from the walls to meet Bolingbroke in the base court, a piece of staging that settles the question before either man says what he wants. The garden scene turns the collapse into an argument about husbandry.

scenes.title: Bristol
scenes.summary: Bolingbroke sends Bushy and Green to execution, itemising their offences first.

scenes.title: The coast of Wales
scenes.summary: Richard argues that no sea can wash the balm from a king, and then hears the reports that undo the claim.

scenes.title: Flint Castle
scenes.summary: Northumberland delivers Bolingbroke's terms; Richard comes down to the base court and is taken to London.

scenes.title: The garden
scenes.summary: A gardener and his man read the state of England off a neglected garden, and the Queen overhears the news of the deposition.

structure.label: Act IV
structure.title: Westminster Hall, and a king unmaking himself
structure.summary: One scene, and the whole political argument is inside it. Carlisle predicts civil war if a subject crowns himself, and is arrested for saying so. Richard is made to hand over the crown in public, and turns the ceremony into a performance of his own undoing, calling for a mirror and breaking it.

scenes.title: The deposition
scenes.summary: Gages fly over Gloucester's death, Carlisle prophesies, Richard resigns the crown and smashes the glass.

structure.label: Act V
structure.title: A new reign begins with a murder it did not order
structure.summary: Richard is parted from the Queen and sent north. York uncovers his own son in a plot and denounces him, which shows what loyalty now costs a family. In prison Richard thinks his way through the only kingdom he has left, and Exton kills him on the strength of a question Bolingbroke asked aloud and never answered.

scenes.title: The parting
scenes.summary: Richard and the Queen say goodbye on the way to the Tower; she is sent to France.

scenes.title: Aumerle's plot
scenes.summary: York finds a treasonous bond on his son and rides to betray him to the new king.

scenes.title: The pardon
scenes.summary: Father and mother plead on opposite sides; Henry pardons Aumerle and hunts the rest.

scenes.title: Exton hears a wish
scenes.summary: Exton repeats the king's question about a living fear and decides it was an order.

scenes.title: Pomfret
scenes.summary: Richard compares his cell to the world, hears music out of time, and is killed.

scenes.title: Windsor
scenes.summary: Henry receives the rebels' heads and then Richard's coffin, banishes Exton and vows a crusade.

characters.name: King Richard II
characters.role: King of England, grandson of Edward III
characters.summary: He begins as a king who thinks the title does the work for him, and becomes, once it is taken away, the best speaker in the play. Everything he loses politically he recovers as language, which is why an audience that would not follow him into battle follows him into prison.
characters.clue: He calls for a looking-glass in the middle of losing a kingdom, and dashes it on the floor when the face in it is still his own.

relationships.label: cousin, rival and prisoner of
relationships.note: They are grandsons of the same king, which is the whole difficulty.

characters.name: Henry Bolingbroke
characters.role: Duke of Hereford, later King Henry IV
characters.summary: He says very little about what he wants and gets all of it. The play never gives him a soliloquy, so an audience must judge him by timing alone: he lands to claim an inheritance, accepts a crown he never demands, and ends by disowning the murder he asked for out loud.
characters.clue: He comes home for his father's land, says nothing about the throne, and is king within two acts.

characters.name: John of Gaunt
characters.role: Duke of Lancaster, Richard's uncle
characters.summary: He refuses to avenge his brother's murder because the king ordered it, and then spends his last scene saying everything he has held back. His speech on England is a complaint about leases and parchment bonds, not a patriotic anthem, and the play takes his estate away before his body is cold.
characters.clue: Dying, he puns on his own name, calls the king a landlord, and says England has conquered itself.

characters.name: Duke of York
characters.role: Edmund of Langley, Richard's uncle and Lord Governor of England
characters.summary: Left to hold the kingdom with no troops and no instructions, he changes sides slowly and in public, which makes him the play's honest measure of how fast legitimacy moves. By Act V he is denouncing his own son to prove a loyalty nobody asked him for.
characters.clue: He is told to defend a kingdom with an empty treasury, meets the invader on the road, and cannot decide whether to arrest him or dine with him.

characters.name: Thomas Mowbray
characters.role: Duke of Norfolk
characters.summary: Accused of Gloucester's murder, he defends himself without ever explaining what happened, because the truth would implicate the king who is judging him. His farewell is about losing English, not England, and he dies offstage in Venice, the first of the play's exiles.
characters.clue: Banished for life, he grieves for his mother tongue and compares his own speech to a viol with the strings taken off.

characters.name: Earl of Northumberland
characters.role: Henry Percy, Bolingbroke's chief supporter
characters.summary: He does the work Bolingbroke will not be seen doing: carrying the demands to Flint, pressing Richard to read the list of crimes aloud, ordering him to the Tower. The Henry IV plays begin with the bill for his service arriving.
characters.clue: He never asks for the crown himself, but he is the man sent up to the castle wall to say what its terms will be.

characters.name: The Queen
characters.role: Richard's wife, Isabel of Valois
characters.summary: Shakespeare ages a child bride into an adult woman so that the fall has a private witness. Her grief arrives before its cause does, and she is the only character who tells Richard to fight rather than to talk, which he cannot do.
characters.clue: She feels a sorrow with no name in it before any messenger arrives, and later hears the worst news of her life from a gardener.

characters.name: Bishop of Carlisle
characters.role: A churchman at the deposition
characters.summary: He makes the one speech in the play that names the consequence of what is happening, and is arrested before he finishes hearing the answer. His prophecy of English blood on English ground is also a trailer for the seven history plays Shakespeare had already written or would write.
characters.clue: He tells a hall full of lords that if they crown this man, the ground itself will be manured with English blood.

characters.name: The Gardener
characters.role: A servant in the Duke of York's garden
characters.summary: He has no name, one scene and the clearest political analysis in the play: a state is a plot of ground that needs pruning, and Richard has let the weeds take the light. He also knows about the deposition before the Queen does, which says something about how news travels.
characters.clue: He tells his man to bind up the apricocks, and turns a day's weeding into a verdict on the reign.

themes.name: Divine right and the anointed body
themes.canonicalName: Divine right and the anointed body
themes.summary: Richard's whole defence is that kingship is a physical fact done to him with holy oil, not an office he holds on conditions. The play does not simply refute him: Bolingbroke wins, but the crown he takes never stops being described as stolen, and the next four plays pay for it.
themes.development: Asserted at full length in 3.2, tested against a landing army in 3.3, formally undone in 4.1, and mourned by the man who broke it in 5.6.

themes.name: Inheritance and the law of succession
themes.summary: Seizing Gaunt's estate is the hinge of the plot because Richard's own title comes from exactly the rule he breaks. York says so to his face: take away the right of an heir to succeed, and you have taken away the argument for being king. The play makes constitutional law a matter of personal cash flow.
themes.development: Richard leases the realm in 1.4, confiscates Lancaster in 2.1, and by 2.3 Bolingbroke is back claiming only what the law says is his.

themes.name: Words, names and what they can do
themes.summary: Banishment is measured in breath, a name is a thing that can be taken off, and the deposition is conducted as a reading aloud. Richard discovers that a word from a king used to be an action and is now only a word, and he becomes a poet at the exact moment the sentence stops working.
themes.development: Bolingbroke counts four years cut from his exile in 1.3; Richard resigns his name in 4.1; at Pomfret in 5.5 he sets one biblical word against another and can settle nothing.

themes.name: England as a garden and an estate
themes.canonicalName: England as a garden and an estate
themes.summary: The country is never an abstraction here. It is soil Richard greets by hand, a lease signed on rotten parchment, a sea-walled garden full of weeds, and a plot whose caterpillars Bolingbroke promises to pluck away. The metaphor lets servants pass judgement on kings without leaving their own subject.
themes.development: Gaunt's blessed plot in 2.1 is answered by the gardener's choked-up beds in 3.4, and by Carlisle's ground manured with English blood in 4.1.

themes.name: Time and its keeping
themes.summary: Richard is repeatedly late: late to hear Gaunt, late back from Ireland, late to fight. In prison he works the image out fully, turning himself into a clock whose hands are his own fingers and whose sound is his groans, and concludes that the keeper of time has become time's object.
themes.development: He wastes it in Acts I and II, hears music played out of time in 5.5, and admits the reversal in a single line before the keepers arrive.

themes.name: Ceremony and performance
themes.summary: Nearly every public event in the play is staged by someone: a trial by combat stopped at the trumpet, a descent from a castle wall, a resignation carried out with a crown held between two pairs of hands. Richard is the better performer and the worse politician, and the play refuses to say those are the same thing.
themes.development: Richard controls the ritual in 1.3, loses control of the staging at Flint in 3.3, and in 4.1 seizes the only role left by directing his own deposition.

techniques.name: Unbroken verse
techniques.definition: A play written entirely in metrical lines, with no prose scenes for servants, clowns or low life.
techniques.bookDefinition: A play written entirely in metrical lines, with no prose scenes for servants, clowns or low life.
techniques.inThisBook: Gardeners, grooms and murderers all speak verse here, so there is no linguistic ground below the court to stand on and judge it from — the Henry IV plays open that ground immediately.

techniques.name: Extended conceit
techniques.definition: A single comparison developed at length until it has been pushed as far as it will go.
techniques.bookDefinition: A single comparison developed at length until it has been pushed as far as it will go.
techniques.inThisBook: The crown as a well with two buckets and the prisoner as a clock are both worked out line by line, which is how Richard fills the time he can no longer command.

techniques.name: Allegory
techniques.definition: A scene in which the surface action stands throughout for something else.
techniques.bookDefinition: A scene in which the surface action stands throughout for something else.
techniques.inThisBook: The garden in 3.4 is a working garden and a diagram of the realm at once, and the gardener never has to explain the second meaning.

techniques.name: Ritual inversion
techniques.definition: Taking the form of a ceremony and running it backwards.
techniques.bookDefinition: Taking the form of a ceremony and running it backwards.
techniques.inThisBook: The deposition in 4.1 uses the shape of a coronation — crown, sceptre, oath, anointing — with every element handed back instead of received.

techniques.name: Prophecy
techniques.definition: A statement about the future that shapes the action by being believed, whether or not it is true.
techniques.bookDefinition: A speech that predicts consequences the audience can check against history.
techniques.inThisBook: Gaunt foretells Richard's burn-out and Carlisle foretells civil war; an Elizabethan audience knew the second prophecy had a hundred years of fulfilment behind it.

techniques.name: Loaded stage properties
techniques.definition: An object handled on stage that carries far more weight than its use in the scene explains.
techniques.bookDefinition: An object handled on stage that carries the argument of a scene.
techniques.inThisBook: Gages thrown on the floor, a crown held between two men, and a mirror shattered in public do the work that a soliloquy would do elsewhere.

quotations.text: How long a time lies in one little word! Four lagging winters and four wanton springs End in a word: such is the breath of kings.
quotations.speaker: Bolingbroke
quotations.context: Richard has just cut Bolingbroke's banishment from ten years to six.
quotations.analysis: Four years are measured in seasons rather than numbers, so the mercy is felt as weather before it is understood as arithmetic. The couplet closes on 'breath', which makes royal authority a matter of air moving — a definition Bolingbroke will spend the play quietly disproving by using armies instead.

quotations.text: The language I have learn'd these forty years, My native English, now I must forego: And now my tongue's use is to me no more Than an unstringed viol or a harp,
quotations.speaker: Mowbray
quotations.context: Sentenced to perpetual banishment, before he leaves for Italy.
quotations.analysis: Exile is described as a speech impediment rather than a loss of land, which sets the play's terms early: to be removed from England is to be removed from English. The instrument images are all of things still intact and simply unusable, and Richard will reach for the same idea when his own name is taken away.

quotations.text: Teach thy necessity to reason thus; There is no virtue like necessity.
quotations.speaker: John of Gaunt
quotations.context: Gaunt tries to console his banished son at the gate.
quotations.analysis: The advice is to argue backwards from what cannot be changed until it looks like a choice, and Bolingbroke refuses it outright in the lines that follow. It is worth noticing that Richard adopts precisely this habit of mind from Act III onwards, at which point Gaunt's consolation reads as a description of political defeat.

quotations.text: Methinks I am a prophet new inspired And thus expiring do foretell of him: His rash fierce blaze of riot cannot last, For violent fires soon burn out themselves;
quotations.speaker: John of Gaunt
quotations.context: Dying at Ely House, waiting for the king to arrive.
quotations.analysis: 'Expiring' does double duty: it means dying and it means breathing out, so the prophecy and the last breath are the same event. Gaunt claims authority not from office but from proximity to death, which is the only position from which anyone in this play tells Richard the truth to his face.

quotations.text: This royal throne of kings, this scepter'd isle, This earth of majesty, this seat of Mars, This other Eden, demi-paradise, This fortress built by Nature for herself Against infection and the hand of war,
quotations.speaker: John of Gaunt
quotations.context: The opening of Gaunt's speech on England, still waiting for Richard.
quotations.analysis: The famous passage is a single sentence that does not reach its main verb for more than twenty lines, and when it arrives the verb is 'Is now leased out'. Quoted on its own the speech sounds like praise; read to the end of its grammar it is a complaint about a property transaction, and the delay is the point.

quotations.text: That England, that was wont to conquer others, Hath made a shameful conquest of itself.
quotations.speaker: John of Gaunt
quotations.context: The close of the England speech, moments before Richard enters.
quotations.analysis: The couplet turns a war verb inwards, so that the country becomes both army and territory. It is also the play's structural thesis in two lines: nobody invades England here, and every wound in the next four acts is administered by an Englishman to another Englishman's title.

quotations.text: Landlord of England art thou now, not king: Thy state of law is bondslave to the law; And thou--
quotations.speaker: John of Gaunt
quotations.context: The quarrel with Richard at the bedside, cut off by the king.
quotations.analysis: Gaunt swaps one title for another and the whole indictment is done. A landlord holds property for income; a king holds a country in trust, and the difference is the lease Richard has just signed. The dash marks the sentence Richard interrupts, and it is the last time anyone at court speaks to him like this.

quotations.text: The ripest fruit first falls, and so doth he; His time is spent, our pilgrimage must be. So much for that. Now for our Irish wars:
quotations.speaker: King Richard II
quotations.context: Richard's response to the news that Gaunt is dead.
quotations.analysis: Two lines of decorous condolence, then 'So much for that', and the tone drops from elegy to agenda inside a single verse line. The switch is the seizure of the Lancastrian estate happening at the level of style, several seconds before Richard says the word 'seize'.

quotations.text: The caterpillars of the commonwealth, Which I have sworn to weed and pluck away.
quotations.speaker: Bolingbroke
quotations.context: Explaining to York, on the road in Gloucestershire, why he has come back armed.
quotations.analysis: Bolingbroke gives his invasion a horticultural justification: he is not raising an army, he is doing the weeding the owner has neglected. The gardener in 3.4 will use exactly this vocabulary without knowing it has already been used as a war aim, and the repetition is how the play checks Bolingbroke's claim against a disinterested witness.

quotations.text: Not all the water in the rough rude sea Can wash the balm off from an anointed king; The breath of worldly men cannot depose The deputy elected by the Lord:
quotations.speaker: King Richard II
quotations.context: Newly landed from Ireland, before the bad news begins to arrive.
quotations.analysis: The claim is made in the language of chemistry — oil that water cannot lift — and it is answered within fifty lines not by an argument but by a series of reports. Note that the sentence concedes more than it means to: if worldly breath cannot depose a king, the play then shows a king deposed by worldly hands instead.

quotations.text: For God's sake, let us sit upon the ground And tell sad stories of the death of kings; How some have been deposed; some slain in war, Some haunted by the ghosts they have deposed;
quotations.speaker: King Richard II
quotations.context: After hearing that his Welsh army has dispersed and his favourites are dead.
quotations.analysis: Richard proposes the one activity no king can afford, which is sitting down, and he does it in the first person plural, recruiting the stage and the audience into an audience of his own. The list that follows is a catalogue of history-play plots, so he is effectively asking to be read rather than obeyed.

quotations.text: All murder'd: for within the hollow crown That rounds the mortal temples of a king Keeps Death his court and there the antic sits, Scoffing his state and grinning at his pomp,
quotations.speaker: King Richard II
quotations.context: The middle of the same speech on the coast of Wales.
quotations.analysis: The crown stops being an ornament and becomes an architectural space with a tenant in it, and the tenant is a jester. 'Hollow' is doing two jobs at once — the shape of the metal, and the emptiness of the office — and the word will still be working in 4.1 when Richard hands the thing over and finds nothing inside it.

quotations.text: I live with bread like you, feel want, Taste grief, need friends: subjected thus, How can you say to me, I am a king?
quotations.speaker: King Richard II
quotations.context: Rebuking his followers for trying to comfort him.
quotations.analysis: 'Subjected' is the key word: it means made into a subject and also made liable to, and Richard hears both meanings at once. Having spent a hundred lines insisting that a king is a different order of being, he now proves the opposite from the evidence of his own appetite.

quotations.text: What must the king do now? must he submit? The king shall do it: must he be deposed? The king shall be contented: must he lose The name of king? o' God's name, let it go:
quotations.speaker: King Richard II
quotations.context: On the walls at Flint Castle, after Northumberland brings Bolingbroke's demands.
quotations.analysis: Richard refers to himself in the third person throughout, as though reading the part of a king from a script someone else is writing. The questions are rhetorical but the answers are real concessions, so the speech gives away the kingdom in the grammar while the surface sounds like defiance.

quotations.text: Down, down I come; like glistering Phaethon, Wanting the manage of unruly jades. In the base court? Base court, where kings grow base, To come at traitors' calls and do them grace.
quotations.speaker: King Richard II
quotations.context: Descending from the castle wall to meet Bolingbroke in the lower courtyard.
quotations.analysis: Richard narrates his own stage movement, turning a walk downstairs into the fall of a boy who could not hold his father's horses. The pun on 'base' — the name of the yard, and a moral judgement — lets him lose the high ground physically while claiming it verbally, which is the whole tactic of his last three acts.

quotations.text: When our sea-walled garden, the whole land, Is full of weeds, her fairest flowers choked up, Her fruit-trees all upturned, her hedges ruin'd, Her knots disorder'd and her wholesome herbs Swarming with caterpillars?
quotations.speaker: A gardener's man
quotations.context: In the Duke of York's garden at Langley, while the Queen listens unseen.
quotations.analysis: A servant asks why he should tend one garden when the larger one is ruined, and in doing so repeats Gaunt's sea-wall and Bolingbroke's caterpillars from a position with nothing to gain. The play's political analysis is given to people with no rank at all, and delivered as a question about work.

quotations.text: And if you crown him, let me prophesy: The blood of English shall manure the ground, And future ages groan for this foul act; Peace shall go sleep with Turks and infidels,
quotations.speaker: Bishop of Carlisle
quotations.context: Interrupting the deposition in Westminster Hall; he is arrested for treason immediately afterwards.
quotations.analysis: 'Manure' is an agricultural word placed in a cathedral register, and it keeps the garden imagery running into the political climax. The prophecy is unusual in Shakespeare for being entirely accurate and entirely useless: the audience already knows the Wars of the Roses happened, and the men on stage crown Bolingbroke anyway.

quotations.text: God save the king! Will no man say amen? Am I both priest and clerk? well then, amen.
quotations.speaker: King Richard II
quotations.context: Brought into Westminster Hall to surrender the crown in public.
quotations.analysis: He offers the loyal shout and then has to supply the response himself, playing both halves of a church service to an audience that will not join in. The line measures the deposition better than any argument in the scene: the form still exists, and nobody is willing to take part in it.

quotations.text: Now is this golden crown like a deep well That owes two buckets, filling one another, The emptier ever dancing in the air, The other down, unseen and full of water:
quotations.speaker: King Richard II
quotations.context: Holding one side of the crown while Bolingbroke holds the other.
quotations.analysis: Two men gripping a single object become a mechanism in which neither can rise without the other falling. The conceit also quietly insults the winner: the bucket that goes up is the empty one, and it is 'dancing in the air' while the full one sits unseen at the bottom.

quotations.text: Ay, no; no, ay; for I must nothing be; Therefore no no, for I resign to thee. Now mark me, how I will undo myself;
quotations.speaker: King Richard II
quotations.context: Asked directly whether he is content to resign the crown.
quotations.analysis: The line will not settle into an answer: 'Ay' and 'I' sounded alike, so 'Ay, no' is also 'I, no', a man agreeing and cancelling himself in the same breath. It is the shortest statement in the play of what deposition does to a person whose identity was an office.

quotations.text: Was this the face that faced so many follies, And was at last out-faced by Bolingbroke? A brittle glory shineth in this face: As brittle as the glory is the face;
quotations.speaker: King Richard II
quotations.context: Looking into the mirror he has demanded, immediately before smashing it.
quotations.analysis: 'Face' is used as noun and verb within one line, so the word for a countenance becomes the word for bluffing, and the pun diagnoses his reign. Breaking the glass is meant to prove that grief has changed him; Bolingbroke's reply, that he has only destroyed the shadow of his face, is the coldest line in the play.

quotations.text: I have been studying how I may compare This prison where I live unto the world: And for because the world is populous And here is not a creature but myself, I cannot do it; yet I'll hammer it out.
quotations.speaker: King Richard II
quotations.context: Alone in the cell at Pomfret Castle.
quotations.analysis: This is the only soliloquy Richard has, and it opens by admitting that the comparison he wants to make does not work. 'Hammer it out' is a smith's phrase for beating metal into shape, so the thinking is presented as manual labour — the first honest work the play lets him do.

quotations.text: I wasted time, and now doth time waste me; For now hath time made me his numbering clock: My thoughts are minutes; and with sighs they jar Their watches on unto mine eyes, the outward watch,
quotations.speaker: King Richard II
quotations.context: Hearing music played badly in time, in the cell at Pomfret.
quotations.analysis: The chiasmus puts the same two words on either side of the verb and swaps who is doing what, which is the play's plot in nine syllables. What follows is not self-pity but mechanism: a man itemising his own body as clockwork, down to the finger wiping tears off a dial.

quotations.text: 'Have I no friend will rid me of this living fear?' Was it not so?
quotations.speaker: Exton
quotations.context: Exton repeating to a servant what he heard the new king say.
quotations.analysis: The murder is commissioned by a question left hanging in a room, and the play stages the moment of interpretation rather than the moment of ordering. Because Exton has to check the wording twice with a servant, Bolingbroke keeps the deniability that lets him banish the killer in the last scene.

quotations.text: I'll make a voyage to the Holy Land, To wash this blood off from my guilty hand:
quotations.speaker: Bolingbroke, now King Henry IV
quotations.context: The last lines of the play, spoken over Richard's coffin.
quotations.analysis: The new reign opens with a promise of expiation that the two parts of Henry IV never allow him to keep; he is still planning the same crusade, and still failing to leave, in the play that follows. Washing also picks up Richard's claim that no water could remove the balm of kingship, and applies the image to a stain instead of a blessing.

atAGlance.label: Written
atAGlance.note: Early enough that the two parts of Henry IV and Henry V are still ahead of it.

atAGlance.label: First printed
atAGlance.note: A quarto printed by Valentine Simmes for Andrew Wise; the deposition material was advertised as an addition only in 1608.

atAGlance.label: Chief source
atAGlance.note: Shakespeare keeps the chronicle sequence and invents the interior life that goes with it.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.note: Act IV is a single scene, and it is the longest and most dangerous in the play.

criticalViews.position: A tragedy of a bad king who becomes a great poet
criticalViews.summary: The oldest reading treats the play as the study of a temperament: a ruler whose gifts are entirely verbal and whose imagination only switches on once power is gone.
criticalViews.counter: It tends to leave Bolingbroke as a blank, when the play's silences around him look deliberate rather than empty.

criticalViews.position: A play about the king's two bodies
criticalViews.summary: Legal and constitutional readings take Richard's insistence on anointing seriously, and follow what happens when the sacred person and the political office are pulled apart in public.
criticalViews.counter: Richard's own behaviour undermines the doctrine before Bolingbroke does: he breaks the law of inheritance that makes him king in the first place.

criticalViews.position: A play read for its politics in its own time
criticalViews.summary: The printing history and the performance on the eve of the Essex rising have long encouraged readings that treat the deposition as live and dangerous material for an Elizabethan audience.
criticalViews.counter: The evidence is thinner than the story suggests, and reading backwards from 1601 can flatten a play that spends most of its length on private grief.

essayQuestions.question: Is Richard deposed by Bolingbroke, or does he depose himself?
essayQuestions.focus: Agency, ceremony and the deposition scene
plan: Establish the legal position first: the seizure of Gaunt's estate in 2.1 breaks the inheritance rule that Richard's own title depends on, and York says so on stage.
Show Bolingbroke never stating a claim: track what he actually says in 2.3 and 3.3 against what his army achieves.
Read 3.3 as staging — the descent to the base court happens before any terms are agreed.
Take 4.1 slowly: Richard runs the ceremony, supplies the responses, calls for the mirror and narrates his own undoing.
Conclude on 5.4, where the new king's power is exercised by a question rather than a command, and ask which man is more responsible for the outcome.

essayQuestions.question: What does the garden scene contribute that the court scenes cannot?
essayQuestions.focus: Allegory, class and political judgement
plan: Set the scene in its place: 3.4 sits between the surrender at Flint and the deposition at Westminster, and nothing in the plot happens in it.
Trace the garden imagery backwards to Gaunt's sea-wall in 2.1 and Bolingbroke's caterpillars in 2.3.
Note that the gardener has no rank and no interest, which is what gives his judgement its authority.
Look at how the Queen's overhearing turns political analysis into personal grief in the same scene.
Close on the fact that the servants speak verse: the play offers no comic underclass, so this is as far outside the court as it can reach.

essayQuestions.question: How does the play's language change once Richard stops being king?
essayQuestions.focus: Style, self-knowledge and the limits of eloquence
plan: Compare Richard's public style in Act I — royal plural, third person, crisp sentences of command — with his speech after 3.2.
Use the hollow crown speech to show the conceits lengthening as his options shorten.
Examine 4.1 for wordplay that works against him: 'face' as noun and verb, 'Ay, no' heard as 'I, no'.
Turn to 5.5 and the prison soliloquy, where he admits at the start that the comparison will not hold.
Judge whether the eloquence is compensation, self-deception, or the only form of understanding the play allows him.

essayQuestions.question: Does the play take sides between an incompetent king and a capable usurper?
essayQuestions.focus: Legitimacy, order and the cost of both
plan: Set out Richard's record honestly: the murder of Gloucester behind the action, the farming of the realm in 1.4, the confiscation in 2.1.
Set out Bolingbroke's: no soliloquy, no stated claim, and a competence the play never denies.
Weigh Carlisle's prophecy in 4.1, which is both treasonous and, on the historical record, correct.
Consider Aumerle's plot in 5.2 and 5.3 as the first instalment of the disorder Carlisle predicted.
Finish on the last twenty lines, where the new king inherits a corpse, a guilt and a crusade he will never make.

discussionQuestions: Bolingbroke is given no soliloquy at all. Does that make him unreadable, or is the silence itself the characterisation?
Gaunt calls England a blessed plot and then says it has conquered itself. Which half of the speech does the rest of the play support?
Richard smashes the mirror to prove that sorrow has changed his face. What does it mean that the face is unchanged?
Why does Shakespeare give the clearest account of the kingdom's condition to a gardener with no name?
The play never lets anyone speak prose. What would be gained, and what lost, if the gardeners or the grooms did?

timeline.label: Richard of Bordeaux is born
timeline.detail: Son of Edward the Black Prince, and grandson of Edward III.

timeline.label: Richard becomes king as a child
timeline.detail: He succeeds his grandfather Edward III at the age of ten, his own father having died the year before.

timeline.label: The Peasants' Revolt
timeline.detail: The young king faces the rebels in person, an episode Shakespeare leaves out of a play that begins seventeen years later.

timeline.label: Bolingbroke and Mowbray are banished
timeline.detail: The quarrel with which the play opens ends in exile rather than trial by combat.

timeline.label: Gaunt dies, Bolingbroke returns, Richard is deposed
timeline.detail: The confiscation of the Lancastrian inheritance and the landing at Ravenspurgh fall in the same year as the surrender of the crown.

timeline.label: Richard dies in captivity at Pontefract
timeline.detail: The play calls the castle Pomfret and gives him a murderer; the historical cause of death is not certain.

timeline.label: Holinshed's Chronicles reissued
timeline.detail: The second edition gave Shakespeare the sequence of events for this play and the ones that follow it.

timeline.label: The play is written
timeline.detail: Usually dated to about this year, which places it at the head of the second sequence of English histories.

timeline.label: The first quarto is printed
timeline.detail: Printed by Valentine Simmes for Andrew Wise, without the deposition passage in 4.1.

timeline.label: A Richard II play is staged before the Essex rising
timeline.detail: Supporters of the Earl of Essex paid for a performance of a play about Richard II on the eve of the revolt; the record does not name Shakespeare's text outright, but the subject was enough to make it dangerous.

timeline.label: A quarto advertises new additions
timeline.detail: The title page announces the Parliament scene and the deposing of King Richard as material now in print.

timeline.label: The First Folio
timeline.detail: The play is printed among the histories, fixing its place at the start of the run to Henry V.

places.name: Coventry
places.note: The lists where the trial by combat is stopped at the trumpet in 1.3.

places.name: Westminster Hall, London
places.note: The single scene of Act IV: Carlisle's prophecy, the resignation of the crown and the broken mirror.

places.name: Ravenspurgh, Humber estuary
places.note: Bolingbroke's landing place, long since lost to the sea near Spurn Head.

places.name: Flint Castle
places.note: Where Richard comes down from the walls into the base court in 3.3.

places.name: Pontefract Castle
places.note: Pomfret in the play: the cell of the prison soliloquy and the murder in 5.5.

places.name: Berkeley Castle
places.note: Where York meets Bolingbroke's advancing force and fails to arrest it.

related.why: The direct sequel: Bolingbroke on the throne, paying for this play's bargains with Northumberland and the Percys.
Where the promise to wash the blood off in the Holy Land finally catches up with the man who made it.
The end of the sequence, in which Richard's murder is still being prayed about on the night before Agincourt.
The other Richard, and the far end of the civil war that Carlisle predicts in Westminster Hall.
An earlier English history built on the same problem: a crown held by a man whose right to it will not stand examination.

books.title: Richard III
books.author: William Shakespeare
books.setting: England at the end of the Wars of the Roses: London, the Tower, Pomfret, Salisbury and Bosworth Field
books.lengthNote: Around 3,600 lines — after Hamlet, the longest play in the Folio
books.openingLine: Now is the winter of our discontent Made glorious summer by this sun of York;
books.summary: A man tells the audience in the first forty lines exactly what he intends to do, and then does it while everyone on stage fails to notice. Richard's method is not secrecy but performance: he grieves for the brother he has imprisoned, refuses a crown he has arranged to be offered, and takes the audience into a confidence he offers nobody else. The play's problem is that the confidence works — and that it stops working in Act IV, when the jokes dry up and the women take over the stage.

sourceText.label: Globe/Moby text of Richard III
sourceText.note: The quarto and Folio texts differ substantially; line numbers here follow the traditional Globe numbering of the conflated text.

structure.label: Act I
structure.title: A programme announced, and two people removed
structure.summary: Richard sets out his intentions to the audience before anyone else appears, has Clarence sent to the Tower on a manufactured prophecy, and wins Lady Anne beside the corpse of the king he helped kill. Margaret arrives to curse everyone present, and the play files the curses for later use.

scenes.title: The winter of our discontent
scenes.summary: Richard explains the peace, his own body and his plan, then greets the brother he has just had arrested.

scenes.title: The wooing of Anne
scenes.summary: Interrupting Henry VI's funeral procession, Richard talks the dead king's daughter-in-law into accepting his ring.

scenes.title: Margaret's curses
scenes.summary: The old Lancastrian queen walks into a Yorkist quarrel and names the deaths that will follow, in order.

scenes.title: Clarence in the Tower
scenes.summary: Clarence describes a dream of drowning and judgement, then argues theology with the murderers his brother has sent.

structure.label: Act II
structure.title: A king dies and the peace he made dies with him
structure.summary: Edward IV has just reconciled his court when Richard tells him Clarence is dead, and the news kills him. The queen's relatives are arrested on the road, the citizens in the street can see what is coming, and the young heir is brought to London under escort by the man who intends to take his place.

scenes.title: The broken reconciliation
scenes.summary: Edward makes his court swear friendship; Richard announces Clarence's death and lets the guilt settle where it falls.

scenes.title: Three grieving women
scenes.summary: The Duchess of York, Queen Elizabeth and Clarence's children compete in mourning while Richard proposes a quiet escort for the prince.

scenes.title: Citizens in the street
scenes.summary: Three ordinary Londoners weigh a child king against ambitious kin and fear the worst.

scenes.title: Sanctuary
scenes.summary: News of the arrests at Pomfret sends the queen and the younger prince into sanctuary.

structure.label: Act III
structure.title: The Tower, the council table and the pretended refusal
structure.summary: The princes are lodged in the Tower with courteous menace, Hastings is executed between one sentence and the next, and the crown is offered to a man who has rehearsed his reluctance with Buckingham beforehand. The theatre here is public and cynical, and the citizens' silence is part of the record.

scenes.title: The princes lodged
scenes.summary: The young Duke of York jokes about his uncle's shoulders; both boys are sent to the Tower for their safety.

scenes.title: Hastings ignores a dream
scenes.summary: Warned by Stanley's nightmare, Hastings decides that his standing with Richard makes him safe.

scenes.title: Pomfret
scenes.summary: Rivers, Grey and Vaughan are executed, and remember Margaret's curse as they go.

scenes.title: Strawberries and a head
scenes.summary: Richard asks for strawberries, leaves the council, returns accusing Hastings of witchcraft, and has him killed before dinner.

scenes.title: Managing the mayor
