scenes.summary: Richard and Buckingham stage an emergency in rusty armour and explain the execution to the city.

scenes.title: The scrivener
scenes.summary: A clerk notes that the indictment of Hastings was written out before the man was accused.

scenes.title: The refusal
scenes.summary: Richard appears between two bishops and declines the crown twice before accepting it.

structure.label: Act IV
structure.title: The crown, and the first things it cannot buy
structure.summary: Richard is king by the middle of the act and immediately less interesting to himself: the soliloquies stop, Buckingham hesitates over the princes and is dropped, and Tyrrel does the work. The long fourth scene gives the stage to three women who have nothing left to lose, and to a second wooing that looks like the first and is not.

scenes.title: Shut out of the Tower
scenes.summary: The women are refused admission to the princes; Anne is summoned to be crowned and knows what it means.

scenes.title: Not in the giving vein
scenes.summary: Richard sounds Buckingham out about the princes, gets hesitation, and drops him mid-sentence.

scenes.title: Tyrrel's report
scenes.summary: The murder of the princes is described by a man who was not in the room, quoting men who were.

scenes.title: The women, and the second wooing
scenes.summary: Margaret teaches the other queens how to curse; Richard then asks Elizabeth for her daughter and believes he has won.

scenes.title: Stanley's message
scenes.summary: Stanley sends secret word to Richmond that his son is held hostage.

structure.label: Act V
structure.title: Two tents, eleven ghosts, and a horse
structure.summary: Buckingham goes to the block quoting the curse he brought on himself. On the eve of Bosworth the ghosts of everyone Richard has killed visit both tents in turn, cursing one sleeper and blessing the other. Richard wakes into the only soliloquy in which he cannot control who is speaking, and dies on foot.

scenes.title: Buckingham at Salisbury
scenes.summary: Led to execution on All-Souls' day, he recalls the oath he swore and the curse Margaret laid.

scenes.title: Richmond marches
scenes.summary: The invading earl describes the boar in the middle of England and counts his friends.

scenes.title: The night before Bosworth
scenes.summary: Two tents, two prayers, and eleven ghosts who speak the same words twice with opposite meanings.

scenes.title: A horse
scenes.summary: Unhorsed and seeking Richmond in the field, Richard offers his kingdom for a mount.

scenes.title: The two roses
scenes.summary: Richmond takes the crown, pardons the soldiers and announces a marriage that ends the civil wars.

characters.name: Richard, Duke of Gloucester
characters.role: Later King Richard III
characters.summary: He is the funniest person in the play and knows it, which is the trap: the audience laughs at the jokes and is therefore in the room for the murders. He is not a hypocrite in the ordinary sense, because he tells us the truth constantly; he simply tells nobody on stage.
characters.clue: He is his own prologue, announces his plan in the first speech, and by Act V is arguing with himself about whether he is a villain and losing both sides.

characters.name: The Duke of Buckingham
characters.role: Richard's chief accomplice
characters.summary: The only person who is let into part of the plan, and he is good at it: the staged emergency and the bogus refusal of the crown are largely his productions. He hesitates exactly once, over the princes, and discovers that there was never a second place in the arrangement.
characters.clue: He boasts that he can counterfeit the deep tragedian, stage-manages a fake coronation appeal, and is dropped the moment he pauses over a murder.

characters.name: Queen Margaret
characters.role: Widow of Henry VI, survivor of the previous three plays
characters.summary: Historically she was not in England at all by this date, and Shakespeare keeps her anyway because the play needs someone who remembers. Her curses are not magic but memory with a very long reach, and the characters who dismiss her in Act I quote her accurately as they go to the block.
characters.clue: She has no title, no army and no business being there, and every death in the play happens in the order she names it.

characters.name: Queen Elizabeth
characters.role: Edward IV's widow, mother of the princes
characters.summary: She begins as a court politician anxious about her relatives' standing and ends as the one person who holds a long conversation with Richard and gives nothing away. Whether she agrees to give him her daughter or plays for time is a question the text leaves genuinely open.
characters.clue: She loses a husband, two sons and most of her family, then talks for two hundred lines with the man who took them and leaves him thinking he has won.

characters.name: Lady Anne
characters.role: Widow of Prince Edward, later Richard's queen
characters.summary: She is given one great scene, in which she out-argues Richard line for line and then takes his ring anyway, and one short scene four acts later in which she explains what the marriage has cost her. The play never accounts for the change, which is why the scene is still argued about.
characters.clue: She spits at him over a coffin, calls him a fouler toad than any poison ever hung on, and is wearing his ring before the corpse has been carried off.

characters.name: The Duchess of York
characters.role: Mother of Edward IV, Clarence and Richard
characters.summary: She has outlived a husband and is watching her sons destroy one another, and the play gives her the one curse that is delivered by someone with an unquestionable right to it. Her farewell to Richard is a mother's formal withdrawal of blessing, and he asks the drums to drown it.
characters.clue: Three of her sons appear in this play; she buries two of them and sends the third to Bosworth with her heaviest curse instead of a blessing.

characters.name: George, Duke of Clarence
characters.role: Richard's elder brother
characters.summary: He is imprisoned on the strength of a prophecy his brother invented and killed on the strength of a warrant his brother sent, and he spends his last scene describing a dream in which the dead he betrayed at Tewkesbury come for him. He is not innocent, and the murder is still shocking.
characters.clue: A letter of the alphabet sends him to the Tower, where he dreams of drowning among jewels and wakes to two men arguing about conscience.

characters.name: Lord Hastings
characters.role: Lord Chamberlain
characters.summary: He celebrates the execution of his enemies in the morning and is executed himself after lunch, having explained an hour earlier that he knows Richard's face too well to be in danger. His speech on the block is the play's plainest statement about reading the powerful.
characters.clue: He laughs at a warning dream, rejoices at his rivals' deaths at Pomfret, and loses his head between the strawberries and dinner.
traits: briefly right about everything except himself

characters.name: The Earl of Richmond
characters.role: Henry Tudor, later Henry VII
characters.summary: He arrives with fewer than two hundred lines and no interior life at all, which is a choice rather than an oversight: after four acts of a man who talks to us constantly, the play offers a leader who talks only to his army and to God. The Tudor settlement is announced rather than dramatised.
characters.clue: He lands at Milford Haven, sleeps well, is blessed by every ghost that curses his opponent, and ends the play by marrying a woman who never appears in it.

themes.name: Tyranny as performance
themes.summary: Richard does not conceal power so much as dramatise it: a fake arrest, a fake emergency, a fake refusal of the crown, all played to audiences who are given their cues. The play argues that consent can be manufactured in public, in daylight, by people who know they are acting.
themes.development: Private improvisation in Act I becomes a civic production in 3.7, and collapses in Act V when there is nobody left to play to.

themes.name: The audience's complicity
themes.summary: Richard tells us his plans, invites us to admire the workmanship and jokes with us about the people he is about to kill. The discomfort is structural: the play gives the audience a better relationship with the murderer than it gives anyone on stage.
themes.development: The soliloquies stop once he is crowned, and the confidence is withdrawn precisely when the murders become unbearable.

themes.name: Curses, prophecy and memory
themes.summary: Margaret's curses in 1.3 function as a programme for the rest of the play, and the play's dead are its most reliable record-keepers. Whether this is providence or simply the way the guilty are made to remember is left unsettled.
themes.development: Named in Act I, quoted by Rivers at Pomfret, by Hastings on the block and by Buckingham at Salisbury, and finally embodied by the ghosts at Bosworth.

themes.name: Conscience
themes.summary: The word is argued over by two hired murderers before it ever troubles Richard, and their comic debate about the inconvenience of having a conscience sets the terms for his nightmare four acts later. He calls it a word cowards use, in a speech that is itself an attempt to talk himself out of one.
themes.development: A joke in 1.4, an absence through Acts II to IV, and by 5.3 a thousand several tongues, every one of them his.

themes.name: The women and formal lament
themes.summary: Four women who have every reason to hate each other end up sitting on the ground together, comparing dead sons in almost liturgical sequence. It is the one form of speech in the play that Richard cannot enter, interrupt or turn to his advantage.
themes.development: Rivalry in 1.3 and 2.2, shared grief in 4.1, and in 4.4 a set of matched laments that stop the plot for two hundred lines.

themes.name: History and legitimacy
themes.summary: The play inherits a Richard already blackened by Tudor chroniclers writing for the dynasty his defeat created, and it ends by announcing that dynasty as the end of civil war. Any reading has to hold both the play's theatrical delight in Richard and its political obligation to bury him.
themes.development: Yorkist triumph in 1.1, usurpation staged as election in 3.7, and in 5.5 a marriage that joins the roses and closes the sequence begun in the Henry VI plays.

techniques.name: Direct address
techniques.definition: A narrator or speaker turning outward to address the reader or the audience by name.
techniques.bookDefinition: A character speaking straight to the audience, treating them as confidants rather than observers.
techniques.inThisBook: Richard has the first word of the play and spends forty lines alone with us before the plot begins; the technique makes the audience an accessory before the fact.

techniques.name: Stichomythia
techniques.definition: Rapid exchange of single lines, each answering and turning the last.
techniques.bookDefinition: Rapid exchange of single lines, each answering and turning the last.
techniques.inThisBook: The wooing of Anne and the later wooing of Elizabeth are both conducted as line-for-line duels, and the second one is where Richard's version of the trick stops landing cleanly.

techniques.name: Anaphora
techniques.definition: Beginning successive clauses with the same word or phrase.
techniques.bookDefinition: Beginning successive clauses with the same word or phrase.
techniques.inThisBook: Margaret's curses and the women's laments are built on hammered repetition — 'Thou that... Thou slander... Thou loathed' — which turns grief and hatred into something closer to ritual than conversation.

techniques.name: The Vice
techniques.definition: The joking, confiding tempter of the medieval morality plays, who explains his tricks to the audience as he performs them.
techniques.bookDefinition: The joking, confiding tempter of the medieval morality plays, who explains his tricks to the audience as he performs them.
techniques.inThisBook: Richard names the inheritance himself in 3.1, comparing his own double meanings to 'the formal vice, Iniquity' — the play's clearest signal about where its hero's charm comes from.

techniques.name: Dramatic irony
techniques.definition: The audience holding information a character on stage does not.
techniques.bookDefinition: The audience holding information a character on stage does not.
techniques.inThisBook: Because Richard briefs us in advance, almost every scene is watched from inside his plan: Clarence's trust, Hastings's confidence and the citizens' silence are all things we can price and they cannot.

techniques.name: Mirrored scenes
techniques.definition: Two scenes built to the same shape so that the second comments on the first.
techniques.bookDefinition: Two scenes built to the same shape so that the second comments on the first.
techniques.inThisBook: Two wooings, two tents on the night before Bosworth, and eleven ghosts who deliver the same words twice with opposite force: the play thinks in matched pairs.

quotations.text: Now is the winter of our discontent Made glorious summer by this sun of York; And all the clouds that lour'd upon our house In the deep bosom of the ocean buried.
quotations.speaker: Gloucester
quotations.context: The first lines of the play, spoken alone on an empty stage.
quotations.analysis: The famous first clause is only half a sentence, and the half that follows reverses it: the winter is over. 'Sun of York' is a pun on son and on Edward's badge, and the whole passage is a victory speech delivered by the one man in the family who has no use for victory.

quotations.text: Why, I, in this weak piping time of peace, Have no delight to pass away the time, Unless to spy my shadow in the sun And descant on mine own deformity
quotations.speaker: Gloucester
quotations.context: The middle of the opening soliloquy, explaining what peace leaves him to do.
quotations.analysis: 'Descant' is a musical term for improvising above a fixed melody, so his deformity is presented as a theme he performs variations on rather than a fact he suffers. The whole speech is his own account of his motives, which is exactly the reason to treat it with care.

quotations.text: And therefore, since I cannot prove a lover, To entertain these fair well-spoken days, I am determined to prove a villain And hate the idle pleasures of these days.
quotations.speaker: Gloucester
quotations.context: The turn of the opening soliloquy, immediately before Clarence is led across the stage under guard.
quotations.analysis: 'Determined' carries both senses at once — resolved, and settled in advance by something outside him — and the play never chooses between them. Note also that the reasoning is theatrical rather than moral: he cannot get the lover's part, so he takes the other one.

quotations.text: Never hung poison on a fouler toad. Out of my sight! thou dost infect my eyes.
quotations.speaker: Lady Anne
quotations.context: Beside the coffin of Henry VI, answering Richard's compliment on her spitting.
quotations.analysis: She wins this exchange and every other one in the scene, which is what makes the ending of it so hard to explain away. Her images are all of contagion — poison, infection, basilisks — and by the end of the scene she has accepted a ring from the source.

quotations.text: Take up the sword again, or take up me.
quotations.speaker: Gloucester
quotations.context: Kneeling with his breast bared, after Anne has let the sword fall.
quotations.analysis: One line, one repeated verb, two incompatible offers — and the staging does the arguing, since she must physically choose. He has converted a confession of murder into a proposal by making the only alternative another killing, which she has just refused to perform.

quotations.text: Was ever woman in this humour woo'd? Was ever woman in this humour won? I'll have her; but I will not keep her long.
quotations.speaker: Gloucester
quotations.context: Alone, the moment Anne has left the stage.
quotations.analysis: Two rhetorical questions to us, and then the third line disposes of her in eleven words. The rhyme of woo'd and won makes the whole seduction sound like a completed piece of business, and the audience is being invited to applaud a performance whose victim has only just walked off.

quotations.text: Shine out, fair sun, till I have bought a glass, That I may see my shadow as I pass.
quotations.speaker: Gloucester
quotations.context: The couplet that closes the wooing scene.
quotations.analysis: The shadow he could only 'descant on' in the first scene is now something he wants to look at, and he intends to buy a mirror to do it. Success has not altered how he sees his body; it has simply made him curious about the man who could pull this off.

quotations.text: Thou elvish-mark'd, abortive, rooting hog! Thou that wast seal'd in thy nativity The slave of nature and the son of hell!
quotations.speaker: Queen Margaret
quotations.context: Cursing Richard in front of the whole Yorkist court, which has been trying to ignore her.
quotations.analysis: 'Rooting hog' is his own badge, the white boar, turned into an insult, and 'seal'd in thy nativity' claims that his body was a signature written at birth. Richard's answer is to wait for her to finish and then substitute her name for his at the end of the curse — the only way anyone in the play ever interrupts her.

quotations.text: Why strew'st thou sugar on that bottled spider, Whose deadly web ensnareth thee about? Fool, fool! thou whet'st a knife to kill thyself.
quotations.speaker: Queen Margaret
quotations.context: To Queen Elizabeth, who has just tried to make peace in the quarrel.
quotations.analysis: Margaret is right about everything and heard by nobody, which is her function until Act IV, when Elizabeth comes to her to be taught this vocabulary. The same 'bottled spider' returns from Elizabeth's own mouth in 4.4, quoted almost exactly — the play keeps a record of who was listening.

quotations.text: And thus I clothe my naked villany With old odd ends stolen out of holy writ; And seem a saint, when most I play the devil.
quotations.speaker: Gloucester
quotations.context: Alone after the quarrel scene, explaining his method to the audience.
quotations.analysis: He describes piety as a costume made of offcuts, and the verb 'play' places the whole performance in a theatre. This is a confession no other character will ever hear, and it arrives fifty lines after he has publicly forgiven his enemies for the injuries he invented.

quotations.text: Thus, like the formal vice, Iniquity, I moralize two meanings in one word.
quotations.speaker: Gloucester
quotations.context: An aside, after telling the young prince that fame lives long without characters.
quotations.analysis: He names his own theatrical ancestry: the Vice of the morality plays, who joked with the audience while damning the hero. 'Moralize' means to draw out a meaning, and he is boasting that he can do it twice at once — one meaning for the boy, the other for us.

quotations.text: Off with his head! Now, by Saint Paul I swear, I will not dine until I see the same.
quotations.speaker: Gloucester
quotations.context: At the council table, moments after asking the Bishop of Ely for strawberries.
quotations.analysis: The domestic detail is the horror: an execution is fitted into the gap before lunch, and the oath is sworn on a saint. Hastings has spoken one cautious conditional — 'if they have done this thing' — and the word 'if' is treated as the treason.

quotations.text: O momentary grace of mortal men, Which we more hunt for than the grace of God! Who builds his hopes in air of your good looks, Lives like a drunken sailor on a mast, Ready, with every nod, to tumble down Into the fatal bowels of the deep.
quotations.speaker: Hastings
quotations.context: On the way to the block, an hour after gloating over the executions at Pomfret.
quotations.analysis: The image is exact about what he got wrong: a sailor high on a mast can see further than anybody on deck and is still the first to fall. 'Nod' does double work — the roll of the ship and the small movement of a great man's head — so favour and shipwreck become the same gesture.

quotations.text: Tut, I can counterfeit the deep tragedian; Speak and look back, and pry on every side, Tremble and start at wagging of a straw, Intending deep suspicion
quotations.speaker: Buckingham
quotations.context: Answering Richard's question about whether he can act frightened, just before the mayor arrives.
quotations.analysis: Two men openly rehearse a piece of political theatre in front of the audience, and then perform it badly on purpose so that the citizens will believe it. 'Intending' here means stretching or pretending, and the vocabulary throughout is an actor's: counterfeit, tragedian, offices, stratagems.

quotations.text: I am not in the giving vein to-day.
quotations.speaker: King Richard III
quotations.context: Cutting off Buckingham, who has asked for the earldom he was promised.
quotations.analysis: One flat line of prose rhythm inside the verse ends a partnership that has run since Act I. 'Vein' is a mood and also a blood vessel, and the joke is that Buckingham has just declined to spill any; the alliance ends not in a quarrel but in a change of subject.

quotations.text: 'Lo, thus' quoth Dighton, 'lay those tender babes:' 'Thus, thus,' quoth Forrest, 'girdling one another Within their innocent alabaster arms: Their lips were four red roses on a stalk, Which in their summer beauty kiss'd each other.
quotations.speaker: Tyrrel
quotations.context: Reporting the murder of the princes, which he arranged but did not watch.
quotations.analysis: The play's most terrible act is reported at two removes, by a man quoting the murderers quoting each other, and the language is the prettiest in the play. 'Four red roses on a stalk' puts the Lancastrian emblem on two Yorkist children, which is the civil war reduced to the size of two sleeping boys.

quotations.text: Bloody thou art, bloody will be thy end; Shame serves thy life and doth thy death attend.
quotations.speaker: Duchess of York
quotations.context: The last words Richard's mother speaks to him, as he marches out to meet Richmond.
quotations.analysis: A rhymed couplet from a mother is a formal withdrawal of blessing, and the chiasmus of blood at either end of the first line makes his beginning and his end the same substance. He has had the drums sounded through her speech, so the audience hears it over noise he ordered.

quotations.text: Is the chair empty? is the sword unsway'd? Is the king dead? the empire unpossess'd? What heir of York is there alive but we?
quotations.speaker: King Richard III
quotations.context: On being told that Richmond is at sea, coming to claim the crown.
quotations.analysis: Four questions in two lines, all of them rhetorical, all of them asked by a man who took the chair by proving it was empty when it was not. He has become the legitimacy he used to dismantle, and the argument he now makes is the one his victims could have made against him.

quotations.text: What do I fear? myself? there's none else by: Richard loves Richard; that is, I am I. Is there a murderer here? No. Yes, I am: Then fly. What, from myself?
quotations.speaker: King Richard III
quotations.context: Waking in his tent at midnight after the ghosts have visited.
quotations.analysis: The soliloquy that was always a performance for us becomes a quarrel with no audience at all, and the syntax splits into question and answer as though two people were speaking. 'I am I' should be the most secure sentence in the language; here it is the last thing he can get to hold still.

quotations.text: My conscience hath a thousand several tongues, And every tongue brings in a several tale, And every tale condemns me for a villain.
quotations.speaker: King Richard III
quotations.context: The same speech, a few lines later.
quotations.analysis: The word he chose for himself in the first scene is now the verdict returned against him, and by a court made entirely of voices. Repetition of 'every' turns conscience into a crowd, which is the first time in the play that Richard is outnumbered in a room.

quotations.text: Conscience is but a word that cowards use, Devised at first to keep the strong in awe: Our strong arms be our conscience, swords our law.
quotations.speaker: King Richard III
quotations.context: Addressing his officers on the morning of Bosworth, a hundred lines after the nightmare.
quotations.analysis: He is arguing with the speech he made in the night, in public, in front of men who did not hear it. The claim that conscience was invented to control the powerful is a political theory, and he advances it a few hours before dying on a field where every ghost has voted the other way.

quotations.text: A horse! a horse! my kingdom for a horse!
quotations.speaker: King Richard III
quotations.context: Unhorsed in the field, hunting for Richmond among the decoys.
quotations.analysis: The most quoted line in the play is an offer to trade everything he has killed for back for a single animal, and it is spoken twice within seven lines, so the second time it is not rhetoric. Catesby offers to fetch a horse and Richard refuses, because what he wants is not escape but Richmond.

quotations.text: We will unite the white rose and the red: Smile heaven upon this fair conjunction, That long have frown'd upon their enmity!
quotations.speaker: Richmond
quotations.context: The closing speech, with the crown newly taken from Richard's body.
quotations.analysis: The settlement is announced rather than shown: the bride is a woman who never appears on stage and the peace is described in the future tense throughout. After five acts of a man who told the audience the truth and lied to everyone else, the play ends with a public statement nobody is invited to examine.

quotations.text: England hath long been mad, and scarr'd herself; The brother blindly shed the brother's blood, The father rashly slaughter'd his own son, The son, compell'd, been butcher to the sire
quotations.speaker: Richmond
quotations.context: Summing up the wars, a few lines before the play ends.
quotations.analysis: The lines summarise not just this play but the three Henry VI plays before it, and the father-and-son image is lifted almost directly from a scene in the last of them. The country is given a body that has been wounding itself, which is the only diagnosis the tetralogy offers for civil war.

atAGlance.label: Written
atAGlance.note: It completes the sequence begun by the three Henry VI plays, and assumes an audience that knows them.

atAGlance.label: First printed
atAGlance.note: A quarto printed by Valentine Simmes for Andrew Wise, with no author named. The 1598 second quarto adds Shakespeare's name.

atAGlance.label: Chief sources
atAGlance.note: Thomas More's hostile life of Richard reached Shakespeare through the Tudor chronicles, already shaped into a villain.

atAGlance.label: Two texts
atAGlance.note: The Folio text is longer and differs from the quarto tradition throughout; the relationship between them is still an open editorial question.

criticalViews.position: A providential history
criticalViews.summary: The reading that takes Margaret's curses at face value: the play traces a pattern of retribution running back through the Henry VI plays and closing with the Tudor marriage, so that Richard is the instrument by which England is scourged and cleansed.
criticalViews.counter: It has to explain why the scourge gets the best lines, the jokes and the audience's attention for four acts.

criticalViews.position: A play about political theatre
criticalViews.summary: On this account the subject is the manufacture of consent: the staged arrest, the fake emergency at 3.5, the rehearsed refusal at 3.7, and the citizens who say nothing. Tyranny here works in public and depends on witnesses agreeing to be an audience.
criticalViews.counter: The last act abandons that interest almost completely for ghosts, dreams and a battle, which is a strange way to end a play about spin.

criticalViews.position: Richard as a role rather than a character
criticalViews.summary: Criticism has long treated the part as an inheritance from the morality-play Vice, a job of work for a virtuoso actor, which is why its stage history is a history of performers rather than of interpretations.
criticalViews.counter: It underrates 5.3, where the play insists on giving the role an interior at exactly the moment the performance stops.

criticalViews.position: Deformity, and who is doing the describing
criticalViews.summary: Disability criticism has examined how consistently the play lets Richard's body be read as a moral text — by Margaret, by the Duchess, and by Richard himself — and asked whether the play endorses that reading or exhibits it.
criticalViews.counter: Richard supplies most of the descriptions himself, which makes it hard to separate the play's view from his performance of one.

essayQuestions.question: How does Shakespeare make an audience enjoy the company of a murderer?
essayQuestions.focus: Direct address, humour and complicity
plan: Start with the structural fact: Richard speaks first, alone, and briefs us before the plot begins.
Analyse the jokes — the Vice comparison at 3.1, the two-meaning asides, the flat dismissal of Anne at 1.2.242.
Show how dramatic irony makes the audience an insider at every scene of trust, from Clarence to Hastings.
Mark the withdrawal: once Richard is crowned the soliloquies stop, and the murders arrive by report instead.
Conclude on 5.3, where he talks to himself because there is nobody else, and ask what the play has done to us by then.

essayQuestions.question: What is the function of the women in the play?
essayQuestions.focus: Lament, memory and the limits of Richard's method
plan: Begin with Margaret's anomalous presence: historically absent, dramatically indispensable as the play's memory.
Trace the curses of 1.3 through Rivers at Pomfret, Hastings on the block and Buckingham at Salisbury.
Read 4.4 as a formal set piece — matched laments, shared arithmetic of dead sons — that Richard cannot interrupt.
Compare the two wooing scenes, and weigh the case that Elizabeth is playing for time rather than consenting.
Decide whether the women are the play's moral centre or its chorus, and what difference that makes to the ending.

essayQuestions.question: 'The play is about theatre, not about history.' Discuss.
essayQuestions.focus: Performance, staging and the Tudor settlement
plan: Collect the play's own theatrical vocabulary: counterfeit, tragedian, vice, plot, induction, stratagem.
Analyse 3.5 and 3.7 as staged productions with scripts, props, cues and a silent audience of citizens.
Set against this the historical apparatus — the chroniclers, the tetralogy, the marriage that closes it.
Test the claim on Act V, which replaces performance with dreams, ghosts and a battle.
Conclude on Richmond, who makes a public statement no one is allowed to examine, and ask which mode wins.

essayQuestions.question: How far does the play invite sympathy for Richard?
essayQuestions.focus: Deformity, self-description and the nightmare
plan: Open with the problem of evidence: nearly everything said about Richard's body is said by Richard or by his enemies.
Read the opening soliloquy as self-presentation rather than confession, noting 'descant' and 'determined'.
Weigh Margaret's and the Duchess's language against his own, and ask whether the play shares their view.
Examine 5.3 closely: the first speech in which he is not in control of who is talking.
Conclude on the difference between sympathy, fascination and complicity, and which of the three the play actually produces.

discussionQuestions: Richard tells us his plan in the first forty lines. Why is the play still suspenseful?
Anne accepts the ring of the man who killed her husband and her father-in-law. Is that scene believable, and does it need to be?
Margaret has no legal standing, no power and no business being in England. What does the play lose if a production cuts her, as many have?
The princes are murdered offstage and described in some of the play's loveliest language. Why that choice?
Richmond has almost no interiority at all. Is that a failure of the writing or a deliberate contrast?

timeline.label: Tewkesbury, and the death of Henry VI
timeline.detail: Two killings the play keeps returning to: Prince Edward at the battle and his father in the Tower.

timeline.label: Edward IV dies and Richard takes the throne
timeline.detail: The events of Acts II to IV are compressed from a few months of this year.

timeline.label: Bosworth Field
timeline.detail: Richard is killed on 22 August and Henry Tudor is crowned; the Wars of the Roses are conventionally dated from here to their end.

timeline.label: Thomas More's history of Richard III printed
timeline.detail: Written decades earlier and left unfinished, it supplied the Tudor chroniclers with the calculating, theatrical Richard Shakespeare inherited.

timeline.label: Holinshed's Chronicles reissued
timeline.detail: Shakespeare's immediate source, which carries More's account through Hall into the material of the play.

timeline.label: The True Tragedy of Richard the Third printed
timeline.detail: An anonymous play on the same story, evidence that Richard was already established stage material.

timeline.label: First quarto
timeline.detail: Printed by Valentine Simmes for Andrew Wise, and reprinted repeatedly over the next four decades.

timeline.label: Second quarto names Shakespeare
timeline.detail: The first of his plays to be widely reprinted in his lifetime carries his name from this edition onwards.

timeline.label: First Folio
timeline.detail: A substantially different and longer text, printed among the histories.

timeline.label: Colley Cibber's adaptation
timeline.detail: A shortened rewriting that cut Margaret altogether and held the English stage for the best part of two centuries.

timeline.label: Garrick's debut as Richard
timeline.detail: The role made his name in London, and made the part an actor's proving ground.

timeline.label: Edmund Kean's Richard at Drury Lane
timeline.detail: A fast, unheroic reading that became the standard against which nineteenth-century Richards were measured.

timeline.label: Laurence Olivier's film
timeline.detail: Still using much of Cibber's shape, it fixed the opening soliloquy in the popular ear for a century of listeners.

timeline.label: Richard III's remains found in Leicester
timeline.detail: The skeleton showed severe scoliosis, reopening old arguments about how much of the play's body is Tudor invention.

places.name: The Tower of London
places.note: Clarence's cell, the princes' lodging, and the council chamber where Hastings is condemned.

places.name: London
places.note: The streets, the palace and Baynard's Castle, where Richard performs his refusal of the crown.

places.name: Pontefract Castle

places.name: Bosworth Field
places.note: The two tents, the ghosts and the battle in which Richard is killed.

related.why: Richard's first long soliloquy is there, and this play begins in the middle of a conversation started in it.
The other deposition play, and the opposite temperament: a king who cannot stop talking about himself and has no plan at all.
A later study of the same material — a usurper, a prophecy and a battlefield — with the jokes and the audience's company taken away.
Another history built around a child in the way of a crown, and a man who hesitates over the order to remove him.
The other Shakespearean study of a leader who understands that ruling is partly a performance, and is admired for it.

books.title: Robinson Crusoe
books.author: Daniel Defoe
books.setting: York, the Barbary coast, Brazil, and an uninhabited island near the mouth of the Orinoco, between 1651 and 1687
books.lengthNote: Around 121,000 words; the familiar twenty chapters are an editorial convenience, since the first edition ran without them
books.openingLine: I was born in the year 1632, in the city of York, of a good family, though not of that country
books.summary: A young man who will not stay in the middle station of life is enslaved at Salé, prospers in Brazil, joins a voyage to buy Africans and is wrecked alone for twenty-eight years. Most of the book is work: salvage, fencing, baking, pottery, a canoe he cannot move to the water. Defoe makes an account-book out of a life, and the same habit that counts the goatskins also counts the mercies and calls the total Providence.

sourceText.label: Standard Ebooks text of Robinson Crusoe
sourceText.note: A proofed transcription with modernised spelling. References give the chapter numbers of this reading text; the chapter division is editorial, since the 1719 edition prints the narrative continuously.

structure.label: Chapters I–III
structure.title: York, Salé and the Brazilian plantation
structure.summary: Crusoe leaves against his father’s advice, is wrecked within days of his first voyage and goes to sea again anyway. Captured by a Salé rover, he escapes in a boat with a boy called Xury, sells him to the Portuguese captain who rescues them both, and becomes a planter in Brazil. He is prosperous and bored when he agrees to fetch enslaved Africans from Guinea.

scenes.title: Start in Life
scenes.summary: The father’s argument for the middle station, the storm off Yarmouth, and the obstinacy that survives it.

scenes.title: Slavery and Escape
scenes.summary: Two years a slave at Salé, then a stolen boat, the African coast and a Portuguese ship bound for Brazil.

scenes.title: Wrecked on a Desert Island
scenes.summary: Xury is sold, the plantation thrives, and a voyage for slaves ends on a sandbank; Crusoe alone reaches the shore.

structure.label: Chapters IV–V
structure.title: The wreck, the raft and the dated record
structure.summary: Eleven trips to the wreck bring off tools, guns, powder, ink and money he laughs at and keeps. He builds a fortified dwelling, notches a post to hold the calendar, draws up a ledger of evil against good, and then starts the narrative again from the beginning in the form of a dated journal, so the same months are told twice at two distances.

scenes.title: First Weeks on the Island
scenes.summary: Salvage, the tent under the hill, and the balance sheet of comforts against miseries.

scenes.title: Builds a House — The Journal
scenes.summary: The dated journal opens on 30 September 1659 and runs until the ink begins to fail.

structure.label: Chapters VI–VIII
structure.title: Fever, tobacco and a Bible opened at random
structure.summary: An earthquake and then a long fever break the routine. Crusoe dreams of a figure with a flame about him, steeps tobacco in rum, opens a Bible at a verse about the day of trouble and dates his deliverance from that reading rather than from any rescue. The barley he first called a miracle is traced back to a bag he shook out himself.

scenes.title: Ill and Conscience-Stricken
scenes.summary: The fever, the dream, the tobacco cure and the first prayer he calls sincere.

scenes.title: Agricultural Experience
scenes.summary: Seasons learned by loss, seed hoarded, and a survey of the island that leaves him lord of all he sees.

scenes.title: Surveys His Position
scenes.summary: The calendar corrected, the Sabbath kept, and a settled comparison between this life and the one he led before.

structure.label: Chapters IX–X
structure.title: Work, failure and a second dwelling
structure.summary: The middle of the book is a record of processes: a canoe too heavy to launch, earthenware discovered by accident in the ashes, bread made from grinding to baking, goats tamed and penned. Defoe gives as much space to the failures as to the successes, which is what separates the whole novel from every abridgement of it.

scenes.title: A Boat
scenes.summary: A canoe hollowed out over months and left where it lies; the country house, the grapes, the parrot.

scenes.title: Tames Goats
scenes.summary: Pottery, a grindstone, a flock of his own, and a coasting voyage that nearly carries him out to sea for good.

structure.label: Chapters XI–XIII
structure.title: One footprint, and fifteen years of fear
structure.summary: A single print in the sand undoes twenty years of security. Crusoe fortifies, hides his goats, plans massacres and argues himself out of them on the ground that the cannibals have committed no crime against him. The chapters are a long study of what fear does to a man who has nobody to check his reasoning.

scenes.title: Finds Print of Man’s Foot on the Sand
scenes.summary: The print, the thunderstruck stop, and two years of broken sleep.

scenes.title: A Cave Retreat
scenes.summary: The bones on the shore, the plan to kill, and the argument that stops him.

scenes.title: Wreck of a Spanish Ship
scenes.summary: A second wreck, more salvage, and the wish for one companion that shapes the rest of the book.

structure.label: Chapters XIV–XVI
structure.title: Friday, and an island with subjects on it
structure.summary: Crusoe dreams of rescuing a prisoner who will serve him, and then does it. Friday is named for a date, taught to say Master before he is taught anything else, and converted — until he asks why God does not simply kill the devil. By the time a Spaniard and Friday’s father arrive, Crusoe is describing himself as lord and lawgiver of three subjects and three religions.

scenes.title: A Dream Realised
scenes.summary: The dream of a servant, the pursuit across the sand, and the token of submission Friday offers on the beach.

scenes.title: Friday’s Education
scenes.summary: Language, clothes, roast meat instead of human flesh, and a theological question Crusoe cannot answer.

scenes.title: Rescue of Prisoners from Cannibals
scenes.summary: The Spaniard and Friday’s father are saved; the island acquires a population and a constitution.

structure.label: Chapters XVII–XX
structure.title: The mutiny, the passage home and the reckoning
structure.summary: An English ship arrives with a captain and his officers about to be marooned by their own crew. Crusoe presents himself as the island’s governor, takes the ship, and sails after twenty-eight years to find that the Brazilian plantation has been making him rich in his absence. The last chapter crosses the Pyrenees in snow and ends with wolves, which is the book refusing to finish on the beach.

scenes.title: Visit of Mutineers
scenes.summary: Three men set ashore, the captain rescued, and a governor invented for the occasion.

scenes.title: The Ship Recovered
scenes.summary: The ship retaken, the ringleader hanged at the yardarm, and the worst of the mutineers left on the island in Crusoe’s place.

scenes.title: Return to England
scenes.summary: Lisbon, the old Portuguese captain, and an estate that has quietly accumulated for two decades.

scenes.title: Fight Between Friday and a Bear
scenes.summary: The overland journey through the Pyrenees, a wolf pack, and a promise of a second part.

characters.name: Robinson Crusoe
characters.role: Merchant, planter, slave, castaway, and self-appointed governor
characters.summary: A man who narrates his own life twice over: once as it happened and once as he later decides it should be understood. He is practical, repetitive and exhaustive about work, and equally exhaustive about accounting for his soul, using the same arithmetic of loss and gain for both.
characters.clue: He notches a post to keep the date, draws up his miseries and comforts in two columns like a ledger, and calls an island he never leaves for twenty-eight years his own property.

relationships.label: rescued and dealt fairly with by

characters.name: Crusoe’s father
characters.role: A merchant of Bremen settled at York
characters.summary: He appears for one speech and is quoted for the rest of the book. His case for the middle station — fewest disasters, fewest distempers, peace and plenty — is the standard against which Crusoe measures every subsequent calamity, usually while calling himself a warning to others.

characters.name: Xury
characters.role: A boy enslaved with Crusoe at Salé
characters.summary: He escapes with Crusoe, keeps watch through the nights on the African coast, offers to go ashore first and be shot first, and is sold within a chapter for sixty pieces of eight. Defoe records Crusoe’s reluctance and the terms of the sale in the same sentence, which is as close as the book comes to an admission.
characters.clue: He promises to be faithful and go all over the world with the man who then sells him to a Portuguese captain, with freedom offered in ten years if he turns Christian.

characters.name: The Portuguese captain
characters.role: The master who picks Crusoe up off the African coast
characters.summary: The one figure in the book who is repeatedly generous without calculation: he takes nothing for the passage, buys the boat at a price Crusoe does not set, and twenty years later hands over the Brazilian accounts to the penny. Defoe uses him as evidence that honest dealing is possible, and therefore that its absence elsewhere is a choice.

characters.name: Friday
characters.role: A prisoner rescued from cannibals on the shore
characters.summary: He is given a name from the calendar, taught the word Master before he is taught yes and no, and shown enormous affection within a relationship he never had the option of refusing. He is also the only character who asks Crusoe a question he cannot answer, and the book lets that stand.
characters.clue: Named after the day of his rescue, taught to call his rescuer Master, and the one person who asks why God does not simply kill the devil.

characters.name: Friday’s father
characters.role: An old prisoner saved from the canoe
characters.summary: His arrival turns the island from a household into a settlement and gives Friday the one relationship that is not owed to Crusoe. The reunion is the most straightforwardly felt scene in the book, and Crusoe reports it with some surprise at the strength of a feeling he has not arranged.

characters.name: The Spaniard
characters.role: A survivor of the wrecked ship, saved from the same canoe
characters.summary: He brings news that sixteen more of his countrymen are living on the mainland, and with him the island becomes a colonial question rather than a solitary one: who feeds them, who governs them, and on what terms they may be brought over. Crusoe draws up conditions before he will allow it.

characters.name: The English captain
characters.role: Master of the ship taken by mutineers
characters.summary: His arrival converts Crusoe’s private kingdom into something with a flag: the captain is told he is dealing with the governor, and the fiction is maintained through the whole recapture. He supplies the means of rescue and, in return, legitimacy for a claim Crusoe has been making to himself for years.

themes.name: Providence and interpretation
themes.summary: The book is less interested in whether God intervenes than in how Crusoe reads events. Barley springs up and is a miracle until he remembers the bag; an earthquake is a judgement until the fever supplies a better one. Defoe keeps the event, the first reading and the later reading visibly separate, so belief is shown being made rather than simply held.
themes.development: Warnings ignored in the storms of Chapters I–II, a conversion dated to a verse opened at random in Chapter VI, and a settled providential account of the whole life by Chapter XIV.

themes.name: Work and property
themes.summary: Crusoe turns survival into ownership: what he has made or fenced or fed becomes his, and the island follows. The novel gives unusual space to unsuccessful work — a canoe he cannot launch, a ruined first harvest, pots that collapse — so the claim to possession is built visibly out of hours rather than asserted.
themes.development: Salvage first, then manufacture, then agriculture and livestock; by Chapter IX he calls himself lord of the whole manor, and by Chapter XVI lord and lawgiver over people.

themes.name: Solitude and company
themes.summary: Twenty-four years pass before another human being is added, and the loneliness is described mostly through its substitutes: the parrot taught his own name, the dog at the table, the journal addressed to nobody. What Crusoe wants is not conversation but a servant, and the book grants that wish exactly.
themes.development: Comfort in routine, then terror at the footprint, then a dream of rescuing a man who will serve him — and the dream is what actually happens.

themes.name: Slavery, service and empire
themes.summary: Crusoe is enslaved at Salé, sells Xury, is wrecked on a voyage to buy Africans, and ends with three subjects of three religions and a fleet of settlers to place. The novel neither hides this sequence nor comments on it; the connections are all in the plot, waiting for a reader to make them.
themes.development: Slave in Chapter II, slave-trader in Chapter III, master in Chapter XIV, governor and proprietor by Chapter XVIII.

themes.name: Fear and its arithmetic
themes.summary: The footprint changes nothing material and everything else: the same island, the same stores, fifteen years of bad sleep. Defoe is precise about how fear reasons — it plans massacres, invents enemies, and then has to be argued down by an appeal to law and jurisdiction that Crusoe constructs himself.
themes.development: Storms and drowning at first, then the sea, then other people; the last fear is the ordinary one of losing the money he has accumulated by post.

themes.name: Keeping the account
themes.summary: Crusoe counts everything: days on a post, seeds, goats, pieces of eight, mercies against afflictions in two columns. The novel is written in the idiom of a merchant’s books, and it takes the form seriously enough to let the ink run out and the journal stop, which is a limit no spiritual autobiography would admit.
themes.development: The tally-post, the ledger of evil and good, the dated journal, and finally the Lisbon accounts that pay out eight-and-twenty years of profits.

techniques.name: Retrospective first person
techniques.definition: A narrator telling their own earlier life, with the distance between the two selves doing the judging.
techniques.bookDefinition: A narrator recounting his own past with the benefit of knowing how it ended.
techniques.inThisBook: Crusoe repeatedly corrects his younger self — what he then took for a miracle, what he now sees was a bag of chicken feed — so the book contains its own commentary.

techniques.name: The interpolated journal
techniques.definition: A dated record set inside a continuous narrative, covering ground the narrative has already told.
techniques.bookDefinition: A dated record set inside a continuous narrative, covering ground the narrative has already told.
techniques.inThisBook: Chapter V begins the island story again from 30 September 1659 at a different distance, and the two accounts of the same months can be read against each other.

techniques.name: Circumstantial realism
techniques.definition: Conviction produced by the quantity and dullness of physical detail.
techniques.bookDefinition: Conviction produced by the quantity and dullness of physical detail.
techniques.inThisBook: Eleven trips to the wreck, the exact list of what each raft carried, the months spent on a canoe that is never launched: the novel is persuasive because it is willing to be tedious.

techniques.name: Providential reading
techniques.definition: Treating events as a message and looking for what they are meant to teach.
techniques.bookDefinition: Treating events as a message and looking for what they are meant to teach.
techniques.inThisBook: A Bible opened at random supplies the date of his conversion, and thereafter every deliverance is entered on the credit side of a spiritual account.

techniques.name: Self-justification
techniques.definition: Reasoning conducted to license a course of action already wanted.
techniques.bookDefinition: Reasoning conducted to license a course of action already wanted.
techniques.inThisBook: The argument that the cannibals have committed no crime against him stops a massacre; the same faculty finds no difficulty at all in the sale of Xury.

techniques.name: The inventory
techniques.definition: A list of goods used as narrative rather than as background.
techniques.bookDefinition: A list of goods used as narrative rather than as background.
techniques.inThisBook: Tools, powder, clothes, money and Bibles are counted off the wreck, and the running stock-take doubles as the measure of how far the island has been turned into an estate.

quotations.text: I was born in the year 1632, in the city of York, of a good family, though not of that country, my father being a foreigner of Bremen
quotations.context: The first sentence of the book.
quotations.analysis: Year, city, family standing and the father’s country of origin, in that order: the opening is the form a deposition or a parish record takes, not the form a story takes. Defoe buys credit with it before a single event has happened, and many first readers spent it on believing the book was true.

quotations.text: the middle station of life was calculated for all kind of virtue and all kind of enjoyments; that peace and plenty were the handmaids of a middle fortune
quotations.context: Crusoe’s father arguing against a life at sea, in the one long speech he is given.
quotations.analysis: The father does not moralise; he makes an actuarial case, listing the distempers and vicissitudes that fall on the ranks above and below. The word ‘calculated’ gives the game away — virtue here is a matter of exposure and risk, and Crusoe spends the rest of the book proving his father’s figures right.

quotations.text: But my ill fate pushed me on now with an obstinacy that nothing could resist; and though I had several times loud calls from my reason and my more composed judgment to go home, yet I had no power to do it.
quotations.context: After the wreck off Yarmouth, going on to London by land rather than home to York.
quotations.analysis: He describes a compulsion and simultaneously reports that his reason was calling him home, so the sentence holds both explanations — fate, and a man choosing. Defoe uses that doubleness throughout: Crusoe is never so determined by Providence that he is not also answerable.

quotations.text: He offered me also sixty pieces of eight more for my boy Xury, which I was loth to take; not that I was unwilling to let the captain have him, but I was very loth to sell the poor boy’s liberty, who had assisted me so
quotations.context: The Portuguese captain’s offer, after the boy has spent weeks keeping watch on the African coast.
quotations.analysis: The reluctance and the price are in the same sentence, and the price wins. Crusoe records that he was loth to sell the boy’s liberty, which shows he knows exactly what is being sold; the transaction is entered in the narrative with the same care as the eighty pieces of eight for the boat.

quotations.text: he would give the boy an obligation to set him free in ten years, if he turned Christian: upon this, and Xury saying he was willing to go to him, I let the captain have him.
quotations.context: The terms on which Crusoe agrees to let the captain have Xury.
quotations.analysis: Conversion is made a condition of freedom, and the deal satisfies Crusoe’s conscience completely. Read this beside Friday, who is taught to say Master before he is taught yes and no: the book uses the same settlement twice and calls it kindness both times.

quotations.text: I stated very impartially, like debtor and creditor, the comforts I enjoyed against the miseries I suffered
quotations.context: Setting out his situation in two columns after the first weeks ashore.
quotations.analysis: The simile is not decorative: what follows is literally ruled into evil and good, item against item, cast off wretched against alive when the rest drowned. A merchant’s habit is applied to the state of a soul, and the comfort Crusoe draws from it comes from the form rather than from anything in the entries.

quotations.text: September 30, 1659⁠—I, poor miserable Robinson Crusoe, being shipwrecked during a dreadful storm in the offing, came on shore on this dismal, unfortunate island, which I called “The Island of Despair”; all the rest of the ship’s company being drowned, and myself almost dead.
quotations.context: The opening entry of the journal, written up later but dated to the day of the wreck.
quotations.analysis: The entry is dated to a day on which he had neither ink nor the heart to write, so the journal is a reconstruction pretending to be immediate. Naming the place is the first act of possession in the book, and the name he gives it will be quietly dropped as the island becomes an estate.

quotations.text: I began to suggest that God had miraculously caused His grain to grow without any help of seed sown, and that it was so directed purely for my sustenance on that wild, miserable place.
quotations.context: Finding green barley stalks growing near his fortification.
quotations.analysis: The reasoning is careful — no seed was sown, therefore the cause is supernatural, therefore it is directed at him — and every step of it is sound except the first. Defoe shows a man deriving personal providence from an incomplete inventory of his own actions.

quotations.text: At last it occurred to my thoughts that I shook a bag of chickens’ meat out in that place; and then the wonder began to cease; and I must confess my religious thankfulness to God’s providence began to abate, too
quotations.context: Remembering, a little later, what he emptied out at that spot.
quotations.analysis: The correction is the most interesting sentence in the religious argument of the book, and Defoe lets Crusoe admit that his thankfulness abated with the wonder. Nothing is retracted — he goes on to say the hand of Providence was in it anyway — but the reader has now watched the machinery of a miracle being dismantled and rebuilt.

quotations.text: “Call on Me in the day of trouble, and I will deliver thee, and thou shalt glorify Me.”
quotations.context: The verse he lights on when he opens a Bible during the fever.
quotations.analysis: He opens the book casually, as he says, and the method is the one Betteredge uses with Robinson Crusoe itself in The Moonstone a century and a half later. Crusoe dates his deliverance from this reading rather than from any rescue, so the turning point of the novel is an act of interpretation.

quotations.text: I was king and lord of all this country indefensibly, and had a right of possession; and if I could convey it, I might have it in inheritance as completely as any lord of a manor in England.
quotations.context: Surveying the fertile side of the island for the first time.
quotations.analysis: Title, possession and inheritance arrive in one breath, and the legal vocabulary is exact: indefeasible right, conveyance, a manor in England. Crusoe cannot convey it to anybody and says so, which makes the claim a piece of pure form — ownership asserted because there is nobody present to dispute it.

quotations.text: how much more happy this life I now led was, with all its miserable circumstances, than the wicked, cursed, abominable life I led all the past part of my days
quotations.context: Reviewing his condition after the conversion, with the calendar and the Sabbath restored.
quotations.analysis: The comparison is between two lives and not two places, and it is the argument the whole island section rests on: solitude with belief is preferable to society without it. Defoe needs this settled before the footprint arrives, because everything after Chapter XI tests it.

quotations.text: I was lord of the whole manor; or, if I pleased, I might call myself king or emperor over the whole country which I had possession of: there were no rivals; I had no competitor, none to dispute sovereignty or command with me
quotations.context: Reflecting on how little his stores of corn and goats actually mean to him.
quotations.analysis: The passage climbs from manor to king to emperor and then collapses, because sovereignty with no rivals is indistinguishable from having nothing. Defoe puts the emptiness and the grandeur in the same sentence, and the reflection that follows — that he had nothing to covet — is the nearest the novel comes to contentment.

quotations.text: I was exceedingly surprised with the print of a man’s naked foot on the shore, which was very plain to be seen on the sand. I stood like one thunderstruck, or as if I had seen an apparition.
quotations.context: Walking towards his boat about noon, fifteen years into his stay.
quotations.analysis: Everything hangs on the singular: one print, and no others, which is why it cannot be explained and cannot be ignored. Defoe surrounds it with sober detail — about noon, very plain to be seen — and the effect of that plainness is the most frightening moment in eighteenth-century English fiction.

quotations.text: they were national, and I ought to leave them to the justice of God, who is the Governor of nations, and knows how, by national punishments, to make a just retribution for national offences
quotations.context: Arguing himself out of a plan to ambush and kill the cannibals.
quotations.analysis: The reasoning is jurisdictional: these are national crimes, so they belong to a court he is not sitting in. It is the best moral thinking Crusoe does in the book, and it should be set against Chapter III, where the same faculty found no difficulty whatever in selling a boy.

quotations.text: I have been, in all my circumstances, a memento to those who are touched with the general plague of mankind, whence, for aught I know, one half of their miseries flow
quotations.context: Looking back over the whole course of his life from the settled island.
quotations.analysis: He offers himself as an exhibit, which is what a providential autobiography is supposed to do, and names the disease as discontent with one’s station. The claim sits oddly beside a narrator who is at that moment fortifying an island he has declared his own property.

quotations.text: kissed the ground, and laid his head upon the ground, and taking me by the foot, set my foot upon his head; this, it seems, was in token of swearing to be my slave forever.
quotations.context: On the shore, immediately after the rescue.
quotations.analysis: Crusoe reports the gesture and supplies its meaning in the same breath — ‘this, it seems’ — although he has no language in common with the man making it. The relationship is therefore interpreted into existence by the person it benefits, before a single word has been exchanged.

quotations.text: I let him know his name should be Friday, which was the day I saved his life; I called him so for the memory of the time. I likewise taught him to say “Master”; and then let him know that was to be my name
quotations.context: The first lesson, on the way back to the fortification.
quotations.analysis: A man is named after a date in Crusoe’s calendar, and the second word he is taught is the name of his owner; yes and no come afterwards. The order of instruction is the whole relationship, and Defoe sets it down without a syllable of comment.

quotations.text: if God much stronger, much might as the wicked devil, why God no kill the devil, so make him no more do wicked?”
quotations.context: Friday’s reply during a lesson on the devil and temptation.
quotations.analysis: The question is the oldest difficulty in Christian apologetics, put by a man who has been learning English for a few months, and Crusoe admits he was strangely surprised and ill qualified to answer. It is the only argument in the book that the narrator loses.

quotations.text: My island was now peopled, and I thought myself very rich in subjects; and it was a merry reflection, which I frequently made, how like a king I looked. First of all, the whole country was my own property, so that I had an undoubted right of dominion. Secondly, my people were perfectly subjected⁠—I was absolutely lord and lawgiver⁠—they all owed their lives to me, and were ready to lay down their lives, if there had been occasion for it, for me. It was remarkable, too, I had but three subjects, and they were of three different religions⁠—my man Friday was a Protestant, his father was a Pagan and a cannibal, and the Spaniard was a Papist. However, I allowed liberty of conscience throughout my dominions.
quotations.context: With Friday, Friday’s father and the Spaniard all on the island.
quotations.analysis: Three men become dominion, property and a constitutional settlement, complete with liberty of conscience granted from above to a Protestant, a pagan and a Catholic. The passage is offered as a merry reflection, and it is also a precise short description of how a colony describes itself.

quotations.text: And thus I left the island, the 19th of December, as I found by the ship’s account, in the year 1686, after I had been upon it eight-and-twenty years, two months, and nineteen days
quotations.context: Sailing at last, twenty-eight years after the wreck.
quotations.analysis: The great release of the book is given as an arithmetic result to the day, checked against the ship’s account rather than his own post. After a lifetime of counting, the final figure is the only celebration Crusoe permits himself.

atAGlance.label: First published
atAGlance.note: By William Taylor in London, presented as a life written by Crusoe himself.

atAGlance.label: Full first title
atAGlance.value: The Life and Strange Surprizing Adventures of Robinson Crusoe
atAGlance.note: Defoe’s name appears nowhere on it; many first readers took the book for a genuine memoir.

atAGlance.label: Continuations
atAGlance.note: The Farther Adventures followed within months, and Serious Reflections in 1720.

atAGlance.label: Time on the island
atAGlance.note: From 30 September 1659 to 19 December 1686, by the reckoning Crusoe keeps on a post.

criticalViews.position: A spiritual autobiography
criticalViews.summary: The book follows the Dissenting pattern exactly: a warning ignored, a career of disobedience, an affliction, a conversion dated to a text, and a life afterwards read backwards as Providence. On this account the island is a punishment that becomes a mercy.
criticalViews.counter: The form is there, but Defoe keeps showing the reading being constructed — the barley, the abating thankfulness — which a straightforward spiritual autobiography would not risk.

criticalViews.position: The first novel of economic man
criticalViews.summary: Crusoe measures his life in labour, stock and profit; the island is improved rather than merely survived, and the book’s realism is inseparable from its accounting. Much criticism since the 1950s has treated it as the founding text of the novel’s middle-class subject matter.
criticalViews.counter: It risks losing the religion, which is not decoration: Crusoe keeps two sets of books, and he takes the spiritual one at least as seriously.

criticalViews.position: A colonial narrative
criticalViews.summary: The plot moves from being enslaved to selling a boy to being wrecked on a slaving voyage to owning an island and granting its inhabitants liberty of conscience. The sequence is the novel’s own, and Friday’s first English word is Master.
criticalViews.counter: Reading it only as an apology for empire flattens the passages where Crusoe argues himself out of violence, and the book’s unusual willingness to record what the transactions cost.

essayQuestions.question: How does Defoe make an invented life convincing?
essayQuestions.focus: Realism, detail and documentary form
plan: Start with the opening sentence and what its order of information — year, city, family, origins — borrows from record-keeping.
Examine the inventories: eleven trips to the wreck, the goods on each raft, the money he mocks and keeps.
Show how failure earns belief: the canoe that cannot be launched, the first pots, the ruined sowing.
Read the journal as a deliberate formal risk, including the admission that the ink is running out.
Weigh the cost of the method: what a novel gives up in shapeliness to be believed.

essayQuestions.question: ‘Crusoe converts everything he touches into property.’ Discuss.
essayQuestions.focus: Labour, ownership and government
plan: Trace the sequence from salvage to manufacture to agriculture, and the point at which use becomes title.
Read the survey in Chapter VII, where he calls himself king and lord indefeasibly of land he cannot convey.
Set the reflection in Chapter IX — lord of the whole manor, with nothing to covet — against that claim.
Follow the logic into people: three subjects, three religions, liberty of conscience granted from above.
Decide whether the novel endorses the process or simply records it with unusual completeness.

essayQuestions.question: What part does Providence play in the novel, and how far does Crusoe make it himself?
essayQuestions.focus: Belief, interpretation and revision
plan: Distinguish the event, Crusoe’s first reading of it, and the reading he settles on later.
Use the barley and the shaken bag as the clearest case, including the abating thankfulness.
Examine the conversion in Chapter VI: a fever, a dream, tobacco, and a Bible opened casually.
Consider the warnings of Chapters I and II, which are only warnings once the outcome is known.
Conclude on what the novel shows about how a providential account of a life gets written.

essayQuestions.question: How should a reader today handle the novel’s treatment of Xury and Friday?
essayQuestions.focus: Slavery, service and the book’s silences
plan: Set out the plot facts in order: enslaved at Salé, sells Xury, wrecked on a slaving voyage, acquires Friday.
Read the sale of Xury closely, noting that Crusoe records his own reluctance and the price in one sentence.
Examine the order in which Friday is taught English, and what the first two words establish.
Give full weight to Friday’s question about the devil, the one argument Crusoe admits he cannot answer.
Judge how far the novel is aware of the pattern it lays out, and whether awareness would change the reckoning.

discussionQuestions: Defoe spends whole chapters on baking bread and firing pots. What would be lost if they were cut, as they usually are?
Crusoe remembers the bag of chicken feed and his thankfulness abates. Does the novel believe in Providence or in Crusoe’s need for it?
One footprint frightens him for fifteen years. Why is a single print more disturbing than a crowd would be?
Friday is named for a day and taught ‘Master’ before ‘yes’. How much does Defoe see of what he has written down?
The book does not end when the ship arrives; it ends with wolves in the Pyrenees. What is that last chapter for?

timeline.label: Crusoe born at York
timeline.detail: The first sentence of the novel gives the year, the city and his father’s origins in Bremen.

timeline.label: He sails from Hull against his father’s advice
timeline.detail: Dated 1 September 1651 in the text, and wrecked off Yarmouth within days.

timeline.label: Wrecked on the island
timeline.detail: 30 September 1659, the date the journal opens on and the day notched at the head of the post.

timeline.label: Daniel Defoe born in London
timeline.detail: The son of a tallow chandler, educated for the Dissenting ministry and afterwards a merchant, bankrupt and pamphleteer.

timeline.label: Crusoe leaves the island
timeline.detail: 19 December 1686, after eight-and-twenty years, two months and nineteen days.

timeline.label: Defoe pilloried for The Shortest Way with the Dissenters
timeline.detail: A satire taken for the thing it imitated — an early demonstration of how completely he could disappear into a voice.

timeline.label: Alexander Selkirk is put ashore on Juan Fernández
timeline.detail: He was taken off in 1709; his case was widely reported and is the nearest thing the novel has to a documented source.

timeline.label: Robinson Crusoe published
timeline.detail: 25 April, by William Taylor, with no author’s name and a title page promising a life written by Crusoe himself.

timeline.label: The Farther Adventures follows
timeline.detail: Published in August of the same year, taking Crusoe back to the island and on to China and Siberia.

timeline.label: Serious Reflections During the Life of Robinson Crusoe
timeline.detail: A third volume of essays, in which the story is defended as an allegory of Defoe’s own life.

timeline.label: Defoe dies in Ropemaker’s Alley, London
timeline.detail: In lodgings, evading creditors, having written more than most of his contemporaries had read.

timeline.label: Rousseau makes it the one book in Émile’s library
timeline.detail: In Émile, Robinson Crusoe is recommended as the whole of a boy’s early reading — the beginning of its career as an educational text.

places.name: York
places.note: Crusoe’s birthplace, and the middle station of life he refuses.

places.name: Hull
places.note: Where he goes on board in September 1651 without his parents’ knowledge.

places.name: Yarmouth Roads
places.note: The anchorage where his first ship founders, and where he ignores the first warning.

places.name: Salé
places.note: The Moroccan port whose rovers take him; he is a slave there for two years.

places.name: Bahia, Brazil
places.note: Where he lands after his escape and builds the plantation that makes him rich in his absence.

places.name: Mouth of the Orinoco
places.note: The stretch of coast the island is placed off, which is why the canoes and the Spaniards come from the mainland.

places.name: Lisbon
places.note: Where the old Portuguese captain renders twenty-eight years of accounts to the penny.

related.why: The satirical answer to it, published seven years later and wearing the same documentary clothes.
Betteredge treats Robinson Crusoe as an oracle, opening it at random for guidance — one foundational English story used inside another.
An earlier first-person account from the plantations, and a direct view of what Crusoe’s Guinea voyage was for.
The other great novel of work at sea, equally willing to stop the story to explain a process in full.
The next decade’s experiment in making fiction out of a plain private record, and another book that persuaded readers it was real.

books.title: Romeo and Juliet
books.author: William Shakespeare
books.setting: Verona, with one day in Mantua, across roughly four days of high summer
books.lengthNote: Around 3,000 lines, and the whole of it takes four days
books.openingLine: Two households, both alike in dignity, In fair Verona, where we lay our scene,
books.summary: A Chorus gives away the ending in fourteen lines, and the play then spends four days showing how quickly two children can reach it. Shakespeare took a story that had run over months in his sources and pressed it into a single hot week, so that every adult delay, every sealed-off street and every letter that fails to arrive lands on lovers who have no time to spare.

sourceText.label: Globe/Moby text of Romeo and Juliet
sourceText.note: Line numbers follow the traditional Globe numbering, which runs the Prologue as 1.0. Modern editions differ by a line or two.

structure.label: Act I
structure.title: A brawl, a feast, and a sonnet between strangers
structure.summary: Two servants start a street fight over nothing, the Prince threatens death for the next offence, and Romeo is in love with a woman who will not have him. At the Capulet feast he meets Juliet, and the two build a sonnet between them before either learns the other's name.

scenes.title: Prologue
scenes.summary: The Chorus announces the feud, the lovers and their deaths in fourteen lines.

scenes.title: Coals and swords
scenes.summary: A servants' quarrel becomes a civic riot; the Prince sets death as the penalty for the next one.

scenes.title: Paris asks
scenes.summary: Capulet tells Paris his daughter is too young, and then invites him to the feast anyway.

scenes.title: Fourteen
scenes.summary: Lady Capulet raises marriage; the Nurse answers with a long, fond, indecent memory.

scenes.title: Queen Mab
scenes.summary: Mercutio's fantasy about the dreams of sleepers runs out of control on the way to the party.

scenes.title: The feast
scenes.summary: Romeo sees Juliet, Tybalt is restrained by Capulet, and the two lovers learn each other's surnames last.

structure.label: Act II
structure.title: A marriage arranged in a night and a morning
structure.summary: Romeo climbs the orchard wall and hears Juliet say aloud what she would never have told him. She proposes marriage herself, and by the following afternoon Friar Laurence has performed it, hoping a secret wedding will do what the Prince's threats cannot.

scenes.title: Prologue
scenes.summary: A second Chorus sonnet marks the change from old love to new.

scenes.title: The wall
scenes.summary: Mercutio conjures for Romeo bawdily in the lane while Romeo hides on the other side.

scenes.title: The orchard
scenes.summary: Juliet, overheard, argues with a name; before the scene ends she has proposed marriage.

scenes.title: The cell
scenes.summary: Friar Laurence, gathering herbs, agrees to marry them for political reasons of his own.

scenes.title: Wit in the street
scenes.summary: Mercutio finds Romeo restored to sociable joking; the Nurse arrives on her errand.

scenes.title: The Nurse delays
scenes.summary: Juliet waits three hours for news and is teased with aching bones before she gets it.

scenes.title: The wedding
scenes.summary: The Friar warns against violent delights and marries them within the same speech.

structure.label: Act III
structure.title: Two deaths at noon and a banishment
structure.summary: Mercutio dies under Romeo's arm, Romeo kills Tybalt within minutes, and the Prince commutes death to exile. Juliet spends her wedding night with a husband who must leave at dawn, and wakes to a father who will disown her if she does not marry Paris on Thursday.

scenes.title: The street at noon
scenes.summary: Mercutio and Tybalt are killed in quick succession; Romeo is banished, not executed.

scenes.title: Juliet hears
scenes.summary: The Nurse's garbled news makes Juliet think Romeo dead, then curse him, then defend him.

scenes.title: On the floor
scenes.summary: Romeo will not hear the word banished; the Friar and the Nurse get him to Juliet.

scenes.title: Thursday
scenes.summary: Capulet fixes the wedding to Paris while his daughter is upstairs with her husband.

scenes.title: Dawn and after
scenes.summary: The lovers part; Capulet threatens to turn Juliet out, and the Nurse advises bigamy.

structure.label: Act IV
structure.title: A drug, a false death and a house of mourning
structure.summary: Juliet takes the Friar's vial without telling anyone, and the scene in which she swallows it is the longest she is ever left alone. The Capulets wake to find her cold, and the household turns its wedding preparations into a funeral in the space of one scene.

scenes.title: The plan
scenes.summary: Juliet meets Paris at the Friar's cell and is given a potion and a forty-two-hour lie.

scenes.title: Obedience
scenes.summary: Juliet apologises to her father, who joyfully brings the wedding forward a day.

scenes.title: The vial
scenes.summary: Alone, Juliet imagines waking among bones, and drinks anyway.

scenes.title: Morning in the kitchen
scenes.summary: Capulet fusses over pastry and logs while his daughter lies drugged upstairs.

scenes.title: The discovery
