characters.role: Worcestershire farm boy, soldier, overseer, convict, and the narrator of chapter XII
characters.summary: He loses a leg to a crocodile, keeps coolies at work on an indigo plantation, helps murder a merchant for a rajah’s jewels and serves twenty years for it. His one fixed virtue is that he keeps faith with his three Indian partners, which the two English officers do not. His account is vivid, self-serving and the only one there is; nobody else alive was at Agra.
characters.clue: He has his name on a plan beside three others, a wooden stump that sinks in Thames mud, and a grievance against the justice system that he states better than anyone answers it.

characters.name: Tonga
characters.role: An Andaman Islander; Small’s companion and the killer of Bartholomew Sholto
characters.summary: He has no line of speech in the book. He is assembled out of a gazetteer entry, a footprint, Watson’s horror and Small’s patronage, and every one of those sources calls him hideous or a savage. What he actually does is recover from an illness, stay with the man who nursed him, sail an open canoe for ten days, get shown at fairs for pennies, and die in the river. Doyle took the portrait from colonial print and added to its errors; it is the part of the novel that most needs to be read against.
characters.clue: The book first knows him as a naked footprint half the size of a man’s, and last sees him as a pair of eyes in the white swirl of the waters.
traits: described only by his enemies and his keeper

characters.name: Mahomet Singh, Abdullah Khan and Dost Akbar
characters.role: Small’s three partners in the sign of the four
characters.summary: Two troopers on a fort gate and a foster-brother who lures the merchant in. Small calls them Sikhs, and Doyle has given them names that are mostly Muslim, which says how closely he was looking. They plan the murder, recruit Small at knife-point and then keep their word to him for thirty years, and he to them. At the end they are still in the Andaman convict-barracks, and nobody in London gives them another thought.
characters.clue: Three of the four names on Captain Morstan’s paper; the ones the English officers left out when they took the treasure.

characters.name: Athelney Jones
characters.role: Scotland Yard detective
characters.summary: Stout, wheezing and quick to a theory, he arrests Thaddeus, the housekeeper, the gatekeeper and the Indian butler within an hour and has to release two of them the next day. He is not a fool so much as a man who decides first. By chapter IX he is asking for help, and he takes the official credit for an arrest he would have made at the wrong place.
characters.clue: He announces that facts are better than theories while holding a theory that fits none of the facts in the room.

themes.name: Empire, loot and what comes home
themes.summary: Every fortune in the book was made in India and none of it honestly. A rajah hedging his bets in 1857, four guards at a gate, two officers with gambling debts: the chest passes by murder and fraud into a villa in Norwood, and the consequences follow it up the Thames. Small’s word for it throughout is loot. The novel lets that word stand, and an Indian partner gets the sharpest line on the subject, yet it never imagines the jewels going back; the only possible ends are an English heiress or the riverbed.
themes.development: Pearls in a cardboard box, then an Eastern room in a suburban terrace, then a garden dug up like a goldfield, and finally the story of Agra, told by a man who went out at eighteen with the Queen’s shilling.

themes.name: Race and the colonial gazetteer
themes.summary: Holmes identifies the second man by reading aloud from a reference book, and what it says about the Andaman Islanders — stunted, hideous, cannibal, untameable — is false in nearly every particular. The novel presents it as the latest authority and then confirms it with Watson’s own eyes on the river. Small’s language about India is of the same kind. None of this is incidental colour: the plot needs a killer nobody will mourn, and it builds one out of the prejudices of its sources.
themes.development: A Hindu servant who looks incongruous in a doorway; a footprint read by racial type; the gazetteer; a face on a launch; and a last chapter that talks of black devils while showing the Indian partners keeping faith and the English officers breaking it.

themes.name: Observation, inference and proof
themes.summary: Holmes’s method is set out as doctrine in the first chapter and tested in a garret in the sixth. It is impressive and it has limits the book is frank about. The watch trick wounds a friend. The trail ends at a barrel of creosote. Days pass with nothing. The launch is found by legwork, and the motive is not deduced at all but told. Detection here gets the men; it does not get the treasure or the truth about Agra.
themes.development: Monographs on tobacco ash and footprints, a demonstration on a watch, a reconstruction from a rope and a thorn, a false scent, a disguise, and then a long silence while the prisoner talks.

themes.name: Justice, oaths and rightful owners
themes.summary: The four call their mark on Major Sholto’s body an act of justice, and the book does not quite laugh at them. Small murdered for the jewels, but he was then cheated by officers who had sworn an oath to him, and his argument from the dock — who has earned this, if not the men who paid twenty years for it? — goes unanswered by Holmes, Watson or Jones. English law can hang him. It has no view on whose the treasure was.
themes.development: An anonymous letter promises a wronged woman justice in chapter II; a card on a corpse claims it in chapter V; Small shouts the word back at a policeman in chapter XII.

themes.name: Marriage and the golden barrier
themes.summary: Watson’s romance is governed by arithmetic. A half-pay surgeon may court a governess; he may not court the richest heiress in England without looking like what he fears he is. So the love story can only end well if the detective story ends badly, and it does. The neatness is a little chilling: Mary’s legal inheritance is destroyed by a criminal, and the man who loves her thanks God for it to her face.
themes.development: Attraction at first sight, selfishness at the mention of the sum, hands held in the dark garden at Norwood, and a proposal over an empty iron box.

themes.name: Appetite and habit
themes.summary: The book opens on an addiction and keeps finding others. Holmes needs cocaine when he has no problem to work on and says so without shame. Major Sholto could not bear to part with a single pearl he never used. Small’s craving passes from the jewels to revenge. The case cures nobody: it is only, for Holmes, a better stimulant than the one in the morocco case, and when it is over he returns to the first.
themes.development: Three injections a day on the first page, a miser’s deathbed in chapter IV, a lifetime spent on one hatred in chapter XII, and the long white hand going up to the mantelpiece on the last.

themes.name: London, its suburbs and its river
themes.canonicalName: London, its suburbs and its river
themes.summary: Doyle maps the case across a city that is growing faster than it can be known. Holmes recites the streets south of the river from inside a cab; the brick terraces are tentacles; Norwood hides an Indian fortune behind a wall topped with glass. The Thames is the way the empire’s goods come in and the way the fugitives mean to get out, and the chase ends on marshland that is barely London at all.
themes.development: Fog in the Strand, a new terrace near the Wandsworth Road, a suburban villa, the wharves opposite Millbank, the Pool, and the mud flats by Plumstead.

techniques.name: The chain of inference
techniques.definition: A conclusion presented as a series of small observations, each of which the reader is invited to check.
techniques.bookDefinition: A conclusion presented as a series of small observations, each of which the reader is invited to check.
techniques.inThisBook: The watch in chapter I is the model: conclusion first, protest from Watson, then the scratches round the keyhole and the pawnbroker’s numbers. The garret in chapter VI repeats it with a rope, a stump-mark and a footprint.

techniques.name: Watson’s retrospective narration
techniques.definition: A narrator telling their own earlier life, with the distance between the two selves doing the judging.
techniques.bookDefinition: An account given after the event by a narrator who already knows how it ends.
techniques.inThisBook: Watson writes as Mary’s husband — as she has often told me, he says in the garden scene — so the love plot is never in doubt, and his fear of her fortune is confessed from the safety of knowing it was lost.

techniques.name: Embedded histories
techniques.definition: A second, older story told by a character to explain the present one.
techniques.bookDefinition: A second, older story told by a character to explain the present one.
techniques.inThisBook: Three are nested in order of distance: Mary’s ten years, Thaddeus’s account of his father’s death, and Small’s thirty-year narrative, which takes over the last chapter and moves the book from Norwood to Agra.

techniques.name: The material clue
techniques.definition: A physical trace that carries the solution before anybody can read it.
techniques.bookDefinition: A physical trace that carries the solution before anybody can read it.
techniques.inThisBook: A small bare footprint in creosote, a thorn, a stone-headed club and a scrap of paper with four names: each is on the page before it is understood, and the creosote is both the best clue and the one that leads to a barrel.

techniques.name: Reading faces
techniques.definition: Treating physical appearance as evidence of character, in the manner of Victorian physiognomy.
techniques.bookDefinition: Treating physical appearance as evidence of character, in the manner of Victorian physiognomy.
techniques.inThisBook: Watson reads refinement in Mary’s face, resolve in Small’s chin and bestiality in Tonga’s features, all with the same confidence. Holmes does it with handwriting. The habit passes as observation and works as prejudice.

techniques.name: Gothic machinery
techniques.definition: The stock furniture of Gothic writing — the ruin, the storm, the locked room, the buried secret — put to a particular use.
techniques.bookDefinition: Isolated houses, locked rooms, moonlight, inherited guilt and faces at the window used to produce dread.
techniques.inThisBook: Pondicherry Lodge has a walled garden, a hidden garret, a curse-bearing treasure and a dead man grinning through a keyhole. Doyle then has Holmes measure the room with a tape.

techniques.name: Foils
techniques.definition: A character constructed to throw another's choices into relief by making different ones.
techniques.bookDefinition: Characters placed side by side so that each shows up what the other lacks.
techniques.inThisBook: Jones’s instant theory against Holmes’s patience; Watson’s feeling against Holmes’s declared coldness; one twin generous and one grasping; and, in Small’s story, three Indian partners who keep an oath beside two English officers who do not.

techniques.name: Interested witnesses
techniques.definition: Narrators with reasons to shape what they report.
techniques.bookDefinition: Narrators with reasons to shape what they report.
techniques.inThisBook: Small expects to be tried for his life and tells his story to the men who will give evidence. He was forced at knife-point; he never touched Sholto; his heart softened before he tripped the merchant. It may all be so. He even says, maybe you gentlemen think that I am just making out a case for myself.

quotations.text: “It is cocaine,” he said,—“a seven-per-cent. solution. Would you care to try it?”
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.context: Watson has at last asked which it is today, morphine or cocaine.
quotations.analysis: The offer is the shock. Holmes does not hide the habit or defend it; he states the concentration like a chemist and passes the case across as he might a cigar. Doyle, a practising doctor writing in 1889, gives Watson the medical objection and gives Holmes the better lines, and the drug was legal. The scene sets the terms of the book: a mind that treats its own body as apparatus.

quotations.text: “My mind,” he said, “rebels at stagnation. Give me problems, give me work, give me the most abstruse cryptogram or the most intricate analysis, and I am in my own proper atmosphere.
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.context: His answer to Watson’s warning about what the drug will do to him.
quotations.analysis: Give me, three times: the grammar is a craving. Holmes describes work and cocaine as substitutes for one another, which makes crime a kind of supply. The client who knocks a few pages later is welcome for the reason the syringe was, and the last sentence of the novel will confirm that the case was only ever an interval between doses.

quotations.text: Detection is, or ought to be, an exact science, and should be treated in the same cold and unemotional manner.
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.context: Holmes reviewing Watson’s pamphlet on the Jefferson Hope case, which he thinks was spoiled by romance.
quotations.analysis: Is, or ought to be: the correction concedes that it is not yet. Holmes goes on to compare Watson’s book to an elopement worked into a proposition of Euclid, and the novel that follows is exactly that — a love story run through a problem. Doyle lets his detective condemn the form of the book he is in, and then writes it anyway.

quotations.text: Was ever such a dreary, dismal, unprofitable world? See how the yellow fog swirls down the street and drifts across the dun-coloured houses.
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.context: At the window, just before the landlady brings up Mary Morstan’s card.
quotations.analysis: Unprofitable is Hamlet’s word for the uses of this world, and Holmes borrows the pose with it. The fog is doing two jobs. It is the London the case will be conducted in, and it is the inside of his head without a problem: yellow, dun, nothing with an edge. A reader is being shown that the great reasoner’s complaint is closer to melancholy than to logic.

quotations.text: “You really are an automaton,—a calculating-machine!” I cried. “There is something positively inhuman in you at times.”
quotations.speaker: Dr John Watson
quotations.context: Watson has remarked on how attractive the client is; Holmes says he did not observe it.
quotations.analysis: Watson is stung on Mary’s behalf, within minutes of meeting her. Holmes answers that the most winning woman he ever knew was hanged for poisoning three children, so the exchange sets feeling against statistics, and the book will need both: Watson’s attention keeps Mary a person, and Holmes’s keeps her a case. The word inhuman will come back, far less playfully, when Watson looks at Tonga.

quotations.text: In an experience of women which extends over many nations and three separate continents, I have never looked upon a face which gave a clearer promise of a refined and sensitive nature.
quotations.context: Watson’s first description of Mary Morstan as she sits down in Baker Street.
quotations.analysis: The boast is comic and Doyle surely knows it, but the method is serious: Watson reads character straight off a face and treats the reading as a promise. He is right about Mary. He will use the identical procedure on the launch in chapter X and find bestiality, and the novel never suggests that a technique which works on a governess might fail on a stranger from the Andamans.

quotations.text: There was something strangely incongruous in this Oriental figure framed in the commonplace doorway of a third-rate suburban dwelling-house.
quotations.context: A servant in a yellow turban opens Thaddeus Sholto’s front door.
quotations.analysis: Watson finds the man incongruous; the plot says he is nothing of the kind. A suburb like this is where Indian money was spent, and the servant is in the doorway because a major came home rich. The sentence frames him like a picture, which is how the book treats almost every Indian it shows in London: as décor that came back with the furniture.

quotations.text: An oasis of art in the howling desert of South London.
quotations.speaker: Thaddeus Sholto
quotations.context: Thaddeus showing his guests into a room of tapestries, tiger-skins and a hookah.
quotations.analysis: Doyle had dined with Oscar Wilde the evening this novel was commissioned, and Thaddeus is an aesthete drawn for laughs. The joke has a point he cannot see. His oasis is furnished from a murdered man’s jewel-box, and the desert he despises is the ordinary England his father’s money let him withdraw from. Taste, in this room, is what plunder looks like a generation on.

quotations.text: The cursed greed which has been my besetting sin through life has withheld from her the treasure, half at least of which should have been hers.
quotations.speaker: Major John Sholto
quotations.context: The Major’s deathbed confession to his sons, as Thaddeus reports it.
quotations.analysis: Half at least should have been hers — and the rest? The dying man reckons only with the English claim on the jewels, his dead friend’s daughter. The four convicts whose secret he bought with an oath, and the rajah before them, do not enter the account. He adds that he made no use of the treasure; possession was the whole pleasure. It is a miser’s confession and it is also, on a small scale, a colonial one.

quotations.text: Surely it was the place of a loyal friend to rejoice at such news; yet I am ashamed to say that selfishness took me by the soul, and that my heart turned as heavy as lead within me.
quotations.context: Thaddeus has put the value of the treasure at not less than half a million sterling.
quotations.analysis: Watson is honest about a feeling that does him no credit, and that honesty is what keeps him likeable through the book. It also gives the narrator a private stake in the outcome. From here the man telling the story of the hunt for the treasure wants it lost, and the reader should hold that in mind when he reports his relief in chapter XI as if it were simple.

quotations.text: How often have I said to you that when you have eliminated the impossible whatever remains, however improbable, must be the truth?
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.context: In the locked room, asking Watson how the second intruder got in.
quotations.analysis: The most quoted rule in detective fiction, and here it is doing modest work: not the door, not the window, not the chimney, so the hole in the roof. As logic it is sound only if the list of possibilities is complete, and Holmes never shows that it is. What the sentence really supplies is tone. It turns a guess that happens to be right into a law, and how often makes Watson, and the reader, the slow pupil.

quotations.text: I could not but think what a terrible criminal he would have made had he turned his energy and sagacity against the law, instead of exerting them in its defence.
quotations.context: Watson watching Holmes go over the floor on his knees with a lens and a tape measure.
quotations.analysis: The sentence before this compares Holmes to a trained blood-hound and gives him beady eyes like a bird’s, so the detective is drawn in animal terms chapters before the Islander is. Watson means a compliment. But the book has already shown a Holmes who works for stimulation rather than for justice, and the thought that his side of the law is a matter of temperament is left sitting in the reader’s mind.

quotations.text: Facts are better than mere theories, after all.
quotations.speaker: Athelney Jones
quotations.context: Jones coming down from the garret, having found the trap-door Holmes had already shown Watson.
quotations.analysis: He is quoting Holmes’s creed back at him and has it upside down. Jones found one fact and hung a prepared theory on it — the brother did it, for the money — while the footprint, the thorn and the wooden stump are all in the room and fit none of it. Doyle makes the official detective the theorist and the amateur the empiricist, and the joke costs Thaddeus Sholto a night in the cells.

quotations.text: It was soothing to catch even that passing glimpse of a tranquil English home in the midst of the wild, dark business which had absorbed us.
quotations.context: Watson leaving Mary at Mrs Forrester’s door at two in the morning: hall-light, stained glass, barometer, stair-rods.
quotations.analysis: English home on one side, wild and dark on the other: Watson sorts the night into domestic and foreign. The case will not let the division stand. The wild business is an English major’s fraud carried out from an English villa, and the income that built such halls came, often enough, from where the treasure did. The glimpse soothes him because it lets him forget that.

quotations.text: They are naturally hideous, having large, misshapen heads, small, fierce eyes, and distorted features.
quotations.context: Holmes reading aloud from the first volume of a new gazetteer, under Andaman Islands.
quotations.analysis: Holmes, who never guesses, takes this on trust because it is in print. The entry goes on to put the people’s height below four feet and to end every shipwreck with a cannibal feast; none of it is true of the Andamanese, who were not cannibals and did not use blowpipes either. Naturally is the word to watch. It turns a judgement about looks into a fact of nature, and the chapter treats a book of colonial hearsay as the same kind of evidence as a footprint.

quotations.text: An injured lady, half a million in treasure, a black cannibal, and a wooden-legged ruffian. They take the place of the conventional dragon or wicked earl.
quotations.speaker: Mrs Cecil Forrester
quotations.context: Mary’s employer, hearing Watson’s account of the case over tea.
quotations.analysis: Doyle lets a character name the genre. Mrs Forrester hears a list of stock parts, and she is right: a man has been cast as the dragon. The remark is light, and it is the most self-aware line in the book, since it admits that the black cannibal is a role the story required rather than a person it met. Mary’s reply, that she cares nothing for the money, quietly declines the role written for her as well.

quotations.text: Never have I seen features so deeply marked with all bestiality and cruelty.
quotations.context: The searchlight falls on the second figure on the Aurora’s deck, seconds before the shooting.
quotations.analysis: This is the only look the novel takes at Tonga alive, and it is a verdict. Watson has been told what to expect by the gazetteer and sees it: the paragraph calls him a creature, gives him half animal fury, and has both men draw revolvers at the sight of him before he moves. A doctor who prides himself on reading faces reads this one as not human, and the narrative then shoots him. The sentence should be quoted as evidence about Watson and his sources, not about the Andamanese.

quotations.text: Somewhere in the dark ooze at the bottom of the Thames lie the bones of that strange visitor to our shores.
quotations.context: The police launch sweeps the water with its light and finds no body.
quotations.analysis: After creature and savage, visitor is almost courteous, and our shores makes the death a matter of geography: he was not from here. The present tense is the detail to notice. Watson, writing later, leaves the bones in the river beside the jewels, as though the two foreign things the Thames swallowed that night were of a kind. There is no inquest, and nobody asks whether firing was necessary.

quotations.text: To him it brought murder, to Major Sholto it brought fear and guilt, to me it has meant slavery for life.
quotations.speaker: Jonathan Small
quotations.context: Small in the launch’s cabin, facing the iron box, before his full story.
quotations.analysis: The cursed Indian jewel was a familiar device by 1890, and it is a convenient one: a curse puts the harm in the stones rather than in the men who stole them. Small’s own sentence undoes the superstition. Murder, fear, guilt and penal labour are what theft and the law produce without supernatural help. Note also who is missing from his list of victims: the rajah who owned it, and Tonga, who has just died for it.

quotations.text: Whoever had lost a treasure, I knew that night that I had gained one.
quotations.context: Mary has accepted Watson beside the empty chest.
quotations.analysis: The pun closes the love story and gives away its logic. Mary takes the place of the jewels in Watson’s sentence, something gained as the other thing is lost, and whoever waves off the question of whose loss it was. It was hers, in law. The line is meant as tenderness and largely is, but it also completes a plot in which the woman’s fortune had to be destroyed before the man could speak.

quotations.text: Whose loot is this, if it is not ours? Where is the justice that I should give it up to those who have never earned it?
quotations.speaker: Jonathan Small
quotations.context: Athelney Jones has told him that he has thwarted justice by sinking the jewels.
quotations.analysis: Loot came into English from Hindi, and Small uses it without embarrassment: he does not claim the treasure was clean, only that nobody in the room has a better title. Earned is a grotesque word for murder followed by twenty years in a swamp, yet the challenge stands. The Sholtos’ claim rests on fraud and the Crown’s on conquest. Doyle gives the argument to a convict in handcuffs and lets no one reply.

quotations.text: One month India lay as still and peaceful, to all appearance, as Surrey or Kent; the next there were two hundred thousand black devils let loose, and the country was a perfect hell.
quotations.speaker: Jonathan Small
quotations.context: Small, an overseer on an indigo plantation near Muttra, describing the outbreak of 1857.
quotations.analysis: This is how the rebellion was told in Britain for a generation: a sleeping county, then fiends, with no cause in between. To all appearance is the phrase that lets daylight in, since a country that only looked like Surrey had reasons of its own. The voice is Small’s, a half-educated soldier’s, and Doyle may be characterising him; but nothing in the novel contradicts him, and his Indian partners are the only Indians it allows a motive.

quotations.text: We only ask you to do that which your countrymen come to this land for. We ask you to be rich.
quotations.speaker: Abdullah Khan
quotations.context: At the fort gate in Agra, with a knife at Small’s throat, proposing the murder of the merchant Achmet.
quotations.analysis: The clearest statement about empire in the book, and Doyle gives it to an Indian conspirator by way of an English convict. It removes any difference between what the four are about to do at a side-gate and what the East India Company did at large: both are people coming to this land to be rich. Small does not dispute it. He asks for three minutes and takes the oath, and the sign of the four is, from that moment, a joint venture.

quotations.text: He was stanch and true, was little Tonga. No man ever had a more faithful mate.
quotations.speaker: Jonathan Small
quotations.context: Small describing the escape from the Andamans in Tonga’s canoe.
quotations.analysis: Set this beside Watson’s bestiality and cruelty: the only man who knew Tonga calls him faithful, and means it. But the praise is a master’s. Little, mate and, elsewhere, hell-hound, imp and poor Tonga are the words for a dog or a child, and the same speaker beat him with a rope’s end. The book offers two accounts of the Islander, a monster and a pet, and no third in which he might have had reasons of his own.

quotations.text: We earned a living at this time by my exhibiting poor Tonga at fairs and other such places as the black cannibal. He would eat raw meat and dance his war-dance: so we always had a hatful of pennies after a day’s work.
quotations.speaker: Jonathan Small
quotations.context: How the two of them lived in England while Small watched Pondicherry Lodge.
quotations.analysis: Here the novel shows, almost by accident, how its own monster was made. The black cannibal is an act, put on for an English crowd that pays to be frightened, and Small knows it is an act; the raw meat is a turn. Mrs Forrester used the same phrase over tea in chapter IX. Doyle sees the fairground trick clearly enough to describe it and does not notice that the gazetteer, and chapter X, are selling the same show.

quotations.text: But love is an emotional thing, and whatever is emotional is opposed to that true cold reason which I place above all things.
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.context: Holmes declining to congratulate Watson on his engagement.
quotations.analysis: He has just praised Mary’s genius for the work, in keeping the Agra plan out of all her father’s papers, so the objection is not to her. It is a creed, and the book has tested it. Cold reason found two men and lost half a million pounds; it took a night and a dog to do what a confession then made unnecessary. Holmes places reason above all things in the same breath as he admits to feeling limp as a rag.

quotations.text: “For me,” said Sherlock Holmes, “there still remains the cocaine-bottle.” And he stretched his long white hand up for it.
quotations.speaker: Sherlock Holmes
quotations.context: The last lines. Watson has observed that he gets a wife and Jones the credit, and asked what is left for Holmes.
quotations.analysis: The novel ends on the gesture it began with, the long white hand and the bottle on the mantelpiece, so the whole case is enclosed between two doses. It is an oddly bleak finish for an adventure story. Everyone else is paid in the ordinary coin of plots, marriage, promotion, the gallows; the hero’s reward is the return of his boredom. Doyle had not yet decided that Holmes would be a series, and he closes him here as a character study of a man who cannot bear to be unoccupied.

atAGlance.label: Written
atAGlance.note: At Southsea, where Doyle was still in practice as a doctor, after an American editor asked him for a story over dinner at the Langham Hotel.

atAGlance.label: First published
atAGlance.note: Complete in one issue of Lippincott’s Monthly Magazine; Spencer Blackett’s book followed in October as The Sign of Four.

atAGlance.label: Place in the series
atAGlance.note: After A Study in Scarlet and before the short stories that made Holmes famous. The cocaine, the boredom and Watson’s marriage all start here.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.value: Eleven chapters of pursuit, one of confession
atAGlance.note: Holmes identifies the culprits by the end of chapter VIII. What he cannot supply is the reason, which takes Jonathan Small a whole chapter and thirty years.

criticalViews.position: An imperial Gothic: the colony comes back to haunt the suburb
criticalViews.summary: On this reading the detective plot is a way of managing a fear. Wealth taken in India returns to England bringing violence with it, the suburban villa turns out to be built on a crime at Agra, and Holmes’s task is to find the foreign element and remove it. The Thames chase restores a border; the ending tidies the empire’s consequences out of sight.
criticalViews.counter: It can make the book more knowing than it is. Doyle’s sympathies are mixed rather than critical: he lets Small call the jewels loot and lets an Indian name the motive of conquest, but he also prints the gazetteer as fact and has his heroes shoot first. A novel can expose a guilty conscience without having one.

criticalViews.position: A racist text that should be taught as one
criticalViews.summary: The portrait of Tonga is drawn from colonial ethnography at its worst, given Holmes’s authority and confirmed by a narrator the reader trusts. He is denied speech, called a creature, and killed without regret. On this view the honest way to read the novel is to say so plainly and to set the gazetteer beside what is actually known of the Andamanese.
criticalViews.counter: The objection is not that this is wrong but that it can stop too soon. The book contains materials that work against its own caricature — Small’s testimony to Tonga’s loyalty, the fairground act, the faith kept by the Indian partners and broken by the officers — and a reading that only condemns will miss how the prejudice is put together.

criticalViews.position: The triumph of scientific method
criticalViews.summary: The traditional account: this is the novel that codifies Holmes. The watch, the monographs, the rule about the impossible and the reconstruction in the garret establish detection as applied reasoning, and the bungling of Athelney Jones shows what it replaces.
criticalViews.counter: Count the results. The trail ends at a barrel, the launch is found by visiting sixteen boatyards, the treasure is lost and the motive is supplied by confession. Holmes’s one recourse to printed authority is the gazetteer, which is worthless. The method is a performance of certainty as much as a means to it, and the framing scenes with the syringe suggest Doyle knew that.

essayQuestions.question: How does Doyle present the Agra treasure, and what does the novel finally do with it?
essayQuestions.focus: Empire, ownership and the ending
plan: Trace the chest’s owners in order — rajah, merchant, the four, Major Sholto, Bartholomew, Small — and note that every transfer is a crime.
Use Abdullah Khan’s we ask you to be rich to show the novel comparing private murder with the business of empire.
Set Major Sholto’s half at least should have been hers against Small’s whose loot is this, and ask whose claims each man leaves out.
Consider the curse as a device that shifts blame from people to stones, and how Small’s own list undoes it.
Weigh the ending: the jewels cannot go to an English heiress without taint and the book cannot picture them returning to India, so they go into the river.

essayQuestions.question: Examine the presentation of Tonga. How far does the novel invite a reader to question it?
essayQuestions.focus: Race, sources and narrative authority
plan: Begin with how he is assembled before he appears: a footprint typed by race, then the gazetteer read aloud by Holmes.
Analyse Watson’s description in chapter X — creature, bestiality, half animal fury — and the fact that both men draw before he moves.
Bring in Small’s account: nursed back to health, stanch and true, beaten with a rope’s end, exhibited at fairs as the black cannibal.
Note what the book never gives him: a word of speech, a motive, a burial, an inquest.
Conclude on the limits of the invitation: the materials for doubt are present, but no character voices it and the narrator’s view is never corrected.

essayQuestions.question: Is The Sign of the Four a celebration of reason?
essayQuestions.focus: Holmes’s method, its successes and its failures
plan: Set out the doctrine of chapter I: exact science, never guessing, the monographs, the watch.
Show the method at its best in the garret, with the rope, the stump and the rule about eliminating the impossible.
List what goes wrong: the creosote barrel, the vanished launch, the blank days of chapter IX, the empty chest.
Contrast Holmes with Athelney Jones, and then with Watson, whose feeling the final chapter refuses to rank below cold reason.
End with the frame: a reasoner who needs cocaine when reason has nothing to work on.

essayQuestions.question: What part does Watson’s love story play in the novel?
essayQuestions.focus: Narration, money and genre
plan: Start with Holmes’s complaint that Watson worked a love-story into Euclid, and observe that Doyle proceeds to do so.
Follow the golden barrier from Watson’s selfishness in the cab to Thank God over the box.
Ask what Mary Morstan is allowed to do: a model client in chapter II, largely a prize by chapter XI.
Consider what a narrator who wants the treasure lost does to a reader’s trust in his account.
Compare the three rewards in the last lines — a wife, the credit, the bottle — and what the book thinks each is worth.

discussionQuestions: Holmes and Watson fire at Tonga together, and nobody in the book asks afterwards whether they had to. Should a reader?
Small says the treasure belongs to the four because they earned it. Who, if anyone, has a better claim?
Thaddeus Sholto is made ridiculous and behaves better than anyone else. Why might Doyle have combined those two things?
Watson thanks God that Mary has lost a fortune. Is that love, or self-interest, or both?
The gazetteer is wrong about the Andaman Islanders and Holmes believes it. What does that do to his authority in the rest of the book?
The novel begins and ends with the cocaine bottle. Does the case change Holmes at all?

timeline.label: The Indian Rebellion
timeline.detail: Beginning among sepoys of the Bengal army in May and spreading across northern India. Europeans from the surrounding country took refuge in the fort at Agra, as Small does, and an action was fought outside the city early in July.

timeline.label: A penal settlement is founded at Port Blair
timeline.detail: The British opened the convict colony on the Andaman Islands in the aftermath of the rebellion, and many of its first prisoners were men sentenced for their part in it. Small and his three partners are sent there.

timeline.label: Arthur Conan Doyle is born in Edinburgh
timeline.detail: He studied medicine at the university there and went into general practice at Southsea in 1882.

timeline.label: Wilkie Collins publishes The Moonstone
timeline.detail: The earlier English novel of an Indian jewel looted in wartime and followed home. Collins sends the stone back; Doyle sends it to the bottom of the river.

timeline.label: A Study in Scarlet appears in Beeton’s Christmas Annual
timeline.detail: Holmes and Watson’s first case, which Holmes criticises in the opening chapter of this one. It made little stir.

timeline.label: Dinner at the Langham Hotel
timeline.detail: On 30 August Joseph Marshall Stoddart, over from Philadelphia for Lippincott’s, entertained Doyle and Oscar Wilde and came away with a promise of a story from each. Doyle wrote his that autumn. Wilde’s was The Picture of Dorian Gray. The Langham is where Captain Morstan vanishes.

timeline.label: Lippincott’s Monthly Magazine prints the novel complete
timeline.detail: In the February number, as The Sign of the Four; or, The Problem of the Sholtos.

timeline.label: Spencer Blackett publishes the first book edition
timeline.detail: In October, under the shorter title The Sign of Four, which many later editions keep.

timeline.label: The Holmes short stories begin in the Strand Magazine
timeline.detail: A Scandal in Bohemia appeared in July. It was the monthly stories, not the two novels, that made Holmes a public figure, and sent readers back to this book.

timeline.label: Maurice Elvey films the novel for Stoll Pictures
timeline.detail: A silent feature with Eille Norwood as Holmes, the last of his long run in the part.

timeline.label: Doyle dies at Crowborough in Sussex
timeline.detail: Knighted in 1902, and by then far better known for Holmes than for the historical novels he valued more.

timeline.label: Arthur Wontner plays Holmes in a sound film of the story
timeline.detail: Directed by Graham Cutts, with Ian Hunter as Watson; the plot is rearranged so that the Agra backstory comes first.

timeline.label: Granada Television’s feature-length adaptation
timeline.detail: Jeremy Brett as Holmes and Edward Hardwicke as Watson, directed by Peter Hammond. It drops Watson’s engagement altogether.

places.name: Baker Street, London
places.note: The sitting-room where the novel begins and ends, with the bottle on the corner of the mantelpiece.

places.name: Lyceum Theatre, Strand
places.note: The third pillar from the left, where Mary Morstan is told to wait at seven, and where a coachman collects the three of them in the fog.

places.name: Upper Norwood
places.note: Pondicherry Lodge: Major Sholto’s walled villa, its grounds dug over for six years in search of the chest that was in the roof.

places.name: Langham Hotel, Portland Place
places.note: Captain Morstan’s address on the night he disappeared in 1878, and the hotel where the novel was commissioned over dinner.

places.name: Plumstead Marshes
places.note: The melancholy south bank where the Aurora runs aground, Small’s wooden leg sinks in the mud, and the treasure and the Islander are both lost to the river.

places.name: Agra Fort
places.note: The Mughal fortress on the Yamuna where Small guards a side door in 1857, the merchant Achmet is murdered, and the jewels are first hidden in a wall.

places.name: Port Blair, Andaman Islands
places.note: The convict settlement in the Bay of Bengal where Small serves his sentence, the two officers play cards, and Tonga is found sick in the woods.

places.name: Southsea, Portsmouth
places.note: Where Doyle was in practice as a doctor when he wrote the book, some distance from the London it maps so confidently.

related.why: The book this one is answering: an Indian jewel seized in a siege, a curse that follows it to an English house, and a very different decision about where it should end up.
The twelve stories that came next and made Holmes famous, with the method intact and Watson now married to the client of this case.
Commissioned at the same dinner by the same editor, and another London book in which a beautiful room is paid for by something kept out of sight upstairs.
Four years earlier: the same fog, the same professional men, and a respectable household with a small, violent figure coming and going by the back way.
Another English fortune with a colonial source and another character from overseas whom the narrator describes as barely human; the comparison sharpens both.

books.title: The Taming of the Shrew
books.author: William Shakespeare
books.setting: Padua and a country house on the road to Verona, framed by an English alehouse
books.lengthNote: Around 2,600 lines, of which the first 270 belong to a drunk who then disappears
books.openingLine: I'll pheeze you, in faith.
books.summary: A tinker is picked up drunk outside an alehouse and persuaded by a bored lord that he is a nobleman recovering from madness. The play performed for him is about a man who marries a woman for her dowry and then starves and contradicts her into agreement, and about a younger sister whose suitors buy their way into her house disguised as tutors. Shakespeare never returns to the tinker, so the audience is left holding a frame with nothing on the other end of it.

sourceText.label: Globe/Moby text of The Taming of the Shrew
sourceText.note: Line numbers follow the traditional Globe numbering. The two Induction scenes are numbered 0.1 and 0.2 in the digital text used for checking, and are cited here as Induction 1 and Induction 2.

structure.label: Induction
structure.title: A tinker is told he is a lord
structure.summary: Christopher Sly is thrown out of an alehouse for breaking glasses and falls asleep. A lord returning from hunting decides, as a joke, to have him carried home, dressed in fine clothes and told that his old life was a fifteen-year delusion. Sly holds out for about a hundred lines and then accepts it, and a company of players is brought in to perform the Padua comedy for him.

scenes.title: The alehouse
scenes.summary: Sly refuses to pay for the glasses, passes out, and is found by a lord with an idea.

scenes.title: The bedchamber
scenes.summary: Sly is waited on, given a page dressed as his wife, and settles down to watch a play.

structure.label: Act I
structure.title: One daughter unsellable, the other on the market
structure.summary: Baptista announces that Bianca may not marry until her elder sister is off his hands, which makes Katherina an obstacle before the audience has heard her speak twenty lines. Lucentio falls in love at first sight and swaps clothes with his servant so that he can enter the house as a tutor. Petruchio arrives from Verona and says plainly that he has come to marry money.

scenes.title: The condition
scenes.summary: Baptista sets his terms; Katherina is insulted in public; Lucentio and Tranio exchange identities.

scenes.title: The suitor from Verona
scenes.summary: Petruchio states his price, hears about Katherina's temper, and is undeterred; Hortensio disguises himself as a music master.

structure.label: Act II
structure.title: A courtship conducted at speed
structure.summary: Katherina has tied up her sister and is striking her when their father walks in, which is the one scene that shows what the household is actually like. Petruchio then meets her, matches her insult for insult for a hundred lines, tells her father they have privately agreed to marry, and settles the dowry. The wedding is fixed for Sunday before Katherina has consented to anything.

scenes.title: The wooing
scenes.summary: Katherina beats Bianca; Petruchio conducts a wit duel, declares a match, and bargains with Baptista; Tranio outbids Gremio for Bianca.

structure.label: Act III
structure.title: A wedding treated as a piece of theatre
structure.summary: Two disguised suitors compete for Bianca's attention under cover of a Latin lesson and a music lesson. Petruchio arrives hours late for his own wedding in deliberately ridiculous clothes, behaves outrageously in church, and then removes his wife before the dinner, announcing that she is his property and pretending to rescue her from thieves.

scenes.title: The lessons
scenes.summary: Lucentio courts Bianca through a construed Latin sentence; Hortensio through a gamut; Bianca sets the terms.

scenes.title: The wedding
scenes.summary: Petruchio comes late and badly dressed, marries Katherina, and carries her off before the feast.

structure.label: Act IV
structure.title: The taming, and a father invented
structure.summary: At Petruchio's house the food is sent back, the bed is pulled apart and a tailor is abused, all in the name of Katherina's comfort. Petruchio explains the method to the audience in falconry terms. On the road back to Padua he makes her agree that the sun is the moon; in Padua a passing pedant is recruited to impersonate Lucentio's father, and the real one arrives.

scenes.title: The country house
scenes.summary: Servants are beaten, the meat is thrown out, and Petruchio sets out his plan alone on stage.

scenes.title: Substitutions
scenes.summary: Hortensio gives up on Bianca and marries a widow; Tranio recruits a pedant to play Vincentio.

scenes.title: The cap and the gown
scenes.summary: Katherina insists on her right to speak; the tailor's work is destroyed; the journey is cancelled over the time of day.

scenes.title: The false father
scenes.summary: The pedant settles the marriage terms as Vincentio, and Lucentio and Bianca slip away to be married.

scenes.title: Sun and moon
scenes.summary: Katherina agrees that the sun is the moon, then greets old Vincentio as a budding virgin.

structure.label: Act V
structure.title: The wager
structure.summary: The real Vincentio meets his impostor and is nearly arrested; the secret marriage is revealed and forgiven. At the wedding feast the three husbands bet on which wife will come when sent for. Katherina comes, fetches the other two, and delivers forty-four lines on a wife's duty to a room of men who have just staked money on her behaviour.

scenes.title: Two Vincentios
scenes.summary: The impersonation collapses; Lucentio confesses the marriage; the fathers are reconciled.

scenes.title: The feast
scenes.summary: The wager is laid and won, and Katherina speaks on obedience before the company.

characters.name: Katherina
characters.role: Baptista's elder daughter
characters.summary: She is called a devil, a fiend and a shrew before she has done anything on stage except resent being auctioned second. Her wit is faster than anyone else's in Padua and she is never once allowed to use it without being punished for it, which is the strongest argument the play makes on her side.
characters.clue: The elder sister nobody will bid for, who ties up the younger one, matches a stranger joke for joke, and ends by telling a room of men to put their hands under their husbands' feet.

characters.name: Petruchio
characters.role: A gentleman of Verona, come to Padua to marry
characters.summary: He announces his financial motive in his first scene and never withdraws it, which makes him harder to sentimentalise than productions often allow. His method is entirely theatrical — arriving in absurd clothes, praising food he is about to throw away, insisting the sun is the moon — and he explains it to the audience in the language of hawking.
characters.clue: He comes to Padua to wive it wealthily, turns up to his own wedding in rags on a broken-down horse, and starves his bride in the name of kindness.

characters.name: Bianca
characters.role: Baptista's younger daughter
characters.summary: She is silent and obedient for as long as it is useful, and the moment she has tutors alone in a room she tells them she will learn as she pleases. By the last scene she has married in secret, refuses to come when sent for, and calls her husband a fool for betting on her — the play's quietest joke at the taming plot's expense.
characters.clue: Everyone's idea of a good daughter, who arranges her own marriage behind her father's back and then will not come when her husband calls.

characters.name: Baptista Minola
characters.role: A wealthy gentleman of Padua, father of both sisters
characters.summary: He runs his household as a market and says so: Bianca goes to the highest bidder, Katherina to anyone who will take her. He asks his elder daughter for her consent exactly once, receives an answer that is plainly not one, and proceeds anyway.

characters.name: Lucentio
characters.role: A student from Pisa, in love with Bianca
characters.summary: He arrives in Padua announcing that he has come for philosophy and falls in love before the end of his first speech. His solution is to become his own servant and teach Latin, which means the romantic lead spends most of the play pretending to be someone poorer than he is.

characters.name: Tranio
characters.role: Lucentio's servant, impersonating his master
characters.summary: Given his master's clothes, he negotiates with Baptista, outbids a rich old man, hires an impostor father and keeps three deceptions running at once. The play's most competent social performer is a servant, and it lets him get away with all of it.
traits: better at being a gentleman than his master

characters.name: Hortensio
characters.role: A suitor to Bianca, disguised as the music master Litio
characters.summary: He disguises himself, is beaten over the head with his own lute, gives up on Bianca when he sees her flirting with a Latin tutor, and marries a widow out of pique. He then loses the wager in the last scene, which is the play's verdict on choosing a wife in a temper.

characters.name: Gremio
characters.role: An elderly, rich suitor to Bianca
characters.summary: He is the pantaloon of Italian comedy, bidding his plate and his hangings and his ships against a young man's invented inheritance. Beaten in the auction, he is left to report on the wedding — and his account of Petruchio in church is the only description of it the play gives.

characters.name: Grumio
characters.role: Petruchio's servant
characters.summary: He is beaten in the first scene for misunderstanding an instruction and spends the rest of the play as the taming's foot soldier: withholding food, describing the journey, playing along with a master he plainly finds frightening. His account of the ride to the country house is the closest the play comes to showing what the marriage looks like from outside.

characters.name: Christopher Sly
characters.role: A tinker, and the audience for the Padua play
characters.summary: He is talked out of his own identity in under a hundred lines by people who find it funny, which is the experiment the rest of the play repeats on a wife. Shakespeare's text drops him after the first act and never brings him back, and every production has to decide what to do about that.
characters.clue: A tinker who will not pay for the glasses he has broken, claims the family came in with Richard Conqueror, and wakes up being offered sack and a wife.

themes.name: Marriage as a market
themes.summary: Nobody in Padua marries without a negotiation. Baptista will not release Bianca until Katherina is sold, Gremio bids his tapestries against Tranio's imaginary ships, Petruchio states his price in his first scene, and the last act is a wager laid on wives. The romance is real but it is always conducted over a contract.
themes.development: Baptista's condition in 1.1, the dowry settled in 2.1, the auction for Bianca in the same scene, and twenty thousand crowns added as a second dowry in 5.2.

themes.name: Taming
themes.summary: The method is deprivation dressed as care: no food, no sleep, no clothes, every refusal delivered as concern for her comfort. Petruchio borrows the vocabulary of hawking to describe it, which is the play at its most disquieting — the language assumes a creature that can be reduced to obedience by hunger and then flown.
themes.development: Announced as an intention in 2.1, explained to the audience in 4.1, tested on the road in 4.5 and displayed as a finished result in 5.2.

themes.name: Disguise and substitution
themes.summary: A servant becomes his master, a master becomes a tutor, a suitor becomes a music teacher, a passing pedant becomes a father, and a tinker becomes a lord. Identity in this play is a matter of clothes and repetition, which is exactly the assumption the taming plot is built on.
themes.development: Lucentio and Tranio change places in 1.1; the false Vincentio is recruited in 4.2 and exposed in 5.1; Sly's transformation in the Induction sets the pattern for all of them.

themes.name: The obedience speech
themes.summary: Forty-four lines on a wife's duty to her lord, delivered in front of men who have just bet money on whether she would come when called. Nothing in the text settles the tone, which is why the speech has been played as surrender, as irony, as a private arrangement between two people and as a public humiliation.
themes.development: Katherina refuses to be silenced in 4.3, agrees to call the sun the moon in 4.5, and in 5.2 tells two other women that their lances are but straws.

themes.name: Naming and contradiction
themes.summary: Petruchio's chief weapon is insisting on his own version of the words: she is Kate, the food is burnt, the cap is a bauble, the sun is the moon. Katherina's resistance is equally verbal, and the marriage is settled not by force but by who gets to decide what things are called.
themes.development: The wit duel of 2.1 is fought on equal terms; by 4.5 one party is naming and the other assenting; the last speech is the naming done in her own voice.

themes.name: Who is watching
themes.summary: Almost everything in the play is performed for an onstage audience: Sly watches the comedy, Gremio reports the wedding, Hortensio spies on Bianca, and the obedience speech is delivered to a room of spectators who have money on it. The Induction makes watching a subject before the main plot has begun.
themes.development: The frame is set up in the Induction and abandoned after 1.1; the wager scene reinstates the same arrangement, with the husbands as the lord and Katherina as Sly.

techniques.name: The unclosed frame
techniques.definition: A story told inside another story, so that every account reaches the reader through somebody with an interest in it.
techniques.bookDefinition: A story enclosing another story, here left open at one end.
techniques.inThisBook: Sly is set up as the play's audience and then simply dropped. The related 1594 quarto A Shrew brings him back at the end, which is why eighteenth-century editors borrowed that ending and why modern directors still have to choose.

techniques.name: Disguise plot
techniques.definition: A character concealing their identity, so that the audience knows more than the people on stage do.
techniques.bookDefinition: Comedy driven by exchanged and counterfeited identities.
techniques.inThisBook: Inherited from Gascoigne's Supposes, itself from Ariosto: a servant in his master's gown, two suitors as tutors and a stranger hired to play a father, all running at once and colliding in 5.1.

techniques.name: Falconry imagery
techniques.definition: Sustained comparison of a person to a hawk being trained.
techniques.bookDefinition: Sustained comparison of a person to a hawk being trained.
techniques.inThisBook: Petruchio's soliloquy in 4.1 uses the technical vocabulary exactly — sharp, full-gorged, lure, man my haggard, watch her — so the audience is told the method in the language of a manual rather than a metaphor.

techniques.name: Stichomythia
techniques.definition: Rapid exchange of single lines between two speakers.
techniques.bookDefinition: Rapid exchange of single lines between two speakers.
techniques.inThisBook: The wooing scene in 2.1 runs on it for over eighty lines: joined-stool, ass, jade, buzzard, each answer taking the previous line's word and turning it round. It is the only sustained conversation in which Katherina is a match for anyone.

techniques.name: Soliloquy
techniques.definition: A character alone on stage, telling the audience what they are doing.
techniques.bookDefinition: A character alone on stage, telling the audience what they are doing.
techniques.inThisBook: Petruchio gets one and Katherina does not. His speech at the end of 4.1 hands the audience the whole strategy and then asks whether anybody knows a better way, which makes the spectators accomplices.

techniques.name: Wordplay
techniques.definition: Puns and quibbles used as attack and defence.
techniques.bookDefinition: Puns and quibbles used as attack and defence.
techniques.inThisBook: Kate, cate and Kates in 2.1; a cap that is a custard-coffin, a bauble and a silken pie in 4.3. The play keeps showing that whoever controls the joke controls the scene.

quotations.text: Ye are a baggage: the Slys are no rogues; look in the chronicles; we came in with Richard Conqueror.
quotations.speaker: Sly
quotations.context: Outside the alehouse, refusing to pay for the glasses he has broken.
quotations.analysis: He defends his family's standing by appealing to a history book he has never read and getting the Conqueror's name wrong. The play's first words are therefore a man insisting on an identity he cannot support — which is exactly the trick the lord is about to play on him from the other direction.
quotations.source: Globe/Moby text, Induction 1, lines 3-4 (numbered 0.1.3-4 in the digital text)

quotations.text: Come, madam wife, sit by my side and let the world slip: we shall ne'er be younger.
quotations.speaker: Sly
quotations.context: The last thing Sly says before the Padua play begins.
quotations.analysis: He has accepted the lordship, the wife who is a page in a dress, and the play about to be performed for him, all within a scene. These are almost his final words in the text: the character who has just learned to let the world slip is himself allowed to slip out of the comedy without explanation.
quotations.source: Globe/Moby text, Induction 2, lines 143-144 (numbered 0.2.143-144 in the digital text)

quotations.text: To see fair Padua, nursery of arts
quotations.speaker: Lucentio
quotations.context: Arriving in the city to study.
quotations.analysis: The play he has walked into is not about arts but about prices, and he will abandon the university within forty lines for a disguise and a marriage. Padua's reputation is set up in the second line of the main plot precisely so that everything that follows can ignore it.

quotations.text: Her eldest sister is so curst and shrewd That till the father rid his hands of her, Master, your love must live a maid at home;
quotations.speaker: Tranio
quotations.context: Explaining the household's rules to Lucentio.
quotations.analysis: Katherina is introduced to the audience as a problem of logistics: a thing the father must be rid of before the real business can proceed. 'Curst' and 'shrewd' are both technical terms of abuse for women rather than descriptions, and they are applied by a servant who has seen her once.

quotations.text: I come to wive it wealthily in Padua; If wealthily, then happily in Padua.
quotations.speaker: Petruchio
quotations.context: Telling Hortensio what kind of wife he is looking for.
quotations.analysis: The couplet makes wealth the condition of happiness in so many words, and the repetition of 'in Padua' turns the city into a marketplace with a location. Nothing later in the play retracts this; the love, if it is there, arrives after the terms have been agreed.

quotations.text: What, will you not suffer me? Nay, now I see She is your treasure, she must have a husband; I must dance bare-foot on her wedding day And for your love to her lead apes in hell.
quotations.speaker: Katherina
quotations.context: To her father, who has just sent Bianca out of the room after Katherina struck her.
quotations.analysis: The violence of the scene is real and so is the grievance underneath it: she is describing, accurately, a household in which one daughter is the treasure and the other the obstacle. Dancing barefoot at a younger sister's wedding and leading apes in hell were both proverbial fates of the unmarried, so she is naming the future arranged for her.

quotations.text: Asses are made to bear, and so are you.
quotations.speaker: Katherina
quotations.context: In the middle of the wit duel, after Petruchio invites her to sit on him.
quotations.analysis: She takes his innuendo and returns it as an insult in the same number of syllables, which is what the whole scene consists of. His reply — 'Women are made to bear, and so are you' — changes bearing weight into bearing children, and the exchange shows the two of them evenly matched at the only game either of them is playing.

quotations.text: Thus in plain terms: your father hath consented That you shall be my wife; your dowry 'greed on; And, Will you, nill you, I will marry you.
quotations.speaker: Petruchio
quotations.context: Ending the wooing scene, before her father returns.
quotations.analysis: Three clauses, and her consent is not among them: the father has agreed, the money has been agreed, and the remaining matter is announced rather than asked. 'Will you, nill you' — whether you are willing or not — is the plainest sentence in the play about how the marriage is made.

quotations.text: For I am he am born to tame you Kate, And bring you from a wild Kate to a Kate Conformable as other household Kates.
quotations.speaker: Petruchio
quotations.context: Immediately before Baptista comes back to hear how the wooing went.
quotations.analysis: The pun runs through wild cat, Kate and cates, which were delicacies laid on a table — three meanings of a name she has already told him she does not use. Renaming is the first move of the taming, and it is done here in front of her while she is being told what she will become.

quotations.text: Why, gentlemen, you do me double wrong, To strive for that which resteth in my choice: I am no breeching scholar in the schools; I'll not be tied to hours nor 'pointed times, But learn my lessons as I please myself.
quotations.speaker: Bianca
quotations.context: To her two disguised suitors, who are arguing about who teaches her first.
quotations.analysis: The obedient daughter, alone with two men and out of her father's hearing, says that the choice rests with her and sets the timetable herself. A breeching scholar is a schoolboy still young enough to be whipped, and she is refusing the position the whole household has assigned her.

quotations.text: To me she's married, not unto my clothes:
quotations.speaker: Petruchio
quotations.context: Refusing to change out of the ridiculous outfit he has worn to his wedding.
quotations.analysis: It is a good argument, and it is made by a man who has spent the morning proving the opposite: the clothes are the entire point of the performance, as the Induction has already demonstrated on a tinker. He will use the same principle in reverse in 4.3, when a cap and a gown become grounds for ruining a tailor.

quotations.text: I see a woman may be made a fool, If she had not a spirit to resist.
quotations.speaker: Katherina
quotations.context: At the wedding, being told she will not be staying for the dinner.
quotations.analysis: It is the clearest statement of her position in the play, and it is made in public at her own wedding feast. The conditional is doing the work: she is not saying she has resisted successfully, only that resistance is the one thing standing between her and being made ridiculous — and four lines later she is carried out of the door.

quotations.text: I will be master of what is mine own: She is my goods, my chattels; she is my house, My household stuff, my field, my barn, My horse, my ox, my ass, my any thing;
quotations.speaker: Petruchio
quotations.context: Removing Katherina from her own wedding feast, pretending to defend her from thieves.
quotations.analysis: The list descends from buildings to livestock to 'my any thing', and the legal terms are accurate: a wife's goods did pass to her husband. What makes the speech theatre rather than doctrine is the pantomime around it — he draws a weapon on an imaginary gang in order to carry her off as a rescue.

quotations.text: My falcon now is sharp and passing empty; And till she stoop she must not be full-gorged, For then she never looks upon her lure.
quotations.speaker: Petruchio
quotations.context: Alone on stage at the country house, after the food has been thrown away.
quotations.analysis: Every word is technical: a sharp hawk is hungry, stooping is the dive to the lure, full-gorged is fed. The audience is being handed a working method rather than a metaphor, and the calm of the vocabulary is what makes the speech disturbing — this is a man describing standard practice.

quotations.text: This is a way to kill a wife with kindness; And thus I'll curb her mad and headstrong humour. He that knows better how to tame a shrew, Now let him speak: 'tis charity to show.
quotations.speaker: Petruchio
quotations.context: The end of the same soliloquy.
quotations.analysis: The phrase now used to mean overwhelming someone with affection is invented here to describe starvation and enforced sleeplessness carried out in the name of care. The closing invitation to the audience is the sharpest thing in the play: he asks a theatre full of husbands whether anyone has a better method, and waits.

quotations.text: Why, sir, I trust I may have leave to speak; And speak I will; I am no child, no babe: Your betters have endured me say my mind, And if you cannot, best you stop your ears.
quotations.speaker: Katherina
quotations.context: When the cap she has asked for is taken away from her.
quotations.analysis: She claims the right to speak rather than the cap, and the argument she makes is about who has authority over her tongue. Her next lines say that if her heart conceals its anger it will break — a physiological claim, not a rhetorical one, and the strongest case in the play for reading the last speech as something other than a change of mind.

quotations.text: Then, God be bless'd, it is the blessed sun: But sun it is not, when you say it is not; And the moon changes even as your mind.
quotations.speaker: Katherina
quotations.context: On the road to Padua, after agreeing that the sun is the moon and being contradicted again.
quotations.analysis: She gives him the answer he wants and then explains the rule she has worked out: truth is whatever he last said. The third line is not obedience but a description of his behaviour, and productions that play the scene as a shared joke and productions that play it as defeat are both working from the same words.

quotations.text: Marry, peace it bodes, and love and quiet life, And awful rule and right supremacy; And, to be short, what not, that's sweet and happy?
quotations.speaker: Petruchio
quotations.context: When Katherina goes to fetch the other two wives.
quotations.analysis: Peace, love and quiet life are listed in the same breath as awful rule and right supremacy, as though they were the same thing rather than its price. 'Awful' here means awe-inspiring, which makes the sentence a definition of the household he thinks he has built.

quotations.text: The wager thou hast won; and I will add Unto their losses twenty thousand crowns; Another dowry to another daughter, For she is changed, as she had never been.
quotations.speaker: Baptista
quotations.context: After Katherina comes when sent for.
quotations.analysis: A father watches his daughter obey and responds by paying out: the transformation is priced at twenty thousand crowns and described as producing a different daughter altogether. It is the last word of the marriage market that opened the play, and it makes the obedience speech that follows a piece of after-sales demonstration.

quotations.text: Thy husband is thy lord, thy life, thy keeper, Thy head, thy sovereign; one that cares for thee, And for thy maintenance commits his body To painful labour both by sea and land,
quotations.speaker: Katherina
quotations.context: Instructing Bianca and the Widow on a wife's duty.
quotations.analysis: The argument is contractual: he labours by sea and land, she keeps warm at home, and obedience is the payment due. It is also a description of a marriage that is not hers — Petruchio has been at no sea, and the man who earned his wife by refusing her food is standing in the room while she says it.

quotations.text: My mind hath been as big as one of yours, My heart as great, my reason haply more, To bandy word for word and frown for frown; But now I see our lances are but straws,
quotations.speaker: Katherina
quotations.context: Near the end of the obedience speech.
quotations.analysis: The past tense is doing something the rest of the speech does not: she tells the other women that she was their equal in mind and their superior in reason, and then says the weapons were never real. 'Bandy word for word' is an exact description of what she did to Petruchio in 2.1, so the speech remembers the wit duel even as it disowns it.

quotations.text: Then vail your stomachs, for it is no boot, And place your hands below your husband's foot: In token of which duty, if he please, My hand is ready; may it do him ease.
quotations.speaker: Katherina
quotations.context: The last lines of the speech, and almost her last in the play.
quotations.analysis: Everything hangs on 'if he please' and on what the actor does with a hand that is offered rather than placed. The gesture is conditional, the token is symbolic, and Petruchio's reply is not thanks but a summons to bed — after which Katherina says nothing at all for the remaining eleven lines of the play.

atAGlance.label: Written
atAGlance.note: Usually placed among the earliest comedies; no document fixes the year.

atAGlance.label: First printed
atAGlance.note: There is no quarto of Shakespeare's Shrew before the First Folio; a 1631 quarto was set from the Folio text.

atAGlance.label: The other Shrew
atAGlance.note: A Pleasant Conceited Historie, called The taming of a Shrew was printed in quarto — closely related, differently worded, and still unexplained.

atAGlance.label: Chief source
atAGlance.note: The Bianca plot comes from Gascoigne's 1566 translation of Ariosto; the taming plot has analogues but no single source.

criticalViews.position: The play as farce
criticalViews.summary: One long tradition treats the taming as broad comic business in the manner of commedia dell'arte: exaggerated, unreal and not to be examined for a theory of marriage.
criticalViews.counter: The falconry soliloquy is not farcical in tone, and the deprivation it describes is precise rather than cartoonish.

criticalViews.position: The play as ironic
criticalViews.summary: A widespread modern reading takes the obedience speech as performance: Katherina has learned Petruchio's own game of saying what the occasion requires, and is playing it in public for the couple's joint profit.
criticalViews.counter: Nothing in the text marks the irony, and the reading relies on staging decisions the words do not require; it can also make a very long speech into a wink.

criticalViews.position: The play as a study of coercion
criticalViews.summary: A third position takes the Induction seriously: a man is talked out of his identity for other people's amusement, and the play then repeats the experiment on a wife, with a wager at the end to confirm the result.
criticalViews.counter: It has to account for the comedy actually working in performance, and for Bianca and the Widow, who refuse to come when called and are not punished for it.

essayQuestions.question: How should Katherina's final speech be played?
essayQuestions.focus: Obedience, irony and the evidence in the text
plan: Set out the staging facts first: forty-four lines, delivered in public, to two women, in a room where money has just changed hands on her conduct.
Trace her earlier language — the refusal to be silenced in 4.3 and the account of his changing mind in 4.5 — as the material an actor has to build on.
Read the speech's own past tense: my mind hath been as big as one of yours, my reason haply more.
Test the ironic reading against 'place your hands below your husband's foot', and the sincere reading against the wager that produced it.
Conclude with what follows: Petruchio's reply, Lucentio's last line about froward women, and Katherina's silence.

essayQuestions.question: What does the Induction do to the rest of the play?
essayQuestions.focus: Frames, spectatorship and the missing ending
plan: Describe what happens to Sly: an identity dismantled and replaced by repetition, clothes and other people's insistence.
Show that the Padua plot repeats the method on a wife, and that Petruchio's technique is the lord's technique.
Note that the Folio never returns to Sly, and that the 1594 A Shrew does — and that editors once borrowed that ending.
Consider the wager scene as a reinstated frame: husbands watching, a woman performing, money on the outcome.
Decide whether a production that cuts the Induction is playing a different play.

essayQuestions.question: 'Every courtship in the play is a negotiation.' Discuss.
essayQuestions.focus: Money, contracts and consent
plan: Begin with Baptista's condition in 1.1, which makes one daughter's marriage the price of the other's.
Use Petruchio's 'wive it wealthily' and the settlement of the dowry in 2.1 before any consent is sought.
Set the auction for Bianca — plate, hangings, an argosy — against the romance Lucentio believes he is conducting.
Examine what Bianca actually does: takes the tutor, marries in secret, and refuses to come when called.
Close on 5.2, where a second dowry is paid for a change in behaviour.

essayQuestions.question: How does disguise work in the play, and what does it prove?
essayQuestions.focus: Identity, clothes and the Supposes plot
plan: List the disguises and note how many of them are of social rank rather than sex: servant as master, gentleman as tutor, stranger as father.
Connect the machinery to Gascoigne's Supposes, and to the comic tradition of substitution the audience would have recognised.
Show that Tranio is better at being a gentleman than Lucentio, and ask what the play does with that.
Set the disguises against Petruchio's wedding clothes and his claim that she is married to him and not to his clothes.
Return to Sly, whose transformation is achieved with nothing but a gown and a consistent story.

discussionQuestions: Christopher Sly never comes back. Should a production invent an ending for him?
Petruchio asks the audience directly whether anyone knows a better way to tame a shrew. What is that question doing in a comedy?
Bianca and the Widow refuse to come when their husbands send for them, and nothing happens to them. Does that undercut the taming plot or confirm it?
Katherina and Petruchio are evenly matched in the wooing scene of Act II. Is anything of that match left by Act V?
The play is still funny in performance. Is that a problem, and for whom?

timeline.label: Gascoigne's Supposes performed at Gray's Inn
timeline.detail: An English version of Ariosto's I Suppositi, and the source of the Bianca plot's disguises and substituted fathers.

timeline.label: Supposes printed
timeline.detail: Its availability in print is what makes the borrowing traceable.

timeline.label: The Taming of the Shrew probably written
timeline.detail: Usually placed around 1590-92 among the earliest comedies; nothing fixes the year.

timeline.label: A Pleasant Conceited Historie, called The taming of a Shrew printed
timeline.detail: A closely related play with different names and wording, reprinted in 1596 and 1607. Source, memorial report, adaptation or early draft: the question is still open.

timeline.label: Fletcher's The Woman's Prize, or The Tamer Tamed
timeline.detail: Usually dated around 1609-11. Petruchio remarries after Katherina's death and is resisted by a second wife, which shows the play was being answered within its own generation.

timeline.label: First Folio
timeline.detail: The first secure printed text of Shakespeare's Shrew, with the Induction and no return to Sly.

timeline.label: A quarto printed from the Folio text
timeline.detail: Not an independent witness; it confirms that the Folio was the version in circulation.

timeline.label: John Lacy's Sauny the Scot
timeline.detail: A Restoration adaptation in prose that expanded Grumio into a Scottish servant and made Petruchio harsher.

timeline.label: Garrick's Catharine and Petruchio
timeline.detail: Three acts, no Sly, almost no Bianca — and the version most audiences saw for well over a century.

timeline.label: Sam Taylor's film with Mary Pickford and Douglas Fairbanks
timeline.detail: Widely cited as the first sound Shakespeare film; Pickford's wink during the last speech became part of the play's argument with itself.

timeline.label: Kiss Me, Kate opens on Broadway
timeline.detail: Cole Porter's musical puts the play inside a backstage quarrel — a twentieth-century replacement for the abandoned Sly frame.

timeline.label: Michael Bogdanov's RSC production
timeline.detail: Sly disrupted the auditorium before the Padua story began, treating the taming plot as a problem rather than a farce.

timeline.label: Justin Audibert's gender-reversed RSC production
timeline.detail: Set in a matriarchal Elizabethan England, with Petruchia and Katherine, so that the hierarchy itself became visible as a construction.

places.name: Padua
places.note: Baptista's city, described as a nursery of arts and run as a marriage market.

places.name: Verona
places.note: Petruchio's home, which he leaves in the first scene of Act I to find a wealthy wife.

places.name: Pisa
places.note: Lucentio's city, and Vincentio's — the identity a passing pedant is hired to counterfeit.

places.name: Venice
places.note: Where Petruchio goes for rings and fine array between the betrothal and the wedding.

places.name: Mantua
places.note: The pedant's home, and the city he is told it is dangerous to have come from.

places.name: Barton-on-the-Heath
