places.note: Sly's Burtonheath: a Warwickshire village a few miles from Stratford, where Shakespeare had relatives by marriage.

related.why: Beatrice and Benedick are the later, kinder version of a courtship conducted entirely through insult.
Another early comedy of disguise, servants and travel between Italian cities, with an ending readers have argued about for as long.
The other early play built out of mistaken identity and substitution, taken from Roman comedy rather than from Ariosto.
Disguise used to court on someone else's behalf, with the consequences taken seriously.
A comedy in which a woman directs her own courtship, and speaks the epilogue herself.

books.title: Tess of the d’Urbervilles
books.author: Thomas Hardy
books.setting: Hardy’s Wessex: the Vale of Blackmoor, the Var valley, the uplands at Flintcomb-Ash, and Stonehenge
books.lengthNote: Fifty-nine chapters gathered into seven named phases
books.openingLine: On an evening in the latter part of May a middle-aged man was walking homeward from Shaston to the village of Marlott, in the adjoining Vale of Blakemore, or Blackmoor.
books.summary: A parson tells a haggler on a Dorset road that he is descended from knights, and the boast costs his daughter everything. Hardy tracks Tess Durbeyfield through four employers, two men and one dead child, and arranges the novel so that every disaster arrives through ordinary machinery: a horse on a dark road, a letter under a carpet, a threshing engine that will not stop. The subtitle is an argument, and the book is built to win it.

sourceText.label: Standard Ebooks text of Tess of the d’Urbervilles
sourceText.note: Chapters are numbered continuously in Roman numerals from I to LIX across the seven phases; references below give the phase as well, since the phases are the divisions Hardy himself named.

structure.label: Phase the First
structure.title: The Maiden
structure.summary: A chance meeting on the road tells John Durbeyfield he is a d’Urberville, and the family’s drunken celebration puts Tess in charge of the horse. Prince is killed, the family loses its living, and Tess is sent to claim kin from a household that bought the name.

scenes.title: The name
scenes.summary: Parson Tringham’s antiquarian civility turns a haggler into a knight, and the club-walking gives Angel Clare his first, unused sight of Tess.

scenes.title: Prince
scenes.summary: Tess takes the beehives to market at night, falls asleep, and the mail-cart kills the horse; the guilt sends her to Trantridge.

scenes.title: The Chase
scenes.summary: Alec installs her in the poultry farm, follows her through the fog after the dance at Chaseborough, and the novel’s central assault is narrated in the dark and in the dark of the prose.

structure.label: Phase the Second
structure.title: Maiden No More
structure.summary: Tess walks home, refuses Alec’s offer of support, and works the harvest with her child at the field edge. Sorrow is baptised by his mother when the parson is refused and buried in the unconsecrated corner with the drunkards and the stillborn.

scenes.title: The return
scenes.summary: She goes back to Marlott and asks her mother why she was never warned.

scenes.title: Sorrow
scenes.summary: The harvest scene, the home baptism, the refused burial, and the two years of silence that follow.

structure.label: Phase the Third
structure.title: The Rally
structure.summary: At Talbothays the work is skilled, the valley is fertile and Tess is briefly an employee rather than a victim. Angel Clare, learning dairying before emigrating, watches her across three months of summer and decides that she is Nature itself, which is the beginning of the trouble.

scenes.title: The Var valley
scenes.summary: A larger landscape, real skill at the milking, and the harp heard across the garden.

scenes.title: Summer
scenes.summary: The dairy’s three other milkmaids love Angel too, and the novel keeps them in view; Angel declares himself in a cart full of milk.

structure.label: Phase the Fourth
structure.title: The Consequence
structure.summary: Tess refuses Angel repeatedly and then accepts, tries four times to tell him, and finally writes it down. The letter goes under the carpet as well as under the door, and the confession she owes is postponed to the wedding night, where he makes his own first.

scenes.title: The engagement
scenes.summary: Angel’s family, his brothers’ respectability, and the ride to the station where Tess begins and abandons her history.

scenes.title: The letter
scenes.summary: The note that is never read, the wedding at last, and Angel’s confession of his own forty-eight hours in London.

structure.label: Phase the Fifth
structure.title: The Woman Pays
structure.summary: Angel hears the same offence he has just confessed and finds it a different thing entirely. He leaves for Brazil; Tess sends money home, is turned away from dairy work, and ends at Flintcomb-Ash pulling swedes in the rain and feeding a threshing machine.

scenes.title: The rejection
scenes.summary: The confession, the sleepwalking, the coffin, and the separation dressed as a temporary arrangement.

scenes.title: Flintcomb-Ash
scenes.summary: The starve-acre farm, Marian and Izz, and the walk to Emminster that ends with Tess overhearing the Clare brothers and turning back.

structure.label: Phase the Sixth
structure.title: The Convert
structure.summary: Alec reappears as a ranting preacher and abandons the pulpit within a fortnight of seeing her again, telling her the backsliding is her fault. He follows her to the rick, offers to keep her family, and waits for her father’s death to do the arguing for him.

scenes.title: The preacher
scenes.summary: The conversion, the pursuit across the uplands, and the confrontation on the threshing rick.

scenes.title: Lady Day
scenes.summary: The unanswered letter, John Durbeyfield’s death, the loss of the cottage, and the night in the churchyard at Kingsbere.

structure.label: Phase the Seventh
structure.title: Fulfilment
structure.summary: Angel comes back from Brazil thin and altered, and finds Tess installed in a boarding house at Sandbourne under another man’s protection. She kills Alec, the two of them walk north for five days, and the police take her at dawn on the stone at Stonehenge.

scenes.title: Sandbourne
scenes.summary: The return, the landlady’s staircase, and the spreading stain on the ceiling below.

scenes.title: Stonehenge and Wintoncester
scenes.summary: The empty house in the New Forest, the sleep on the altar stone, the arrest at sunrise, and the black flag over the city gaol.

characters.name: Tess Durbeyfield
characters.role: A field-woman, sixteen at the opening
characters.summary: Hardy gives her the intelligence of a National-school education and the position of an unskilled labourer, and the gap between the two is where the novel lives. She is judged by everyone she meets on evidence she was never allowed to present, and the subtitle exists because Hardy expected his readers to join in.
characters.clue: She baptises her own child with a jug of water because the parson will not come, and names him for a word out of the Bible.

relationships.label: assaulted, pursued and finally killed by her hand

characters.name: Alec d’Urberville
characters.role: Son of a Stoke family that purchased the name
characters.summary: His ancestry is bought and his power is entirely current: money, a gig, a poultry farm, a mother who cannot see. He converts, preaches, relapses and proposes with the same unembarrassed energy, and blames Tess for each turn.
characters.clue: He drives too fast downhill, feeds a girl strawberries she has not asked for, and later preaches in a barn about the sin he committed.

characters.name: Angel Clare
characters.role: A parson’s youngest son, learning farming
characters.summary: He has rejected his father’s church and kept every one of its judgements. The cruelty of the wedding night is not hypocrisy in the ordinary sense — he has genuinely convinced himself that the woman in front of him is a different person from the one he proposed to.
characters.clue: He confesses forty-eight hours of dissipation, is forgiven in a sentence, and cannot manage the same for a confession he has just been given.

characters.name: Joan Durbeyfield
characters.role: Tess’s mother
characters.summary: She sends her daughter to claim kin in a clean dress and never explains why a clean dress might matter. Hardy is precise about the gap between them: the mother’s world is ballads and a fortune-telling book, the daughter’s is the Sixth Standard, and two hundred years lie between the two.
characters.clue: She keeps a fortune-telling book in the thatch because she will not have it in the house at night.

characters.name: John Durbeyfield
characters.role: A haggler of Marlott
characters.summary: He is given a title and no money, and spends the rest of his short life being carried home. His death is the event that empties the cottage, because the lease was on his life: the novel’s cruellest joke is that the ancestry which ruined his daughter also fails to house her.
characters.clue: Told on the road that he is descended from knights, he immediately orders a carriage to take him the rest of the way home.

characters.name: Marian
characters.role: A dairymaid at Talbothays, later at Flintcomb-Ash
characters.summary: She loves Angel, loses him without resentment, and is the one who finds Tess work when nobody else will. Her drinking at the starve-acre farm is treated as a fact about the work rather than a fault in her.
characters.clue: The stoutest of the three milkmaids who lie awake listening for a man’s footstep, and the one who later writes to warn of a danger she cannot name.

characters.name: Izz Huett
characters.role: A dairymaid at Talbothays
characters.summary: Asked by Angel to come to Brazil with him, she agrees, and then tells him the truth about how much Tess loved him, which ends the proposal. It is the most disinterested act in the book and nobody thanks her for it.
characters.clue: She is offered a passage to Brazil and talks the man out of it by telling him what another woman would have done for him.

characters.name: Liza-Lu
characters.role: Tess’s younger sister
characters.summary: She is barely characterised until the last pages, when Tess asks Angel to marry her — a request the novel neither endorses nor refuses. She walks away from Wintoncester holding his hand, which is as close to a future as the book offers.
characters.clue: A girl of about sixteen, described as having her sister’s face without her sister’s history, who is handed that history at the end.

themes.name: Purity and the verdict
themes.summary: The subtitle picks a fight before the first page. Hardy’s method is to show the judgement being made — by Angel, by the parson who will not bury Sorrow, by Tess herself — and then to show the evidence on which it rests, which is always somebody else’s conduct.
themes.development: From the refused burial in Phase the Second, through the wedding night in Phase the Fifth, to the narrator’s flat statement that she had broken an accepted social law and no law known to her environment.

themes.name: Class and ancestry
themes.summary: The d’Urberville name is the novel’s original accident: it is worthless as property, potent as fantasy, and purchasable by anyone with money. Hardy sets a family that owns the name legitimately and has nothing against a family that bought it and has everything.
themes.development: Announced on the road in Chapter I, exploited at Trantridge, revived at Kingsbere when the family sleeps under the window of its own vault, and finally irrelevant at the gallows.

themes.name: Work and the land
themes.summary: Nobody in this novel is ever outside the labour market. Tess moves between a poultry farm, a dairy, a swede field and a threshing rick, and each place has its own skills, wages, weather and physical cost, described with the accuracy of someone who had watched it done.
themes.development: The fertile Var valley of Phase the Third is set against the starve-acre uplands of Phase the Fifth, and the threshing machine in Phase the Sixth makes the pace of work no longer human.

themes.name: Chance, timing and cause
themes.summary: A letter slides under a carpet, a horse meets a mail-cart, a man arrives a week too late. Hardy is not arguing that Tess is unlucky; he is arguing that a woman with no money and no standing cannot survive the ordinary accidents that other people absorb.
themes.development: Each phase turns on a small mistimed event, and the narrator repeatedly refuses to call any of them fate while allowing the characters to do so.

themes.name: Religion and its officers
themes.summary: The novel is full of clergy and empty of comfort. A vicar refuses a Christian burial and then privately says it makes no difference; a rake preaches in a barn and abandons it in a fortnight; Angel keeps his father’s morality after discarding his father’s creed.
themes.development: The home baptism in Phase the Second is the book’s one act of genuine sacrament, and it is performed by an unmarried mother in a cottage bedroom.

themes.name: The double standard
themes.summary: Hardy constructs the wedding night as a controlled experiment: two confessions, the same offence, told within an hour of each other, with the sexes reversed. Angel is forgiven in a sentence; the novel then watches him fail to return the favour for the next hundred pages.
themes.development: Set up by the paired confessions in Phase the Fifth, named by the title of that phase, and never retracted — Angel’s eventual forgiveness arrives after it can do any good.

techniques.name: The named phases
techniques.definition: Dividing a novel into large titled units that carry an argument of their own.
techniques.bookDefinition: Dividing a novel into large titled units that carry an argument of their own.
techniques.inThisBook: Hardy calls his seven divisions phases rather than books or parts, and names them so that the contents page reads as a sentence: The Maiden, Maiden No More, The Rally, The Consequence, The Woman Pays, The Convert, Fulfilment.

techniques.name: Landscape as pressure
techniques.definition: Place and weather made to press on the people living in them, rather than serving as scenery.
techniques.bookDefinition: Using terrain, weather and scale to exert force on the characters rather than to decorate them.
techniques.inThisBook: The Var valley makes bodies fertile and Flintcomb-Ash makes them cold; the same woman doing the same work is a different creature in each, and Hardy changes his vocabulary accordingly.

techniques.name: Narratorial intervention
techniques.definition: A narrator stepping out of the story to contest the judgement the story is receiving.
techniques.bookDefinition: A narrator stepping out of the story to contest the judgement the story is receiving.
techniques.inThisBook: The narrator asks where Tess’s guardian angel was, declares that she had broken no law known to her surroundings, and closes with a sentence about the President of the Immortals that is deliberately unfair to the universe.

techniques.name: Machinery
techniques.definition: Industrial equipment introduced into a rural setting as an agent in the plot.
techniques.bookDefinition: Industrial equipment introduced into a rural setting as an agent in the plot.
techniques.inThisBook: The threshing machine at Flintcomb-Ash sets the tempo of a whole chapter: the engineer is described as a stranger from another world, and Tess cannot leave the platform while it runs.

techniques.name: Dialect and register
techniques.definition: Spelling and grammar used to mark where a speaker comes from, and what being heard that way costs them.
techniques.bookDefinition: Marking class and education through the grammar characters are given.
techniques.inThisBook: Tess speaks two languages — the dialect at home and ordinary English at school and abroad — and Hardy says so explicitly, which makes the gap between her and her mother measurable in sentences.

techniques.name: Omens and retrospect
techniques.definition: Planting details whose significance is only available on a second reading.
techniques.bookDefinition: Planting details whose significance is only available on a second reading.
techniques.inThisBook: The cock that crows in the afternoon, the d’Urberville coach, the blood on the ceiling at Sandbourne: the superstitions belong to the characters, and the patterning belongs to Hardy.

quotations.text: Then what might your meaning be in calling me ‘Sir John’ these different times, when I be plain Jack Durbeyfield, the haggler?
quotations.speaker: John Durbeyfield
quotations.context: On the road to Marlott, to Parson Tringham, who has greeted him by a title.
quotations.analysis: He states his own name and trade accurately and in dialect, and it is the last time in the book anyone does so without embarrassment. The sentence is the hinge of the whole plot: a man asks for an explanation of a courtesy, and is given an ancestry he cannot afford.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Phase the First, Chapter I

quotations.text: ’Tis because we be on a blighted star, and not a sound one, isn’t it, Tess?
quotations.speaker: Abraham Durbeyfield
quotations.context: In the cart on the road to Casterbridge, after Tess has explained the stars to him, and before the mail-cart kills the horse.
quotations.analysis: A child converts an astronomy lesson into a theory of his family’s luck, and the novel lets it stand as the best available explanation. The image is agricultural rather than cosmic — the blighted apple on the stubbard-tree — so the cosmology is made out of the only materials the Durbeyfields have.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Phase the First, Chapter IV

quotations.text: might some say, where was Tess’s guardian angel? where was the providence of her simple faith? Perhaps, like that other god of whom the ironical Tishbite spoke, he was talking, or he was pursuing, or he was in a journey, or he was sleeping and not to be awaked.
quotations.context: In The Chase, at the moment the narrative declines to describe.
quotations.analysis: The question is put into the mouth of an imagined objector — ‘might some say’ — so that the narrator can ask it without quite owning it. The answer comes from Elijah mocking the priests of Baal, which turns a plea for providence into a joke about a god who is out of the office.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Phase the First, Chapter XI

quotations.text: Why it was that upon this beautiful feminine tissue, sensitive as gossamer, and practically blank as snow as yet, there should have been traced such a coarse pattern as it was doomed to receive; why so often the coarse appropriates the finer thus, the wrong man the woman, the wrong woman the man, many thousand years of analytical philosophy have failed to explain to our sense of order.
quotations.context: Immediately after the assault, in the narrator’s own voice.
quotations.analysis: Tess is described as fabric and the assault as a pattern traced on it, which keeps the violence entirely out of the grammar: there is no assailant in the sentence, only a coarseness that appropriates a fineness. The evasion has been read both as Hardy’s delicacy and as his failure of nerve.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Phase the First, Chapter XI

quotations.text: An immeasurable social chasm was to divide our heroine’s personality thereafter from that previous self of hers who stepped from her mother’s door to try her fortune at Trantridge poultry-farm.
quotations.context: The last sentence of the first phase.
quotations.analysis: The damage is described as social rather than personal: what has changed is not Tess but the distance between two versions of her, and the chasm is measured from her mother’s door to a poultry farm. Hardy ends the phase on a job title, which is where the novel always puts its weight.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Phase the First, Chapter XI

quotations.text: How could I be expected to know? I was a child when I left this house four months ago. Why didn’t you tell me there was danger in menfolk? Why didn’t you warn me? Ladies know what to fend hands against, because they read novels that tell them of these tricks; but I never had the chance o’ learning in that way, and you did not help me!
quotations.speaker: Tess Durbeyfield
quotations.context: Back at Marlott, answering her mother’s complaint that she has not managed to get Alec to marry her.
quotations.analysis: The accusation is about information, not morality: ladies read novels and therefore know, and Tess had no access to the warning. It is the only moment in the book where she names the mechanism of her own ruin, and she names it as a class fact.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Phase the Second, Chapter XII

quotations.text: But all the while she was making a distinction where there was no difference. Feeling herself in antagonism, she was quite in accord. She had been made to break an accepted social law, but no law known to the environment in which she fancied herself such an anomaly.
quotations.context: Walking at night after her return, believing herself a figure of guilt among innocent birds and hedges.
quotations.analysis: The sentence performs a small legal argument: there is an accepted social law and there is the law of the environment, and only the first has been broken. ‘Feeling herself in antagonism, she was quite in accord’ inverts her self-accusation without arguing with it, which is Hardy’s usual method of defence.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Phase the Second, Chapter XIII

quotations.text: Sorrow, I baptize thee in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost.
quotations.speaker: Tess Durbeyfield
quotations.context: In the bedroom at Marlott, at one in the morning, her father having locked the door against the parson.
quotations.analysis: She uses the exact liturgical formula, which is why the vicar afterwards cannot say the rite was invalid — only that it will not buy a place in the churchyard. The child’s name is a common noun, so the sentence baptises an emotion, and the form of words is the one piece of institutional authority Tess is able to take for herself.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Phase the Second, Chapter XIV

quotations.text: So passed away Sorrow the Undesired⁠—that intrusive creature, that bastard gift of shameless Nature, who respects not the social law
quotations.context: After the burial in the corner of the churchyard reserved for the unbaptised and the suicides.
quotations.analysis: Three epithets in one clause, each in a different voice: the mother’s, the parish’s and the narrator’s. ‘Shameless Nature, who respects not the social law’ sets the two jurisdictions of the whole novel against each other in eight words, and leaves no doubt which one Hardy thinks is real.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Phase the Second, Chapter XIV

quotations.text: The world was drawn to a larger pattern here. The enclosures numbered fifty acres instead of ten
quotations.context: Tess’s first sight of the Var valley from the ridge, on the way to Talbothays.
quotations.analysis: The change of scene is registered as a change of measurement: fields, herds and horizons all get bigger, and so does the room she has to move in. Hardy is careful to make the relief agricultural — this is better land, and better land means steadier work.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Phase the Third, Chapter XVI

quotations.text: What a fresh and virginal daughter of Nature that milkmaid is!
quotations.speaker: Angel Clare
quotations.context: Angel identifying the new milkmaid, to himself, at Talbothays.
quotations.analysis: Every word of it is a category rather than a person, and two of them will be used against her within a year. He is not lying and he is not looking: the sentence is a piece of pastoral criticism applied to a colleague, and the novel records that he said it to himself.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Phase the Third, Chapter XVIII

quotations.text: There was hardly a touch of earth in her love for Clare. To her sublime trustfulness he was all that goodness could be⁠—knew all that a guide, philosopher, and friend should know. She thought every line in the contour of his person the perfection of masculine beauty, his soul the soul of a saint, his intellect that of a seer.
quotations.context: During the engagement at Talbothays.
quotations.analysis: Her love is described as having no earth in it, in a book where earth is the one thing that can be relied on. The triple structure — guide, philosopher and friend, then saint and seer — makes her devotion sound liturgical, and prepares the exact ground on which he will later refuse her.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Phase the Fourth, Chapter XXXI

quotations.text: under the edge of the carpet she discerned the faint white margin of the envelope containing her letter to him, which he obviously had never seen, owing to her having in her haste thrust it beneath the carpet as well as beneath the door.
quotations.context: The morning of the wedding, in the room where Angel has been sleeping.
quotations.analysis: The disaster is a matter of half an inch of floor covering, and Hardy makes the reader watch her find it rather than reporting it afterwards. Note that the sentence assigns the error to her haste, not to malice or fate: the novel’s catastrophes are almost always this small and this domestic.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Phase the Fourth, Chapter XXXIII

quotations.text: I repeat, the woman I have been loving is not you.
quotations.speaker: Angel Clare
quotations.context: At the old d’Urberville farmhouse, hours after his own confession has been forgiven.
quotations.analysis: ‘I repeat’ tells us he has already said it once, which is the cruellest word in the sentence. He does not accuse her of anything; he unmakes her, replacing a person with a category error, and the novel has spent a whole phase showing that the category was his invention.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Phase the Fifth, Chapter XXXV

quotations.text: How can we live together while that man lives?⁠—he being your husband in nature, and not I.
quotations.speaker: Angel Clare
quotations.context: Refusing Tess’s plea to be allowed to stay with him as a servant if not as a wife.
quotations.analysis: He converts an assault into a marriage and then reasons from it: the man who forced her is ‘your husband in nature’. The argument is legal in shape and biological in content, and it is the clearest statement in the book of the belief the subtitle was written to attack.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Phase the Fifth, Chapter XXXVI

quotations.text: Close under the eaves of the stack, and as yet barely visible, was the red tyrant that the women had come to serve⁠—a timber-framed construction, with straps and wheels appertaining⁠—the threshing-machine which, whilst it was going, kept up a despotic demand upon the endurance of their muscles and nerves.
quotations.context: Dawn at Flintcomb-Ash, as the threshing gang assembles.
quotations.analysis: The machine is given a colour, a title and a household of servants before it is given a technical description. ‘Despotic demand’ converts a wage relationship into a political one, and the women are the last link in it: the engine sets the speed, and Tess cannot step off the platform while it runs.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Phase the Sixth, Chapter XLVII

quotations.text: Whip me, crush me; you need not mind those people under the rick! I shall not cry out. Once victim, always victim⁠—that’s the law!
quotations.speaker: Tess Durbeyfield
quotations.context: On the threshing rick, after striking Alec across the mouth with her leather glove.
quotations.analysis: She invites the punishment and states the principle in the same breath, and the word she chooses is ‘law’. It is the same word the narrator used in Phase the Second about the accepted social law she had broken, and here Tess speaks it as if it were physics.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Phase the Sixth, Chapter XLVII

quotations.text: Remember, my lady, I was your master once! I will be your master again. If you are any man’s wife you are mine!
quotations.speaker: Alec d’Urberville
quotations.context: Holding her by the shoulders on the rick, after she has refused his offer to keep her family.
quotations.analysis: Three sentences, three tenses: was, will be, are. The vocabulary is of ownership throughout, and ‘my lady’ is a sneer at the ancestry that brought her to him in the first place. The threat is also a prediction, and the novel lets it come true.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Phase the Sixth, Chapter XLVII

quotations.text: I must cry to you in my trouble⁠—I have no one else! I am so exposed to temptation, Angel. I fear to say who it is, and I do not like to write about it at all. But I cling to you in a way you cannot think! Can you not come to me now, at once, before anything terrible happens?
quotations.speaker: Tess Durbeyfield
quotations.context: The letter written at Flintcomb-Ash and sent to Angel’s parents to be forwarded to Brazil.
quotations.analysis: She will not name the danger even in a private letter, which is exactly the reticence that has cost her twice already. The phrase ‘before anything terrible happens’ is the novel’s only piece of accurate forecasting, and the distance to Brazil guarantees that it arrives too late to be one.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Phase the Sixth, Chapter XLVIII

quotations.text: Angel, I am almost glad⁠—yes, glad! This happiness could not have lasted. It was too much. I have had enough; and now I shall not live for you to despise me!
quotations.speaker: Tess Durbeyfield
quotations.context: Waking on the stone at Stonehenge as the police close in at dawn.
quotations.analysis: Her last argument is about time rather than justice: the happiness was too much, so it could not have lasted, so ending it now is a form of thrift. ‘I shall not live for you to despise me’ shows that the wedding night is still the governing event of her life, five years and two men later.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Phase the Seventh, Chapter LVIII

quotations.text: the President of the Immortals, in Aeschylean phrase, had ended his sport with Tess.
quotations.context: As the black flag rises over Wintoncester gaol and Angel and Liza-Lu watch from the hill.
quotations.analysis: Hardy puts ‘Justice’ in quotation marks and then hands the credit to a figure out of Aeschylus, which lets him blame a god he does not believe in for a sentence passed by an English court. The evasion is deliberate: no judge, no juror and no clergyman is named, and the reader is left to supply them.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Phase the Seventh, Chapter LIX

atAGlance.label: Serialised
atAGlance.note: Weekly in The Graphic from July to December, cut and altered to suit a family illustrated paper.

atAGlance.label: First book edition
atAGlance.note: Three volumes from James R. Osgood, McIlvaine and Co., with the material the serial had removed restored.

atAGlance.label: Subtitle
atAGlance.note: Not a description but a verdict, and the reason much of the first reviewing was about morality rather than the novel.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.note: Hardy names them — The Maiden, Maiden No More, The Rally, The Consequence, The Woman Pays, The Convert, Fulfilment — so that the table of contents reads as a sentence about a life.

criticalViews.position: A tragedy of circumstance
criticalViews.summary: The oldest reading treats Tess as a modern tragic heroine destroyed by forces larger than herself — heredity, chance, the decay of the rural economy — with the President of the Immortals as the novel’s own summary of the case.
criticalViews.counter: It risks letting Alec and Angel off as instruments of fate, when the book is careful to show each of them choosing, at leisure, what to do next.

criticalViews.position: A social and economic novel
criticalViews.summary: Criticism attentive to the work has read the book as a record of the late-Victorian agricultural labour market: the annual hirings, the loss of lifehold cottages, the arrival of steam threshing, and what all of that does to a woman without a settlement.
criticalViews.counter: Read only this way, the marriage plot becomes an interruption, and the novel’s very deliberate arguments about purity and judgement go unanswered.

criticalViews.position: A novel about who is allowed to speak
criticalViews.summary: Later criticism, particularly feminist criticism from the 1970s onwards, has focused on the narration itself: Tess is described, painted, watched and argued over, and the scene on which everything turns is narrated in her absence from the prose.
criticalViews.counter: Hardy’s defenders point out that the same narrator is the only voice in the book that consistently argues on her side, and that the subtitle cost him a great deal.

essayQuestions.question: How does Hardy use the seven phases to shape the reader’s judgement of Tess?
essayQuestions.focus: Structure as argument
plan: Set out the titles in order and show that they form a narrative sentence about a life rather than a list of parts.
Contrast The Maiden and Maiden No More: the second title is imposed by other people, and the phase opens with Tess walking home.
Use The Rally to show Hardy granting a recovery that the structure has already told us is temporary.
Read The Woman Pays as the book’s thesis statement, and check it against the paired confessions that open the phase.
Weigh Fulfilment: an ironic title, a religious one, or an accurate description of what Tess says on the stone at Stonehenge.

essayQuestions.question: ‘Tess is destroyed by circumstance, not by character.’ Discuss.
essayQuestions.focus: Chance, agency and blame
plan: List the accidents: the mail-cart, the letter under the carpet, the Clare brothers on the road, Angel’s return a few weeks late.
Show that each one is small, domestic and survivable by somebody with money — and that Hardy makes that point rather than the reader.
Set against this the decisions actually taken: Alec at Trantridge, Angel on the wedding night, Joan Durbeyfield sending her daughter to claim kin.
Examine the narrator’s own interventions, which repeatedly refuse fate as an explanation while allowing the characters to reach for it.
Test the last paragraph: does the President of the Immortals settle the question or dodge it?

essayQuestions.question: Examine Hardy’s presentation of work in the novel.
essayQuestions.focus: Labour, land and machinery
plan: Start with the fact that Tess is always employed, and track the four workplaces in order: Trantridge, Talbothays, Flintcomb-Ash, Sandbourne.
Show how the prose changes with the land — the Var valley’s abundance against the flint uplands’ grey, and how each is described through the body doing the work.
Read the threshing scene closely: the machine’s tempo, the engineer as a stranger, and the fact that Tess cannot leave the platform.
Connect labour to power: every one of Alec’s advantages is contractual, from the poultry farm to the offer to keep her family.
Conclude on Lady Day and the lost cottage, where a lifehold agreement does more damage than either man.

essayQuestions.question: How far does the novel earn its subtitle?
essayQuestions.focus: A Pure Woman Faithfully Presented
plan: Establish what the subtitle claims and whom it is addressed to: not Tess, but the readers who will judge her.
Use the refused burial and the home baptism to show institutions and individuals reaching opposite verdicts on the same child.
Read the wedding night as a controlled experiment in the double standard, with the same offence confessed twice in an hour.
Consider the cost of the defence: Tess is repeatedly described rather than heard, and the assault itself happens outside the prose.
Decide whether Hardy’s narrator persuades or merely insists, and whether the last sentence helps or weakens the case.

discussionQuestions: Hardy does not describe what happens in The Chase. Is that restraint, evasion, or a way of making the reader supply the verdict?
Angel confesses first and is forgiven in a sentence. What would the novel lose if that order were reversed?
The letter goes under the carpet as well as under the door. Does that small accident convince you, or does it feel arranged?
Alec’s conversion lasts a fortnight. Is the novel attacking religion, or attacking him?
Tess asks Angel to marry her sister. What is being offered, and what is being taken away?

timeline.label: Thomas Hardy born at Higher Bockhampton
timeline.detail: In a cottage on the edge of the heath, three miles from Dorchester, into a family of builders and masons.

timeline.label: The Elementary Education Act
timeline.detail: The schooling that gives Tess her Sixth Standard English and opens the two-hundred-year gap Hardy describes between her and her mother.

timeline.label: Far from the Madding Crowd
timeline.detail: The novel that made Hardy’s name and fixed Wessex as a place readers expected to revisit.

timeline.label: The Mayor of Casterbridge
timeline.detail: Dorchester under its Wessex name, and the same interest in a man ruined by a single early act.

timeline.label: Serialised in The Graphic
timeline.detail: Weekly from July to December, with the seduction, the baptism and other material cut or altered for a family illustrated paper.

timeline.label: First book edition
timeline.detail: Three volumes from James R. Osgood, McIlvaine and Co., restoring the excised material and carrying the subtitle A Pure Woman Faithfully Presented.

timeline.label: One-volume edition
timeline.detail: A cheaper single volume widens the readership, and Hardy goes on revising the text in later issues.

timeline.label: Jude the Obscure
timeline.detail: The reception of Hardy’s last novel effectively ended his career as a novelist; he wrote poetry for the next thirty years.

timeline.label: Lorimer Stoddard’s stage version opens in New York
timeline.detail: Minnie Maddern Fiske played Tess from 2 March, and made the part a major role in the American theatre.

timeline.label: Silent film with Blanche Sweet
timeline.detail: Blanche Sweet as Tess, Stuart Holmes as Alec and Conrad Nagel as Angel; the film is now considered lost.

timeline.label: Hardy dies
timeline.detail: His ashes were buried in Westminster Abbey and his heart at Stinsford, which is the most Hardyan fact about him.

timeline.label: Roman Polanski’s Tess
timeline.detail: Nastassja Kinski in the title role; the film won Academy Awards for cinematography, art direction and costume design.

timeline.label: BBC four-part adaptation
timeline.detail: Written by David Nicholls and directed by David Blair, with Gemma Arterton as Tess.

places.name: Marnhull, Dorset
places.note: Hardy’s Marlott, in the Vale of Blackmoor: the club-walking, the cottage, and the night journey with the beehives.

places.name: Cranborne Chase
places.note: The Chase, the oldest wood in England in Hardy’s description, and the place the novel refuses to describe.

places.name: Dorchester
places.note: Casterbridge, the market town Tess is driving towards when the mail-cart kills Prince.

places.name: Bournemouth
places.note: Sandbourne, a resort of villas and bath-chairs grown up in a generation, where Angel finds Tess in a boarding house called The Herons.

places.name: Stonehenge
places.note: The heathen temple where Tess sleeps on the altar stone and asks whether Liza-Lu may have her place.

places.name: Winchester
places.note: Wintoncester, the cathedral city whose gaol flies the black flag in the last paragraph.

related.why: Another dependent woman whose employer’s household turns out to hold a prior claim, and who walks out of it onto the moor with nothing.
A community’s verdict on an unmarried mother, and a child named for the circumstances of her birth.
Published eight years later, and equally interested in what a woman is permitted to want once the marriage is in place.
A life reorganised around a fantasy of gentility, and a fortune whose real source is nothing like the imagined one.
Landscape as an agent rather than a setting, and a plot in which class humiliation is passed down a generation.

books.title: The Adventures of Tom Sawyer
books.author: Mark Twain
books.setting: St Petersburg, a Mississippi river town in Missouri, in the decades before the Civil War
books.written: Drafted in the early 1870s at Hartford and Quarry Farm
books.lengthNote: Thirty-five chapters, a preface and a conclusion that explains why the book stops
books.openingLine: “Tom!”
books.summary: A boy in a slaveholding river town dodges school, trades a whitewashing job for other boys’ treasures, and then watches a murder in a graveyard at midnight. Twain keeps the two halves in the same book on purpose: the comedy of Sunday-school tickets and dead cats runs straight into a perjured trial, a man left to starve behind a cave door, and twelve thousand dollars that buys a boy into respectability he does not want. The narrator is an adult looking back with affection and no illusions, and the Conclusion admits that the story stops because its hero is about to stop being a boy.

sourceText.label: Standard Ebooks text of The Adventures of Tom Sawyer
sourceText.note: The thirty-five chapters are numbered I to XXXV in the text and cited here by Arabic numeral; the Preface and Conclusion are cited by name. Twain’s spelling and dialect forms are retained.

structure.label: Chapters 1–7
structure.title: The fence, the Sunday school and Becky Thatcher
structure.summary: Tom dodges Aunt Polly, converts a punishment into a profitable enterprise, and exchanges traded tickets for a Bible prize he cannot answer a single question about. Becky Thatcher arrives, is engaged to him inside a day, and discovers she is not the first.

structure.label: Chapters 8–11
structure.title: The graveyard, the oath and Muff Potter
structure.summary: Tom and Huck take a dead cat to a new grave to cure warts and see a doctor killed, a drunk framed and a knife left in the right hands. They swear a blood oath to keep mum, and for three chapters the comedy is interrupted by a boy who cannot sleep.

structure.label: Chapters 12–18
structure.title: Jackson’s Island and the funeral
structure.summary: Three boys run away to be pirates, live on bacon and stolen watermelons, and hear their own town firing a cannon over the water to raise their bodies. Tom’s masterpiece is to come back for the funeral, and the congregation sings the doxology over three boys standing in the aisle.

structure.label: Chapters 19–24
structure.title: The trial
structure.summary: Tom takes Becky’s whipping, sits through an examination evening of borrowed compositions, and finally breaks the oath in open court. Muff Potter is saved, Injun Joe goes through the window, and Tom becomes a hero by day and a terrified child at night.

structure.label: Chapters 25–29
structure.title: Treasure, the haunted house and the revenge job
structure.summary: A game of digging for buried money turns real when two men count out gold under the floor of a haunted house. Huck follows them, learns that the Widow Douglas is the object of a revenge, and fetches the Welshman and his sons up Cardiff Hill in the middle of the night.

structure.label: Chapters 30–33
structure.title: The cave, and the door that was already shut
structure.summary: Tom and Becky are lost in McDougal’s cave for three days, and Tom sees a hand holding a candle that belongs to the man he testified against. The cave door is sealed by the town, and when it is opened again Injun Joe is lying dead against it with a broken knife.

structure.label: Chapters 34–35
structure.title: Twelve thousand dollars and a hogshead
structure.summary: The boys are rich, invested at six per cent, and Huck is taken into the Widow Douglas’s house, where he is washed, combed and made to eat by the clock. He lasts three weeks, and Tom can only get him back by promising that the robber gang has an entry requirement: respectability.

characters.name: Tom Sawyer
characters.role: A boy in the care of his dead mother’s sister
characters.summary: He is a showman first and a hero second, and the book is unusually clear that the two are often the same thing: he returns from the dead for the effect, takes a whipping for Becky in front of an audience, and tells the truth in court only when it can be done at the last possible dramatic moment. His courage is real, and it is always staged.
characters.clue: He sells the right to whitewash a fence, collects enough traded tickets to win a Bible he has not read, and comes back from the dead in time to hear his own funeral sermon.
traits: braver than he expects to be

characters.name: Huckleberry Finn
characters.role: Son of the town drunkard
characters.summary: He sleeps in empty hogsheads, comes and goes as he likes, and is envied by every boy whose mother has forbidden him. Twain gives him the novel’s only sustained resistance to the town’s values, and the last chapter is an argument he loses — for now, and in one book’s time not at all.
characters.clue: Cast-off clothes too big for him, a life without school, church, shoes or bedtime, and three weeks of being washed and combed before he runs for a hogshead.

characters.name: Aunt Polly
characters.role: Tom’s guardian, his dead sister’s aunt
characters.summary: She believes in duty, the rod and patent medicines, and is defeated in advance by her own affection — the novel’s first long speech is her explaining to herself why she will not punish him. Her grief in the funeral chapters is the strongest feeling in the book and is played, uncomfortably, for comedy.
characters.clue: She keeps her spectacles for style rather than service, doses a boy with Pain-killer, and can be disarmed by any joke made at the right moment.

characters.name: Becky Thatcher
characters.role: The judge’s daughter, newly arrived in St Petersburg
characters.summary: She is courted, jilted, insulted and reconciled within a few chapters, and then given the novel’s longest ordeal in the cave, where she is the one who runs out of strength first. Twain grants her a genuine moment of moral weight — the torn schoolbook and Tom’s whipping — and then returns her to the plot as somebody to be rescued.
characters.clue: Yellow hair in two long tails, a new face in a small school, and a torn page in the master’s anatomy book that somebody else is thrashed for.

relationships.label: engaged to, and lost in the cave with

characters.name: Injun Joe
characters.role: The murderer of Dr Robinson
characters.summary: He is the book’s engine of fear and the clearest sign of its limits: a character built almost entirely out of period assumptions about mixed and Native ancestry, given a grudge, a knife and no inner life. His death behind the sealed cave door is the most disturbing scene Twain wrote for children, and the town treats it as a spectacle.
characters.clue: He is whipped as a vagrant by a judge and repays it in the doctor’s own graveyard; later he is found dead against a door with a broken bowie-knife and a hollow in the stone under a dripping stalactite.
traits: given no interior by the book

characters.name: Muff Potter
characters.role: The town drunk, tried for murder
characters.summary: He is persuaded by the real killer that he did it himself, and thanks the two boys who are letting him hang for the small kindnesses they smuggle through the jail window. His gratitude is what finally breaks Tom’s oath, which makes him the novel’s most effective moral argument.
characters.clue: Told he committed a murder he slept through, he believes it, and thanks the boys at the grating for tobacco and matches while they say nothing that would save him.

characters.name: Sid
characters.role: Tom’s half-brother
characters.summary: He is quiet, clean and an informer, and exists to show what the town actually rewards. Twain uses him to keep the reader from mistaking the novel for a morality tale: the model boy is the one nobody, including the narrator, likes.
characters.clue: He notices that the thread in a collar has changed colour, and tells.

characters.name: The Widow Douglas
characters.role: The kindest and richest person in St Petersburg
characters.summary: She is marked for mutilation by Injun Joe because her dead husband once had him horsewhipped, and she is saved by a boy who has no reason to care except that she was once kind to him. Her reward for Huck is to civilise him, which the novel presents as both genuine generosity and a kind of confinement.
characters.clue: Her house is at the top of the hill, she has ice-cream most days, and she is saved from a knife by a barefoot boy who will not give his name to the men he fetches.
traits: well meaning about other people’s lives

themes.name: Play, work and the difference between them
themes.canonicalName: Play, work and the difference between them
themes.summary: The whitewashing chapter states a general law — that work is whatever you are obliged to do — and the rest of the novel tests it. Pirating, robbing, digging for treasure and being dead are all games until somebody starts firing a cannon over the river or counting out real gold, at which point the game does not stop; it simply acquires consequences.
themes.development: A fence sold in Chapter 2, a pirate camp in Chapter 13, a robber gang still being planned in Chapter 35 — with a murder trial, a manhunt and a cave in between.

themes.name: Conscience, and keeping mum
themes.summary: Tom’s oath makes silence a point of honour and lets a man go to trial for a murder two children watched. Twain writes conscience as physical symptom — sleeplessness, a week of dread, inquests on dead cats that will not leave him alone — and the confession, when it comes, is extracted by gratitude rather than by principle.
themes.development: A blood oath in Chapter 10, a smuggled plug of tobacco through a jail grating in Chapter 11, and a witness box in Chapter 23 where the truth arrives at the last possible moment.

themes.name: Respectable St Petersburg
themes.summary: The town runs on visible virtue: Sunday-school tickets that can be traded rather than earned, examination compositions copied from the same handful of moral endings, and mothers who forbid their sons to speak to the boy they all envy. Twain does not despise the village, but he never lets the reader confuse its standards with goodness.
themes.development: A Bible won by commerce in Chapter 4, a model boy loathed in Chapter 1, and in the last chapter the same standards applied to Huck with a hairbrush and a clock.

themes.name: Warts, spunk-water and signs
themes.summary: The boys’ world is governed by an elaborate system of charms, oaths and cures that they discuss with the precision of theologians, and the book takes it seriously as a working technology of childhood. It is also what puts them in the graveyard at midnight, so the novel’s central crime enters through a folk remedy for warts.
themes.development: Dead cats and bean-burying in Chapter 6, an oath written in blood in Chapter 10, and the marked candles, superstitions and omens that structure the treasure hunt.

themes.name: Who counts in St Petersburg
themes.summary: The town is a slaveholding one, and its hierarchy is reported as ordinary fact: enslaved people do the work in the background, and the man the plot needs as its monster is identified almost entirely by his ancestry. A modern reading has to hold two things together — the accuracy of the record and the assumptions of the telling.
themes.development: Present from the first chapters as the town’s ordinary furniture, concentrated in the treatment of Injun Joe, and left unexamined by an ending in which the whole village comes to see him buried.

themes.name: Where boyhood stops
themes.summary: Twain ends the book with a note explaining that it must stop here, because to go on would be to write the history of a man. The novel is built to that boundary: it can hold murder, perjury and starvation, but not marriage, work or the future, and everything in it is dated by an adult who knows the town is gone.
themes.development: Signalled by the Preface’s claim on real events, sustained by a narrator who keeps stepping outside the summer, and stated outright in the Conclusion.

techniques.name: Dialect
techniques.definition: Spelling and grammar used to mark where a speaker comes from, and what being heard that way costs them.
techniques.bookDefinition: Regional speech written phonetically.
techniques.inThisBook: Huck’s speech is spelled as it sounds — ’pears, widder, hain’t — against a narrator with a full literary vocabulary, and the gap between the two is the book’s chief source of both comedy and sympathy.

techniques.name: Narratorial irony
techniques.definition: Saying one thing in a form that invites the opposite judgement.
techniques.bookDefinition: A narrator whose tone quietly judges what it reports.
techniques.inThisBook: The mayor and his wife are introduced ‘among other unnecessaries’, and the whitewashing law of human action is credited to a great and wise philosopher — the writer of this book.

techniques.name: Satire of institutions
techniques.definition: Comic exposure of the machinery by which a community measures virtue.
techniques.bookDefinition: Comic exposure of the machinery by which a community measures virtue.
techniques.inThisBook: The Sunday school, the examination evening and the Cadets of Temperance are each given a full set piece, and each is shown rewarding performance rather than the thing performed.

techniques.name: Mock-heroic
techniques.definition: Epic apparatus — arms, councils, homecomings — applied to small domestic events.
techniques.bookDefinition: Epic apparatus — arms, councils, homecomings — applied to small domestic events.
techniques.inThisBook: Three boys on a sandbar style themselves the Black Avenger of the Spanish Main, the Terror of the Seas and the Red-Handed, and the Conclusion measures the whole book against the convention that a novel ends with a marriage.

techniques.name: The comic set piece
techniques.definition: A self-contained episode built to a single effect and complete in itself, whether comic or ceremonial.
techniques.bookDefinition: A self-contained episode built to a single disaster, complete in one chapter.
techniques.inThisBook: The fence, the Bible prize, the Pain-killer and the poodle on the pinch-bug each occupy a chapter, and each is constructed so that Tom’s humiliation and Tom’s triumph are the same event.

techniques.name: Melodrama inside the idyll
techniques.definition: Stage-villain plotting — oaths, graveyards, disguises, buried gold — running underneath a realist surface.
techniques.bookDefinition: Stage-villain plotting — oaths, graveyards, disguises, buried gold — running underneath a realist surface.
techniques.inThisBook: A midnight murder, a framed innocent, a masked revenge and a treasure under a cross are imported wholesale from popular drama, and are the reason the summer chapters acquire a body count.

quotations.text: Most of the adventures recorded in this book really occurred; one or two were experiences of my own, the rest those of boys who were schoolmates of mine.
quotations.context: The opening of Twain’s preface, signed before the story begins.
quotations.analysis: The claim is made in the flat voice of a deposition, and it is doing two jobs: it licenses the book’s cruelties as reportage and it warns the reader not to look for a moral design. Twain goes on to say that Tom is a composite of three boys and therefore belongs to the composite order of architecture — a joke that quietly admits how much arranging has been done.

quotations.text: He was not the Model Boy of the village. He knew the model boy very well though⁠—and loathed him.
quotations.context: Introducing Tom, after the first chase round the house.
quotations.analysis: The capital letters make the Model Boy an office rather than a person, and the drop to lower case in the second sentence quietly demotes him. ‘Loathed’ is much stronger than the joke requires, and it sets the book’s position early: the village’s system of rewards is not being satirised from outside but hated from within.

quotations.text: Every time I let him off, my conscience does hurt me so, and every time I hit him my old heart most breaks.
quotations.speaker: Aunt Polly
quotations.context: Alone in the kitchen, after Tom has escaped over the fence.
quotations.analysis: Her dilemma is stated as a perfect trap with no third option, and the balanced grammar — every time, every time — is the sound of an argument she has had with herself for years. It tells the reader before Chapter 2 that punishment in this book is a ritual nobody expects to work.

quotations.text: “Like it? Well, I don’t see why I oughtn’t to like it. Does a boy get a chance to whitewash a fence every day?”
quotations.speaker: Tom Sawyer
quotations.context: Answering Ben Rogers, who has come to jeer at him for working on a Saturday.
quotations.analysis: The rhetorical question does all the work: scarcity is invented out of nothing, and Ben is converted in four lines. Tom never claims the job is pleasant — he claims it is rare, which is the distinction the next paragraph turns into a law of human action.

quotations.text: He had discovered a great law of human action, without knowing it⁠—namely, that in order to make a man or a boy covet a thing, it is only necessary to make the thing difficult to attain.
quotations.context: After the fence has been whitewashed three times over by other boys who paid for the privilege.
quotations.analysis: The narrator takes a boy’s trick and restates it as economics, and the phrase ‘without knowing it’ opens the distance between the adult telling and the child acting that the whole book runs on. It is also a rare instance of Twain giving the reader the moral of an episode outright, and he immediately undercuts it with a joke about the wise philosopher who wrote the book.

quotations.text: Work consists of whatever a body is obliged to do, and that Play consists of whatever a body is not obliged to do.
quotations.context: The narrator continuing his commentary on the whitewashing.
quotations.analysis: Both definitions turn on obligation rather than effort, which is why the book can put pirates, treasure-hunting and a three-day ordeal in a cave on the same side of the line as a game. The examples that follow — treadmills against Mont Blanc — make the point that the difference is in who is making you do it.

quotations.text: Huckleberry was cordially hated and dreaded by all the mothers of the town, because he was idle and lawless and vulgar and bad⁠—and because all their children admired him so, and delighted in his forbidden society, and wished they dared to be like him.
quotations.context: Tom meets the juvenile pariah of the village on his way to school.
quotations.analysis: The sentence gives the official reason and the real one in the same breath, joined by an ‘and’ that pretends they are the same kind of thing. Note the order of the adjectives — idle first, bad last — which is the town’s scale of values rather than a moral one.

quotations.text: “Say⁠—what is dead cats good for, Huck?”
quotations.speaker: Tom Sawyer
quotations.context: Tom has just noticed what Huck is swinging by the tail.
quotations.analysis: The question is asked in the tone of one specialist consulting another, and the discussion that follows — spunk-water, bean-burying, the exact words to say — has the structure of a technical seminar. It is also the hinge of the plot: this conversation is what takes two children into a graveyard at midnight.

quotations.text: “Tom, we got to keep mum. You know that. That Injun devil wouldn’t make any more of drownding us than a couple of cats, if we was to squeak ’bout this and they didn’t hang him.
quotations.speaker: Huckleberry Finn
quotations.context: The two boys in the old tannery, an hour after the murder.
quotations.analysis: Huck’s reasoning is entirely practical and entirely correct, and it is the practical argument, not the oath, that binds them. The simile about cats returns the reader to the dead cat that took them to the graveyard, which is Twain’s habit of letting the comic props reappear as threats.

quotations.text: “Huck Finn and Tom Sawyer swears they will keep mum about This and They wish They may Drop down dead in Their Tracks if They ever Tell and Rot.”
quotations.context: The oath written on a pine shingle in red keel and signed in blood.
quotations.analysis: The capital letters are the boys’ idea of what a legal document looks like, copied from nothing they have ever read properly. The document is a game and a binding contract at once — this is the point in the novel where play stops being separable from consequence, and a man goes to trial because two children have signed a shingle.

quotations.text: Tom’s fearful secret and gnawing conscience disturbed his sleep for as much as a week after this
quotations.context: The days following Muff Potter’s arrest.
quotations.analysis: ‘For as much as a week’ is the sentence’s sting: the narrator measures a child’s remorse against an adult’s and finds it short. Twain neither excuses Tom nor makes him a monster — he simply records the duration, and then lets the guilt come back every time the schoolboys hold another inquest on a dead cat.

quotations.text: The pipe dropped from the fingers of the Red-Handed, and he slept the sleep of the conscience-free and the weary.
quotations.context: The first night on Jackson’s Island, in the pirate camp.
quotations.analysis: The boys’ chosen titles are used straight-faced by the narrator, so that ‘the Red-Handed’ and ‘conscience-free’ sit in the same clause. The joke has an edge: Huck, who has no conscience to trouble him about running away, is the one of the three with a murder on his mind and can still sleep.

quotations.text: the congregation rose and stared while the three dead boys came marching up the aisle
quotations.context: In the middle of the funeral sermon preached over Tom, Joe and Huck.
quotations.analysis: The narration keeps calling them dead after they have walked in, which is exactly how the congregation sees them for the length of a held breath. Tom has engineered the best entrance available to a human being, and the novel notes a few lines later that Huck, who has no family in the church, gets no share of the welcome.

quotations.text: “Speak out, my boy⁠—don’t be diffident. The truth is always respectable. What did you take there?”
quotations.context: Counsel for the defence examining Tom in the murder trial.
quotations.analysis: The lawyer’s maxim collides immediately with the answer — a dead cat — and the court laughs. Twain places the book’s most solemn statement about truth one line before its silliest object, which is his standard method for keeping a moral from hardening into a lesson.

quotations.text: Tom began⁠—hesitatingly at first, but as he warmed to his subject his words flowed more and more easily; in a little while every sound ceased but his own voice; every eye fixed itself upon him
quotations.context: Tom breaking the oath in open court, with Injun Joe sitting in the room.
quotations.analysis: The act of conscience is described in exactly the vocabulary the book uses for his performances — warming to his subject, every eye on him — so that the bravest thing Tom does is also his best entrance. Twain does not let the reader separate the two, and the chapter ends with the witness terrified for months afterwards.

quotations.text: There were some that believed he would be President, yet, if he escaped hanging.
quotations.context: St Petersburg’s verdict on Tom after the trial.
quotations.analysis: The village’s two available futures for a remarkable boy are the highest office in the country and the gallows, and it cannot tell which is coming. The sentence also dates the book precisely: this is a river town’s idea of how far a bright, unmanageable child might go, and the joke was old enough by 1876 to be affectionate.

quotations.text: “Tom, Tom, we’re lost! we’re lost! We never can get out of this awful place! Oh, why did we ever leave the others!”
quotations.speaker: Becky Thatcher
quotations.context: In McDougal’s cave, after the candles have shown them an unfamiliar passage.
quotations.analysis: Becky is given the plain statement of the situation while Tom is still constructing reassurances, which reverses the usual distribution of realism in the novel. The exclamation marks and the repetition are the only hysteria the book allows anybody, and it is immediately followed by Tom keeping his voice cheerful — a performance, and the thing that gets them out.

quotations.text: Injun Joe’s bowie-knife lay close by, its blade broken in two. The great foundation-beam of the door had been chipped and hacked through, with tedious labor; useless labor, too, it was, for the native rock formed a sill outside it
quotations.context: When the cave door is opened, a fortnight after the town sealed it.
quotations.analysis: The passage is written as a forensic reconstruction — knife, beam, sill, the hollow worn in stone by dripping water — and the repetition of ‘labor’ makes the dying man’s work sound like the whitewashing chapter turned inside out. Twain then has the town hold a picnic at the cave mouth for the funeral, which is the harshest judgement in the book and is delivered without comment.

quotations.text: “Don’t talk about it, Tom. I’ve tried it, and it don’t work; it don’t work, Tom. It ain’t for me; I ain’t used to it.
quotations.speaker: Huckleberry Finn
quotations.context: Found in an empty hogshead after three weeks in the Widow Douglas’s house.
quotations.analysis: The repetition is not rhetoric but exhaustion, and the complaint that follows is entirely about the body: washing, combing, clothes that let no air through, meals by the clock. Huck makes the only sustained case in the novel against what the town calls kindness, and Tom defeats it with an argument about club membership.

quotations.text: So endeth this chronicle. It being strictly a history of a boy, it must stop here; the story could not go much further without becoming the history of a man.
quotations.context: The first sentences of the Conclusion, after the last chapter.
quotations.analysis: The archaism of ‘So endeth’ borrows the cadence of a lesson read in church, and is then used to explain a purely technical decision about where a book stops. The remark about novels of grown people ending with a marriage also tells you what Twain thinks he has avoided — and Huckleberry Finn, nine years later, is the history of a boy who does not stop.

atAGlance.label: First published
atAGlance.note: Chatto & Windus issued the first edition months before the authorised American one.

atAGlance.label: Pirated
atAGlance.note: Belford Brothers brought out an unauthorised Canadian edition; the American Publishing Company’s followed in December.

atAGlance.label: Source town
atAGlance.note: St Petersburg is built from the town Samuel Clemens grew up in, rearranged rather than copied.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.note: Two plots: the summer of games, and the murder that the games keep running into.

criticalViews.position: An idyll with a body in it
criticalViews.summary: The most common account of the book treats it as a summer idyll — fence, island, cave — into which a melodrama of murder and buried gold has been imported from popular theatre. The interest then lies in how the two survive in one volume, and in what the games look like once a real knife has appeared.
criticalViews.counter: The division is too neat: the oath, the trial and the treasure are all continuations of games the boys were already playing.

criticalViews.position: A record of a slaveholding town
criticalViews.summary: Read as social history, the novel documents an antebellum Missouri village in exact detail — its church, school, courtroom and hierarchy — including the enslaved labour that makes the boys’ freedom possible and is reported as ordinary background.
criticalViews.counter: Documentation is not examination; the book notices the town’s order without ever putting it on trial, which is the work Twain left to Huckleberry Finn and Pudd’nhead Wilson.

criticalViews.position: The problem of Injun Joe
criticalViews.summary: Modern criticism concentrates on a villain constructed from period assumptions about Native and mixed ancestry, given a grievance and no interiority, and finally starved to death behind a door while the town holds a picnic. How a study of childhood handles that character is now part of how it is taught.
criticalViews.counter: The novel does record the whipping and the public humiliation that produced his grudge, which is more than the town itself is willing to remember.

criticalViews.position: Tom as performer
criticalViews.summary: A reading that runs through the whole book: every act of courage is also a scene, from the funeral entrance to the whipping taken for Becky to the testimony delivered at the last possible moment. The question is whether performance disqualifies the courage or is simply the form it takes in a boy raised on adventure stories.
criticalViews.counter: The cave chapters give him three days with no audience at all, and he behaves exactly the same.

essayQuestions.question: How does Twain hold the comic and criminal halves of the novel together?
essayQuestions.focus: Structure, tone and consequence
plan: Set out the two plots and where they first intersect: a wart cure that requires a graveyard at midnight.
Show how comic props return as threats — the dead cat at the trial, the cave as a picnic spot and then a tomb.
Use the oath in Chapter 10 to argue that play and consequence are never separable in this book.
Consider the funeral chapter, which is simultaneously the funniest and the cruellest thing in the novel.
Conclude with the Conclusion, and the boundary Twain says he has to stop at.

essayQuestions.question: ‘Tom’s courage is always a performance.’ Discuss.
essayQuestions.focus: Character, audience and the trial
plan: Begin with the whitewashing, where Tom’s talent is identified as salesmanship before anything else.
Read the return from the dead as the purest case: real grief, deliberately produced, for an entrance.
Analyse the trial in Chapter 23, where the narrator uses performance vocabulary for an act of conscience.
Test the claim against the cave, where he has no audience but Becky and no advantage to gain.
Weigh the ending, in which he recruits Huck back to respectability by making a gang membership of it.

essayQuestions.question: What does the novel show, and what does it decline to examine, about St Petersburg?
essayQuestions.focus: Community, hierarchy and the limits of the narrator
plan: Gather the institutions Twain satirises directly: the Sunday school, the examination evening, the Cadets of Temperance.
Show the town’s hierarchy as the book reports it, including the enslaved labour that appears as ordinary furniture.
Examine the treatment of Injun Joe and of Huck: two outsiders, one demonised and one envied.
Consider the picnic at the cave mouth after the funeral as the novel’s sharpest unspoken judgement.
Decide whether the adult narrator’s irony amounts to a critique or only to affection with good eyesight.

essayQuestions.question: How does Twain use Huckleberry Finn in this book?
essayQuestions.focus: Freedom, dialect and the ending
plan: Describe how Huck is introduced: through the mothers’ verdict and the children’s envy in the same sentence.
Contrast his speech with the narrator’s and with Tom’s, and show what the dialect is doing beyond comedy.
Follow his independent plot — the haunted house, the hill, the Welshman — in which he acts alone and refuses credit.
Read Chapter 35 as a serious argument about civilisation conducted in a hogshead.
Conclude by considering what it means that Twain had to write another novel to let Huck answer back.

discussionQuestions: Two children watch a murder and let an innocent man go to trial. Does the novel hold them responsible?
Aunt Polly’s grief in the funeral chapters is genuine, and it is played for laughs. Does the book get away with it?
Huck says that being civilised does not work. Is the last chapter a happy ending for him?
The town seals the cave and then holds a picnic at its mouth. What is Twain doing by reporting this without comment?
The Conclusion says the story must stop before its hero becomes a man. What could this novel not have contained?

timeline.label: Samuel Langhorne Clemens born at Florida, Missouri
timeline.detail: The family moved to Hannibal on the Mississippi four years later.

timeline.label: The Clemens family moves to Hannibal
timeline.detail: The river town, its cave, its hill and its social order supply nearly everything St Petersburg is made of.

timeline.label: The Civil War begins
timeline.detail: The book, written afterwards, looks back at a Missouri slaveholding town and never says so directly.

timeline.label: First edition published in London
timeline.detail: Chatto & Windus issued the book on 9 June, ahead of any authorised American printing.

timeline.label: Pirated in Toronto, and published in the United States
timeline.detail: Belford Brothers’ unauthorised Canadian edition appeared on 29 July; the American Publishing Company’s illustrated edition followed in December.

timeline.label: True W. Williams illustrates the American edition
timeline.detail: His pictures shaped how the book was sold by subscription, and are discussed rather than reproduced in the Astor edition.

timeline.label: Adventures of Huckleberry Finn published in Britain
timeline.detail: The American edition followed in 1885; the sequel gives the narration to the boy Tom treats as an accessory.

timeline.label: Pudd’nhead Wilson published
timeline.detail: Twain returns to the same river town and puts slavery, identity and the law at the centre rather than the edge.

timeline.label: Mark Twain dies at Redding, Connecticut
timeline.detail: By then Tom Sawyer had long outsold its first, disappointing season.

timeline.label: The Technicolor film adaptation
timeline.detail: Produced by David O. Selznick, it fixed the fence, the cave and the funeral as the story’s three scenes for a mass audience.

places.name: Hannibal, Missouri
places.note: The river town Clemens grew up in, and the source of St Petersburg’s streets, church, school and social order.

places.name: Cardiff Hill (Holliday’s Hill)
places.note: The hill above the town, Cardiff Hill in the novel, up which Huck follows Injun Joe to the Widow Douglas’s house.

places.name: Mark Twain Cave, south of Hannibal
places.note: The limestone cave behind McDougal’s cave, where Tom and Becky are lost and Injun Joe is sealed in.

places.name: Hartford, Connecticut
places.note: Twain’s home while he wrote the book, and the base of the American Publishing Company that issued the December 1876 edition.

places.name: London
places.note: Chatto & Windus published the true first edition here in June 1876, before American readers could buy it.

places.name: Toronto
places.note: Belford Brothers’ unauthorised edition of July 1876 reached readers ahead of the authorised American book.

related.why: The sequel that hands the narration to Huck and turns the same river into a moral problem rather than a playground.
Twain returning to the same kind of river town with slavery, identity and the courtroom moved to the centre.
The same narrator’s voice turned on chivalry and progress, with the comedy carrying a much darker argument.
Another episodic novel about a child in a small community, and a useful contrast in how much harm each book will admit.
Childhood as a set of adventures with adult catastrophe kept just offstage, written a generation later and on another continent.

books.title: The Awakening
books.author: Kate Chopin
books.setting: Grand Isle and Chênière Caminada on the Louisiana coast, and the Creole quarter of New Orleans
books.lengthNote: Thirty-nine chapters, several of them under two pages
books.openingLine: A green and yellow parrot, which hung in a cage outside the door, kept repeating over and over: “Allez vous-en! Allez vous-en! Sapristi! That’s all right!”
books.summary: A New Orleans broker's wife spends a summer at a Gulf resort, learns to swim at twenty-eight, and comes back to the city unwilling to keep her Tuesdays at home. Chopin tracks what follows with almost no editorial comment: the painting, the money, the smaller house, the two men, the friend who tells her to think of the children. The novel was reviewed as immoral, went quietly out of print, and was read properly seventy years later.

sourceText.label: Standard Ebooks text of The Awakening
sourceText.note: Chapters are numbered I to XXXIX, following the 1899 first edition; references below give the chapter only.

structure.label: Chapters I–XIII
structure.title: A summer at the shore
structure.summary: Léonce Pontellier looks up from his newspaper at a sunburnt wife and sees damaged property. Over the weeks that follow Edna sits with Adèle Ratignolle, hears Mademoiselle Reisz play, and finally swims out alone at night further than she has strength to return. The next morning she and Robert Lebrun cross to Chênière Caminada and she sleeps through most of a day.

scenes.title: The gallery
scenes.summary: The parrot, the husband's newspaper, the Creole frankness Edna cannot match, and Robert attached to her for the season.

scenes.title: Two kinds of music
scenes.summary: Adèle's playing keeps company; Mademoiselle Reisz's undoes Edna entirely in a room full of people.

scenes.title: The swim
scenes.summary: Edna swims out alone, refuses to be walked home, and crosses to the Chênière the following morning with Robert.

structure.label: Chapters XIV–XVIII
structure.title: Robert goes to Mexico, and the season ends
structure.summary: Robert announces at a few hours' notice that he is leaving for Mexico, and Edna discovers how much has been arranged without reference to her. Back in New Orleans she abandons her reception day, throws her wedding ring on the carpet, and finds that her husband's response is to consult a doctor about her health.

scenes.title: The announcement
scenes.summary: Robert's departure; Edna tells Adèle that she would give her life for her children but not herself.

scenes.title: The city
scenes.summary: The abandoned Tuesday, the ring on the carpet, and a visit to the Ratignolles that leaves her flat.

structure.label: Chapters XIX–XXVIII
structure.title: Painting, money, and two visitors
structure.summary: Edna paints in the atelier, goes to the races, lets Alcée Arobin into the house, and begins to keep accounts of her own. Mademoiselle Reisz reads her Robert's letters and tells her what it takes to be an artist; her father visits, her husband goes to New York, and the children are sent to their grandmother.

scenes.title: Doing as she likes
scenes.summary: The atelier, the abandoned household routine, and Doctor Mandelet's cautious diagnosis.

scenes.title: The races and the letters
scenes.summary: Arobin's attentions, Reisz's test of her shoulder blades, and the decision to take a small house of her own.

scenes.title: After
scenes.summary: A night with Arobin, and a morning of understanding rather than shame.

structure.label: Chapters XXIX–XXXIV
