Machiavelli's Italy in the same decade as the play's action, and the plain case for the policy that Webster's courtiers practise and his malcontent despises.

books.title: The Great Gatsby
books.author: F. Scott Fitzgerald
books.setting: Long Island and Manhattan, in the summer of 1922, with Louisville and the Midwest behind them
books.lengthNote: Nine chapters and fewer than fifty thousand words — short enough to be read in an evening, and built to be
books.openingLine: In my younger and more vulnerable years my father gave me some advice that I’ve been turning over in my mind ever since.
books.summary: A bond salesman rents a cottage next to a mansion whose owner gives parties for strangers, and gradually works out that the parties are addressed to one woman across the bay. Fitzgerald releases the facts about Gatsby in the wrong order on purpose, so that a rumour becomes a host, then a lover, then a poor farm boy called James Gatz. The summer ends with two people dead, a third shot in a swimming pool, and a narrator who has decided that the people who survive are the ones with enough money to leave.

sourceText.label: Standard Ebooks text of The Great Gatsby
sourceText.note: References give the chapter. This transcription carries British spellings in places where the 1925 American first edition differs, and the quotations here follow it exactly.

structure.label: Chapter 1
structure.title: Two houses and a light across the water
structure.summary: Nick Carraway introduces himself as a suspended judge, rents a small house in West Egg, and dines across the bay with his cousin Daisy and her husband Tom, who is reading about the decline of the white race and taking a telephone call from his mistress. On the way home he sees his neighbour on the lawn, reaching towards a green light.

scenes.title: The dinner at East Egg
scenes.summary: Daisy's voice, Jordan's boredom, Tom's theories, and a telephone that will not stop ringing.

structure.label: Chapter 2
structure.title: The valley of ashes
structure.summary: The road from Long Island to New York runs through a landscape made of the city's waste, watched over by a faded oculist's hoarding. Tom takes Nick to a garage there, collects Myrtle Wilson from her husband's business, and continues to a flat in Manhattan where the afternoon ends with a broken nose.

scenes.title: The apartment on 158th Street
scenes.summary: A party of six, a dog bought on the street, and Tom breaking Myrtle's nose for saying Daisy's name.

structure.label: Chapter 3
structure.title: The party, and the host who is not at it
structure.summary: Nick is one of the few guests who has been invited. He hears three contradictory biographies of Gatsby before meeting him, finds a drunk in the library marvelling that the books are real, and leaves at the end of a night that closes with a car in a ditch and a driver who does not understand that wheels are involved.

scenes.title: Owl Eyes in the library
scenes.summary: A man in enormous spectacles establishes that the books have pages, which he treats as evidence of thoroughness.

structure.label: Chapter 4
structure.title: A war record, a photograph, and a man with cufflinks
structure.summary: Driving into the city, Gatsby produces documents: a medal from Montenegro, a photograph from Oxford. Lunch introduces Meyer Wolfshiem, who fixed a World Series. Then Jordan tells Nick, in the Plaza's tea garden, the story of a white roadster in Louisville in 1917, and what the parties have actually been for.

scenes.title: Jordan's account
scenes.summary: Daisy in 1917, a letter the night before her wedding, and a request relayed from the man next door.

structure.label: Chapter 5
structure.title: Tea in the rain
structure.summary: Gatsby has Nick's lawn cut and fills his house with flowers for a meeting arranged four chapters and five years in advance. He knocks over a clock, recovers, and takes Daisy through the mansion, throwing shirts onto a table until she cries into them. The rain stops on cue. The green light becomes a light on a dock.

scenes.title: The shirts
scenes.summary: The house is exhibited as evidence; the tour ends with Daisy weeping over imported linen.

structure.label: Chapter 6
structure.title: James Gatz of North Dakota
structure.summary: The history the reader has been waiting for arrives at last: a boy who rowed out to a millionaire's yacht and changed his name at seventeen. Daisy comes to a party and does not enjoy it. Gatsby explains to Nick that Daisy must tell Tom she never loved him, and Nick suggests that the past cannot be repeated.

scenes.title: Dan Cody's yacht
scenes.summary: A name is invented on Lake Superior, and an inheritance of twenty-five thousand dollars is taken away by a lawyer.

structure.label: Chapter 7
structure.title: The hottest day
structure.summary: The parties stop and the servants are replaced. Five people drive to the Plaza in the heat and Gatsby asks Daisy to erase four years of her marriage; she cannot say the sentence. On the way back a yellow car kills Myrtle Wilson at the garage, and Nick learns who was driving. Gatsby stands in the shrubbery all night watching nothing.

scenes.title: The suite at the Plaza
scenes.summary: Tom takes the argument apart with the one fact Gatsby cannot dispose of: Daisy's past is her own.

scenes.title: The accident
scenes.summary: The exchanged cars make the wrong person responsible, which is how responsibility works in this book.

structure.label: Chapter 8
structure.title: The telephone that does not ring
structure.summary: Nick hears the Louisville story from Gatsby himself, tells him he is worth the whole lot of them, and goes to work. Gatsby waits for a call, swims for the first time all summer, and is shot in the pool by George Wilson, who has spent the morning being pointed at the wrong car by the man who owned the right one.

scenes.title: The pool
scenes.summary: A gardener's plan to drain the pool is postponed by a day, and the day is the last one.

structure.label: Chapter 9
structure.title: Three people at a funeral
structure.summary: Nobody comes. Wolfshiem sends regrets, Daisy and Tom have left no address, and the only mourners are Nick, Gatsby's father with a boyhood schedule written in the back of a book, and the drunk from the library. Nick breaks with Jordan, meets Tom on Fifth Avenue, and goes back to the Midwest.

scenes.title: The last page
scenes.summary: Nick lies on the beach at night and turns one man's backward-looking project into a history of the continent.

characters.name: Nick Carraway
characters.role: Narrator; a bond salesman from the Midwest
characters.summary: He opens by claiming a habit of suspended judgement and then spends nine chapters judging everyone he meets, often by their voices and their hands. The contradiction is the book's engine: reserving judgement is what gets him invited everywhere, and writing the account afterwards is where the verdict is finally delivered.
characters.clue: He rents the small house between two mansions, claims to be one of the few honest people he has ever known, and writes the whole thing down after going home.

relationships.label: neighbour, confidant and only mourner of

characters.name: Jay Gatsby
characters.role: Owner of the house next door; formerly James Gatz
characters.summary: A farm boy who invented a wealthy self at seventeen and then spent fifteen years assembling the evidence for him: a name, an accent, a war record, a mansion positioned directly across the water from one particular dock. His crime is not the bootlegging but the belief that five years can be cancelled if you buy enough.
characters.clue: He throws parties he barely attends for guests he has not invited, and every one of them is aimed at a single house across the bay.
traits: formal to the point of strangeness

characters.name: Daisy Buchanan
characters.role: Tom's wife, Nick's cousin, and the object of the whole scheme
characters.summary: She is charming in a way the novel presents as an audible property of money, and she is not stupid — her remark about wanting her daughter to be a beautiful little fool is a report on what her intelligence has been worth to her. When the choice comes she does not make it, and she is not there when the bill arrives.
characters.clue: Her voice is the thing everyone remembers, she cries over a pile of shirts, and she lets someone else take the blame for a car.

relationships.label: loved by, and briefly in love with
kills, without knowing who she was

characters.name: Tom Buchanan
characters.role: A polo player with inherited money
characters.summary: Physically enormous, intellectually credulous, and secure in a way the novel treats as structural rather than personal. He conducts an affair openly, reads racial pseudo-science aloud at dinner, and wins the crucial argument not by being right about anything but by being the one person in the room whose past cannot be revised.
characters.clue: He brought a string of polo ponies east, breaks a woman's nose over dinner, and tells a man with a gun which car to look for.

characters.name: Jordan Baker
characters.role: A golfer
characters.summary: A professional sportswoman who once moved a ball in a semi-final and left the rumour to die on its own. She is the novel's other unreliable narrator: it is her account in Chapter 4 that carries the history Nick cannot get from Gatsby, and she is careless in exactly the way Nick claims to despise.
characters.clue: She lies about a golf ball, drives badly on principle, and tells the story that explains the parties.

characters.name: Myrtle Wilson
characters.role: Wife of a garage proprietor in the valley of ashes
characters.summary: She has one room in Manhattan in which she is a different person, and the novel is precise about what her ambition can actually buy: a dog collar, some magazines, a tea set. She is the only character who dies because she believed a car was coming for her, and it was.
characters.clue: She keeps a small flat with a puppy in it, says a name she has been forbidden to say, and runs into the road at the wrong car.

characters.name: George Wilson
characters.role: Garage proprietor under the eyes of Doctor T. J. Eckleburg
characters.summary: The only poor man in the novel, and the only one who acts on a moral conviction. He locks his wife in a room, mistakes an advertising hoarding for God, is given a name and an address by the man who has been sleeping with her, and does what he is pointed at.
characters.clue: He sells petrol beneath a pair of painted eyes, decides they belong to God, and is handed a description of a yellow car.

characters.name: Meyer Wolfshiem
characters.role: Gatsby's business connection
characters.summary: Introduced as the man who fixed a World Series, and written with a stereotyping that a modern reader has to see and name. He is also the novel's clearest statement of how Gatsby's money was made, and the one associate who explains, in a letter, that he cannot afford to attend the funeral.
characters.clue: He wears cuff buttons made of human molars and made the reputation of a whole business, then sends his regrets in writing.

themes.name: The past as property
themes.summary: Gatsby's demand is not that Daisy love him but that she withdraw four years of her life from the record. The novel treats time the way it treats everything else in Gatsby's hands — as something he assumes money and effort can acquire — and the last page enlarges the same error into a national habit.
themes.development: Stated as a plan in Chapter 6, put to Daisy in the Plaza suite in Chapter 7, and turned into a history of the continent in the final paragraphs.

themes.name: Money you can hear
themes.summary: Fitzgerald keeps making class audible and spatial rather than numerical: a voice full of money, two eggs identical in shape and unlike in everything else, a valley between the houses and the city. Gatsby can buy the mansion, the shirts and the car, and the one thing he cannot buy is the sound of not having had to.
themes.development: Set up by the geography of Chapter 1, made explicit in Gatsby's remark about Daisy's voice in Chapter 7, and enforced by Tom in the same chapter.

themes.name: Self-invention
themes.summary: James Gatz becomes Jay Gatsby at seventeen on the shore of Lake Superior, and the novel calls it a Platonic conception — an idea of himself that he then has to furnish. Everything from the Oxford photograph to the word 'old sport' is evidence being assembled for a case nobody has formally brought.
themes.development: Withheld through four chapters of rumour, delivered in Chapter 6, and completed in Chapter 9 by a father with a boy's timetable written in the back of a book.

themes.name: Carelessness
themes.summary: The word runs from Jordan's driving in Chapter 3 to Nick's summary of the Buchanans in Chapter 9, and it is deliberately not the same as cruelty. Carelessness is what money makes possible: the ability to damage something and then to be somewhere else, with the address unavailable.
themes.development: Introduced as a joke about a badly parked car, and paid out when a woman is killed by one and nobody who was in it is inconvenienced.

themes.name: Ashes and eggs
themes.summary: The novel's map does the sociology. East Egg holds inherited money, West Egg new money, Manhattan the places where the rules are suspended, and between them a valley where the city's ash is dumped and the people who shovel it live. Every fatal event in the book happens on the road through that valley.
themes.development: Laid out in Chapter 2, revisited on the way to the Plaza in Chapter 7, and the site of the accident on the way back.

themes.name: Judgement withheld and delivered
themes.summary: Nick's opening claim to reserve judgement is worth testing sentence by sentence against what he actually does, which is to assign moral, social and aesthetic value continually. The novel is his account, written after he has left, and the reader's task is to notice whose interior life he grants and whose he does not.
themes.development: Claimed in Chapter 1, complicated by his silence about the accident in Chapter 7, and declared outright in Chapter 9 when he tells Tom what he thinks of him.

techniques.name: Retrospective first person
techniques.definition: A narrator telling their own earlier life, with the distance between the two selves doing the judging.
techniques.bookDefinition: A narrator telling, after the event, a story in which he took part.
techniques.inThisBook: Nick is writing from the Midwest the following autumn, which is why the judgements he claims to withhold are already in the prose: the verdict was reached before the first sentence was written.

techniques.name: Delayed disclosure
techniques.definition: Withholding the facts of a character's life until the reader has formed an impression without them.
techniques.bookDefinition: Withholding the facts of a character's life until the reader has formed an impression without them.
techniques.inThisBook: Gatsby is a rumour in Chapter 3, a host in Chapter 4, a lover in Chapter 5, and only in Chapter 6 a poor boy from North Dakota — so the reader meets the invention before the man.

techniques.name: Symbol under revision
techniques.definition: An object whose meaning changes as a character's knowledge of it changes.
techniques.bookDefinition: An object whose meaning changes as a character's knowledge of it changes.
techniques.inThisBook: The green light is an unexplained gesture in Chapter 1, a dock light in Chapter 5 once Daisy is in the room, and a figure for the whole continent's appetite in Chapter 9.

techniques.name: Catalogue
techniques.definition: A list allowed to run on past the point of usefulness, so that the accumulation itself becomes the effect.
techniques.bookDefinition: A list used for social observation rather than description.
techniques.inThisBook: The guest list written on a railway timetable gives two pages of names and small disasters, and demonstrates without comment that nobody at the parties knows the host.

techniques.name: Weather as staging
techniques.definition: Using heat, rain and light to time the emotional register of a scene.
techniques.bookDefinition: Using heat, rain and light to time the emotional register of a scene.
techniques.inThisBook: Gatsby's reunion with Daisy is scheduled in rain that stops at the moment it should, and the Plaza confrontation is staged on the hottest day of the summer with a wedding band playing downstairs.

techniques.name: The lyric close
techniques.definition: Shifting at the end of a passage from reported speech and event into sustained rhythmic prose.
techniques.bookDefinition: Shifting at the end of a passage from reported speech and event into sustained rhythmic prose.
techniques.inThisBook: The last two pages leave the plot entirely for a meditation on Dutch sailors and the current, and the final sentence is built out of one subject, two participles and a metaphor that reverses the direction of travel.

quotations.text: “Whenever you feel like criticizing anyone,” he told me, “just remember that all the people in this world haven’t had the advantages that you’ve had.”
quotations.speaker: Nick's father
quotations.context: The advice Nick reports in the second sentence of the novel.
quotations.analysis: The sentence sounds like generosity and is actually an instruction in class: it assumes both speaker and listener are on the advantaged side, and says nothing about what to do with that. Nick spends the novel among people who have had more advantages than he has, and never once applies the rule to them.

quotations.text: In consequence, I’m inclined to reserve all judgements, a habit that has opened up many curious natures to me and also made me the victim of not a few veteran bores.
quotations.context: Nick explaining the effect his father's advice has had on him.
quotations.analysis: The second half of the sentence gives the reason: suspending judgement is a technique for being told things. Within two pages he has called Tom's family enormously wealthy, Jordan incurably dishonest and the East a place he wanted in uniform, which is the contradiction the whole narration runs on — the reserve is a method, not a temperament.

quotations.text: it was an extraordinary gift for hope, a romantic readiness such as I have never found in any other person and which it is not likely I shall ever find again
quotations.context: The first description of Gatsby, given before the reader has met him.
quotations.analysis: The verdict is delivered in the opening pages, so the novel is not a mystery about whether Gatsby is admirable but an account of how Nick got there. 'Readiness' is the exact word: it names a capacity waiting for an object, which is what makes Daisy interchangeable with any sufficiently distant light.

quotations.text: ‘All right,’ I said, ‘I’m glad it’s a girl. And I hope she’ll be a fool⁠—that’s the best thing a girl can be in this world, a beautiful little fool.’
quotations.speaker: Daisy Buchanan
quotations.context: Daisy quoting what she said on waking from the ether after her daughter was born.
quotations.analysis: It is a quotation inside a quotation, which lets her disown it while saying it, and the setting matters: she is describing the hour in which her husband was elsewhere. The line is often read as cynicism about women, but it is a piece of career advice from someone who has calculated exactly what her own intelligence has been worth to her.

quotations.text: Involuntarily I glanced seaward⁠—and distinguished nothing except a single green light, minute and far away, that might have been the end of a dock.
quotations.context: Watching his neighbour stretch his arms towards the water at the end of the first chapter.
quotations.analysis: Three qualifications in one clause — nothing except, might have been — keep the light from meaning anything yet, which is precisely why it can later mean everything. Nick sees the gesture without the explanation, and the novel's method is set: the reader is given the reaching arms four chapters before the reason for them.

quotations.text: This is a valley of ashes⁠—a fantastic farm where ashes grow like wheat into ridges and hills and grotesque gardens; where ashes take the forms of houses and chimneys and rising smoke and, finally, with a transcendent effort, of ash-grey men, who move dimly and already crumbling through the powdery air.
quotations.context: The opening of the second chapter, describing the land between West Egg and New York.
quotations.analysis: The metaphor is agricultural — a farm, wheat, gardens — applied to industrial waste, so the valley is described as growing what the city throws away. The sentence takes four clauses to arrive at the men, and by the time it does they are made of the same material as the landscape, which is the book's flattest statement about who is disposable.

quotations.text: The eyes of Doctor T. J. Eckleburg are blue and gigantic⁠—their retinas are one yard high. They look out of no face, but, instead, from a pair of enormous yellow spectacles which pass over a nonexistent nose.
quotations.context: The hoarding above the valley of ashes, left by an oculist who moved away.
quotations.analysis: The measurements are given in the present tense and in yards, as though the reader might go and check, and the eyes are explicitly attached to nothing — no face, no nose, no oculist. George Wilson will later decide they are God's, and the novel's care in establishing that they are an abandoned advertisement is what makes his mistake so exact.

quotations.text: I believe that on the first night I went to Gatsby’s house I was one of the few guests who had actually been invited. People were not invited⁠—they went there.
quotations.context: The opening of the first party scene.
quotations.analysis: The verb is repeated three times in two sentences so that invitation, the basic transaction of hospitality, can be shown to have collapsed. Nick's one small distinction — he was asked — is what qualifies him to narrate, and it also tells the reader that the parties are not for the people at them.

quotations.text: “I hope I never will,” she answered. “I hate careless people. That’s why I like you.”
quotations.speaker: Jordan Baker
quotations.context: Jordan, who has just nearly hit a workman's coat with her car, explaining why bad driving does not worry her.
quotations.analysis: She has explained that it takes two to make an accident, so her own carelessness is safe until she meets another one — and then says she hates careless people. The word she introduces here is the one Nick will use, six chapters later, to sum up Tom and Daisy; she hands him the term for the novel's central charge while demonstrating the offence.

quotations.text: “You’re a rotten driver,” I protested. “Either you ought to be more careful, or you oughtn’t to drive at all.”
quotations.speaker: Nick Carraway
quotations.context: In the car with Jordan, on the way back from a party.
quotations.analysis: Driving is the novel's practical test of character, and every collision in it involves someone who thought the other party would take care. The exchange also establishes the alternative Nick is offering the reader — be careful or get out — which is exactly the choice he takes himself at the end by going home.

quotations.text: “If it wasn’t for the mist we could see your home across the bay,” said Gatsby. “You always have a green light that burns all night at the end of your dock.”
quotations.speaker: Jay Gatsby
quotations.context: Showing Daisy the view from his own house, minutes after their reunion.
quotations.analysis: He tells her about the light in the flattest possible way — a fact about her property — and the sentence 'you always have' quietly admits five years of watching. This is the moment the symbol is handed over to its owner, and the next paragraph records what it cost him.

quotations.text: Now it was again a green light on a dock. His count of enchanted objects had diminished by one.
quotations.context: Nick watching Gatsby immediately after he has pointed the light out to Daisy.
quotations.analysis: 'Count' is an accountant's word, and it suggests Gatsby keeps an inventory of enchantments the way he keeps one of shirts. The loss is caused by getting what he wanted: the light only worked at a distance, and the whole tragedy is compressed into the arithmetic of that second sentence.

quotations.text: There must have been moments even that afternoon when Daisy tumbled short of his dreams⁠—not through her own fault, but because of the colossal vitality of his illusion.
quotations.context: The end of the reunion chapter, as Nick leaves the two of them together.
quotations.analysis: The exoneration is explicit — not through her own fault — which makes it much harder to read the novel as a case against Daisy. 'Vitality' gives the illusion a life of its own, something grown rather than held, and by this measure Gatsby's tragedy is not that he lost her but that no actual person could have been what he had spent five years building.

quotations.text: The truth was that Jay Gatsby of West Egg, Long Island, sprang from his Platonic conception of himself. He was a son of God⁠—a phrase which, if it means anything, means just that⁠—and he must be about His Father’s business, the service of a vast, vulgar, and meretricious beauty.
quotations.context: The chapter that finally gives James Gatz's history, seventeen years old on the shore of Lake Superior.
quotations.analysis: Two incompatible vocabularies are welded together: Platonic philosophy and the Gospel of Luke, both used to explain a boy changing his name. The aside — if it means anything — is Nick refusing to guarantee his own sentence, and the last three adjectives make the object of worship squarely commercial without withdrawing the religious language.

quotations.text: “Can’t repeat the past?” he cried incredulously. “Why of course you can!”
quotations.speaker: Jay Gatsby
quotations.context: Answering Nick's suggestion that he should not ask so much of Daisy.
quotations.analysis: The adverb is the whole characterisation: he is not arguing, he is astonished that anyone would doubt it. Grammatically he treats the past as a direct object — something one performs again — and the rest of the novel is the demonstration that it is the one commodity his money cannot reach.

quotations.text: He wanted nothing less of Daisy than that she should go to Tom and say: “I never loved you.”
quotations.context: Nick explaining what Gatsby is actually asking for.
quotations.analysis: The demand is for a sentence, not an action, which tells the reader that Gatsby's project is editorial: he wants the record amended. When she cannot produce the words in Chapter 7 it is not cowardice but accuracy that stops her, and the failure of one clause brings down the entire five-year scheme.

quotations.text: “Her voice is full of money,” he said suddenly.
quotations.speaker: Jay Gatsby
quotations.context: In Gatsby's house on the hottest afternoon of the summer, while Daisy is speaking in the next room.
quotations.analysis: Nick has spent two chapters failing to describe Daisy's voice and Gatsby settles it in five words, which is the one moment in the book where he sees more clearly than the narrator. It is also the diagnosis of his own defeat: what he loves in her is a sound produced by a security he was not born into and cannot purchase.

quotations.text: “They’re a rotten crowd,” I shouted across the lawn. “You’re worth the whole damn bunch put together.”
quotations.speaker: Nick Carraway
quotations.context: Leaving for work on the last morning of Gatsby's life, after a night of listening to the Louisville story.
quotations.analysis: Nick reports immediately afterwards that it was the only compliment he ever paid him, and that he disapproved of him from beginning to end — so the sentence is offered with the disapproval attached. The staging matters too: it is shouted across a lawn, at a distance, by a man on his way to the office, and it is the last thing Gatsby hears from anybody.

quotations.text: A new world, material without being real, where poor ghosts, breathing dreams like air, drifted fortuitously about
quotations.context: Nick's reconstruction of Gatsby's last hours, waiting beside a telephone that does not ring.
quotations.analysis: Everything solid in the novel is here declared unreal at the moment the illusion fails, and the ghosts are poor — the adjective does double duty for pity and for money. Nick admits he is guessing at all of this, so the most metaphysical passage in the book is explicitly an invention, made by a narrator about a man who invented himself.

quotations.text: “The poor son-of-a-bitch,” he said.
quotations.speaker: Owl Eyes
quotations.context: At the graveside, spoken by the drunk who admired the library in Chapter 3.
quotations.analysis: The only epitaph Gatsby gets comes from a man who went to one party and never met him, and it is four words of profanity. Set it against the two pages of lyric prose that close the book: the novel gives the plain human verdict first, and the grand one afterwards, and does not say which is truer.

quotations.text: They were careless people, Tom and Daisy⁠—they smashed up things and creatures and then retreated back into their money or their vast carelessness, or whatever it was that kept them together, and let other people clean up the mess they had made
quotations.context: After meeting Tom on Fifth Avenue and learning what he told George Wilson.
quotations.analysis: 'Things and creatures' declines to say people, which is how the sentence performs the carelessness it is describing. The judgement Nick promised on the first page to reserve is delivered here in the past tense, and the most damning phrase is the vaguest — 'or whatever it was' — because he has stopped trying to understand them.

quotations.text: gradually I became aware of the old island here that flowered once for Dutch sailors’ eyes⁠—a fresh, green breast of the new world
quotations.context: Lying on the beach at night before leaving the East for good.
quotations.analysis: The houses are made to melt away so that a seventeenth-century landscape can be laid over a twentieth-century one, and the colour green arrives from the dock light three hundred pages earlier. The move enlarges one man's obsession into a continental habit without ever quite saying that Gatsby stands for America.

quotations.text: Gatsby believed in the green light, the orgiastic future that year by year recedes before us.
quotations.context: The penultimate paragraph of the novel.
quotations.analysis: The verb 'recedes' does the work: the future is not ahead but retreating, so pursuing it is already a backward motion. Nick has also switched to the first person plural here, which quietly enrols the reader in Gatsby's error two sentences before the famous image of the boats.

quotations.text: So we beat on, boats against the current, borne back ceaselessly into the past.
quotations.context: The last sentence of the novel.
quotations.analysis: Two participles pulling opposite ways — beating forward, borne backwards — leave the sentence with no net motion at all, which is the exact shape of Gatsby's five years. 'We' has replaced 'he' by now, and the last word of a book about the future is 'past'.

quotations.text: “I’m thirty,” I said. “I’m five years too old to lie to myself and call it honour.”
quotations.speaker: Nick Carraway
quotations.context: Ending the affair with Jordan Baker, who has accused him of throwing her over on the telephone.
quotations.analysis: He turns his birthday into a moral unit of measurement, as though self-deception had an age limit, and the arithmetic quietly puts the honest years at twenty-five. Jordan's reply — that she thought he was an honest, straightforward person — is the novel's last word on his opening claim.

atAGlance.label: Published
atAGlance.note: Charles Scribner's Sons, New York, with Francis Cugat's jacket painting.

atAGlance.label: Set in
atAGlance.note: Prohibition is three years old and the dates inside the novel fix the year precisely.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.note: Gatsby's history arrives in Chapter 6, when four chapters of performance have already been established.

atAGlance.label: Earlier titles
atAGlance.note: Forms of the name of Petronius's party-giving freedman survived into the galleys Fitzgerald revised in Rome.

atAGlance.label: Reception
atAGlance.note: The reviews were mixed and the sales worse; the reputation the book now has was built after 1940.

criticalViews.position: The novel as a critique of the American dream
criticalViews.summary: The reading that took hold after the 1945 revival: Gatsby's rise and death are a verdict on a national promise that has become a demand for money and a woman, with the last page enlarging one man's case into a continental one.
criticalViews.counter: The novel never quite equates Gatsby with America — Nick makes the connection himself, in prose he has already admitted is reconstruction.

criticalViews.position: The novel as a study of its narrator
criticalViews.summary: Attention shifts from Gatsby to Nick: what he omits, whom he grants an interior life, how much of the last two chapters he has invented, and what it means that he claims reserve while assigning value in every paragraph.
criticalViews.counter: Pressed hard, this can make the book a puzzle about reliability and lose the fact that Nick's judgements are mostly accurate.

criticalViews.position: The novel as social history of 1922
criticalViews.summary: A reading grounded in Prohibition economics, the motor car, the geography of new and inherited money on Long Island, and the racial anxieties Tom reads aloud at dinner in the first chapter.
criticalViews.counter: The novel is not a documentary; its dates and prices are exact, but its shape is closer to a fable than to a report.

criticalViews.position: The novel as a book about women who are not permitted to act
criticalViews.summary: Daisy, Jordan and Myrtle are given three different strategies — retreat into charm, professional coolness, and a rented room — and all three are punished or contained. The demand Gatsby makes of Daisy is that she revise her own history to suit his.
criticalViews.counter: The narration grants none of them much interiority, so the argument must be built from what Nick does not report.

essayQuestions.question: How reliable is Nick Carraway?
essayQuestions.focus: Narration, omission and retrospective judgement
plan: Start with the opening claim to reserve judgement and set it against the judgements made in the same three pages.
Use Chapter 3 to show reserve working as a technique: it is what makes people talk to him.
Examine what he does not do after the accident in Chapter 7, and how little space the novel gives to that silence.
Look at Chapter 8, where he reconstructs a dying man's thoughts and admits he is guessing.
Conclude with Chapter 9: he delivers the verdict he promised to withhold, and the reader has to decide whether the account earns it.

essayQuestions.question: Discuss the function of place in The Great Gatsby.
essayQuestions.focus: East Egg, West Egg, the valley of ashes and the Midwest
plan: Map the four settings and what kind of money each one holds.
Read Chapter 2 closely: the valley is between the houses and the city, so everyone must drive through it.
Note that every death in the novel happens on that road or in a swimming pool built with new money.
Use the Plaza in Chapter 7 as a neutral ground where the geography is temporarily suspended and the argument can be had.
Close on Nick's return to the Midwest, and on whether the novel treats it as a refuge or as a retreat.

essayQuestions.question: 'Gatsby's tragedy is that he got what he wanted.' Discuss.
essayQuestions.focus: Desire, distance and the green light
plan: Trace the green light through Chapters 1, 5 and 9 and note who is looking at it each time.
Use the count of enchanted objects in Chapter 5 to show possession working as subtraction.
Set against this Gatsby's actual demand in Chapter 6 — a sentence from Daisy, not a life with her.
Weigh Chapter 7, where Daisy's inability to say she never loved Tom defeats him before Myrtle dies.
Decide whether Chapter 8's unreal new world is Gatsby's discovery or Nick's invention.

essayQuestions.question: How does the novel present carelessness?
essayQuestions.focus: Money, consequence and who clears up
plan: Begin with Jordan's driving in Chapter 3 and her claim that it takes two to make an accident.
Follow the motif through the drunk in the ditch, the exchanged cars, and the wrong driver being blamed.
Note that the only people who cannot retreat are the Wilsons, and that both of them die.
Use Nick's verdict in Chapter 9 and examine its vocabulary — things and creatures, mess, whatever it was.
Ask whether Nick's own departure counts as an escape of the same kind.

discussionQuestions: Gatsby's history is withheld until Chapter 6. What would be lost if it came first?
Daisy is given almost no interior life by the narrator. Is that a limitation of the book or a statement by it?
The eyes of Doctor T. J. Eckleburg are an abandoned advertisement. Does it matter that George Wilson takes them for God?
Nobody comes to the funeral. What does the novel want the reader to conclude from a guest list of three?
Nick says he disapproved of Gatsby from beginning to end. Do the last two pages agree with him?
Tom tells George Wilson which car to look for. How much of the ending is an accident?

timeline.label: F. Scott Fitzgerald born in Saint Paul, Minnesota
timeline.detail: Named for a distant relative who wrote the words of The Star-Spangled Banner.

timeline.label: Fitzgerald meets Zelda Sayre while stationed in Alabama
timeline.detail: The courtship, the refusal and the eventual acceptance after his first novel sold all feed the Louisville chapters.

timeline.label: The World Series is fixed
timeline.detail: The scandal that gives Meyer Wolfshiem his introduction in Chapter 4, and dates the world Gatsby's money comes from.

timeline.label: National prohibition takes effect, and This Side of Paradise is published
timeline.detail: The law that creates Gatsby's business and the book that made his author famous arrive in the same year.

timeline.label: The summer the novel is set in
timeline.detail: Fitzgerald was living at Great Neck on Long Island and beginning to plan a third novel.

timeline.label: The main draft is written in France
timeline.detail: A pencil manuscript of more than two hundred and fifty pages, then galleys revised so heavily in Rome that whole chapters changed shape.

timeline.label: The Great Gatsby is published on 10 April
timeline.detail: Charles Scribner's Sons, New York. The reviews were mixed and the sales well short of Fitzgerald's hopes.

timeline.label: Fitzgerald dies in Hollywood
timeline.detail: He was forty-four, at work on a novel about the film industry, and his reputation was at its lowest.

timeline.label: The Armed Services Editions distribute 155,000 copies
timeline.detail: A free paperback for service personnel put the novel into more hands in a year than it had reached in twenty.

timeline.label: Works published in 1925 enter the United States public domain
timeline.detail: The first-edition text became freely available for independent editions on 1 January.

related.why: The other great retrospective narration by a young man remade by money he did not understand the source of.
Published the same year, and the other 1925 novel in which a single day exposes what a decade has cost.
An earlier American account of a woman who tries to act on her own account, and what the society around her does about it.
The same country seen from the other end of the economy, with a smash on a winter hill instead of a road accident.
Another study of a beautiful invented self maintained by spending, and of the people who pay for it.

books.title: The Iliad
books.author: Homer
books.setting: The plain of Troy, between the city walls and the Greek ships drawn up on the shore, with the gods watching from Olympus and Mount Ida, over some fifty days in the tenth year of the war
books.written: Composed in Greek, probably in the second half of the eighth century BCE; Samuel Butler's English prose translation appeared in 1898
books.lengthNote: A poem of about 15,700 lines of Greek hexameter verse in twenty-four books, nearly a third as long again as the Odyssey. Butler translates it into continuous English prose, so it reads like a novel, but it is recorded here as a poem because that is what Homer made.
books.openingLine: Sing, O goddess, the anger of Achilles son of Peleus, that brought countless ills upon the Achaeans.
books.summary: The most famous war poem ever made leaves out the war's beginning and its end. It covers some fifty days in the tenth year of the siege of Troy, and its subject, named in its first line, is one man's anger. Achilles, publicly shamed by his commander over a captive woman, withdraws from the fighting and asks the gods to let his own side be beaten until they beg for him. They are beaten, and the price is his closest friend. His anger then turns on Hector, the Trojan prince who killed Patroclus, and the poem follows it through a river choked with bodies to the point where it burns out. The last book is not a victory but a supper: the old king of Troy kisses the hands that killed his son, and the man who killed him weeps with him.
books.referenceStyle: book — Butler's prose translation carries no line numbers, so quotations are placed by book alone (Book 1 to Book 24)

sourceText.label: Samuel Butler's prose translation of the Iliad (1898), Project Gutenberg eBook 2199
sourceText.note: Quotations are given exactly as they stand in this transcription, and Butler used the Roman names then usual in English: Jove for Zeus, Juno for Hera, Minerva for Athene, Neptune for Poseidon, Mars for Ares, Venus for Aphrodite, Vulcan for Hephaestus, Mercury for Hermes, Saturn for Cronus and Ulysses for Odysseus. He also writes Diomed for Diomedes, and Alexandrus as often as Paris. Unlike the Astor Odyssey, the Astor Iliad keeps Butler's Roman names and explains them in its notes. Outside quotations, the commentary uses the Greek names. Achaeans, Argives and Danaans all mean the Greek army.

structure.label: Books 1–4
structure.title: The quarrel and the armies
structure.summary: The whole disaster begins in a public meeting, with a priest's daughter, a plague and an insult. Achilles withdraws and his mother wins Zeus's promise to punish the Greeks. The next three books show the war he has left: an army nearly talked into going home, a duel meant to settle everything that settles nothing, and a truce broken by a single arrow.

scenes.title: The quarrel
scenes.summary: Agamemnon must return Chryseis to end Apollo's plague, takes Briseis from Achilles instead, and Achilles withdraws; Thetis wins Zeus's nod.

scenes.title: The dream and the catalogue
scenes.summary: Zeus sends Agamemnon a false dream; a test of the army's nerve becomes a stampede for the ships; Odysseus beats Thersites; the forces are listed.

scenes.title: Paris and Menelaus
scenes.summary: Helen's two husbands fight a duel for her, watched from the wall by Priam and Helen; Aphrodite snatches Paris away to his bedroom.

scenes.title: The truce broken
scenes.summary: Athene persuades Pandarus to shoot Menelaus; Agamemnon goes round his captains, and the armies close.

structure.label: Books 5–8
structure.title: The war without Achilles
structure.summary: With the best fighter sitting out, the poem finds out what the others are made of. Diomedes wounds two gods in a day. Hector goes back into the city and meets, one after another, the women he is fighting for. Then Zeus begins to keep his promise, and by nightfall the Trojans are camped on the plain within sight of the ships.

scenes.title: Diomedes' day
scenes.summary: Athene fills Diomedes with strength; he wounds Aphrodite as she rescues Aeneas, and later wounds Ares himself.

scenes.title: Hector in Troy
scenes.summary: Glaucus and Diomedes find their grandfathers were guest-friends and exchange armour; Hector sees his mother, Helen and Paris, then Andromache and their son at the Scaean gate.

scenes.title: Hector and Ajax
scenes.summary: A duel is broken off at nightfall with an exchange of gifts; both sides bury their dead, and the Greeks build a wall and trench round their ships.

scenes.title: Zeus turns the battle
scenes.summary: Zeus forbids the gods to interfere, weighs the two armies' fates in his scales, and drives the Greeks behind their wall.

structure.label: Books 9–12
structure.title: The embassy and the wall
structure.summary: Agamemnon admits his mistake and offers a fortune to have Achilles back, and Achilles turns it down in a speech that questions the whole bargain of heroic life. Without him the Greek leaders are wounded one after another, Patroclus is sent on an errand that will lead to his death, and Hector smashes his way through the wall.

scenes.title: The embassy to Achilles
scenes.summary: Odysseus, Phoenix and Ajax carry Agamemnon's offer of gifts; Achilles refuses and threatens to sail for home in the morning.

scenes.title: The night raid
scenes.summary: Odysseus and Diomedes go out as spies, catch the Trojan scout Dolon, kill him, and steal the horses of the Thracian king Rhesus.

scenes.title: The leaders wounded
scenes.summary: Agamemnon, Diomedes and Odysseus are wounded in turn; Achilles sends Patroclus to ask after a wounded man, and Nestor urges Patroclus to fight in Achilles' armour.

scenes.title: The wall breached
scenes.summary: Sarpedon tells Glaucus why princes must fight in front; Hector breaks the gate with a stone and the Trojans pour through.

structure.label: Books 13–16
structure.title: Battle at the ships
structure.summary: The fighting reaches the beach and the gods break Zeus's orders to join it: Poseidon rallies the Greeks, and Hera puts Zeus to sleep by seducing him. When he wakes, the Trojans are driven on to the ships with fire. Only then does Achilles let Patroclus go out in his armour, and the substitute does too well.

scenes.title: Poseidon at the ships
scenes.summary: Poseidon, watching from Samothrace, comes down to rally the Greeks; Idomeneus leads the defence while Hector presses on.

scenes.title: Hera deceives Zeus
scenes.summary: Hera borrows Aphrodite's embroidered girdle, seduces Zeus on Mount Ida and sends him to sleep; Ajax fells Hector with a stone.

scenes.title: Zeus wakes
scenes.summary: Zeus sends Apollo to revive Hector; the Trojans reach the ships, and Ajax fights them off from the decks.

scenes.title: Patroclus
scenes.summary: Patroclus drives the Trojans back and kills Sarpedon, son of Zeus; Apollo strips him of his armour, and Euphorbus and Hector kill him.

structure.label: Books 17–20
structure.title: Grief, armour and return
structure.summary: The poem slows down around a body. Greeks and Trojans fight all day over Patroclus's corpse; the news reaches Achilles, who pours dust over his head; his mother goes to Hephaestus for new armour, and the shield is described at length before a blow is struck with it. The reconciliation with Agamemnon, when it comes, is brisk, because nobody now cares about the gifts.

scenes.title: The fight for the body
scenes.summary: Menelaus and Ajax defend Patroclus's corpse; Achilles' immortal horses stand weeping in the battle; Hector wears Achilles' armour.

scenes.title: The shield
scenes.summary: Achilles hears the news and chooses death; his shout from the trench throws the Trojans into panic; Hephaestus makes the shield.

scenes.title: The reconciliation
scenes.summary: Agamemnon blames Zeus and Folly for the quarrel; Briseis mourns Patroclus; Achilles' horse Xanthus foretells his death.

scenes.title: The gods take sides
scenes.summary: Zeus lets the gods join the fighting; Poseidon snatches Aeneas away from Achilles because he is fated to survive.

structure.label: Books 21–24
structure.title: Revenge and ransom
structure.summary: Achilles fills the river with bodies until the river itself fights him, then kills Hector under the walls and drags the corpse behind his chariot. Two whole books remain. The funeral games for Patroclus hand out prizes and settle disputes without bloodshed; then Priam crosses the Greek camp at night to ransom his son, and the poem ends with a funeral in Troy.

scenes.title: The river
scenes.summary: Achilles kills Lycaon and chokes the Scamander with the dead; the river rises against him until Hephaestus burns it back; the gods fight one another.

scenes.title: The death of Hector
scenes.summary: Hector waits outside the gates, runs three times round the walls, is tricked by Athene in the shape of his brother, and dies; Achilles drags the body away.

scenes.title: The funeral games
scenes.summary: Patroclus's ghost asks for burial; twelve Trojan captives die on his pyre; Achilles presides over races and contests and keeps the peace among the winners.

scenes.title: Priam and Achilles
scenes.summary: Hermes leads Priam to Achilles' tent; the two men weep together, eat, and agree a truce for Hector's funeral.

characters.name: Achilles
characters.role: Son of Peleus and the sea-goddess Thetis, the best fighter at Troy
characters.summary: He knows two things the other heroes can only suspect: that he will die young if he stays, and that the honour he is dying for can be taken from him by a worse man with a bigger army. The poem is about what that knowledge does to him. His anger is justified in Book 1, excessive by Book 9, catastrophic in Book 16 and monstrous in Book 22, and it ends not in triumph but in a meal shared with his enemy's father.
characters.clue: He refuses a king's fortune in Book 9 and accepts an old man's ransom in Book 24.

relationships.label: quarrels with, and is reconciled to
kills, and drags behind his chariot

characters.name: Hector
characters.role: Eldest son of Priam and the chief defender of Troy
characters.summary: The poem's most sympathetic fighter is on the losing side, and it gives him what it never gives Achilles: a wife, a baby and a city of people who depend on him. He knows Troy will fall and fights anyway, from shame rather than hope. His judgement slips as his success grows. He overrules sound advice, puts on the armour he stripped from Patroclus, and when Achilles finally comes for him, he runs.
characters.clue: He takes off his helmet so that his baby son will stop crying, and dies wearing armour stripped from a man he killed.

relationships.label: kind to, when others are not

characters.name: Agamemnon
characters.role: King of Mycenae and commander of the Greek army
characters.summary: He holds the largest command and the least authority, and knows it: many of his speeches are attempts to make others acknowledge a rank that ought to speak for itself. He takes Briseis to prove that he is the stronger and proves the opposite. His apology in Book 19 blames Zeus, Fate and Folly, which is true to the poem's theology and convenient for him. On the battlefield, to be fair, he is brave.
characters.clue: He proposes that the army give up and sail home three times, and only the first time is it a test.

relationships.label: insults, then tries to buy back

characters.name: Patroclus
characters.role: Achilles' companion and squire, son of Menoetius
characters.summary: He is the gentlest man in the Greek camp — Briseis remembers him as the one who told her not to weep — and the poem makes him the price of Achilles' anger. Sent out in borrowed armour to frighten the Trojans away from the ships, he forgets his orders and chases them to the walls. The narrator speaks to him directly as he goes, as if he could still be warned.
characters.clue: He came to Achilles' father as a child refugee, after killing another boy in a quarrel over dice.

characters.name: Priam
characters.role: King of Troy, father of fifty sons
characters.summary: Too old to fight, he watches the war from the walls and loses most of his sons to it. He refuses to blame Helen. In the last book he does what nobody in the poem has dared to do: crosses the enemy camp at night, with only a herald and a disguised god, and kisses the hands that killed Hector. His courage is the poem's last and least warlike kind.
characters.clue: He asks Helen to name the Greek leaders for him from the wall, and tells her the gods are to blame, not she.

characters.name: Andromache
characters.role: Wife of Hector, daughter of Eetion of Thebe
characters.summary: Everything she has lost, she has lost to Achilles, who killed her father and seven brothers in one day. She appears three times, and each time the poem stops for her. She tells Hector where the wall is weakest, and he sends her back to her loom; she heats his bath while he dies; she leads the lament over his body, and the lament is mostly about what will now happen to their son.
characters.clue: The shuttle falls from her hands when she hears the cry from the wall.

characters.name: Helen
characters.role: Wife of Menelaus, taken to Troy by Paris
characters.summary: The cause of the war speaks of herself with a disgust nobody else voices, wishes a whirlwind had carried her off at birth, and has no illusions about Paris. She alone seems to know that she is living inside a story that will be sung. She is also the poem's last mourner: her lament for Hector remembers him as the one Trojan who was never unkind to her.
characters.clue: She is found in her room embroidering the battles that are being fought over her.

characters.name: Paris (Butler's Alexandrus)
characters.role: Son of Priam, whose seizure of Helen began the war
characters.summary: Beautiful, capable and absent whenever it matters. He challenges the best of the Greeks and then shrinks from Menelaus, and Aphrodite lifts him out of the duel to his bed. The poem does not simply despise him: he takes Hector's rebukes gracefully, fights well enough when he chooses, and is named in Hector's dying words as the man who will kill Achilles.
characters.clue: Told off by his brother, he agrees at once, then asks him to wait while he puts his armour on.

characters.name: Thetis
characters.role: A sea-goddess, mother of Achilles
characters.summary: She was married to a mortal 'sorely against my will', as she tells Hephaestus, and she knows her son must die young. Every time Achilles weeps she rises out of the sea to comfort him, and every time she can do nothing about what is really wrong. It is her plea that turns Zeus against the Greeks in Book 1, and her errand to Hephaestus that arms her son for the death she has just foretold.
characters.clue: She tells her son his death will follow Hector's, and then goes to fetch him new armour.

characters.name: Zeus (Butler's Jove)
characters.role: King of the gods
characters.summary: He has promised Thetis to honour Achilles, and he keeps his word at the cost of thousands of lives. He also feels pity — for Hector, for his own son Sarpedon, for Achilles' horses — and in each case lets the pity go. His golden scales weigh out deaths he could apparently prevent and chooses not to. The poem's highest power is capable of sympathy and unwilling to spend it.
characters.clue: He nods, and Olympus reels; he weighs two fates, and one sinks.

characters.name: Odysseus (Butler's Ulysses)
characters.role: King of Ithaca, the Greeks' best speaker
characters.summary: He is not yet the hero of his own poem but already recognisably himself: he stops a mutiny with a sceptre across Thersites' back, leads the embassy to Achilles, goes spying by night, and reminds the army that men must eat before they fight. Achilles' reply to him in Book 9 — that he hates a man who says one thing and hides another — is aimed at exactly the skill the Odyssey will celebrate.
characters.clue: From the wall Priam picks him out as shorter than Agamemnon by a head, pacing the ranks like a ram among ewes.

characters.name: Briseis
characters.role: A captive woman, Achilles' prize, taken from him by Agamemnon
characters.summary: The woman the quarrel is about is led away 'loth to go' in Book 1 and speaks only once, in Book 19, over Patroclus's body. Her lament tells us what the heroes never mention: that Achilles killed her husband and three brothers when he sacked her city, and that Patroclus promised to make Achilles marry her. She is a prize to the men and a widow to herself.
characters.clue: Her one speech is a lament for the only Greek who was kind to her.

themes.name: The anger of Achilles
themes.summary: The poem announces its subject in its first word, and the word means a lasting, almost divine rage rather than a burst of temper. It is justified at first: Achilles has been publicly robbed. The poem's interest is in what happens when a just grievance outlives its cause, becomes a pleasure in itself, and is transferred, when Patroclus dies, from a commander to an enemy.
themes.development: Provoked in Book 1, hardened into refusal in Book 9, released on Hector from Book 18, glutted at the river in Book 21 and on Hector's corpse in Book 22, and exhausted, not conquered, in Book 24.

themes.name: Honour, prizes and glory
themes.summary: Honour in the Iliad is concrete. It is a captive, a tripod, the best cut of meat, and a name that lives in songs after the body is gone. That makes it measurable and so confiscable, and the quarrel exposes the system's weakness. Once Achilles sees that a worse man can take his prize, he starts to ask what glory is worth to someone who will die for it.
themes.development: Taken from Achilles in Book 1, offered back with interest in Book 9 and refused, redefined by Sarpedon in Book 12, and sought by Hector at the last in the only form left to him: a death worth telling.

themes.name: Death and the body
themes.summary: The gods cannot die and so cannot be heroes; men can, and that is the only reason courage means anything. The poem gives every minor warrior a father, a home and a moment of dying, and its great speeches about death come from men who know how little time they have. It cares just as much about what happens afterwards: a body stripped, fought over, left for dogs, or washed and given back for burial.
themes.development: A 'little season' in Book 1, leaves on the trees in Book 6, a choice of two deaths in Book 9, a whole book fought over Patroclus's corpse in Book 17, Hector's body dragged in Book 22 and ransomed in Book 24.

themes.name: Fate and the will of Zeus
themes.summary: The poem opens by saying that the counsels of Zeus were being fulfilled, and it is full of foreknowledge: Thetis knows, Achilles knows, even the horses know. Yet nothing is excused by it. Men choose inside a frame they cannot alter, and the gods, who could sometimes alter it, weigh the fates in golden scales and let them fall.
themes.development: Set in motion by Zeus's nod in Book 1, weighed in the scales in Books 8 and 22, argued over when Zeus considers saving Sarpedon and Hector, and blamed by Agamemnon for everything in Book 19.

themes.name: Home, and the city behind the wall
themes.summary: The Greeks are far from home and the Trojans are fighting in front of theirs, and the poem keeps showing what the war is being fought across: washing-troughs where women did laundry in peacetime, a baby frightened by a helmet, a bath heating for a man already dead. Achilles gives up his homecoming for glory. Hector dies within sight of his.
themes.development: Hector's visit to the city in Book 6, Achilles' choice between Phthia and fame in Book 9, the lost peace of the springs in Book 22, and the body brought home through the gates in Book 24.

themes.name: Hosts, guests and strangers
themes.summary: The war began as a crime against hospitality — Paris was Menelaus's guest when he took Helen — and the poem's two moments of peace between enemies both rest on the same code. Glaucus and Diomedes stop fighting when they find their grandfathers were host and guest; Priam comes to Achilles as a suppliant, and Achilles feeds him.
themes.development: Broken before the poem begins, honoured on the battlefield in Book 6, refused at Hector's death in Book 22, and restored in the tent in Book 24, where the killer becomes the host.

themes.name: Prizes, captives and mourners
themes.summary: In a poem about men at war, women are the prizes the quarrel is about, the captives the sack of a city produces, and the mourners who have the last word. The heroes send their wives back to the loom; the poem keeps following them there. Andromache, Hecuba, Helen and Briseis speak its most searching lines about what the fighting is for.
themes.development: Briseis led away in Book 1, Helen weaving the war in Book 3, Andromache at the gate in Book 6, the captive women's double mourning in Book 19, and the three formal laments that end Book 24.

techniques.name: Invocation
techniques.definition: An opening address to a muse or god, asking for the song and announcing its subject.
techniques.bookDefinition: An opening address to a muse or god, asking for the song and announcing its subject.
techniques.inThisBook: The goddess is asked to sing 'the anger of Achilles', and the invocation plunges straight into the tenth year of the war with the quarrel already under way. Nothing of the ten years before is narrated. The poem calls on the Muses again before the catalogue of ships in Book 2, and at later crises, when it needs names and numbers rather than inspiration.

techniques.name: Epithets and formulae
techniques.definition: Fixed descriptive phrases attached to a person or thing and repeated whenever they recur, a working tool of poetry composed in performance.
techniques.bookDefinition: Fixed descriptive phrases attached to a person or thing and repeated whenever they recur, a working tool of poetry composed in performance.
techniques.inThisBook: Achilles is 'son of Peleus', Hector 'tamer of horses', Dawn 'rosy-fingered', and whole scenes — sacrifice, arming, a warrior's soul leaving his body — recur almost word for word. The lines for a soul leaving the body, flying to Hades to mourn 'its sad fate' and the youth it has lost, are used for Patroclus and again for Hector, so the second death is heard through the first.

techniques.name: Extended simile
techniques.definition: A comparison developed over several lines until it becomes a small scene of its own, typically closed with 'even so'.
techniques.bookDefinition: A comparison developed over several lines until it becomes a small scene of its own, typically closed with 'even so'.
techniques.inThisBook: The Iliad's similes carry the reader out of the battle into the world the battle is not: shepherds, harvests, children, storms, a woman weighing wool to earn her children's bread. They are also where the poem thinks hardest. Glaucus compares men to leaves; the arrival of Priam in Book 24 is compared, very strangely, to the arrival of a murderer.

techniques.name: Apostrophe
techniques.definition: A speaker or narrator turning away from the audience to address someone, usually absent or unable to answer, as 'you'.
techniques.bookDefinition: A speaker or narrator turning away from the audience to address someone, usually absent or unable to answer, as 'you'.
techniques.inThisBook: Homer's narrator occasionally speaks to a character directly, and in Book 16 he does it again and again to Patroclus — 'O knight Patroclus' — as the young man goes to his death. The effect is of a narrator who knows what is coming and cannot stop it, which is exactly the position of the audience.

techniques.name: Prophecy and foreknowledge
techniques.definition: A statement about the future that shapes the action by being believed, whether or not it is true.
techniques.bookDefinition: Statements about the future that shape how the present is read, whether they come from gods, seers or the characters' own fears.
techniques.inThisBook: Almost nothing in the Iliad comes as a surprise. Achilles knows the terms of his life from Book 1; Hector knows Troy will fall; Patroclus, dying, predicts Hector's death, and Hector, dying, predicts Achilles'. Suspense is replaced by dread, and attention moves from what will happen to how people behave knowing it will.

techniques.name: Dramatic irony
techniques.definition: The audience knows something that a character speaking or acting does not.
techniques.bookDefinition: The audience knows something that a character speaking or acting does not.
techniques.inThisBook: The poem's audience knows the ending of the war and most of its heroes' deaths, and the characters mostly speak without that knowledge. Hector bargains in Book 7 for the return of a dead champion's body, never imagining his own; Andromache heats water for a man already dead.

techniques.name: Objects that carry the argument
techniques.definition: An object the narrative keeps returning to until it stands for the argument rather than illustrating it.
techniques.bookDefinition: Physical things that the narrative returns to until they stand for a relationship or an idea.
techniques.inThisBook: Achilles' armour passes from his body to Patroclus's to Hector's, so that in Book 22 Achilles is in effect fighting his own old self. The sceptre he swears by and throws down in Book 1, stripped of leaf and bark and never to sprout again, is the authority of kings he is about to defy. The new shield carries cities at peace into battle, and Hector's helmet frightens his son.

techniques.name: Mirrored scenes
techniques.definition: Scenes built to echo one another, so that the second is read through the first and the difference between them carries the meaning.
techniques.bookDefinition: Scenes built to echo one another, so that the second is read through the first and the difference between them carries the meaning.
techniques.inThisBook: The poem begins with an old father, Chryses, coming to the Greek camp with a ransom for his child and being sent roughly away, and ends with an old father, Priam, coming with a ransom for his son and being fed. The quarrel over a prize in Book 1 is answered by the fairly judged prizes of the funeral games in Book 23.

quotations.text: Sing, O goddess, the anger of Achilles son of Peleus, that brought countless ills upon the Achaeans. Many a brave soul did it send hurrying down to Hades, and many a hero did it yield a prey to dogs and vultures, for so were the counsels of Jove fulfilled.
quotations.context: The opening of the poem.
quotations.analysis: The first noun is anger, and the sentence cares about its consequences rather than its cause: souls sent to Hades, bodies left for dogs and vultures. That last threat is not decoration. Whether a corpse is buried or eaten becomes the question the whole poem turns on, up to the ransoming of Hector. And 'the counsels of Jove' are fulfilled through this anger: the first sentence already puts a god's plan and a man's temper inside the same machine.
quotations.source: Butler's translation, Project Gutenberg text, Book I

quotations.text: I came not warring here for any ill the Trojans had done me. I have no quarrel with them. They have not raided my cattle nor my horses, nor cut down my harvests on the rich plains of Phthia.
quotations.speaker: Achilles
quotations.context: In the assembly, after Agamemnon threatens to take Achilles' prize to make up for the one he must give back.
quotations.analysis: The most subversive thing anyone says in the poem is said in its first book. Achilles has no grievance against Troy; he is there to win satisfaction for Agamemnon and Menelaus, and his reward comes in the form of prizes. Once a prize can be confiscated, the whole contract is exposed. His refusal of the embassy in Book 9 grows out of this speech: if the war is not his quarrel, only honour kept him in it.
quotations.source: Butler's translation, Project Gutenberg text, Book I

quotations.text: you bore me doomed to live but for a little season; surely Jove, who thunders from Olympus, might have made that little glorious. It is not so.
quotations.speaker: Achilles
quotations.context: Alone by the sea after Briseis has been led away, Achilles calls on his mother.
quotations.analysis: Achilles' bargain is a short life in exchange for glory, and here he complains that he is being cheated on the glory. The phrasing is exact: the 'little season' is accepted, only the 'glorious' is in dispute. It is also the first time the most feared man in the army weeps, and he does it at the water's edge like a child calling for its mother. The poem never treats his tears as weakness.
quotations.source: Butler's translation, Project Gutenberg text, Book I

quotations.text: Small wonder that Trojans and Achaeans should endure so much and so long, for the sake of a woman so marvellously and divinely lovely. Still, fair though she be, let them take her and go, or she will breed sorrow for us and for our children after us.
quotations.speaker: The elders of Troy
quotations.context: Helen comes to the Scaean gate to watch the duel that is to decide whose wife she is; the old men of Troy, too old to fight, see her approach.
quotations.analysis: The elders say two opposite things in two sentences and mean both. Her beauty explains ten years of war; she should be sent back anyway. It is the most generous verdict on Helen in the poem and it is spoken softly, among themselves. Notice who is judging: men past fighting, sitting on the tower 'like cicales', who will see their city burn for a decision nobody on the wall made.
quotations.source: Butler's translation, Project Gutenberg text, Book III

quotations.text: Men come and go as leaves year by year upon the trees. Those of autumn the wind sheds upon the ground, but when spring returns the forest buds forth with fresh vines. Even so is it with the generations of mankind, the new spring up as the old are passing away.
quotations.speaker: Glaucus
quotations.context: Diomedes, meeting a stranger in battle, asks who he is before he fights him. Glaucus begins his answer by questioning the question.
quotations.analysis: A warrior asked for his pedigree replies that pedigrees are like leaves, and then gives his at great length. The simile is the poem's most famous statement of mortality, and a comment on heroic ancestry: what lasts is the kind, not the individual. Yet the genealogy that follows saves his life, because his grandfather turns out to have been the guest of Diomedes' grandfather. The leaves fall; the obligation survives.
quotations.source: Butler's translation, Project Gutenberg text, Book VI

quotations.text: it is you who bear the brunt of that toil that has been caused by my hateful self and by the sin of Alexandrus—both of whom Jove has doomed to be a theme of song among those that shall be born hereafter.
quotations.speaker: Helen
quotations.context: In Paris's house, Helen invites Hector to sit and rest; he refuses and goes to find his wife.
quotations.analysis: Helen is the one character who seems to know she is in a poem. Her sense that she and Paris exist to become 'a theme of song' is a bleak consolation: the suffering has a purpose, and the purpose is entertainment for people not yet born. Heroes fight so that songs will be sung about them. Helen, who had no choice, has worked out what being sung about costs, and she says it to the man who is paying.
quotations.source: Butler's translation, Project Gutenberg text, Book VI

quotations.text: He stretched his arms towards his child, but the boy cried and nestled in his nurse’s bosom, scared at the sight of his father’s armour, and at the horse-hair plume that nodded fiercely from his helmet.
quotations.context: At the Scaean gate, Hector reaches for his baby son Astyanax before returning to the battle.
quotations.analysis: The one warrior in the poem shown with a child is undone by his own equipment. Everything that makes Hector a hero — the bronze, the plume that 'nodded fiercely' — is exactly what a baby cannot read. The parents laugh, and Hector takes the helmet off: for a moment the poem shows a man choosing between his two roles and choosing the smaller one. A few lines later he picks the helmet up again.
quotations.source: Butler's translation, Project Gutenberg text, Book VI

quotations.text: Go, then, within the house, and busy yourself with your daily duties, your loom, your distaff, and the ordering of your servants; for war is man’s matter, and mine above all others of them that have been born in Ilius.
quotations.speaker: Hector
quotations.context: Hector's last words to Andromache before he goes back to the fighting.
quotations.analysis: Andromache has just given him sound advice about the weak point in the wall, and he answers by sending her to her loom. The sentence is a formula: the Odyssey gives it almost word for word to Telemachus, with 'war' changed to 'speech'. Here it is tender rather than rude, since he has just told her not to grieve before her time, but it draws the line the poem keeps. Men decide; women mourn the decisions. Book 24 gives the women the last word.
quotations.source: Butler's translation, Project Gutenberg text, Book VI

quotations.text: Then will one say hereafter as he sails his ship over the sea, ‘This is the monument of one who died long since a champion who was slain by mighty Hector.’ Thus will one say, and my fame shall not be lost.
quotations.speaker: Hector
quotations.context: Hector challenges the best of the Greeks to single combat, and sets terms for what will happen to the loser's body.
quotations.analysis: Hector pictures his fame as something a stranger will say about a tomb, and in doing so he lays down the rule the poem will later test: the winner keeps the armour and the body goes home to be buried. When he asks the same of Achilles in Book 22, Achilles refuses outright. The barrow he imagines is the Greek champion's; it does not occur to him that it may be his own, or that he may be denied one.
quotations.source: Butler's translation, Project Gutenberg text, Book VII

quotations.text: Him do I hate even as the gates of hell who says one thing while he hides another in his heart; therefore I will say what I mean.
quotations.speaker: Achilles
quotations.context: Odysseus has repeated Agamemnon's offer of gifts, leaving out Agamemnon's closing demand that Achilles submit to him as the more royal man.
quotations.analysis: Whether or not Achilles guesses what has been left out, he names the fault exactly, and he names it to the one man in the camp who most deserves it. Odysseus's own poem will celebrate the skill of saying one thing and hiding another. Achilles' refusal to do so is his integrity, and also his isolation: a man who says only what he means has no way to climb down.
quotations.source: Butler's translation, Project Gutenberg text, Book IX

quotations.text: My mother Thetis tells me that there are two ways in which I may meet my end. If I stay here and fight, I shall not return alive but my name will live for ever: whereas if I go home my name will die, but it will be long ere death shall take me.
quotations.speaker: Achilles
quotations.context: Achilles tells the embassy that he will sail for Phthia in the morning.
quotations.analysis: The choice that defines Achilles is set out like a sum, and on this night he chooses the long life. He reverses the choice only when Patroclus dies. What makes the speech shocking is that it doubts the arithmetic heroes live by: glory is a name, and a name is worth less than a life that, as he has just said, 'can neither be bought nor harried back again'. He is the only man at Troy who knows the price for certain.
quotations.source: Butler's translation, Project Gutenberg text, Book IX

quotations.text: My good friend, if, when we were once out of this fight, we could escape old age and death thenceforward and forever, I should neither press forward myself nor bid you do so, but death in ten thousand shapes hangs ever over our heads, and no man can elude him; therefore let us go forward and either win glory for ourselves, or yield it to another.
quotations.speaker: Sarpedon
quotations.context: Sarpedon, prince of the Lycians and a son of Zeus, rouses his friend Glaucus to attack the Greek wall.
quotations.analysis: The clearest short account of why Homeric heroes fight. Privilege — the best seats, the fullest cups — is repaid by standing in front, and if men could not die there would be no point in courage at all. It is Achilles' argument from Book 9 turned inside out: because death is certain, glory is worth pursuing. Sarpedon dies at Patroclus's hands in Book 16, and his father, who could save him, lets him go.
quotations.source: Butler's translation, Project Gutenberg text, Book XII

quotations.text: You know no pity; knight Peleus was not your father nor Thetis your mother, but the grey sea bore you and the sheer cliffs begot you, so cruel and remorseless are you.
quotations.speaker: Patroclus
quotations.context: The Trojans are setting fire to the Greek ships. Patroclus comes to Achilles in tears and begs to be allowed to fight.
quotations.analysis: Patroclus disowns Achilles' parents on his behalf: no man and no goddess could have produced this, only rocks and the sea. It is the harshest thing said to Achilles by anyone who loves him, and it works where the embassy's gifts did not. Achilles gives way — not by fighting, but by lending his armour. The cruelty Patroclus names here is the quality that will make Achilles' revenge for him so terrible.
quotations.source: Butler's translation, Project Gutenberg text, Book XVI

quotations.text: but as he was coming on like a god for a time, then, O Patroclus, was the hour of your end approaching, for Phoebus fought you in fell earnest.
quotations.context: Patroclus has driven the Trojans back towards their walls, killing nine men in each of three charges.
quotations.analysis: The narrator turns and speaks to Patroclus, as if to warn him, at the moment the warning is useless. The grammar changes the killing: the audience is put in the position of someone watching a friend walk into danger and unable to shout. 'Your end' is announced before we see how it comes. When it does, the poem's gentlest man is struck from behind by a god he never sees.
quotations.source: Butler's translation, Project Gutenberg text, Book XVI

quotations.text: Poor things, why did we give you to King Peleus who is a mortal, while you are yourselves ageless and immortal? Was it that you might share the sorrows that befall mankind? for of all creatures that live and move upon the earth there is none so pitiable as he is.
quotations.speaker: Zeus (Butler's Jove)
quotations.context: Achilles' immortal horses stand motionless in the battle, heads bowed, weeping for Patroclus.
quotations.analysis: Looking at two grieving horses, the king of the gods arrives at the poem's bleakest general statement, and he says it about the race he rules. The horses were never meant to share human grief, and have caught it. Zeus's pity is real and changes nothing: he goes straight on to explain that the Trojans will keep killing until dark. The gods of the Iliad can feel for men without being moved to spare them.
quotations.source: Butler's translation, Project Gutenberg text, Book XVII

quotations.text: Therefore, perish strife both from among gods and men, and anger, wherein even a righteous man will harden his heart—which rises up in the soul of a man like smoke, and the taste thereof is sweeter than drops of honey.
quotations.speaker: Achilles
