quotations.context: Told that Patroclus is dead, Achilles tells Thetis he will kill Hector, though he knows his own death must follow.
quotations.analysis: This is the nearest the poem comes to analysing its own subject. Anger is described from the inside as a pleasure — it rises 'like smoke' and tastes 'sweeter than drops of honey' — which is why it is so hard to give up. Achilles renounces his anger against Agamemnon in the same breath as he takes up a far worse one against Hector. He sees the mechanism clearly and cannot step out of it.
quotations.source: Butler's translation, Project Gutenberg text, Book XVIII

quotations.text: Meanwhile the people were gathered in assembly, for there was a quarrel, and two men were wrangling about the blood-money for a man who had been killed, the one saying before the people that he had paid damages in full, and the other that he had not been paid.
quotations.context: One of the scenes Hephaestus works into the new shield he makes for Achilles.
quotations.analysis: On the shield of the angriest man in the poem is a quarrel about compensation for a killing, argued in public and settled by elders, with a prize for whoever judges most fairly. It is the Iliad in miniature. Achilles refused Agamemnon's compensation in Book 9 and will accept Priam's in Book 24. The shield shows a city solving the problem its heroes cannot, and hands the picture to a man going out to kill.
quotations.source: Butler's translation, Project Gutenberg text, Book XVIII

quotations.text: but it was not I that did it: Jove, and Fate, and Erinys that walks in darkness struck me mad when we were assembled on the day that I took from Achilles the meed that had been awarded to him.
quotations.speaker: Agamemnon
quotations.context: At the formal reconciliation, Agamemnon speaks from his place rather than stepping into the middle of the assembly.
quotations.analysis: Agamemnon apologises by explaining that he is not to blame, and goes on to tell a long story about Folly deceiving Zeus himself. In the poem's theology this is not simply an excuse: gods do cloud men's minds. But it is convenient, and it is addressed to an army that has paid for his mistake with its dead. The Odyssey opens with Zeus complaining about precisely this kind of speech.
quotations.source: Butler's translation, Project Gutenberg text, Book XIX

quotations.text: She wept as she spoke, and the women joined in her lament-making as though their tears were for Patroclus, but in truth each was weeping for her own sorrows.
quotations.context: Briseis, returned to Achilles at last, sees Patroclus's body and mourns him as the one Greek who was kind to her.
quotations.analysis: One sentence lets the captive women's mourning be seen for what it is: a public lament for a Greek hero that is really private grief for their own dead husbands, fathers and freedom. Briseis has just said that Achilles killed her husband and three brothers. The narrator does not comment further, but he has admitted that the women the heroes fight over are living through a war of their own.
quotations.source: Butler's translation, Project Gutenberg text, Book XIX

quotations.text: Therefore, my friend, you too shall die. Why should you whine in this way? Patroclus fell, and he was a better man than you are.
quotations.speaker: Achilles
quotations.context: Lycaon, a son of Priam whom Achilles once captured and sold, clasps his knees at the river and begs to be ransomed.
quotations.analysis: The word 'friend' is the most chilling thing in the passage. Achilles is not in a frenzy; he is calm, almost companionable, because he now includes himself among the dead-to-be, and goes on to say his own death will come 'at dawn or dark, or at the noontide'. Before Patroclus died, captives were sold. The same fact — that everyone dies — which will let him pity Priam in Book 24, is here his reason to show no mercy.
quotations.source: Butler's translation, Project Gutenberg text, Book XXI

quotations.text: She told her maids to set a large tripod on the fire, so as to have a warm bath ready for Hector when he came out of battle; poor woman, she knew not that he was now beyond the reach of baths.
quotations.context: Andromache, at her loom in an inner room, has not yet heard that Hector is dead.
quotations.analysis: The poem cuts from the killing to a woman weaving flowers into a purple cloth, and the ordinary kindness of heating water for a tired husband becomes unbearable because we know more than she does. 'Poor woman' is the narrator stepping in. The bath matters for another reason: washing the body is the first rite of a funeral, and this body is being dragged through the dust towards the ships.
quotations.source: Butler's translation, Project Gutenberg text, Book XXII

quotations.text: My doom has come upon me; let me not then die ingloriously and without a struggle, but let me first do some great thing that shall be told among men hereafter.
quotations.speaker: Hector
quotations.context: Hector has thrown his spear and turned for a second one, only to find that the brother at his side was Athene in disguise.
quotations.analysis: Tricked by a goddess and without a spear, Hector gives up on survival and falls back on the one thing he can still control: the story. It is the hope of his challenge in Book 7, fame spoken 'hereafter', now reduced to the manner of his death. After running three times round the walls, he turns and charges with his sword. The poem grants what he asks, since it is still telling it.
quotations.source: Butler's translation, Project Gutenberg text, Book XXII

quotations.text: As when some cruel spite has befallen a man that he should have killed some one in his own country, and must fly to a great man’s protection in a land of strangers, and all marvel who see him, even so did Achilles marvel as he beheld Priam.
quotations.context: Priam, guided by Hermes, has entered Achilles' tent unseen, clasped his knees and kissed his hands.
quotations.analysis: The simile makes the wrong man a killer. It is Achilles who has killed and Priam who has lost, yet the comparison casts the old king as a murderer seeking refuge in a stranger's house. It fits someone else exactly: Patroclus, who as a boy killed a playmate over dice and was taken in by Peleus, as his ghost recalls in Book 23. By reversing the roles, the poem makes Achilles see a suppliant, and prepares the recognition between the two men.
quotations.source: Butler's translation, Project Gutenberg text, Book XXIV

quotations.text: Fear, O Achilles, the wrath of heaven; think on your own father and have compassion upon me, who am the more pitiable, for I have steeled myself as no man yet has ever steeled himself before me, and have raised to my lips the hand of him who slew my son.
quotations.speaker: Priam
quotations.context: The end of Priam's plea, after he has asked Achilles to think of his own old father, Peleus.
quotations.analysis: Priam rests his claim to pity on an act rather than a loss: he has done what no man has done before. The last clause holds the whole horror of the scene — a father's lips on the hand that killed his son. It also mirrors the poem's opening, where another old father, Chryses, came to the Greek camp with ransom for his child and was sent roughly away. This time the ransom is taken, and the father is fed.
quotations.source: Butler's translation, Project Gutenberg text, Book XXIV

quotations.text: The immortals know no care, yet the lot they spin for man is full of sorrow; on the floor of Jove’s palace there stand two urns, the one filled with evil gifts, and the other with good ones.
quotations.speaker: Achilles
quotations.context: After the two men have wept together, Achilles raises Priam from the ground and tells him to sit.
quotations.analysis: The youngest great man at Troy offers the oldest a philosophy, and it is not a comforting one. Zeus gives some men a mixture and some men only evil; nobody receives only good. Achilles applies it at once to Peleus and to Priam, which is the point: the speech is how he comes to see his enemy's father as his own. Grief is shared by everyone. Justice is not on offer.
quotations.source: Butler's translation, Project Gutenberg text, Book XXIV

quotations.text: Thus, then, did they celebrate the funeral of Hector tamer of horses.
quotations.context: The last sentence of the poem, after Hector's bones have been gathered into a golden urn and buried under a barrow.
quotations.analysis: A poem that began with the anger of Achilles ends with the funeral of the man he killed, and gives Hector the plainest of his fixed epithets, one that belongs to peacetime skill rather than battle. The fall of Troy, which everyone knows is coming, is left out. The poem stops at the one thing its first sentence feared would be denied: a body properly burned, mourned and buried.
quotations.source: Butler's translation, Project Gutenberg text, Book XXIV

atAGlance.label: Composed
atAGlance.note: A scholarly estimate, not a record. Most scholars place the Iliad somewhat before the Odyssey; nobody knows when, or whether, a single poet fixed it.

atAGlance.label: This translation
atAGlance.note: Samuel Butler, novelist and author of Erewhon, published his prose Iliad two years before his Odyssey, 'for the use of those who cannot read the original'.

atAGlance.label: Length
atAGlance.note: The division into twenty-four books is ancient but later than the poem, and is usually credited to the scholars of Alexandria.

atAGlance.label: Time covered
atAGlance.note: Out of a ten-year war. The death of Achilles and the fall of the city lie outside the poem, which foresees both and narrates neither.

criticalViews.position: A poem against war
criticalViews.summary: On this reading the Iliad's sympathies lie with the victims. It gives nameless spearmen fathers and fields they will never see again, fills its battles with similes of peacetime work, lets the Trojans be as human as the Greeks, and ends not in victory but in lament. Its real subject is force, and what force does to the people who use it as well as to those it destroys.
criticalViews.counter: The poem also relishes killing, describing wounds with a connoisseur's precision, and its heroes want nothing more than glory won in battle. It never imagines a world without war: even the shield, its picture of civil life, has a city under siege on it. Pity and delight in prowess sit side by side, and neither cancels the other.

criticalViews.position: Achilles learns
criticalViews.summary: Some readers see the poem as the education of Achilles. His anger isolates him from the community of Book 1; Patroclus's death shows him what that anger costs; and in Book 24 he reaches an understanding of shared mortality that lets him weep with his enemy's father. The shape of the poem, from quarrel to reconciliation, supports a story of moral growth.
criticalViews.counter: Achilles in Book 24 is still dangerous: he warns Priam not to provoke him in case he kills him, and he gives up the body partly because the gods have ordered it. The truce lasts eleven days and Troy will still burn. It may be truer to say the poem shows a moment of understanding than a changed man.

criticalViews.position: The work of a tradition rather than an author
criticalViews.summary: The repeated epithets and whole repeated scenes, the loose ends and inconsistencies, point to poetry composed in performance and built up by generations of singers. On this view there is no single author in the modern sense, and parts of the poem — Book 10, the night raid, has been suspected since ancient times — may be later additions to an older core.
criticalViews.counter: Whatever the tradition behind it, the poem's large design argues for one controlling intelligence. The mirroring of Books 1 and 24, the long foreshadowing of Patroclus's death from Book 11, and the passing of Achilles' armour from body to body are architecture, not accumulation.

essayQuestions.question: Is Achilles right to refuse Agamemnon's gifts in Book 9?
essayQuestions.focus: Honour, compensation and the limits of the heroic code
plan: Set out the offence in Book 1: honour in this poem is a prize won in public, so taking Briseis is a public stripping of status, not a private slight.

Weigh the offer. It is enormous, but Odysseus has quietly left out Agamemnon's demand that Achilles yield to him as the kinglier man, and Achilles' hatred of a man who 'hides another in his heart' may be a response to that.
Examine the argument of the refusal: if coward and hero are honoured alike, and life cannot be bought back, the whole exchange of risk for reward is exposed.
Count the cost. Phoenix's warning and Patroclus's reproach in Book 16 show others paying for Achilles' principle, and his own words in Book 18 admit the anger was a pleasure.
Conclude by comparing Book 24, where he accepts a ransom he could refuse. Consider whether the poem judges him wrong to refuse in Book 9, or wrong only in what he did next.

essayQuestions.question: How does the Iliad present the Trojans, and why might a Greek poem be so generous to its enemies?
essayQuestions.focus: Sympathy, perspective and the shape of the poem
plan: Begin with Book 6, where the poem goes inside Troy and shows Hector among the women of his family: something it never does for a Greek.

Consider Hector's flaws as well as his virtues — his overconfidence after Book 8, his rejection of Polydamas's advice, his flight round the walls — and argue that sympathy is not the same as idealisation.
Look at Priam and Helen on the wall in Book 3, and at the elders' refusal to blame her, as the poem's most humane judgements.
Examine Book 22 through the eyes of Hector's family, especially the bath prepared by Andromache.
Conclude with Book 24: the poem ends in Troy, with a Trojan funeral, and the last word goes to the defeated. Ask what an audience that knew the city's fate would take from that.

essayQuestions.question: What part do women play in a poem about men at war?
essayQuestions.focus: Prizes, captives and mourners
plan: Start with Chryseis and Briseis in Book 1: women as prizes whose transfer measures men's honour.
Turn to Helen weaving the battles in Book 3 and calling herself a theme of song in Book 6, as the one character aware of the story being made.
Read Andromache's scenes in Books 6 and 22 as a continuous argument about what war costs a household, including Hector's picture of her enslaved in Argos.
Use the captive women in Book 19, weeping 'each for her own sorrows', to show the narrator acknowledging a second, hidden war.
End with the three laments of Book 24 and consider whether giving the women the last word changes the meaning of the men's glory.

essayQuestions.question: How do the similes change the way we see the fighting?
essayQuestions.focus: Extended simile and the world beyond the battlefield
plan: Explain the form: a comparison developed into a small scene of its own, often drawn from farming, weather, hunting or family life.
Take Glaucus's leaves in Book 6 as a simile that turns a battlefield boast into a meditation on mortality.
Show how similes bring peacetime into war: the washing-troughs beside the springs in Book 22 and the scenes of harvest and dancing on the shield work in the same way.
Analyse the reversed simile in Book 24, where Priam is compared to a murderer seeking refuge, and link it to Patroclus's history.
Conclude that the similes are where the poem's sympathy is most visible, while noting that many similes also glorify the killer as a lion or a fire.

discussionQuestions: Achilles says he has no quarrel with the Trojans. If that is true, what is he fighting for, and what are the others fighting for?
Hector takes off his helmet for his son and then puts it back on. What would it have meant for him to stay inside the walls?
The narrator speaks directly to Patroclus as he goes to his death. How does that change your experience of the scene?
Zeus pities Hector, Sarpedon and even Achilles' horses, and saves none of them. What kind of gods does this poem believe in?
Is the meeting of Priam and Achilles in Book 24 a reconciliation, or only a pause before Troy burns?
The poem ends with Hector's funeral rather than the fall of Troy. Why stop there?

timeline.label: The traditional date for the fall of Troy
timeline.detail: Calculated centuries later by the Greek scholar Eratosthenes from the genealogies of legend. It is not a record, though it falls close to a destruction that archaeologists date to around 1180 BCE at Hisarlik. The poem foresees the fall and never narrates it.

timeline.label: The Iliad takes something like its present form
timeline.detail: A scholarly estimate: probably the second half of the eighth century BCE, perhaps a little later, and probably somewhat before the Odyssey. It grew out of generations of sung poetry about the war.

timeline.label: Alexander the Great at Troy
timeline.detail: Crossing into Asia, Alexander is said by his ancient biographers to have sacrificed at Ilium and honoured the tomb of Achilles, and to have carried a copy of the Iliad on campaign.

timeline.label: Virgil dies, leaving the Aeneid
timeline.detail: The second half of Rome's epic replays the Iliad in Italy, with a Trojan now in the invader's role and a local prince, Turnus, dying at the end as Hector did.

timeline.label: Homer printed for the first time
timeline.detail: The first printed edition of the Greek text of both epics appeared in Florence, edited by Demetrius Chalcondyles.

timeline.label: Chapman's Iliad completed
timeline.detail: George Chapman published seven books of the Iliad in 1598 and the whole poem in English verse around 1611. It is the translation Keats would read two centuries later.

timeline.label: Pope's Iliad completed
timeline.detail: Alexander Pope's version in heroic couplets appeared in six volumes from 1715 and made his fortune. For a century it was the Iliad most English readers knew.

timeline.label: Keats's sonnet on Chapman's Homer
timeline.detail: 'On First Looking into Chapman's Homer', written in October 1816, compares first reading Homer in Chapman's English to sighting a new planet or an unknown ocean.

timeline.label: Samuel Butler born
timeline.detail: The translator was born at Langar in Nottinghamshire, a clergyman's son. Before he turned to Homer he farmed sheep in New Zealand, painted, wrote the satire Erewhon and argued in print against Darwin's account of evolution.

timeline.label: Schliemann digs at Hisarlik
timeline.detail: Heinrich Schliemann began large-scale excavation of the mound that Frank Calvert, who owned part of it, had already identified as Troy. The site holds many cities one above another, and which of them, if any, is Homer's is still argued.

timeline.label: Butler's prose Iliad published
timeline.detail: Rendered, as the title page says, 'for the use of those who cannot read the original', in the plain prose of Butler's own day. His Odyssey followed in 1900, and he died in 1902.

timeline.label: Troy in the Hittite archives?
timeline.detail: In the mid-1920s scholars reading Hittite diplomatic texts proposed that Wilusa, a kingdom in western Anatolia, was Homer's Ilios, and that its ruler Alaksandu bore the name Alexandros — Paris's other name. The identification is widely accepted; what it proves about a Trojan war is not.

timeline.label: Milman Parry's study of the Homeric epithet
timeline.detail: Parry showed that phrases like 'Hector tamer of horses' form a system fitted to the metre, of the kind a poet composing aloud would need. Fieldwork among singers in Yugoslavia in the 1930s supported the case that Homeric verse grew out of oral performance.

places.name: Troy (Hisarlik)
places.note: The mound at Hisarlik in north-west Turkey, generally accepted as the site of Troy, a city rebuilt layer upon layer over more than three thousand years. The poem rarely goes inside the walls, but when it does — to Priam's palace, to the Scaean gate — it is the only city we are shown from within.

places.name: The Hellespont (Dardanelles)
places.note: The strait between Europe and Asia, a few miles from Troy. The Greek ships are drawn up on the shore near its mouth; Achilles threatens to be rowing out on it by morning in Book 9, and Hector pictures a champion's barrow beside it in Book 7.

places.name: Mount Ida (Kaz Dağı)
places.note: The mountain range south-east of Troy, 'many-fountained Ida' in Butler. Zeus watches the battle from its highest peak, Gargarus, and it is there that Hera lulls him to sleep in Book 14.

places.name: Samothrace
places.note: The mountainous island in the northern Aegean from whose heights Poseidon watches the battle in Book 13 — a seat from which, the poem says, he could see Ida, Priam's city and the Greek ships.

places.name: Lemnos
places.note: The island where Hephaestus landed when Zeus threw him out of heaven, as he tells it in Book 1, and where Achilles sold Lycaon before meeting him again at the river in Book 21. Ships from Lemnos bring wine to the Greek camp.

places.name: Mycenae
places.note: Agamemnon's citadel in the Argolid, 'the strong city of Mycenae' in the catalogue of ships. Schliemann dug there in 1876; the gold from its shaft graves is centuries older than any date proposed for a Trojan war.

places.name: Xanthos (Lycia)
places.note: The ancient city on the Lycian river Xanthus in south-west Turkey. Sarpedon and Glaucus lead the Lycians 'by the eddying waters of the Xanthus', and the estate Sarpedon describes in Book 12 lies on its banks — not to be confused with Troy's own river, which the gods also call Xanthus.

related.why: The sequel about getting home, in the same Butler translation. Its hero is the Iliad's best speaker, and in its Book 11 the ghost of Achilles takes back the choice he made in Book 9.
A close reading of the scene at the Scaean gate, where Hector's son is frightened by his father's helmet.
Virgil's reply from the Trojan side: a survivor of the fall whose second six books refight the Iliad in Italy.
Shakespeare's version of the same war and the same men — Achilles sulking, Hector chivalrous, Helen barely worth it — seen with none of Homer's reverence.
Marlowe's Faustus addresses the face that launched the thousand ships, the Helen the Trojan elders thought worth the war and wanted sent home.

books.title: The Importance of Being Earnest
books.author: Oscar Wilde
books.setting: A flat in Half-Moon Street, Mayfair, and the garden and drawing room of a manor house at Woolton, Hertfordshire
books.lengthNote: Three acts of continuous prose dialogue, reduced by Wilde from an earlier four-act version
books.openingLine: Did you hear what I was playing, Lane?
books.summary: Two young men have each invented a person who does not exist in order to get out of obligations, and both find themselves engaged to women who will only marry a man called Ernest. Wilde builds a farce in which the plot is entirely conventional and the sentences are not: every line of feeling arrives inverted, and the discovery that resolves everything is produced out of a hand-bag left in a railway cloakroom.
books.referenceStyle: act. The play is continuous prose dialogue and the text checked against carries no line numbers, so quotations are placed by act and by the point in the action they belong to.

sourceText.label: Standard Ebooks text of The Importance of Being Earnest
sourceText.note: The three-act text, following the first book edition of 1899. Because it is prose without line numbering, references give the act alone.

structure.label: Act I
structure.title: Half-Moon Street: a cigarette case and an interview
structure.summary: Algernon produces an inscribed cigarette case and forces Jack to confess that he is Jack in the country and Ernest in town. Gwendolen accepts a proposal on the strength of a name, and her mother interviews the candidate, finds his origins to be a railway cloakroom, and refuses.

scenes.summary: Lane and the cucumber sandwiches; Algernon extracts the truth about Cecily and the double life.
Jack's imaginary brother is matched against Algernon's imaginary invalid.
Gwendolen announces that her ideal has always been to love a man called Ernest, and Jack proposes on his knees.
Lady Bracknell's examination of income, politics, property and parentage ends at the hand-bag.

structure.label: Act II
structure.title: The garden at Woolton: two Ernests at once
structure.summary: Algernon arrives in the country as the wicked brother and is engaged to Cecily inside half an hour, having been engaged to her in her diary for months already. Jack comes home in mourning for a brother who is standing on the lawn, and the two women meet over tea and discover they are engaged to the same name.

scenes.summary: Miss Prism, Dr Chasuble and a chapter on the Fall of the Rupee that may be omitted.
Algernon presents himself as Jack's brother and Cecily produces the record of their engagement.
Jack returns in black to announce a death that contradicts the guest in the garden.
Gwendolen and Cecily compare diaries, sugar and cake, and conclude they have both been deceived.
Both men book the same clergyman for the same afternoon and the same name.

structure.label: Act III
structure.title: The drawing room: a hand-bag, and a christening cancelled
structure.summary: Lady Bracknell arrives, approves of Cecily's money and forbids Algernon's engagement until Jack forbids Cecily's, at which point Miss Prism is recognised, the hand-bag is produced and Jack turns out to be Algernon's elder brother. His father's name is looked up in an Army List and is, inevitably, Ernest.

scenes.summary: Lady Bracknell's objections to Cecily evaporate on hearing the figure in the Funds.
Jack refuses consent for Cecily until his own engagement is allowed.
A governess, a perambulator, a three-volume novel and a hand-bag left at Victoria Station.
Jack's real name is found in print, and the title of the play is spoken as its last line.

characters.name: John Worthing, J.P.
characters.role: A country landowner and magistrate, Cecily's guardian
characters.summary: He maintains a wicked younger brother in town so that he can be respectable in Hertfordshire, and takes the high moral tone in the country because he has invented somewhere else to be immoral. He is the only character who wants a settled identity, and the plot hands him one he has been using by accident for years.
characters.clue: He was found in a hand-bag at a railway cloakroom, is a magistrate in one county and a scoundrel in another, and turns out to have been telling the truth all along.

relationships.label: friend of, and unknowingly brother to

characters.name: Algernon Moncrieff
characters.role: Lady Bracknell's nephew, of Half-Moon Street
characters.summary: He eats continuously, owes money everywhere, and has invented a permanently ill friend whose relapses can be timed to avoid any dinner he does not want. He is the play's theorist, supplying most of its paradoxes, and the only person in it who is entirely unembarrassed by his own behaviour.
characters.clue: He keeps an invalid friend whose health fails precisely when a family dinner is proposed, and eats every muffin in the dish while a crisis is going on.

relationships.label: friend and, it emerges, brother of

characters.name: Hon. Gwendolen Fairfax
characters.role: Lady Bracknell's daughter
characters.summary: She speaks in her mother's cadences about entirely different things, and she has settled the question of whom she will marry before meeting anyone: it must be a man called Ernest. Her certainty is unshakeable and her reasoning is decorative, which makes her a comic character and also, in the tea scene, a formidable one.
characters.clue: She will only marry a man with one particular name, and travels with a diary so that she always has something sensational to read.

characters.name: Cecily Cardew
characters.role: Jack's ward, at the Manor House
characters.summary: She has been conducting an engagement to a man she has never met for three months in a diary, including the letters he wrote her and the week they were broken off. Wilde gives the country ingenue the most thoroughly fictional inner life in the play, and it is entirely in writing.
characters.clue: She waters roses to avoid German grammar and has already recorded, in her diary, the proposal she is about to receive.

characters.name: Lady Bracknell
characters.role: Gwendolen's mother, Algernon's aunt
characters.summary: She conducts marriage as a matter of lists, incomes and addresses, and delivers her most outrageous positions in the tone of settled common sense. She was herself without fortune when she married, which she mentions once, and that single admission is the crack in an otherwise seamless piece of masonry.
characters.clue: She keeps a list of eligible young men, disapproves of education on the grounds that ignorance is a delicate fruit, and changes her mind about a girl the moment she hears the figure.

characters.name: Miss Prism
characters.role: Cecily's governess
characters.summary: She wrote a three-volume novel of more than usually revolting sentimentality, mislaid it in a perambulator and deposited the baby in a hand-bag at Victoria Station. The play's entire machinery of discovery rests on a woman who has spent two acts recommending moral fiction and disapproving of everybody.
characters.clue: She once put a manuscript where a baby should have been, and has been giving German lessons ever since.

characters.name: Rev. Canon Chasuble, D.D.
characters.role: Rector of the parish
characters.summary: He has a sermon adaptable to almost any occasion, joyful or distressing, and is prepared to christen two grown men in one afternoon. His courtship of Miss Prism proceeds entirely in metaphors about bees and education, and neither party ever says anything directly until the last minute of the play.
characters.clue: He has one sermon he has preached at harvest celebrations, christenings, confirmations and days of humiliation, and is prepared to baptise two grown men in one afternoon.

characters.name: Lane
characters.role: Algernon's manservant
characters.summary: He drinks the champagne, keeps the accounts of the cucumber sandwiches and declines to have opinions in a way that is itself an opinion. His handful of lines are placed where they will deflate his employer's, and they do it without ever ceasing to be perfectly correct.
characters.clue: He did not think it polite to listen to the piano, and explains that in married households the champagne is rarely of a first-rate brand.

themes.name: Earnestness and triviality
themes.summary: The play takes the highest Victorian virtue and reduces it to a name that can be acquired at a christening for half a crown. Nobody in it is sincere and nobody suffers for that; the characters who talk most about duty, morality and improving literature are the ones caught out, and the ones who admit to inventing their lives get what they want.
themes.development: Jack adopts a high moral tone in Act I because he has somewhere else to misbehave; by the last line the word earnest has been converted into a proper noun and a joke.

themes.name: Names and identity
themes.summary: Two women will marry a name rather than a man, and two men undertake to be rechristened to supply it. Jack's search for his parents is, in the end, a search for an entry in a printed list, and the play's happy ending consists of a fact being looked up in the Army Lists rather than felt.
themes.development: A name invented in Act I, promised to two women in Act II, and finally discovered to have been legally correct from the start in Act III.

themes.name: Marriage as a transaction
themes.summary: Lady Bracknell conducts courtship as due diligence: income, investments, town address, politics, parentage. Wilde's joke is not that she is wrong about how it works but that she says so out loud, and her objections to Cecily disappear the instant a number is mentioned.
themes.development: A list of eligible young men in Act I, a valuation of a Hertfordshire estate, and an about-turn in Act III on the strength of a figure in the Funds.

themes.name: Town and country, and the double life
themes.canonicalName: Town and country, and the double life
themes.summary: Bunburying is the play's word for the arrangement that lets a respectable life continue: a place where one is not, and a person one is not, held in reserve. The comedy's geography is moral, and the two halves have to be kept from meeting, which is exactly what Act II arranges.
themes.development: Two invented people in Act I, both physically present in Act II, and both killed off before the christenings can be booked.

themes.name: Diaries, letters and the written record
themes.canonicalName: Diaries, letters and the written record
themes.summary: Nearly every fact in the play is documented before it happens. Cecily's engagement exists in her diary, Gwendolen carries hers for the sensational reading, Miss Prism's novel is lost in a perambulator and Jack's name is confirmed by the Army Lists. Writing here does not record events; it creates them.
themes.development: An inscription inside a cigarette case in Act I, two diaries in conflict in Act II, and a shelf of Army Lists settling the plot in Act III.

themes.name: Servants, food and appetite
themes.summary: Cucumber sandwiches, bread and butter, muffins, tea and sugar are the currency of every quarrel, and the servants keep the accounts. Emotional crises in this play are conducted over plates, and Wilde uses eating as the only honest appetite anybody displays.
themes.development: Sandwiches ordered for an aunt and eaten before she arrives in Act I, sugar and cake used as weapons in Act II, and muffins consumed during the collapse of both engagements.

techniques.name: Epigram
techniques.definition: A short balanced sentence that sounds like settled wisdom and usually turns a received idea inside out.
techniques.bookDefinition: A short, polished statement that sounds like settled wisdom.
techniques.inThisBook: Wilde gives the epigrams to the characters least entitled to them, so that a manservant, an idler and a snob all speak with the authority of a proverb.

techniques.name: Inversion
techniques.definition: Reversing a received sentiment so that the expected term ends up in the wrong place.
techniques.bookDefinition: Reversing a received sentiment so that the expected term ends up in the wrong place.
techniques.inThisBook: Divorces made in heaven, three being company in marriage, style mattering more than sincerity: the form is always a maxim and the content is always its opposite.

techniques.name: Bathos
techniques.definition: A sentence that descends abruptly from the elevated to the trivial.
techniques.bookDefinition: A sentence that descends abruptly from the elevated to the trivial.
techniques.inThisBook: Lady Bracknell moves from the excesses of the French Revolution to a cloakroom at a railway station, and the drop is the joke.

techniques.name: Farce structure
techniques.definition: Symmetrical plotting in which two of everything collide.
techniques.bookDefinition: Symmetrical plotting in which two of everything collide.
techniques.inThisBook: Two invented people, two men called Ernest, two engagements, two christenings booked with one clergyman for the same afternoon, and one hand-bag to undo it all.

techniques.name: The stage property
techniques.definition: An object handled on stage that carries far more weight than its use in the scene explains.
techniques.bookDefinition: An object that carries the plot rather than decorating it.
techniques.inThisBook: The inscribed cigarette case exposes Jack, the diaries authorise both engagements, and the hand-bag delivers the recognition scene.

techniques.name: The deflating servant
techniques.definition: A subordinate whose brief, correct replies undercut the speaker above them.
techniques.bookDefinition: A subordinate whose brief, correct replies undercut the speaker above them.
techniques.inThisBook: Lane's refusal to have listened to the piano, and his account of married households and champagne, set the play's tone before Jack has entered.

quotations.text: I didn’t think it polite to listen, sir.
quotations.speaker: Lane
quotations.context: Answering Algernon's question about the piano, in the play's fourth line.
quotations.analysis: The servant declines to have heard something everyone in the theatre has just heard, and does it by appealing to manners rather than to fact. Within four lines Wilde has established the rule the whole play runs on: politeness is a technique for not knowing things.

quotations.text: The truth is rarely pure and never simple.
quotations.speaker: Algernon
quotations.context: Pressing Jack to admit that Cecily exists.
quotations.analysis: The line is an epigram in defence of an interrogation, which is a peculiar use for it. Wilde puts the play's most quotable statement about truth in the mouth of the man currently telling the fewest lies, and follows it immediately with a joke about modern literature.

quotations.text: Divorces are made in Heaven
quotations.speaker: Algernon
quotations.context: On marriage, moments before defending the cucumber sandwiches.
quotations.analysis: One word is swapped in a proverb and the sentiment is reversed without a syllable of argument. The line is also interrupted mid-breath by Algernon stopping Jack taking a sandwich, so that the epigram and the appetite share a sentence.

quotations.text: You have invented a very useful younger brother called Ernest, in order that you may be able to come up to town as often as you like. I have invented an invaluable permanent invalid called Bunbury, in order that I may be able to go down into the country whenever I choose.
quotations.speaker: Algernon
quotations.context: Naming Jack's deception and matching it with his own.
quotations.analysis: The two fictions are laid out in parallel clauses, and the symmetry is the play's architecture in advance: town and country, brother and invalid, each man needing somewhere he is not. Note that both inventions are described as useful, which is the only virtue either man claims for them.

quotations.text: You don’t seem to realise, that in married life three is company and two is none.
quotations.speaker: Algernon
quotations.context: Warning Jack that a married man will need Bunbury.
quotations.analysis: Two is company, three is none goes in and comes out reversed, so that adultery is described in the vocabulary of good manners. It is also a plot prediction: by Act II there are indeed three people in each engagement, and one of them does not exist.

quotations.text: I hate people who are not serious about meals. It is so shallow of them.
quotations.speaker: Algernon
quotations.context: Interrupting a discussion of the evening's arrangements.
quotations.analysis: Seriousness, the quality the whole play is named for, is transferred to dinner, and shallowness becomes a charge against people who are not hungry. The joke works because Algernon means it entirely: his appetite is the one sincere thing in the comedy.

quotations.text: The fact is constantly mentioned in the more expensive monthly magazines, and has reached the provincial pulpits, I am told; and my ideal has always been to love someone of the name of Ernest. There is something in that name that inspires absolute confidence.
quotations.speaker: Gwendolen
quotations.context: Explaining to Jack, before he has proposed, why she has decided to love him.
quotations.analysis: Her ideal is not a man but a set of syllables, and she supports it with the monthly magazines and the provincial pulpits, as though it were a matter of public opinion. Everything Jack has invented to make himself free has turned out to be the one condition he cannot meet.

quotations.text: To lose one parent, Mr. Worthing, may be regarded as a misfortune; to lose both looks like carelessness.
quotations.speaker: Lady Bracknell
quotations.context: During the interview, on learning that Jack has lost both his parents.
quotations.analysis: Bereavement is reclassified as a lapse of organisation, and the balance of the sentence, misfortune against carelessness, does the reclassifying without an argument. It is the clearest example in the play of Wilde giving a monstrous position the rhythm of common sense.

quotations.text: A handbag?
quotations.speaker: Lady Bracknell
quotations.context: On being told where Jack was found as a baby.
quotations.analysis: Two words, and they are the most famous in the English comic theatre because the actor has to decide the entire character on them. The line is a question that is not asking for information; it is a whole social order failing to accommodate a piece of luggage.

quotations.text: I do not approve of anything that tampers with natural ignorance. Ignorance is like a delicate exotic fruit; touch it and the bloom is gone.
quotations.speaker: Lady Bracknell
quotations.context: On being told that Jack knows nothing.
quotations.analysis: Ignorance is given the vocabulary of horticulture and the protection usually reserved for virtue. The sentence that follows extends the compliment to English education on the grounds that it produces no effect whatsoever, which is Wilde attacking his own class from inside its drawing room.

quotations.text: What between the duties expected of one during one’s lifetime, and the duties exacted from one after one’s death, land has ceased to be either a profit or a pleasure. It gives one position, and prevents one from keeping it up. That’s all that can be said about land.
quotations.speaker: Lady Bracknell
quotations.context: Assessing Jack's Hertfordshire estate during the interview.
quotations.analysis: This is the play's one piece of genuine economics, spoken by its least reflective character: agricultural land in the 1890s really had stopped paying, and estates really were maintained for the position they conferred. The joke is that she states the whole agricultural depression as a social inconvenience.

quotations.text: Cecily, you will read your Political Economy in my absence. The chapter on the Fall of the Rupee you may omit. It is somewhat too sensational. Even these metallic problems have their melodramatic side.
quotations.speaker: Miss Prism
quotations.context: Leaving Cecily to her lessons while she walks with Dr Chasuble.
quotations.analysis: The collapse of the rupee had ruined real fortunes and salaries across the Empire, which is precisely why it is too sensational for a schoolroom. Wilde's governess protects her pupil from the one subject in the curriculum that describes the world she actually lives in.

quotations.text: The good ended happily, and the bad unhappily. That is what Fiction means.
quotations.speaker: Miss Prism
quotations.context: Describing the three-volume novel she once wrote.
quotations.analysis: A whole theory of the improving Victorian novel in fourteen words, delivered by the woman whose own carelessness with a perambulator will supply this play's ending. The capital letter on Fiction is doing the work: she is defining a genre, not describing a book.

quotations.text: I hope you have not been leading a double life, pretending to be wicked and being really good all the time. That would be hypocrisy.
quotations.speaker: Cecily
quotations.context: To Algernon, who is at that moment leading a double life in the other direction.
quotations.analysis: Hypocrisy is redefined as the pretence of wickedness, which inverts the standard Victorian charge exactly. Cecily is right about the double life and wrong about which way round it runs, and the audience is the only party in the garden that knows both halves.

quotations.text: You must not laugh at me, darling, but it had always been a girlish dream of mine to love someone whose name was Ernest.
quotations.speaker: Cecily
quotations.context: Accepting Algernon while explaining the condition she has always attached.
quotations.analysis: The second woman arrives at the identical requirement independently, and Wilde makes no attempt to explain the coincidence because the play is not interested in psychology. The effect is to turn a private preference into something more like a law of nature.

quotations.text: I never travel without my diary. One should always have something sensational to read in the train.
quotations.speaker: Gwendolen
quotations.context: Producing documentary evidence during the tea-table confrontation with Cecily.
quotations.analysis: The diary is introduced as proof and described as entertainment in consecutive sentences, which tells the audience exactly how much the evidence is worth. Both women are now arguing from written records of events that never happened.

quotations.text: This is no time for wearing the shallow mask of manners. When I see a spade I call it a spade.
quotations.speaker: Cecily
quotations.context: At the height of the tea-table quarrel with Gwendolen.
quotations.analysis: The country girl claims plain speaking as a virtue, in a sentence that is itself a cliche about not using cliches. Gwendolen's reply, that she is glad to say she has never seen a spade, turns the claim into a statement about class within two lines.

quotations.text: I am glad to say that I have never seen a spade. It is obvious that our social spheres have been widely different.
quotations.speaker: Gwendolen
quotations.context: Answering Cecily, marked in the text as spoken satirically.
quotations.analysis: She takes a dead metaphor completely literally and converts it into evidence of rank, which is the fastest piece of social violence in the play. The second sentence is delivered as a neutral observation, and that flatness is what makes it cut.

quotations.text: In matters of grave importance, style, not sincerity is the vital thing.
quotations.speaker: Gwendolen
quotations.context: Agreeing with Cecily on how to receive the men's explanations.
quotations.analysis: This is the play's own defence, stated by a character as a rule of etiquette. It also inverts the usual hierarchy under which sincerity excuses a clumsy apology, and it arrives just before both women accept explanations they know to be worthless.

quotations.text: Never speak disrespectfully of Society, Algernon. Only people who can’t get into it do that.
quotations.speaker: Lady Bracknell
quotations.context: Rebuking her nephew during the negotiation over Cecily.
quotations.analysis: The defence of Society is conducted entirely by sneering at outsiders, which concedes the criticism while appearing to refuse it. Wilde, who was about to be put outside it himself, gives the line to the character with the most to lose from anyone examining the claim.

quotations.text: On the contrary, Aunt Augusta, I’ve now realised for the first time in my life the vital Importance of Being Earnest.
quotations.speaker: Jack
quotations.context: The last line of the play, answering the charge that he has been trivial.
quotations.analysis: The title arrives as a pun that has taken three acts to load: the quality and the name have become the same word, and the discovery that resolves everything is a matter of spelling. Wilde ends a comedy about sincerity by proving that the hero was accurate all along, and entirely by accident.

atAGlance.label: First performed
atAGlance.note: At the St James's Theatre, London, managed by George Alexander, who played Jack.

atAGlance.label: First book edition
atAGlance.note: Published by Leonard Smithers; the title page names the author through Lady Windermere's Fan rather than printing his name.

atAGlance.label: Subtitle
atAGlance.value: A Trivial Comedy for Serious People
atAGlance.note: The joke is the arrangement: triviality is the discipline, seriousness the affliction.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.note: Cut down from a four-act draft, which removed an entire subplot about a solicitor come to arrest Ernest for unpaid dinners.

criticalViews.position: A perfect farce and nothing more
criticalViews.summary: The oldest account, and Wilde's own framing in the subtitle: a comedy whose subject is its own construction, where the plotting is symmetrical, the dialogue is polished and the pleasure is entirely formal.
criticalViews.counter: It has to ignore how much of the laughter comes from money, rank and the machinery of a marriage market that the play describes with considerable accuracy.

criticalViews.position: A comedy about the double life
criticalViews.summary: Criticism since the middle of the twentieth century has read Bunburying as a figure for lives lived in two places at once, written months before Wilde's own prosecution made the arrangement a matter of public record.
criticalViews.counter: Read too directly, it turns a play whose whole method is surface into a coded confession, which is the one thing its style refuses to be.

criticalViews.position: A satire of the late-Victorian ruling class
criticalViews.summary: Lady Bracknell's interview, the agricultural depression, the Funds, the London season and the servants' commentary place the comedy precisely in a class whose income and confidence were both under pressure in the 1890s.
criticalViews.counter: The satire is affectionate enough to be enjoyed by its targets, and the play ends by rewarding everyone in it with money and a title.

essayQuestions.question: How does Wilde use the idea of earnestness in the play?
essayQuestions.focus: The title, the name and the Victorian virtue
plan: Separate the two senses at once: the moral quality and the proper noun, and show how the play keeps them colliding.
Use Jack's high moral tone in Act I, adopted precisely so that he can misbehave elsewhere.
Examine the two women's requirement that a husband be called Ernest, and the fact that neither offers a reason.
Set the christenings against the discovery in the Army Lists: one is a decision, the other a fact.
Close on the last line and decide what Wilde has proved about sincerity by making it a question of spelling.

essayQuestions.question: Discuss Lady Bracknell's function in the comedy.
essayQuestions.focus: Authority, money and the sound of common sense
plan: Analyse the interview in Act I as a procedure: income, investments, address, politics, parentage, in that order.
Show how Wilde gives outrageous positions the cadence of settled wisdom, using the lines on ignorance and on land.
Note the single admission that she married without a fortune, and what it does to her authority.
Track the reversal in Act III when Cecily's money is mentioned, and how quickly the objections dissolve.
Assess whether she is a satirical target, a comic engine, or the only character who tells the truth about the system.

essayQuestions.question: What part do written documents play in the plot?
essayQuestions.focus: Diaries, inscriptions, novels and lists
plan: Start with the cigarette case, whose inscription begins the exposure of Jack's arrangement.
Compare Cecily's diary, which records an engagement that has not happened, with Gwendolen's, which is carried for entertainment.
Consider Miss Prism's three-volume novel and the perambulator, the play's most consequential piece of writing.
Examine the Army Lists as the instrument of resolution, and what it means that a fact is settled by looking it up.
Conclude on the pattern: in this play writing does not record events, it authorises them.

essayQuestions.question: 'A play in which nobody is sincere and nobody suffers for it.' Discuss.
essayQuestions.focus: Morality, consequence and the shape of the ending
plan: List the deceptions in play by the end of Act II and note that none of them is punished.
Contrast the characters who preach improvement, Miss Prism and Chasuble, with those who admit to invention.
Test the statement against Lady Bracknell, who is never deceived and never apologises for anything.
Weigh the ending: two marriages, a fortune, a brother and a name, all delivered by coincidence.
Decide whether the absence of consequence is a moral evasion or the precise point of the form.

discussionQuestions: Both women insist on marrying a man called Ernest, and neither will say why. Does the play want us to find a reason?
Algernon eats through every crisis in the play. What does his appetite do that his epigrams cannot?
Lady Bracknell says the most outrageous things in the calmest voice. Is she a monster, or simply the only character stating the terms out loud?
The plot is resolved by a hand-bag and a shelf of Army Lists. Is that a weakness in the play or the whole joke?
Lane speaks about a dozen lines. Why does Wilde open the play with him rather than with Algernon?

timeline.label: Oscar Wilde born in Dublin
timeline.detail: Educated at Trinity College Dublin and Magdalen College, Oxford.

timeline.label: The Picture of Dorian Gray published in book form
timeline.detail: Expanded from the magazine version of the previous year, with a preface answering its critics.

timeline.label: Lady Windermere's Fan opens at the St James's Theatre
timeline.detail: The first of the society comedies, and the play the title page of the 1899 Earnest uses to identify its author.

timeline.label: A Woman of No Importance opens
timeline.detail: The second society comedy, at the Haymarket.

timeline.label: Earnest written, largely at Worthing
timeline.detail: Wilde took a house on the Sussex coast with his family for the late summer; the hero's surname comes from the town.

timeline.detail: For a few weeks in early 1895 Wilde had two plays running in the West End at once.

timeline.detail: At the St James's Theatre, with George Alexander as Jack; the run ended within months when Wilde was tried and imprisoned.

timeline.detail: He left England for France and never returned.

places.name: Half-Moon Street, Mayfair
places.note: Algernon's flat, and the setting of the whole first act.

places.name: St James's Theatre, King Street
places.note: Where the play opened on 14 February 1895 under George Alexander's management; the building was demolished in 1957.

places.name: Victoria Station
places.note: The cloakroom where the hand-bag was deposited, on the Brighton line.

places.name: Worthing, West Sussex
places.note: Where Wilde wrote the play in the late summer of 1894, and where the hero got his surname.

places.name: Dublin
places.note: Wilde's birthplace and the city of his education before Oxford.

related.why: Wilde's novel of the same decade, with the same epigrams put to an entirely unfunny purpose.
The comic ancestor: two couples, a wit who will not admit to feeling, and a plot driven by what people are told rather than what is true.
The other great English comedy of income, property and a formidable older woman investigating a marriage.
Assumed identities, mistaken names and a resolution that arrives when two people who look alike are finally in the same room.
The same 1890s society viewed from several rungs down, and also told through a diary that its keeper takes very seriously.

books.title: The Merchant of Venice
books.author: William Shakespeare
books.setting: Venice — the Rialto, a private house, a court of justice — and Belmont, a country estate a day's journey away
books.lengthNote: Around 2,600 lines, of which the trial takes nearly four hundred
books.openingLine: In sooth, I know not why I am so sad:
books.summary: A merchant borrows money he does not need, on terms he thinks are a joke, so that a friend can go courting. The comedy that follows has a courtroom at its centre, and the clever rescue there is also a confiscation: Shylock loses his money, his profession and his religion in the space of forty lines, and the play then moves to a moonlit garden and refuses to mention him again.

sourceText.label: Globe/Moby text of The Merchant of Venice
sourceText.note: Line numbers follow the traditional Globe numbering, which counts the prose scenes continuously. Modern editions vary.

structure.label: Act I
structure.title: A sad merchant, a locked test, and a bond made in jest
structure.summary: Antonio cannot say why he is unhappy. Bassanio needs money to court an heiress whose father has left her unable to choose her own husband, and Shylock lends it on a forfeit of a pound of flesh — proposed, and accepted, as a piece of friendly humour by men who have just insulted each other.

scenes.title: The Rialto
scenes.summary: Antonio's friends try to explain his melancholy; Bassanio asks for a further loan to go to Belmont.

scenes.title: The will of a dead father
scenes.summary: Portia reviews her suitors with Nerissa and complains of a lottery she cannot refuse.

scenes.title: The merry bond
scenes.summary: Shylock recalls years of public abuse, then lends interest-free against a pound of Antonio's flesh.

structure.label: Act II
structure.title: Two wrong caskets and a daughter gone
structure.summary: Morocco and Arragon choose gold and silver and are beaten by their own assumptions about worth. In Venice, Jessica leaves her father's house dressed as a boy, taking money and jewels with her, and the Christian gentlemen of the Rialto turn Shylock's public grief into a street entertainment.

scenes.title: Morocco arrives
scenes.summary: He asks not to be judged by his complexion and is told the terms of the lottery.

scenes.title: Launcelot changes master
scenes.summary: The clown argues with his own conscience and leaves Shylock for Bassanio.

scenes.title: Jessica's plan
scenes.summary: She calls her father's house hell and asks Launcelot to carry a letter to Lorenzo.

scenes.title: The masque
scenes.summary: Lorenzo learns what gold and jewels she will bring with her.

scenes.title: Locking up
scenes.summary: Shylock, going out to supper against his judgement, tells Jessica to shut the windows.

scenes.title: The elopement
scenes.summary: Jessica throws down a casket and escapes in boy's clothes, ashamed of the disguise.

scenes.title: Gold
scenes.summary: Morocco opens the golden casket and finds a skull and a rhyme about glittering.

scenes.title: Reported grief
scenes.summary: Salanio performs Shylock's cries about his daughter and his ducats for laughs.

scenes.title: Silver
scenes.summary: Arragon takes what he deserves and is handed the portrait of a blinking idiot.

structure.label: Act III
structure.title: Lead won, ships lost, and a speech about eyes
structure.summary: Bassanio rejects ornament, chooses lead and wins Portia within the hour. In the same act Shylock, taunted in the street about his daughter, answers with the play's most famous demand for common humanity and ends it by promising revenge. News arrives that Antonio's ships are gone.

scenes.title: On the Rialto
scenes.summary: Salarino and Salanio bait Shylock; Tubal brings news of Jessica's spending and of a wrecked argosy.

scenes.title: Lead
scenes.summary: Bassanio chooses correctly; the rings are given; a letter from Antonio interrupts the betrothal.

scenes.title: No more speaking
scenes.summary: Shylock refuses to hear Antonio and repeats that he will have his bond.

scenes.title: Padua
scenes.summary: Portia sends for legal papers from Doctor Bellario and tells Nerissa they will go disguised.

scenes.title: Salvation and bacon
scenes.summary: Launcelot jokes that converting Jews will raise the price of pork; Jessica changes the subject.

structure.label: Act IV
structure.title: The court, and what mercy turns out to mean
structure.summary: The longest scene in the play. Shylock refuses three times the money, Portia arrives disguised as a lawyer from Padua and preaches mercy, and then wins by reading the bond more strictly than its holder. Within forty lines Shylock has lost his estate, his livelihood and his religion.

scenes.title: The trial
scenes.summary: Mercy is argued, the bond is enforced to the letter, and an alien statute is produced against the plaintiff.

scenes.title: The rings
scenes.summary: Portia and Nerissa, still disguised, collect the rings their husbands swore never to part with.

structure.label: Act V
structure.title: Music at Belmont, and one man missing
structure.summary: Lorenzo and Jessica trade stories of lovers who came to bad ends, the wives expose the business of the rings, and Antonio learns that three of his ships are safe after all. Shylock is not mentioned. The comedy closes with everybody paired except the merchant it is named after.

scenes.title: Moonlight
scenes.summary: Music, the ring quarrel, the revelation of the disguise, and news that Antonio's argosies have come home.

characters.name: Shylock
characters.role: A Jewish moneylender of Venice
characters.summary: He appears in five scenes and dominates the play. Shakespeare gives him the abuse he has taken in detail — the spitting, the name-calling, the kicks — and then has him turn that history into a legal instrument. The play neither excuses what he does nor lets his enemies off the account he reads them.
characters.clue: He keeps a ledger of insults as exactly as one of debts, asks whether a dog has money, and leaves the stage saying he is not well.

characters.name: Portia
characters.role: An heiress of Belmont
characters.summary: Rich, quick and confined: her father's will means she may neither choose nor refuse. She takes the only freedom available by leaving Belmont in a man's gown, and the same intelligence that saves Antonio is later used to trap her own husband over a ring.
characters.clue: She may neither choose a husband nor refuse one, so she borrows a lawyer's gown from Padua and wins the biggest case in Venice.
traits: less merciful than her own speech

relationships.label: rescuer of, and rival for Bassanio
prosecutes in the guise of defending

characters.name: Antonio
characters.role: A merchant of Venice
characters.summary: The title character speaks the first line of the play and almost nothing in the last scene. His sadness is never explained; his willingness to die for Bassanio is stated plainly, and so is his intention to go on spitting on Shylock. He is the only major figure who ends the play unpaired.
characters.clue: He opens the play saying he does not know why he is sad, offers his own body as security for a friend's courtship, and ends it the only one without a partner.

characters.name: Bassanio
characters.role: A Venetian gentleman, Antonio's friend
characters.summary: He has run through his money and proposes to repair it by marrying a fortune, which he explains to Antonio without embarrassment. His casket speech rejects outward show in terms that apply uncomfortably well to his own courtship, financed by a borrowed appearance of wealth.
characters.clue: He argues that the world is deceived by ornament while wearing clothes bought with a friend's borrowed money.

characters.name: Jessica
characters.role: Shylock's daughter
characters.summary: She robs her father, sells her mother's ring for a monkey, and converts. Shakespeare gives her the discomfort as well as the escape: she is ashamed of her boy's clothes, and in the last act she and Lorenzo exchange a string of stories about lovers whose nights ended badly.
characters.clue: She leaves her father's house in a boy's coat with his ducats in a casket, and spends the last act naming lovers who came to grief.

characters.name: Lorenzo
characters.role: A friend of Bassanio and Antonio
characters.summary: He plans the elopement as a raid, is pleased about the gold, and then speaks the play's most beautiful verse about music and the harmony of the spheres. The distance between those two facts is one of the things the last act is for.
characters.clue: He organises a theft and an elopement in the same breath, and later explains that a man with no music in him is fit for treasons.

characters.name: Nerissa
characters.role: Portia's waiting-gentlewoman
characters.summary: She doubles Portia at every level: she gives the sceptical answer in 1.2, marries the friend rather than the principal, disguises herself as a clerk, and runs the same trick with the same ring. The play works by these pairings, and she is the clearest of them.
characters.clue: She dresses as a lawyer's clerk, marries the friend rather than the hero, and plays the ring trick a second time.

characters.name: Gratiano
characters.role: A friend of Bassanio
characters.summary: Bassanio says he speaks an infinite deal of nothing, and for three acts that is a joke about a harmless talker. In the courtroom he becomes the voice that cheers each reversal and asks for Shylock to be hanged, which is where the comic licence stops being comic.
characters.clue: A friend says he speaks an infinite deal of nothing; in court he applauds every turn of the verdict and offers the defeated man a free halter.

themes.name: Bonds and binding
themes.summary: The word runs through every plot in the play: a bond is a loan agreement, a tie of friendship, a marriage, a ring, and finally a piece of writing that can take a man's life. Venice runs on written obligation, and the tragedy is that Shylock is the only character who treats the writing as meaning exactly what it says.
themes.development: A bond is sealed in 1.3, tested in 4.1 and replaced in 5.1 by a ring — which is another bond, and also broken.

themes.name: Mercy and justice
themes.summary: Portia's argument is that mercy cannot be compelled, which is true, and she then compels Shylock into receiving it. The court offers him his life on condition that he give up his religion, and calls that leniency. The play stages the gap between the doctrine and the settlement enacted in its name.
themes.development: Mercy is preached at 4.1.191, refused by Shylock at 4.1.213, and delivered at 4.1.396 as a set of conditions including forced conversion.

themes.name: Antisemitism and the outsider
themes.summary: The Christians of Venice call Shylock dog, devil and cur to his face and in his absence, and Antonio says plainly that he will do it again. The play lets Shylock answer, at length and in prose, and then ends with his enemies in a garden and his name unmentioned.
themes.development: The abuse is itemised by its victim in 1.3, answered in 3.1, and given legal form in 4.1, where an alien is found to have no standing against a citizen.

themes.name: Worth, ornament and risk
themes.summary: Three caskets ask what a thing is worth; three suitors answer with what they think they deserve. The same question runs through the merchant plot, where ships are venture capital and a pound of flesh is valued, out loud, against mutton and beef.
themes.development: Morocco buys the outside, Arragon buys his own merit, Bassanio buys the risk — and the man who has hazarded everything has borrowed the stake.

themes.name: Friendship, marriage and rivalry
themes.summary: Antonio's feeling for Bassanio is the strongest attachment in the play and has no name available to it. Portia understands the competition exactly, which is why the ring she gives her husband is the one thing she makes him swear never to surrender, and why she has it taken from him in a courtroom.
themes.development: Antonio offers his body for Bassanio in Act I, is outbid in Act IV when Bassanio says he would give up his wife to save him, and is given a ring to return in Act V.

themes.name: Disguise and the law
themes.summary: Nothing in the trial scene is what it appears: the lawyer is a woman, the clerk is her maid, the mercy is a threat and the rescue is a confiscation. Belmont's women enter the Venetian court by the only door available to them and leave it having beaten the men at their own document.
themes.development: Jessica's boy's clothes in Act II rehearse the device; Portia's gown in Act IV makes it the machinery of the plot.

techniques.name: The legal quibble
techniques.definition: A judgment that turns on the exact words of a document rather than its evident intention.
techniques.bookDefinition: A judgment that turns on the exact words of a document rather than its evident intention.
techniques.inThisBook: Portia defeats the bond by noting that it grants flesh and says nothing of blood — a stricter reading than Shylock's own, delivered by someone who has just argued that strictness damns us all.

techniques.name: Parallel plotting
techniques.definition: A second story running beside the first, repeating its problem in another key and commenting on it.
techniques.bookDefinition: Two or more actions built on the same shape, so that each comments on the other.
techniques.inThisBook: The caskets, the bond and the rings are all tests in which a man must choose what to give up, and all three are set by someone with more control than he realises.

techniques.name: Prose against verse
techniques.definition: The shift between unmetered speech and blank verse as a marker of register, class or feeling.
techniques.bookDefinition: The shift between unmetered speech and blank verse as a marker of register, class or feeling.
techniques.inThisBook: Shylock's great answer to Salarino is in prose, which is what gives it the sound of a man speaking rather than performing; Portia's mercy speech is verse, and sounds like a set piece because it is one.

techniques.name: Accumulated rhetorical questions
techniques.definition: A run of questions whose answers are obvious, used to make denial impossible.
techniques.bookDefinition: A run of questions whose answers are obvious, used to make denial impossible.
techniques.inThisBook: Eyes, hands, organs, dimensions, senses, affections, passions: the questions pile up until the last one changes direction and asks about revenge instead of about bleeding.

techniques.name: Flesh and blood
techniques.definition: A physical image repeated until it binds unrelated scenes together.
techniques.bookDefinition: A physical image repeated until it binds unrelated scenes together.
techniques.inThisBook: The bond's pound of flesh is only the plainest instance; Shylock calls Jessica his own flesh and blood, and the court eventually divides his property along the same line between body and estate.

techniques.name: Scriptural argument
techniques.definition: Quoting or contesting scripture as a way of settling a dispute.
techniques.bookDefinition: Quoting or contesting scripture as a way of settling a dispute.
techniques.inThisBook: Shylock and Antonio argue over Jacob's sheep in 1.3, each claiming the Old Testament, and Portia's mercy speech borrows the language of the Lord's Prayer to address a man who does not say it.

quotations.text: In sooth, I know not why I am so sad:
quotations.speaker: Antonio
quotations.context: The opening line of the play, to Salarino and Salanio on the Rialto.
quotations.analysis: A comedy begins with a man announcing an unexplained depression, and the play never supplies the explanation — his friends propose his ships and then love, and he denies both. The refusal to account for it leaves a hole at the centre of the title role that every production has to fill with something.

quotations.text: so is the will of a living daughter curbed by the will of a dead father
quotations.speaker: Portia
quotations.context: In prose to Nerissa, listing the suitors she cannot refuse.
quotations.analysis: The sentence turns on one word used twice: 'will' as desire and 'will' as legal document. Portia's problem is stated as a pun, which is a warning about the kind of play this is — the trial in Act IV will also be won by a word that carries two meanings at once.

quotations.text: Still have I borne it with a patient shrug, For sufferance is the badge of all our tribe.
quotations.speaker: Shylock
quotations.context: Answering Antonio's request for a loan by recalling how Antonio has treated him.
quotations.analysis: A badge in Venice was not a metaphor: Jews were required to wear identifying marks, and Shylock takes that fact and makes endurance itself the uniform. The shrug is the detail that does the work — a small physical gesture, repeated over years, standing in for everything he has swallowed.

quotations.text: 'Hath a dog money? is it possible A cur can lend three thousand ducats?'
quotations.speaker: Shylock
quotations.context: Quoting back to Antonio the names Antonio has called him.
quotations.analysis: He performs the insult rather than complaining of it, putting Antonio's own vocabulary into a speech Antonio has to stand and listen to. Quotation marks are a weapon here: the abuse is returned intact, with the arithmetic of the loan sitting inside it.

quotations.text: I am as like to call thee so again, To spit on thee again, to spurn thee too.
quotations.speaker: Antonio
quotations.context: His reply, immediately before asking for the loan anyway.
quotations.analysis: He does not deny a word of the account; he promises to repeat it. The couplet is the reason the bond is not simply a piece of villainy — the borrower has just told the lender to his face that nothing will change, and then asks to be lent the money as to an enemy.

quotations.text: Give him direction for this merry bond,
quotations.speaker: Shylock
quotations.context: Sending Antonio to the notary to seal the agreement.
quotations.analysis: 'Merry' is doing a great deal of work, and nobody in the scene challenges it. The forfeit is framed as a joke between men who have just exchanged threats, which is exactly what allows Antonio to sign it: a penalty that cannot be meant does not need to be feared.

quotations.text: Hie thee, gentle Jew. The Hebrew will turn Christian: he grows kind.
quotations.speaker: Antonio
quotations.context: As Shylock leaves to fetch the ducats.
quotations.analysis: 'Gentle' and 'gentile' were near-homophones, so the compliment is also a joke about conversion — and the joke turns out to be a prophecy the court will enforce at knife-point in Act IV. Antonio can praise the man only by imagining him becoming someone else.

quotations.text: Our house is hell, and thou, a merry devil, Didst rob it of some taste of tediousness.
quotations.speaker: Jessica
quotations.context: Saying goodbye to Launcelot, who is leaving her father's service.
quotations.analysis: Her complaint is not cruelty but dullness — the house is hell because it is tedious, and the clown made it bearable. It is the only account the play gives of what living with Shylock was like, and it comes from someone about to rob him.

quotations.text: All that glitters is not gold; Often have you heard that told: Many a man his life hath sold But my outside to behold:
quotations.speaker: Morocco
quotations.context: Reading the scroll found inside the golden casket, beside a skull.
quotations.analysis: The verse is in short rhyming lines, a nursery metre for a lesson everybody claims to know already, and the casket answers in the first person as though the gold were speaking. Morocco has just argued himself into gold by reasoning about what the world values — the scroll's point is that he was reasoning at all.

quotations.text: 'My daughter! O my ducats! O my daughter! Fled with a Christian! O my Christian ducats!
quotations.speaker: Salanio
quotations.context: Salanio and Salarino imitating Shylock's behaviour in the street after Jessica's flight.
quotations.analysis: The audience never sees Shylock discover the loss; it is reported as an impersonation by a man doing the voice for a laugh. Whether the alternation of daughter and ducats is grief or greed depends entirely on how far you trust the reporter, and the play deliberately gives you no other witness.

quotations.text: I am a Jew. Hath not a Jew eyes? hath not a Jew hands, organs, dimensions, senses, affections, passions? fed with the same food, hurt with the same weapons, subject to the same diseases, healed by the same means, warmed and cooled by the same winter and summer, as a Christian is?
quotations.speaker: Shylock
quotations.context: In the street, to Salarino, who has just asked what a pound of flesh is good for.
quotations.analysis: The argument is built entirely on the body, not on doctrine, and the repetitions of 'the same' make the shared ground impossible to refuse. It is in prose, which is why it sounds like a man talking rather than a set speech, and its logic is deliberately unfinished — everything so far has been about suffering, and the next sentence will apply the same equality to revenge.

quotations.text: The villany you teach me, I will execute, and it shall go hard but I will better the instruction.
quotations.speaker: Shylock
quotations.context: The end of the same speech, after the questions about bleeding and laughing.
quotations.analysis: He claims to be a pupil, which puts the responsibility on the teachers and leaves him doing the thing anyway. 'Better the instruction' is the sentence's cold centre: he intends not merely to match Christian revenge but to improve on it, and the play holds him to that promise in the courtroom.

quotations.text: So may the outward shows be least themselves: The world is still deceived with ornament.
quotations.speaker: Bassanio
quotations.context: Deliberating in front of the three caskets at Belmont.
quotations.analysis: He wins by distrusting appearances, having arrived in Belmont on borrowed money precisely in order to look the part. 'Still' means always, and the line indicts a world Bassanio has been working rather successfully; the play lets him say the true thing without noticing that it applies to him.

quotations.text: Which is the merchant here, and which the Jew?
quotations.speaker: Portia
quotations.context: Her first words on entering the court in the gown of a doctor of laws.
quotations.analysis: The question establishes her impartiality and is also unanswerable by sight, which is the play's point about what Venice thinks it can see. She already knows which is which, so the line is a performance of neutrality by the one person in the room who has come to win.

quotations.text: The quality of mercy is not strain'd, It droppeth as the gentle rain from heaven Upon the place beneath: it is twice blest; It blesseth him that gives and him that takes:
quotations.speaker: Portia
quotations.context: Answering Shylock's question: on what compulsion must he be merciful?
quotations.analysis: The whole speech depends on mercy being uncompelled, which is a direct answer to the word 'compulsion' in Shylock's question. What follows in the scene contradicts it: the court will compel mercy out of Shylock at the price of his religion, and the word for what he receives will still be mercy.

quotations.text: My deeds upon my head! I crave the law,
quotations.speaker: Shylock
quotations.context: Refusing Portia's appeal and asking for judgment on the bond.
quotations.analysis: He takes the consequences onto himself in the words of a formula that Shakespeare's audience would have heard as an echo of the Gospel account of Christ's condemnation, and which was used for centuries to justify persecution. Giving Shylock that sentence is the harshest thing the play does to him, and he says it in the act of asking only for what he is owed.

quotations.text: Tarry a little; there is something else. This bond doth give thee here no jot of blood; The words expressly are 'a pound of flesh:'
quotations.speaker: Portia
quotations.context: Stopping Shylock as he prepares to cut.
quotations.analysis: She has let the case run to the point of the knife before producing the objection, which means the trap was set several hundred lines earlier. Her method is not mercy but a stricter literalism than Shylock's own: he asked for what the words say, and she gives him exactly that and no more.

quotations.text: Nay, take my life and all; pardon not that: You take my house when you do take the prop That doth sustain my house; you take my life When you do take the means whereby I live.
quotations.speaker: Shylock
