quotations.context: After the court has divided his estate and offered to commute the fine.
quotations.analysis: The repetition of 'take' four times in four lines turns the verdict into an inventory. He refuses the distinction the court is congratulating itself on — between killing a man and removing his livelihood — and the play gives him the argument without letting him win it.

quotations.text: Two things provided more, that, for this favour, He presently become a Christian;
quotations.speaker: Antonio
quotations.context: Stating his terms for giving up his half of Shylock's goods.
quotations.analysis: It is called a favour, and it is attached as a condition to a pardon Shylock cannot refuse. 'Presently' means at once: the man who has just been prevented from taking a pound of flesh is required to change religion on the spot, and the scene treats this as the merciful outcome.

quotations.text: I am content.
quotations.speaker: Shylock
quotations.context: Asked by Portia whether he accepts the court's terms.
quotations.analysis: Three words, and then four more lines asking to be allowed to leave because he is not well. Antonio had used the same phrase twelve lines earlier while dictating the terms, so the play puts the identical sentence in two mouths in one scene and lets the difference between them stand without comment.

quotations.text: How sweet the moonlight sleeps upon this bank! Here will we sit and let the sounds of music Creep in our ears:
quotations.speaker: Lorenzo
quotations.context: In the garden at Belmont with Jessica, waiting for Portia's return.
quotations.analysis: The last act opens by changing the weather completely: after four hundred lines of courtroom prose the play produces its most lyrical verse, and does it in the mouth of the man who organised the elopement and the theft. Shakespeare buys the comedy its ending with music, and the person who says she is never merry when she hears it is sitting next to him.

quotations.text: I am never merry when I hear sweet music.
quotations.speaker: Jessica
quotations.context: Her reply to Lorenzo's account of music's power over wild animals.
quotations.analysis: It is the last thing she says in the play. Lorenzo talks her out of it immediately, explaining that attentiveness only looks like sadness, and she does not answer — a silence that productions can play as agreement, exhaustion or something colder.

atAGlance.label: Written
atAGlance.note: Topical references and the style of the verse place composition in the later 1590s.

atAGlance.label: First printed
atAGlance.note: The First Quarto, which remains the basis of most modern editions.

atAGlance.label: Chief source
atAGlance.note: The bond, the trial and the disguised lady-lawyer come from a tale in Ser Giovanni Fiorentino's Italian collection.

atAGlance.label: At court
atAGlance.note: The first recorded performance was on 10 February 1605, and the play was repeated before the court two days later.

criticalViews.position: A romantic comedy with an obstacle
criticalViews.summary: On this reading the play's business is three marriages and a rescue, Shylock is the blocking figure whom comedy must remove, and Act V is the proper ending rather than an evasion.
criticalViews.counter: It requires the audience to accept a forced conversion as a happy outcome, and it cannot explain why Shakespeare gave the obstacle the best prose in the play.

criticalViews.position: A play whose antisemitism is its subject rather than its accident
criticalViews.summary: Much modern criticism argues that the Christians are shown behaving exactly as Shylock describes them — spitting, mocking, confiscating — so that the comedy is built to expose the society it flatters.
criticalViews.counter: The play still ends in that society's garden, with its victim offstage, and the text nowhere condemns what the court does.

criticalViews.position: A study of contract and obligation
criticalViews.summary: Bonds, wills, caskets and rings are all binding documents, and the play tests what happens when a written promise meets the intention behind it. The trial is then less about race than about how far a society will honour its own paperwork.
criticalViews.counter: The verdict turns on a statute about aliens, which makes Shylock's standing under Venetian law inseparable from his religion.

essayQuestions.question: How does Shakespeare present Shylock?
essayQuestions.focus: Sympathy, hostility and the limits of both
plan: Note first that he appears in only five scenes and never speaks after 4.1.412.
Use 1.3 to show him giving an itemised account of the abuse, and Antonio confirming every word of it.
Read 3.1 carefully: the questions establish common humanity, and the same logic then licenses revenge.
Set the reported grief of 2.8 against the direct speech of 4.1.388 and ask which the audience is allowed to trust.
Close on his exit line and on the fact that Act V does not mention him.

essayQuestions.question: 'Mercy in this play is something the powerful do to the powerless.' Discuss.
essayQuestions.focus: Justice, law and the trial scene
plan: Begin with Shylock's question at 4.1.190 — on what compulsion? — and show that Portia's speech is a direct answer to it.
Trace the reversal: mercy preached, refused, then imposed as a set of conditions at 4.1.394-404.
Examine the alien statute and what it says about who counts as a citizen of Venice.
Weigh Antonio's terms, including the conversion, against his conduct in 1.3.
Decide whether the play endorses the verdict, exposes it, or simply stages it and moves on.

essayQuestions.question: What is the function of Belmont?
essayQuestions.focus: Place, wealth and the structure of the play
plan: Set out the alternation: Venice for business and law, Belmont for music, riddles and marriage.
Show that Belmont is also governed by a document — a dead man's will — and so is less free than it looks.
Use the casket scenes to argue that the two worlds share one question: how do you value what you cannot see?
Note that Portia's money resolves nothing in Venice; it is her legal reading that wins.
Judge whether Act V restores Belmont or merely relocates the play's unfinished business.

essayQuestions.question: Discuss the presentation of women in The Merchant of Venice.
essayQuestions.focus: Portia, Nerissa, Jessica and the uses of disguise
plan: Start from the constraint: Portia cannot choose, Jessica is locked in, Nerissa marries where her mistress does.
Show disguise as the only available instrument — a boy's coat for one, a doctor's gown for another.
Read the trial as Portia acquiring, temporarily, a competence the play otherwise reserves for men.
Use the ring plot to argue that she brings the courtroom's methods home with her.
Ask what happens to that competence in Act V, when the gowns come off.

discussionQuestions: Antonio never explains his sadness. Should a production decide what it is?
Shylock's greatest speech ends by promising revenge. Does that ending change what the speech is worth?
Portia argues that mercy cannot be compelled, and then compels it. Is she a hypocrite, or is the court?
Jessica's last line is that she is never merry when she hears sweet music. What should she do for the rest of the scene?
The play is classed as a comedy. What would have to change for it to be a tragedy?

timeline.label: Il Pecorone reaches print
timeline.detail: Ser Giovanni Fiorentino's fourteenth-century collection contains the bond, the trial and the lady disguised as a lawyer.

timeline.label: Roderigo Lopez is executed in London
timeline.detail: The queen's Portuguese physician, of Jewish descent, was convicted of conspiracy; the trial fed a wave of public feeling in the years just before the play.

timeline.label: Entered in the Stationers' Register
timeline.detail: Registered to James Roberts as the Merchant of Venice, two years before it was printed.

timeline.label: First Quarto
timeline.detail: The earliest printed text, and the basis of most modern editions.

timeline.label: Performed at court
timeline.detail: The first recorded performance, on 10 February, with a repeat before the court two days later.

timeline.label: First Folio
timeline.detail: Printed among the comedies, following the quarto text closely.

timeline.label: Charles Macklin plays Shylock at Drury Lane
timeline.detail: He abandoned the comic red wig of the Restoration stage and played the part seriously, which changed the play's reputation.

timeline.label: Edmund Kean's London debut as Shylock
timeline.detail: A performance that made the moneylender a figure of tragic force rather than a stage villain.

timeline.label: Henry Irving's Shylock at the Lyceum
timeline.detail: Irving's dignified, sympathetic reading dominated the late Victorian stage and shaped expectations for decades.

timeline.label: Michael Radford's film
timeline.detail: A screen version set in a carefully reconstructed Venice, with Al Pacino as Shylock and an opening sequence about the ghetto.

places.name: Venice
places.note: The city of the bond, the street insults and the court of justice.

places.name: The Rialto
places.note: The commercial exchange where news of ships travels and where Antonio has abused Shylock in public.

places.name: Genoa
places.note: Where Tubal reports Jessica spending her father's ducats and trading her mother's ring.

places.name: Padua
places.note: Home of Doctor Bellario, whose legal opinion and borrowed credentials get Portia into the courtroom.

places.name: Tripoli
places.note: One of the ports named for Antonio's argosies, and the destination of the ship reported lost.

related.why: The other Venetian play, and the other outsider whom the city uses and then discards.
A comedy that also stops for a long argument about mercy and the letter of the law, and also ends in silence.
Another heroine who puts on a man's clothes, with the same interest in what a disguise makes possible.
The other great breeches role of these years, and a comic world built on the same device pushed in the opposite direction.
A comedy of the same period that turns for a whole act into something close to tragedy before recovering.

books.title: The Moonstone
books.author: Wilkie Collins
books.setting: Seringapatam in 1799, then a house on the Yorkshire coast and London in 1848–49, and finally Kattiawar in 1850
books.lengthNote: Around 195,000 words, written for thirty-two weekly instalments and divided among eleven separate narrators
books.openingLine: I address these lines⁠—written in India⁠—to my relatives in England.
books.summary: A diamond taken during the storming of Seringapatam arrives in a Yorkshire drawing room as a birthday present and vanishes the same night. Collins gives the case to eleven witnesses in turn, each writing to order and each certain of a different thing, so the mystery is solved less by a detective than by comparing accounts that do not fit. The solution turns on a dose of laudanum given without the patient’s knowledge, and the stone goes back to India.
books.referenceStyle: period and narrative, with the chapter where a narrative is divided

sourceText.label: Standard Ebooks text of The Moonstone
sourceText.note: A proofed transcription of Collins’s text. References follow the book’s own divisions — Prologue, First Period, the numbered Narratives of the Second Period, and Epilogue — rather than a running chapter count.

structure.label: Prologue
structure.title: The Storming of Seringapatam (1799)
structure.summary: An unnamed cousin writes to his family explaining why he will never speak to John Herncastle again. In the confusion of the sack he finds Herncastle with a torch and a bloody dagger and two dead Indians at his feet, and hears the third man curse the stone as he dies. Nothing is proved, and the letter is deliberately left as a private accusation.

scenes.title: A letter that accuses nobody in public
scenes.summary: The legend of the yellow diamond, its removal from Somnauth, and a death in a doorway that the writer will not report to his colonel.

structure.label: First Period
structure.title: The Loss of the Diamond (1848), told by Gabriel Betteredge
structure.summary: The house steward writes twenty-three chapters of the birthday, the theft and the investigation, in a voice built out of Robinson Crusoe, household hierarchy and an unshakeable belief that women are the cause of most trouble. Sergeant Cuff arrives, reads the smeared paint on a door correctly and the people entirely wrongly, Rosanna Spearman drowns herself in the quicksand, and Rachel leaves in a fury nobody can explain.

scenes.title: The steward sets the scene
scenes.summary: Betteredge is commissioned to write, opens Robinson Crusoe for guidance, and introduces the household, Lady Verinder and the Shivering Sand.

scenes.title: The diamond arrives
scenes.summary: Franklin Blake brings the legacy from the wicked Colonel; three Indian jugglers appear at the gate; Rachel is given the stone on her eighteenth birthday.

scenes.title: The night and the morning after
scenes.summary: The dinner party, Murthwaite’s warning, the missing diamond, the local superintendent’s failure, and the sending for Sergeant Cuff.

scenes.title: Cuff’s investigation
scenes.summary: The smeared door, the missing nightgown, Cuff’s theory of Rachel’s debts, and Rosanna’s journey to Frizinghall and to the sand.

scenes.title: The case abandoned
scenes.summary: Rosanna drowns, Rachel refuses to be questioned, Cuff is dismissed with three predictions, and Franklin Blake leaves England.

structure.label: Second Period, First Narrative
structure.title: Contributed by Miss Clack
structure.summary: A poor relation with a bag of religious tracts takes the story to London, and reveals far more than she intends. Miss Clack is present at Godfrey Ablewhite’s proposal, at Rachel’s refusal and at Lady Verinder’s death, and reports all three through a haze of self-congratulation. Collins prints Franklin Blake’s letters declining her extracts inside her own narrative, so the reader watches her being edited.

scenes.ref: Second Period, First Narrative, Chapters I–III
scenes.title: Tracts and a proposal
scenes.summary: Clack distributes improving literature, hides behind a curtain, and hears Godfrey Ablewhite propose to Rachel.

scenes.ref: Second Period, First Narrative, Chapters IV–VI
scenes.title: A will and a death
scenes.summary: Lady Verinder’s illness and will; Clack’s campaign of anonymous extracts; the correspondence in which Blake refuses to print them.

scenes.ref: Second Period, First Narrative, Chapters VII–VIII
scenes.title: The engagement broken
scenes.summary: Rachel breaks with Godfrey once his father’s inquiries are made, and Clack records his composure as saintliness.

structure.label: Second Period, Second Narrative
structure.title: Contributed by Mathew Bruff, Solicitor
structure.summary: The family lawyer supplies what only a lawyer would have: the terms of Lady Verinder’s will, the reason Godfrey’s interest in Rachel cooled, and an interview with an Indian client who wanted to know the law on pledged property. Bruff is shrewd, useful and quite sure that women cannot administer a trust, which is the kind of blind spot Collins gives to every witness.

scenes.ref: Second Period, Second Narrative, Chapter I
scenes.title: The will
scenes.summary: Rachel has only a life interest, which removes Godfrey’s motive for marrying her and supplies Bruff’s explanation of his conduct.

scenes.ref: Second Period, Second Narrative, Chapters II–III
scenes.title: The diamond in the bank
scenes.summary: A question about the Indian law of pledges, and Murthwaite’s reading of the conspiracy at a London dinner table.

structure.label: Second Period, Third Narrative
structure.title: Contributed by Franklin Blake
structure.summary: Blake returns, commissions the whole record, and follows Rosanna’s posthumous letter to a tin box buried under the Shivering Sand. In it is a paint-stained nightgown marked with his own name. He then hears from Rachel that she watched him take the diamond with her own eyes, and the novel’s central problem becomes a contradiction rather than a mystery.

scenes.ref: Second Period, Third Narrative, Chapters I–III
scenes.title: The buried box
scenes.summary: Betteredge, the quicksand, the chain, and a nightgown that carries the wrong name — his own.

scenes.ref: Second Period, Third Narrative, Chapters IV–VII
scenes.title: Rosanna’s letter and Rachel’s evidence
scenes.summary: Rosanna’s account of her silence and her love; Rachel, confronted at last, says she saw him do it.

scenes.ref: Second Period, Third Narrative, Chapters VIII–X
scenes.title: Ezra Jennings
scenes.summary: Mr. Candy’s wandering memory, and an assistant nobody in the town will speak to, who has the means of reconstructing what was said at the birthday dinner.

structure.label: Second Period, Fourth Narrative
structure.title: Extracted from the Journal of Ezra Jennings
structure.summary: A dying man with a disgraced past and an opium habit designs the experiment that solves the case: reproduce the conditions of the birthday night, give the same dose, and see what Blake does. The journal is the most intimate document in the book, and it is kept by the only narrator who has nothing to gain and no reputation to protect.

scenes.title: The reconstruction
scenes.summary: Consent obtained from Rachel and Mr. Bruff, the house restored to its 1848 state, the laudanum given, and Blake watched through the night.

structure.label: Second Period, Fifth to Eighth Narratives
structure.title: Blake resumed, Cuff, Mr. Candy and Betteredge
structure.summary: The experiment proves what Blake did and not where the diamond went, so the last movement follows the stone to a London bank, a disguise and a murder in a cheap tavern. Sergeant Cuff returns to write out the case he got wrong, naming a man whose reputation for charity had been paid for out of a trust he had robbed. Betteredge closes the book with Robinson Crusoe, as he opened it.

scenes.title: The pursuit to London
scenes.summary: The pledged diamond, the watch on the bank, and a bearded man followed to a tavern in Shore Lane.

scenes.title: Contributed by Sergeant Cuff
scenes.summary: Cuff’s written account of Godfrey Ablewhite’s two lives, the trust he had emptied, and the debt the diamond was raised to pay.

scenes.title: In a Letter from Mr. Candy
scenes.summary: The doctor supplies the last medical detail and the news of Ezra Jennings’s death.

scenes.title: Contributed by Gabriel Betteredge
scenes.summary: The steward is given the last word, and uses it on a marriage, a baby and his own favourite book.

structure.label: Epilogue
structure.title: The Finding of the Diamond
structure.summary: Three short statements move the story out of English hands. Cuff’s man and a ship’s captain trace the three Indians as far as Bombay, and then Murthwaite, travelling in Kattiawar, watches a night ceremony at Somnauth and sees the yellow diamond back in the forehead of the god. The English narrators complete their record and lose the object it was about.

scenes.title: The Statement of Sergeant Cuff’s Man (1849)
scenes.summary: Three Hindus board a steamer bound for Rotterdam and are followed no further.

scenes.title: The Statement of the Captain (1849)
scenes.summary: Three passengers go overboard off the Indian coast and swim for the shore.

scenes.title: The Statement of Mr. Murthwaite (1850)
scenes.summary: A pilgrimage at Somnauth, three penitents parting for ever, and the Moonstone restored to the god of the Moon.

characters.name: Gabriel Betteredge
characters.role: House steward at Lady Verinder’s, and first narrator
characters.summary: Seventy years old, in service since he was a footman, and entirely convinced that a household runs on precedence and that Robinson Crusoe will answer any question put to it. His prejudices are visible on every page, which is precisely what makes his evidence usable: the reader can see the shape of what he is leaving out.
characters.clue: He has worn out six copies of one book, opens it at random whenever he needs advice, and calls his sudden interest in the investigation a disease.

characters.name: Rachel Verinder
characters.role: The owner of the diamond, on her eighteenth birthday
characters.summary: She is the only person in the book who knows a central fact from the first morning and refuses to give it up, and her silence is read by everyone as guilt, temper or debt. Collins gives her no narrative of her own, so she is constructed entirely out of other people’s accounts of a woman they have decided is behaving badly.
characters.clue: She saw the theft with her own eyes and will not say what she saw, because saying it would ruin the man she loves.

relationships.label: loves, and believes she saw steal the diamond

characters.name: Franklin Blake
characters.role: Lady Verinder’s nephew, and the compiler of the record
characters.summary: He brings the diamond from London, commissions every narrative in the book, and turns out to be the man who took it. Educated in Germany, France and Italy, he argues with himself in three national manners, and his greatest discovery is that his own memory holds nothing at all of the most important night of his life.
characters.clue: He collects everybody else’s testimony in order to find a thief, and finds his own name on the evidence.

characters.name: Rosanna Spearman
characters.role: Second housemaid, formerly a thief
characters.summary: Taken from a reformatory, deformed in one shoulder, and in love with a gentleman who does not notice she exists. She hides the paint-stained nightgown to protect him, is suspected because of her record, and walks into the Shivering Sand. Her letter, read fifty chapters later, is the most painful document in the book.
characters.clue: A housemaid with a prison record and a crooked shoulder, who buries the evidence that would convict a man who has never once looked at her.

characters.name: Sergeant Cuff
characters.role: A detective officer from Scotland Yard
characters.summary: Grizzled, softly spoken and interested chiefly in roses, he reads a smear of paint faster than anybody and misreads a young woman completely. Collins makes him formidable and wrong at once, which is unusual in the genre he helped invent: the great detective leaves the case with three predictions, two of which come true for reasons he never understood.
characters.clue: He whistles ‘The Last Rose of Summer’ when he is thinking, and means to give up catching thieves for a nursery garden.

characters.name: Drusilla Clack
characters.role: A poor cousin, and the second period’s first narrator
characters.summary: She lives on a small income in Brittany, distributes tracts with titles like ‘Satan in the Hair Brush’, and writes her narrative for the fee. Everything she reports is accurate and every judgement she attaches to it is wrong, which makes her the clearest demonstration of Collins’s method: evidence and interpretation arriving in the same sentence and needing to be separated by the reader.
characters.clue: She leaves improving pamphlets in hat-boxes and under sofa cushions, and hides behind a curtain to witness a proposal of marriage.
characters.firstAppearance: Second Period, First Narrative, Chapter I

characters.name: Godfrey Ablewhite
characters.role: A barrister and celebrated charitable speaker
characters.summary: The favourite of the Ladies’ committees, a large fair man who is kind to everybody and is living two lives at the expense of a trust he was supposed to hold. Collins makes him the one figure in the book whose public character is entirely manufactured, and the novel’s method — many witnesses, each partial — is exactly what is needed to catch him.
characters.clue: The ladies’ favourite platform speaker, whose charity is funded by a minor’s money he has already spent.

characters.name: Ezra Jennings
characters.role: Mr. Candy’s assistant, and the designer of the experiment
characters.summary: Of mixed birth, piebald hair, dying of an incurable disease and ruined years ago by an accusation he will not describe, he is the only person willing to test an idea rather than assert one. He reconstructs the birthday night as a controlled trial and insists that Rachel’s consent be freely given, and he asks for nothing except to be remembered.
characters.clue: His hair is black on one side and white on the other, the town will not speak to him, and he keeps himself alive on the drug that solves the case.
characters.firstAppearance: Second Period, Third Narrative, Chapter IX

characters.name: Mathew Bruff
characters.role: Solicitor, of Gray’s Inn Square
characters.summary: He drew Sir John’s will in ten minutes and has kept the family’s secrets ever since, and his narrative supplies the legal machinery the plot turns on. He is also the proof that competence is no protection against prejudice: he explains Rachel’s troubles shrewdly and states in the same breath that hardly one woman in a thousand could manage a trust.
characters.firstAppearance: Second Period, Second Narrative, Chapter I

characters.name: The three Indians
characters.role: Brahmin guardians of the Moonstone, travelling as jugglers
characters.summary: They appear at the gate, at a London bank and finally at Somnauth, and they are the only characters with a claim to the diamond that predates every English one. Collins filters them through Victorian conventions of mystery and disguise, and still gives them the last word: the stone goes home and the English lose sight of it for ever.

characters.name: Mr. Murthwaite
characters.role: A traveller in India, and the last witness
characters.summary: He is the only Englishman in the book who can speak to the three Indians in their own language and the only one who states plainly what they will do to recover the stone. His statement closes the novel from Kattiawar, which puts the final act of interpretation outside the English record entirely.

characters.name: Lady Julia Verinder
characters.role: Rachel’s mother, mistress of the house
characters.summary: She refuses to have her daughter questioned, sends Cuff away rather than let him proceed, and dies before the case is reopened. Her judgement is the one the household runs on, and it is exercised in the teeth of the professional advice she is paying for.

themes.name: Testimony and its limits
themes.summary: Every narrator is instructed to write only what they saw, and every one of them breaks the rule by supplying motive. The novel is built so that the truth exists nowhere in a single document: it has to be assembled by a reader setting Betteredge’s prejudice against Clack’s piety against Bruff’s professional certainty.
themes.development: Betteredge establishes the method and its weakness; Clack pushes unreliability to comedy; Jennings’s journal is the one narrative with nothing to defend, which is why it can solve the case.

themes.name: Empire and possession
themes.summary: The stone is stolen twice — from Somnauth in the eleventh century and from Seringapatam in 1799 — before it becomes an English birthday present. Collins keeps the adjective ‘Indian’ attached to it through every drawing room and bank vault, so English law can hold the diamond but never quite naturalise it.
themes.development: A private letter of accusation in the Prologue, a legacy designed as a weapon in the First Period, and a restitution in the Epilogue that the English narrators can record but not control.

themes.name: Detection and its blind spots
themes.summary: Cuff reads objects brilliantly and people badly, and the case is finally opened not by inference but by an experiment. The novel insists that clues belong to several disciplines at once — policing, medicine, law, household routine — and that a detective who owns only one of them will get it wrong.
themes.development: Local incompetence, then professional inference, then a collapse of the professional theory, and finally a reconstruction under laboratory conditions.

themes.name: Class, service and suspicion
themes.summary: Rosanna is suspected because she was a thief; the servants are examined first; Betteredge measures every visitor by the manner in which the household should receive them. The book is unusually clear that a criminal record and a crooked shoulder are treated as evidence, while a reputation for charity is treated as an alibi.
themes.development: The servants’ rooms are searched in the First Period; the man nobody suspects is exposed in the Sixth Narrative, by which time he has been dead for chapters.

themes.name: Memory, medicine and the unwitnessed act
themes.summary: The solution requires a state in which a man acts with purpose and retains nothing. Collins builds it out of contemporary argument about opium, nervous disease and the conditions under which an experiment can be repeated, and he is careful that the drug proves nothing on its own — Jennings has to design, observe and interpret.
themes.development: A dose given as a joke at the birthday dinner, a year of contradiction, and a second dose given deliberately with witnesses, consent and a written protocol.

themes.name: Respectability as a disguise
themes.summary: The novel’s two most public characters — a platform philanthropist and a tract-distributing spinster — are the ones least able to see themselves. Collins sets professed virtue against conduct repeatedly, and reserves his admiration for a reformed thief, a dying outcast and an old servant who admits he reads one book for comfort.
themes.development: Godfrey’s charity funds itself from a trust; Clack’s piety is paid for by the page; Jennings, whom nobody will speak to, is the only person who asks for consent before he acts.

techniques.name: Multiple narration
techniques.definition: A story assembled from separate first-person accounts, each limited to what the writer witnessed.
techniques.bookDefinition: A story assembled from separate first-person accounts, each limited to what the writer witnessed.
techniques.inThisBook: Eleven narrators write in turn to Franklin Blake’s commission, and none of them can revise another’s pages, so the contradictions stay on the record.

techniques.name: The documentary frame
techniques.definition: A novel presented as a dossier of letters, journals, statements and reports.
techniques.bookDefinition: A novel presented as a dossier of letters, journals, statements and reports.
techniques.inThisBook: Blake’s commission is explained in Chapter I and the correspondence about what may be included is printed inside the narrative it belongs to.

techniques.name: The unreliable narrator
techniques.definition: A witness whose facts can be trusted and whose judgements cannot.
techniques.bookDefinition: A witness whose facts can be trusted and whose judgements cannot.
techniques.inThisBook: Miss Clack reports a proposal, a will and a death accurately while describing all three as tributes to her own Christian usefulness.

techniques.name: The material clue
techniques.definition: A physical trace that carries the solution before anybody can read it.
techniques.bookDefinition: A physical trace that carries the solution before anybody can read it.
techniques.inThisBook: A smear in wet paint fixes the time, a buried nightgown fixes the name, and both are in the reader’s hands long before they are understood.

techniques.name: Serial suspense
techniques.definition: Structure shaped by weekly publication — withheld information, instalment endings, deliberate recurrence.
techniques.bookDefinition: Structure shaped by weekly publication — withheld information, instalment endings, deliberate recurrence.
techniques.inThisBook: Thirty-two weeks meant readers had to carry a detail for months, so Collins repeats the quicksand, the paint and the Indians at intervals rather than relying on memory.

techniques.name: Written voice
techniques.definition: A speech habit belonging to one character alone, so that they can be recognised before they are named.
techniques.bookDefinition: Characterisation carried by the habits of a narrator’s prose rather than by description.
techniques.inThisBook: Betteredge digresses and quotes Defoe, Clack italicises her own virtues, Bruff numbers his points, and Jennings writes in dated fragments between doses.

quotations.text: the Mohammedan conqueror, Mahmoud of Ghizni, crossed India; seized on the holy city of Somnauth; and stripped of its treasures the famous temple, which had stood for centuries⁠—the shrine of Hindu pilgrimage, and the wonder of the Eastern world.
quotations.context: The family legend of the diamond, as the letter-writer has heard it in camp.
quotations.analysis: The theft the English commit in 1799 is not the first: Collins puts an eleventh-century sack at the head of the book so that the stone arrives with a history of plunder already attached. The Epilogue returns to exactly this city, which turns the novel’s shape into a circle rather than a chase.

quotations.text: “The Moonstone will have its vengeance yet on you and yours!” He spoke those words, and fell dead on the floor.
quotations.context: The last of the three guardians, dying in the armoury doorway at Seringapatam.
quotations.analysis: The curse is the one supernatural claim in a novel that otherwise explains everything by paint, law and medicine, and Collins puts it in a language the narrator has to have translated for him. Every subsequent misfortune can be read as fulfilment or coincidence, and the book never adjudicates.

quotations.text: In the first part of Robinson Crusoe, at page one hundred and twenty-nine, you will find it thus written:
quotations.context: The opening sentence of Betteredge’s narrative.
quotations.analysis: A detective novel begins by citing another book by page number, and the citation is exact where everything else in Betteredge’s testimony will be approximate. Collins is announcing his method in the first line: this story will arrive as a document that quotes its sources.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, First Period, Chapter I

quotations.text: When my spirits are bad⁠—Robinson Crusoe. When I want advice⁠—Robinson Crusoe. In past times when my wife plagued me; in present times when I have had a drop too much⁠—Robinson Crusoe. I have worn out six stout Robinson Crusoes
quotations.context: Betteredge explaining what the book is for.
quotations.analysis: The list runs from low spirits to marital trouble to drink, and the remedy never changes; six worn-out copies is the detail that turns a joke into a portrait of a life. It also plants a foundational story of English trade and mastery inside a novel about stolen colonial property, and Collins leaves the reader to notice.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, First Period, Chapter I

quotations.text: trembling in a manner most remarkable to see, and which has given to it, among the people in our parts, the name of the Shivering Sand.
quotations.context: Betteredge describing the quicksand in the little bay below the house.
quotations.analysis: The name comes from the local people rather than from a map, which is how Collins keeps the place both real and slightly outside ordinary jurisdiction. The sand does the work a Gothic castle would once have done: it swallows a woman, hides the only physical evidence, and gives it back a year later intact.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, First Period, Chapter IV

quotations.text: here was our quiet English house suddenly invaded by a devilish Indian Diamond⁠—bringing after it a conspiracy of living rogues, set loose on us by the vengeance of a dead man.
quotations.context: Betteredge taking in what Franklin Blake has just told him about the legacy.
quotations.analysis: The sentence sets ‘quiet English house’ against ‘devilish Indian Diamond’ as though the two belonged to different worlds, which is the assumption the whole novel dismantles. The conspiracy of living rogues turns out to include an English barrister, and the vengeance of a dead man to be an English colonel’s.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, First Period, Chapter V

quotations.text: Send the Diamond tomorrow (under guard of more than one man) to be cut up at Amsterdam. Make half a dozen diamonds of it, instead of one. There is an end of its sacred identity as The Moonstone
quotations.context: Murthwaite’s advice at the birthday dinner on how to end the danger.
quotations.analysis: The one solution offered that would actually work is refused because it would destroy the value of the stone as a stone. Murthwaite has identified precisely what makes the object dangerous — its sacred identity — and the English response is to bank it instead, which guarantees the rest of the plot.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, First Period, Chapter X

quotations.text: One of these days (please God) I shall retire from catching thieves, and try my hand at growing roses.
quotations.context: The Sergeant’s first conversation on arriving, conducted with the gardener about grass walks.
quotations.analysis: Collins gives his detective a private life before he gives him a theory, and the roses are not a quirk but a measure: Cuff is at his most attentive and most accurate when the subject is not human. The same man will shortly read Rachel Verinder as a young woman in debt.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, First Period, Chapter XII

quotations.text: “Nobody has stolen the Diamond,” answered Sergeant Cuff.
quotations.context: Overheard by Betteredge at the threshold, in reply to Franklin Blake’s question.
quotations.analysis: The line is the first statement of the book’s real problem: not who took it, but whether taking it was a theft at all. Cuff means that Rachel has removed her own property to raise money; he is wrong about the person and right about the grammar, since the man who carried the diamond out of the room had no criminal intention either.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, First Period, Chapter XII

quotations.text: If there is such a thing known at the doctor’s shop as a detective-fever, that disease had now got fast hold of your humble servant.
quotations.context: Following Cuff down to the beach on the track of Rosanna Spearman.
quotations.analysis: Betteredge coins the phrase to excuse himself, and it names something the novel makes formally true: once Cuff begins asking questions, every detail in the house looks like a clue and every servant like a suspect. The word ‘fever’ also carries the warning — the appetite for a solution is what produces the wrong one.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, First Period, Chapter XV

quotations.text: having always a few tracts in my bag, I selected one which proved to be quite providentially applicable to the person who answered the door.
quotations.reference: Second Period, First Narrative, Chapter I
quotations.context: Waiting in the hall of her aunt’s London house.
quotations.analysis: The pamphlet is chosen for the servant who opened the door, which means a stranger has been diagnosed in the time it takes to cross a hall. Clack’s own word — providentially — does the work of concealing a judgement as a piece of divine good fortune, and she uses the same manoeuvre on every person in her narrative.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Second Period, First Narrative, Chapter I

quotations.text: The chapters best adapted to female perusal are “Satan in the Hair Brush;” “Satan behind the Looking Glass;” “Satan under the Tea Table;” “Satan out of the Window”
quotations.reference: Second Period, First Narrative, Chapter IV
quotations.context: Describing the book she leaves for Lady Verinder to find.
quotations.analysis: The comedy is in the domestic inventory — brush, looking glass, tea table, window — which turns the devil into a fixture of the furniture. Collins is also making a point about method: Clack finds significance in ordinary household objects with exactly the confidence Sergeant Cuff brings to a smear of paint.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Second Period, First Narrative, Chapter IV

quotations.text: he will refrain from mentioning any personal objection which he may entertain to this species of literature
quotations.reference: Second Period, First Narrative, Chapter VI
quotations.context: One of the letters Collins prints inside Clack’s own narrative, refusing her extracts.
quotations.analysis: The editor of the record appears inside the record, and the reader watches the dossier being assembled and trimmed. Blake’s courtesy is lethal — he declines to mention his personal objection while mentioning it — and the exchange quietly tells us that every narrative in the book has passed through one man’s hands.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Second Period, First Narrative, Chapter VI

quotations.text: to be also capable of properly administering a trust (which, in my experience of the fair sex, not one in a thousand of them is competent to do)
quotations.reference: Second Period, Second Narrative, Chapter I
quotations.context: Explaining why Sir John’s will left everything to his wife.
quotations.analysis: The parenthesis is the whole point: Bruff praises Lady Verinder’s competence and generalises about her sex in the same sentence, without noticing the contradiction. Collins gives his most reliable witness a prejudice he cannot see, which is the exact defect the novel’s many-narrator structure exists to expose.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Second Period, Second Narrative, Chapter I

quotations.text: I looked back again at the letters. My own name. Plainly confronting me
quotations.reference: Second Period, Third Narrative, Chapter III
quotations.context: Opening the tin case recovered from under the Shivering Sand and reading the mark on the nightgown.
quotations.analysis: Collins breaks the paragraph into fragments so that the sentence has to be read twice, which is what Blake is doing on the page. The buried evidence solves the mystery and destroys the investigator in the same instant, and the novel still has three hundred pages to run.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Second Period, Third Narrative, Chapter III

quotations.text: And, on the unanswerable evidence of the paint-stain, I had discovered myself as the thief.
quotations.reference: Second Period, Third Narrative, Chapter III
quotations.context: The end of the same scene, with Betteredge walking towards him along the sand.
quotations.analysis: ‘Unanswerable’ is the word a lawyer would use, and Blake is applying the standard of proof he has been gathering testimony under. The sentence also fuses detective and criminal into one grammatical subject, which is the structural joke the entire second half depends on.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Second Period, Third Narrative, Chapter III

quotations.text: His gipsy-complexion, his fleshless cheeks, his gaunt facial bones, his dreamy eyes, his extraordinary parti-coloured hair, the puzzling contradiction between his face and figure which made him look old and young both together
quotations.reference: Second Period, Third Narrative, Chapter IX
quotations.context: Franklin Blake’s first close look at Mr. Candy’s assistant.
quotations.analysis: Blake catalogues the features that have made a whole town refuse to employ Jennings and admits that his own first impression is unfavourable. The doubleness — old and young, black hair and white — is the book’s picture of a man read wrongly by everybody, which is precisely the condition Rachel and Rosanna are also in.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Second Period, Third Narrative, Chapter IX

quotations.text: The one effectual palliative in my case, is⁠—opium. To that all-potent and all-merciful drug I am indebted for a respite of many years from my sentence of death.
quotations.reference: Second Period, Third Narrative, Chapter IX
quotations.context: Jennings explaining his own illness to Franklin Blake.
quotations.analysis: The drug that lost Blake a night of his life is the same drug keeping Jennings alive, and the man who explains it is speaking from inside the experiment he is about to run. Collins, who took laudanum himself for years, refuses to let opium be either a poison or a miracle: it is a treatment with a stated limit.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Second Period, Third Narrative, Chapter IX

quotations.text: It leaves her entirely mistress of her own decision. If she consents to assist the experiment, she consents of her own free will
quotations.context: From Jennings’s journal, on the letter he has drafted asking Rachel to permit the experiment.
quotations.analysis: Consent is written into the protocol before the laudanum is measured, by the one character the town has decided is disreputable. Set it beside the birthday dinner, where the first dose was administered to Blake as a practical joke without his knowledge, and the novel’s moral arrangement is complete.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Second Period, Fourth Narrative

quotations.text: And there, in the forehead of the deity, gleamed the yellow Diamond, whose splendour had last shone on me in England, from the bosom of a woman’s dress!
quotations.context: Murthwaite at the shrine in Kattiawar, watching the curtain drawn aside.
quotations.analysis: The last time the diamond was described it was on a woman’s dress at a birthday party, and Collins puts both settings into one sentence so the reader makes the comparison. The stone has not been recovered by anybody in the English narrative; it has simply gone back to where the Prologue took it from.

quotations.text: So the years pass, and repeat each other; so the same events revolve in the cycles of time. What will be the next adventures of the Moonstone? Who can tell?
quotations.context: The last sentences of the book.
quotations.analysis: A detective novel ends on an open question, and the question is not who did it but what happens next. The cycle Collins describes is the one the Prologue began — conquest, theft, restitution, conquest — and by refusing to close it he keeps the English portion of the story a single episode rather than the whole account.

atAGlance.label: Serialised
atAGlance.note: Thirty-two weekly instalments in Dickens’s All the Year Round, and simultaneously in Harper’s Weekly.

atAGlance.label: First edition
atAGlance.note: Tinsley Brothers, three volumes, published in London before the serial had finished running.

atAGlance.label: Narrators
atAGlance.note: All writing to Franklin Blake’s commission, each confined to what they personally saw.

atAGlance.label: Historical anchor
atAGlance.note: The prologue places the theft during a documented assault of the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War.

criticalViews.position: A founding text of the detective novel
criticalViews.summary: The country-house theft, the professional detective, the false suspect, the material clue and the final reconstruction are all here in one book, and much later crime fiction can be described in its terms.
criticalViews.counter: Prose mysteries and investigating figures existed before 1868, and the claim can flatten what is unusual here — a detective who is wrong, and a solution nobody deduces.

criticalViews.position: A novel about testimony rather than crime
criticalViews.summary: On this reading the subject is how evidence is produced: who is asked, what they are allowed to say, and how religion, class and vanity shape what a witness notices. The structure does the arguing, since no single document is sufficient.
criticalViews.counter: It risks treating the plot as a pretext, when Collins plainly took great care to make the mechanism of the theft work in medical and legal detail.

criticalViews.position: An imperial novel
criticalViews.summary: The stone is taken by force, held under English law, and returned outside it, and the Prologue and Epilogue frame the domestic mystery with acts of conquest and restitution the English narrators cannot control.
criticalViews.counter: The Indian characters are still filtered through Victorian conventions of disguise and inscrutability, and they are given no narrative of their own in a novel made entirely of narratives.

essayQuestions.question: What does Collins gain, and what does he give up, by telling the story through many narrators?
essayQuestions.focus: Structure, testimony and the reader’s work
plan: Set out the commission in the First Period: each witness confined to what they personally saw.
Use Betteredge to show the method’s strength — visible prejudice makes the omissions legible.
Read Miss Clack as the limiting case, where accurate facts arrive wrapped in judgements nobody can accept.
Weigh the cost: Rachel, the person who knows most, is never given a narrative, and the Indians none at all.
Conclude on what the form asks of a reader that a single detective’s account would not.

essayQuestions.question: ‘Sergeant Cuff is the most impressive person in the book and he gets it wrong.’ Discuss.
essayQuestions.focus: Detection, inference and class
plan: Establish his real competence: the paint, the timing, the missing garment, the deduction about the town.
Show where the inference fails and why — a theory of Rachel’s debts that fits everything except Rachel.
Examine the part played by Rosanna’s record and appearance in making the wrong suspect plausible.
Set his method against Ezra Jennings’s: inference from traces, versus an experiment designed to produce new evidence.
Assess the Sixth Narrative, where Cuff writes up the truth and thereby admits what his first theory cost.

essayQuestions.question: How far is the Prologue necessary to The Moonstone?
essayQuestions.focus: Empire, framing and the ending
plan: Describe what the Prologue establishes: an eleventh-century sack, a documented 1799 assault, a private accusation, a curse.
Trace how Herncastle’s legacy works as a weapon rather than a gift, and what that makes of the birthday.
Follow the adjective ‘Indian’ through the English chapters, where the stone is repeatedly given a geography.
Read the Epilogue as the Prologue completed, and note that no English narrator is present for the restitution.
Decide whether the frame is a moral argument, an exotic device, or both at once.

essayQuestions.question: Examine Collins’s treatment of respectability and reputation.
essayQuestions.focus: Godfrey Ablewhite, Miss Clack, Rosanna Spearman and Ezra Jennings
plan: Pair the characters by reputation: the celebrated philanthropist and the reformatory housemaid, the tract-giver and the outcast assistant.
Show how suspicion is distributed in the First Period, and on what evidence.
Read Clack’s narrative for the mechanics of self-approval, using her own word ‘providentially’.
Use Cuff’s Sixth Narrative to establish what Godfrey’s public character was actually financed by.
Close on Jennings, who asks for consent and asks for nothing else, and on what the novel does with him.

discussionQuestions: Rachel knows the answer from the first morning and says nothing. Is her silence admirable, or does the novel punish her for it?
Betteredge consults Robinson Crusoe as an oracle. What does Collins gain by putting one famous English story inside another?
Miss Clack is ridiculous and every fact she reports is true. How should a reader use a witness like that?
Ezra Jennings solves the case and dies asking only to be forgotten. Why does Collins give the solution to the man nobody will employ?
The diamond goes back to India and the English characters never learn how. Is that an ending or a refusal to end?

timeline.label: The storming of Seringapatam
timeline.detail: British forces take the city in the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War; Collins places the theft of the diamond in the confusion of the assault.

timeline.label: Wilkie Collins born in London
timeline.detail: The son of the landscape painter William Collins, and later trained for the law at Lincoln’s Inn.

timeline.label: Collins meets Charles Dickens
timeline.detail: The beginning of a collaboration and a friendship that gave Collins his serial platforms.

timeline.label: The Woman in White begins in All the Year Round
timeline.detail: Collins’s first great multiple-narrator novel, and the commercial proof of the method used again here.

timeline.label: The Moonstone serialised
timeline.detail: Thirty-two weekly instalments from 4 January to 8 August, in All the Year Round and in Harper’s Weekly.

timeline.label: Three-volume edition published
timeline.detail: Tinsley Brothers issue the London book in July, before the weekly serial has finished.

timeline.label: Revised one-volume text
timeline.detail: Smith, Elder issue a revised text with a new preface for a different market and format.

timeline.label: Collins’s own dramatisation staged
timeline.detail: He adapted the novel for the theatre himself, cutting the many-narrator structure the book was built on.

timeline.label: Collins dies in London
timeline.detail: He had used laudanum for years against the pain of rheumatic illness, as Ezra Jennings does in the novel.

timeline.label: First sound film version
timeline.detail: One of a long line of adaptations that keep the theft and drop most of the narrators.

timeline.label: BBC television serial
timeline.detail: The first of several British television versions to attempt the novel’s sequence of witnesses.

places.name: Seringapatam (Srirangapatna)
places.note: Where the diamond passes into English hands during the assault of 1799.

places.name: Somnauth (Somnath)
places.note: The sacred city the stone was taken from in the eleventh century, and the shrine it returns to in the Epilogue.

places.name: Gray’s Inn Square, London
places.note: Mr. Bruff’s office, where the will is drawn and the Indian client asks about the law of pledges.

places.name: Hampstead
places.note: Bruff’s private house, where Rachel takes refuge after her mother’s death.

places.name: Brighton
places.note: Where Lady Verinder takes a house, and where the story is brought back together after the Yorkshire investigation collapses.

places.name: Amsterdam
places.note: The city where Murthwaite advises the diamond be cut into half a dozen stones, which would have ended the danger and the plot.

related.why: Collins’s earlier experiment with the same method, where the witnesses are assembled as though for a trial.
The detective story after Cuff: inference raised to a system, and a investigator who is never wrong.
Betteredge’s oracle, opened at random for guidance throughout the First Period and quoted by page number in the first line.
Another All the Year Round serial built on a concealed benefactor and a fortune whose origins will not bear examination.
A later novel assembled from journals, letters and statements, and equally interested in what a dossier can prove.

books.title: The Odyssey
books.author: Homer
books.setting: Ithaca, Pylos, Sparta, and the seas and islands between Troy and home, in the tenth year after the fall of Troy
books.written: Composed in Greek, probably in the late eighth or early seventh century BCE; Samuel Butler's English prose translation appeared in 1900
books.lengthNote: A poem of about 12,000 lines of Greek hexameter verse in twenty-four books. Butler translates it into continuous English prose, so it reads like a novel, but it is recorded here as a poem because that is what Homer made.
books.openingLine: Tell me, O Muse, of that ingenious hero who travelled far and wide after he had sacked the famous town of Troy.
books.summary: A war poem has a sequel about getting home, and it turns out that getting home is the harder job. Odysseus has been gone twenty years; his son has grown up without him, his wife is holding off a hundred and eight suitors with a piece of weaving, and he himself is sitting on a beach crying. The poem spends half its length on the voyage everyone remembers and the other half in one house on one island, where a man dressed as a beggar has to find out who is still loyal to him before anybody finds out who he is. Its hero wins by lying, and the poem admires him for it; its last great test is set not by a monster but by his wife.
books.referenceStyle: book — Butler's prose translation carries no line numbers, so quotations are placed by book alone (Book 1 to Book 24)

sourceText.label: Samuel Butler's prose translation of the Odyssey (1900), Project Gutenberg eBook 1727
sourceText.note: Quotations are given exactly as Butler first printed them, and Butler used the Roman names then usual in English: Ulysses for Odysseus, Minerva for Athene, Jove for Zeus, Neptune for Poseidon, Mercury for Hermes, Proserpine for Persephone. The Astor edition prints the same translation with the familiar Greek names restored, so a quotation here that says Ulysses will say Odysseus there. Outside quotations, the commentary uses the Greek names.

structure.label: Books 1–4
structure.title: The son goes looking
structure.summary: The hero of the poem does not appear for four books. Instead we get the hole he has left: a house being eaten by his wife's suitors, and a son of twenty who has never had to act. Athene sends Telemachus abroad to ask after his father, and what he brings back is less news than an education in how a great house ought to be run.

scenes.title: The council of the gods
scenes.summary: Zeus complains that mortals blame the gods for their own folly; Athene, disguised as Mentes, stirs Telemachus to act.

scenes.title: The assembly in Ithaca
scenes.summary: Telemachus denounces the suitors in public, Antinous tells the story of Penelope's web, and the boy sails by night.

scenes.title: Nestor at Pylos
scenes.summary: Nestor receives the strangers with sacrifice and talk, and tells how the Greek fleet broke up after Troy.

scenes.title: Menelaus and Helen at Sparta
scenes.summary: Husband and wife tell rival stories about Odysseus at Troy; in Ithaca the suitors plan to murder Telemachus on his way home.

structure.label: Books 5–8
structure.title: From Calypso's island to the Phaeacian court
structure.summary: Odysseus enters his own poem weeping on a beach, refuses immortality, builds a raft, is wrecked by Poseidon and crawls ashore naked among strangers. The Phaeacians test the rules of hospitality from the host's side, and their blind bard sings the Trojan war back to a guest who turns out to have been in it.

scenes.title: The raft
scenes.summary: Hermes orders Calypso to release Odysseus; he turns down eternal life, sails for seventeen days and is wrecked within sight of land.

scenes.title: Nausicaa
scenes.summary: A princess doing the laundry meets a naked castaway, who talks his way to safety with a speech about marriage.

scenes.title: The palace of Alcinous
scenes.summary: Odysseus is received as a suppliant and promised a ship home before anybody has asked his name.

scenes.title: Games and songs
scenes.summary: Demodocus sings of Troy and of Ares and Aphrodite; the guest weeps twice, and Alcinous finally asks who he is.

structure.label: Books 9–12
structure.title: The wanderings, told by the wanderer
structure.summary: Everything most readers think of as the Odyssey — Cyclops, Circe, the dead, the Sirens, Scylla — is here, and all of it is narrated by Odysseus himself after dinner to hosts who are about to give him presents. He leaves Troy with twelve ships and ends the story alone, and the poem leaves the reader to decide how much of the account to take on trust.

scenes.title: Lotus-eaters and Cyclops
scenes.summary: Odysseus blinds Polyphemus under the name Noman, then shouts his real name from the ship and earns Poseidon's curse.

scenes.title: Aeolus, the Laestrygonians, Circe
scenes.summary: The bag of winds is opened in sight of home; eleven ships are destroyed; Circe turns men to pigs and then keeps them a year.

scenes.title: The land of the dead
scenes.summary: Tiresias prophesies the way home and the journey after it; Odysseus meets his mother, Agamemnon and Achilles.

scenes.title: Sirens, Scylla and the cattle of the Sun
scenes.summary: Odysseus hears the Sirens tied to the mast, loses six men to Scylla, and loses everyone else when the crew eat the Sun's cattle.

structure.label: Books 13–16
structure.title: Ithaca, unrecognised
structure.summary: The Phaeacians put Odysseus ashore asleep, and he wakes not knowing where he is. From here the poem slows right down. Athene turns him into an old beggar, he shelters with the swineherd Eumaeus, and father and son meet in a hut, where the first thing they do after weeping is count the enemy.

scenes.title: The landing
scenes.summary: Odysseus lies to a shepherd boy who is really Athene; she is delighted, and the two of them plan the suitors' deaths.

scenes.title: The swineherd's hut
scenes.summary: Eumaeus feeds a beggar he takes for a stranger and refuses to believe the beggar's news that his master is coming home.

scenes.title: Telemachus returns
scenes.summary: Telemachus leaves Sparta, slips past the ambush, and Eumaeus tells the story of how he was sold as a child.

scenes.title: Father and son
scenes.summary: Athene restores Odysseus's looks for a moment; Telemachus takes him for a god, then believes him, and they plot.

structure.label: Books 17–20
structure.title: The beggar in the hall
structure.summary: Odysseus goes into his own house in rags and is kicked, pelted and laughed at in it. These books are a long audit of loyalty: the dog knows him and dies, the nurse knows him and is silenced, the goatherd and the maids insult him, and Penelope questions him by firelight without, apparently, knowing who he is.

scenes.title: Argos
scenes.summary: The old hound recognises his master from the dung heap; inside, Antinous throws a footstool at the beggar.

scenes.title: The fight with Irus
scenes.summary: Odysseus boxes the resident beggar for the suitors' amusement and warns the one decent suitor, Amphinomus, to leave.

scenes.title: The interview and the scar
scenes.summary: Penelope and the beggar talk alone; Eurycleia washes his feet and knows the scar; Penelope announces the contest of the bow.

scenes.title: The last feast
scenes.summary: A sleepless night, thunder from a clear sky, and the prophet Theoclymenus sees the hall running with blood while the suitors laugh.

structure.label: Books 21–24
structure.title: The bow, the bed and the truce
structure.summary: The beggar strings the bow nobody else can bend, and the hall becomes a battlefield with the doors locked. The killing is followed by a second test, which Odysseus does not set but sits: Penelope's trick about the bed. The final book goes down to the dead and out to Laertes' farm, and stops a civil war by divine order.

scenes.title: The contest
scenes.summary: The suitors fail to string the bow; Odysseus strings it like a lyre and shoots through the twelve axes.

scenes.title: The slaughter
scenes.summary: Antinous dies first with a cup at his lips; all the suitors are killed, and twelve maidservants are hanged.

scenes.title: The bed
scenes.summary: Penelope will not accept him until he proves he knows how their bed was built; then the night is lengthened for them.

scenes.title: The dead, Laertes, and peace
scenes.summary: The suitors' ghosts reach Hades, Odysseus tests his father in the orchard, and Athene halts the suitors' kin.

characters.name: Odysseus (Butler's Ulysses)
characters.role: King of Ithaca, ten years at Troy and ten more getting back
characters.summary: The Iliad's heroes are strong; this one is clever, and the poem treats cleverness as a kind of endurance. He can build a raft, a bed and a lie with equal care, and he tells five separate false life-stories once he is home. He is also the only survivor of his expedition, a fact he narrates himself and for which he never quite takes the blame.
characters.clue: He gives a giant a false name and gets away with it, then cannot resist shouting the real one, and pays ten years for the pleasure.

characters.name: Penelope
characters.role: Wife of Odysseus, besieged in her own house
characters.summary: She has no army, no husband and a son too young to help, and she holds a hundred-odd men off for three years with a loom. The poem never quite says when she recognises the beggar, and her decision to set the bow contest on the very day he arrives can be read as despair, luck or collusion. She is the only person in the poem who out-tricks Odysseus.
characters.clue: She weaves by day, unpicks by night, and at the end orders a bed moved that she knows cannot be moved.

characters.name: Telemachus
characters.role: Son of Odysseus, a baby when his father sailed
characters.summary: The first four books are his, and they show a young man who has been told all his life whose son he is and has no way to check. His journey finds out very little about Odysseus and a good deal about himself. By Book 21 he is giving orders to his mother and could, the poem hints, have strung the bow himself.
characters.clue: He tells his mother that talking is men's business in Book 1, and that the bow is men's business in Book 21, in almost the same words.

characters.name: Athene (Butler's Minerva)
characters.role: Goddess of craft and war, daughter of Zeus
characters.summary: She opens the plot by lobbying her father while Poseidon is out of the room, and she stays in it to the last line. She appears as Mentes, as Mentor, as a little girl with a pitcher and as a shepherd boy, and she likes Odysseus for the quality a moralist would disapprove of: he lies as well as she does.
characters.clue: Caught being lied to by her favourite mortal, she smiles, strokes his hand and compliments his technique.

characters.name: Poseidon (Butler's Neptune)
characters.role: God of the sea, father of the Cyclops
characters.summary: His anger is the reason a voyage of a few weeks takes ten years, and it has a specific cause: Odysseus blinded his son and then supplied a name for the curse. He cannot kill Odysseus, because fate has settled that the man gets home, so he settles for making it slow, solitary and expensive, and takes out the remainder on the Phaeacians.
characters.clue: He is away at a feast among the Ethiopians when the poem begins, which is the only reason anything can start.

characters.name: Polyphemus
characters.role: A Cyclops, shepherd and cannibal
characters.summary: He is the poem's clearest picture of a host who breaks every rule: he asks his guests' business before feeding them, eats them, and offers as his guest-gift the favour of being eaten last. Yet he is tender with his ram, and Odysseus was in his cave uninvited, helping himself to cheese. The episode is less one-sided than its teller makes it sound.
characters.clue: His neighbours ask who is hurting him, and he gives them an answer that sends them back to bed.

characters.name: Calypso
characters.role: A nymph, daughter of Atlas, on the island of Ogygia
characters.summary: Her name comes from the Greek for hiding, and she has hidden Odysseus from the world for seven years. She offers the one thing no Homeric hero is otherwise offered — never to die — and he declines it for a woman he concedes is less beautiful. Told to release him, she protests that gods are allowed mortal lovers and goddesses are not.
characters.clue: She offers a man immortality and ends up lending him an axe.

characters.name: Circe
characters.role: A goddess and enchantress on the island of Aeaea
characters.summary: She turns half the crew into pigs, fails to turn Odysseus, and then becomes the most useful ally of the whole voyage. It is Circe who sends him to the dead and who briefs him, point by point, on the Sirens, Scylla and the cattle of the Sun. He stays a year, and it is the crew who have to remind him about home.
characters.clue: Her guests arrive as men and are penned as pigs, with their minds unchanged.

characters.name: Nausicaa
characters.role: Daughter of Alcinous, king of the Phaeacians
characters.summary: She is the only person on the beach who does not run away from the salt-caked stranger, and she manages the encounter better than he could have hoped, down to the instruction to walk behind her wagon so that nobody gossips. The poem lets her think of him as a husband and then quietly sends him home to someone else.
characters.clue: She goes to the river to wash her brothers' clothes and comes back with the hero of the Trojan war.

characters.name: Eumaeus
characters.role: Swineherd to Odysseus, born a king's son and sold as a child
characters.summary: He is the poem's model host, and he is a slave with a hut and a herd of pigs. He gives a beggar the best cut of pork and his own cloak, and refuses to believe the beggar's good news because he has been lied to before. The narrator addresses him directly as 'you', a courtesy the poem extends to nobody else in Ithaca.
characters.clue: He has been told so often that his master is coming home that he will not believe it from the master himself.

characters.name: Eurycleia
characters.role: The old nurse of Odysseus and of Telemachus
characters.summary: She knows the house better than anyone in it, and she knows Odysseus by touch: the scar on his leg tells her what twenty years and a goddess's disguise were hiding from everybody else. Her reward is a hand at her throat. After the killing it is she who names the twelve disloyal maids.
characters.clue: She drops his foot into the basin, the water spills, and he grips her by the throat before she can speak.

characters.name: Antinous and the suitors
characters.role: The ringleader of the hundred and eight men courting Penelope
characters.summary: The suitors are guests who will not leave, and their offence is described again and again as eating. Antinous is the worst of them: he proposes Telemachus's murder and throws a stool at a beggar in another man's hall. Yet his account of Penelope's web in Book 2 is half admiring, and the suitors' kin have a grievance the last book takes seriously.
characters.clue: He dies with a gold cup raised to his lips, thinking about his wine.

themes.name: Homecoming
themes.summary: The Greek word is nostos, and the poem measures its hero against other men's returns: Agamemnon got home quickly and was murdered at dinner; Menelaus got home rich and sits beside a wife he cannot quite trust. Arriving is the easy part. Home has to be re-entered carefully, in disguise, and won back room by room.
themes.development: A longing on Calypso's beach in Book 5, a coastline glimpsed and lost in Book 10, an unrecognised shore in Book 13, and finally an olive-tree bedpost in Book 23 — after which Tiresias's prophecy quietly says he must leave again.

themes.name: Hosts, guests and strangers
themes.summary: Nearly every episode is a test of how a household treats someone who turns up at the door. The rule — feed the stranger first, ask his name afterwards, send him on with a gift — is under the protection of Zeus. Nestor, Menelaus, the Phaeacians and a swineherd keep it; the Cyclops inverts it; the suitors break it from the guest's side by never leaving.
themes.development: Shown working in Books 3, 4 and 7, parodied in the Cyclops's cave, kept by the poorest household in Book 14, and enforced in Book 22 with a bow.

themes.name: Names, fame and recognition
themes.summary: Odysseus survives by being nobody and cannot bear it. A hero exists in what is said about him, so the man who calls himself Noman has to shout his name and address from the ship. In Ithaca the process runs the other way: he withholds his name and is recognised piece by piece, by a dog, a scar, a bow and a bed.
themes.development: Withheld for a whole book at the Phaeacian court, declared with pride in Book 9, hidden again from Book 13, and then surrendered in stages to son, nurse, servants, wife and father.

themes.name: Cunning, lies and disguise
themes.summary: The poem's word for its hero is polytropos — of many turns — and it admires the quality without apology. Athene loves him because he lies well; Penelope matches him with the web and the bed. But deceit corrodes as well as protects: by Book 24 he cannot greet his own grieving father without first trying a false story on him.
themes.development: A tactic against the Cyclops, a habit by Book 13, a household policy in Books 17 to 21, and something close to a compulsion in the orchard scene of Book 24.

themes.name: Loyalty and the audit of the household
themes.summary: Twenty years is long enough for everyone to have made a choice, and the second half of the poem goes through the household finding out what each one chose. Penelope, Eumaeus, Eurycleia, the cowherd Philoetius and the dog pass. Melanthius the goatherd and twelve of the fifty maids do not, and the poem's punishment of them is harsher than modern readers find comfortable.
themes.development: Tested quietly in the swineherd's hut, brutally in the hall, intimately at the footbath, and paid out in Book 22.

themes.name: Justice, revenge and the gods
themes.summary: Zeus opens the poem by saying that mortals bring suffering on themselves beyond what is fated, and offers Aegisthus as the example. The crew who eat the Sun's cattle and the suitors who eat Odysseus's are both warned and both destroyed. Whether what happens in the hall is justice or a massacre is a question the final book raises and then closes by decree.
themes.development: Stated as a principle in Book 1, illustrated on Thrinacia in Book 12, carried out in Book 22, and challenged by the dead men's families in Book 24.

themes.name: Storytelling and who gets to tell it
themes.summary: This is a poem full of poets. Phemius sings in Ithaca, Demodocus at the Phaeacian court, and Odysseus himself is compared to a bard by his host. The famous adventures reach us only in his words, to an audience he needs to impress, and the same man tells elaborate false autobiographies in Ithaca with exactly the same fluency.
themes.development: A bard's song makes Penelope weep in Book 1 and Odysseus weep in Book 8; he takes over as narrator for Books 9 to 12, and strings the bow in Book 21 like a singer tuning a lyre.

techniques.name: Beginning in the middle
techniques.definition: Opening an epic late in its story and supplying the earlier events afterwards, usually through a character's own narration.
techniques.bookDefinition: Opening an epic late in its story and supplying the earlier events afterwards, usually through a character's own narration.
techniques.inThisBook: The poem starts in the twentieth year, and with the wrong person: four books about Telemachus before Odysseus appears. The ten years of wandering are then folded into one evening's talk, so that the poem's present is only about forty days long.

techniques.name: Invocation
techniques.definition: An opening address to a muse or god, asking for the song and announcing its subject.
techniques.bookDefinition: An opening address to a muse or god, asking for the song and announcing its subject.
techniques.inThisBook: The proem asks the Muse for 'that ingenious hero' and does not name him until the second paragraph. It also gets its excuses in early, blaming the crew's deaths on 'their own sheer folly' before we have heard a word of the evidence.

techniques.name: Epithets and formulae
techniques.definition: Fixed descriptive phrases attached to a person or thing and repeated whenever they recur, a working tool of poetry composed in performance.
techniques.bookDefinition: Fixed descriptive phrases attached to a person or thing and repeated whenever they recur, a working tool of poetry composed in performance.
techniques.inThisBook: Dawn is 'rosy-fingered' every time she appears, and whole blocks of lines — arming, washing, serving a meal — recur word for word. Butler keeps many of these in his prose. The repetitions are not padding: they make each dawn and each dinner the same ritual, so a breach of the ritual shows at once.

techniques.name: Extended simile
techniques.definition: A comparison developed over several lines until it becomes a small scene of its own, typically closed with 'even so'.
techniques.bookDefinition: A comparison developed over several lines until it becomes a small scene of its own, typically closed with 'even so'.
techniques.inThisBook: The Odyssey's similes have a habit of crossing sides. The victor of Troy weeps like a woman being dragged into slavery from a sacked town; Penelope greets her husband like a shipwrecked sailor reaching land, which is his experience, not hers. The comparisons make characters change places with those their stories have harmed or left behind.

techniques.name: The hero as his own narrator
techniques.definition: A narrator telling their own earlier life, with the distance between the two selves doing the judging.
techniques.bookDefinition: A story told after the event by someone who was in it, with the advantages and the unreliability that implies.
techniques.inThisBook: Books 9 to 12 are in the first person, and the poem has taken care to show us beforehand that the speaker is a gifted liar who wants a ship and presents from his audience. Nothing confirms or denies his account except Poseidon's anger, which is real enough.

techniques.name: Dramatic irony
techniques.definition: The audience knows something that a character speaking or acting does not.
techniques.bookDefinition: The audience knows something that a character speaking or acting does not.
techniques.inThisBook: From Book 13 onwards almost every conversation in Ithaca is conducted with a man whose identity we know and the speakers do not. Eumaeus mourns his master to his master's face; the suitors wish the beggar luck 'in other things' as he strings the bow that will kill them.

techniques.name: Recognition scene
techniques.definition: A scene in which one character discovers who another really is, often by means of a token or sign.
techniques.bookDefinition: A scene in which one character discovers who another really is, often by means of a token or sign.
techniques.inThisBook: The second half is built as a ladder of these, each with a different token and a different cost: Telemachus by a goddess's help, Argos by scent, Eurycleia by a scar, the herdsmen by being shown it, the suitors by an arrow, Penelope by the bed, Laertes by the orchard trees counted out to a child.

techniques.name: Objects that carry the argument
techniques.definition: An object the narrative keeps returning to until it stands for the argument rather than illustrating it.
techniques.bookDefinition: Physical things that the narrative returns to until they stand for a relationship or an idea.
techniques.inThisBook: The web that is never finished is Penelope's marriage kept open. The bow that only one man can string is the kingship. The bed built round a living olive tree is a marriage that cannot be moved without being killed — and the poem makes the point by having someone threaten to move it.

quotations.text: Tell me, O Muse, of that ingenious hero who travelled far and wide after he had sacked the famous town of Troy. Many cities did he visit, and many were the nations with whose manners and customs he was acquainted
quotations.context: The opening of the poem.
quotations.analysis: The Iliad's first noun is anger; this poem's is a man, and an unnamed one. 'Ingenious' is Butler's word for the Greek polytropos, 'of many turns', which can mean much-travelled or much-twisting, and the sentence allows both. Note too what he is credited with: not killing, but visiting cities and learning customs. The hero is introduced as a kind of tourist with a sack of Troy behind him.
quotations.source: Butler's translation, Project Gutenberg text, Book I

quotations.text: See now, how men lay blame upon us gods for what is after all nothing but their own folly.
