characters.name: The Hermit
characters.role: The holy man of the wood by the harbour
characters.summary: He is the poem's picture of religion lived at ease in nature: he sings hymns of his own making, kneels on a mossy oak-stump and likes talking to sailors. The Mariner expects him to wash the blood away. What the Hermit actually does is cross himself and ask a question, and the answer to that question is the first telling of the tale, so that the confessor starts the compulsion rather than ending it.
characters.clue: He compares the ship's sails to dead leaves in his forest brook, urges the boat on when the Pilot is afraid, and can scarcely stand when he steps ashore.

relationships.label: questions, and so becomes the first listener of

characters.name: The Pilot
characters.role: The harbour pilot who rows out to the ship
characters.summary: An ordinary working man brought to the edge of the supernatural, he serves to measure how the Mariner now looks to the world he has come back to. He thinks the ship fiendish before he reaches it, and when the drowned-looking body in his boat moves its lips he shrieks and falls down in a fit.
characters.clue: He says he is afraid, is told to push on, and collapses when the man he has rescued tries to speak.

characters.name: The Pilot's boy
characters.role: The lad in the rescue boat
characters.summary: He has the poem's most disturbing line after the shooting itself. Watching the Mariner take the oars, he laughs long and loud with his eyes going to and fro, and says what the adults are too frightened or too pious to say. The Mariner adds, in passing and in the present tense, that the boy is mad now, which is the cost of the homecoming to somebody who only came out in a boat.
characters.clue: He laughs, names the Devil as the oarsman, and is mentioned once more as one who now goes crazy.

relationships.label: driven mad by the sight of

themes.name: A crime without a motive
themes.summary: The shooting is given one clause and no reason, and the poem never goes back to supply one. That omission is the centre of the work: guilt here is not the consequence of a bad intention that can be examined and repented, but a fact that attaches to a man and has to be carried, first as a dead bird and then as a story. The crew's guilt is different in kind, a matter of approving after the event, and is punished more severely.
themes.development: Stated in a line at the end of Part I, made visible as a burden at the end of Part II, lifted from the neck in Part IV, and shown in Part VII to have moved inwards, where it returns at uncertain hours.

themes.name: The living world, slimy and beautiful
themes.summary: The same sea creatures appear twice. In Part II they are slimy things crawling on a rotting sea, and in Part IV they are water-snakes in blue, green and velvet black, shedding light as they rear. Nothing about them has altered except the way they are looked at, and the poem locates the Mariner's release in that change of looking. The sun in this poem tends to preside over suffering and the moon over relief, a pattern too consistent to be accidental and too loose to be a code.
themes.development: From the bird treated as a guest and then as a target in Part I, through disgust in Part II and unwilled love in Part IV, to the closing claim that prayer and the love of creatures are one act.

themes.name: Alone on a wide wide sea
themes.summary: The Mariner's punishment is solitude in company: two hundred bodies on deck, every one with its eyes open, and nobody to speak to. The poem treats loneliness as a spiritual condition as well as a physical one, since at its worst he cannot pray either. His later longing is touchingly modest. He does not ask for the wedding feast, only to walk to church in a crowd.
themes.development: Introduced when the ship breaks into a sea nobody has entered, brought to its extreme in Part IV, and carried home in Part VII, where the man who praises company passes like night from land to land and belongs nowhere.

themes.name: Penance without an end
themes.summary: The poem borrows the vocabulary of confession, with its shrieving and penance and a hermit to hear it, and then declines to complete the sacrament. The albatross falls off, the curse is snapped and the ship comes home, yet a voice has already said that more penance is to come, and the Hermit gives a question instead of absolution. Release in this poem is real but partial, and it is never declared finished.
themes.development: First relief in Part IV; the verdict of the second voice at the end of Part V; the hope of being shrieved at the end of Part VI; and in Part VII the discovery that telling the tale frees him only until the next time.

themes.name: The tale that has to be told
themes.summary: The poem is about being told a story as much as about the story. It opens on a listener being stopped and closes on what listening has done to him, and in between the teller explains that he does not choose his moments or his audience. Storytelling is therefore shown from both ends as something undergone. It is a penance for the speaker and, the last stanza suggests, an injury as well as an education for the hearer.
themes.development: The frame is set in the first stanza, interrupts the voyage at its most frightening points in Parts I, IV and V, and takes over completely in Part VII, where the origin and mechanism of the compulsion are finally given.

themes.name: Prayer, chance and an unsteady providence
themes.summary: The Mariner's world is thick with Christian reference, from vespers and the Virgin to the holy rood and guardian saints, and he reads his rescue as grace. But the poem also shows his fate settled by a throw of dice between two spectres, and a sea so lonely that God himself scarcely seemed to be there. It holds both pictures without choosing, which is why it has been read as an orthodox parable and as a nightmare with a parable pinned to it.
themes.development: The bird is greeted in God's name in Part I; the dice fall in Part III; prayer fails and then succeeds in Part IV; and Part VII ends with a creed whose comfort the listener's condition does not quite confirm.

techniques.name: Frame narrative
techniques.definition: A story told inside another story, so that every account reaches the reader through somebody with an interest in it.
techniques.bookDefinition: A story told inside another story, so that every account reaches the reader through somebody with an interest in it.
techniques.inThisBook: The voyage is enclosed in an encounter on a road outside a wedding. The frame breaks in whenever the Wedding-Guest can bear no more, and it supplies the ending: the last two stanzas are about him, not the Mariner. After 1817 a second frame, the prose gloss in the margin, tells the story again in a confident scholarly voice that knows more, or claims to, than the verse does.

techniques.name: Ballad stanza
techniques.definition: A four-line stanza alternating four-stress and three-stress lines, rhymed on the second and fourth, inherited from traditional sung narrative.
techniques.bookDefinition: A four-line stanza alternating four-stress and three-stress lines, rhymed on the second and fourth, inherited from traditional sung narrative.
techniques.inThisBook: Coleridge keeps the old measure for speed and plainness and then breaks it for effect. When the storm drives the ship, when the spectre-bark closes in, when the fiend treads behind on the lonesome road, the stanza swells to five or six lines, so that the reader waits longer than expected for the rhyme to close.

techniques.name: Internal rhyme
techniques.definition: A rhyme between the middle and the end of a single line, rather than between line-endings.
techniques.bookDefinition: A rhyme between the middle and the end of a single line, rather than between line-endings.
techniques.inThisBook: Many of the long lines chime at the half-way point: guests met and feast set, the ice that did split with a thunder-fit, the first that ever burst. The effect is a gallop in the passages of motion and, in the becalmed passages, a kind of locked echo in which the line seems unable to get away from itself.

techniques.name: Refrain
techniques.definition: A phrase brought back at intervals, so that its meaning shifts with what has happened since.
techniques.bookDefinition: A phrase brought back at intervals, so that its meaning shifts with what has happened since.
techniques.inThisBook: Repetition works at every scale, from doubled words within a line to whole stanzas that return altered. The sun that came up upon the left in Part I rises upon the right in Part II, which is how the poem says the ship has rounded the ice; the lighthouse, hill and kirk of the departure come back in reverse order at the homecoming; and the word 'alone' is struck five times in two lines.

techniques.name: Archaism
techniques.definition: The deliberate use of words and forms already old-fashioned when the work was written.
techniques.bookDefinition: The deliberate use of words and forms already old-fashioned when the work was written.
techniques.inThisBook: Words such as eftsoons, swound, gramercy, clomb and I wist give the poem the air of something found rather than written, and the 1798 text went further with antique spelling throughout. Coleridge pared much of this away in revision, but kept enough that the tale seems to come from no particular century, which suits a teller who is himself out of time.

techniques.name: Simile
techniques.definition: A comparison made explicit with 'like' or 'as', so that the two things are held side by side rather than fused.
techniques.bookDefinition: A comparison made explicit with 'like' or 'as', so that the two things are held side by side rather than fused.
techniques.inThisBook: The similes repeatedly reach away from the sea towards the land the Mariner has lost: a hidden brook in the leafy month of June, a meadow-gale of spring, April hoar-frost. Others turn the ship into a picture or a prison, as with the painted ship and the sun peering through a dungeon-grate. The most famous of them, the man on the lonesome road, describes fear by refusing to look at its cause.

techniques.name: The unstable symbol
techniques.definition: An object placed at the centre of a work whose meaning is never settled by it.
techniques.bookDefinition: An object placed at the centre of a work whose meaning is never settled by it.
techniques.inThisBook: The albatross is hailed as a soul, credited with the wind, blamed for the fog, hung in the place of a cross and mourned by a spirit, all by characters with reasons of their own. The verse itself never says what the bird means, only what is done with it. Readings that make it Christ, nature, the imagination or an innocent stranger are all continuing the crew's habit of deciding after the fact.

quotations.text: It is an ancient Mariner, And he stoppeth one of three.
quotations.context: The opening couplet, before anybody has spoken.
quotations.analysis: 'It is', not 'there was': the present tense puts the Mariner in front of us as something encountered, almost as a thing, and the same tense will return at the end when we learn he is still doing this. 'One of three' is never explained. Two men walk on into the wedding, and the poem's first act is a selection without a stated reason, which prepares for a story built on another.

quotations.text: He holds him with his glittering eye-- The Wedding-Guest stood still, And listens like a three years child: The Mariner hath his will.
quotations.context: The Mariner has been told to take his hand away, and does; this is what he uses instead.
quotations.analysis: The hand fails and the eye succeeds, so the hold is not physical and the guest's consent is not asked. Comparing a grown man to a three years child makes listening a return to helplessness. 'Hath his will' is a phrase of mastery, and it sits oddly on a man we later learn has no will of his own in the matter, since the tale compels him as he compels the guest.

quotations.text: As if it had been a Christian soul, We hailed it in God's name.
quotations.context: The albatross comes through the fog to a ship surrounded by ice, where no living thing has been seen.
quotations.analysis: The sailors greet the first creature they have met in the ice as one greets a person, and the 'as if' keeps the comparison honest: nobody claims the bird is a soul. What the line establishes is hospitality. The bird is received as a guest, fed, and called to, so that the shooting nine evenings later is a breach of welcome before it is anything more mysterious.

quotations.text: "God save thee, ancient Mariner! From the fiends, that plague thee thus!-- Why look'st thou so?"--With my cross-bow I shot the ALBATROSS.
quotations.context: The Wedding-Guest breaks in at the sight of the Mariner's face, and the answer closes the first part.
quotations.analysis: The confession is made in reply to a question about his expression, not about his conduct, and it answers 'why' with 'what'. The instrument comes first and the verb is the plainest available. There is no because, then or afterwards. Placing the act at the very end of the part, after a stanza of moonshine and vespers, gives it the abruptness of the thing itself, and the capitals are the text's way of letting the word ring.

quotations.text: For all averred, I had killed the bird That made the breeze to blow.
quotations.context: The first verdict of the shipmates, while the wind still holds but the bird no longer follows.
quotations.analysis: 'Averred' is a word for sworn testimony, and the crew use it twice, a stanza apart, for opposite findings: that he killed the bird that brought the breeze, and that he killed the bird that brought the fog. Their morality is a weather report. The poem quietly treats the second verdict as the fatal one, since approving the act afterwards is the only thing the two hundred ever do to deserve what follows.

quotations.text: We were the first that ever burst Into that silent sea.
quotations.context: The ship, running north with a fair wind, enters waters no ship has sailed.
quotations.analysis: For two lines the poem sounds like the voyage narratives Coleridge had been reading, with the explorer's boast of priority. 'Burst' is a violent verb for an arrival, and it rhymes inside the line with 'first', so that discovery and intrusion are heard as one sound. The silence they break into is about to become their own: in the next stanza the wind drops, and they speak only to hear something.

quotations.text: Day after day, day after day, We stuck, nor breath nor motion; As idle as a painted ship Upon a painted ocean.
quotations.context: The ship is becalmed under a copper sky.
quotations.analysis: The first line does what it describes, repeating itself because nothing has happened to report. The simile is stranger than it looks. A becalmed ship is compared to a picture of a ship, which is to say to art, and the comparison is a complaint: to be a painting is to be without breath. In a poem so concerned with what it is to be fixed by a tale, the image of people trapped in a representation is not idle.

quotations.text: Water, water, every where, And all the boards did shrink; Water, water, every where, Nor any drop to drink.
quotations.context: Thirst begins among the becalmed crew.
quotations.analysis: The line most people know is usually misquoted, and the true second line is the more exact observation: salt water and sun are shrinking the planks of the ship itself, so the sea surrounds them and is also pulling their shelter apart. The stanza is a riddle of abundance as deprivation. It prepares for Part IV, where the Mariner is surrounded by life and cannot be part of it until he sees it differently.

quotations.text: Instead of the cross, the Albatross About my neck was hung.
quotations.context: The close of Part II: the crew, too parched to speak, express themselves in an act.
quotations.analysis: The rhyme of 'cross' and 'Albatross' falls inside one line and makes the substitution audible. The passive voice matters: he does not take the bird up, it is hung on him by men who have themselves approved the killing, which makes this a scapegoating as much as a penance. Whether the bird is thereby likened to Christ, or whether the emblem of forgiveness has simply been replaced by the evidence of the offence, the line declines to say.

quotations.text: I bit my arm, I sucked the blood, And cried, A sail! a sail!
quotations.context: A shape has been sighted, and nobody on board has moisture enough in his mouth to call out.
quotations.analysis: To speak at all he has to drink from himself, and the poem sets down the fact in two short clauses without comment. It is the first time speech costs the Mariner blood, and it will not be the last: every later telling of the tale is wrung from him by a bodily agony. The hope he pays for so dearly is also mistaken, since the sail is the spectre-bark.

quotations.text: Her lips were red, her looks were free, Her locks were yellow as gold: Her skin was as white as leprosy, The Night-Mare LIFE-IN-DEATH was she, Who thicks man's blood with cold.
quotations.context: The Mariner sees the two figures on the skeleton ship as it comes alongside.
quotations.analysis: The first two lines are the stock portrait of a ballad heroine, and the third spoils it with a single noun. Red, gold and white are the colours of beauty, and white is also the colour of the disease, so the portrait turns on its own palette. The stanza runs to five lines because the name needs a line to itself. 'Thicks' is used as a verb, an old usage that makes the cold seem to act inside the listener's own veins.

quotations.text: The game is done! I've won! I've won!
quotations.context: Death and Life-in-Death have been casting dice on the deck of the hulk; this is her cry.
quotations.analysis: The poem's only glimpse of how sentences are passed in its universe is a game of chance, and the winner's glee is a child's. If the Mariner's survival is a prize in a dice game, then the moral economy of sin, penance and grace that he later describes has a rival explanation underneath it. The gloss of 1817 tidies this scene into a judgement; the verse leaves it as a throw.

quotations.text: And every soul, it passed me by, Like the whizz of my CROSS-BOW!
quotations.context: The last lines of Part III: two hundred men have dropped dead, and their souls leave their bodies.
quotations.analysis: Each part of the poem so far has ended on the bird or the weapon, and this one brings the weapon back as a sound. Two hundred deaths are heard as two hundred repetitions of the one shot, so that the simile does the accusing that no character has done aloud. The poem will not say where the souls go: they fled to bliss or woe, and the Mariner knows only that they went past him.

quotations.text: Alone, alone, all, all alone, Alone on a wide wide sea! And never a saint took pity on My soul in agony.
quotations.context: The Mariner has just reassured the Wedding-Guest that he is not a ghost, and resumes.
quotations.analysis: The first two lines contain almost nothing but one word and its near-rhymes: 'alone', 'all', 'a'. Long open vowels and the doubled 'wide wide' stretch the line out to the horizon it describes. The loneliness is then made vertical as well as horizontal, since no saint looks down either. He is not literally alone, as the next stanza cruelly points out; he has two hundred companions on deck.

quotations.text: The many men, so beautiful! And they all dead did lie: And a thousand thousand slimy things Lived on; and so did I.
quotations.context: Alone on deck among the bodies of the crew, looking from them to the sea.
quotations.analysis: The men are beautiful only now that they are dead; alive, they were evil looks from old and young. Against them he sets the slimy things and then, after a semicolon that works like a flinch, himself. The grammar files him with the creatures he despises. This self-disgust is the state from which he cannot pray, and the stanza needs to be remembered when the same creatures reappear transformed.

quotations.text: The moving Moon went up the sky, And no where did abide: Softly she was going up, And a star or two beside.
quotations.context: After seven days and nights under the dead men's curse, the Mariner looks up.
quotations.analysis: After stanzas clogged with rot, reek and curses, this one is almost empty, and the change of pace is the change of heart beginning. The moon is 'moving' and the Mariner is stuck; she abides nowhere and yet is accompanied, a star or two beside her, while he is fixed and alone. Nothing is asked of the image. It simply turns his eyes outward, and the water-snakes come two stanzas later.

quotations.text: O happy living things! no tongue Their beauty might declare: A spring of love gushed from my heart, And I blessed them unaware
quotations.context: The Mariner has been watching the water-snakes coil and swim in the shadow of the ship.
quotations.analysis: The turning point of the poem is an action its agent does not know he is performing. 'Unaware' is said twice in the stanza, and it matches the unexplained shooting exactly: he did not decide to kill and he does not decide to bless. 'A spring of love gushed' is water imagery arriving in a drought, and it comes from inside him before any rain falls. Note too that no tongue can declare their beauty, from a man whose whole later life is declaring.

quotations.text: The self same moment I could pray; And from my neck so free The Albatross fell off, and sank Like lead into the sea.
quotations.context: The end of Part IV, immediately after the blessing.
quotations.analysis: Prayer is not the cause of the release but its sign: the blessing came first and was not a prayer at all. The bird, which flew and perched and came to a call, leaves the poem as dead weight, and 'like lead' will be used once more, of the ship itself going down in Part VII. Both burdens sink, and neither sinking ends the matter, which is why this stanza closes a part and not the poem.

quotations.text: They raised their limbs like lifeless tools-- We were a ghastly crew.
quotations.context: The dead sailors rise without speaking and work the ship as it moves without wind.
quotations.analysis: The simile turns the men into the equipment they are handling, and then the pronoun does something worse: 'we'. The Mariner counts himself among them, hauling on a rope beside his own nephew's body. Life-in-Death has won him, and here the phrase is shown from the inside, as a living man doing a shift with corpses and unable to tell himself apart from the gang.

quotations.text: Quoth he, "The man hath penance done, And penance more will do."
quotations.context: The Mariner lies in a faint and hears two voices in the air discussing him; this is the softer one.
quotations.analysis: The sentence is passed in his hearing but not to his face, by speakers who are never identified, and it is the most exact statement of his condition in the poem: penance in the past tense and the future tense, with no present in which it is complete. The soft voice, as soft as honey-dew, delivers the harder news. Everything in Parts VI and VII should be read under this line.

quotations.text: Like one that on a lonesome road Doth walk in fear and dread, And having once turned round walks on, And turns no more his head; Because he knows, a frightful fiend Doth close behind him tread.
quotations.context: The spell of the dead men's eyes has just snapped, and the Mariner looks out over the sea again, but sees little.
quotations.analysis: The simile leaves the sea for a road on land, the place where we first met the Mariner, and describes a man who has looked once and will not look again. The fiend is never seen; knowledge of it is enough. The stanza takes six lines instead of four, so the reader, like the walker, is kept going past the point where rest was expected. Mary Shelley has Frankenstein quote it as he flees his creature.

quotations.text: "Ha! ha!" quoth he, "full plain I see, The Devil knows how to row."
quotations.context: The Pilot has fainted and the Hermit is praying, so the Mariner takes the oars of the rescue boat himself.
quotations.analysis: The boy's joke is the judgement of the ordinary world on the returning Mariner, and it is delivered in laughter by a child who is losing his mind as he speaks. The poem reports his madness in the present tense, in a subordinate clause, as a casualty nobody stops to count. It is a reminder that the tale harms those it touches, which bears on how we read the Wedding-Guest's condition at the end.

quotations.text: Since then, at an uncertain hour, That agony returns; And till my ghastly tale is told, This heart within me burns.
quotations.context: The Mariner has described how the Hermit's question forced the tale out of him, and explains what has happened since.
quotations.analysis: 'Uncertain' removes the last comfort of routine: the penance has no calendar. The burning has moved from the sky and the sea of Part II into his chest, so the tropics are now internal. 'Ghastly' is the word he used of the dead crew at the ropes, and he applies it to his own story. Telling brings relief, which means every listener is being used as medicine, and the Wedding-Guest is only the latest dose.

quotations.text: I pass, like night, from land to land; I have strange power of speech
quotations.context: The Mariner describes his life since the voyage and how he chooses, or is given, his listeners.
quotations.analysis: He compares himself to night, the thing that fell at one stride when the crew died, and the comparison makes him a natural force that arrives everywhere and stays nowhere. 'Strange power of speech' is as close as the poem comes to describing itself. Coleridge, a famous talker who held rooms for hours, gives the gift of eloquence to a man for whom it is a symptom.

quotations.text: He prayeth best, who loveth best All things both great and small; For the dear God who loveth us He made and loveth all.
quotations.context: The Mariner's farewell to the Wedding-Guest.
quotations.analysis: The rhythm goes nursery-simple and the diction could be a hymn for children, which is either the hard-won plainness of a man who has been to the bottom or a formula too small for what it follows. The poem gives grounds for both. The creed says God loves all; the narrative has shown two hundred men killed for a change of opinion. It is worth asking who needs this stanza more, the listener or the speaker.

quotations.text: A sadder and a wiser man, He rose the morrow morn.
quotations.context: The last two lines of the poem; the Mariner has gone, and the Wedding-Guest has turned from the bridegroom's door.
quotations.analysis: The poem ends on the listener, and the order of the adjectives is the verdict: sadder first. The stanza before says he went like one stunned and of sense forlorn, language closer to injury than to enlightenment. He has missed the wedding of his own kin to acquire this wisdom. If the Mariner's moral were the whole meaning, the guest ought to be gladder, and that gap is where the poem's interpretation properly begins.

atAGlance.label: First published
atAGlance.note: Anonymously, as the opening poem of Lyrical Ballads, under the title 'The Rime of the Ancyent Marinere'.

atAGlance.label: Marginal gloss added
atAGlance.note: In Sibylline Leaves, where the poem first appeared under Coleridge's own name, with a Latin epigraph in place of the old prose Argument.

atAGlance.label: Text followed here
atAGlance.note: The last version Coleridge saw through the press, in the year of his death.

atAGlance.label: Form
atAGlance.note: Alternating four- and three-stress lines, rhymed on the short lines, with internal rhyme in many of the long ones.

criticalViews.position: The sacramental reading: a coherent parable of sin, penance and grace
criticalViews.summary: On this view the poem means what its Mariner says it means. The killing is a breach of the bond between all living things; the becalming and the deaths are its consequences; the blessing of the water-snakes is an act of love that restores the bond; and the homecoming and the moral complete a pattern of fall and redemption. The gloss of 1817 is Coleridge making that pattern explicit.
criticalViews.counter: It has to pass over the dice game, the wildly unequal punishment of the crew, the Hermit's failure to absolve, and a penance explicitly said to have no end. It also takes the gloss as the poem's own voice, when the gloss is written in a different persona and sometimes asserts what the verse leaves open.

criticalViews.position: The nightmare reading: a universe without reliable justice
criticalViews.summary: Here the poem's power lies in the mismatch between act and consequence. A thoughtless shot brings cosmic retribution; chance decides who lives; spirits pursue their own quarrels; and the pious moral at the end is a frightened man's attempt to make sense of what happened to him. The poem is closer to a bad dream than to a sermon, and its terror is that of guilt felt without a crime understood.
criticalViews.counter: The release in Part IV is too carefully prepared and too exactly mirrors the shooting to be arbitrary, and the Christian imagery is not only in the Mariner's mouth but in the structure of events. To call the moral mere consolation is to decide in advance that the poem cannot mean what it says.

criticalViews.position: The double-text reading: verse and gloss as rival narrators
criticalViews.summary: A third position takes the 1817 page, with ballad in the centre and learned commentary in the margin, as the real work. The gloss names the spirits, assigns motives and draws lessons; the verse does none of these things. The poem thereby stages the act of interpretation itself, and shows a later, tidier mind trying to master an older and wilder story, much as the Mariner's moral tries to master his experience.
criticalViews.counter: For nineteen years the poem existed and was read without any gloss, and it was already strange and already complete. A reading that depends on the margin risks treating an afterthought as the design, and cannot explain the force of the 1798 text.

essayQuestions.question: How far does the Mariner's closing moral account for the poem that precedes it?
essayQuestions.focus: The relation between the stated lesson and the narrated events
plan: Set out the moral exactly: prayer and love of all creatures are one thing, because God made and loves them all. Note its hymn-like simplicity and who speaks it.
Show what it does explain: the hospitality shown to the bird in Part I, its violation, and the unwilled blessing of the water-snakes in Part IV, where love precedes prayer.
Turn to what it leaves out: the dice game in Part III, the deaths of two hundred men for approving an act, and the Pilot's boy driven mad.
Consider the speaker's situation. A man told that more penance is to come, and still seized by agony at uncertain hours, has reasons to want a simple creed.
Conclude with the Wedding-Guest, stunned, forlorn and sadder before he is wiser, as the poem's own evidence that the tale outweighs its moral.

essayQuestions.question: Explore the significance of the Wedding-Guest and the frame in which the tale is told.
essayQuestions.focus: Frame narrative, interruption and the effects of listening
plan: Begin with the opening as an act of selection and restraint: one of three, the hand and then the eye, the guest who cannot choose but hear.
Track the interruptions in Parts I, IV and V, and show that each comes where the tale is most frightening, so the frame regulates the reader's fear.
Set the wedding against the voyage: music, kin and company within earshot of a story about total solitude, and the Mariner's preference for the kirk over the feast.
Use Part VII to show that the frame is also the subject: the origin of the telling in the Hermit's question, and the mechanism of compulsion.
End on the last stanza, which belongs to the guest, and weigh whether the poem presents storytelling as gift, contagion or both.

essayQuestions.question: 'The albatross means whatever the characters need it to mean.' Discuss Coleridge's handling of the bird.
essayQuestions.focus: Symbolism, interpretation and the crew's changing verdicts
plan: Establish what the verse actually shows the bird doing, which is little: arriving, eating, circling, perching, answering a call.
Follow the meanings laid on it in sequence: a Christian soul in simile, the bringer of the breeze, the bringer of the fog, a substitute for the cross, the beloved of a spirit.
Argue that the crew's two sworn verdicts in Part II make interpretation itself a moral act with consequences.
Consider the falling of the bird in Part IV, where it becomes pure weight and sinks like lead, and what is and is not resolved by that.
Relate this to the gloss and to later readings, each of which repeats the crew's gesture of deciding afterwards what the bird was.

essayQuestions.question: How does Coleridge use the ballad form to create a sense of the supernatural?
essayQuestions.focus: Stanza, rhyme, repetition and archaic diction
plan: Describe the inherited form and what it brings with it: speed, impersonality, a teller who does not explain, and an air of age supported by archaic words.
Show internal rhyme and repetition producing both momentum, in the storm and the homecoming, and paralysis, in the becalmed stanzas of Part II.
Examine the stanzas that overrun four lines, such as the portrait of Life-in-Death and the lonesome road, and what the delay of the rhyme does to the reader.
Look at how plainly the uncanny is stated: the shooting, the dead men rising, the ship sinking are each given in the flattest syntax available.
Conclude that the form's refusal to comment is what lets the natural and the supernatural share a single tone, so that neither can be dismissed.

discussionQuestions: The poem never says why the Mariner shot the albatross. Would any reason make the poem better, or is the absence of one the point?
The crew die and the man who fired the shot lives. Is there any account of justice on which that is fair, and does the poem want there to be?
The water-snakes of Part IV are the slimy things of Part II. What has changed, and who or what changed it?
The Hermit is asked for absolution and replies with a question. Is that a failure on his part, or the only honest response available?
Is the Wedding-Guest better off for having heard the tale? What would you need to know about the next morning to decide?
If you read the poem with the 1817 gloss beside it, does the margin help you, or does it seem to be talking about a slightly different poem?

timeline.label: George Shelvocke's A Voyage Round the World published
timeline.detail: Its account of a rough passage round Cape Horn includes an officer shooting a black albatross in the hope of better weather. Wordsworth later recalled suggesting the incident to Coleridge.

timeline.label: Samuel Taylor Coleridge born at Ottery St Mary, Devon
timeline.detail: The youngest child of the vicar and schoolmaster of the town; he was sent to school at Christ's Hospital in London after his father's death.

timeline.label: Cook's Resolution crosses the Antarctic Circle
timeline.detail: The expedition's astronomer, William Wales, afterwards taught mathematics at Christ's Hospital while Coleridge was a pupil there, a possible route by which descriptions of polar ice reached the poem.

timeline.label: The poem is planned on a November walk in Somerset
timeline.detail: Coleridge, living at Nether Stowey, set out with William and Dorothy Wordsworth from Alfoxden towards the coast. A joint ballad was proposed to pay for the trip, and soon became Coleridge's alone.

timeline.label: Finished in March and published in Lyrical Ballads
timeline.detail: The anonymous volume, printed in Bristol, opened with 'The Rime of the Ancyent Marinere' in deliberately antique spelling, prefaced by a short prose Argument.

timeline.label: Second edition of Lyrical Ballads
timeline.detail: The spelling was modernised, the title shortened, the poem moved from the front of the volume, and Wordsworth added a note listing what he took to be its defects alongside its merits.

timeline.label: Coleridge moves to Highgate
timeline.detail: He went to live in the household of the surgeon James Gillman, seeking help with his dependence on opium, and stayed for the rest of his life.

timeline.label: Sibylline Leaves adds the marginal gloss
timeline.detail: The poem appeared under Coleridge's name for the first time, with a Latin epigraph from Thomas Burnet and a prose commentary in the margin. Biographia Literaria, with his retrospective account of the Lyrical Ballads plan, came out the same year.

timeline.label: Frankenstein quotes the poem
timeline.detail: Mary Shelley's novel gives Walton an allusion to the albatross and has Victor recite the stanza of the lonesome road, an early sign of the poem's hold on the Gothic imagination.

timeline.label: Final lifetime text; Coleridge dies at Highgate
timeline.detail: The last collected Poetical Works he oversaw prints the version now standard. He died on 25 July.

timeline.label: Gustave Doré's illustrated edition (c. 1876)
timeline.detail: Doré's large engravings of the ice, the becalmed ship and the spectre-bark fixed the poem's look for generations of readers.

places.name: Nether Stowey, Somerset
places.note: Coleridge's cottage from the end of 1796, where the poem was written.

places.name: Alfoxden, near Holford
places.note: The house William and Dorothy Wordsworth rented in 1797 and 1798, a few miles' walk from Stowey; the November walk began here.

places.name: Watchet harbour
places.note: The small Bristol Channel port on the route of the 1797 walk, by local tradition the model for the harbour with its kirk, hill and lighthouse. The poem itself names no place.

places.name: Bristol
places.note: Where Joseph Cottle had Lyrical Ballads printed in 1798.

places.name: Cape Horn
places.note: The poem gives no bearings, but a ship driven south to the ice that then runs north into an unvisited sea follows the Horn route of Shelvocke's voyage, and the gloss calls the second sea the Pacific.

places.name: Ottery St Mary, Devon
places.note: Coleridge's birthplace, where his father was vicar.

places.name: Highgate, London
places.note: Coleridge's home from 1816 until his death in 1834, and where the later revisions of the poem were made.

related.why: The 1798 volume the poem opened, where it sits beside Wordsworth's poems of ordinary life and shows how odd a companion it was.
For 'Christabel', 'Kubla Khan' and the conversation poems written in the same Somerset months.
A close reading of the becalmed stanzas of Part II, line by line.
Mary Shelley's novel borrows the poem's frame of a compelled teller and a captive listener, and quotes it twice.
Another voyage in which a single creature is loaded with more meaning than it can settle, told by a sole survivor.
The poem that closed the 1798 Lyrical Ballads, and Wordsworth's very different account of how nature acts on the mind.

books.title: The Scarlet Letter
books.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
books.setting: Boston in the Massachusetts Bay Colony, in the 1640s, reached through a Salem custom house of the 1840s
books.lengthNote: Twenty-four chapters, preceded by an introductory sketch nearly a sixth of the book's length
books.openingLine: A throng of bearded men, in sad-colored garments, and gray, steeple-crowned hats, intermixed with women, some wearing hoods and others bareheaded, was assembled in front of a wooden edifice, the door of which was heavily timbered with oak, and studded with iron spikes.
books.summary: A woman is sentenced to wear an embroidered letter for the rest of her life, refuses to name the father of her child, and outlives the sentence without ever being released from it. Hawthorne is less interested in the adultery, which has already happened when the book opens, than in what seven years of public meaning does to four people: the woman who is marked, the minister who is not, the husband who turns diagnosis into revenge, and the child who is made to stand for all of it.

sourceText.label: Standard Ebooks text of The Scarlet Letter
sourceText.note: References give the chapter, or the introductory sketch, which this text titles 'The Customhouse'.

structure.label: The Customhouse
structure.title: A found manuscript that was never found
structure.summary: A surveyor of customs at Salem describes the dozing office he worked in and the parcel he claims to have turned up in the upper storey: a worn scrap of embroidered cloth and some papers about the woman who wore it. He puts the letter on his own breast and feels it burn. Every document in this sketch is invented, and the sketch is where the book keeps its honesty about invention.

scenes.title: The upper storey
scenes.summary: The narrator finds the rag of scarlet cloth and Surveyor Pue's papers, and takes the burn on his chest as a commission.

structure.label: Chapters 1–8
structure.title: The prison door and the first scaffold
structure.summary: Hester Prynne comes out of the jail with a three-month-old child and a letter she has embroidered far beyond the sentence. She refuses to name the father while he stands above her on the balcony and asks her to. In the crowd is the husband nobody has seen for two years, who makes her swear to keep his identity secret and settles into Boston as a physician.

scenes.title: The Marketplace
scenes.summary: Hester emerges with Pearl and the letter, and the women of the town discuss what a proper punishment would have been.

scenes.title: The Recognition
scenes.summary: Dimmesdale is ordered to exhort her to name her partner; she refuses him to his face.

scenes.title: The Interview
scenes.summary: In the prison Chillingworth binds her to silence about his name and swears to find the man.

scenes.title: The Elf-Child and the Minister
scenes.summary: The magistrates consider removing Pearl; Hester appeals to Dimmesdale, who argues successfully for her.

structure.label: Chapters 9–12
structure.title: The physician moves in
structure.summary: Chillingworth attaches himself to the failing minister as doctor and lodger, and begins an investigation conducted entirely through sympathy. Dimmesdale's sermons grow more powerful as his health collapses; he scourges himself in a locked closet and cannot say the one sentence that would end it. At last he climbs the scaffold at midnight, where nobody can see him confess.

scenes.title: The Leech and His Patient
scenes.summary: Chillingworth opens the sleeping minister's vestment and sees something on his chest; the narrator does not say what.

scenes.title: The Interior of a Heart
scenes.summary: The more Dimmesdale accuses himself in the pulpit in general terms, the holier his congregation thinks him.

scenes.title: The Minister's Vigil
scenes.summary: A midnight confession with an audience of three, a meteor in the shape of a letter, and a glove left on the scaffold.

structure.label: Chapters 13–15
structure.title: What seven years have made of her
structure.summary: Hester has become the town's unpaid nurse, and the townspeople have begun to read her letter as 'Able'. Hawthorne notes what that respectability has cost: passion turned into thought, a woman who now speculates freely because she has nothing left to lose socially. She confronts Chillingworth, tells him she means to break her promise, and looks at what he has become.

scenes.title: Another View of Hester
scenes.summary: The letter's meaning has drifted, and the narrator counts the price of the drift.

scenes.title: Hester and the Physician
scenes.summary: She releases herself from her oath; he declines to forgive and calls it fate.

scenes.title: Hester and Pearl
scenes.summary: Hester admits to herself that she hates her husband, and Pearl asks what the letter means.

structure.label: Chapters 16–19
structure.title: The one place the letter can come off
structure.summary: Hester intercepts Dimmesdale on a forest path, tells him who the physician is, and is forgiven. They plan a ship to Europe. She throws the letter into the leaves, lets down her hair, and the sunshine arrives on cue — until Pearl, on the far bank of a brook, refuses to cross until her mother puts the letter back on.

scenes.title: The Pastor and His Parishioner
scenes.summary: Two people who have not spoken in seven years argue about what their sin actually was.

scenes.title: A Flood of Sunshine
scenes.summary: The letter comes off and the forest changes lighting.

scenes.title: The Child at the Brook-Side
scenes.summary: Pearl will not recognise a mother without the letter, and screams until it is fastened on again.

structure.label: Chapters 20–24
structure.title: Election Day
structure.summary: Dimmesdale walks back through the town nearly deranged with the effort of pretending, writes the sermon of his life in one night, and preaches it. Then he asks Hester and Pearl to help him onto the scaffold in daylight, tells the colony what he is, tears open his shirt and dies. The witnesses immediately begin to disagree about what they saw.

scenes.title: The New England Holiday
scenes.summary: The whole colony gathers; Hester learns that Chillingworth has taken passage on the same ship.

scenes.title: The Revelation of the Scarlet Letter
scenes.summary: The confession, the chest, and Chillingworth's collapse.

scenes.title: Conclusion
scenes.summary: Several accounts of what was on the minister's breast, Pearl's inheritance and marriage abroad, and Hester's return to resume the letter voluntarily.

characters.name: Hester Prynne
characters.role: A needleworker sentenced to wear the letter A
characters.summary: She is the only person in the book who never lies, and the only one who is punished. Left to support a child on embroidery, she gradually makes herself indispensable to the town that sentenced her, and the change in her — from passion to speculation, from beauty to a kind of marble calm — is described by the narrator as a loss rather than a triumph.
characters.clue: She embroiders her own sentence in gold thread, refuses for seven years to name the man, and comes back at the end to put the badge on again when nobody is making her.

characters.name: Arthur Dimmesdale
characters.role: Minister of the Boston congregation
characters.summary: A young clergyman of great ability whose sermons improve in exact proportion as his health fails, because the congregation hears the suffering and mistakes it for holiness. He confesses constantly in terms so general that every confession makes him more revered, and the novel is merciless about how comfortable that arrangement is.
characters.clue: He keeps his hand over his heart, preaches better the worse he gets, and confesses at midnight where nobody can hear.

characters.name: Roger Chillingworth
characters.role: Physician, and Hester's husband under another name
characters.summary: A scholar who sent a much younger wife ahead to a colony and arrived two years late to find her on a scaffold. He is right about everything — he identifies the man, he reads the symptoms, he proves his case — and the book treats the accuracy as the crime, because he uses a doctor's access to get inside a heart and stay there.
characters.clue: He arrives from the forest with one shoulder higher than the other, takes a new name at the prison door, and spends seven years being right.

characters.name: Pearl
characters.role: Hester's daughter
characters.summary: Adults keep calling her a symbol — the scarlet letter given life, a demon child, evidence of sin — and she keeps behaving like a bright, neglected, furiously observant little girl. Her questions are the most exact in the book precisely because nobody has taught her what may not be asked.
characters.clue: Dressed in scarlet and gold to match her mother's badge, she throws flowers at it, and will not cross a brook until it is put back on.

characters.name: The Surveyor of Customs
characters.role: Narrator of 'The Customhouse'
characters.summary: A version of Hawthorne who spent three years counting cargo, lost the job to a change of administration, and claims to have found the story in an attic. He is the reason the book is called a romance rather than a history: he hands the reader a forged provenance and says so in the same breath.
characters.clue: He is dismissed from a government post, blames the guillotine of politics, and produces a manuscript nobody else has ever seen.

relationships.label: claims to have found the papers about

characters.name: Governor Bellingham
characters.role: Magistrate of the colony
characters.summary: He owns the grandest house in Boston, complete with a suit of armour that distorts Hester's letter into a monstrous size, and considers taking Pearl away from her mother for the child's spiritual good. He is the book's ordinary face of authority: not cruel, merely certain.
characters.clue: His polished breastplate makes the letter look enormous, and he has to be argued out of removing a child from her mother.

characters.name: Mistress Hibbins
characters.role: The Governor's sister, reputed a witch
characters.summary: She invites Hester to the forest to meet the Black Man, recognises Dimmesdale's condition on sight, and is later executed for witchcraft. Hawthorne uses her to keep an unsettling possibility open: that the forest bargain the townspeople believe in is one the narrator will neither confirm nor rule out.
characters.clue: She keeps offering people a night ride to the forest, and is hanged for it in the end.

characters.name: The people of Boston
characters.role: The judging crowd
characters.summary: They open the book demanding a branding iron and close it deciding that the letter means Able and that the minister's confession was a parable. As a character they have one consistent trait: whatever they believe, they believe it unanimously and without memory of having believed anything else.
characters.clue: They gather at the same scaffold three times, and give three different verdicts without noticing that they have changed their minds.

themes.name: Punishment in public
themes.summary: The sentence is not the prison term, which is already over when the book opens; it is being looked at for life. Hawthorne is precise about what that does — it makes Hester's every errand a performance, converts strangers into an audience, and eventually turns the badge into a qualification, which is not the same as a pardon.
themes.development: From the scaffold hour in Chapter 2, through the years of errands in Chapter 13, to the voluntary resumption of the letter at the end, when there is no magistrate left to require it.

themes.name: Secrecy and the body
themes.summary: What is hidden in this book does not stay abstract: it gets into the chest, the complexion, the hand that keeps rising to the heart. Dimmesdale's concealment is treated as a medical condition with a physician in attendance, and the physician is the injured husband, which makes the diagnosis a form of torture.
themes.development: Announced in Chapter 11's account of a life so false it hollows out reality, staged at midnight in Chapter 12, and finally exhibited on the scaffold in Chapter 23 — where the witnesses cannot agree what they saw.

themes.name: A sign that will not hold still
themes.canonicalName: A sign that will not hold still
themes.summary: The magistrates intend the A as a fixed sentence; Hester's embroidery has already altered it before she leaves the prison. Over seven years the same three stitches are read as adultery, as ability, as an angel in the sky, and as a judgement on a minister's chest. Meaning is not infinite here — it is contested, and the contest has winners.
themes.development: Set up by the gold thread in Chapter 2, restated as a matter of town opinion in Chapter 13, and left unresolved in Chapter 24, which offers several accounts and refuses to choose.

themes.name: Revenge as a vocation
themes.summary: Chillingworth does not strike; he settles in. The novel's harshest judgement falls not on the adultery but on a man who makes another person's inner life his life's work, and it is put as a violation of the heart's sanctuary rather than as cruelty. When his subject dies he has nothing left and is gone within the year.
themes.development: Begins as a scholar's curiosity in Chapter 4, hardens into a profession by Chapter 10, and is named the blacker sin by Dimmesdale himself in Chapter 17.

themes.name: Town, forest and brook
themes.summary: The settlement is where the letter is enforced and the forest is where it can be taken off, but Hawthorne will not let the forest be simply free: it is also where Mistress Hibbins signs her book and where Hester admits her thinking has run wild. The brook between mother and child is the book's most exact piece of geography.
themes.development: The rosebush at the prison door in Chapter 1 sets the terms; Chapters 16 to 19 test them, and Pearl's refusal to cross the water withdraws the offer.

themes.name: Ancestors and offices
themes.summary: 'The Customhouse' puts two histories in front of the romance: a Salem judge in the family line, and the narrator's own appointment to a federal post. Both are ways of belonging to an institution that judges people, and the seventeenth-century story is written by a man uneasily aware that he has inherited the bench.
themes.development: Stated in the introductory sketch, carried into the fiction by magistrates who are never villains, and left with Pearl, who inherits a murderer's money and leaves the country.

techniques.name: The invented frame
techniques.definition: A story told inside another story, so that every account reaches the reader through somebody with an interest in it.
techniques.bookDefinition: Presenting fiction as a document the narrator merely discovered and edited.
techniques.inThisBook: 'The Customhouse' produces a rag of cloth and Surveyor Pue's papers, gives the narrator a burn on the chest as authorisation, and never once pretends the reader should believe it.

techniques.name: The multiple explanation
techniques.definition: Offering natural and supernatural accounts of the same event without deciding between them.
techniques.bookDefinition: Offering natural and supernatural accounts of the same event without deciding between them.
techniques.inThisBook: The meteor in Chapter 12 is a sign, an optical effect, or a symptom of a diseased conscience; the mark on Dimmesdale's chest gets four separate explanations in Chapter 24, including the theory that there was nothing there.

techniques.name: The repeated tableau
techniques.definition: Staging the same arrangement of characters in the same place at intervals, so the changes register.
techniques.bookDefinition: Staging the same arrangement of characters in the same place at intervals, so the changes register.
techniques.inThisBook: Three scaffold scenes — noon, midnight, noon — with the same three people and a different distribution of knowledge each time.

techniques.name: Emblem
techniques.definition: An object made to stand for an idea, in the tradition of the emblem book and the heraldic device.
techniques.bookDefinition: An object made to stand for an idea, in the tradition of the emblem book and the heraldic device.
techniques.inThisBook: The book ends on a coat of arms, 'On a field, sable, the letter A, gules', turning a punishment into the formal blazon of a tombstone.

techniques.name: The intruding narrator
techniques.definition: A narrator who steps forward to generalise, moralise or admit uncertainty.
techniques.bookDefinition: A narrator who steps forward to generalise, moralise or admit uncertainty.
techniques.inThisBook: He tells us what Chillingworth's face is doing and then says he cannot be sure; he draws a moral in Chapter 24 and puts it in quotation marks, as if reporting somebody else's.

techniques.name: Names that argue
techniques.definition: Giving characters names that carry a judgement or a quality.
techniques.bookDefinition: Giving characters names that carry a judgement or a quality.
techniques.inThisBook: A physician who chills, a minister whose name contains a dimming, and a child named for a thing of great price bought at the cost of everything else.

quotations.text: which evidently found something congenial in the soil that had so early borne the black flower of civilized society, a prison
quotations.context: Describing the weeds on the grass-plot in front of the jail, in the book's opening paragraph.
quotations.analysis: The prison is called a flower, which makes punishment an organic product of settlement rather than a response to crime — and the chapter has already noted that every new colony lays out a graveyard and a jail before anything else. The rosebush beside the door arrives one sentence later, so the book's first image is a pair of flowers, one of them a building.

quotations.text: On the breast of her gown, in fine red cloth, surrounded with an elaborate embroidery and fantastic flourishes of gold-thread, appeared the letter A.
quotations.context: Hester's first appearance, coming out of the prison door with Pearl in her arms.
quotations.analysis: The sentence puts four clauses of craftsmanship in front of the letter itself, so the reader meets the needlework before the charge. Hester has been given a sentence and has answered it with her trade: the gold thread exceeds what the magistrates ordered, which is why the goodwives in the crowd are so angry about it.

quotations.text: “I will not speak!” answered Hester, turning pale as death, but responding to this voice, which she too surely recognized. “And my child must seek a heavenly Father; she shall never know an earthly one!”
quotations.speaker: Hester Prynne
quotations.context: Refusing, from the scaffold, to name Pearl's father, after Dimmesdale has been ordered to exhort her.
quotations.analysis: The refusal is addressed to the man asking for it, and the narrator's aside — she recognised the voice — lets the reader in on the arrangement a hundred pages before the town gets there. Her second sentence is not defiance but a legal fiction, a father invented to fill an empty space on a record, which is the same manoeuvre Dimmesdale will use for seven years.

quotations.text: It irks me, nevertheless, that the partner of her iniquity should not, at least, stand on the scaffold by her side. But he will be known!⁠—he will be known!⁠—he will be known!
quotations.speaker: Roger Chillingworth
quotations.context: Spoken by the stranger in the crowd, who has not yet given anyone his name.
quotations.analysis: Three identical clauses, and each one is a promise rather than a prediction — he is describing work he intends to do. The irony is that he is standing in a crowd deciding not to be known himself, so the sentence that launches his revenge is also the moment he takes a false name.

quotations.text: she felt or fancied, then, that the scarlet letter had endowed her with a new sense
quotations.context: After Hester settles in a cottage on the edge of the settlement and begins to support herself by her needle.
quotations.analysis: 'Felt or fancied' is the book's characteristic hedge, offered before the claim rather than after it. The sense she acquires is a detector for concealed sin in respectable people, which is either a supernatural gift or the ordinary consequence of being the only person in town with nothing left to hide.

quotations.text: It was the scarlet letter in another form; the scarlet letter endowed with life!
quotations.context: Describing the crimson and gold tunic Hester has made for Pearl to wear to the Governor's hall.
quotations.analysis: Hester has dressed her daughter to match her own badge, which is either an act of defiance or a confession that she can no longer imagine the child apart from the crime. The exclamation mark belongs to the narrator, and it is worth noticing how often the adults in this book need Pearl to be a symbol rather than a three-year-old with good clothes.

quotations.text: “God gave me the child!” cried she. “He gave her in requital of all things else, which ye had taken from me. She is my happiness!⁠—she is my torture, none the less! Pearl keeps me here in life! Pearl punishes me too!
quotations.speaker: Hester Prynne
quotations.context: Arguing against the magistrates' proposal to take Pearl away and have her brought up elsewhere.
quotations.analysis: She wins the argument by conceding the prosecution's case: yes, the child is a punishment, and that is the reason to leave her where she is. The two exclamations balance on the same verb, and the strategy is one Hester uses throughout — she never denies what the colony says about her, she simply refuses to draw its conclusions.

quotations.text: To the untrue man, the whole universe is false⁠—it is impalpable⁠—it shrinks to nothing within his grasp.
quotations.context: Explaining why Dimmesdale's visions of his dead parents and his congregation feel more solid to him than furniture.
quotations.analysis: The falsehood is described as spreading outward from the liar until it reaches the walls, which is a much stronger claim than that lying is wrong. It also explains the shape of Dimmesdale's sermons: the only thing he can still feel is the anguish, so the anguish is the only thing he can preach, and it is exactly what makes him beloved.

quotations.text: “Come up hither, Hester, thou and little Pearl,” said the Reverend Mr. Dimmesdale. “Ye have both been here before, but I was not with you. Come up hither once again, and we will stand all three together!”
quotations.speaker: Arthur Dimmesdale
quotations.context: On the scaffold at midnight, when no one in Boston is awake to see it.
quotations.analysis: Every word of this would be a confession at noon, and the sentence is grammatically identical to the one he will finally speak in Chapter 23. The only variable is the hour, which is the book's point about him: he has never lacked the words, only the daylight.

quotations.text: many people refused to interpret the scarlet A by its original signification. They said that it meant Able; so strong was Hester Prynne, with a woman’s strength.
quotations.context: After seven years of nursing the sick and clothing the poor.
quotations.analysis: The town has not forgiven her; it has relabelled her, which is cheaper. Note the passive shape of the reading — 'they said that it meant' — and note that the letter itself has not moved an inch: the same three stitches now certify a virtue, so the badge has proved capable of holding whatever the community needs it to hold.

quotations.text: Thou hadst great elements. Peradventure, hadst thou met earlier with a better love than mine, this evil had not been. I pity thee, for the good that has been wasted in thy nature!
quotations.speaker: Roger Chillingworth
quotations.context: By the shore, when Hester tells him she means to break her promise of secrecy.
quotations.analysis: It is the fairest judgement anyone passes on Hester and it comes from the man ruining her lover, which is the novel's way of showing that accuracy is not the same as goodness. The conditional in the middle sentence also admits what the whole plot depends on: a marriage arranged between an old scholar and a young woman is where the evil actually started.

quotations.text: Ye that have wronged me are not sinful, save in a kind of typical illusion; neither am I fiend-like, who have snatched a fiend’s office from his hands. It is our fate. Let the black flower blossom as it may!
quotations.speaker: Roger Chillingworth
quotations.context: Refusing Hester's suggestion that he forgive, in the same conversation.
quotations.analysis: He describes his own vocation in the language of employment — he has taken over a post that belonged to a fiend — and then abolishes all responsibility by calling it fate. The image returns from the first page, where the prison was a black flower growing out of the soil of settlement; here revenge is a plant too, and the gardener denies having planted it.

quotations.text: Let men tremble to win the hand of woman, unless they win along with it the utmost passion of her heart!
quotations.context: The narrator, after Hester admits to herself that she hates her husband.
quotations.analysis: The warning is addressed to men in general and delivered in the imperative, which is as close as this narrator comes to taking a side. It also quietly relocates the novel's original sin from the forest to the wedding: the marriage was contracted without the wife's heart, and everything after it follows.

quotations.text: “Mother,” said little Pearl, “the sunshine does not love you. It runs away and hides itself, because it is afraid of something on your bosom. Now, see! There it is, playing, a good way off. Stand you here, and let me run and catch it. I am but a child. It will not flee from me; for I wear nothing on my bosom yet!”
quotations.speaker: Pearl
quotations.context: On the forest path, walking to the meeting with Dimmesdale.
quotations.analysis: A child's observation about where the light happens to fall becomes the most efficient statement of the book's premise, and the last word does the damage: 'yet' assumes she will wear one in time. Pearl has worked out the rule of her mother's world without being told it, and she expects to inherit it.

quotations.text: “Never, never!” whispered she. “What we did had a consecration of its own. We felt it so! We said so to each other! Hast thou forgotten it?”
quotations.speaker: Hester Prynne
quotations.context: Answering Dimmesdale's question whether they are past hope.
quotations.analysis: She uses the vocabulary of the church to describe the act the church punished, and the tense is the point — 'had', not 'has', so she is defending the past rather than proposing a future. In 1850 this was the sentence reviewers objected to, and the novel neither retracts it nor lets her act on it.

quotations.text: There is one worse than even the polluted priest! That old man’s revenge has been blacker than my sin. He has violated, in cold blood, the sanctity of a human heart. Thou and I, Hester, never did so!
quotations.speaker: Arthur Dimmesdale
quotations.context: On learning that his physician and lodger is Hester's husband.
quotations.analysis: This is the moral scale the novel actually uses, and it is delivered by the man with the most to gain from it. 'In cold blood' is the operative phrase: the adultery is not excused, it is reclassified as a warm-blooded fault, while the sin the book cannot forgive is the deliberate, patient occupation of somebody else's inner life.

quotations.text: The scarlet letter was her passport into regions where other women dared not tread. Shame, Despair, Solitude! These had been her teachers⁠—stern and wild ones⁠—and they had made her strong, but taught her much amiss.
quotations.context: Explaining why Hester can contemplate flight and Dimmesdale cannot.
quotations.analysis: A punishment is redescribed as a travel document, which is the boldest reversal in the book — and then the final clause takes most of it back. 'Taught her much amiss' is the narrator declining to endorse his own heroine, and readers have been arguing ever since about whether that is Hawthorne's caution or Hawthorne's honesty.

quotations.text: The mystic token alighted on the hither verge of the stream. With a hand’s breadth farther flight it would have fallen into the water
quotations.context: Immediately after Hester unfastens the letter and throws it away among the leaves.
quotations.analysis: The narrator measures the miss in inches, which is the cruellest sentence in the chapter: the letter lands on this side of the brook, still retrievable, and so the whole flood of sunshine that follows is provisional. Pearl will make her pick it up within the hour, and the geography has already said she will have to.

quotations.text: “Is not this better,” murmured he, “than what we dreamed of in the forest?”
quotations.speaker: Arthur Dimmesdale
quotations.context: To Hester, as she supports him up the scaffold steps in front of the whole colony.
quotations.analysis: He is asking her to agree that public death is preferable to private escape, and she does not answer. The question is the last of his half-confessions: even at the end he needs the other person to pronounce the verdict, and Hawthorne withholds her reply so that the reader has to make it instead.

quotations.text: “Thou hast escaped me!” he repeated more than once. “Thou hast escaped me!”
quotations.speaker: Roger Chillingworth
quotations.context: Kneeling beside the scaffold as Dimmesdale confesses.
quotations.analysis: The verb makes the physician a gaoler rather than an avenger, which is what he has been for seven years — the point was never to punish the man but to keep him. Within a year Chillingworth is dead, and the book says plainly that he had nothing else left to do, which is as close as it comes to defining what revenge costs the avenger.

quotations.text: Be true! Be true! Be true! Show freely to the world, if not your worst, yet some trait whereby the worst may be inferred!
quotations.context: The moral the narrator draws from Dimmesdale's case, and puts in quotation marks.
quotations.analysis: Three imperatives and then an immediate discount: not the worst, only enough of a hint that the worst could be worked out. It is a morality of adequate disclosure rather than honesty, and the narrator has just spent a chapter reporting four incompatible accounts of the minister's chest — which suggests he knows how little inference can be trusted.

quotations.text: Here had been her sin; here, her sorrow; and here was yet to be her penitence.
quotations.context: Explaining why Hester comes back to the cottage on the edge of Boston years after she was free to leave.
quotations.analysis: Three clauses on the same adverb, and the tenses walk forward through them — had been, was, was yet to be — so the sentence turns a place into a chronology. The return is voluntary: the narrator notes that not the sternest magistrate would have required it, which makes the letter, at the very end, the only thing she has ever chosen to wear.

quotations.text: “On a field, sable, the letter A, gules.”
quotations.context: The last line of the book: the device carved on the slab that covers Hester and Dimmesdale.
quotations.analysis: The novel ends in heraldic French, a language of inherited honour, applied to a mark of shame — and the two words for the colours, black and red, are the only description of the grave we get. A punishment has become a coat of arms, which is either the final rehabilitation of the letter or proof that it will outlast everyone who tried to fix its meaning.

quotations.text: it seemed to me, then, that I experienced a sensation not altogether physical, yet almost so, of burning heat; and as if the letter were not of red cloth, but red-hot iron. I shuddered, and involuntarily let it fall upon the floor.
quotations.context: The narrator places the found scrap of embroidery on his own chest in the disused upper room of the Salem custom house.
quotations.analysis: The hedging is doing serious work — not altogether physical, yet almost so — and it establishes the rule for every marvel in the romance that follows. A man who will not commit himself to a sensation he has just had is the right narrator for a book whose final chapter cannot decide whether there was anything on Dimmesdale's chest at all.

quotations.text: the floor of our familiar room has become a neutral territory, somewhere between the real world and fairyland, where the Actual and the Imaginary may meet, and each imbue itself with the nature of the other
quotations.context: Describing moonlight in a room he cannot write in, near the end of the introductory sketch.
quotations.analysis: This is Hawthorne defining the romance as a form before he writes one, and the capital letters on Actual and Imaginary make it a diagram rather than a mood. It also explains why the novel keeps offering two explanations for everything: a neutral territory has to remain neutral, and a narrator who settled the meteor would have surrendered the ground.

atAGlance.label: Published
atAGlance.note: Ticknor, Reed and Fields, Boston. A second edition followed within weeks.

atAGlance.label: Called
atAGlance.note: Hawthorne's own subtitle, and a claim about the kind of truth the book is offering.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.note: Daylight, midnight, daylight — the book's structure is a stage used three times.

atAGlance.label: Span
atAGlance.note: From Pearl at three months old to the Election Day sermon.

atAGlance.label: Frame
atAGlance.note: A sketch of Hawthorne's own surveyorship, which invents an archival source for everything that follows.

criticalViews.position: A psychological study of concealment
criticalViews.summary: The longest-standing reading takes the book's subject to be what secrecy does to a mind and a body, with Dimmesdale as the case and Chillingworth as the pathology of the observer.
criticalViews.counter: It tends to make Hester the occasion for two men's inner lives, when she is the only character in the book who acts.

criticalViews.position: A romance about historical inheritance
criticalViews.summary: Read with 'The Customhouse' attached, the novel is a nineteenth-century writer negotiating with a Puritan ancestry — a judge in the family, a federal post of his own — rather than a reconstruction of the 1640s.
criticalViews.counter: The frame can be treated as so decisive that the seventeenth-century story becomes merely illustrative, which is not how it reads.

criticalViews.position: A book about the government of women
criticalViews.summary: Criticism since the 1970s has concentrated on Hester's needle as the only economic independence available to her, on the magistrates' proposal to remove her child, and on the closing prophecy of a truth that could not be entrusted to a woman stained with sin.
criticalViews.counter: The final chapter's retreat — Hester returns, resumes the badge, and defers the revelation to someone purer — is hard to read as either endorsement or critique, and both sides claim it.

criticalViews.position: A study of interpretation itself
criticalViews.summary: The A is read half a dozen ways by half a dozen parties, the meteor gets three explanations, and the minister's chest gets four. On this account the romance is about communities deciding what marks mean, and the power that decision carries.
criticalViews.counter: Pushed far enough it turns a novel with real suffering in it into an essay on signs.

essayQuestions.question: How does Hawthorne use the three scaffold scenes to structure the novel?
essayQuestions.focus: Repetition, staging and the distribution of knowledge
plan: Set the three scenes side by side: Chapter 2 at noon, Chapter 12 at midnight, Chapter 23 at noon again.
Track who is present, who is watching, and who knows what at each of the three points.
Show that Dimmesdale's midnight words are nearly identical to his final ones, so the variable is the audience.
Use Chillingworth's position in each scene — in the crowd, at the foot, kneeling — to measure his progress.
Close on what the third scene fails to settle: the witnesses in Chapter 24 cannot agree what they saw.

essayQuestions.question: 'The letter changes meaning, but never stops working.' Discuss.
essayQuestions.focus: The unstable sign and the power behind it
plan: Begin with the gold thread in Chapter 2: Hester alters the sentence before she has served an hour of it.
Trace the readings — adultery, Able, an angel in the sky, a mark on a minister's chest.
Note who does the reading each time, and that the object itself never changes.
Test the case with Chapter 18, where the letter comes off and the forest brightens, and Chapter 19, where it goes back on.
Decide what it means that Hester resumes the badge when nobody is enforcing it.

essayQuestions.question: Is Chillingworth the villain of The Scarlet Letter?
essayQuestions.focus: Revenge, marriage and the ethics of observation
plan: Establish the facts he is right about, and the accuracy of his diagnosis in Chapter 10.
Use Chapter 14 to show him passing the fairest judgement anyone passes on Hester.
Set against that Dimmesdale's verdict in Chapter 17 — the violation of a human heart in cold blood.
Consider the marriage itself, and Chapter 15's warning to men who win a hand without a heart.
Weigh the conclusion: he dies within the year and leaves his property to the child of the man he destroyed.

essayQuestions.question: What does 'The Customhouse' do for the romance that follows?
essayQuestions.focus: Frame, provenance and the claims a romance makes
plan: Describe what the sketch claims: a scrap of cloth, Surveyor Pue's papers, a burn on the chest.
Note that all of it is invented, and that the sketch tells us so by its tone.
Use the moonlit room and the neutral territory as Hawthorne's own definition of the form.
Connect the narrator's ancestry and his federal office to the magistrates in the story.
Ask what would be lost if a modern edition printed the twenty-four chapters alone.

discussionQuestions: Hester is punished, Dimmesdale is revered, and Chillingworth is free. Does the ending correct any of that, or only end it?
Pearl is called a demon, an elf and the scarlet letter given life. What happens if you read her simply as a child?
The novel never dramatises the adultery. Why does Hawthorne begin after it, and what would change if he had not?
Chapter 24 gives four accounts of what was on Dimmesdale's chest, including the claim that there was nothing. Which one does the book prefer?
The forest lets the letter come off and the brook puts it back. Is nature on Hester's side in this book?
Hester says what they did had a consecration of its own. Does the novel ever answer her?

timeline.label: The approximate date of the opening scene
timeline.detail: The novel places Pearl's birth in the early 1640s, some fifteen or twenty years after the settlement of Boston.

timeline.label: Governor John Winthrop dies
timeline.detail: The historical death the novel puts on the night of Dimmesdale's midnight vigil, with a meteor over the town.

timeline.label: The Salem witch trials
timeline.detail: John Hathorne sat as one of the examining magistrates; the novelist added a w to the family name.

timeline.label: Nathaniel Hawthorne born in Salem
timeline.detail: His father, a ship's captain, died in Surinam four years later.

timeline.label: Twice-Told Tales
timeline.detail: The collection that made his name among writers, if not yet among book-buyers.

timeline.label: Hawthorne is appointed Surveyor of the Port of Salem
timeline.detail: Three years in the custom house gave him the material for the book's introductory sketch.

timeline.label: He loses the post, and his mother dies
timeline.detail: The dismissal followed a change of administration; the romance was written in the months after both events.

timeline.label: The Scarlet Letter is published in Boston
timeline.detail: Ticknor, Reed and Fields issued it in March; it sold out quickly enough to need a second printing at once.

timeline.label: A second edition carries a new preface
timeline.detail: Salem had taken 'The Customhouse' personally, and Hawthorne declined to withdraw a word of it.

timeline.label: The House of the Seven Gables
