timeline.detail: Written in the Berkshires, where Melville was his neighbour and about to dedicate Moby-Dick to him.

timeline.label: Hawthorne dies at Plymouth, New Hampshire
timeline.detail: He was buried at Sleepy Hollow Cemetery in Concord, Massachusetts.

timeline.label: Victor Sjöström films the novel with Lillian Gish as Hester
timeline.detail: The silent version fixed a popular image of the story that stayed in circulation for decades.

places.name: Salem, Massachusetts
places.note: Hawthorne's birthplace, the custom house of the frame, and the town his ancestor judged witches in.

places.name: Boston, Massachusetts
places.note: The colonial settlement of the romance: prison, marketplace, scaffold, Governor's hall and meeting-house.

places.name: King's Chapel Burying Ground
places.note: The old churchyard named in the first chapter, and the kind of ground the final slab belongs to.

places.name: Amsterdam
places.note: Where Hester and her husband lived before she sailed ahead of him to Massachusetts.

places.name: Concord, Massachusetts
places.note: The Old Manse, where Hawthorne wrote before Salem, and the cemetery where he was buried.

places.name: Lenox, Massachusetts
places.note: The Berkshire cottage he moved to months after publication, and where Melville rode over to see him.

related.why: Dedicated to Hawthorne a year later by a neighbour who had just read this book, and the other great American argument with a symbol.
The same case tried in England fifty years on: a woman marked by an event and judged for the rest of her life.
A later American novel about a woman whose independence is available only outside the settled community.
Another study of a first-person conscience formed against an institution, and of a secret kept inside a respectable house.
The other American book about a conscience that has been trained wrong by the community it belongs to.

books.title: The Tempest
books.author: William Shakespeare
books.setting: A ship in a storm, then an unnamed island, across a single afternoon
books.lengthNote: Around 2,000 lines — one of the shortest plays in the Folio
books.openingLine: Boatswain!
books.summary: A magician who was once Duke of Milan raises a storm to bring his enemies ashore on the island where he has lived in exile for twelve years. He has the whole afternoon planned before the play begins, and the interest lies in watching a man with absolute power discover what he actually wants to do with it. Almost alone among Shakespeare's plays it keeps to a single place and a few hours, so that the action and the performance take roughly the same time.

sourceText.label: Globe/Moby text of The Tempest
sourceText.note: Line numbers follow the traditional Globe numbering; modern editions differ by a line or two. Ariel's songs are printed inside another speaker's text in some settings, and are attributed here to Ariel.

structure.label: Act I
structure.title: A storm, and the twelve years behind it
structure.summary: The shipwreck is staged first and explained second. Prospero then tells Miranda the history she has never been told, wakes and dispatches Ariel, insults Caliban, and steers Ferdinand into meeting his daughter — four interviews in one scene, each conducted by a man who already knows how it ends.

scenes.title: The ship
scenes.summary: Courtiers get in the way of the crew; the Boatswain tells them rank means nothing to the weather.

scenes.title: The island
scenes.summary: Prospero recounts the usurpation to Miranda, sets Ariel back to work, curses Caliban and arranges Ferdinand's arrival.

structure.label: Act II
structure.title: Two conspiracies, one serious and one drunk
structure.summary: On one part of the island Gonzalo imagines a commonwealth with no trade, law or labour and is mocked for it; within fifty lines Antonio has talked Sebastian into murdering his brother. On another, Caliban meets a butler with a bottle and decides that a new master is the same thing as freedom.

scenes.title: The courtiers
scenes.summary: Gonzalo's utopia is laughed down; Antonio persuades Sebastian to kill the sleeping Alonso, and Ariel wakes them.

scenes.title: The bottle
scenes.summary: Trinculo shelters under Caliban's cloak, Stephano arrives with wine, and Caliban swears allegiance to a drunkard.

structure.label: Act III
structure.title: A betrothal, a plot and a banquet that vanishes
structure.summary: Miranda proposes marriage to Ferdinand while her father watches unseen. Caliban lays out a workable murder — take the books first — and is repeatedly interrupted by Ariel's mimicry. The act ends with the courtiers accused of their old crime by a spirit dressed as a harpy.

scenes.title: The log-pile
scenes.summary: Ferdinand carries wood; Miranda offers herself as wife, and Prospero approves from a distance.

scenes.title: The conspiracy
scenes.summary: Caliban explains how to kill Prospero; Ariel sows confusion by throwing his voice.

scenes.title: The harpy
scenes.summary: A banquet appears and disappears; Ariel indicts Alonso, Antonio and Sebastian to their faces.

structure.label: Act IV
structure.title: A masque, broken off
structure.summary: Prospero gives the young couple a wedding entertainment performed by spirits, and then stops it mid-dance because he has remembered Caliban. The interruption is the hinge of the play: the most beautiful thing he makes is abandoned because of the one creature he cannot govern by art.

scenes.title: The masque and the line of clothes
scenes.summary: Iris, Ceres and Juno bless the betrothal; Prospero breaks off the show, then traps the conspirators with a rack of glittering clothes.

structure.label: Act V
structure.title: Forgiveness, and the end of the magic
structure.summary: Ariel describes the suffering of the charmed courtiers and Prospero chooses mercy — before he has heard a word of apology from any of them. He abjures his art, restores Ferdinand to his father, claims Caliban as his own, frees Ariel, and steps forward to ask the audience for release.

scenes.title: The circle, and the epilogue
scenes.summary: Prospero breaks his staff, forgives his brother, discovers the lovers at chess, frees Ariel and asks for applause as absolution.

characters.name: Prospero
characters.role: The exiled Duke of Milan, and the island's magician
characters.summary: He lost a dukedom by preferring his library to government and has spent twelve years acquiring a power no government could match. Almost every event in the play is something he has arranged, which makes the one decision he has not rehearsed — to forgive rather than punish — the only genuine action in it.
characters.clue: A scholar who lost a dukedom to his own reading, and who runs an island the way a director runs a rehearsal room, down to the storm.

characters.name: Miranda
characters.role: Prospero's daughter, aged about fifteen
characters.summary: She has met three people in her life and remembers none of her own history until her father decides she should. Her instincts are consistently better than his: she pities the shipwrecked before she knows who they are, and she proposes marriage herself rather than waiting to be arranged into it.
characters.clue: She has seen three human faces in her life, weeps for strangers drowning, and asks a log-carrier to marry her before he can ask her.

characters.name: Ariel
characters.role: A spirit of the air, bound to Prospero's service
characters.summary: Everything the audience calls Prospero's magic is in fact Ariel's labour: the storm, the songs, the harpy, the masque, the invisible mischief. The relationship runs on a promise of freedom that is repeatedly deferred, and the play's most surprising moment is Ariel telling a human what pity would look like.
characters.clue: Invisible, tireless and unpaid: the one who actually raises the storm, sings the drowned father's song and asks, again, when the promise will be kept.

characters.name: Caliban
characters.role: Son of the witch Sycorax; the island's earlier inhabitant
characters.summary: He welcomed Prospero, showed him the fresh water and the fertile ground, and was enslaved for it after attempting to rape Miranda. The play gives him the case against his master and the best verse about the island, and then refuses to let either cancel the other out.
characters.clue: He showed the newcomer where the fresh springs were and has been carrying his firewood ever since; he speaks the loveliest lines about the island he says is his.

characters.name: Ferdinand
characters.role: Prince of Naples, Alonso's son
characters.summary: He is separated from the ship, told his father has drowned, and set to carrying logs — a trial that has no purpose except to make Miranda seem hard-won. He accepts the labour without complaint, which is the only test Prospero can devise and the only one he passes.

characters.name: Alonso
characters.role: King of Naples
characters.summary: He put Antonio into Prospero's dukedom and spends the play believing he has lost his son as a consequence. Grief, not argument, is what breaks him: by Act V he is the only one of the three guilty men who says anything resembling an apology.

characters.name: Antonio
characters.role: Prospero's brother, the usurping Duke of Milan
characters.summary: He took a dukedom once and, within an hour of washing ashore, is arranging a second murder for someone else's benefit. He is forgiven in the last scene and does not reply, a silence that most productions have to make a decision about.
characters.clue: He took his brother's title while the man was reading, and washes ashore only to start talking another younger brother into the same crime.

characters.name: Sebastian
characters.role: Alonso's brother
characters.summary: A mocker of other men's speeches who turns out to need only one conversation to be talked into killing his sleeping brother. He is the proof that Antonio's crime was not a single aberration but a piece of ordinary political reasoning.

characters.name: Gonzalo
characters.role: An old counsellor of Naples
characters.summary: He is the reason Prospero survived: he stocked the leaking boat with food, water and the books. His imagined commonwealth without money or magistrates is mocked on stage as nonsense, and it is also the only vision in the play of an island run by nobody.

characters.name: Stephano
characters.role: Alonso's butler, washed ashore with a butt of wine
characters.summary: Given a bottle and a worshipper, he declares himself king of the island within a scene. His plot against Prospero is the same plot as Antonio's, played by a drunk, and the parallel is the play's sharpest joke about how little ambition requires.

themes.name: Rule and service
themes.summary: Every relationship on the island is a version of master and servant: Prospero and Ariel, Prospero and Caliban, Prospero and Ferdinand at the log-pile, Stephano and his new subject. The play sets them side by side so that the differences between labour, slavery, apprenticeship and worship become visible.
themes.development: The first act establishes three servants with three grievances; the last frees one, claims another and says nothing at all about the third.

themes.name: Whose island is it
themes.summary: Caliban's claim is stated plainly in the first act and never refuted, only overruled. Shakespeare gives the dispossessed party the historical facts and the finest description of the place, and gives the occupier the power, which is why the play has been unignorable in the century of decolonisation.
themes.development: 'This island's mine' in 1.2 sets the terms; Gonzalo's commonwealth in 2.1 imagines an island belonging to nobody; the play ends without saying who is left on it.

themes.name: Magic as theatre
themes.summary: Prospero's art is indistinguishable from stagecraft: costumes, music, entrances, illusions, an interrupted masque. When he describes his own show dissolving he uses the words 'the great globe itself', spoken in a theatre of that name, and the metaphor stops being a metaphor.
themes.development: The storm is staged in 1.1, exposed as a production in 1.2, perfected in the masque of 4.1, renounced in 5.1, and handed to the audience in the epilogue.

themes.name: Freedom and what is mistaken for it
themes.summary: Three characters want to be free and each means something different by it: Ariel wants release from service, Caliban wants his island back, and Stephano's crew want a bottle and a crown. The play is careful to make the drunkards' freedom song ridiculous without making Caliban's demand ridiculous.
themes.development: Ariel asks in 1.2 and is refused; Caliban sings of a new master in 2.2; Ariel is released in the last twenty lines, and Prospero then asks to be freed himself.

themes.name: Revenge given up
themes.summary: Prospero has the power to do anything he likes to the men who ruined him, and the decisive scene is the one in which he decides not to. What makes it strange is the timing: he chooses mercy after a spirit has described their suffering to him, and before any of them has asked for it.
themes.development: Twelve years of grievance are recited in 1.2; the harpy indicts the guilty in 3.3; 5.1 turns on Ariel's remark that he would feel pity if he were human.

themes.name: Nature and nurture
themes.summary: Prospero insists that Caliban is a devil on whom nurture will never stick, having spent years teaching him. Miranda, raised on the same island by the same man with the same books, is his counter-example, and the play leaves the argument standing unresolved between them.
themes.development: Caliban is taught language in 1.2 and uses it to curse; Prospero's verdict comes in 4.1; the masque of Ceres and Juno makes fertility itself a thing to be blessed and supervised.

techniques.name: Retrospective exposition
techniques.definition: Putting the backstory into a single long scene of telling rather than showing.
techniques.bookDefinition: Putting the backstory into a single long scene of telling rather than showing.
techniques.inThisBook: Act I Scene 2 is nearly a third of the play and consists largely of Prospero explaining the past to people who interrupt him. Because he controls what is told and when, the exposition is also a demonstration of his character.

techniques.name: The court masque
techniques.definition: A courtly entertainment of gods, song, dance and blessing, staged for an occasion rather than a plot.
techniques.bookDefinition: A courtly entertainment of gods, song, dance and blessing, staged for an occasion rather than a plot.
techniques.inThisBook: The betrothal masque of 4.1 imports an entire Jacobean art form into the play and then breaks it off in the middle, which no masque at court would ever have done.

techniques.name: Metatheatre
techniques.definition: A play drawing attention to the fact that it is a play.
techniques.bookDefinition: A play drawing attention to the fact that it is a play.
techniques.inThisBook: Prospero's actors are spirits, his revels end, the great globe dissolves, and the last speech asks the audience to release him with their hands. The illusion is dismantled in front of the people it was made for.

techniques.name: Song
techniques.definition: A sung passage standing outside the dialogue, free to say what the speaking characters cannot.
techniques.bookDefinition: Sung lyric used to carry information a speech cannot.
techniques.inThisBook: Ariel's songs lead Ferdinand ashore, tell him his father is dead in language too beautiful to be grief, and wake Gonzalo in time to prevent a murder. The music does the work the plot would otherwise need scenes for.

techniques.name: Parody subplot
techniques.definition: A low plot that repeats the main plot's action in a debased form.
techniques.bookDefinition: A low plot that repeats the main plot's action in a debased form.
techniques.inThisBook: Stephano, Trinculo and Caliban plan exactly the crime Antonio and Sebastian plan, one scene apart, with a bottle in place of a sword — and are treated as a farce while the courtiers are treated as a threat.

techniques.name: The classical unities
techniques.definition: Keeping a play to one place, one day and one action.
techniques.bookDefinition: Keeping a play to one place, one day and one action.
techniques.inThisBook: Alone among the late plays, this one observes them: the characters repeatedly state the time, and the three hours of the story run at roughly the speed of the performance.

quotations.text: What cares these roarers for the name of king? To cabin: silence! trouble us not.
quotations.speaker: Boatswain
quotations.context: In the storm, ordering the king and his councillors below deck.
quotations.analysis: The play's first political statement is made by a working sailor to a monarch, and it is about the limits of titles. Within a hundred lines the audience learns that the storm was manufactured, so the one moment when rank genuinely counts for nothing turns out to have been arranged by a duke.

quotations.text: If by your art, my dearest father, you have Put the wild waters in this roar, allay them.
quotations.speaker: Miranda
quotations.context: Her first words in the play, watching the wreck from the shore.
quotations.analysis: She knows at once that the storm is her father's doing, which tells the audience more about the household than any description could. The conditional 'if' is politeness rather than doubt, and the sentence ends in an imperative: the only person on the island who gives Prospero orders is fifteen.

quotations.text: What seest thou else In the dark backward and abysm of time?
quotations.speaker: Prospero
quotations.context: Testing how much Miranda remembers of her life before the island.
quotations.analysis: 'Backward' is used as a noun, which is not ordinary English then or now; the phrase makes the past a place you could fall into. He is checking the extent of her ignorance before deciding how much of it to repair, and the grandeur of the image conceals a piece of information management.

quotations.text: Hell is empty And all the devils are here.
quotations.speaker: Ariel
quotations.context: Reporting how Ferdinand leapt from the burning ship.
quotations.analysis: Ariel is quoting a terrified boy, so the most famous line in the first act belongs to a character who never says it again. The joke underneath it is theological: the devils on this island are a spirit doing as it is told and a man who was once a duke.

quotations.text: Is there more toil? Since thou dost give me pains, Let me remember thee what thou hast promised, Which is not yet perform'd me.
quotations.speaker: Ariel
quotations.context: After performing the storm, before being sent out again.
quotations.analysis: The complaint is contractual rather than emotional: work has been done, a promise was made, the promise is outstanding. Prospero's answer is to recite the rescue from the cloven pine, which is the standard reply of an employer who would rather discuss gratitude than terms.

quotations.text: This island's mine, by Sycorax my mother, Which thou takest from me.
quotations.speaker: Caliban
quotations.context: Answering Prospero's summons, before the quarrel about his attempt on Miranda.
quotations.analysis: The claim is made in the language of inheritance law — by his mother, therefore his — which is exactly how Prospero would argue for Milan. Nobody on stage disputes the facts; they change the subject to his conduct, and the play never returns to settle the question of title.

quotations.text: You taught me language; and my profit on't Is, I know how to curse. The red plague rid you For learning me your language!
quotations.speaker: Caliban
quotations.context: The end of his argument with Prospero and Miranda about his education.
quotations.analysis: The complaint is delivered in fluent blank verse, which quietly contradicts it: he has plainly got more from the lessons than curses. 'Profit' is a merchant's word, and 'learning' here means teaching — the exchange is being audited, and the pupil finds it a bad bargain.

quotations.text: Full fathom five thy father lies; Of his bones are coral made; Those are pearls that were his eyes: Nothing of him that doth fade But doth suffer a sea-change Into something rich and strange.
quotations.speaker: Ariel
quotations.context: Sung invisibly to Ferdinand, who believes his father has drowned.
quotations.analysis: The song tells a lie — Alonso is alive — in the gentlest possible form, turning a corpse into jewellery so that grief arrives already consoled. 'Sea-change' enters English here, and the whole lyric is an argument that loss can be transformation, which is the claim the last act will have to make good.
quotations.source: Globe/Moby text, 1.2.461-466; sung by Ariel within Ferdinand's scene

quotations.text: I' the commonwealth I would by contraries Execute all things; for no kind of traffic Would I admit; no name of magistrate;
quotations.speaker: Gonzalo
quotations.context: Imagining what he would do if he were king of the island.
quotations.analysis: The speech follows Florio's translation of Montaigne closely enough that the borrowing is visible, and Shakespeare stages it as a joke: Antonio and Sebastian point out that a commonwealth with no sovereignty has just been proposed by a man who began by saying he would be king of it. The mockery does not dispose of the idea, and the contradiction is the play's own.

quotations.text: And by that destiny to perform an act Whereof what's past is prologue, what to come In yours and my discharge.
quotations.speaker: Antonio
quotations.context: Persuading Sebastian to murder the sleeping Alonso.
quotations.analysis: The line is now quoted as though it were wisdom about history; in the play it is a murderer's argument that the past is merely the warm-up and the killing is the real performance. 'Prologue' and 'act' are theatre words, put into the mouth of the man whose plot competes with Prospero's for control of the island's plot.

quotations.text: Be not afeard; the isle is full of noises, Sounds and sweet airs, that give delight and hurt not.
quotations.speaker: Caliban
quotations.context: Reassuring Stephano and Trinculo, who have heard Ariel playing on an invisible pipe.
quotations.analysis: The drunkards are frightened and the so-called monster is the one who knows the island is safe. Shakespeare gives the play's most delicate verse to the character everyone on stage calls a beast, three minutes after he has explained how to drive a nail into a man's skull.

quotations.text: Remember First to possess his books; for without them He's but a sot, as I am, nor hath not One spirit to command
quotations.speaker: Caliban
quotations.context: Instructing Stephano on how the murder of Prospero must be done.
quotations.analysis: It is the most accurate piece of political analysis in the play, and it comes from the servant: the power is not in the man, it is in the library. Prospero lost Milan to his books and now holds the island by them, and the only character who understands the mechanism is the one with no share in it.

quotations.text: I am your wife, if you will marry me; If not, I'll die your maid: to be your fellow You may deny me; but I'll be your servant, Whether you will or no.
quotations.speaker: Miranda
quotations.context: Proposing to Ferdinand at the log-pile, with Prospero watching unseen.
quotations.analysis: She proposes, sets out the alternatives and closes off the last of them: the grammar moves from a condition to a refusal to accept one. Having been given no information about her own life for twelve years, she takes the single decision available to her without consulting the man who arranged the meeting.

quotations.text: Our revels now are ended. These our actors, As I foretold you, were all spirits and Are melted into air, into thin air:
quotations.speaker: Prospero
quotations.context: Breaking off the wedding masque on remembering Caliban's conspiracy.
quotations.analysis: He is apologising to his son-in-law for a cancelled entertainment, and the apology grows into the play's largest statement about existence within eight lines. Note that he says 'as I foretold you': the consolation is that the disappearance was always in the design, which is true of a masque and is what he needs to believe about a dukedom.

quotations.text: We are such stuff As dreams are made on, and our little life Is rounded with a sleep.
quotations.speaker: Prospero
quotations.context: The close of the same speech, before he admits his mind is troubled.
quotations.analysis: 'Made on' means made of, so human beings are built out of the same material as the vanished spirits — not that life resembles a dream but that it is cut from it. 'Rounded' can mean surrounded or finished off, and the line declines to choose, which is why it can be read as consolation or as the bleakest sentence in the play.

quotations.text: A devil, a born devil, on whose nature Nurture can never stick; on whom my pains, Humanely taken, all, all lost, quite lost;
quotations.speaker: Prospero
quotations.context: Alone, immediately after breaking off the masque.
quotations.analysis: The verdict is delivered by a man who has just spent years teaching the creature he says cannot be taught, and the repetitions — 'all, all lost, quite lost' — are those of someone arguing with himself. It is also the play's clearest statement of the position Miranda's existence contradicts.

quotations.text: Though with their high wrongs I am struck to the quick, Yet with my nobler reason 'gaitist my fury Do I take part: the rarer action is In virtue than in vengeance
quotations.speaker: Prospero
quotations.context: Immediately after Ariel says that he would pity the charmed courtiers if he were human.
quotations.analysis: The decision that ends twelve years of planning is made in four lines and prompted by a spirit. 'Rarer' means both more unusual and finer, which concedes that mercy is the less natural response; and the reason he gives is not that they deserve it but that it is the better piece of work.

quotations.text: But this rough magic I here abjure, and, when I have required Some heavenly music, which even now I do, To work mine end upon their senses that This airy charm is for, I'll break my staff, Bury it certain fathoms in the earth, And deeper than did ever plummet sound I'll drown my book.
quotations.speaker: Prospero
quotations.context: Ending the long invocation of the elves of hills, brooks and groves.
quotations.analysis: He renounces the art in the middle of using it: the sentence that abjures magic also orders up the heavenly music that will disarm his enemies. The staff is broken, but the book is drowned deeper than any sounding line can reach, which is a peculiar precaution against an object he says he no longer wants.

quotations.text: How beauteous mankind is! O brave new world, That has such people in't!
quotations.speaker: Miranda
quotations.context: On seeing the assembled courtiers for the first time.
quotations.analysis: The people she is admiring include the two men who set her adrift to die and a third who tried to murder his brother two days ago. Prospero's reply — three words, 'Tis new to thee — is the most economical piece of irony in Shakespeare, and it is the last thing he says to his daughter in the play.

quotations.text: Two of these fellows you Must know and own; this thing of darkness! Acknowledge mine.
quotations.speaker: Prospero
quotations.context: Presenting the three conspirators to Alonso.
quotations.analysis: The sentence is built to balance: two servants belong to the king, one belongs to me. 'Acknowledge' is doing a great deal of work — it can mean simply claiming a possession, or admitting a kinship, and the entire modern performance history of the play turns on which of those an actor decides to play.

quotations.text: As you from crimes would pardon'd be, Let your indulgence set me free.
quotations.speaker: Prospero
quotations.context: The last two lines of the epilogue, spoken alone to the audience.
quotations.analysis: The man who has spent the play releasing or refusing to release other people ends by asking to be released himself, and the currency is applause. 'Indulgence' was also the word for a remission of punishment granted by the Church, so the audience is being asked to perform an absolution that the play's own theology could not quite supply.

atAGlance.label: Written
atAGlance.note: After reports of the 1609 Sea Venture wreck reached London, and before the recorded court performance of November 1611.

atAGlance.label: First printed
atAGlance.note: No quarto exists. The First Folio prints it first in the volume, at the head of the comedies.

atAGlance.label: Sources
atAGlance.note: Shipwreck pamphlets, Florio's Montaigne, Ovid and the court masque, combined rather than adapted.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.note: Act I Scene 2 alone runs to about a third of the play.

criticalViews.position: The play as Shakespeare's farewell
criticalViews.summary: The oldest popular reading takes Prospero's renunciation of magic as the dramatist laying down his own art, and the epilogue as a retirement speech.
criticalViews.counter: It sits badly with the facts of the career: Shakespeare went on to collaborate on at least two more plays, and the epilogue is a conventional appeal for applause of a kind other plays also make.

criticalViews.position: The play as a colonial document
criticalViews.summary: Read beside the Bermuda pamphlets and the Virginia venture, the island becomes a place with an inhabitant, a claim and an occupation, and Caliban's case is the one the drama cannot dispose of.
criticalViews.counter: The Mediterranean geography is insistent — Milan, Naples, Tunis, Algiers — and a reading built entirely on the Atlantic has to work around it.

criticalViews.position: The play as a study of service
criticalViews.summary: A third approach puts Ariel rather than Caliban at the centre and reads the island as a workplace: promised wages, deferred release, labour that is invisible because it is magical.
criticalViews.counter: It risks flattening the difference between a spirit who is freed in the last scene and a man whose future the play never mentions.

essayQuestions.question: How far does The Tempest endorse Prospero's rule of the island?
essayQuestions.focus: Authority, service and the limits of art
plan: Begin with the fact that the audience is shown the storm before it is told who made it, so the first experience of his power is as a catastrophe.
Set Ariel's petition in 1.2 beside Caliban's claim in the same scene: two servants, two grievances, two completely different answers from the same master.
Use the breaking of the masque in 4.1 to show that his control is dependent on his attention, and collapses the moment he remembers a threat.
Weigh the decision in 5.1: mercy chosen freely, but only after a spirit has had to describe what pity is.
Close on the epilogue, where a man who has ruled everything asks an audience for the power to leave.

essayQuestions.question: 'The most eloquent character in the play is its slave.' Discuss Caliban.
essayQuestions.focus: Language, dispossession and sympathy
plan: Establish what Caliban actually claims in 1.2 and note that nobody on stage denies the history, only changes the subject.
Examine the verse of 'the isle is full of noises' and ask why Shakespeare gives this speech to this character at this point in a conspiracy scene.
Balance the sympathy against 1.2 and the attempt on Miranda, which the play states plainly and does not excuse.
Compare his understanding of Prospero's power — take the books first — with the courtiers' failure to understand anything.
Finish with 'this thing of darkness', and with the play's silence about what becomes of him.

essayQuestions.question: What is the effect of staging the masque in Act IV and then interrupting it?
essayQuestions.focus: Spectacle, form and control
plan: Describe what a Jacobean masque was for: blessing, order, flattery of the ruler who paid for it.
Show how the Ceres and Juno masque fits that description exactly, down to the banishing of Venus and Cupid from the betrothal.
Identify the interruption as the only point where Prospero's plan is affected by something outside it.
Read the 'revels' speech as an attempt to convert a failure of stage management into a philosophy.
Consider the staging consequences: how a production makes the spirits vanish determines how seriously it takes the speech.

essayQuestions.question: Is the ending of The Tempest a reconciliation?
essayQuestions.focus: Forgiveness, silence and what is left unresolved
plan: List what is settled in 5.1: the dukedom restored, the marriage arranged, Ariel freed, the ship repaired.
Set against it what is not: Antonio says nothing, Sebastian jokes, Caliban's future is never mentioned.
Look closely at Miranda's 'brave new world' and Prospero's reply as a test of how much the audience is being asked to believe.
Use Gonzalo's summary at 5.1.235-241 — all of us found ourselves when no man was his own — and ask whether the play has earned it.
Decide what the epilogue changes: a character stepping out of the fiction to ask for pardon from people who have not been wronged.

discussionQuestions: Prospero forgives his enemies before any of them apologises. Does that make the forgiveness stronger or emptier?
Ariel and Caliban are both unfree. Why does the play release one and say nothing about the other?
Miranda has been told nothing about her own history until the day the play begins. What does her father gain from that?
The conspiracy of the drunkards repeats the conspiracy of the courtiers almost exactly. Why is one funny?
If a production cuts the epilogue, what is lost?

timeline.label: Florio's translation of Montaigne published
timeline.detail: The English 'Of the Cannibals' behind Gonzalo's commonwealth speech becomes available.

timeline.label: The Sea Venture wrecked on Bermuda
timeline.detail: Bound for Virginia, the ship broke up on the reefs; the survivors reached Jamestown the following year.

timeline.label: Jourdain's A Discovery of the Barmudas printed
timeline.detail: One of the pamphlets that turned the wreck into a London story of storm, survival and abundant islands.

timeline.label: Performed before James I at Whitehall on 1 November
timeline.detail: The Revels record is the earliest firm evidence that the play existed and was being acted.

timeline.label: Played at court during the festivities for Princess Elizabeth's marriage
timeline.detail: One of a group of plays given by the King's Men that winter for the betrothal and wedding celebrations.

timeline.label: First Folio
timeline.detail: The only early text, and the volume opens with it — unusually well printed, with full stage directions and a cast list.

timeline.label: Dryden and Davenant's The Enchanted Island
timeline.detail: A Restoration rewriting that gave Miranda a sister and Caliban a mate, and held the stage for well over a century.

timeline.label: Peter Brook directs John Gielgud as Prospero
timeline.detail: At the Shakespeare Memorial Theatre; remembered for a Prospero of severity rather than serenity.

timeline.label: Jonathan Miller's colonial production
timeline.detail: Casting made the island's politics explicit, and helped establish a reading British theatre has not since put down.

timeline.label: Peter Greenaway's Prospero's Books
timeline.detail: A film that takes the library rather than the island as the centre of the play.

timeline.label: Julie Taymor's film, with Helen Mirren as Prospera
timeline.detail: Changing the magician's sex reorganises the play's questions about parenthood, exile and authority.

places.name: Milan
places.note: The dukedom Prospero lost to his brother while he studied.

places.name: Naples
places.note: Alonso's kingdom, and the wedding party the shipwrecked court was returning from.

places.name: Tunis
places.note: Where Claribel was married, and the voyage home from which the storm interrupts.

places.name: Algiers
places.note: Argier in the text: the city from which Sycorax was banished to the island.

places.name: Bermuda
places.note: The still-vex'd Bermoothes of Ariel's speech, and the site of the 1609 wreck behind the play's storm.

places.name: Whitehall Palace, London
places.note: Where the first recorded performance was given before James I on 1 November 1611.

related.why: The other late play in which a ruler's damage is repaired after years, though there the miracle is a statue rather than a storm.
Written at about the same time, and equally willing to let romance conventions do work that tragedy would refuse.
Shipwreck, a lost daughter and reunion at sea: the pattern The Tempest compresses into one afternoon.
More's island commonwealth stands behind the tradition Gonzalo is drawing on, and being mocked for.
The earlier play of spirits, spells and interrupted entertainments, with the magic used for comedy rather than government.

books.title: The Turn of the Screw
books.author: Henry James
books.setting: Bly, an old family place in Essex, across one summer and autumn, with a Christmas-Eve frame in another old house
books.lengthNote: A prologue and twenty-four short chapters; the governess who writes most of it is never named
books.openingLine: The story had held us, round the fire, sufficiently breathless, but except the obvious remark that it was gruesome, as, on Christmas Eve in an old house, a strange tale should essentially be, I remember no comment uttered till somebody happened to say that it was the only case he had met in which such a visitation had fallen on a child.
books.summary: A young woman takes charge of two orphaned children in a country house on the condition that she never trouble their guardian about anything. She begins to see a man on a tower and a woman by a lake, learns from the housekeeper that both are dead, and concludes that they have come back for the children. Whether that conclusion is a rescue or the thing the children need rescuing from is the question James spends twenty-four chapters refusing to answer.
books.referenceStyle: chapter, with the frame narrative given as Prologue

sourceText.label: Standard Ebooks text of The Turn of the Screw
sourceText.note: The frame is headed Prologue; the governess's manuscript runs in unheaded chapters numbered I to XXIV, and references here use those numerals.

structure.label: Prologue
structure.title: Christmas Eve, and a manuscript in a locked drawer
structure.summary: Guests at a country house are trading ghost stories when Douglas offers one he has kept to himself for years. He has to send to town for the manuscript, which delays the telling by two nights, and he dies before the outer narrator makes the copy the reader is holding.

scenes.summary: A story about a child prompts Douglas to promise one about two.
A young clergyman's daughter answers an advertisement in Harley Street and accepts a post nobody else will take.
She promises never to appeal to her employer about anything, and never sees him again.

structure.label: Chapters I-IV
structure.title: Bly, two beautiful children, and a man on the tower
structure.summary: The governess arrives to find Flora enchanting, Mrs Grose welcoming and the house larger than she expected. A letter says Miles has been expelled and gives no reason; she decides to ask nobody. Twice she sees a strange man, once on the tower and once looking in through the dining-room window.

scenes.summary: First evening at Bly, and a place that seems to her like a great drifting ship.
The school's letter is burned in conversation rather than answered.
Miles arrives; at the end of her own hour a figure appears at the top of the tower.
The same man looks in at a window, and the governess goes out to take his place at the glass.

structure.label: Chapters V-VIII
structure.title: The housekeeper names two of the dead
structure.summary: From the governess's description, Mrs Grose identifies Peter Quint, a former valet who is dead, and then Miss Jessel, the previous governess, also dead. What Mrs Grose actually says about the pair is much less than what the governess takes from it, and the difference between the two is the engine of the rest of the book.

scenes.summary: The description is given, and Mrs Grose's face finishes it.
Quint was too free with the boy; the governess decides she is a screen between the children and the dead.
A woman in black across the lake, seen while Flora plays with her back to the water.
Mrs Grose is pressed on what she knew and admits she said nothing at the time.

structure.label: Chapters IX-XIV
structure.title: Night stairs, and children who are never caught
structure.summary: The governess keeps watch by night and finds Quint on the staircase, Miss Jessel on the stair below, Flora at the window and Miles on the lawn looking up. Every incident is explained away charmingly by one child or the other, and she begins to read the charm itself as the proof.

scenes.summary: A figure on the staircase in the small hours, met without a candle.
Flora is found at the window; Miles admits he was out on the lawn to be, for once, bad.
The governess reconstructs the night with Mrs Grose in the daylight.
She concludes that the children belong to the dead and always have.
Weeks of unspoken watching, in which nobody names anything.
Miles, walking to church, asks when he is to go back to school.

structure.label: Chapters XV-XXI
structure.title: A letter, a lake, and Flora sent away
structure.summary: The governess writes to the guardian at last, finds Miss Jessel at her own schoolroom desk, and takes Mrs Grose to the lake to force Flora into an admission. Flora sees nothing, turns on her, and is taken to London the next morning; the letter never left the house.

scenes.summary: Miss Jessel is found in the schoolroom and addressed aloud.
The governess agrees to write to the children's uncle.
A night scene at Miles's bedside, ended by a gust that blows out the candle.
Miles plays the piano while Flora slips out of the house.
The search leads to the lake, where the boat has been moved.
The governess names Miss Jessel across the water; Flora sees nothing and asks to be taken away.
Mrs Grose reports Flora's new vocabulary, and the letter is found to have been stolen.

structure.label: Chapters XXII-XXIV
structure.title: Alone in the house with Miles
structure.summary: With Flora and Mrs Grose gone, the governess sets out to get a confession over a dish of mutton. Miles admits he said things at school; the white face appears at the window; and in getting the name out of him she is holding a child whose heart has stopped.

scenes.summary: The house's servants stare, and dinner is served downstairs like a trial.
Miles asks to be let alone and is not.
The confession, the figure at the glass, and the last three words of the book.

characters.name: The governess
characters.role: Twenty years old, a country parson's youngest daughter, in her first post
characters.summary: She writes the account, so every fact in it has already passed through her. She is brave, observant and entirely alone with a responsibility she has promised not to share, and the novella gives the reader no instrument for telling her courage apart from her certainty.
characters.clue: She takes a post on condition that she never write to her employer, and then never does, even when she has a reason that would justify it.

characters.name: Mrs Grose
characters.role: The housekeeper at Bly
characters.summary: She cannot read, which means every written thing at Bly passes through the governess, and she knows the household's history but volunteers almost none of it. Her agreement is usually a repetition of what she has just been told, and the governess treats each repetition as independent evidence.
characters.clue: She keeps the keys and the past of the house, and has to ask somebody else to read her letters.

characters.name: Miles
characters.role: Ten years old, sent down from school
characters.summary: Expelled for something the school will not put in writing and he will not put into words, he is courteous, oddly adult and perfectly capable of managing the woman in charge of him. The single thing he finally admits, that he said things to boys he liked, is small enough to be anything at all.
characters.clue: A boy of ten who cannot go back to school, plays the piano to cover his sister's escape, and dies at the moment he gives up a name.

characters.name: Flora
characters.role: Eight years old, Miles's sister
characters.summary: For half the book she is the most charming child in English fiction and for one page she is something else, refusing to look where she is told to look and turning a face on the governess that the narrative calls hard. She is removed to London and never gets to give her account.
characters.clue: She shows a new governess round a house like a small chatelaine, and later begs to be taken away from her.

characters.name: Peter Quint
characters.role: The master's former valet, dead before the story begins
characters.summary: Described before he is named, in a passage of clothes and hair and a habit of going bareheaded, and identified by a housekeeper who has heard the description rather than seen the man. He died on the ice coming back from a public house, and everything else said about him at Bly is inference.
characters.clue: He wore his master's waistcoats without permission and was found dead on a road one winter morning.

characters.name: Miss Jessel
characters.role: The previous governess, dead before the story begins
characters.summary: She left Bly and died, and the reason is given only in hints that the present governess completes for herself. Seen in black across the lake and at the schoolroom desk, she is the position the narrator currently occupies, which is a large part of why she is so frightening.
characters.clue: She sat at this desk before, left in the middle of a summer, and is seen again on the other side of the water.

characters.name: The master
characters.role: The children's uncle, in Harley Street
characters.summary: Handsome, busy and entirely offstage after the prologue, he creates the conditions of the story by refusing to be part of it. His prohibition removes the one person who could confirm or dismiss anything the governess believes, and she keeps to it long after keeping to it has stopped making sense.
characters.clue: He is handsome, lives in London, and requires only that nobody ever tell him anything.

characters.name: Douglas
characters.role: The reader of the manuscript, in the frame
characters.summary: He knew the governess when he was an undergraduate and she was his sister's governess, kept her manuscript in a locked drawer for years, and admits she was in love with her employer before he begins. He dies soon afterwards and sends the papers to the narrator, so the text arrives with its witness already gone.
characters.clue: He keeps a story in a locked drawer for forty years and has to send to town for it before he can tell it.
traits: dead before the account is copied

themes.name: Evidence and the single witness
themes.summary: Nobody else in the story ever sees an apparition. The governess's proof is that Mrs Grose recognises a description, and Mrs Grose is being asked to recognise it after being told what to expect. James keeps the reader in exactly the position of a juror with one witness and no corroboration, and then stops.
themes.development: Corroboration in Chapter V feels total; by Chapter XX, when Flora looks at an empty stretch of water, the same procedure produces nothing at all.

themes.name: Innocence and what adults do with it
themes.canonicalName: Innocence and what adults do with it
themes.summary: The children's beauty is described in religious terms and then read as a disguise, and the reading comes first: the governess decides what she is looking for and then finds the children charming in a way that confirms it. Whatever is wrong at Bly, the adults' certainty about it is doing measurable harm by the last chapter.
themes.development: A passion of tenderness in Chapter III, a theory of possession in Chapter XII, and a boy held to his confession until his heart stops in Chapter XXIV.

themes.name: The unsaid
themes.summary: Nothing in this book is ever specified. The school will not state Miles's offence, Mrs Grose will not describe what Quint did, and the governess repeatedly decides that naming a thing would be worse than leaving it. James makes the reader supply the content, which is why no two readers frighten themselves in quite the same way.
themes.development: A letter that gives no reason, a housekeeper who says only that Quint was too free, and a confession that amounts to saying things to boys who liked him.

themes.name: Class, service and who may speak
themes.summary: Everyone at Bly is somebody's employee, and the horror is organised by rank: a valet who wore his master's waistcoats, a governess who is neither family nor servant, a housekeeper who cannot read, and a master who has purchased the right not to be told. Quint's real offence, as Bly describes it, is a matter of position before it is anything else.
themes.development: The prohibition in the Prologue, the too-free valet in Chapter VI, and the schoolroom desk that two women occupy in turn.

themes.name: Possession, influence and rescue
themes.summary: The governess understands herself as standing between the children and the dead, a screen, a shield, the one person who will act. That self-description is heroic and also exactly what a frightening adult would say, and the story ends with the rescue and the fatality being the same gesture.
themes.development: The screen in Chapter VI, the demons in Chapter XII, and the embrace in Chapter XXIV that is both a saving grip and the thing that kills.

themes.name: The frame, and how a story gets to us
themes.canonicalName: The frame, and how a story gets to us
themes.summary: Three narrators and a forty-year delay stand between the reader and Bly. The manuscript is in a locked drawer, its keeper is in love with its author, and by the time it is copied out both of them are dead, so the text arrives with every route back to a fact closed off.
themes.development: Douglas promises a second turn of the screw in the Prologue and then dies; the novella never returns to the fire, and no outer narrator comments at the end.

techniques.name: Frame narrative
techniques.definition: A story told inside another story, so that every account reaches the reader through somebody with an interest in it.
techniques.bookDefinition: A story told inside another story, by a narrator with his own interests.
techniques.inThisBook: The Christmas-Eve frame gives the story a title, a delay, a champion for the governess and, crucially, no way of checking her: it closes without returning to the fireside.

techniques.name: Withheld specifics
techniques.definition: Refusing to name the act, the word or the offence that the plot turns on.
techniques.bookDefinition: Refusing to name the act, the word or the offence that the plot turns on.
techniques.inThisBook: Miles's expulsion, Quint's freedom and Miss Jessel's disgrace are all left as gaps, and readers fill them with material James never supplied.

techniques.name: Suspended syntax
techniques.definition: Sentences that qualify themselves clause by clause before reaching the verb that matters.
techniques.bookDefinition: Sentences that qualify themselves clause by clause before reaching the verb that matters.
techniques.inThisBook: The governess's prose delays its own conclusions with dashes and parentheses, so that the reader experiences her habit of thought as much as her account of events.

techniques.name: The reported sighting
techniques.definition: An apparition given only as one person's report, never as an event the narrative confirms.
techniques.bookDefinition: An apparition given only as one person's report, never as an event the narrative confirms.
techniques.inThisBook: James never writes that Quint is there; he writes that she saw him, and the difference is the whole argument between a century of readings.

techniques.name: Leading questions
techniques.definition: Producing testimony by supplying the answer inside the question.
techniques.bookDefinition: Producing testimony by supplying the answer inside the question.
techniques.inThisBook: Mrs Grose is asked whether the man had no hat, and Flora is asked where Miss Jessel is; one witness agrees and one does not, by the same method.

techniques.name: Doubling
techniques.definition: Pairing characters so that one occupies another's position.
techniques.bookDefinition: Pairing characters so that one occupies another's position.
techniques.inThisBook: Two governesses at one desk, two children, two dead servants, and a title that promises a second turn of a screw already turned once.

quotations.text: The story had held us, round the fire, sufficiently breathless, but except the obvious remark that it was gruesome, as, on Christmas Eve in an old house, a strange tale should essentially be, I remember no comment uttered till somebody happened to say that it was the only case he had met in which such a visitation had fallen on a child.
quotations.context: The opening sentence, in the voice of the outermost narrator.
quotations.analysis: The sentence is a hundred words long and arrives at its subject, a child, only at the very end, which is the book's method in miniature. Note also that the first thing we are told about the story we are about to read is that it is not the one being told.

quotations.text: If the child gives the effect another turn of the screw, what do you say to two children
quotations.speaker: Douglas
quotations.context: Offering his story in answer to one about a single haunted child.
quotations.analysis: The title is produced as a piece of after-dinner arithmetic: horror treated as a quantity that can be doubled. It also sets the terms on which everything that follows will be judged, because a story introduced as an intensification has to deliver one.

quotations.text: The story won’t tell
quotations.speaker: Douglas
quotations.context: Asked whether the story will say what the governess felt for her employer.
quotations.analysis: He is answering a question about motive, and the refusal is attributed to the manuscript rather than to himself. James thus establishes in the frame that the document is capable of not telling, and readers are warned before the first chapter that omission here is deliberate.

quotations.text: That she should never trouble him⁠—but never, never: neither appeal nor complain nor write about anything; only meet all questions herself, receive all moneys from his solicitor, take the whole thing over and let him alone.
quotations.speaker: Douglas
quotations.context: Describing the one condition attached to the post, which several other applicants had refused.
quotations.analysis: Every verb in the list is one the governess is forbidden to perform, and the accumulation makes the prohibition sound like a courtesy. The plot that follows is simply this sentence being kept: there is no adult she is permitted to consult, and she never breaks it.

quotations.text: He was incredibly beautiful, and Mrs. Grose had put her finger on it: everything but a sort of passion of tenderness for him was swept away by his presence.
quotations.context: Meeting Miles at the inn, the day after the school's letter arrives.
quotations.analysis: She decides the charge against him is impossible on the evidence of his face, and says so before she has asked him a single question. The verb swept away is worth keeping: her judgement of Miles is described from the start as something that happens to her rather than something she does.

quotations.text: Someone would appear there at the turn of a path and would stand before me and smile and approve.
quotations.context: Her habitual daydream during the free hour she takes in the grounds before dark.
quotations.analysis: This is the wish that the first apparition answers, and James puts it on the page a paragraph before Quint appears. The man she wants is the employer she has promised not to write to, so the figure on the tower arrives in a space her own longing has already prepared.

quotations.text: What arrested me on the spot⁠—and with a shock much greater than any vision had allowed for⁠—was the sense that my imagination had, in a flash, turned real.
quotations.context: The instant she catches sight of a man at the top of the tower.
quotations.analysis: The phrasing is doing two incompatible jobs at once: an imagination turning real is either a ghost or a symptom, and the sentence commits to neither. Almost every sighting in the book is worded with the same care.

quotations.text: So I saw him as I see the letters I form on this page
quotations.context: Insisting on the clarity of the first sighting.
quotations.analysis: She guarantees the apparition by comparing it with her own handwriting, which is the only thing the reader actually has. The comparison is meant as proof and works as a warning: everything we can see is the writing.

quotations.text: Quint was much too free.
quotations.speaker: Mrs Grose
quotations.context: Explaining why the valet was so often with the boy.
quotations.analysis: Four words, and they are the entire documented case against Peter Quint. Free is a word about rank as much as conduct, and the governess converts it into something much larger over the following chapters without ever being given more.

quotations.text: He was looking for little Miles.
quotations.speaker: The governess
quotations.context: Concluding what Quint wanted when he looked in at the window.
quotations.analysis: She calls this a portentous clearness, and it is the first time she states a motive for an apparition rather than a fact about one. From here the sightings stop being events to be explained and become moves in a campaign she believes she has understood.

quotations.text: I was a screen⁠—I was to stand before them. The more I saw, the less they would.
quotations.context: Working out what her role in the household now is.
quotations.analysis: The image makes her heroism and her monopoly the same thing: standing in front of the children means standing between them and any other account of what is happening. The arithmetic in the second sentence is stated as a certainty and never once tested.

quotations.text: They’re not mine⁠—they’re not ours. They’re his and they’re hers!
quotations.speaker: The governess
quotations.context: Telling Mrs Grose what she has concluded about the children's good behaviour.
quotations.analysis: The children's goodness has been reinterpreted as evidence against them, which means no conduct of theirs can now count in their favour. Possession is stated grammatically, in four possessive pronouns, and the sentence takes them away from Mrs Grose as well.

quotations.text: For the love of all the evil that, in those dreadful days, the pair put into them. And to ply them with that evil still, to keep up the work of demons, is what brings the others back.
quotations.context: Answering Mrs Grose's question about why the dead should return.
quotations.analysis: Demons is the point at which her vocabulary leaves the household and enters theology, and the others is the phrase she now uses for people she has named. Once the case is put in these terms, any intervention at all can be justified as rescue.

quotations.text: You terrible, miserable woman!
quotations.speaker: The governess
quotations.context: Finding a figure seated at her own desk in the schoolroom.
quotations.analysis: She has just recorded the extraordinary chill of feeling that she was the intruder, and the outburst is what that feeling turns into. Both women have sat at this desk in charge of these children, which is why the insult lands so close to home.

quotations.text: She’s there, she’s there!
quotations.speaker: The governess
quotations.context: At the lake, seizing Mrs Grose's arm and pointing across the water at Flora's back.
quotations.analysis: This is the one moment when the apparition is put to a public test, in daylight, with two other people present. Neither of them sees anything, and the governess's response is not doubt but a louder assertion, which tells the reader what kind of proof she is now capable of accepting.

quotations.text: Take me away, take me away⁠—oh, take me away from her!
quotations.speaker: Flora
quotations.context: Buried in Mrs Grose's skirts, moments after being asked where Miss Jessel is.
quotations.analysis: The child's only sustained utterance in the book is a plea to be removed from her protector, and the pronoun at the end is unambiguous. Whatever else is at Bly, this is the sentence the reader has to place any reading of the governess against.

quotations.text: I could only get on at all by taking “nature” into my confidence and my account, by treating my monstrous ordeal as a push in a direction unusual, of course, and unpleasant, but demanding, after all, for a fair front, only another turn of the screw of ordinary human virtue.
quotations.context: Steadying herself before dinner on the first day alone with Miles.
quotations.analysis: She reaches for the title herself, and applies it not to the horror but to her own endurance, as though virtue were a thing that could be tightened. The phrase quietly admits that what she is about to do to a ten-year-old is an extremity rather than a duty.

quotations.text: For there again, against the glass, as if to blight his confession and stay his answer, was the hideous author of our woe⁠—the white face of damnation.
quotations.context: The figure appears at the window just as Miles begins to answer her.
quotations.analysis: The apparition arrives precisely when a confession is about to be completed, which is convenient for the reading that it is a projection and equally convenient for the reading that it is a rival. James supplies no third possibility and no narrator to adjudicate.

quotations.text: Peter Quint⁠—you devil!
quotations.speaker: Miles
quotations.context: His answer when asked whom he means by 'he'.
quotations.analysis: The line can be read two ways with no change of wording: the devil is either Quint at the window or the woman holding him. The governess takes it as her triumph and calls it his supreme surrender of the name, which is a phrase about an interrogation rather than a haunting.

quotations.text: We were alone with the quiet day, and his little heart, dispossessed, had stopped.
quotations.context: The last sentence of the novella.
quotations.analysis: Dispossessed is the governess's word and it claims a success: the demon has been evicted. Placed between two commas in a sentence that ends with stopped, it also reads as the cause of death, and James lets both meanings stand without a syllable of comment from anyone outside her account.

atAGlance.label: Serialised
atAGlance.note: In Collier's Weekly, before its book appearance.

atAGlance.label: First collected
atAGlance.note: Printed with Covering End, a comedy in James's other register entirely.

atAGlance.label: Narrators
atAGlance.note: An unnamed guest reports Douglas, who reads a manuscript by a governess who is also not named.

atAGlance.label: The condition
atAGlance.note: The guardian's one requirement is the plot: no adult with authority can be consulted about anything that happens.

criticalViews.position: The apparitions are real
criticalViews.summary: The oldest reading, and the one the text supports most directly: a governess of ordinary good sense describes a man she has never seen or heard of, and a housekeeper who knew him recognises him from the description.
criticalViews.counter: Mrs Grose is told a great deal before she confirms anything, and no second person ever sees a figure at any point in the story.

criticalViews.position: The apparitions are the governess's own
criticalViews.summary: A reading associated with Edmund Wilson and developed by much twentieth-century criticism, which treats the sightings as projections of a young woman's isolation, her feeling for her employer and her fear of what she has taken on.
criticalViews.counter: It has to explain how she describes Quint's clothes and habits before anyone has told her about him, and it can make Flora's terror and Miles's death seem like a foregone conclusion rather than a horror.

criticalViews.position: The ambiguity is the design
criticalViews.summary: A third position holds that the story is built so that neither reading can win, and that James's preface and the frame narrative are both engineered to withhold the evidence a decision would need.
criticalViews.counter: It risks treating a cruel and specific story about two children as a clever machine, and it can leave nothing to say about what actually happens at the lake.

essayQuestions.question: How does James make it impossible to decide whether the ghosts are real?
essayQuestions.focus: Evidence, corroboration and the single witness
plan: Set out what a reader is actually given: one person's manuscript, copied after her death, with no outer narrator returning to comment.
Examine the identification of Quint in Chapter V closely, distinguishing what the governess supplies from what Mrs Grose supplies.
Contrast the lakeside scene in Chapter XX, where the same method is used in daylight and produces nothing.
Consider the wording of the sightings themselves, which report seeing rather than asserting presence.
Conclude on the frame: Douglas is in love with the author of the manuscript, and both are dead before it is copied.

essayQuestions.question: Discuss the presentation of the children.
essayQuestions.focus: Innocence, charm and adult interpretation
plan: Begin with the language of Chapter III, where beauty is described in religious terms and used as evidence.
Trace the reversal in Chapter XII, at which good behaviour becomes proof of corruption.
Use Flora's outburst at the lake and Miles's confession about saying things as the only direct evidence either child offers.
Weigh what Miles is actually accused of against what readers have traditionally supplied.
Decide what the last chapter shows: a child freed, or a child questioned to death.

essayQuestions.question: What does the prologue contribute to the story?
essayQuestions.focus: Frame narrative and the title
plan: Describe the layers: an unnamed guest, Douglas, a locked drawer, a manuscript, and a forty-year delay.
Show how the title is produced as a figure of speech about intensifying horror before the story begins.
Note what Douglas says and refuses to say about the governess's feelings for her employer.
Examine the master's condition as the plot's precondition rather than an item of background.
Consider the effect of never returning to the fireside: the story ends without anyone to receive it.

essayQuestions.question: 'The horror at Bly is a matter of class before it is a matter of ghosts.' Discuss.
essayQuestions.focus: Service, rank and the unsaid
plan: Establish everyone's position: master, governess, housekeeper, valet, and children who belong to none of them.
Read what is said about Quint, noting that the phrase used against him is about freedom rather than any named act.
Consider Mrs Grose's illiteracy, which puts every document in the house under the governess's control.
Set the two governesses at one desk beside each other, and ask what happened to the first.
Test the statement against the ending: Miles's expulsion concerns words said to other boys, and no adult will repeat them.

discussionQuestions: Nobody but the governess ever sees anything. Does that settle the question, or is it exactly what a ghost story requires?
Mrs Grose agrees with almost everything she is told. Is she a witness at all?
Miles is expelled for something the school will not name and he will barely describe. Why does James leave the gap open?
At the lake, Flora asks to be taken away from the governess. How much weight should a reader give that?
The story is told by three people and heard by none of them at the end. What does the missing return to the fireside do to the ending?

timeline.label: Henry James born in New York
timeline.detail: Into a family that moved repeatedly between America and Europe throughout his childhood.

timeline.label: James settles in London
timeline.detail: He spent most of the rest of his life in England and became a British subject in 1915.

timeline.label: Guy Domville fails at the St James's Theatre
timeline.detail: James was booed at his own curtain call and abandoned writing for the stage; the fiction of the following years is markedly more compressed and dramatic.

timeline.label: What Maisie Knew published
timeline.detail: Another book built on a child's partial understanding of adults, written immediately before this one.

timeline.label: Serialised in Collier's Weekly
timeline.detail: The story reached its first readers in a popular illustrated weekly rather than a literary quarterly.

timeline.label: Collected in The Two Magics
timeline.detail: Published with Covering End, so that the ghost story shared a volume with a comedy.

timeline.label: Revised for the New York Edition
timeline.detail: James reworked the text and added a preface discussing how the story was made.

timeline.label: James dies in London
timeline.detail: He had taken British nationality the previous year, during the war.

timeline.label: Britten's opera premieres in Venice
timeline.detail: The Turn of the Screw set for chamber orchestra, with Quint written for a tenor who sings, which the novella's Quint never does.

timeline.label: The Innocents released
timeline.detail: Jack Clayton's film, with Deborah Kerr as the governess and a screenplay that keeps the ambiguity deliberately open.

places.name: Harley Street, London
places.note: The guardian's house, where the governess is interviewed and gives her promise.

places.name: Essex
places.note: Bly is described only as an old family place in Essex; James names no town and draws no map.

places.name: De Vere Gardens, Kensington
places.note: James's London flat through the 1890s, the years of Maisie and this story.

places.name: Rye, East Sussex
places.note: Lamb House, where James lived and worked for the last phase of his career.

places.name: New York
places.note: James's birthplace, and the city whose collected edition he revised the story for in 1908.

related.why: An earlier English novel assembled entirely from partial testimonies, and equally interested in who is allowed to be believed.
The other great governess narrative: a young woman alone in a large house with a secret she is not told and an employer she must not question.
The Christmas-Eve tradition the prologue is sitting in, gathered as a collection.
The other great turn-of-the-century ghost writer, and the opposite method: everything specified, dated and documented.
A near-contemporary American story told by a woman whose account of a room nobody else will credit.

books.title: The Wind in the Willows
books.author: Kenneth Grahame
books.setting: An English river bank, the Wild Wood beyond it, and the roads, courts and railways of Edwardian England
books.written: Out of bedtime stories and letters sent to the author’s son in 1907
books.lengthNote: Twelve chapters, of which only six concern Toad at all
books.openingLine: The Mole had been working very hard all the morning, spring-cleaning his little home.
books.summary: A mole abandons his spring-cleaning, finds a river, and acquires three friends and a way of life within a single afternoon. Around that quiet centre Grahame builds two very different books: a farce in which a rich amphibian steals a motorcar and goes to prison, and a set of chapters about homesickness, wandering and awe that have no jokes in them at all. The animals are the size of their own houses and of human courtrooms by turns, and the novel never explains the discrepancy because it does not need to.

sourceText.label: Standard Ebooks text of The Wind in the Willows
sourceText.note: The twelve chapters are numbered I to XII and carry titles in the text; they are cited here by Arabic numeral.

structure.label: Chapters 1–2
structure.title: The River Bank and the Open Road
structure.summary: Mole throws down his whitewash brush, comes up into the sunlight and meets a Rat who owns a boat and a picnic hamper. Within a chapter he has a new life; within two, Toad has abandoned a caravan for a motorcar he has only heard, and the book’s two rhythms are both running.

structure.label: Chapters 3–4
structure.title: The Wild Wood and Mr Badger
structure.summary: Mole goes into the Wild Wood alone to call on Badger, is frightened by faces and whistling, and is found asleep in a hollow tree by a Rat carrying pistols. Badger’s underground house turns out to be built in the cellars of a vanished city, and the terror of the wood becomes a lecture on who lasts.

structure.label: Chapters 5–6
structure.title: Dulce Domum and Mr Toad
structure.summary: On a winter walk Mole catches the smell of his own abandoned house and breaks down in the road; Rat takes him back, and the field-mice sing carols at the door. Then Badger, Rat and Mole put Toad under house arrest, and he escapes out of a bedroom window by knotted sheets before lunch.

structure.label: Chapters 7–8
structure.title: The Piper at the Gates of Dawn and Toad’s Adventures
structure.summary: Searching at night for Otter’s lost son, Rat and Mole hear piping on an island and see something they are then mercifully allowed to forget. Alongside that chapter sits Toad in a dungeon, weeping over bubble-and-squeak, and the gaoler’s daughter proposing a washerwoman’s dress.

structure.label: Chapters 9–10
structure.title: Wayfarers All and the Further Adventures of Toad
structure.summary: A Sea Rat talks the Water Rat into a trance of harbours and southern ports, and Mole has to hold him down and put a pencil in his paw. Toad meanwhile escapes by train, barge and stolen horse, sells the horse to a gipsy, and boasts his way into a river.

structure.label: Chapters 11–12
structure.title: The tears of Toad and the return to Toad Hall
structure.summary: Toad comes home to find his house occupied by stoats and weasels and, for once, listens while Badger explains a plan. The four of them retake the hall through a tunnel, and Toad’s banquet is remarkable chiefly for the speeches and songs he does not give.

characters.name: Mole
characters.role: A householder who leaves his house
characters.summary: He begins the book as the reader’s proxy — ignorant, enthusiastic and easily impressed — and ends it as the animal who thinks of the tunnel and holds the line in the fight. His crisis in Chapter 5 is the emotional centre of the novel: he is the one who discovers that leaving home does not end the claim it has on you.
characters.clue: Whitewash on the fur, a brush thrown down on the floor, and a scrape up into the sunlight; later, the one who smells his own front door in the dark and cannot stop crying.

characters.name: Water Rat
characters.role: Riverbank poet, boatman and host
characters.summary: He is competent in everything the river requires and incurious about everything beyond it, and the book both loves him for the first and tests him on the second. His collapse in Chapter 9, when a wandering Sea Rat almost carries him off southward, shows how thin the difference is between a settled life and a refusal to look up.
characters.clue: He keeps a boat, a hamper and a paper of half-finished verses, and tells a new friend that the Wide World is something that does not matter either to him or to anybody else.

characters.name: Toad of Toad Hall
characters.role: A rich animal with a new enthusiasm every season
characters.summary: Boats, caravans and motorcars pass through him in turn, each one described as a conversion. He is the only character with money, a hall and a name in the newspapers, and the plot punishes him with prison and dispossession while the narration keeps enjoying him — a tension the ending resolves only by making him behave.
characters.clue: Goggles, gaiters, a bright red car on approval, twenty years’ imprisonment, a washerwoman’s dress, and a song about himself sung twice over in front of a mirror.

characters.name: Badger
characters.role: The authority of the Wild Wood
characters.summary: He hates society, keeps no fixed hours and is treated by every other animal as the last word. His house, built into the cellars of a city that has disappeared, gives him the long view that the rest of the book lacks, and it is why his rebukes to Toad carry weight that Rat’s do not.
characters.clue: A long, gloomy, shabby passage, a kitchen with a fire in it and no invitation ever issued; he is out, or asleep, or busy, and everyone waits for him anyway.

characters.name: Otter
characters.role: A riverbank neighbour, and Portly’s father
characters.summary: He appears in the margins of the sociable chapters and then, in Chapter 7, supplies the emergency that takes Rat and Mole up the river at night. His grief is reported rather than shown, which is what allows the vision on the island to happen to somebody else.
characters.clue: He comes out of the water beside a picnic and shakes himself dry, and later stands all night at a ford waiting for a small son who cannot swim well enough yet.

characters.name: The Sea Rat
characters.role: A wayfarer out of the south
characters.summary: He arrives for one chapter, eats a meal, talks about harbours, and leaves the Water Rat glassy-eyed and packing. He is the book’s argument against itself: everything the river stands for is put at risk by a stranger who is better at describing places than Rat is at defending his own.
characters.clue: Lean, keen-featured and dusty, with a story of Constantinople, Venice and a little grey sea town, and a voice that works on the listener like wine.

characters.name: The gaoler’s daughter
characters.role: A girl in the castle where Toad is imprisoned
characters.summary: She is fond of animals, sees through Toad completely, and arranges his escape by lending him her aunt’s washerwoman’s dress for a consideration. She is one of the very few humans in the book with a will of her own, and the plot of the second half depends entirely on her.
characters.clue: She is fond of animals and keeps several of her own, and it is her aunt’s trade, her aunt’s gown and her own arithmetic that get a prisoner out through a gate.

characters.name: The stoats, weasels and ferrets
characters.role: Inhabitants of the Wild Wood, and squatters at Toad Hall
characters.summary: They frighten Mole in Chapter 3 and occupy Toad Hall in Chapter 11, and the book never grants them a named individual or a line of reported thought. They are the clearest sign of the novel’s politics: the riverbankers own houses, and the animals from the wood get them only by seizure.
characters.clue: Wicked little faces in holes, whistling and pattering behind the traveller, and later a banquet in somebody else’s dining room with sentries at the gate.

themes.name: Home, and the claim it keeps
themes.summary: Every animal in the book is defined by a dwelling — a hole in a bank, a house under a wood, a hall with a banqueting room — and the plot repeatedly takes one away. Grahame’s most serious writing is about the moment a house you abandoned calls you back, and about how difficult it is to admit that the call has been heard.
