themes.development: Mole leaves his house in Chapter 1 without a backward look, is ambushed by the smell of it in Chapter 5, and by Chapter 12 is planning the recovery of somebody else’s.

themes.name: Wandering and the Wide World
themes.summary: Against the riverbank sits everything outside it: the Wide World Rat refuses to discuss, the open road Toad takes up as a fashion, and the southern ports the Sea Rat describes until Rat starts packing. The book is honest enough to make the case for leaving eloquent, and then to treat it as an illness to be nursed.
themes.development: Refused as a topic in Chapter 1, played as farce by Toad in Chapter 2, and taken seriously enough in Chapter 9 to require physical restraint and a sheet of paper.

themes.name: Friendship as management
themes.summary: Loyalty here looks like supervision: Rat feeds and teaches Mole, Badger and Rat put Toad under house arrest, and Mole holds a struggling friend down on the floor until the fit passes. Affection in this book is rarely declared and almost always expressed as taking charge of somebody.
themes.development: Hospitality in Chapter 1, rescue in Chapter 3, house arrest in Chapter 6, physical restraint in Chapter 9, and a military operation in Chapter 11.

themes.name: Halls, holes and the lower orders
themes.summary: Toad has a hall, a boathouse and a solicitor; the Wild Wooders have holes and no names. The novel’s comedy of a gentleman in a washerwoman’s dress depends on the assumption that both women and stoats are types rather than people, and its happy ending restores a landowner to his property by force.
themes.development: Signalled in the ‘Private. No landing allowed’ notice-board in Chapter 2, tested in the barge-woman’s kitchen, and settled at the point of a cudgel in Chapter 11.

themes.name: The motorcar against the old road
themes.summary: The car arrives first as a noise, then as a cloud of dust, then as a court case, and the book records what it does to everyone else on the road: a horse in the ditch, a cart on its side, a canary in a cage. Grahame published in the years when speed limits, licences and registration plates were new law, not prophecy.
themes.development: A hum like a distant bee in Chapter 2, an obsession by the end of it, twenty years’ imprisonment in Chapter 6, and a promise in the last chapter that is entirely believed by nobody.

themes.name: Wonder, and the gift of forgetfulness
themes.canonicalName: Wonder, and the gift of forgetfulness
themes.summary: One chapter steps outside the comedy altogether: two animals hear piping at dawn, see something they can only call the Friend and Helper, and are then given oblivion as a kindness. The book will not let awe be kept, catalogued or used later, which is why the experience leaves no mark on the plot.
themes.development: Announced by music on an island in Chapter 7, granted and immediately withdrawn, and echoed faintly in the Sea Rat’s spell two chapters later.

techniques.name: Shifting registers
techniques.definition: Moving between comic, domestic and exalted styles within one book, without harmonising them.
techniques.bookDefinition: Moving between comic, domestic and exalted styles within one book, without harmonising them.
techniques.inThisBook: Chapter 7 is written in the cadences of the King James Bible and Chapter 10 in those of a music-hall sketch; the same four animals appear in both, and neither chapter apologises for the other.

techniques.name: Animals on a sliding scale
techniques.definition: Keeping creatures simultaneously animal and human in size, station and behaviour, and never resolving the contradiction.
techniques.bookDefinition: Keeping creatures simultaneously animal and human in size, station and behaviour, and never resolving the contradiction.
techniques.inThisBook: Toad is small enough to be picked up by a barge-woman and large enough to drive a motorcar and stand trial; Mole is the size of his own front door and of a punt seat by turns.

techniques.name: Catalogue
techniques.definition: A list allowed to run on past the point of usefulness, so that the accumulation itself becomes the effect.
techniques.bookDefinition: A long list of objects or names used in place of narrative.
techniques.inThisBook: The luncheon basket is emptied in a single unpunctuated word — coldtonguecoldham and the rest — so that abundance arrives as a sound rather than an inventory.

techniques.name: Song
techniques.definition: A sung passage standing outside the dialogue, free to say what the speaking characters cannot.
techniques.bookDefinition: Sung lyric used to carry information a speech cannot.
techniques.inThisBook: The field-mice carol at Mole’s door, the Rat hears verse in the reeds, and Toad composes a hymn to himself in a bedroom and sings it twice — the surest sign that his reform is skin-deep.

techniques.name: Idiolect
techniques.definition: A speech habit belonging to one character alone, so that they can be recognised before they are named.
techniques.bookDefinition: Giving each character a distinct and consistent way of speaking.
techniques.inThisBook: Rat's sentences drift and trail off, Badger's are short and final, and Toad speaks almost entirely in exclamations about himself; the four voices can be told apart without attribution.

techniques.name: Doors and thresholds
techniques.definition: Doors, windows, gates and stairs used to mark what may be crossed, by whom, and at what cost.
techniques.bookDefinition: Physical barriers used to carry an idea about what is concealed behind them.
techniques.inThisBook: Badger’s door in the snow, ‘Mole End’ in Gothic lettering over a bellpull, a cell door, and finally a forgotten tunnel that opens inside the butler’s pantry.

techniques.name: Mock-heroic
techniques.definition: Epic apparatus — arms, councils, homecomings — applied to small domestic events.
techniques.bookDefinition: Epic apparatus — arms, councils, homecomings — applied to small domestic events.
techniques.inThisBook: The last chapter is called ‘The Return of Ulysses’, the weapons are laid out in rows on the table, and the battle for a dining room is fought by four animals with sticks.

quotations.text: Spring was moving in the air above and in the earth below and around him, penetrating even his dark and lowly little house with its spirit of divine discontent and longing.
quotations.context: The third sentence of the novel, while Mole is still at work with the whitewash.
quotations.analysis: The season is the subject of the sentence and Mole merely the place it reaches, which sets up a book in which characters are acted on by weather, smells and calls rather than by decisions. ‘Divine discontent’ is a phrase from the pulpit and the essay, and it arrives four lines before the word ‘Bother!’ — the two registers of the whole novel established on its first page.

quotations.text: he suddenly flung down his brush on the floor, said, “Bother!” and “O blow!” and also “Hang spring-cleaning!”
quotations.context: The moment Mole abandons the house he has spent all morning cleaning.
quotations.analysis: Three exclamations in ascending order of daring, and all of them mild: the most rebellious thing Mole can say is a word about housework. The comedy is that a life is being abandoned in the vocabulary of a slightly cross uncle, and the novel keeps that gap between small language and large events all the way to the battle at the end.

quotations.text: there is nothing⁠—absolute nothing⁠—half so much worth doing as simply messing about in boats.
quotations.speaker: Water Rat
quotations.context: Rowing Mole downstream on the morning they meet.
quotations.analysis: The famous sentence is usually quoted as ‘absolutely nothing’; Grahame wrote ‘absolute nothing’, and the slight wrongness is part of Rat’s dreamy delivery, which trails off a line later into ‘messing—about—in—boats; messing—’. The philosophy being proposed is the refusal of purpose, and the sentence enacts it by losing its own thread.

quotations.text: “There’s cold chicken inside it,” replied the Rat briefly: “coldtonguecoldhamcoldbeefpickledgherkinssaladfrenchrollscresssandwichespottedmeatgingerbeerlemonadesodawater⁠—”
quotations.speaker: Water Rat
quotations.context: Mole asks what is in the fat wicker luncheon basket.
quotations.analysis: The spaces are removed so that the list is read at the speed Rat says it, and the effect is of a rope of food paying out without a breath. ‘Briefly’ is the joke: the narrator calls a sixteen-item catalogue brief because for Rat the river’s abundance genuinely goes without saying.

quotations.text: “Beyond the Wild Wood comes the Wide World,” said the Rat. “And that’s something that doesn’t matter, either to you or me. I’ve never been there, and I’m never going, nor you either, if you’ve got any sense at all. Don’t ever refer to it again, please.
quotations.speaker: Water Rat
quotations.context: Mole has asked what lies past the smoke on the horizon.
quotations.analysis: Rat answers a question about geography with a prohibition, and the sentence that closes the subject — ‘Don’t ever refer to it again, please’ — is the politest thing in the book and the most frightened. Chapter 9 will collect on it: the animal who refuses to discuss the world outside turns out to be the one most easily carried off by a stranger’s description of it.

quotations.text: They found him in a sort of a trance, a happy smile on his face, his eyes still fixed on the dusty wake of their destroyer. At intervals he was still heard to murmur “Poop-poop!”
quotations.context: The motorcar has just put the caravan in the ditch and disappeared down the road.
quotations.analysis: The car is converted into a sound and the sound into a possession: Toad has learned the vocabulary of the new machine before he has touched one. ‘Their destroyer’ is the narrator’s word, not Toad’s, and it keeps the wrecked cart and the terrified horse in view while the joke is being made.

quotations.text: “Glorious, stirring sight!” murmured Toad, never offering to move. “The poetry of motion! The real way to travel! The only way to travel!
quotations.speaker: Toad
quotations.context: Still sitting in the road where the car has left him.
quotations.analysis: ‘Never offering to move’ is placed inside a speech about motion, and the contradiction is the whole of Toad: his enthusiasms are states of mind rather than activities. The three exclamations escalate from description to doctrine in nine words, which is how every one of his conversions is reported.

quotations.text: I want to show you the world! I’m going to make an animal of you, my boy!
quotations.speaker: Toad
quotations.context: Persuading Rat to come on the caravan expedition.
quotations.analysis: ‘Make a man of you’ is the phrase the sentence is built on, and swapping in ‘animal’ is the book’s only direct joke about its own premise. It also reveals Toad’s theory of friendship: other people are raw material for his current enthusiasm, which is why he never notices that Rat has said no.

quotations.text: he thought that he had never seen so far and so intimately into the insides of things as on that winter day when Nature was deep in her annual slumber and seemed to have kicked the clothes off.
quotations.context: Mole setting out alone for the Wild Wood on a cold, still afternoon.
quotations.analysis: A sentence of grave Latinate observation ends with somebody kicking off the bedclothes, and the joint is invisible. This is Grahame’s characteristic move — the natural world made domestic rather than sublime — and it explains why a wood can be terrifying in this book without ever becoming supernatural.

quotations.text: We river-bankers, we hardly ever come here by ourselves. If we have to come, we come in couples at least; then we’re generally all right.
quotations.speaker: Water Rat
quotations.context: Comforting Mole in the hollow tree after finding him in the snow.
quotations.analysis: ‘We river-bankers’ is the first time the book names a class, and it does so to explain where that class does not go. The reassurance is really a set of rules of caste — passwords, signs, sayings which have power and effect — and the Wild Wood is dangerous chiefly because it belongs to animals who have not been introduced.

quotations.text: “People come⁠—they stay for a while, they flourish, they build⁠—and they go. It is their way. But we remain.
quotations.speaker: Badger
quotations.context: Explaining that his house is built in the cellars of a city that once stood where the Wild Wood now grows.
quotations.analysis: The dashes let the whole of human history pass in a single line, and the verbs get shorter as it goes. ‘But we remain’ is the book’s one moment of geological time, and it quietly reverses the usual arrangement in which animals are temporary and people permanent.

quotations.text: Home! That was what they meant, those caressing appeals, those soft touches wafted through the air, those invisible little hands pulling and tugging, all one way!
quotations.context: On the winter road, when Mole catches the smell of the house he abandoned in Chapter 1.
quotations.analysis: The summons is written entirely as touch — appeals, touches, hands — so that homesickness arrives as a physical assault rather than a thought. Grahame delays the explanation for a whole paragraph after the word ‘Home!’, which reproduces the order in which Mole himself works it out.

quotations.text: directly facing them was Mole’s little front door, with “Mole End” painted, in Gothic lettering, over the bellpull at the side.
quotations.context: Rat following Mole down the long passage to the house he left in the spring.
quotations.analysis: Gothic lettering over a bellpull is suburban gentility rendered in a hole in the ground, and it tells you what Mole was before he met the river. The detail also does the work that Mole’s tears could not: the house is shown to be modest, cared for and named by its owner, all in one line.

quotations.text: he looked in the very eyes of the Friend and Helper; saw the backward sweep of the curved horns, gleaming in the growing daylight; saw the stern, hooked nose between the kindly eyes that were looking down on them humorously
quotations.context: Dawn on the island, at the end of the night search for Otter’s son.
quotations.analysis: The god is never named in the chapter, only titled, and the description is built out of a repeated ‘saw’ that turns looking into a liturgy. Note the adverb ‘humorously’ dropped into the middle of an awe-struck sentence: even here Grahame will not let the sublime arrive without a domestic detail to steady it.

quotations.text: “Afraid?” murmured the Rat, his eyes shining with unutterable love. “Afraid! Of Him? O, never, never! And yet⁠—and yet⁠—O, Mole, I am afraid!”
quotations.speaker: Water Rat
quotations.context: Mole has whispered the question while both animals are crouching on the island.
quotations.analysis: The speech contradicts itself twice in eighteen words and means all three positions at once, which is a precise account of religious awe rather than a muddle. It is also the only time in the novel that Rat, the competent one, is given a sentence he cannot finish.

quotations.text: For this is the last best gift that the kindly demigod is careful to bestow on those to whom he has revealed himself in their helping: the gift of forgetfulness.
quotations.context: A breeze crosses the island and both animals lose the memory of what they have seen.
quotations.analysis: The vision is removed from the characters by the narrator rather than by them, and the colon lands on ‘forgetfulness’ as though it were a reward. This is why the chapter leaves no trace on the plot: Grahame has decided that an experience of this kind cannot be carried back into a book about picnics and motorcars.

quotations.text: “And you, you will come too, young brother; for the days pass, and never return, and the South still waits for you. Take the adventure, heed the call, now ere the irrevocable moment passes!
quotations.speaker: The Sea Rat
quotations.context: The end of the Sea Rat’s account of his travels, told over a meal on the riverbank.
quotations.analysis: The rhythm is deliberately liturgical — three clauses, then a command, then a warning — and it works on Rat precisely because he has no counter-vocabulary for it. Set beside Chapter 7, the chapter is unnerving: the same trance-like language that produced a god here produces a travel brochure.

quotations.text: It is true that he sucked a good deal more than he scribbled; but it was joy to the Mole to know that the cure had at least begun.
quotations.context: After Mole has held Rat down through his fit and then put paper and pencil in front of him.
quotations.analysis: Wanting to go to sea is treated here as an illness with a treatment, and the treatment is writing poetry. It is the most revealing sentence in the book about its own making: the longing is real, the departure is impossible, and what is left is a man at a desk sucking a pencil.

quotations.text: “Ho, ho!” he said to himself, as he marched along with his chin in the air, “what a clever Toad I am! There is surely no animal equal to me for cleverness in the whole world!
quotations.speaker: Toad
quotations.context: Walking away from the barge, having just stolen the barge-woman’s horse.
quotations.analysis: Every escape in the second half has been arranged by somebody else — a girl with a dress, an engine-driver, a gipsy with cash — and Toad’s self-congratulation edits all of them out. The narrator lets him do it at length and then puts him in a river, which is the book’s standard method of argument.

quotations.text: The Toad⁠—came⁠—home!
quotations.speaker: Toad
quotations.context: The refrain of the song Toad composes in his bedroom before the banquet, and sings twice over.
quotations.analysis: The dashes are stage directions for a singer pausing to be admired, and the third person is the point: Toad writes about himself as a public event. The chapter is called ‘The Return of Ulysses’, and the returning hero’s first act is to compose his own ballad.

quotations.text: “Badger’s was the master mind; the Mole and the Water Rat bore the brunt of the fighting; I merely served in the ranks and did little or nothing.”
quotations.speaker: Toad
quotations.context: Disengaging himself from Otter’s embrace at the banquet.
quotations.analysis: It is an accurate account of the battle, delivered by the one animal who has never given an accurate account of anything. The modesty is a new performance rather than a new character, and the narrator confirms it two lines later by noting how closely Toad watches Badger and Rat for their reaction.

quotations.text: He was indeed an altered Toad!
quotations.context: After Toad has declined to make a speech or sing a song at his own banquet.
quotations.analysis: One sentence, one paragraph, and an exclamation mark that could be admiration or disbelief. The reform is real enough to be observed and light enough to be withdrawn, which is why the book can end with a promise about motorcars that nobody in the room believes.

atAGlance.label: First published
atAGlance.note: Methuen, London, with a frontispiece by W. Graham Robertson and no other pictures.

atAGlance.label: Origin
atAGlance.note: Grahame sent animal-story letters to his young son in 1907; the Bodleian holds fifteen of them.

atAGlance.label: The author’s day job
atAGlance.value: Secretary of the Bank of England
atAGlance.note: He had entered the Bank in 1879 and resigned in June 1908, four months before the book appeared.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.note: The Toad farce runs through six of them; the other six are about home, wonder and going away.

criticalViews.position: Two books bound as one
criticalViews.summary: The most persistent critical observation is that the Toad chapters and the riverbank chapters belong to different works — one a picaresque farce with a plot, the other a set of static essays on home, awe and longing. Readers who love one often skip the other, and adaptations almost always choose the farce.
criticalViews.counter: The seam is the point: both halves are about leaving a house, and only Toad is allowed to make it funny.

criticalViews.position: A pastoral written against the motorcar
criticalViews.summary: Read as Edwardian social record, the book is a defence of an older road and river culture at the moment it was being displaced, published five years after the Motor Car Act and by a man who had spent his career in the City.
criticalViews.counter: The novel gives the machine all the best noises and its most memorable character, and the countryside it defends has servants, halls and no visible labour.

criticalViews.position: The politics of the riverbank
criticalViews.summary: Later criticism has looked hard at who owns what: a gentleman’s hall recovered by force from animals who are never individually named, a class of ‘river-bankers’ with passwords, and women who appear mainly as gaolers’ daughters and barge-women.
criticalViews.counter: Badger’s speech about vanished cities cuts against any settled order, and the book’s final image of respect from the Wild Wood is uneasy rather than triumphant.

criticalViews.position: The mystical chapter
criticalViews.summary: ‘The Piper at the Gates of Dawn’ has been read as late-Victorian nature religion, as a private elegy, and as the one place where Grahame’s essayist’s prose is given a subject large enough for it. Its removal from the plot by the gift of forgetfulness is the crux of every reading.
criticalViews.counter: It can also be read as an evasion: the book raises something it cannot use and then deletes it before the next chapter.

essayQuestions.question: ‘A book about home, interrupted by a book about Toad.’ How convincing is this account of the novel?
essayQuestions.focus: Structure, tone and the two plots
plan: Set out the division precisely: which chapters concern Toad, and which of the others have any plot at all.
Use Chapter 5 to show what the quiet chapters do that the farce cannot — homesickness as a physical event rather than a comic reversal.
Show the two plots touching: Toad’s dispossession in Chapter 11 is also a story about a house, and Mole is the one who solves it.
Test the claim against Chapter 9, which is neither farce nor domestic comfort and belongs to neither half cleanly.
Conclude on the ending, where the returning hero, the recovered house and the suppressed song are all in the same room.

essayQuestions.question: How does Grahame use the Wild Wood?
essayQuestions.focus: Fear, class and the geography of the book
plan: Begin with the wood as Mole meets it: faces, whistling, pattering, and no actual attack.
Read Rat’s explanation as a statement of caste — river-bankers, passwords, and animals who have not been introduced.
Turn to Badger’s house, which converts the frightening wood into history and makes the ruins of a city its foundation.
Follow the Wild Wooders to Toad Hall and ask what changes when the frightening neighbours become squatters in a dining room.
Weigh the final paragraph’s picture of mother-weasels teaching respect: reassurance, or an occupation confirmed?

essayQuestions.question: What is ‘The Piper at the Gates of Dawn’ doing in this novel?
essayQuestions.focus: Register, the numinous and narrative consequence
plan: Describe the chapter’s prose: the repeated ‘saw’, the refusal to name the god, the single humorous adjective.
Establish what prompts it — a lost child and a night search — so that the vision is framed by an ordinary emergency.
Analyse the gift of forgetfulness as a narrative device: nothing may be carried forward into the following chapters.
Compare the Sea Rat’s spell in Chapter 9, which uses the same trance-like rhythms for a worldly purpose.
Decide whether the chapter enlarges the book or exposes the limits of what the rest of it can hold.

essayQuestions.question: Is Toad reformed?
essayQuestions.focus: Character, comedy and the ending
plan: Chart the conversions in order — boats, caravan, motorcar — and note that each is announced in the same language.
Examine the mechanisms of his escapes and how little of each one he actually performs himself.
Read the bedroom song as evidence: private, third-person, and sung twice.
Set the modest speech at the banquet against his sideways glances at Badger and Rat.
Conclude with the promise about the first motorcar he sees, and whether the book wants reform or only good manners.

discussionQuestions: Rat refuses even to discuss the Wide World, and is nearly carried off by it. Is his life on the river a choice or an avoidance?
The animals are sometimes the size of a boat and sometimes the size of a courtroom. Does the book lose anything by never resolving this?
Mole is the only character who cries in the novel. Why does Grahame give the breakdown to him rather than to Toad?
Toad Hall is recovered by force from animals who have no names or speeches. What would change if the stoats were given either?
Why does the vision on the island have to be forgotten?

timeline.label: Kenneth Grahame born in Edinburgh
timeline.detail: He was brought up largely by relatives in Berkshire after his mother’s death, on the stretch of the Thames the book keeps returning to.

timeline.label: Grahame enters the Bank of England
timeline.detail: He worked there for nearly thirty years while publishing essays and stories in his own time.

timeline.label: The Golden Age published
timeline.detail: Sketches of childhood seen from the child’s side; Dream Days followed in 1898.

timeline.label: Grahame becomes Secretary of the Bank of England
timeline.detail: The most senior post he held, and the one he resigned a few months before the novel appeared.

timeline.label: The Motor Car Act
timeline.detail: Registration, driving licences and a twenty-mile-an-hour limit — the legal background to Toad’s career on the road.

timeline.label: The letters to Alastair
timeline.detail: Grahame sent his young son a series of animal-story letters; fifteen survive in the Bodleian with manuscript material for the novel.

timeline.label: Retirement, and publication
timeline.detail: Grahame resigned from the Bank in June; Methuen published The Wind in the Willows on 8 October.

timeline.label: Alastair Grahame dies at Oxford
timeline.detail: The son the stories were first told to; he was nineteen.

timeline.label: A. A. Milne’s Toad of Toad Hall staged
timeline.detail: The dramatisation keeps the Toad plot and drops the chapters that have no jokes in them, a division most adaptations have followed.

timeline.label: E. H. Shepard illustrates the book
timeline.detail: His drawings fixed the appearance of the four animals for most readers; the 1908 first edition had a frontispiece and nothing else.

timeline.label: Grahame dies at Pangbourne
timeline.detail: He is buried at Oxford, beside Alastair.

places.name: Cookham Dean, Berkshire
places.note: Where Grahame spent part of his childhood beside the Thames, and the country the riverbank chapters draw on.

places.name: Quarry Wood, near Marlow
places.note: The wood on the hill above Cookham Dean, long identified locally with the Wild Wood.

places.name: Pangbourne
places.note: Grahame’s last home, on the same river, where he died in 1932.

places.name: Fowey, Cornwall
places.note: The harbour town Grahame knew well, and the kind of grey sea town the Sea Rat describes to a spellbound listener.

places.name: Bank of England, London
places.note: Grahame’s office for nearly thirty years, and the working life the riverbank is usually read against.

places.name: Bodleian Library, Oxford
places.note: Holds the surviving letters to Alastair and manuscript material for the novel.

related.why: The other English classic in which animals hold conversations, and a much less comfortable one about manners.
Published two years earlier, and built on the same Edwardian machinery — railways, courts and a house lost and regained.
The Thames as a comic idyll of picnics, hampers and incompetent boating, twenty years before Rat took up the sculls.
An animal book from the other extreme: no speech, no houses, and instinct treated as a matter of survival rather than character.
Blackwood’s riverside terror of the same decade, where the water and the willows are not friendly at all.

books.title: The Winter's Tale
books.author: William Shakespeare
books.setting: The court of Sicilia and, sixteen years later, a sheep-shearing feast on the coast of Bohemia
books.lengthNote: Around 3,000 lines, with a sixteen-year gap opened in the middle of them
books.openingLine: If you shall chance, Camillo, to visit Bohemia, on the like occasion whereon my services are now on foot
books.summary: A king watches his wife be courteous to his oldest friend and decides, in the space of nine lines, that she has betrayed him. Three acts later a bear has eaten a nobleman, a baby has been left on a beach and sixteen years have gone past in a speech. What returns is not the world he broke but a second one built beside it, and the play's last scene asks an audience to believe a thing it has been told twice is impossible.

sourceText.label: Globe/Moby text of The Winter's Tale
sourceText.note: Line numbers follow the traditional Globe numbering. The only early text is the First Folio, generally thought to have been set from a scribal transcript.

structure.label: Act I
structure.title: Nine lines, and a marriage destroyed
structure.summary: Polixenes has been visiting for nine months and means to leave; Hermione persuades him to stay because her husband asked her to. Watching them talk, Leontes decides they are lovers, and there is no Iago, no handkerchief and no evidence of any kind. By the end of the act he has ordered his most trusted counsellor to poison a king.

scenes.title: Two courtiers
scenes.summary: Camillo and Archidamus praise the friendship of the kings and the promise of the young prince.

scenes.title: Too hot, too hot
scenes.summary: Hermione wins the argument her husband could not, and Leontes watches her hand in another man's and goes mad in public.

structure.label: Act II
structure.title: A queen arrested and an oracle sent for
structure.summary: Hermione is taken from her son in the middle of a ghost story and imprisoned; she gives birth in the cell. Paulina carries the baby to the king expecting the sight of it to work, and is called a witch for her trouble. Leontes has already sent to Delphos, and announces that he will believe the god whatever the god says.

scenes.title: The sad tale
scenes.summary: Mamillius begins a winter's tale and is interrupted by his father's guards; Hermione is charged and taken away.

scenes.title: The prison
scenes.summary: Paulina learns of the birth and decides to carry the child to its father herself.

scenes.title: The infant refused
scenes.summary: Paulina lays the baby at the king's feet and argues; Antigonus is sworn to carry it to a desert place and leave it.

structure.label: Act III
structure.title: The oracle, the deaths, and the bear
structure.summary: Hermione defends herself in the clearest speech in the play, the oracle clears her in five clauses, and Leontes rejects it out loud. His son dies within a minute of the blasphemy and his wife within two. Then the play changes countries, a storm sinks a ship, a bear takes Antigonus, and a shepherd finds a baby and says the first kind thing anyone has said for three acts.

scenes.title: Returning from Delphos
scenes.summary: Cleomenes and Dion describe the sweet air and the deafening voice of the oracle, and hope for a good outcome.

scenes.title: The trial
scenes.summary: Hermione speaks for her honour, the oracle is read, Leontes denies it, and Mamillius and Hermione are both reported dead.

scenes.title: Things dying, things newborn
scenes.summary: Antigonus leaves the baby on the Bohemian coast and exits pursued by a bear; a shepherd and his son find the child and the wreck.

structure.label: Act IV
structure.title: Sixteen years, a sheep-shearing and a pedlar
structure.summary: Time appears as a chorus, turns the glass and moves the play on. In Bohemia the foundling is a shepherd's daughter presiding over a feast, a prince is courting her under a false name, and a thief with a ballad-sheet is working the crowd. Then Polixenes tears off his disguise and threatens everyone, and the young couple run for Sicilia with the help of the man who fled it.

scenes.title: Time
scenes.summary: The chorus turns his hourglass, apologises for the leap and sets the second half in motion.

scenes.title: Camillo asks to go home
scenes.summary: Polixenes refuses, and they agree to go in disguise to the shepherd's cottage where the prince keeps disappearing.

scenes.title: Autolycus
scenes.summary: A pedlar and former courtier sings on the road, picks the Clown's pocket by pretending to be robbed, and goes to the feast.

scenes.title: The sheep-shearing
scenes.summary: Perdita gives out flowers and argues about art and nature with a disguised king who then forbids the match and threatens her with death.

structure.label: Act V
structure.title: Recognitions, and a chapel
structure.summary: Leontes has spent sixteen years doing penance under Paulina's supervision. The lovers arrive, the pursuing king arrives, the tokens are produced and the reunion of father and daughter is deliberately kept offstage and reported by gentlemen. The play saves its one visible wonder for last, in a chapel, with a curtain and a piece of music.

scenes.title: Penitence
scenes.summary: Leontes is urged to remarry and Paulina forbids it; Florizel and Perdita arrive claiming a diplomatic errand.

scenes.title: The reunion, reported
scenes.summary: Three gentlemen describe the discovery of Perdita's identity to one another, and the Clown becomes a gentleman born.

scenes.title: The statue
scenes.summary: Paulina draws a curtain on a figure of Hermione aged sixteen years, requires the onlookers to awake their faith, and calls for music.

characters.name: Leontes
characters.role: King of Sicilia
characters.summary: His jealousy has no source outside himself, and the play makes that a formal problem: the verse breaks apart into half-lines, parentheses and obscene punning within seconds of the first suspicion. He is given the longest penance in Shakespeare and the play never quite says it has been enough.
characters.clue: He needs no villain to persuade him, convicts a queen on the evidence of a handshake, and spends sixteen years visiting a grave at the instruction of the woman who chose it.

characters.name: Hermione
characters.role: Queen of Sicilia
characters.summary: She is witty and entirely at ease in the first scene, which is what condemns her, and at the trial she argues from honour rather than innocence because innocence has already been ruled inadmissible. She has perhaps eighty lines after the trial and none at all to her husband in the final scene.
characters.clue: She wins an argument on her husband's behalf and is charged with adultery for it; sixteen years later she is a statue with wrinkles.

characters.name: Paulina
characters.role: A lady of the Sicilian court, Antigonus's wife
characters.summary: She says the unsayable to a king in Act III and then organises the next sixteen years of his life. Whether she hid a living woman for that long or performed a miracle is left deliberately unresolved, and she loses a husband to a bear and is handed a new one in the last thirty lines.
characters.clue: She calls a king a tyrant to his face, keeps something behind a curtain for sixteen years, and tells a court that it is required to awake its faith.

characters.name: Perdita
characters.role: Leontes and Hermione's lost daughter, raised as a shepherd's child
characters.summary: She presides over the sheep-shearing in borrowed finery and is uncomfortable in it, and she holds her own in an argument about grafting against a king. The play is careful that her authority looks natural without ever settling whether that is breeding, upbringing or the pastoral convention doing its work.
characters.clue: She is dressed as a goddess for a feast she thinks is above her, refuses to grow streaked flowers, and wants spring flowers for a living lover rather than a corpse.

characters.name: Polixenes
characters.role: King of Bohemia
characters.summary: He begins as the innocent party and ends the fourth act threatening to have a shepherd's daughter's face scratched with briars. The play gives him the elegant argument that art is itself a part of nature, and then has him forbid exactly the kind of grafting he has just defended.
characters.clue: He argues that crossing a noble bud with a baser stock is nature's own art, and forty lines later threatens death to anyone who lets his son marry a shepherdess.

characters.name: Camillo
characters.role: A Sicilian lord, later Polixenes's counsellor
characters.summary: Ordered to commit a murder, he warns the victim and leaves with him, which is the one action in the first half that prevents a death. He then spends sixteen years homesick and engineers the escape to Sicilia largely because he wants to see the place again.
characters.clue: Told to poison a king, he takes him abroad instead, and later sends a prince and a shepherdess to the country he is longing for.

characters.name: Florizel
characters.role: Prince of Bohemia, courting as Doricles
characters.summary: He is in the same disguise Rosalind and Viola wear, and he uses it only to be poorer than he is. His praise of Perdita dancing is the most beautiful speech in the play and also, read carefully, a wish that she would never do anything else.
characters.clue: He courts under a false name in shepherd's clothes and tells his love he wishes she could dance for ever, which is a compliment with a door in it.
traits: readier to lose a kingdom than to argue for one

characters.name: Autolycus
characters.role: A pedlar, ballad-seller and pickpocket
characters.summary: He arrives after the interval of sixteen years and changes the play's weather entirely, singing, cheating and selling printed ballads about impossible events to people who buy them because they are printed. He is the only character who profits from the happy ending without contributing anything to it.
characters.clue: Named after the son of Mercury, littered under the same planet, he picks a pocket by pretending to have been robbed and sells ballads of fish and usurers' wives.

characters.name: Mamillius
characters.role: The young prince of Sicilia
characters.summary: He is beginning a ghost story for his mother — a sad tale, because it is winter — when the guards come in, and the play takes its title from the tale he never finishes. He dies of what a servant calls mere conceit and fear, and nothing in the last act replaces him.
characters.clue: He is told a sad tale is best for winter, gets two lines into one, and is the reason the ending cannot be called a restoration.

characters.name: Antigonus
characters.role: A Sicilian lord, Paulina's husband
characters.summary: He argues for the queen, is bullied into swearing an oath, and then keeps it — which is the play's clearest illustration of how obedience does the damage that tyranny orders. His death is the most famous stage direction in the language, and his last line is one of the quietest.
characters.clue: He carries a baby to a beach because he swore he would, says he is gone for ever, and is right.

themes.name: Jealousy without a cause
themes.summary: Shakespeare had already written the version with a tempter; here he removes him. Leontes supplies his own evidence, his own interpretation and his own verdict inside a single speech, and the play shows the process in the grammar — clauses that start over, brackets inside brackets, words that turn obscene as he handles them.
themes.development: It arrives fully formed in 1.2, hardens into law in 2.1 and 2.3, and survives even the oracle in 3.2 until a child's death breaks it in a single line.

themes.name: Time and what it cannot mend
themes.summary: The play's hinge is a chorus who turns an hourglass and moves the action on sixteen years, and everything after that is about what can and cannot be recovered. The daughter comes back and the wife comes back; the son does not, and neither does Antigonus.
themes.development: A boy's unfinished tale in 2.1, the leap of Act IV, and in 5.3 a statue deliberately carved with sixteen years of age on it so that the time cannot be pretended away.

themes.name: Art and nature
themes.summary: The argument is conducted explicitly over grafted flowers in 4.4 and then acted out in the last scene, where a woman is presented as a painted stone. Perdita will not have improved carnations; Paulina asks a court to accept a work of art that breathes.
themes.development: Polixenes argues that the art itself is nature and immediately contradicts himself in practice; the statue scene answers him by refusing to say which it is.

themes.name: Faith, oracles and wonder
themes.summary: An oracle is read out, believed by everyone except the one man who sent for it, and vindicated by a death within the minute. In the last scene nothing supernatural is claimed and everything depends on whether the onlookers will do what Paulina asks and awake their faith.
themes.development: Apollo in Act III speaks and is denied; in Act V there is no god at all, only music, a curtain and an instruction.

themes.name: The women who hold the line
themes.canonicalName: The women who hold the line
themes.summary: Hermione argues for her honour in a court that has already convicted her; Paulina tells a king he is a tyrant and then runs his conscience for sixteen years; Perdita refuses a king's argument about breeding to his face. The men in this play give orders and the women decide what will actually happen.
themes.development: Hermione's defence in 3.2, Paulina's denunciation a hundred lines later, and in 5.3 a woman directing every other character on stage, including two kings.

themes.name: Court and country, tragedy and comedy
themes.canonicalName: Court and country, tragedy and comedy
themes.summary: The play is built in two unequal halves and refuses to blend them: a claustrophobic court where a man watches his wife's hands, and an open field with a pedlar, a dance and a cheat. The famous impossible bear stands exactly between them.
themes.development: Three acts of tragedy, an exit pursued by a bear, and a shepherd's remark about things dying and things newborn — which is the play describing its own form.

techniques.name: Broken syntax
techniques.definition: Sentences that fracture, restart or bury themselves in parenthesis to show a mind under strain.
techniques.bookDefinition: Sentences that fracture, restart or bury themselves in parenthesis to show a mind under strain.
techniques.inThisBook: Leontes's speeches in 1.2 and 2.1 are among the hardest passages Shakespeare wrote, and the difficulty is the point: the audience has to work out the thought at the same speed he is failing to.

techniques.name: The Chorus
techniques.definition: A narrator who addresses the audience directly between the acts.
techniques.bookDefinition: A figure outside the action who addresses the audience and moves it through time or space.
techniques.inThisBook: Time appears at the start of Act IV to turn his glass and skip sixteen years, apologising for the liberty — a device Sidney had mocked in print, used here without embarrassment.

techniques.name: The reported scene
techniques.definition: A major event described by witnesses rather than performed.
techniques.bookDefinition: A major event described by witnesses rather than performed.
techniques.inThisBook: The reunion of Leontes and Perdita — the scene any other play would build to — is handed to three gentlemen in 5.2, so that the statue can be the only wonder the audience actually sees.

techniques.name: Festival and song
techniques.definition: A set-piece of country celebration, with dance, ballads and the giving of flowers.
techniques.bookDefinition: A set-piece of country celebration, with dance, ballads and the giving of flowers.
techniques.inThisBook: The sheep-shearing in 4.4 is the longest scene in Shakespeare, and it is built of ballads, a pedlar's pack and a flower speech that turns into a lament halfway through.

techniques.name: The sustained stage image
techniques.definition: A piece of staging held long enough to become the play's argument.
techniques.bookDefinition: A piece of staging held long enough to become the play's argument.
techniques.inThisBook: A woman standing motionless behind a curtain for eighty lines while a court talks about her: the last scene works because nobody is allowed to touch her until she moves.

techniques.name: Tragicomic structure
techniques.definition: A play that goes as far as tragedy will take it and then turns.
techniques.bookDefinition: A play that goes as far as tragedy will take it and then turns.
techniques.inThisBook: Two deaths and an abandonment in Act III are followed by a stage direction about a bear and a scene of comic misunderstanding; the join is left visible on purpose.

quotations.text: Too hot, too hot! To mingle friendship far is mingling bloods. I have tremor cordis on me: my heart dances; But not for joy; not joy.
quotations.speaker: Leontes
quotations.context: An aside, the instant Hermione succeeds in persuading Polixenes to stay.
quotations.analysis: This is the whole onset of the jealousy, and it occupies four lines. 'Tremor cordis' is a physician's term, so he reaches for a diagnosis before he reaches for an accusation; the repetitions — too hot, mingle and mingling, not for joy, not joy — are a man arguing with something already decided.

quotations.text: But to be paddling palms and pinching fingers, As now they are, and making practised smiles, As in a looking-glass, and then to sigh, as 'twere The mort o' the deer
quotations.speaker: Leontes
quotations.context: Continuing the aside, describing what he can see across the stage.
quotations.analysis: Everything he lists is something the audience can watch happening, which is what makes the scene so uncomfortable to stage: a director must decide how much of this is true. The hunting horn blown at a deer's death was a stock image for the sigh after sex, so the innuendo is doing the work that evidence cannot.

quotations.text: A sad tale's best for winter: I have one Of sprites and goblins.
quotations.speaker: Mamillius
quotations.context: Beginning a story for his mother and her ladies, moments before the guards arrive.
quotations.analysis: The play takes its title from a child's game and then interrupts it for good: he gets two lines further before his father walks in. Placing the phrase here rather than in the happy fifth act makes the title a description of Acts I to III, not of the ending.

quotations.text: There may be in the cup A spider steep'd, and one may drink, depart, And yet partake no venom, for his knowledge Is not infected: but if one present The abhorr'd ingredient to his eye, make known How he hath drunk, he cracks his gorge, his sides, With violent hefts.
quotations.speaker: Leontes
quotations.context: On being told that Polixenes and Camillo have fled by ship.
quotations.analysis: It is a brilliant image and it proves nothing whatever: the argument is that knowing makes the poison work, which conveniently means his own conviction is itself the evidence. He ends the sentence with 'I have drunk, and seen the spider', having drunk nothing and seen only two men leaving in a hurry.

quotations.text: You speak a language that I understand not: My life stands in the level of your dreams, Which I'll lay down.
quotations.speaker: Hermione
quotations.context: At her trial, answering the charge of conspiracy.
quotations.analysis: 'In the level of' is an archery term — she is standing in the line of his aim — and the aim is a dream. Leontes answers by taking the word off her: 'Your actions are my dreams', which is the play's most compact statement of how a delusion defends itself.

quotations.text: if powers divine Behold our human actions, as they do, I doubt not then but innocence shall make False accusation blush and tyranny Tremble at patience.
quotations.speaker: Hermione
quotations.context: The opening of her defence, before the court.
quotations.analysis: She makes blushing and trembling the business of the accusers rather than the accused, which reverses the whole physical vocabulary of a trial. The conditional at the start — 'if powers divine behold' — is the risk she is taking, and within a hundred lines Apollo answers it, and Leontes refuses the answer.

quotations.text: Hermione is chaste; Polixenes blameless; Camillo a true subject; Leontes a jealous tyrant; his innocent babe truly begotten; and the king shall live without an heir, if that which is lost be not found.
quotations.speaker: An Officer
quotations.context: Reading the sealed oracle aloud in the courtroom.
quotations.analysis: Five flat verdicts and then one condition, and the condition is the plot of the last two acts. Everything before the final clause is in the present tense and settled; the play's whole second half hangs on the word 'if', which is the only uncertainty Apollo allows.

quotations.text: Apollo's angry; and the heavens themselves Do strike at my injustice.
quotations.speaker: Leontes
quotations.context: One line after a servant reports that his son is dead.
quotations.analysis: The delusion that survived a god's direct testimony collapses the moment a child dies, which is a brutal piece of arithmetic on the play's part. Note that he still makes the news about himself — the heavens are striking at his injustice, not at Mamillius.

quotations.text: What studied torments, tyrant, hast for me? What wheels? racks? fires? what flaying? boiling? In leads or oils? what old or newer torture Must I receive, whose every word deserves To taste of thy most worst?
quotations.speaker: Paulina
quotations.context: Returning to the court with the news that the queen is dead.
quotations.analysis: She lists the punishments before she delivers the news, which is a way of making it impossible to silence her: every torment has already been named and accepted. The word 'tyrant' is placed inside the first question, where a king's title would go.

quotations.text: The day frowns more and more: thou'rt like to have A lullaby too rough: I never saw The heavens so dim by day. A savage clamour! Well may I get aboard! This is the chase: I am gone for ever.
quotations.speaker: Antigonus
quotations.context: On the Bohemian coast, having just laid the baby down; the next line of the text is the stage direction.
quotations.analysis: 'A lullaby too rough' is addressed to an infant he is abandoning in a storm, and it is the gentlest thing said in three acts. The last four words are both a cry of terror and a piece of plain information, and the stage direction that follows them is the most famous in the language.

quotations.text: Heavy matters! heavy matters! but look thee here, boy. Now bless thyself: thou mettest with things dying, I with things newborn.
quotations.speaker: Shepherd
quotations.context: To his son, who has just described the shipwreck and the bear, while holding the baby he has found.
quotations.analysis: The play's structure is stated out loud by a man who has no idea he is describing it: one half of the stage has a wreck on it and the other half a child. It is also the only line in Shakespeare that could serve as a definition of tragicomedy, and it is given to a shepherd in prose.

quotations.text: My father named me Autolycus; who being, as I am, littered under Mercury, was likewise a snapper-up of unconsidered trifles.
quotations.speaker: Autolycus
quotations.context: Introducing himself to the audience on the road to the sheep-shearing.
quotations.analysis: Mercury was the god of thieves and of eloquence, and Autolycus in Homer was his son; the name is a joke for anyone who has it and a good name for a pedlar for anyone who has not. 'Littered' is a word for animals, and he applies it to himself without complaint.

quotations.text: You see, sweet maid, we marry A gentler scion to the wildest stock, And make conceive a bark of baser kind By bud of nobler race: this is an art Which does mend nature, change it rather, but The art itself is nature.
quotations.speaker: Polixenes
quotations.context: Disguised at the sheep-shearing, arguing with Perdita about grafted flowers.
quotations.analysis: The argument is that human art is one of nature's own methods, and it is unanswerable — Perdita simply says 'So it is' and then refuses to do it anyway. The joke is savage: within forty lines the same speaker will forbid his noble son to marry a baser stock and threaten the girl with death.

quotations.text: O Proserpina, For the flowers now, that frighted thou let'st fall From Dis's waggon! daffodils, That come before the swallow dares, and take The winds of March with beauty
quotations.speaker: Perdita
quotations.context: Wishing she had spring flowers to give the young women at the feast.
quotations.analysis: Every flower in the speech is one she does not have, so the loveliest passage in the play is a list of absences. Proserpina was also a daughter stolen from her mother and returned for half the year — Perdita invokes her own story without knowing it, which is the closest the play comes to telling her who she is.

quotations.text: when you do dance, I wish you A wave o' the sea, that you might ever do Nothing but that; move still, still so, And own no other function
quotations.speaker: Florizel
quotations.context: Praising Perdita as she moves among the guests.
quotations.analysis: 'Move still, still so' means keep moving and keep still at once, which is what a wave does and what a statue cannot — the play will collect on that image in the last scene. The wish is also faintly alarming: he would like her to do nothing else ever, and the speech turns her actions into a series of held poses.

quotations.text: No more such wives; therefore, no wife: one worse, And better used, would make her sainted spirit Again possess her corpse, and on this stage, Where we're offenders now, appear soul-vex'd, And begin, 'Why to me?'
quotations.speaker: Leontes
quotations.context: Refusing, in front of Paulina, the court's suggestion that he remarry.
quotations.analysis: He imagines his dead wife returning to reproach him, in a theatre, on a stage — and two scenes later she does return, without reproaching him at all. 'Where we're offenders now' turns the court into a playhouse and the living into the guilty party, which is exactly the arrangement of the final scene.

quotations.text: Chide me, dear stone, that I may say indeed Thou art Hermione; or rather, thou art she In thy not chiding, for she was as tender As infancy and grace.
quotations.speaker: Leontes
quotations.context: The first words spoken after Paulina draws the curtain.
quotations.analysis: He asks the statue to scold him and then decides its silence is more like her, which lets him have the rebuke and the forgiveness at once. Everything he says in this scene is addressed to an object, and the audience has been given no more information than he has.

quotations.text: So much the more our carver's excellence; Which lets go by some sixteen years and makes her As she lived now.
quotations.speaker: Paulina
quotations.context: Explaining why the statue looks older than the queen Leontes remembers.
quotations.analysis: The wrinkles are the play's proof that the reconciliation is not a reversal: the sixteen years are carved into the object everyone is looking at. It is also a very good lie, and the audience is invited to notice that a sculptor who aged his subject would be doing something no sculptor does.

quotations.text: It is required You do awake your faith. Then all stand still; On: those that think it is unlawful business I am about, let them depart.
quotations.speaker: Paulina
quotations.context: Before calling for music and telling the statue to descend.
quotations.analysis: The instruction is given to the people on stage and, unavoidably, to the people watching them: a theatre audience is always being asked to do this, and here the request is made out loud. 'Required' is the hardest word in the sentence — not invited, not encouraged, and with an exit offered to anyone who will not.

quotations.text: O, she's warm! If this be magic, let it be an art Lawful as eating.
quotations.speaker: Leontes
quotations.context: Taking Hermione's hand as she steps down from the pedestal.
quotations.analysis: Three words settle a question the whole scene has hung on, and they are about temperature rather than identity. The comparison he reaches for is eating — the most ordinary bodily fact available — which quietly refuses the supernatural reading while leaving it standing.

quotations.text: That she is living, Were it but told you, should be hooted at Like an old tale: but it appears she lives, Though yet she speak not.
quotations.speaker: Paulina
quotations.context: As Hermione embraces Leontes and the others ask where she has been.
quotations.analysis: The play calls its own plot ridiculous for the third time, and the defence is that this one is being seen rather than reported. It is also an exact description of what the audience is doing: accepting on stage what it would hoot at in a story, which is the difference the last act is built to demonstrate.

quotations.text: You gods, look down And from your sacred vials pour your graces Upon my daughter's head!
quotations.speaker: Hermione
quotations.context: Her first words after sixteen years, spoken once Paulina has turned her towards Perdita.
quotations.analysis: She speaks to the gods, then to her daughter, and never once to her husband — the reunion the play has been building towards turns out to be with the child. Her only explanation is that she preserved herself because the oracle gave hope the baby was alive, which makes the marriage a piece of unfinished business the play leaves alone.

atAGlance.label: Written
atAGlance.note: One of the late plays, close in date to Cymbeline and The Tempest.

atAGlance.label: First seen
atAGlance.note: Simon Forman recorded a performance at the Globe and wrote down what he took from it — chiefly a warning about trusting confidence men.

atAGlance.label: Chief source
atAGlance.note: Robert Greene's prose romance of 1588, whose jealous king dies at the end. Shakespeare keeps the plot and refuses the ending.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.note: Three acts of tragedy, a speech from Time, and two acts of pastoral comedy that have to carry the first three.

criticalViews.position: A play about repentance and grace
criticalViews.summary: The oldest reading takes the last scene at its word: sixteen years of penance are answered by something that looks like resurrection, and the language of faith, awakening and redemption is the play's own.
criticalViews.counter: Mamillius and Antigonus stay dead, and the play makes a point of the wrinkles — nothing is given back unaltered.

criticalViews.position: A play about theatre itself
criticalViews.summary: The chorus, the reported reunion, the curtain and the instruction to awake your faith all point at the playhouse: what the last act asks of Leontes is exactly what a performance asks of an audience.
criticalViews.counter: It can make the reconciliation feel like a trick, when the text gives Hermione a plain and unmagical explanation of where she has been.

criticalViews.position: Where was Hermione for sixteen years?
criticalViews.summary: The text supports two readings — a concealment managed by Paulina, or a genuine restoration — and criticism has long argued about which the staging should imply, since the answer changes what kind of play this is.
criticalViews.counter: The scene is written so that neither reading can be ruled out, which suggests the ambiguity is the effect rather than an oversight.

criticalViews.position: The women and the recovery
criticalViews.summary: Feminist criticism has noted how completely the second half depends on women — Paulina's management, Perdita's authority, Hermione's silence — and how little the restored marriage is allowed to say for itself.
criticalViews.counter: The same reading has to account for Paulina being handed a new husband in the last thirty lines, with no line of her own to answer it.

essayQuestions.question: How does Shakespeare present Leontes's jealousy, and what is the effect of giving it no cause?
essayQuestions.focus: Language, evidence and the absence of an Iago
plan: Compare the opening with Othello: there is no tempter here, and the suspicion takes nine lines.
Analyse the syntax of 1.2.134 onward — the restarts, the parentheses, the sexual punning that arrives before the accusation.
Use the spider speech at 2.1.51 to show the jealousy generating its own proof.
Examine 3.2: the oracle is denied, and only a child's death breaks the delusion.
Conclude on what the missing motive does to an audience, which is left with nothing to blame but a mind.

essayQuestions.question: Discuss the function of the play's two halves.
essayQuestions.focus: Structure, genre and the bear
plan: Set out the shape: three acts of tragedy, a chorus, two acts of pastoral comedy.
Read 3.3 closely — the abandonment, the bear, the Clown's comic account of a drowning — as the point where the genres change hands.
Use the Shepherd's 'things dying, I with things newborn' as the play's own description of its form.
Show how the second half keeps the first in view: sixteen years, an aged statue, a dead son never replaced.
Argue whether the join is a flaw the play survives or the whole point of it.

essayQuestions.question: What is Paulina for?
essayQuestions.focus: Authority, conscience and stage management
plan: Begin with 2.2 and 2.3, where she decides on her own initiative to confront a king with his daughter.
Analyse the denunciation at 3.2.192 and note that she lists the tortures before delivering the news.
Trace her control of the sixteen years: the daily visits to the grave, the veto on remarriage in 5.1.
Read 5.3 as a piece of direction — the curtain, the standstill, the music, the instruction about faith.
Weigh the ending, in which the play's most independent character is given a husband in a single line.

essayQuestions.question: 'The last scene works because the audience is asked to do something.' Discuss.
essayQuestions.focus: Faith, wonder and the reported reunion
plan: Note first what the play declines to show: the recognition of Perdita is handed to three gentlemen in 5.2.
Establish what the audience knows and does not know going into 5.3, and what a production can choose to signal.
Analyse 'It is required You do awake your faith' as an instruction aimed past the stage.
Consider 'O, she's warm' and the comparison to eating — the wonder is confirmed by the most ordinary evidence available.
Decide what Hermione's silence towards her husband does to the effect, and whether the scene is a reward or a question.

discussionQuestions: Leontes becomes jealous in nine lines with no evidence at all. Is that harder or easier to watch than Othello's slow poisoning?
The reunion of father and daughter happens offstage and is described by strangers. Why give away the scene most plays would build to?
Was Hermione alive for sixteen years, or restored? Does a production have to decide?
Mamillius never comes back, and nobody in the last scene mentions him. What does that silence do to the ending?
Bohemia has no sea-coast, and the play knows it. Does the impossibility matter, or is it part of the invitation?

timeline.label: Robert Greene's Pandosto published
timeline.detail: The prose romance Shakespeare follows closely, and whose jealous king kills himself at the end.

timeline.label: Greene dies, having attacked Shakespeare in print
timeline.detail: The pamphlet that calls him an upstart crow appeared in the same year; twenty years later Shakespeare took Greene's plot.

timeline.label: The Winter's Tale most likely written
timeline.detail: Usually dated 1609–11, among the late plays and close to Cymbeline and The Tempest.

timeline.label: Simon Forman sees the play at the Globe
timeline.detail: His notebook entry of 15 May records the plot, the bear and, at length, Autolycus; the moral he draws is to beware of trusting feigned beggars.

timeline.label: Played at court for Princess Elizabeth's wedding festivities
timeline.detail: The King's Men gave a long series of plays for the marriage of James's daughter, and this was among them.

timeline.label: Jonson mocks tales and tempests
timeline.detail: The induction to Bartholomew Fair jeers at plays full of servant-monsters and drolleries — a contemporary judgement on exactly this kind of writing.

timeline.label: First Folio
timeline.detail: The only early text, printed last among the comedies and generally thought to have been set from a scribe's transcript.

timeline.label: Garrick's Florizel and Perdita
timeline.detail: An adaptation that kept the pastoral and cut most of the first three acts, and held the stage for decades.

timeline.label: The full play returns to the London stage
timeline.detail: The nineteenth century restored the tragic first half, and the statue scene became one of the great set pieces of the English theatre.

places.name: Sicily
places.note: Leontes's court, the trial, and the chapel in Paulina's house.

places.name: Bohemia
places.note: Polixenes's kingdom and the sheep-shearing — given a sea-coast by the play, which Bohemia has never had.

places.name: Delphi
places.note: The play calls it Delphos and makes it an island; Cleomenes and Dion sail there for the oracle.

places.name: Delos
places.note: The Aegean island sacred to Apollo, routinely confused with Delphi in Shakespeare's day and the reason the ambassadors go by sea.

places.name: The Globe, Bankside
places.note: Where Simon Forman saw the play in May 1611 and wrote down what he made of it.

related.why: The other late play built on loss, a long interval and a reconciliation the text will not quite guarantee.
Written within a year or two, with the same machinery: a wronged wife, a lost child, an oracle and a recognition scene.
The same disease with a cause supplied, which makes the comparison the fastest way to see what this play is doing.
The first of the late romances, with a chorus, a sea and a daughter restored to a father who has stopped speaking.
The earlier pastoral, where the country festival is the whole play rather than the cure for the first half of one.

books.title: The Woman in White
books.author: Wilkie Collins
books.setting: Cumberland, London and a decaying estate in Hampshire, between 1849 and 1851
books.written: Begun 15 August 1859; the manuscript finished 26 July 1860, with the serial still running
books.lengthNote: Three Epochs, assembled out of eleven separate narratives by nine hands
books.openingLine: This is the story of what a woman’s patience can endure, and what a Man’s resolution can achieve.
books.summary: A drawing master meets a frightened woman on the Finchley Road at midnight and learns afterwards that she has escaped from an asylum. Her resemblance to the heiress he is about to teach turns out to be the whole machinery of a conspiracy: two women can be exchanged if the documents say so, and a marriage settlement supplies the motive. Collins tells it as a file of statements by different hands, so that the reader assembles the case as a jury would, out of testimony that nobody has cross-examined.

sourceText.label: Standard Ebooks text of The Woman in White
sourceText.note: References give the epoch, the narrator and the chapter number within that narrative, since the novel numbers its chapters afresh for each new hand.

structure.label: The First Epoch — Hartright
structure.title: The road, Limmeridge and the likeness
structure.summary: Walter Hartright takes a post teaching drawing in Cumberland, having met a woman dressed entirely in white on the Finchley Road and helped her into a cab. At Limmeridge he finds his pupil’s face is the same face, falls in love with an engaged woman, and is quietly removed from the household.

structure.label: The First Epoch — Gilmore
structure.title: The settlement
structure.summary: The family solicitor takes over the narrative and the story becomes a document. Sir Percival’s lawyer refuses to protect Laura’s twenty thousand pounds, Mr Fairlie will not exert himself to object, and Gilmore signs a settlement he says no daughter of his would have been married under.

structure.label: The First Epoch — Marian’s diary
structure.title: The marriage agreed
structure.summary: Marian’s diary begins, and with it the novel’s most immediate voice: dated, unrevised and written by somebody who does not know what happens next. Laura tells Sir Percival the truth about her feelings and he marries her anyway.

structure.label: The Second Epoch — Blackwater Park
structure.title: Fosco, surveillance and a diary interrupted
structure.summary: The couple return with Count and Countess Fosco, and Blackwater Park becomes a place where letters are read and servants are managed. Marian climbs onto the verandah roof in the rain to hear the two men plan, and writes down what she has heard until the fever takes the pen out of her hand.

structure.label: The Second Epoch — other hands
structure.title: The substitution, told by the people who were there
structure.summary: Mr Fairlie, the housekeeper Eliza Michelson, a cook, a doctor and a headstone carry the story through the exchange. Anne Catherick dies in London under Laura’s name; Laura is taken to the asylum under Anne’s, and every step is attested by somebody who saw only a fragment.

structure.label: The Third Epoch — Hartright returns
structure.title: A living woman and her own grave
structure.summary: Walter comes back from Central America to find a stone with Laura’s name on it and a woman nobody will identify. The investigation turns into a search for dates: what is needed is not a confession but proof that the journey to London happened after the death on the certificate.

structure.label: The Third Epoch — Mrs Catherick and Fosco
structure.title: Two confessions, neither of them penitent
structure.summary: Mrs Catherick’s letter explains the vestry, the forged register and the secret Sir Percival died trying to burn. Fosco, writing at pistol point, gives the conspiracy as a piece of intellectual autobiography and awards himself the credit for it.

structure.label: The Third Epoch — the conclusion
structure.title: Identity restored, on paper
structure.summary: Fosco is killed in Paris by the Brotherhood he betrayed, the false inscription is cut away from the stone, and Laura’s name is publicly restored in front of the tenants at Limmeridge. Walter closes the file he has spent the novel assembling and hands the last word to Marian.

characters.name: Walter Hartright
characters.role: A teacher of drawing, later the editor of the whole narrative
characters.summary: He is the novel’s hero and also its archivist, which are two different kinds of power. He collects, orders and introduces every other statement in the book, so the reader’s impression of Marian, Fosco and Laura has already passed through his hands before it arrives.
characters.clue: He is walking back to London at midnight when a hand touches his shoulder, and he spends the rest of the book assembling the paperwork that follows.

characters.name: Marian Halcombe
characters.role: Laura’s half-sister
characters.summary: She is introduced through a description that admires her figure and recoils from her face, and then proceeds to do everything the plot requires: investigate, climb, travel, negotiate and remember. The novel gives her no money, no legal standing and the best prose in the book.
characters.clue: She takes off her shoes, crawls out over a verandah roof in a downpour and writes down what she hears until the fever takes the pen away.
traits: without any legal power at all

characters.name: Laura Fairlie
characters.role: Heiress of Limmeridge, later Lady Glyde
characters.summary: She is the object the conspiracy moves around, and Collins gives her almost no narrative of her own: her testimony is the one thing the plot establishes is legally worthless. What is stolen from her is not money but the acknowledged fact of being herself.
characters.clue: Her name is on a gravestone in Cumberland while she is alive in London, and for a whole epoch nobody in authority will say otherwise.

characters.name: Anne Catherick
characters.role: The woman in white
characters.summary: She is dressed in white because a kind woman once praised her in it, shut up in an asylum because she knew a secret she did not understand, and killed by the conspiracy because her heart gives out at the right moment for it. She gives the novel its title and almost nothing else of her own.
characters.clue: She asks a stranger on the road whether he knows many men of the rank of Baronet, and will not say which one she means.

characters.name: Sir Percival Glyde
characters.role: Baronet, of Blackwater Park
characters.summary: Charming for exactly as long as the settlement takes to sign, and after that a man locking doors. His secret is smaller and more frightening than the plot implies: he has no title at all, only a page added to a parish register, which makes him a forgery rather than a villain.
characters.clue: He dies in the vestry of a country church, trying to burn the book that proves he was never entitled to his own name.
characters.firstAppearance: The First Epoch, Vincent Gilmore’s narrative

characters.name: Count Fosco
characters.role: An Italian exile, Sir Percival’s friend
characters.summary: Enormous, silent-footed, fond of white mice and pastry, and the only character in the novel who thinks in terms of systems. He is also the one who writes his own confession and cannot resist making it a lecture; his vanity is what eventually kills him.
characters.clue: He keeps canaries and white mice, flatters his enemy in her own diary, and is found in the Paris Morgue with a mark cut into his left arm.

characters.name: Frederick Fairlie
characters.role: Laura’s uncle, master of Limmeridge House
characters.summary: A collector of etchings and coins who has made his own nerves into a full-time occupation, and whose refusal to be troubled is what allows every stage of the conspiracy to proceed. Collins hands him a narrative of his own so that he can convict himself in his own voice.
characters.clue: He asks visitors to speak more quietly and to put the tray of coins back themselves, and calls himself a bundle of nerves dressed up to look like a man.

characters.name: Mrs Catherick
characters.role: Anne’s mother, of Welmingham
characters.summary: She sold her silence for respectability and has spent twenty years collecting it in instalments: a house, a clock, and the clergyman’s bow every Sunday. Her narrative is the coldest thing in the book, because she is not ashamed of any of it.
characters.clue: She sits at her window each Sunday to be bowed to by the clergyman, and counts that bow as the price of what she did in a vestry.

characters.name: Vincent Gilmore
characters.role: The Fairlie family solicitor
characters.summary: He writes the second narrative and supplies the novel’s legal spine: the marriage settlement, the twenty thousand pounds, and the clause that makes Laura worth more dead than alive. He sees exactly what is coming and signs anyway, because his client will not be bothered.
characters.clue: He records, twice and in the same words, that no daughter of his would have been married under the settlement he was compelled to draw up.

themes.name: Identity and documents
themes.summary: A person in this novel is whatever the paperwork says. A gravestone, a doctor’s certificate and a parish register are enough to kill a living woman and to make a commoner a baronet, and no amount of embodied self-knowledge will overturn any of them.
themes.development: Anne’s white dress and Laura’s face set up the resemblance; the inscription in Limmeridge churchyard executes it; and the counter-attack, when it comes, is made of dates rather than recognition.

themes.name: Testimony and the record
themes.summary: The book is arranged as evidence in a trial that never takes place, and the arrangement is itself the argument: no single witness sees enough, and the person who compiles them holds the real power. Walter says so in the preamble and then exercises it for six hundred pages.
themes.development: From Hartright’s opening statement of method, through Marian’s dated diary and Mr Fairlie’s self-serving deposition, to Fosco’s written confession extracted at gunpoint.

themes.name: Marriage, money and the law
themes.summary: The conspiracy needs no magic, only a settlement. Laura’s twenty thousand pounds passes to her husband if she dies first, and the whole plot is an attempt to bring that clause forward by about fifty years.
themes.development: Drafted in Gilmore’s narrative, refused correction by an indolent guardian, and executed at Blackwater Park by a man who needs the money before his creditors arrive.

themes.name: Confinement and the asylum
themes.summary: Two women are shut up in this novel and neither is mad. Private asylum admission needed certificates and somebody willing to sign them, and Collins builds his most frightening scenes out of that ordinary administrative fact rather than out of anything Gothic.
themes.development: Anne escapes in the first chapters, Laura is admitted under her name in the second epoch, and the rescue depends on a nurse being bribed rather than on any doubt being raised.

themes.name: What women are allowed to do
themes.summary: The preamble divides the world into a woman’s patience and a man’s resolution, and the novel immediately disobeys it. Marian does the investigating, the climbing and the remembering; Laura’s own word about who she is counts for nothing in law.
themes.development: Stated as a formula in the first paragraph, contradicted throughout Marian’s diary, and quietly restored at the end when the record is closed by Walter and the estate passes to his son.

themes.name: Rank, name and forgery
themes.summary: Sir Percival’s secret is that his rank is a forgery, and the novel treats this as worse than the conspiracy it produced. A title, like an identity, turns out to be a line of writing in a book kept in a badly locked cupboard.
themes.development: Hinted by Anne’s question about men of the rank of Baronet, investigated through the marriage register at Old Welmingham, and settled by a fire in a vestry.

techniques.name: Multiple narrators
techniques.definition: Telling one story through a sequence of first-person accounts by different people.
techniques.bookDefinition: Telling one story through a sequence of first-person accounts by different people.
techniques.inThisBook: Eleven narratives by nine hands, from a solicitor and a housekeeper to a cook, a doctor and a headstone; each witness speaks only of what they saw, and the differences between their voices carry the class comedy as well as the evidence.

techniques.name: Documentary form
techniques.definition: Building a novel out of objects that would exist in the world it describes.
techniques.bookDefinition: Building a novel out of objects that would exist in the world it describes.
