books.title: Uncle Tom’s Cabin
books.author: Harriet Beecher Stowe
books.setting: A Kentucky farm, the Ohio river and the free states, New Orleans, and a cotton plantation on the Red River
books.lengthNote: Forty-five chapters in two volumes, written to a weekly newspaper deadline
books.openingLine: Late in the afternoon of a chilly day in February, two gentlemen were sitting alone over their wine, in a well-furnished dining parlor, in the town of P⁠⸺, in Kentucky.
books.summary: A Kentucky farmer in debt sells two people to settle it, and the novel follows both of them in opposite directions. Eliza runs north with her child across the ice of the Ohio; Tom is carried south through three owners until he reaches a plantation where the arithmetic of cotton makes a man cheaper to replace than to keep. Stowe built the book out of scenes designed to be unbearable to a churchgoing readership, and then told that readership what it was to do about them.

sourceText.label: Standard Ebooks text of Uncle Tom’s Cabin
sourceText.note: Chapters are numbered continuously in Roman numerals from I to XLV across the two volumes of the 1852 book edition; references below give the chapter only.

structure.label: Chapters I–VIII
structure.title: A debt, and two people sold to cover it
structure.summary: Mr Shelby, who considers himself a kind man, settles his accounts by selling Tom and the child Harry to a trader. Eliza overhears the arrangement and runs that night; Tom, who could run, stays because leaving would mean the rest of the estate going instead. The novel's whole argument is set up in a dining parlour before anybody is cruel to anyone.

scenes.title: The bargain
scenes.summary: Haley and Shelby over the wine; Eliza listens at the door; George Harris tells his wife he will not endure it much longer.

scenes.title: The cabin and the flight
scenes.summary: An evening of hymn-singing in Tom's cabin, then Eliza waking Harry at midnight and the household covering for her.

scenes.title: The ice
scenes.summary: Eliza crosses the Ohio on the breaking floes, and the slave-catchers are hired in a tavern.

structure.label: Chapters IX–XIII
structure.title: Free states, and a boat going the other way
structure.summary: The chapters alternate between the fugitives and their cargo counterpart. A senator who voted for the Fugitive Slave Act finds it in his kitchen; George Harris faces down his pursuers on a rock; and Haley, on a steamboat south, sells a woman's infant off her lap and records the consequence in his account book.

scenes.title: Senator Bird
scenes.summary: Mrs Bird argues the law down in her own parlour, and the senator drives Eliza to a safe house himself.

scenes.title: Two directions at once
scenes.summary: Tom is taken from his family and shipped downriver; George Harris, in disguise, declares himself a man without a country.

scenes.title: The Quaker settlement
scenes.summary: Rachel Halliday's kitchen: the novel's model household, run without owning anybody.

structure.label: Chapters XIV–XVIII
structure.title: New Orleans, and a household that means well
structure.summary: Tom saves a child who falls overboard and is bought by her father, and the book's middle section installs him in the most comfortable slavery it can imagine. Augustine St Clare talks brilliantly against the system he profits from; his cousin Ophelia arrives from Vermont opposed to slavery and unable to bear the people held under it.

scenes.title: Eva and the boat
scenes.summary: Tom is bought after pulling Evangeline St Clare out of the Mississippi.

scenes.title: The St Clare house
scenes.summary: Marie's invalidism, Ophelia's efficiency, and St Clare's long argument that knowing better changes nothing.

structure.label: Chapters XIX–XXVIII
structure.title: Two deaths, and the paper that was never signed
structure.summary: St Clare sets out the economics of ownership more clearly than any abolitionist in the book and does nothing. Ophelia is given Topsy to educate and discovers her own revulsion. Eva dies at length and in public, as sentimental fiction required; her father is stabbed in a tavern brawl before he can free Tom, and the household is sold.

scenes.title: The argument
scenes.summary: St Clare on his brother's plantation, on his own idleness, and on what the law actually permits.

scenes.title: Ophelia and Topsy
scenes.summary: A northern woman's antislavery principle meets a child she cannot bring herself to touch.

scenes.title: Two funerals
scenes.summary: Eva's death, St Clare's sudden one, and Marie's decision to sell.

structure.label: Chapters XXIX–XXXVIII
structure.title: The Red River, where manners stop
structure.summary: Tom is sold at auction to Simon Legree and taken to a plantation run on the principle that people are cheaper to work to death than to maintain. Cassy, who has survived it longest, tells Tom her history; Legree, who is afraid of nothing visible, turns out to be terrified of a lock of hair and a noise in the garret.

scenes.title: The warehouse and the wagon
scenes.summary: The New Orleans sale rooms, and the journey upriver with Legree's new purchases.

scenes.title: Legree's arithmetic
scenes.summary: Tom refuses to flog a sick woman; Cassy gives the plantation's history in her own voice.

scenes.title: The garret
scenes.summary: Legree's superstition, Cassy's plan, and Tom's refusal to say where the women have gone.

structure.label: Chapters XXXIX–XLV
structure.title: An escape, a death and an address to the reader
structure.summary: Cassy and Emmeline hide in the haunted garret while the plantation searches the swamp for them. Tom is beaten to death for his silence, and George Shelby arrives two days late with the money to buy him. The scattered family is reassembled improbably, sails for Liberia, and Stowe steps forward to tell her readers what she wants them to do.

scenes.title: The ghost in the garret
scenes.summary: Cassy uses Legree's superstition against him; Tom is flogged and dies; George Shelby buries him.

scenes.title: Reunions
scenes.summary: Cassy discovers that Eliza is her daughter; the Harrises decide on Liberia; George Shelby frees the people at home.

scenes.title: Concluding remarks
scenes.summary: Stowe drops the fiction, states which incidents are drawn from record, and addresses the mothers of America directly.

characters.name: Tom
characters.role: An enslaved man, sold three times in the course of the novel
characters.summary: He is a literate, married man of about forty who reads his Bible slowly with a finger, and the novel's central question is whether his refusal to escape is obedience or a decision. On the Red River he draws a line and will not move it, and the line costs him his life rather than saving it.
characters.clue: He could have run north with the others and did not, because the rest of the estate would have been sold instead; he is killed for refusing to say where two women went.

characters.name: Eliza Harris
characters.role: An enslaved woman in the Shelby household, Harry's mother
characters.summary: She is given the novel's most famous physical action and almost none of its dialogue about principle: she hears the sale discussed through a door and is over the river before anyone has finished arguing. Everything she does afterwards is organised around keeping a five-year-old alive and quiet.
characters.clue: She crossed a river full of moving ice with a child on her hip, and a slave-catcher watching from the bank called the jump the best he had ever seen.

characters.name: George Harris
characters.role: Eliza's husband, hired out to a factory by his owner
characters.summary: He invented a machine for cleaning hemp and was taken out of the factory for it, which is the novel's compressed statement of what slavery wastes. He argues rather than endures, arms himself, and is the one character allowed to reject the country outright rather than appeal to its conscience.
characters.clue: A factory hand whose invention got him sent back to field work, he stands on a rock above a pursuing posse and declares that he has no country at all.

characters.name: Haley
characters.role: A slave trader
characters.summary: Stowe makes him neither a monster nor an aberration but a man with a business model, who prides himself on humane methods because damaged goods sell badly. He supplies the novel's running joke and its coldest passages: the same voice that talks about conscience keeps a ledger of losses.
characters.clue: He boasts of his humanity in the trade, and enters a woman who has drowned herself in his account book under the heading of losses.

characters.name: Mrs Shelby
characters.role: Mistress of the Kentucky farm
characters.summary: She has taught the people she owns to read and to pray and believes this makes the arrangement tolerable; the sale shows her that her opinions have no legal force whatever. Her outrage is genuine and completely ineffective, which is the use Stowe makes of her.
characters.clue: She taught them their catechism and their letters, and found on the morning of the sale that her husband had not consulted her and did not need to.

characters.name: Augustine St Clare
characters.role: A New Orleans gentleman, Tom's second owner
characters.summary: He can describe the economics and the hypocrisy of slavery better than anyone else in the novel, and he keeps a household of people he has not freed. Stowe gives the clearest analysis to a man who will not act on it, which makes his sudden death the most pointed thing that happens in the book.
characters.clue: He calls the whole business accursed of God and man over his brandy, and dies with the manumission papers still unsigned.

characters.name: Evangeline St Clare
characters.role: St Clare's daughter
characters.summary: She is the novel's sentimental engine: a child who says the unanswerable thing and then dies of it slowly enough for everyone to gather. Readers who find her unbearable and readers who weep over her are responding to the same technique, which Stowe deploys with complete deliberation.
characters.clue: A child who tells a grown man she would die for the people he owns, and then does — over most of a chapter, with the household assembled.

characters.name: Miss Ophelia
characters.role: St Clare's cousin, from Vermont
characters.summary: She arrives with northern antislavery opinions and a horror of disorder, and the novel uses her to make the point it most wanted its readers to feel: that opposing slavery in principle and being unable to touch a black child are perfectly compatible. Her slow correction by Topsy is the only conversion in the book that takes work.
characters.clue: A New Englander who disapproved of slavery all her life, and had to be taught by a child that she could not bear to be in the same room as the people she pitied.

relationships.label: given charge of, and educated by

characters.name: Topsy
characters.role: A child in the St Clare household
characters.summary: She answers questions about her origins by saying she had none, and the answer is the most efficient indictment of the trade in the novel. She is also the character in whom Stowe's comic writing comes closest to the minstrel stage, and the two facts have to be held together rather than traded off.
characters.clue: Asked who made her, she says she has no father, no mother and no birth, and supposes she was raised by a speculator.

characters.name: Simon Legree
characters.role: A cotton planter on the Red River, Tom's last owner
characters.summary: He runs his plantation on a stated policy of using people up and buying more, and he sets the enslaved to guard each other so that nobody can be trusted. Stowe makes him a New Englander by birth, which quietly removes the comfort of treating him as a southern problem.
characters.clue: He works people to death on principle because replacements are cheaper than upkeep, and is frightened out of his wits by a lock of hair and a noise upstairs.

characters.name: Cassy
characters.role: An enslaved woman on Legree's plantation
characters.summary: She has been educated, sold repeatedly, separated from three children and driven to kill an infant rather than let it be sold, and she tells all of it herself in the first person. She is also the only person in the novel who defeats a white man by out-thinking him, using his own fear of the house against him.
characters.clue: She reads her owner's terrors better than he does, and escapes by hiding in the one room on the plantation he will not enter.

themes.name: Law, debt and property in people
themes.summary: Stowe's method is to show ownership working through ordinary paperwork rather than through the whip: a debt, a bill of sale, an unsigned deed of manumission, a statute obliging a senator's neighbours to help recapture a stranger. The cruelty of the Red River is the same legal power that the Shelbys exercise politely.
themes.development: A private debt in Chapter I, the Fugitive Slave Act in Senator Bird's parlour, St Clare's failure to sign in Chapter XXVIII, and the auction rooms of Chapter XXX where the law and the market are the same thing.

themes.name: Feeling as political argument
themes.summary: The book asks its readers to imagine an enslaved family through the domestic affections they already honour, and then to act on the recognition. Every device of popular fiction — the deathbed, the lost child, the reunion — is turned toward a legislative end, and the concluding chapter says so explicitly.
themes.development: From the sale overheard in Chapter I, through Eva's death, to the direct instruction in Chapter XLV that the least a reader can do is to see to it that they feel rightly.

themes.name: Christianity on trial
themes.summary: Nearly every character has a religion and the novel spends its length distinguishing between them: the piety that sanctions a sale, the piety that sings hymns in a cabin, the northern church that deplores slavery and returns fugitives. Stowe's final pages put the account squarely at the door of the American churches.
themes.development: Tom's Bible in Chapter IV, Mrs Bird against her husband's vote in Chapter IX, St Clare's mockery of clerical apologists, Legree's use of scripture as a licence, and the judgement pronounced in Chapter XLV.

themes.name: Mothers and children
themes.summary: The novel's engine is separation: a child sold off a lap on a steamboat, a mother crossing broken ice, a woman who poisoned her own infant rather than see it sold, and a reader addressed at the end as a mother who has stood beside a cradle. Stowe treats the destruction of families as slavery's defining product rather than its excess.
themes.development: Eliza's flight in Chapter VII, the unnamed woman on Haley's boat in Chapter XII, Cassy's history in Chapter XXXIV, and the address to the mothers of America in Chapter XLV.

themes.name: Flight and the geography of freedom
themes.canonicalName: Flight and the geography of freedom
themes.summary: North and south are not moral categories in this book but distances with laws attached. Eliza's route runs through Ohio parlours where the Fugitive Slave Act reaches, and ends outside the country altogether; Tom's runs downriver through kinder and kinder owners into the worst place in the novel.
themes.development: The river crossing in Chapter VII, the Quaker settlement in Chapter XIII, George's declaration on the rock in Chapter XVII, and the decision in Chapter XLIII to leave for Liberia rather than stay in a country that will not have them.

themes.name: Race, type and caricature
themes.summary: Stowe assigns temperaments by descent — Tom's patience, George's intellect explained by a white father, Topsy's comic energy — and the novel's sympathy runs along those lines rather than across them. This is the book's deepest and most enduring problem, and it is present in the same scenes that made it politically effective.
themes.development: The narrator's generalisations about African nature in the New Orleans chapters, the handling of Topsy, the whiteness of the characters permitted to argue and escape, and the Liberian ending that removes the freed family from America altogether.

techniques.name: Double plot
techniques.definition: A second story running beside the first, repeating its problem in another key and commenting on it.
techniques.bookDefinition: A second story running beside the first, repeating its problem in another key and commenting on it.
techniques.inThisBook: Eliza going north and Tom going south are told in alternating blocks, so that every act of the flight plot is read against a corresponding stage of the sale plot, and neither is allowed to stand for the whole.

techniques.name: Direct address
techniques.definition: A narrator or speaker turning outward to address the reader or the audience by name.
techniques.bookDefinition: A narrator or speaker turning outward to address the reader or the audience by name.
techniques.inThisBook: Stowe interrupts constantly — to tell a trader's reader that his own heart could be brought to the same place, and finally to address the mothers of America by name in the closing chapter.

techniques.name: The tableau
techniques.definition: A scene composed and held still so that its emotional meaning can be read off it.
techniques.bookDefinition: A scene composed and held still so that its emotional meaning can be read off it.
techniques.inThisBook: The deathbeds, the cabin at hymn-time, the auction block, the child handed across a wagon seat: scenes arranged with the stillness of an engraving, which is one reason the book moved so easily onto the stage.

techniques.name: Dialect
techniques.definition: Spelling and grammar used to mark where a speaker comes from, and what being heard that way costs them.
techniques.bookDefinition: Spelling and grammar used to mark where a speaker comes from, and what being heard that way costs them.
techniques.inThisBook: Stowe writes four or five distinct speech registers — Kentucky field, New Orleans drawing room, Vermont, Quaker plain speech — and uses the gap between them to mark exactly how much education each character has been allowed.

techniques.name: Scriptural argument
techniques.definition: Using scripture as the ground of an argument rather than as decoration.
techniques.bookDefinition: Using scripture as the ground of an argument rather than as decoration.
techniques.inThisBook: Characters quote the same verses at each other for opposite purposes — Legree citing servants obeying masters, Tom answering out of the Gospels — so that the novel stages a dispute about interpretation rather than about belief.

techniques.name: Weekly serial structure
techniques.definition: A narrative shaped by instalments, each needing its own crisis.
techniques.bookDefinition: A narrative shaped by instalments, each needing its own crisis.
techniques.inThisBook: Written to a weekly deadline for The National Era, the book keeps two plots alive by cutting between them, and its most famous set pieces sit exactly where an instalment had to end.

quotations.text: Well, I’ve got just as much conscience as any man in business can afford to keep
quotations.speaker: Haley
quotations.context: The trader, over wine, negotiating the sale of Tom and the child Harry.
quotations.analysis: Conscience is presented as an overhead, priced like any other, and the joke is that the speaker is entirely sincere. Stowe puts the novel's economic case in its first pages and in the mouth of its least reflective character, so that everything said later by thoughtful men is an elaboration of a trader's small talk.

quotations.text: a delicately formed hand and a trim foot and ankle were items of appearance that did not escape the quick eye of the trader, well used to run up at a glance the points of a fine female article.
quotations.context: Eliza has come into the parlour on an errand and gone out again.
quotations.analysis: The sentence begins as a conventional novelistic description of a pretty woman and ends in the vocabulary of livestock, with 'items' and 'points' and 'article' doing the turn. The reader is made to notice that they have been looking at her in the same way the trader has, one clause earlier.

quotations.text: I always thought that I must obey my master and mistress, or I couldn’t be a Christian.
quotations.speaker: Eliza
quotations.context: To George, who has told her he intends to escape.
quotations.analysis: She states the doctrine she has been taught as a condition of her faith, and within four chapters she will break it with a child on her hip. The novel gets its Christian readers to abandon that teaching by letting a good woman hold it first, and then making obedience unthinkable.

quotations.text: It is a sin to hold a slave under laws like ours
quotations.speaker: Mrs Shelby
quotations.context: On learning that her husband has sold Tom and Harry to settle a debt.
quotations.analysis: The qualification is the whole sentence: it is the laws that make it a sin, which leaves open the idea of a slavery conducted decently. Stowe gives her heroine the argument most of her readers actually held, and then spends forty chapters dismantling it by following the paperwork.

quotations.text: God helping me, I crossed on the ice
quotations.speaker: Eliza
quotations.context: In Senator Bird's kitchen, answering the disbelief of everyone in the room.
quotations.analysis: The novel's most spectacular action is reported afterwards, flatly, by the person who performed it, and the room's astonishment does the work that description would. Note that she credits God and the syntax credits herself: the main verb is hers, and the help is a subordinate phrase.

quotations.text: It’s a shameful, wicked, abominable law, and I’ll break it, for one, the first time I get a chance
quotations.speaker: Mrs Bird
quotations.context: To her husband, who has voted for the Fugitive Slave Act.
quotations.analysis: Three adjectives and then a plan, which is the order Stowe wants her readers to follow. The chapter is constructed so that the opportunity arrives within the hour, and the senator who defended the law in the abstract is soon driving a wagon through the mud at midnight.

quotations.text: Mr. Wilson, you have a country; but what country have I, or anyone like me, born of slave mothers?
quotations.speaker: George Harris
quotations.context: In an inn, in disguise, to his former employer from the factory.
quotations.analysis: The question is put to a sympathetic man who has just advised obedience to the law, and it works by simple grammatical contrast: you have, what have I. Stowe lets George reject the national argument rather than appeal to it, which is why he ends the novel outside the United States.

quotations.text: I’ll fight for my liberty to the last breath I breathe. You say your fathers did it; if it was right for them, it is right for me!
quotations.speaker: George Harris
quotations.context: The end of the same speech, having announced that he is armed.
quotations.analysis: He does not ask for the revolution's principles to be extended to him; he points out that they already cover his case and dares his listener to deny it. An American readership in 1852 could refuse the claim only by unsaying its own founding story, which is precisely the trap the sentence sets.

quotations.text: The trader, therefore, sat discontentedly down, with his little account-book, and put down the missing body and soul under the head of losses!
quotations.context: After a woman whose child Haley has sold has gone over the side of the steamboat.
quotations.analysis: A suicide is recorded as a bookkeeping entry, and the sentence adopts the ledger's own calm until the last three words. 'Body and soul' is the trade's own phrase used against it: the column exists because the law allows a soul to be entered as stock.

quotations.text: His heart was exactly where yours, sir, and mine could be brought, with proper effort and cultivation.
quotations.context: Of Haley, who has just watched a mother lose her child without interest.
quotations.analysis: The narrator turns from the trader to the reader mid-paragraph and includes herself in the indictment, which stops the sentence from being a simple accusation. 'Cultivation' is the word a Victorian reader would apply to their own moral improvement, redeployed here to describe the process of learning not to care.

quotations.text: You loathe them as you would a snake or a toad, yet you are indignant at their wrongs.
quotations.speaker: Augustine St Clare
quotations.context: To his cousin Ophelia, on the difference between northern and southern feeling.
quotations.analysis: The line is aimed past Ophelia at the book's actual readership, most of whom lived north of the Ohio and had subscribed to an antislavery paper. Stowe puts her sharpest attack on her own supporters into the mouth of a slaveholder, which makes it harder to dismiss and impossible to enjoy.

quotations.text: This cursed business, accursed of God and man, what is it?
quotations.speaker: Augustine St Clare
quotations.context: Beginning a long explanation of slavery to Ophelia, in his own house, with his own servants in it.
quotations.analysis: He asks the question rhetorically and then answers it in the language of force rather than of race: because I am strong and he is weak, therefore I may. The speech is the most complete argument in the novel, and it is given to the one man in a position to act who never does.

quotations.text: never had no father nor mother, nor nothin’. I was raised by a speculator, with lots of others.
quotations.speaker: Topsy
quotations.context: Answering Ophelia's questions about where she comes from.
quotations.analysis: The scene is played for comedy and the answer is a statement of fact about the domestic trade, which is exactly the difficulty Topsy presents. 'Raised by a speculator' names the only parent the market provided, and the sentence is funny and unanswerable in the same breath.

quotations.text: I would die for them, Tom, if I could
quotations.speaker: Eva St Clare
quotations.context: To Tom in the garden, having heard the stories of the people in the household.
quotations.analysis: The conditional is doing something odd: she is already dying, and the novel is about to spend a chapter arranging her death as a redemptive event. Stowe's sentimental machinery is at its most exposed here — a child's willingness to die is offered as the emotional equivalent of the political act nobody in the house will perform.

quotations.text: Mas’r, if you mean to kill me, kill me; but, as to my raising my hand agin anyone here, I never shall
quotations.speaker: Tom
quotations.context: Refusing Legree's order to flog a sick woman in the field.
quotations.analysis: The refusal is not to be beaten but to beat, and that distinction is the whole of Tom's position: he concedes the body and withholds the act. Legree's plantation runs on making the enslaved police each other, so one man declining to strike is a structural problem rather than a moral gesture.

quotations.text: No! no! no! my soul an’t yours, Mas’r! You haven’t bought it
quotations.speaker: Tom
quotations.context: Answering Legree's demand to know whether he is not his master's, body and soul.
quotations.analysis: Legree has just cited scripture and a purchase price; Tom answers the property claim in property language, conceding the sale and disputing what was in it. The triple 'no' is the only moment in the novel where Tom raises his voice, and he does it about a point of law.

quotations.text: I’ve been on this place five years, body and soul, under this man’s foot; and I hate him as I do the devil!
quotations.speaker: Cassy
quotations.context: Telling Tom what the plantation is, on the night after his first flogging.
quotations.analysis: She uses the same phrase Tom has just refused to concede, and she concedes it, which measures the distance between them. Stowe gives Cassy the plainest hatred in the book and does not require her to repent of it, even while the novel is arranging Tom's forgiveness.

quotations.text: in the judgment day, I will stand up before God, a witness against those that have ruined me and my children, body and soul!
quotations.speaker: Cassy
quotations.context: The end of her account of her own life, told to Tom in the first person.
quotations.analysis: She does not ask the reader for pity; she declares herself a witness in a proceeding that has not yet opened. It is the strongest claim to legal personality in the novel, and it is made by a woman whose testimony no court in Louisiana would have heard.

quotations.text: I’ll give ye all the work of my hands, all my time, all my strength; but my soul I won’t give up to mortal man.
quotations.speaker: Tom
quotations.context: To Legree, who has told him he is broken and offers him a place as an overseer.
quotations.analysis: The offer on the table is promotion — Legree wants Tom to drive the others — so the refusal is of power rather than of suffering. The list of what he concedes is long and specific, which makes the single withheld item look like a legal reservation rather than a pious formula.

quotations.text: they can see to it that they feel right
quotations.context: In the concluding remarks, answering the question of what any individual can do.
quotations.analysis: It is the most-quoted sentence in the book and the most criticised, because it makes the reader's inner state the unit of political action. Read in context it is less passive than it sounds — the paragraph goes on to talk about influence and atmosphere — but the novel does end by asking for feeling and leaving the legislation to follow.

quotations.text: And say, mothers of America, is this a thing to be defended, sympathized with, passed over in silence?
quotations.context: The closing appeal, after a page addressed to farmers, sailors and shipowners by region.
quotations.analysis: Stowe names her actual constituency last and most directly, and the three verbs run from active approval to mere silence, closing every available position. The fiction has been put down by this point: the last chapter is a pamphlet, and the novel has been its evidence.

quotations.text: not surer is the eternal law by which the millstone sinks in the ocean, than that stronger law, by which injustice and cruelty shall bring on nations the wrath of Almighty God!
quotations.context: The last sentence of the book.
quotations.analysis: The comparison is to a physical certainty, so judgement is presented as mechanics rather than as a threat. Nine years before the first shots, Stowe ends a domestic novel by telling the United States that the consequence is already in motion and that repentance is the only variable left.

atAGlance.label: Serialised
atAGlance.note: Weekly in the abolitionist paper The National Era, where it ran far longer than the few instalments originally intended.

atAGlance.label: First book edition
atAGlance.note: Two volumes from John P. Jewett of Boston, published while the serial was still finishing.

atAGlance.label: The law behind it
atAGlance.note: It obliged citizens of free states to assist in returning people who had escaped, which is why so much of the novel is set in northern parlours.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.note: Eliza moves north and out of the book's jurisdiction; Tom moves south and deeper into it. Neither plot resolves the other.

criticalViews.position: The novel as political act
criticalViews.summary: On any measure of effect this is the most consequential American novel of the nineteenth century: it put the domestic slave trade in front of a mass readership that had been able to think of slavery as a distant arrangement, and it made the Fugitive Slave Act a matter of personal conduct rather than policy.
criticalViews.counter: Effect is not the same as accuracy or fairness, and the book's power came partly from techniques — the dying child, the loyal servant — that later did real damage.

criticalViews.position: The objection to its racial typing
criticalViews.summary: The long-standing critical objection is that Stowe's sympathy runs along a racial map: patience and piety are given to Tom as qualities of descent, intellect and rebellion belong to the characters with white fathers, and Topsy is written for laughter in a register the minstrel stage had already established.
criticalViews.counter: The typology was the common property of the period and Stowe used it to move readers who shared it, which is an explanation of the method rather than a defence of it.

criticalViews.position: Sentiment as a political method
criticalViews.summary: Critics since the 1980s have taken the sentimental machinery seriously as a strategy rather than a failing, arguing that domestic feeling was one of the few forms of public authority available to women writers, and that the book was engineered to convert emotion into votes and subscriptions.
criticalViews.counter: The method's limit is stated in the book itself: the final advice to the individual reader is to feel rightly, which asks less than the situation the novel has just described.

criticalViews.position: The book against the 'Tom shows'
criticalViews.summary: For a century the stage versions — unlicensed, altered, often openly racist — were far more widely seen than the novel, and the insult that the name later carried was manufactured largely by them rather than by Stowe's pages.
criticalViews.counter: Separating the two only goes so far: the character's endurance and death are in the novel, and a modern reader still has to decide what the book is asking of him.

criticalViews.position: Fiction beside testimony
criticalViews.summary: Read next to Douglass's Narrative, published seven years earlier, the novel's status changes: Stowe invents and arranges in order to persuade, while Douglass gives names and counties and can be checked.
criticalViews.counter: Stowe answered the charge of invention in 1853 with A Key to Uncle Tom's Cabin, setting out the advertisements, trials and narratives behind her scenes.

essayQuestions.question: How does the novel make slavery a matter of law and money rather than of individual cruelty?
essayQuestions.focus: Debt, contract and the Fugitive Slave Act
plan: Begin with Chapter I: a decent man, a creditor and an ordinary contract are enough to destroy two families.
Follow Haley's account book through Chapter XII, where a death is entered under losses.
Use Senator Bird's kitchen to show the 1850 Act reaching into a free state and a private house.
Weigh St Clare, who understands everything and signs nothing, against Legree, who signs everything and understands nothing.
Close by asking what the ending implies about remedy: individual manumission, or a change in the law.

essayQuestions.question: 'Its abolitionist force and its racial typing are in the same sentences.' Discuss.
essayQuestions.focus: Sympathy, stereotype and method
plan: Set out the case for the book's effect: the scale of its readership and the specific political provocation it answered.
Examine how sympathy is distributed — who argues, who escapes, who endures, and how that maps onto descent in the narrator's own commentary.
Read the Topsy scenes closely, holding the comic register and the documentary content together.
Consider St Clare's attack on northern squeamishness as evidence that Stowe understood at least part of the problem.
Reach a judgement that does not require choosing between historical importance and the objection.

essayQuestions.question: What is the effect of telling Eliza's story and Tom's story at the same time?
essayQuestions.focus: Structure and the double plot
plan: Map the alternation: which chapters belong to the flight and which to the descent.
Show how each plot supplies what the other lacks — speed and hope against endurance and analysis.
Note that the two plots never meet again, and that only one of them ends in freedom.
Consider the serial deadline as a formal cause of the cutting between them.
Ask what the novel would argue if either half were removed.

essayQuestions.question: How does the novel use Christianity, and against whom?
essayQuestions.focus: Scripture, the churches and the last chapter
plan: Distinguish the several religions in the book: Tom's, Mrs Bird's, Legree's use of scripture, and the northern churches at a distance.
Analyse the exchange in Chapter XXXIII, where a purchase price and a Bible verse are produced together.
Set Cassy's refusal to forgive beside Tom's forgiveness, and ask whether the novel treats them as equals.
Use the concluding remarks to show where Stowe finally lays the charge.
Compare Douglass's appendix of 1845, which makes the same distinction from the inside.

discussionQuestions: Tom could have escaped with Eliza and does not. Is that obedience, calculation, or something the novel cannot quite name?
St Clare understands slavery better than any abolitionist in the book and frees nobody. Why does Stowe give the best argument to that character?
The novel's most famous advice is that readers should see to it that they feel rightly. Is that enough, and did Stowe think it was?
Topsy's answers about her origins are played for laughter and are factually exact. How should a reader now hold those two things together?
The freed family sails for Liberia at the end. What does that ending concede about the country the book is addressing?

timeline.label: Harriet Beecher born in Litchfield, Connecticut
timeline.detail: Into a famous clerical family; her father Lyman Beecher and several brothers were preachers.

timeline.label: The Beechers move to Cincinnati
timeline.detail: Eighteen years living on the Ohio, across the river from a slave state, gave her most of what she knew at first hand.

timeline.label: Marriage to Calvin Stowe
timeline.detail: A biblical scholar; the couple later moved to Brunswick, Maine, where the novel was begun.

timeline.label: The Fugitive Slave Act
timeline.detail: Part of the Compromise of 1850, it required citizens of free states to assist in recapture and is the immediate provocation for the book.

timeline.label: Serialisation begins in The National Era
timeline.detail: From June, in an abolitionist weekly in Washington; the story ran far beyond its planned length.

timeline.label: Published in two volumes by John P. Jewett
timeline.detail: It sold on a scale no American novel had reached before, and was pirated and translated across Europe within the year.

timeline.label: The first stage versions appear
timeline.detail: Unlicensed dramatisations began at once; the 'Tom shows' outlived the book's reputation and coarsened everything in it.

timeline.label: A Key to Uncle Tom's Cabin
timeline.detail: Stowe answered accusations of invention by publishing the court records, advertisements and narratives behind her scenes.

timeline.label: The Dred Scott decision
timeline.detail: The Supreme Court held that a black American could not be a citizen, hardening the argument the novel had entered.

timeline.label: The American Civil War begins
timeline.detail: The story that Lincoln greeted Stowe as the little woman who started the war is undocumented and long-lived.

timeline.label: The Thirteenth Amendment
timeline.detail: Slavery abolished in the United States, thirteen years after the book appeared.

timeline.label: Stowe dies at Hartford, Connecticut
timeline.detail: By then the novel's stage afterlife had largely replaced the book in the public mind.

related.why: The first-person testimony published seven years earlier, and the book against which Stowe's inventions have always been measured.
The same river and the same law thirty years later, with a boy deciding to break it and calling the decision wickedness.
Twain on descent, the one-drop rule and the legal fictions of race, written after emancipation had settled nothing.
Published two years earlier: another American novel about public judgement, the churches, and a woman's standing before them.
The other great weekly serial of the period, and a useful comparison for how instalment deadlines shape a plot.

books.title: Utopia
books.author: Thomas More
books.setting: A garden in Antwerp in 1515, a remembered dinner at Cardinal Morton’s table in England some twenty years before, and an island somewhere in the New World that nobody else has seen
books.lengthNote: Two books and about 42,000 words in Burnet’s English. Book I, the argument about England and about counsel, is under a third of the whole; Book II is a single long speech describing the island
books.openingLine: Henry VIII., the unconquered King of England, a prince adorned with all the virtues that become a great monarch, having some differences of no small consequence with Charles the most serene Prince of Castile, sent me into Flanders, as his ambassador, for treating and composing matters between them.
books.summary: An English envoy, waiting on stalled negotiations in Flanders, is introduced by a friend in Antwerp to a sunburnt Portuguese traveller who has sailed with Vespucci. The traveller will not serve any king, and to explain why he describes a dinner at which an English lawyer praised the hanging of thieves twenty to a gibbet. Asked to show that a commonwealth without private property could work, he spends the whole of the second book describing one: fifty-four cities built to a single plan, a six-hour working day, gold used for chamber-pots and slaves’ chains, and a religious peace kept by law. The envoy, who shares the author’s name, thanks him, takes him in to supper and keeps most of his objections to himself.
books.referenceStyle: book, by the work’s own two books; passages in Book II are further placed by the section headings printed in the translation, and its opening pages, which come before the first heading, are cited as ‘Book II, opening’

sourceText.label: Project Gutenberg text of Utopia, in Gilbert Burnet’s translation of 1684, edited by Henry Morley
sourceText.note: The Astor edition’s book page names no translation and links to this Project Gutenberg file, whose editor states in his introduction that the translation is Burnet’s. Burnet turns More’s Latin into late seventeenth-century English, so wording differs from Ralph Robinson’s version of 1551 and from modern translations. This edition leaves out the letters, verses, map and alphabet that surrounded the early printings, and runs the two books on under a single heading: Book II begins at ‘The island of Utopia is in the middle two hundred miles broad’. Because the book is a dialogue, every quotation names its speaker; all of Book II is Hythloday’s speech as the narrator reports it. The Utopians and their officers are listed under characters as groups.

structure.label: Book I
structure.title: An envoy, a friend and a stranger
structure.summary: More describes his embassy to Flanders and his friendship with Peter Giles, who introduces him outside a church in Antwerp to Raphael Hythloday. In More’s garden the three talk about the New World. When Giles and More urge Hythloday to put his learning at a king’s service, he refuses: courts want flattery rather than counsel, and meet every new idea by appealing to what pleased their ancestors.

scenes.title: The embassy
scenes.summary: Henry VIII sends More to Flanders; the talks stall at Bruges and he goes to Antwerp, where Giles’s company eases his homesickness.

scenes.title: Not a seaman but a philosopher
scenes.summary: Giles describes Hythloday’s voyages with Vespucci and his return by way of Ceylon and Calicut.

scenes.title: Why not serve a king?
scenes.summary: Hythloday says he has given his estate away and will not enslave himself to any prince; More replies that a good counsellor can do a whole nation good.

structure.label: Book I
structure.title: Dinner with Cardinal Morton
structure.summary: To show how counsel is received, Hythloday recalls a dinner at the table of John Morton, Archbishop of Canterbury, Cardinal and Chancellor, in about 1497. A lawyer praises the hanging of thieves; Hythloday argues that England makes thieves through idle retainers, enclosure and sheep, and proposes instead the penal labour of the Polylerits. The company scorns the idea until the Cardinal approves it. A fool’s joke about beggars and friars turns into a quarrel with an angry friar, and Morton ends the dinner.

scenes.title: Twenty on one gibbet
scenes.summary: The lawyer praises severe punishment for theft; Hythloday answers that no penalty deters men who have no other way to live.

scenes.title: Sheep that devour men
scenes.summary: Enclosure, rising prices and idle households are blamed for making the thieves the law then hangs.

scenes.title: The Polylerits
scenes.summary: A people tributary to Persia set thieves to public work instead of killing them; Morton proposes a trial of the method.

scenes.title: The fool and the friar
scenes.summary: A jester’s plan for beggars and a friar’s scriptural rage show the table taking its cue from whatever the Cardinal smiles at.

structure.label: Book I
structure.title: Philosophy at court, and the case against property
structure.summary: Hythloday imagines himself in the French king’s council advising against the conquest of Italy, with the example of the Achorians, and among ministers raising money by debasing the coinage and reviving old laws, with the Macarians’ limit on a king’s treasure. More grants that such advice would be ignored but argues for a pliable philosophy that plays its part in the drama in hand. Hythloday answers that the only cure is to abolish property; More objects that nobody would work, and Hythloday promises to describe Utopia after dinner.

scenes.title: The French council
scenes.summary: A king’s advisers plot leagues and invasions; counsel to stay at home and govern well would not be heard.

scenes.title: The treasury
scenes.summary: Ministers propose debasing the coin and selling dispensations; Hythloday would cite the Macarians’ oath never to hold more than a thousand pounds of gold.

scenes.title: A more pliable philosophy
scenes.summary: More compares counsel to acting in a play already under way; Hythloday says the preachers have bent Christ’s teaching like a leaden rule.

scenes.title: No property
scenes.summary: Hythloday names private property as the root of the trouble; More and Giles object, and the three go in to dine.

structure.label: Book II, opening to ‘Of their Trades’
structure.title: The shape of the island
structure.summary: After dinner Hythloday describes a crescent-shaped island, cut off from the mainland by King Utopus’s channel, with fifty-four cities built to one plan and farms worked by townspeople in two-year shifts. Amaurot, the capital, stands on the tidal river Anider, with gardens behind every house and doors that anyone may open. Magistrates are elected by households in thirties and three hundreds, and every citizen works six hours a day at farming and a trade.

scenes.title: The island and its farms
scenes.summary: Utopus digs the channel; the cities stand a day’s walk apart; townspeople take turns on the land.

scenes.ref: Book II, Of their Towns, particularly of Amaurot
scenes.title: Amaurot
scenes.summary: Walls, a stone bridge, uniform streets, houses exchanged by lot every ten years, and gardens kept in rivalry.

scenes.title: Syphogrants and Tranibors
scenes.summary: Elected officers, a prince chosen for life, three days’ debate on any public question, and death for plotting outside the council.

scenes.ref: Book II, Of their Trades, and Manner of Life
scenes.title: The six-hour day
scenes.summary: Everyone farms and learns a trade; idleness is abolished, lectures fill the early mornings, and luxuries are not made.

structure.label: Book II, ‘Of their Traffic’ to ‘Of their Slaves’
structure.title: Living without money
structure.summary: Households of fixed size take what they need from common stores and eat together in halls. Surplus is exported, and the gold it brings is kept for war and made into chamber-pots and chains so that nobody will prize it. Hythloday tells of the Anemolian ambassadors who arrive dressed in gold and are taken for slaves, then sets out the Utopians’ philosophy of pleasure, their appetite for Greek learning, and their laws on slavery, the incurably sick, marriage, divorce and treaties.

scenes.title: Families and halls
scenes.summary: Children moved between households, colonies planted abroad, common stores and common meals, hospitals outside the walls.

scenes.ref: Book II, Of the Travelling of the Utopians
scenes.title: Gold, pleasure and learning
scenes.summary: Travel by passport, gold for chamber-pots, the Anemolian embassy, true and false pleasures, and the Greek books Hythloday left behind.

scenes.ref: Book II, Of their Slaves, and of their Marriages
scenes.title: Bondage, death and marriage
scenes.summary: Slavery as punishment, counselled death for the incurably suffering, betrothed couples shown to each other naked, few laws, no lawyers and no treaties.

structure.label: Book II, ‘Of their Military Discipline’ to the end
structure.title: War, worship and the last word
structure.summary: The Utopians detest war and wage it with bribes, bounties on enemy princes and mercenaries whose deaths they count a service to mankind. Their religions are many and protected by a law of Utopus, provided nobody denies Providence or the soul’s survival. Hythloday closes by calling every other commonwealth a conspiracy of the rich, and pride the serpent that stops the world from following Utopia. More, privately unconvinced, praises the account, leads him in to supper and says he wishes rather than hopes to see such things adopted.

scenes.ref: Book II, Of their Military Discipline
scenes.title: War by other means
scenes.summary: Just causes, rewards for killing an enemy prince, Zapolet mercenaries, wives fighting beside their husbands.

scenes.ref: Book II, Of the Religions of the Utopians
scenes.title: Toleration
scenes.summary: Many faiths under one Supreme Being, Utopus’s law against compulsion, few and holy priests, temples kept dim.

scenes.ref: Book II, Of the Religions of the Utopians
scenes.title: The peroration and the reply
scenes.summary: Hythloday’s attack on money and pride; the narrator’s unspoken objections and his closing wish.

characters.name: Raphael Hythloday
characters.role: A Portuguese traveller and philosopher; the book’s main speaker
characters.summary: He gave his estate to his brothers while young, sailed on three of Vespucci’s four voyages, stayed behind in the New World and lived five years in Utopia. He talks brilliantly, argues from examples, and will not compromise: he refuses royal service because he could neither lie nor be heard, and he names private property as the disease that every other reform only soothes. More gives him a surname that means something like ‘dealer in nonsense’, and the angriest, most persuasive pages in the book.
characters.clue: He has seen the best commonwealth in the world and would rather not advise any real one.

relationships.label: argues with about counsel and property
was a guest of, and admires
argues against the hanging of thieves with
lived five years among, and speaks for

characters.name: More, the narrator
characters.role: An English envoy in Flanders and the teller of the book; not quite the same person as its author
characters.summary: He shares the author’s name, office and family, and the book makes him a little less than the author: courteous, practical, a lawyer who believes a good man should serve the state and work within its bad habits. He argues against Hythloday twice, for a pliable philosophy that plays its part in the drama in hand and against holding all things in common, and at the end he keeps his objections to himself because his guest looks tired. His last sentence is the book’s most quoted hedge.
characters.clue: He was brought up in Cardinal Morton’s household, which is why Hythloday tells the dinner story to him.

relationships.label: was brought up in the household of
the other half of an argument the author may have been having with himself

characters.name: Peter Giles
characters.role: A scholar and city secretary of Antwerp; More’s friend
characters.summary: A real person and a friend of Erasmus, whom More praises at length for his learning, his modesty and his ‘prudent simplicity’. In the fiction he is the introducer: he brings Hythloday to More, urges the traveller to serve a king for his friends’ sake, and doubts that any nation in the New World can be better governed than old Europe. His presence gives the fantasy a real address.
characters.clue: He corrects More’s first impression: the stranger sailed not as a seaman but as a philosopher.

characters.name: Cardinal John Morton
characters.role: Archbishop of Canterbury and Lord Chancellor under Henry VII
characters.summary: The one great man in the book who listens. Hythloday describes him as grave, easy in conversation and fond of testing suitors by speaking sharply; he stops the lawyer’s set speech, asks a real question about how thieves should be punished, and proposes a trial of the Polylerits’ method. Yet his table is where the case against courts is proved. The guests despise an idea until he approves it, and applaud in earnest what he only liked in jest.
characters.clue: His guests laugh when he laughs; he asks for an experiment before a verdict.

characters.name: The lawyer
characters.role: An English lawyer at Morton’s table, later called ‘the Counsellor’
characters.summary: He opens the argument by praising a justice that hangs twenty thieves on one gibbet, and wonders aloud why theft continues. Answered, he prepares a formal rebuttal that will repeat everything in order and answer nothing, and the Cardinal stops him before he starts. His last contribution is a shake of the head and a prediction that the scheme would endanger the whole nation. Burnet’s English calls him ‘the Counsellor’, which makes him the working model of the royal adviser Hythloday refuses to become.
characters.clue: He had got as far as ‘there were four things’ when the Cardinal told him to hold his peace.

characters.name: The Friar
characters.role: A divine at Morton’s table
characters.summary: A grave, morose man who enjoys the Fool’s joke at the monks’ expense until it turns on the friars. He then rails at the jester as knave, backbiter and son of perdition, quotes scripture to prove that his anger is no sin, and threatens the fate of the children who mocked Elisha and a papal bull. He is the book’s portrait of learning used for self-defence.
characters.clue: He insists he is not angry, and cites the Psalms to prove it.

characters.name: The Fool
characters.role: A jester at Morton’s table
characters.summary: He plays the fool so naturally that he seems to be one, and most of his jokes fall flat, but he is the only guest who says something rude and true: that the answer to beggars is to put them in monasteries, and that no vagabonds are like the friars. The company likes the jest in earnest because the Cardinal smiles. Erasmus had lately punned More’s name into folly in The Praise of Folly, and the jester is a small version of the licensed truth-teller the whole book tries to be.
characters.clue: He says he knows no vagabonds like the friars.

relationships.label: says in jest what Hythloday says in earnest

characters.name: King Utopus
characters.role: Conqueror and lawgiver of Utopia
characters.summary: He conquered a peninsula called Abraxa, gave it his own name, and had it cut from the mainland by a fifteen-mile channel dug by his soldiers as well as the natives. He drew the plan of Amaurot and left its ornament to later generations, and he made the law that every man may follow what religion he pleases and argue for it without violence. The ideal commonwealth, it is worth noticing, begins with a conquest.
characters.clue: He found the natives easy to conquer because they were quarrelling about religion.

characters.name: The Utopians
characters.role: The citizens of the island, taken as a people
characters.summary: They are industrious, cheerful, fond of lectures and gardens, contemptuous of gold, jewels, hunting and dice, and quick to learn Greek. They also live in full view of one another, need a passport to leave their city, keep slaves, marry after inspecting each other naked, bar from office anyone who denies Providence, and win wars with bribes. Hythloday presents them almost as a single character with one mind, which is both the attraction of the place and its strangeness.
characters.clue: Their children laugh at foreign ambassadors for wearing jewels like toddlers.

relationships.label: elect, and are watched over by

characters.name: Syphogrants, Tranibors and the Prince
characters.role: Utopia’s elected officers
characters.summary: Every thirty households elect a Syphogrant each year, and every ten Syphogrants answer to a Tranibor; the Syphogrants choose a Prince for life, by secret vote, from four candidates named by the people, and he can be removed if he is suspected of meaning to enslave them. The Syphogrants’ chief business is to see that nobody is idle. The system is built against conspiracy, down to the rule that no question is debated on the day it is raised and the law that makes it death to discuss public affairs outside council.
characters.clue: The Prince wears no crown; a sheaf of corn is carried before him.

themes.name: Property, money and the common store
themes.summary: Hythloday’s central claim is that while there is property, and money is the measure of everything, no nation can be governed either justly or happily. Book II tests the claim: households take what they need from public stores, cities supply one another as though the island were one family, and gold is made into chamber-pots. The book lets the narrator raise the obvious objection, that without hope of gain nobody will work, and answers it with the six-hour day.
themes.development: Named as the root cause at the end of Book I; put into practice in ‘Of their Traffic’ and ‘Of the Travelling of the Utopians’; restated in the closing speech, where every other commonwealth is ‘a conspiracy of the rich’.

themes.name: Crime, punishment and justice
themes.summary: The argument of the book begins at a gallows. Hythloday tells an English lawyer that hanging thieves is neither just nor effective, since a country that drives men off the land and then hangs them for stealing has made the thieves it punishes. The Polylerits’ penal labour, Utopian slavery and the maxim that ‘extreme justice is an extreme injury’ all turn on one question: what punishment is for. The answers are humane by the standards of 1516 and hard by later ones.
themes.development: Morton’s dinner in Book I; the Utopians’ use of slavery in place of death and their few, plain laws in ‘Of their Slaves’; the ‘two sorts of justice’, one for the poor and one for princes, in the same section.

themes.name: Counsel: should the wise serve kings?
themes.canonicalName: Counsel: should the wise serve kings?
themes.summary: Book I is an argument between two men about whether a philosopher can do any good at court. Hythloday says he would be ignored, or corrupted, or blamed for other men’s crimes; More says a man should play his part in the drama in hand and make bad things as little bad as he can. The question was not abstract. Within a few years of writing it the author was in Henry VIII’s service, and he died there.
themes.development: Raised by Peter Giles’s suggestion that Hythloday serve a king; illustrated at Morton’s table; argued to a standstill in the imagined French council; left unsettled when the talk turns to Utopia and again in the narrator’s last sentence.

themes.name: Pleasure, true and false
themes.summary: The Utopians hold that happiness lies in pleasure, and spend pages sorting the true kind from the false: health, learning, a good conscience and music on one side; fine clothes, titles, jewels, hoarded gold, hunting and dice on the other. The philosophy has a religious floor under it, since they think virtue would be madness if it brought no reward after death. It is also the book’s sharpest satire, because it makes the pleasures Europe prizes look like a child’s.
themes.development: Prepared by the gold and the Anemolian ambassadors, argued at length in ‘Of the Travelling of the Utopians’, and carried over into their treatment of the sick and dying in ‘Of their Slaves’.

themes.name: Religion and toleration
themes.summary: Utopus found the island’s people easy to conquer because they were fighting over religion, and made a law that everyone could believe as he pleased and argue for it peacefully. The Utopians worship one Supreme Being under many names, keep their temples dim so each may imagine God in his own way, and are drawn to Christianity partly because it seemed to favour holding goods in common. The toleration has a floor: nobody who denies Providence or the immortality of the soul may hold office.
themes.development: Glimpsed in the Fool’s quarrel with the friar in Book I and in the pleasure philosophy, set out fully in ‘Of the Religions of the Utopians’, and tested by the zealous convert who is banished for stirring up the people rather than for his faith.

themes.name: Order and liberty
themes.summary: Utopia is free of want, and not of supervision. Citizens need a passport to travel and permission to walk in their own district; ‘all men live in full view’; it is death to discuss public affairs outside council; slaves in gold chains do the killing and the dirty work. The book hides none of this. Whether the Utopians have traded one freedom for another, or simply given it up, is a question Hythloday never asks and a reader cannot avoid.
themes.development: The Polylerits’ marked and cropped penal workers in Book I; the magistrates and passports of Book II; the slaves, the counselled deaths and the marriage laws in ‘Of their Slaves, and of their Marriages’.

themes.name: The New World, colonies and war
themes.summary: The book was written within a decade of the printing of Vespucci’s voyages, and its traveller claims to have sailed on them. Utopia borrows the explorer’s report and some of its assumptions: the Utopians plant colonies on land its owners leave unfarmed, and count resistance a just cause of war. Their wars are fought with money, bounties and mercenaries, and the ideal state turns out to know every trick of the powers it despises.
themes.development: Hythloday’s voyages and the compass he teaches the sailors to use in Book I; the colonies in ‘Of their Traffic’; the bribery and the Zapolets in ‘Of their Military Discipline’.

techniques.name: Frame narrative
techniques.definition: A story told inside another story, so that every account reaches the reader through somebody with an interest in it.
techniques.bookDefinition: A story told inside another story, so that every account reaches the reader through somebody with an interest in it.
techniques.inThisBook: Nothing in Utopia reaches the reader directly. More reports a conversation in Antwerp, in which Hythloday reports a dinner in England and then an island he alone has seen, while the narrator holds back his own judgement. The frame lets the author say dangerous things about England in another man’s mouth, and leaves the reader to decide how far to trust a witness whose name means nonsense.

techniques.name: Irony
techniques.definition: Saying one thing in a form that invites the opposite judgement.
techniques.bookDefinition: Saying one thing in a form that invites the opposite judgement.
techniques.inThisBook: More’s irony is usually a straight face held a beat too long. Europe’s princes keep their treaties so religiously, Hythloday says, especially where Christianity is received; the Utopians have no lawyers, because lawyers disguise matters and wrest the laws, in a book by a lawyer. The narrator’s courteous silence at the end works the same way, by saying much less than he thinks.

techniques.name: Names that argue
techniques.definition: Invented names that carry a judgement on the thing named.
techniques.bookDefinition: Invented names that carry a judgement on the thing named.
techniques.inThisBook: The island is No-place. Its capital, Amaurot, is the dim or shadowy city, on the Anider, the waterless river; its prince was called the Ademus, the ruler without a people; the traveller’s surname suggests an expert in nonsense. Hythloday’s model nations are the Achorians, people without a country, the Macarians, the blessed, and the Polylerits, the people of much nonsense. A reader with Greek catches the joke on every page while the institutions are described in earnest.

techniques.name: Objection and reply
techniques.definition: Raising the opponent’s strongest point in order to answer it.
techniques.bookDefinition: Raising the opponent’s strongest point in order to answer it.
techniques.inThisBook: The book is organised around two objections, both given to the narrator: that a wise man should serve princes, and that people will not work where all things are common. Hythloday answers the first with the Morton story and the imagined councils, and the second with the whole of Book II. The final objection, reserved and never spoken, is left for the reader to supply.

techniques.name: Making the familiar strange
techniques.definition: Presenting ordinary customs through outsiders’ eyes so that they look absurd.
techniques.bookDefinition: Presenting ordinary customs through outsiders’ eyes so that they look absurd.
techniques.inThisBook: Utopian children laugh at an ambassador for wearing pearls like a toddler; Utopian philosophers cannot see the pleasure in watching dogs tear a hare or in another man’s taking off his hat. By describing European habits as the Utopians see them, More makes gold, rank and fashion look like what they materially are: metal, ancestry, and wool that was once on a sheep.

techniques.name: Analogy
techniques.definition: Arguing from a comparison with something better understood.
techniques.bookDefinition: Arguing from a comparison with something better understood.
techniques.inThisBook: Hythloday thinks in comparisons: sheep that devour men, schoolmasters who beat rather than teach, a physician who cures one disease by causing another, a king who is a gaoler, a doctrine bent like a leaden rule. More answers in kind, with a play already in performance. The analogies do the persuading, because each carries a judgement that is obvious in ordinary life into politics, where it is not obvious at all.

techniques.name: Argument by example
techniques.definition: Proving a political claim by a case, real or supposed, that shows it working.
techniques.bookDefinition: Proving a political claim by a case, real or supposed, that shows it working.
techniques.inThisBook: Machiavelli argued from Cesare Borgia and the Romans; Hythloday argues from peoples nobody can check, the Polylerits, the Achorians and the Macarians, whose names announce that they do not exist. It is the humanist method of learning from history applied to invented history, and the joke is that the invented cases are more persuasive than most real ones.

quotations.text: his face was tanned, he had a long beard, and his cloak was hanging carelessly about him, so that, by his looks and habit, I concluded he was a seaman.
quotations.speaker: More
quotations.context: Coming out of mass in Antwerp, More sees Peter Giles talking to a stranger.
quotations.analysis: The first impression is a misreading, and Giles corrects it at once: this man sailed ‘as a traveller, or rather a philosopher’. The book opens by showing that appearances are uncertain evidence, a fair warning in a text whose only witness to the island is introduced here by his tan, his beard and his untidy cloak.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg text (Burnet translation), Book I

quotations.text: I think my friends ought to rest contented with this, and not to expect that for their sakes I should enslave myself to any king whatsoever.
quotations.speaker: Hythloday
quotations.context: Giles has suggested that Hythloday enter a king’s service for the good of his friends.
quotations.analysis: Giles says ‘serve’ and Hythloday hears ‘enslave’, and when Giles softens it to ‘assist’ he replies that the change of the word does not alter the matter. The argument of Book I begins as an argument about vocabulary. Having given his estate away young, he owes nobody anything, and the independence that would make him a good counsellor is exactly what makes him unwilling to become one.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg text (Burnet translation), Book I

quotations.text: for the springs both of good and evil flow from the prince over a whole nation, as from a lasting fountain.
quotations.speaker: More
quotations.context: More urges Hythloday to put his philosophy to use in a prince’s council.
quotations.analysis: The image is the orthodox case for counsel: if good and evil flow down from the ruler, the place to improve a nation is at its source. It assumes the fountain can be cleaned from inside. Hythloday attacks the assumption rather than the image, arguing that courtiers poison anything new, and the rest of Book I tests which of the two is right.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg text (Burnet translation), Book I

quotations.text: were then hanged so fast that there were sometimes twenty on one gibbet!
quotations.speaker: The lawyer
quotations.context: At Cardinal Morton’s table an English lawyer praises the severity of the law against thieves, as Hythloday reports it.
quotations.analysis: The exclamation mark is the lawyer’s admiration, and the number is his proof that the system works. He then wonders why so many thieves are left, which is the question the whole dinner turns on. More gives the case for the gallows to a man who has the evidence against it in front of him and draws the wrong conclusion.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg text (Burnet translation), Book I

quotations.text: your sheep, which are naturally mild, and easily kept in order, may be said now to devour men and unpeople, not only villages, but towns
quotations.speaker: Hythloday
quotations.context: Asked by the Cardinal what cause of theft is ‘more peculiar to England’, Hythloday names the increase of pasture.
quotations.analysis: The mildest animal in the kingdom becomes a predator, and the grammar keeps the owners out of sight until the next clause names them: nobility, gentry and ‘those holy men, the abbots’. ‘Unpeople’ is the striking verb, a village emptied rather than destroyed. The argument is economic, about land turned from ploughing to wool, and the image makes it impossible to hear as merely economic.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg text (Burnet translation), Book I

quotations.text: for if you suffer your people to be ill-educated, and their manners to be corrupted from their infancy, and then punish them for those crimes to which their first education disposed them, what else is to be concluded from this but that you first make thieves and then punish them?
quotations.speaker: Hythloday
quotations.context: The end of Hythloday’s answer to the lawyer, after his account of enclosure and idleness.
quotations.analysis: The speech ends on a question that answers itself. Its logic moves the guilt upward, from the thief to the society that formed him, and its last clause gives making and punishing the same subject, ‘you’. It is the book’s plainest statement that crime has causes, and it is addressed to the Lord Chancellor of England at his own table.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg text (Burnet translation), Book I

quotations.text: That it was not easy to form a judgment of its success, since it was a method that never yet had been tried
quotations.speaker: Cardinal Morton
quotations.context: The lawyer has said the Polylerits’ penal labour could never work in England, and the company agrees with him.
quotations.analysis: Morton is the only person at the table who treats a new idea as something to test. He proposes reprieving a condemned thief and trying the method on him, a cautious and entirely reasonable answer. The company, which had despised the idea, now praises it because he has spoken, so the most open-minded man present proves Hythloday’s case against courts.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg text (Burnet translation), Book I

quotations.text: for the Cardinal has provided for you by what he proposed for restraining vagabonds and setting them to work, for I know no vagabonds like you.
quotations.speaker: The Fool
quotations.context: A friar has told the Fool that his plan for beggars will not rid him of begging friars.
quotations.analysis: The jester turns the Cardinal’s scheme for idle vagrants on the mendicant orders, whose members lived by begging. It is Hythloday’s argument about idleness delivered as a joke, and the company laughs because the Cardinal is not displeased. The friar’s furious reply, full of scripture, shows what happens to a man in authority who is told the truth by someone without standing.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg text (Burnet translation), Book I

quotations.text: that they in good earnest applauded those things that he only liked in jest; and from hence you may gather how little courtiers would value either me or my counsels.
quotations.speaker: Hythloday
quotations.context: Hythloday apologises for the length of his story and draws its moral.
quotations.analysis: This is why the dinner was told at all. The company’s judgement moved with the Cardinal’s face, rejecting the Polylerits when a stranger proposed them and applauding the Fool’s joke as policy. Earnest and jest change places, and a book that is itself a jest told in earnest names its own difficulty: readers, like courtiers, take their cue from whoever seems to have authority.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg text (Burnet translation), Book I

quotations.text: but there is another philosophy that is more pliable, that knows its proper scene, accommodates itself to it, and teaches a man with propriety and decency to act that part which has fallen to his share.
quotations.speaker: More
quotations.context: Hythloday has said there is no room for philosophy in the courts of princes. More disagrees.
quotations.analysis: More’s answer is theatrical, and he develops it with a scene: a philosopher who walks into a comedy reciting Seneca spoils the play. The counsellor must work within the drama already in progress and, if he cannot make things good, make them as little bad as possible. It is a serious ethics of compromise, and its author tried to live by it until a king required him to say what he did not believe.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg text (Burnet translation), Book I

quotations.text: as long as there is any property, and while money is the standard of all other things, I cannot think that a nation can be governed either justly or happily
quotations.speaker: Hythloday
quotations.context: Having argued about counsel, Hythloday says what he really thinks.
quotations.analysis: ‘To speak plainly my real sentiments’, the sentence begins, and the level of the argument changes: everything before this was about remedies, and now he names the disease. The two adverbs are unpacked at once, since property makes government unjust by giving the best things to the worst men and unhappy by dividing everything among a few. The claim is so large that the narrator objects immediately.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg text (Burnet translation), Book I

quotations.text: it seems to me that men cannot live conveniently where all things are common. How can there be any plenty where every man will excuse himself from labour?
quotations.speaker: More
quotations.context: The narrator answers Hythloday’s claim that property must be abolished.
quotations.analysis: This is the objection every reader brings to Book II, and More gives it to his narrator first, in its strongest form: without gain nobody will work, and without property nobody will respect the magistrates. Hythloday’s reply is not an argument but an invitation to have seen the place, and Book II is his evidence. The island is set up to answer a particular doubt.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg text (Burnet translation), Book I

quotations.text: Utopus, that conquered it (whose name it still carries, for Abraxa was its first name), brought the rude and uncivilised inhabitants into such a good government, and to that measure of politeness, that they now far excel all the rest of mankind.
quotations.speaker: Hythloday
quotations.context: After dinner Hythloday begins his account of the island with its history.
quotations.analysis: The perfect commonwealth starts with a conquest, and its founder puts his own name on the land he takes. Utopus then turns the peninsula into an island by setting natives and soldiers alike to dig a channel, so the separation from the world that makes Utopia possible is itself an act of power. ‘Rude and uncivilised’ is the explorer’s usual verdict on the people found, and Hythloday repeats it without comment.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg text (Burnet translation), Book II, opening

quotations.text: but they, dividing the day and night into twenty-four hours, appoint six of these for work, three of which are before dinner and three after
quotations.speaker: Hythloday
quotations.reference: Book II, Of their Trades, and Manner of Life
quotations.context: Hythloday contrasts Utopian labour with the toil from morning to night of workmen everywhere else.
quotations.analysis: The number is the book’s answer to the narrator’s objection, and it rests on arithmetic that follows: in Europe women, priests, the rich, their servants and able-bodied beggars do little, and many who do work make luxuries. Put everyone to useful work and six hours suffice. The generosity has a condition, since the Syphogrants’ chief business is ‘to take care that no man may live idle’.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg text (Burnet translation), Book II, Of their Trades, and Manner of Life

quotations.text: it is the fear of want that makes any of the whole race of animals either greedy or ravenous; but, besides fear, there is in man a pride that makes him fancy it a particular glory to excel others in pomp and excess
quotations.speaker: Hythloday
quotations.context: Hythloday explains why nobody takes more than he needs from the common stores.
quotations.analysis: The psychological foundation of the whole system is laid in one sentence. Greed is not natural but a response to insecurity, so a society that guarantees supply removes the motive. The second clause admits something security cannot cure, pride, and Utopian law deals with that separately. The same pride returns in Hythloday’s closing speech as ‘that infernal serpent’.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg text (Burnet translation), Book II, Of their Traffic

quotations.text: for they account it a very just cause of war for a nation to hinder others from possessing a part of that soil of which they make no use, but which is suffered to lie idle and uncultivated
quotations.speaker: Hythloday
quotations.context: When the island grows too populous, the Utopians plant colonies on the neighbouring mainland.
quotations.analysis: The passage anticipates an argument that would justify colonial seizure for centuries: land not farmed is land not really owned. Natives who accept Utopian rule are absorbed; those who refuse are driven out by force.
