Whether More endorses the reasoning or shows how easily a just commonwealth becomes an aggressive one, it is set down in the same calm voice as the arrangements for dinner.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg text (Burnet translation), Book II, Of their Traffic

quotations.text: all men live in full view, so that all are obliged both to perform their ordinary task and to employ themselves well in their spare hours
quotations.speaker: Hythloday
quotations.reference: Book II, Of the Travelling of the Utopians
quotations.context: After describing the passports needed for travel, Hythloday explains why Utopia has no taverns.
quotations.analysis: Offered as praise, the sentence describes a society without privacy. No taverns, no alehouses, no corners, no parties: idleness is prevented by visibility, and ‘obliged’ reaches into the spare hours as well as the working ones. Hythloday sees no conflict between this and the plenty it secures, and that is exactly what makes the passage uneasy for a modern reader.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg text (Burnet translation), Book II, Of the Travelling of the Utopians

quotations.text: They eat and drink out of vessels of earth or glass, which make an agreeable appearance, though formed of brittle materials; while they make their chamber-pots and close-stools of gold and silver
quotations.speaker: Hythloday
quotations.reference: Book II, Of the Travelling of the Utopians
quotations.context: Hythloday explains how the Utopians keep the gold their trade brings in without anyone coming to value it.
quotations.analysis: The joke is precise. Gold kept in a tower would breed suspicion of the rulers and gold made into plate would be loved, so it goes into the lowest objects in the house and into slaves’ fetters. Value, the passage implies, lies not in the metal but in the use a society gives it, and Europe has given its gold the most honoured places.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg text (Burnet translation), Book II, Of the Travelling of the Utopians

quotations.text: See that great fool, that wears pearls and gems as if he were yet a child!
quotations.speaker: A Utopian child
quotations.reference: Book II, Of the Travelling of the Utopians
quotations.context: The Anemolian ambassadors, expecting to dazzle a plainly dressed people, arrive in cloth of gold, chains and jewels.
quotations.analysis: The splendour is read in the only terms the Utopians have for it: gold marks a slave and jewels are toys. The mothers’ reply, that this must be one of the ambassadors’ fools, completes the reversal, since the real dignitaries are taken for the lowest members of their own train. Pride of dress turns out to need an audience that shares the code.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg text (Burnet translation), Book II, Of the Travelling of the Utopians

quotations.text: I have not now the leisure to examine whether they think right or wrong in this matter; nor do I judge it necessary, for I have only undertaken to give you an account of their constitution, but not to defend all their principles.
quotations.speaker: Hythloday
quotations.reference: Book II, Of the Travelling of the Utopians
quotations.context: Hythloday finishes his account of the Utopians’ philosophy of pleasure.
quotations.analysis: The most partisan speaker in the book suddenly takes up a reporter’s neutrality. It is the kind of disclaimer that let a writer describe what he could not openly recommend, and it is undone by the very next sentence, which declares that there is not in the whole world a better people or a happier government. The reader is left holding both.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg text (Burnet translation), Book II, Of the Travelling of the Utopians

quotations.text: They are kept at perpetual labour, and are always chained, but with this difference, that their own natives are treated much worse than others
quotations.speaker: Hythloday
quotations.reference: Book II, Of their Slaves, and of their Marriages
quotations.context: Hythloday describes who the Utopians’ slaves are: their own convicts, criminals bought abroad, and poor foreigners who come of their own accord.
quotations.analysis: The ideal commonwealth runs partly on forced labour, and the account says so in the same even voice it uses for gardens. The logic is the Polylerits’ from Book I, bondage as a more useful punishment than death, and the harsher treatment of native Utopians follows from the belief that those raised so well have less excuse. Hythloday never asks whether a slave would describe Utopia as he does.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg text (Burnet translation), Book II, Of their Slaves, and of their Marriages

quotations.text: We know how religiously they are observed in Europe, more particularly where the Christian doctrine is received, among whom they are sacred and inviolable!
quotations.speaker: Hythloday
quotations.reference: Book II, Of their Slaves, and of their Marriages
quotations.context: The Utopians make no treaties, because the princes around them break theirs.
quotations.analysis: The exclamation mark does the work of a raised eyebrow. In 1516, with popes and Christian kings making and breaking leagues across Italy, no reader could take the sentence straight, and the praise that follows of the popes as the most religious keepers of their promises extends the joke. It is the plainest irony in the book, and a guide to reading its quieter ones.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg text (Burnet translation), Book II, Of their Slaves, and of their Marriages

quotations.text: The Utopians hold this for a maxim, that as they seek out the best sort of men for their own use at home, so they make use of this worst sort of men for the consumption of war
quotations.speaker: Hythloday
quotations.reference: Book II, Of their Military Discipline
quotations.context: Hythloday describes the Zapolets, a fierce people who hire themselves out to any side and change sides for a penny a day.
quotations.analysis: The Utopians hate war and are content to buy it. They pay the Zapolets more than anyone, send them into the worst danger, and reckon their deaths a service to mankind. ‘Consumption’ is an economist’s word, and it treats a people as fuel. Readers have long recognised Europe’s hired Swiss soldiers in the Zapolets, and the calm that abolishes poverty at home here spends foreigners’ lives abroad.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg text (Burnet translation), Book II, Of their Military Discipline

quotations.text: he made a law that every man might be of what religion he pleased, and might endeavour to draw others to it by the force of argument and by amicable and modest ways, but without bitterness against those of other opinions
quotations.speaker: Hythloday
quotations.reference: Book II, Of the Religions of the Utopians
quotations.context: Utopus had found the island’s inhabitants divided by religious quarrels, which made them easy to conquer.
quotations.analysis: The law is justified twice, by public peace and by the interest of religion itself, since truth, Utopus thinks, will prevail if it is argued gently. It is a remarkable principle for 1516, and its author later wrote against Protestant reformers and, as Chancellor, pursued them, one reason readers argue about how far Hythloday speaks for More. The law has its own limit: denying Providence bars a man from office.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg text (Burnet translation), Book II, Of the Religions of the Utopians

quotations.text: I can have no other notion of all the other governments that I see or know, than that they are a conspiracy of the rich, who, on pretence of managing the public, only pursue their private ends
quotations.speaker: Hythloday
quotations.reference: Book II, Of the Religions of the Utopians
quotations.context: Hythloday’s closing speech compares Utopia with every other commonwealth.
quotations.analysis: After two books of description the traveller drops his reporting manner and passes sentence on Europe. ‘Conspiracy’ implies agreement and secrecy, and he goes on to say that the rich then have their devices made into law, having already given hardship ‘the name and colour of justice’. It is the angriest sentence in the book, and it is followed by the narrator’s polite silence.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg text (Burnet translation), Book II, Of the Religions of the Utopians

quotations.text: However, there are many things in the commonwealth of Utopia that I rather wish, than hope, to see followed in our governments.
quotations.speaker: More
quotations.reference: Book II, Of the Religions of the Utopians
quotations.context: The last sentence of the book, after the narrator has led Hythloday in to supper without raising his objections.
quotations.analysis: The sentence is balanced so carefully that it commits to nothing: ‘many things’, not all; ‘wish’, but not ‘hope’; ‘followed’, not established. Having just listed what struck him as absurd, their way of making war, their religion and above all their living in common without money, the narrator ends on a wish, and every reading of Utopia as blueprint or as satire has to make sense of it.
quotations.source: Project Gutenberg text (Burnet translation), Book II, Of the Religions of the Utopians

atAGlance.label: Written
atAGlance.note: The island of Book II was probably written first, late in 1515, after More’s embassy to Flanders; Book I, with its argument about England, followed early in 1516.

atAGlance.label: First printed
atAGlance.note: In Latin, seen through the press by Erasmus, Peter Giles and others of More’s friends. It was not printed in England in his lifetime.

atAGlance.label: In English
atAGlance.note: Ralph Robinson’s translation came sixteen years after More’s execution. The quotations here follow Gilbert Burnet’s version of 1684.

atAGlance.label: The name
atAGlance.note: From Greek ou, ‘not’, and topos, ‘place’, with a pun on eutopia, ‘good place’, made in verses printed with the early editions. Nearly every proper name in the book is a Greek joke of the same kind.

atAGlance.label: The traveller
atAGlance.note: A Portuguese who sailed with Amerigo Vespucci and stayed behind in the New World. His surname is built from Greek words for nonsense.

atAGlance.label: The working day
atAGlance.note: Three before dinner and three after, possible, Hythloday argues, because everybody works and nobody makes luxuries.

criticalViews.position: A serious blueprint
criticalViews.summary: On this reading Hythloday speaks for More, and Utopia is what it appears to be: a reasoned case that private property causes poverty, crime and war, with a working model attached. The anger of Book I at enclosure and hanging is too specific to be play, and later socialist writers recognised an ancestor in the book. The fictional frame was protection, not irony.
criticalViews.counter: The book goes out of its way to undermine its witness: an island called No-place, a traveller named for nonsense, a narrator who objects at the start and the end. The island includes slavery, surveillance, counselled death and wars won by bribery, and the author spent the next two decades serving a king and defending the established church. A blueprint would not advertise its own unreality so insistently.

criticalViews.position: A humanist satire of Europe
criticalViews.summary: Here the island is a mirror rather than a model. Its point is what it shows about Christian Europe: that pagans guided by reason alone live better than those who have revelation, and that gold, rank and fashion are absurd once seen from outside. The Greek puns, the straight-faced praise of treaties and the gold chamber-pots belong to the world of Erasmus’s Praise of Folly, a learned joke with a moral edge.
criticalViews.counter: Satire needs a target, and some Utopian institutions are ones humanists argued for in earnest: education for all, toleration within limits, punishment that reforms. Reading everything as a joke also loses the plain moral force of Book I and of Hythloday’s closing speech, neither of which is written like a joke.

criticalViews.position: A dialogue about counsel
criticalViews.summary: A third view makes Book I the heart of the work. Hythloday and the narrator are two sides of a choice the author faced, whether to enter royal service, and the island is Hythloday’s strongest card in an argument about whether philosophy can work inside an imperfect state. The unresolved ending is then the point: neither pure principle nor accommodation wins.
criticalViews.counter: This makes the larger part of the book an illustration for the smaller, and it leans on biography that the text never mentions. The island has had a life of its own for five centuries because readers found in it more than an example in someone else’s argument.

essayQuestions.question: Does Utopia present its island as a model to be imitated?
essayQuestions.focus: Frame, irony and endorsement
plan: Distinguish three voices: Hythloday, who admires; the narrator, who objects; and the author, who invented both and all the names.
Gather the evidence for endorsement: the cure for theft, the six-hour day, the treatment of gold, toleration, and the passion of the closing speech.
Gather the evidence against: the Greek names, the slavery and surveillance described without comment, the colonies and mercenaries, and the narrator’s reservations.
Treat the last sentence as a key: ‘rather wish, than hope’ allows admiration without advocacy.
Conclude that the book is built to be argued about, and that its method, making Europe look strange, matters more than whether the island could exist.

essayQuestions.question: How does Book I prepare the reader for Book II?
essayQuestions.focus: Structure and argument
plan: Note that Book I was probably written after Book II, and ask what it adds: England, a real Cardinal, real hangings and real enclosures.
Show how Morton’s dinner diagnoses problems, idleness, enclosure and savage punishment, that Book II’s institutions answer one by one.
Read the argument about counsel as a warning about how Book II will be received: ‘how little courtiers would value either me or my counsels’.
Look at the narrator’s objection to common property and how Book II is framed as the reply to it.
Conclude that Book I turns a description into an argument, and seats the reader at Morton’s table deciding whether to laugh.

essayQuestions.question: Compare the presentation of Raphael Hythloday and More the narrator.
essayQuestions.focus: Character, voice and the dialogue form
plan: Set out the difference in their situations: a traveller who has given away his estate, and an envoy with a wife, children and an office.
Compare their images of counsel: the lasting fountain and the play in performance against Plato’s philosopher who stays indoors while others stand in the rain.
Consider tone: Hythloday’s certainty and indignation against the narrator’s courtesy and his silence at the end.
Discuss the names: a traveller called for nonsense who talks the most sense, and a narrator who bears the author’s name and holds back.
Conclude on whether the book sides with either, or deliberately leaves the reader in the space between them.

essayQuestions.question: How does More use the Utopians’ attitudes to gold, jewels and pleasure to criticise Europe?
essayQuestions.focus: Satire and making the familiar strange
plan: Explain the chamber-pots and chains: the reasons given for them, and why value turns out to be a matter of convention.
Analyse the Anemolian ambassadors as a set piece: their mistaken expectations, the children’s laughter, their shame.
Show how the philosophy of true and false pleasure extends the method to fine clothes, titles, gems, dice and hunting.
Consider the limits: the Utopians’ certainty, their contempt for hunters, and the slaves who wear the gold.
Conclude that making Europe look childish is the book’s most effective argument, and ask whether it depends on a people who have never seen anything else.

discussionQuestions: Hythloday says that at court ‘serve’ and ‘enslave’ come to the same thing. Is he right, and does the narrator ever answer him?
Which Utopian institution would you most like to see adopted, and which would you most resist? Does the book seem to expect that division?
The Utopians keep slaves, need passports and ‘live in full view’. Does this weaken the case for the island, or make the account more honest?
Why might a book that argues for toleration make belief in an afterlife a condition of public office?
What is the effect of giving the book’s strongest arguments to a character whose name suggests nonsense?
At Morton’s table the guests applaud whatever the Cardinal approves. Where else do people take their cue from authority rather than argument?

timeline.label: Thomas More born in London
timeline.detail: Son of John More, a lawyer who later became a judge of the King’s Bench. The year usually given is 1478.

timeline.label: A page in Cardinal Morton’s household, c. 1490
timeline.detail: As a boy More waited at the table of John Morton, Archbishop of Canterbury and Chancellor, whom Hythloday describes in Book I.

timeline.label: The Cornish rising crushed
timeline.detail: Hythloday says he was in England ‘not long after the rebellion in the West was suppressed’, which places Morton’s dinner in about this year.

timeline.label: Vespucci’s voyages in print
timeline.detail: An account of Amerigo Vespucci’s four voyages was printed at Saint-Dié with a new map of the world. Hythloday claims to have sailed on three of them.

timeline.label: The Praise of Folly printed
timeline.detail: Erasmus wrote it in More’s London house and titled it Moriae Encomium, a pun on his friend’s name. Utopia comes from the same circle and the same habit of serious joking.

timeline.label: Machiavelli writes The Prince
timeline.detail: Another out-of-office official’s advice to rulers, taking the opposite view of how far a counsellor should accommodate power. It was not printed until 1532.

timeline.label: The embassy to Flanders
timeline.detail: In May More went with Cuthbert Tunstall to negotiate with the commissioners of Charles, Prince of Castile, and in Antwerp became friends with Peter Giles. The island of Book II was probably written later in the year.

timeline.label: First edition, Louvain
timeline.detail: Printed in Latin by Dirk Martens late in the year, with a woodcut map of the island, a Utopian alphabet and letters and verses by More’s friends.

timeline.label: The Basel editions
timeline.detail: Johann Froben printed revised editions at Basel, with woodcuts by Ambrosius Holbein.

timeline.label: More becomes Lord Chancellor
timeline.detail: He succeeded Wolsey in October, in the office Morton had held, and resigned in 1532 as Henry VIII moved against the Church.

timeline.label: More executed
timeline.detail: Beheaded on Tower Hill on 6 July, having refused to accept Henry VIII as supreme head of the church in England.

timeline.label: The first English translation
timeline.detail: Ralph Robinson’s version was printed in the reign of Edward VI, sixteen years after More’s death.

timeline.label: Burnet’s translation
timeline.detail: Gilbert Burnet, later Bishop of Salisbury, translated the book soon after the execution of his friend Lord William Russell. His English is the text quoted here.

timeline.label: More declared a saint
timeline.detail: Pope Pius XI canonised More, with John Fisher, four hundred years after their deaths.

places.name: Antwerp, Cathedral of Our Lady
places.note: More first sees Hythloday after mass at ‘St. Mary’s, which is the chief church’ of the city; the talk moves to the garden of More’s lodging.

places.name: Bruges
places.note: Where Henry VIII’s envoys met the commissioners of Charles, Prince of Castile, and failed to agree.

places.name: Brussels
places.note: Where the Prince’s commissioners went for instructions, leaving More free to visit Antwerp.

places.name: Lambeth Palace, London
places.note: The London residence of the Archbishops of Canterbury, and so of Morton, in whose household More served as a boy. The book does not say where the dinner took place.

places.name: Leuven (Louvain)
places.note: Where Dirk Martens printed the first edition in 1516.

places.name: Basel
places.note: Where Johann Froben printed the revised editions of 1518.

places.name: Calicut (Kozhikode)
places.note: Where Hythloday, having travelled by way of Ceylon, found Portuguese ships to carry him home.

places.name: Tower Hill, London
places.note: Where More was beheaded in 1535.

related.why: A phrase-by-phrase reading of the enclosure passage, in which the mildest animal in England becomes a predator with a landlord behind it.
Written three years earlier by another official out of favour, and the opposite answer to Hythloday: the adviser who takes men as they are and tells princes how to keep power.
The Elizabethan play about More’s rise and fall, in which the London under-sheriff talks a rioting crowd out of violence.
Swift’s traveller also returns from a rational commonwealth unable to bear his own country, and the satire again turns on how seriously to take the report.
Gonzalo’s imagined commonwealth, with no riches, poverty or occupation, belongs to the tradition More began, and is laughed at on stage.
A modern fable about a revolution in common ownership that ends with the pigs at the farmhouse table.

books.title: The War of the Worlds
books.author: H. G. Wells
books.setting: Surrey and London across about three weeks, from a sandpit on Horsell Common to the top of Primrose Hill
books.lengthNote: Two books and twenty-seven chapters, the last of them an epilogue written years after the events
books.openingLine: No one would have believed in the last years of the nineteenth century that this world was being watched keenly and closely by intelligences greater than man’s and yet as mortal as his own; that as men busied themselves about their various concerns they were scrutinised and studied, perhaps almost as narrowly as a man with a microscope might scrutinise the transient creatures that swarm and multiply in a drop of water.
books.summary: A cylinder from Mars lands on a Surrey common, and within a week the largest empire on Earth has been reduced to six million people running along the roads out of London. Wells tells it through a narrator who is never in charge of anything: he watches, runs, hides in a ruined scullery and arrives too late to understand what he has seen. The Martians are killed by bacteria, and the book is careful to insist that this is not a victory.
books.referenceStyle: book and chapter, e.g. Book I, Chapter XVII

sourceText.label: Standard Ebooks text of The War of the Worlds
sourceText.note: The novel divides into Book I, The Coming of the Martians, and Book II, The Earth Under the Martians. Chapters are numbered in Roman within each book and carry titles, which references here give where they help.

structure.label: Book I, Chapters I-IV
structure.title: A light on Mars, and a cylinder in a sandpit
structure.summary: Ten flashes are seen on Mars and reported as a curiosity. The first cylinder lands at night on Horsell Common, a crowd gathers round the pit as it would round a beached whale, and the lid begins to unscrew while the narrator watches from the heather.

scenes.title: The Eve of the War
scenes.summary: The narrator, writing afterwards, describes a world being studied by minds it has never thought about.

scenes.title: The Falling Star
scenes.summary: The cylinder comes down in the small hours and Ogilvy is the first man to reach it.

scenes.title: On Horsell Common
scenes.summary: A holiday crowd assembles round the pit and the newspapers get a paragraph.

scenes.title: The Cylinder Opens
scenes.summary: The first Martian hauls itself out and the watchers discover what they have come to see.

structure.label: Book I, Chapters V-VIII
structure.title: The Heat-Ray, and the evening papers
structure.summary: A deputation walks towards the pit under a white flag and is burned where it stands. The narrator gets home, tells his wife, and finds that the rest of England is still treating the matter as local news; the second cylinder falls while Woking is being evacuated.

scenes.title: The Heat-Ray
scenes.summary: An invisible beam kills the deputation and sets the common alight.

scenes.title: The Heat-Ray in the Chobham Road
scenes.summary: The crowd on the road is caught in the open.

scenes.title: How I Reached Home
scenes.summary: The narrator walks back through burning heather and finds his own dining room unchanged.

scenes.title: Friday Night
scenes.summary: London reads a short paragraph and goes to bed.

structure.label: Book I, Chapters IX-XIV
structure.title: Machines that walk, and a second witness
structure.summary: The fighting-machines rise and the military answer is over almost before it begins. The narrator drives his wife to Leatherhead, comes back into the storm, meets the curate among the ruins of Weybridge, and the narrative opens a second front with his brother in London.

scenes.title: The Fighting Begins
scenes.summary: Guns are dug in on the common; the narrator takes his wife out of Woking.

scenes.title: In the Storm
scenes.summary: A tripod overtakes the dog cart in the lightning.

scenes.title: At the Window
scenes.summary: Soldiers pass the house and the artilleryman tells what happened to his battery.

scenes.title: What I Saw of the Destruction of Weybridge and Shepperton
scenes.summary: A Martian is brought down by artillery, and the river boils.

scenes.title: How I Fell in with the Curate
scenes.summary: A clergyman reads the invasion as the day of judgement and cannot stop talking.

scenes.title: In London
scenes.summary: The narrator's brother finds the capital calm, then reads the morning papers.

structure.label: Book I, Chapters XV-XVII
structure.title: Six million people on the roads
structure.summary: The Black Smoke clears the ground in front of the machines and London empties north and east. The brother's chapters turn the novel from one man's escape into a study of a population in motion, and the Thunder Child gives the book its single moment of successful resistance.

scenes.title: What Had Happened in Surrey
scenes.summary: The Black Smoke is used systematically to kill anything that stays indoors.

scenes.title: The Exodus from London
scenes.summary: The brother joins the stampede and gets two women out through Barnet to the coast.

scenes.title: The Thunder Child
scenes.summary: A torpedo ram rams a fighting-machine and covers the escaping steamers.

structure.label: Book II, Chapters I-V
structure.title: Under foot, with the curate
structure.summary: A fifth cylinder buries the narrator and the curate in a half-collapsed house at Sheen, with a Martian pit on the other side of the wall. For a fortnight the two men watch the invaders feed, ration a dwindling larder and quarrel, until the curate's noise forces the narrator to stop him.

scenes.title: Under Foot
scenes.summary: The narrator is hunted through Sheen and takes shelter in an empty house.

scenes.title: What We Saw from the Ruined House
scenes.summary: Through a crack in the wall the Martians are seen taking human blood.

scenes.title: The Days of Imprisonment
scenes.summary: Hunger, thirst and the curate's voice become the immediate danger.

scenes.title: The Death of the Curate
scenes.summary: The narrator strikes him with the handle of a chopper, and a Martian takes the body.

scenes.title: The Stillness
scenes.summary: The pit is abandoned and the narrator crawls out into a red landscape.

structure.label: Book II, Chapters VI-VII
structure.title: Dethronement, and a plan drawn in a drain
structure.summary: Walking through the red weed, the narrator works out that he is no longer a master but an animal among animals. On Putney Hill he meets the artilleryman again, listens for a night to a magnificent scheme for living underground and rebuilding the species, then looks at the trench the man has actually dug.

scenes.title: The Work of Fifteen Days
scenes.summary: The red weed has taken the Thames valley and the narrator understands what has happened to his species.

scenes.title: The Man on Putney Hill
scenes.summary: The artilleryman's underground future, his champagne, and his unfinished tunnel.

structure.label: Book II, Chapters VIII-X
structure.title: Dead London, and the epilogue
structure.summary: The narrator walks into an empty capital following a howling that stops mid-note, climbs Primrose Hill and finds the Martians dead in their redoubt. The last chapter is written years later by a man who cannot walk down a road without seeing it silent.

scenes.title: Dead London
scenes.summary: The cry of Ulla, ulla ends, and the invaders are found killed by bacteria.

scenes.title: Wreckage
scenes.summary: The narrator breaks down, is taken in at Leatherhead, and gets home to Woking.

scenes.title: The Epilogue
scenes.summary: Unfinished science, a warning about the next opposition, and a man who wakes cold in the night.

characters.name: The narrator
characters.role: A writer on philosophical subjects, living near Woking
characters.summary: A man whose profession is explaining things and who spends the whole invasion failing to. He is never given a name, never holds a weapon that works and never makes a decision that alters events; what he does instead is look carefully and write it down years afterwards, which is the only kind of authority the book allows anyone.
characters.clue: He explains the Zodiac to his wife on a warm evening, and later beats a clergyman senseless in a scullery to stop him being heard.

characters.name: The narrator's brother
characters.role: A medical student in London
characters.summary: He exists so that the book can leave Surrey. His chapters are the only place where the invasion is seen as a problem of crowds, trains, money and roads rather than of one frightened man, and he is also the only character who does something plainly useful: he gets two women out alive.
characters.clue: A London medical student who knocks a man down over a dropped bag of sovereigns and then drives two strangers to the coast.
traits: the book's second pair of eyes

characters.name: Ogilvy
characters.role: An astronomer at Ottershaw
characters.summary: He sees the first jet of gas leave Mars and tells the narrator that the chances against anything manlike there are a million to one. He is the first man to reach the cylinder and one of the first killed by the Heat-Ray, which is the book's briskest way of dealing with confident expertise.
characters.clue: He invites a friend up to look through a telescope, scoffs at the idea of signals from Mars, and dies under a white flag.

characters.name: The curate
characters.role: A clergyman met in the ruins of Weybridge
characters.summary: He meets the invasion with a theology that cannot hold it and collapses into repetition, appetite and noise. Wells does not let the narrator feel superior for long: the two men eat the same rations, and the killing in the scullery is done for the very practical reason that the curate can be heard.
characters.clue: He rebuilt his church three years ago, cannot stop asking why, and eats more than his share in the dark.

characters.name: The artilleryman
characters.role: A survivor of a gun battery destroyed on the common
characters.summary: Twice met and twice differently judged. On the second meeting he lays out a whole underground civilisation of able men who will learn to fly a fighting-machine, and the narrator is carried away by it until morning, when the plan turns out to consist of a short tunnel, a stolen larder and a game of cards.
characters.clue: He can describe the coming underground republic in detail, and has dug about ten yards of it.

characters.name: The Martians
characters.role: The invaders
characters.summary: Heads and hands with no digestive system, moving in machines because Earth's gravity is too heavy for their bodies. They are never given speech, motive or negotiation; the book insists they are neither devils nor monsters but a species whose planet is dying and which is doing what our own has done to other populations.
characters.clue: They cannot walk upright on this planet, take their nourishment straight from other creatures' veins, and are killed by something too small to see.

characters.name: The narrator's wife
characters.role: Left at Leatherhead in the second week
characters.summary: She is driven to relatives for safety in the third chapter of the invasion and is off the page for most of the book, which is exactly what makes the last line work. The narrator counts her among the dead, and she counts him among the dead, for longer than either of them is actually missing.
characters.clue: She has the signal lights of the railway pointed out to her on a warm evening, and is left with cousins at Leatherhead.

themes.name: Imperial reversal
themes.summary: The book asks readers at the centre of the largest empire on Earth to occupy the other position. Wells makes the argument explicit in the first chapter, naming the extermination of the Tasmanians before a single cylinder has landed, so that everything the Martians do afterwards has already been described as something Europeans did first.
themes.development: Stated as history in Book I, Chapter I; enacted as roads, refugees and confiscated homes in the exodus chapters; and left unresolved at the end, because the deliverance is bacterial rather than moral.

themes.name: Dethronement
themes.summary: The invasion's real damage is to a belief rather than to a city: that human beings are the point of the planet. The narrator dates his own loss of it precisely, standing among the red weed and realising that he has become an animal among animals, and the epilogue shows the feeling never quite lifting.
themes.development: Complacency in Chapter I, terror in the middle books, and then a settled and permanent change of position in Book II, Chapters VI and X.

themes.name: Technological asymmetry
themes.summary: Courage makes no difference to the outcome of any engagement in this novel. The Heat-Ray kills before it is understood, the Black Smoke is applied like a weedkiller, and the one human success, the Thunder Child, is achieved by a ship that simply runs at a machine and dies doing it.
themes.development: Artillery at Horsell, a lucky shot at Shepperton, an ironclad off the Essex coast: three attempts, each smaller in its effect than the scale of the force behind it.

themes.name: Witness and report
themes.summary: Everything in the book reaches the reader through somebody who was there and did not understand it at the time. Telegraph, newspaper, rumour and eyewitness are all shown failing in different ways, and the narrator's authority comes from admitting how much of his account is reconstruction.
themes.development: A paragraph in the Daily Telegraph, then contradictory special editions, then no papers at all; and behind them the brother's narrative, which the narrator can only have received second-hand.

themes.name: Evolution and the humblest things
themes.summary: The novel's science is Darwinian before it is mechanical. Mars is old and cooling, its inhabitants have specialised themselves into brains with hands, and Earth's advantage turns out to be an immune system bought by a billion deaths nobody remembers.
themes.development: The cooling planet in Chapter I, the red weed rotting in Book II, and the Martians dead in the redoubt without a shot fired at them.

themes.name: Faith, explanation and nerve
themes.summary: Three ways of meeting a catastrophe are set against each other: the curate's apocalypse, the artilleryman's grand programme and the narrator's habit of writing down what he can see. Two of them are exposed, and the third is not offered as heroism, only as the one that leaves a record.
themes.development: The curate breaks in Book I, Chapter XIII and is silenced in Book II, Chapter IV; the artilleryman is believed for one night and disbelieved by breakfast.

techniques.name: Retrospective first-person narration
techniques.definition: A narrator telling their own earlier life, with the distance between the two selves doing the judging.
techniques.bookDefinition: A narrator telling, years later, events he lived through without understanding them.
techniques.inThisBook: The opening sentence is written from a future the first readers had not reached, which lets Wells put dread and explanation in the same paragraph without either cancelling the other.

techniques.name: The second witness
techniques.definition: Breaking off one character's account to follow another who can see what the first cannot.
techniques.bookDefinition: Breaking off one character's account to follow another who can see what the first cannot.
techniques.inThisBook: The brother's three chapters take the reader to London and the coast, and they are the only way the novel can show six million people moving at once.

techniques.name: Named topography
techniques.definition: Using real, checkable place names rather than invented ones.
techniques.bookDefinition: Using real, checkable place names rather than invented ones.
techniques.inThisBook: Horsell, Ottershaw, Byfleet, Shepperton, Barnet, Putney Hill and Primrose Hill let a first reader trace the invasion across a map they already owned.

techniques.name: Shift of scale
techniques.definition: Moving between the astronomical and the domestic inside a few sentences.
techniques.bookDefinition: Moving between the astronomical and the domestic inside a few sentences.
techniques.inThisBook: Forty million miles of void in one paragraph and a siphon of soda water on a table in the next; later, a balloonist's view of London and then one man's thirst.

techniques.name: The domestic simile
techniques.definition: Describing something unprecedented by comparing it with a familiar household object.
techniques.bookDefinition: Describing something unprecedented by comparing it with a familiar household object.
techniques.inThisBook: The first fighting-machine is a milking stool bowled violently along the ground, and the spreading Black Smoke is ink on blotting paper.

techniques.name: Scientific register
techniques.definition: Borrowing the vocabulary and cadence of a report or a lecture.
techniques.bookDefinition: Borrowing the vocabulary and cadence of a report or a lecture.
techniques.inThisBook: Distances, volumes, spectrum analysis and anatomical description give the terror a tone of measurement, and the epilogue's admissions of ignorance are more convincing than certainty would be.

quotations.text: No one would have believed in the last years of the nineteenth century that this world was being watched keenly and closely by intelligences greater than man’s and yet as mortal as his own; that as men busied themselves about their various concerns they were scrutinised and studied, perhaps almost as narrowly as a man with a microscope might scrutinise the transient creatures that swarm and multiply in a drop of water.
quotations.context: The novel's first sentence.
quotations.analysis: The sentence is built so that the reader is inside the microscope before they know there is one: men are the subject of the verbs for half its length and the object of them by the end. Wells also dates his own book from the future, which quietly guarantees that somebody survived to write it.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Book I, Chapter I

quotations.text: Yet across the gulf of space, minds that are to our minds as ours are to those of the beasts that perish, intellects vast and cool and unsympathetic, regarded this Earth with envious eyes, and slowly and surely drew their plans against us.
quotations.context: Still in the opening pages, after a paragraph about missionary enterprise.
quotations.analysis: Three adjectives do the work of a whole description of the enemy, and none of them is a moral term: cool and unsympathetic are what a scientist aspires to be. The phrase that follows, drew their plans against us, is the language of a committee, and that is the point.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Book I, Chapter I

quotations.text: Are we such apostles of mercy as to complain if the Martians warred in the same spirit?
quotations.context: Immediately after a sentence naming the extermination of the Tasmanians by European settlers.
quotations.analysis: The argument of the whole novel is made in a rhetorical question before the first cylinder has landed. It disarms the reader in advance: any outrage felt over the next two hundred pages has already been booked against an account the reader is on the wrong side of.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Book I, Chapter I

quotations.text: The chances against anything manlike on Mars are a million to one
quotations.speaker: Ogilvy
quotations.context: The astronomer, walking home from the observatory, dismissing the idea that the flashes are signals.
quotations.analysis: The professional is not being stupid; he is being reasonable with the evidence he has, which is what makes the line frightening rather than comic. Wells gives expertise one confident sentence and then kills the man who says it four chapters later.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Book I, Chapter I

quotations.text: A big greyish rounded bulk, the size, perhaps, of a bear, was rising slowly and painfully out of the cylinder. As it bulged up and caught the light, it glistened like wet leather.
quotations.context: The lid of the cylinder falls off and the first Martian appears above the edge of the pit.
quotations.analysis: The first alien in English fiction to be described this closely is measured against a bear and a piece of wet leather, both things a Woking crowd would have handled. Wells withholds the eyes for another sentence, so the thing is an object before it is a gaze.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Book I, Chapter IV

quotations.text: It was sweeping round swiftly and steadily, this flaming death, this invisible, inevitable sword of heat.
quotations.context: The deputation with the white flag has just been burned, and the beam is turning towards the narrator.
quotations.analysis: The weapon is named with a word from an older war, sword, because nothing in the narrator's vocabulary fits it. Every adjective is about motion and none about appearance, which is accurate: he is describing something he cannot see, only infer from what catches fire.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Book I, Chapter V

quotations.text: A monstrous tripod, higher than many houses, striding over the young pine trees, and smashing them aside in its career; a walking engine of glittering metal, striding now across the heather; articulate ropes of steel dangling from it, and the clattering tumult of its passage mingling with the riot of the thunder.
quotations.context: In a thunderstorm on the Maybury road, with his wife already safe at Leatherhead.
quotations.analysis: The machine is assembled in front of the reader out of participles, each clause adding one moving part, because the narrator is seeing it in lightning flashes rather than continuously. A page later he reaches for a milking stool to explain it, and the drop in register is the most honest thing in the chapter.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Book I, Chapter X

quotations.text: This must be the beginning of the end
quotations.speaker: The curate
quotations.context: His first extended speech, among the ruins at Weybridge.
quotations.analysis: He has a framework ready and reaches for it at once, which spares him the work of looking. The novel sets his apocalypse against the narrator's habit of counting cylinders and noting times, and only one of the two men is capable of learning anything new.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Book I, Chapter XIII

quotations.text: All the work⁠—all the Sunday schools⁠—What have we done⁠—what has Weybridge done? Everything gone⁠—everything destroyed. The church! We rebuilt it only three years ago. Gone! Swept out of existence! Why?
quotations.speaker: The curate
quotations.context: Standing in the wreckage of his parish.
quotations.analysis: The grief is real and the accounting is parochial: Sunday schools, a church rebuilt three years ago, a single town. He asks why five times in the chapter and never once asks what, which is the difference between him and the man listening to him.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Book I, Chapter XIII

quotations.text: It was the beginning of the rout of civilisation, of the massacre of mankind.
quotations.context: Summarising the flight of London, seen as if from a balloon above the home counties.
quotations.analysis: Rout is a military word applied to a population that was never an army, and the sentence puts civilisation and mankind in the same grammatical position as a broken regiment. Wells reaches this judgement only after six pages of specific roads and named suburbs, so the abstraction has been earned.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Book I, Chapter XVII

quotations.text: I was no longer a master, but an animal among the animals, under the Martian heel. With us it would be as with them, to lurk and watch, to run and hide; the fear and empire of man had passed away.
quotations.context: Walking through the red weed towards Putney, after seeing navvies digging foundations for a house.
quotations.analysis: The realisation is triggered by the most ordinary sight in the book, men building a house, and the tenses give it away: it would be as with them, the future of a man who has already accepted the position. Empire is the exact word, and it is the same empire the first chapter warned about.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Book II, Chapter VI

quotations.text: It never was a war, any more than there’s war between man and ants.
quotations.speaker: The artilleryman
quotations.context: On Putney Hill, over the first evening of talk.
quotations.analysis: War implies two parties with something to settle, and the artilleryman is right that this is not one. What he cannot see is that the same argument applies backwards: the analogy he has just used is the one the first chapter used about Europeans and the people they cleared.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Book II, Chapter VII

quotations.text: We’re eatable ants.
quotations.speaker: The artilleryman
quotations.context: Closing his comparison of men with insects.
quotations.analysis: Three words, and the adjective is the horror: ants are cleared out of the way, but these ones are also food. It is the only moment in the novel where the human position is stated as a biological fact rather than a political one.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Book II, Chapter VII

quotations.text: Cities, nations, civilisation, progress⁠—it’s all over. That game’s up. We’re beat.
quotations.speaker: The artilleryman
quotations.context: Setting out the principle on which he says he has acted.
quotations.analysis: A list of everything the nineteenth century believed in, dismissed in a sporting idiom. The energy of the speech is what persuades the narrator for a night, and Wells then shows the same man unable to finish a trench, so that the rhetoric and the labour can be compared directly.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Book II, Chapter VII

quotations.text: And scattered about it, some in their overturned war-machines, some in the now rigid handling-machines, and a dozen of them stark and silent and laid in a row, were the Martians⁠—dead!⁠—slain by the putrefactive and disease bacteria against which their systems were unprepared; slain as the red weed was being slain; slain, after all man’s devices had failed, by the humblest things that God, in his wisdom, has put upon this Earth.
quotations.context: On the rampart of the Martian redoubt on Primrose Hill.
quotations.analysis: Slain is repeated three times, each with a different agent, and the last is the smallest thing in the book. The sentence gives the victory to bacteria and the credit to God, which leaves human courage, artillery and strategy with nothing to claim at all.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Book II, Chapter VIII

quotations.text: By the toll of a billion deaths man has bought his birthright of the Earth, and it is his against all comers; it would still be his were the Martians ten times as mighty as they are. For neither do men live nor die in vain.
quotations.context: Explaining why the invaders died and human beings did not.
quotations.analysis: Birthright is a legal and biblical word, and Wells insists it was bought rather than granted, at a price counted in the deaths of people nobody recorded. It is the closest the novel comes to consolation, and it is addressed to the species rather than to anyone in it.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Book II, Chapter VIII

quotations.text: We have learned now that we cannot regard this planet as being fenced in and a secure abiding place for Man; we can never anticipate the unseen good or evil that may come upon us suddenly out of space.
quotations.context: The Epilogue, weighing what the invasion has permanently changed.
quotations.analysis: The image is agricultural, a fenced field, and it is the exact opposite of the imperial map: the planet is no longer property. Wells then refuses the obvious moral by suggesting the invasion may have done humanity good, which is a colder thought than the one it replaces.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Book II, Chapter X

quotations.text: I go to London and see the busy multitudes in Fleet Street and the Strand, and it comes across my mind that they are but the ghosts of the past, haunting the streets that I have seen silent and wretched, going to and fro, phantasms in a dead city, the mockery of life in a galvanised body.
quotations.context: The Epilogue, describing what the narrator still sees years afterwards.
quotations.analysis: The tenses have gone to the present: this is not a memory but a thing that keeps happening. The living crowd is described as the ghost and the emptied street as the real one, which inverts the usual arrangement of a haunting.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Book II, Chapter X

quotations.text: And strangest of all is it to hold my wife’s hand again, and to think that I have counted her, and that she has counted me, among the dead.
quotations.context: The last sentence of the book.
quotations.analysis: Strangest is a superlative reached after tripods, dead London and the redoubt, and it is spent on two people holding hands. The symmetry of the clause, he counted her and she counted him, makes the loss mutual and leaves the novel ending on an arithmetic of the dead rather than on relief.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Book II, Chapter X

atAGlance.label: Serialised
atAGlance.note: In Pearson's Magazine in Britain and Cosmopolitan in the United States, before any book edition.

atAGlance.label: First book edition
atAGlance.note: Published in London by William Heinemann.

atAGlance.label: Where it starts
atAGlance.note: Ordinary common land on the edge of the Surrey town where Wells was living when he planned the book.

atAGlance.label: How it ends
atAGlance.note: No army defeats the Martians. They die of the microbes every human body has already survived.

criticalViews.position: An anti-imperial fable
criticalViews.summary: The reading the book invites in its own first chapter: Britain is made to suffer what British settlers did to peoples they judged inferior, and the novel's sympathies are complicated by the narrator's inability to claim any moral advantage.
criticalViews.counter: The Martians are still presented as biologically alien rather than as colonists with a culture, which lets the comparison work as shock without holding up in detail.

criticalViews.position: A founding text of science fiction
criticalViews.summary: Wells's method, extrapolating from published science and grounding the result in real streets and timetables, set the pattern for the invasion narrative and for a century of catastrophe fiction.
criticalViews.counter: Read only as an origin, the book's peculiar features go missing: its dead time, its long passages of hunger and boredom, and its refusal to give anyone a decisive action.

criticalViews.position: A late-Victorian crisis of confidence
criticalViews.summary: Critics have placed the novel beside invasion-scare fiction, anxieties about national decline and the popular astronomy of the 1890s, reading it as a diagnosis of a society that has mistaken technical superiority for permanence.
criticalViews.counter: The epilogue argues the opposite way, suggesting that losing serene confidence in the future was worth what it cost.

essayQuestions.question: How far does The War of the Worlds ask its readers to see themselves as the Martians?
essayQuestions.focus: Imperial reversal and the novel's first chapter
plan: Start with the Tasmanians sentence in Book I, Chapter I: the comparison is made before any Martian acts.
Trace the vocabulary of empire through the book, especially the narrator's realisation that he is under the Martian heel.
Use the exodus chapters to show English people occupying the position of a displaced population.
Test the limits of the case: the Martians take blood rather than land, and never speak or govern.
Close on the ending, where deliverance is microbial, so no imperial self-justification is available.

essayQuestions.question: What is gained by telling the invasion through a narrator who achieves nothing?
essayQuestions.focus: Narration, authority and the second witness
plan: Establish what the narrator actually does: walks, hides, watches, and writes it up years later.
Contrast him with the artilleryman, who has a plan, and the curate, who has an explanation.
Examine the brother's chapters as a deliberate widening, and ask how the narrator could know them.
Consider the epilogue's admissions of ignorance as a source of credibility rather than a weakness.
Judge whether the book's power depends on this refusal of a hero, comparing any adaptation that supplies one.

essayQuestions.question: Discuss Wells's use of real places and ordinary objects in the novel.
essayQuestions.focus: Topography, simile and the texture of catastrophe
plan: Map the route: Horsell, Byfleet, Weybridge, Sheen, Putney, Primrose Hill, and what naming them does to a local reader.
Collect the domestic comparisons, from the milking stool to ink on blotting paper, and note who is making them.
Show how the Black Smoke and the red weed are described in the language of gardening and public health.
Set the scientific register of the epilogue against the eyewitness register of the middle books.
Conclude on the effect: terror produced by accuracy rather than by invention.

essayQuestions.question: 'The ending is a defeat for humanity, not a victory.' Discuss.
essayQuestions.focus: Bacteria, dethronement and the epilogue
plan: Set out how the Martians die and how little any human action contributes to it.
Read the humblest things sentence closely, noting the three uses of slain and where the agency lies.
Weigh the billion deaths passage, which does claim something for the species, though nothing for individuals.
Use the epilogue's fenced-in image and the return of the narrator's nightmares against any sense of restoration.
Decide what the last sentence about his wife's hand settles, and what it deliberately leaves open.

discussionQuestions: The first chapter tells you the Martians are only doing what Europeans have already done. Does knowing that change how you read the rest of the invasion?
The artilleryman talks brilliantly and digs almost nothing. Why does Wells let him be so persuasive first?
The narrator kills the curate. Does the novel condemn him for it?
Nothing the army does makes any difference, and the Thunder Child dies achieving one small thing. Why keep the episode at all?
Would the book be more or less frightening if the Martians could speak?

timeline.label: H. G. Wells born at Bromley
timeline.detail: He later trained in science in South Kensington under T. H. Huxley.

timeline.label: Schiaparelli maps the canali of Mars
timeline.detail: The Italian word for channels was widely read in English as canals, and the idea of Martian engineering entered popular astronomy.

timeline.label: Percival Lowell opens his observatory at Flagstaff
timeline.detail: Built largely to study Mars; the novel opens with a light seen on the planet at the 1894 opposition.

timeline.label: The Time Machine published
timeline.detail: Wells's first scientific romance, and the beginning of four years that also produced Moreau, The Invisible Man and this book.

timeline.label: The Island of Doctor Moreau published
timeline.detail: Its interest in the boundary between men and animals runs straight into the artilleryman's argument about ants.

timeline.label: Serialised in Pearson's Magazine
timeline.detail: British readers met the invasion in monthly instalments; an American serial ran in Cosmopolitan.

timeline.label: First book edition, William Heinemann
timeline.detail: Harper and Brothers issued the American book edition the same year.

timeline.label: Orson Welles broadcasts the story on CBS
timeline.detail: Howard Koch's adaptation moved the first landing to Grovers Mill, New Jersey, and used the form of a news bulletin.

timeline.label: Wells dies in London
timeline.detail: By then he was known as much for his histories and political writing as for the scientific romances.

timeline.label: George Pal's film released
timeline.detail: Directed by Byron Haskin, it relocated the invasion to mid-century America and replaced the tripods with flying machines.

timeline.label: Jeff Wayne's musical version released
timeline.detail: A concept album narrated by Richard Burton, which kept the novel's structure of a witness reporting after the event.

timeline.label: Steven Spielberg's film released
timeline.detail: Refocused on one family in flight, and on the refugee traffic that occupies the brother's chapters.

related.why: The same decade's other story of an invader arriving by sea, tracked through timetables, telegrams and newspaper cuttings.
Wilde's novel of the 1890s, taking the other route out of Victorian confidence: inward rather than outward.
The earlier argument about what science makes and what it fails to anticipate.
A contemporary English fantasy that also sets one isolated narrator against forces with no interest in him.
Another late-Victorian scientific romance told through documents by a narrator who arrives after the event.

books.title: White Fang
books.author: Jack London
books.setting: The Mackenzie River country of the Canadian North, Fort Yukon and Dawson in the gold-rush summer of 1898, then San Francisco and the Santa Clara Valley in California
books.written: c. 1904–05, in California, as a deliberate companion to The Call of the Wild
books.lengthNote: Five parts and twenty-five titled chapters, about 72,000 words — more than twice the length of The Call of the Wild, and the hero is not born until the sixth chapter
books.openingLine: Dark spruce forest frowned on either side the frozen waterway.
books.summary: A cub that is three-quarters wolf is born in a cave beside a frozen stream, walks into an Indian camp, and spends the rest of the book being made into whatever his owners need: a sled dog for Grey Beaver, a pit fighter for Beauty Smith, and at last a house dog for a mining expert’s family in California. London sets out to prove that character is clay pressed by circumstance, and he is thorough enough to apply the same rule to a camp cook and an escaped convict. The difficulty the novel never quite settles is that its happy ending is also a surrender, and that the thumb which finally presses the wolf into a fairer shape belongs to a man he calls a god.

sourceText.label: Project Gutenberg text of White Fang
sourceText.note: The novel is divided into five parts, and the chapter numbers begin again in each. Parts and chapters carry Roman numerals and titles in the text; they are cited here by Arabic numeral, as Part 3, Chapter 2.

structure.label: Part 1
structure.title: The Wild
structure.summary: Two men, six dogs and a coffin are followed down a frozen river by a starving wolf pack that takes the dogs one by one, lured out by a she-wolf who knows the ways of camps. White Fang is not yet born. The part exists to show the Wild from the position of the meat, so that every later chapter about a hunting cub is read by someone who has already been hunted.

scenes.title: The Trail of the Meat
scenes.summary: Bill and Henry haul the body of Lord Alfred towards Fort McGurry; Bill feeds seven dogs where there should be six, and in the morning Fatty is gone.

scenes.title: The She-Wolf
scenes.summary: Frog and Spanker are taken, the she-wolf shows herself in daylight and decoys One Ear from the traces, and Bill goes after her with three cartridges and does not come back.

scenes.title: The Hunger Cry
scenes.summary: Henry, alone with two dogs, slings the coffin into a tree and holds the pack off from inside a ring of fire until a party of men finds him asleep in the ashes.

structure.label: Part 2
structure.title: Born of the Wild
structure.summary: The pack breaks up, old One Eye wins the she-wolf by killing his rivals, and a litter is born in a cave above a stream. Famine leaves one grey cub alive. He learns fear before he has met anything to be afraid of, tumbles out through the wall of light into a world of ptarmigan, hawks and weasels, and arrives at a law in three words.

scenes.title: The Battle of the Fangs
scenes.summary: The famine ends, the pack divides, and One Eye and a young leader together kill an ambitious three-year-old before One Eye kills the young leader as well.

scenes.title: The Lair
scenes.summary: The she-wolf finds a cave and whelps; One Eye waits out a porcupine and a lynx and carries home what the lynx leaves.

scenes.title: The Grey Cub
scenes.summary: The one grey cub of the litter takes the cave mouth for a wall of light; a second famine kills his brothers and sisters, and the lynx kills his father.

scenes.title: The Wall of the World
scenes.summary: He falls through the wall, eats a nest of ptarmigan chicks, is beaten by the hen, nearly drowned in a stream and nearly killed by a weasel.

scenes.title: The Law of Meat
scenes.summary: The she-wolf robs the lynx’s lair, the lynx comes for the cave, and mother and cub kill her between them; the cub draws the conclusion.

structure.label: Part 3
structure.title: The Gods of the Wild
structure.summary: The cub meets five Indians on the way to the stream, his mother crawls to them at the sound of her name, and he is named and owned in a single speech. In Grey Beaver’s camp he learns clubs, fire, laughter, property and the sled, is made an outcast by the puppy pack under Lip-lip, and comes back of his own accord when he might have stayed wild.

scenes.title: The Makers of Fire
scenes.summary: Grey Beaver recognises Kiche, names the cub and claims him; White Fang meets Lip-lip, burns his nose on a fire, and is laughed at.

scenes.title: The Bondage
scenes.summary: Kiche is handed to Three Eagles to settle a debt, and White Fang, swimming after her canoe, takes his first real beating and learns never to bite a god.

scenes.title: The Outcast
scenes.summary: Lip-lip turns every young dog in the camp against him, and he learns to fight without warning and to go for the throat.

scenes.title: The Trail of the Gods
scenes.summary: He hides when the camp moves in the autumn, finds that freedom is cold and silent, and runs forty hours down the river bank to crawl to Grey Beaver’s fire.

scenes.title: The Covenant
scenes.summary: Harnessed in Mit-sah’s team behind a persecuted Lip-lip, he learns what property is, and defends Mit-sah against a gang of boys.

scenes.title: The Famine
scenes.summary: He faces down old Baseek over a shin-bone, is slashed by a mother who has forgotten him, lives wild through the famine, kills Lip-lip, and goes back to the village.

structure.label: Part 4
structure.title: The Superior Gods
structure.summary: Made sled leader and hated for it, he travels with Grey Beaver to Fort Yukon in the summer of 1898 and is sold for whisky to Beauty Smith, who turns him into the Fighting Wolf. A bulldog he cannot throw gets him by the throat, and a young mining expert pulls the jaws apart, buys him by force and begins, with great patience, to unmake what the pit has made.

scenes.title: The Enemy of His Kind
scenes.summary: Running at the head of a team that wants to tear him down, he crosses the Rockies to Fort Yukon and sees his first white men.

scenes.title: The Mad God
scenes.summary: Beauty Smith, the fort’s cook, buys him from a drunk Grey Beaver with bottles; he gnaws free twice and is twice handed back and beaten.

scenes.title: The Reign of Hate
scenes.summary: Caged, goaded and exhibited at Dawson, he fights dogs, wolves and a full-grown lynx, and never loses his feet.

scenes.title: The Clinging Death
scenes.summary: Tim Keenan’s bulldog Cherokee gets a grip and keeps it; Weedon Scott knocks Beauty Smith down, levers the jaws open with a revolver and pays a hundred and fifty dollars.

scenes.title: The Indomitable
scenes.summary: He kills a sled dog and lays open Scott’s hand, and is reprieved because he knows what a rifle is and has the sense to get out of its way.

scenes.title: The Love-Master
scenes.summary: Scott’s hand comes down without hurting; liking becomes love; White Fang sickens when Scott goes away, and mauls Beauty Smith when he comes to steal him.

structure.label: Part 5
structure.title: The Tame
structure.summary: He breaks through a cabin window to follow Scott aboard the steamer and is taken to the Scott family estate in California, where he has to learn that chickens, cats, children and other dogs are all under the protection of the gods. He pays for his place by killing the convict who comes for the Judge, and ends the book in the sun with puppies climbing on him.

scenes.title: The Long Trail
scenes.summary: Locked in the cabin, he goes through the window and is waiting on the deck of the Aurora; Scott gives in.

scenes.title: The Southland
scenes.summary: San Francisco appals him, a baggage car carries him south, and at Sierra Vista he is met by a deer-hound and by a sheepdog, Collie, who knows a wolf when she sees one.

scenes.title: The God’s Domain
scenes.summary: He learns the household, kills fifty Leghorn hens in one night, is taught better, and wins Scott a bet against the Judge by sitting an afternoon in the chicken yard.

scenes.title: The Call of Kind
scenes.summary: He learns to be laughed at, fetches help when Scott’s horse falls and breaks his leg, barking for the only time in his life, and runs in the woods with Collie.

scenes.title: The Sleeping Wolf
scenes.summary: Jim Hall escapes from San Quentin to kill the Judge who sentenced him; White Fang kills him on the stairs, takes three bullets, and is named the Blessed Wolf.

characters.name: White Fang
characters.role: A wolf-dog, three parts wolf: sled dog, pit fighter, house dog
characters.summary: He is the only survivor of his litter and the quickest learner in every company he enters, and what he learns depends entirely on who has hold of him. The book is careful to make him neither noble nor vicious by nature: he is morose and murderous under Lip-lip and Beauty Smith and devoted under Scott, and London’s point is that it is the same animal each time.
characters.clue: Named in a single sentence by an Indian who has just clouted him, this one never barks but twice in his life, fights without warning, and ends by letting puppies climb over him in the California sun.

relationships.label: cub of, and later a stranger to
gives himself to, and is sold by
persecuted by, and at last kills
hates, and is made to fight by
is harried by, then mates with

characters.name: Kiche, the she-wolf
characters.role: White Fang’s mother; half wolf, half Indian camp dog
characters.summary: In Part 1 she is the red-hued decoy who lures sled dogs out of camp to be eaten, and in Part 2 a fierce and competent mother; in Part 3 she drops to her belly at the sound of her own name. She is the book’s first proof that a creature can belong to the Wild and to men by turns, and her forgetting of her son is given as a plain fact of wolf-motherhood rather than a wound.
characters.clue: She knows enough about campfires to steal from them and enough about men to come when they call her; a year after losing her cub she lays his cheek open to the bone.

characters.name: One Eye
characters.role: An old grey wolf, White Fang’s father
characters.summary: A scarred veteran who runs on the she-wolf’s blind side and wins her by patience and by treachery, killing a rival while the rival is licking a wound. He is a dutiful provider who is rather afraid of his mate, and he dies offstage, killed by the lynx, leaving only the remains his mate finds at the end of his trail.
characters.clue: He has lost the sight on one side and most of his illusions, waits an hour beside a rolled-up porcupine because something may happen, and is found at last as a few remains near a lynx’s lair.

characters.name: Grey Beaver
characters.role: A Mackenzie Indian, White Fang’s first master
characters.summary: He is just by his own lights, never caresses and never beats without cause, and defends his dog against the whole camp when it has killed another man’s. What he offers is a bargain — food, fire and protection for work and obedience — and the novel respects the bargain while insisting it contains no love. Whisky undoes him at Fort Yukon, and he sells for bottles what he had refused to sell for dollars.
characters.clue: He names a cub in one breath and clouts it in the next, holds the door of his tepee against an angry camp, and in the end trades the best sled dog on the Mackenzie for something in a black bottle.

characters.name: Lip-lip
characters.role: A camp puppy, older and larger than White Fang
characters.summary: A bully who wins his first fight with the newcomer and makes a career of it, leading the puppy pack against White Fang until the cub has no companion in the camp but his tied-up mother. The narrator holds him responsible for a good deal: without him, we are told, White Fang might have grown up more doglike and more liking of dogs.
characters.clue: He had fought many puppy fights before the stranger arrived and enjoyed winning them; years later, thin with famine, he meets that stranger alone at the foot of a bluff.

characters.name: Beauty Smith
characters.role: Cook and drudge at Fort Yukon; owner of the Fighting Wolf
characters.summary: Misshapen, cowardly and cruel, he takes out on a caged animal what stronger men have done to him. London describes him at cruel length and then pronounces him not responsible, since the clay of him was moulded that way in the making. The verdict is consistent with the book’s theory, though the chapter’s evident loathing of him is not.
characters.clue: The other men gave him his first name as a joke; he cooks for them, is feared for what he might put in the coffee, and laughs when the thing in the cage goes mad with hate.
traits: patient in getting what he wants

relationships.label: is knocked down and bought out by

characters.name: Weedon Scott
characters.role: A mining expert from California; the love-master
characters.summary: He arrives in the book as a fist in Beauty Smith’s face and then turns out to be its gentlest figure, undertaking the taming as a debt — a way, he thinks, of redeeming mankind from the wrong it had done the dog. He is also a judge’s son with money and connections, and the ease with which he overrides another man’s property rights is something the novel enjoys rather than examines.
characters.clue: He pays a hundred and fifty dollars for a half-dead dog whose owner is not selling, has his hand laid open for his trouble, and sits down on the cabin step next day to try again.

relationships.label: rescues, tames and is loved by

characters.name: Matt
characters.role: Scott’s dog-musher
characters.summary: The practical man of Part 4, who spots the harness marks on White Fang’s chest, argues for giving him a chance, and feeds him for months without ever being accepted as his master. His slangy commentary keeps the taming chapters from turning solemn, and his puzzlement that the dog should love the man who never feeds him is the book’s own question put in plain speech.
characters.clue: He tells his employer to his face that he is seventeen kinds of a fool, and shouts from a gang-plank that the wolf will never stand the climate unless he is clipped.

characters.name: Collie
characters.role: A sheepdog at Sierra Vista
characters.summary: She alone refuses the household’s verdict on the newcomer: generations of guarding flocks tell her what he is, and she nags, nips and shoulders him for months. She is right, as the chicken-yard shows, and the novel lets her be right and lose. By the last chapter she has a litter by the ancient marauder and is still snarling at him.
characters.clue: Her instinct is older than her manners; she drives the newcomer across the fields after the business with the groom, and a season later runs beside him in the woods as another female once ran beside One Eye.

characters.name: Judge Scott
characters.role: Weedon Scott’s father, master of Sierra Vista
characters.summary: A genial retired judge who bets that a chicken-killer cannot be cured and cheerfully pays up when he is. He is also the man who, in good faith and on perjured evidence, sent Jim Hall to prison for fifty years, so the comfortable household that receives White Fang rests on exactly the kind of mistaken sentence the novel has been arguing against.
characters.clue: He must say sixteen times, slowly and solemnly, that the wolf is smarter than he thought; he pooh-poohs the newspapers, though not with reason.

characters.name: Jim Hall
characters.role: A convict escaped from San Quentin
characters.summary: He enters five chapters from the end and is given, in two pages, the same life as the hero: soft clay handled harshly, a cage, a keeper who was as great a beast as he, and teeth used on a throat. The difference is that nobody comes for him. He is innocent of the crime he was sentenced for, and the dog who was saved kills the man who was not.
characters.clue: He was a little pulpy boy in a city slum, lived three years in an iron cell without seeing the sky, and crept one night up a judge’s staircase past something asleep in the hall.

relationships.label: the human double of, killed by

characters.name: Bill and Henry
characters.role: Two dog-drivers carrying a coffin to Fort McGurry
characters.summary: They own Part 1 and then vanish from the book. Bill frets, counts dogs and cartridges and finally goes after the pack with a rifle; Henry eats his beans, reproves him for being off colour, and survives. Their laconic talk across the fire is London’s way of measuring how near death is without having to say so.
characters.clue: One of them counts seven dogs at feeding time when there should be six; the other ends up asleep inside a circle of embers with his mittens burnt through.

themes.name: The clay and the thumb
themes.summary: London states his thesis outright and repeats it at every change of owner: heredity is a life-stuff like clay, and environment is what models it. The cub who would have become a true wolf becomes a wolfish dog, then a fiend in a cage, then a guardian of children, without his nature changing at all. The argument is applied even-handedly to human beings, which is where it becomes uncomfortable.
themes.development: Announced in Part 3, Chapter 6; extended to Beauty Smith, who is pronounced not responsible, in Part 4; turned into the thumb of circumstance, which is Weedon Scott, in Part 4, Chapter 6; and closed with Jim Hall, the soft clay of a San Francisco slum, in the last chapter.

themes.name: Gods, clubs and the power of dead things
themes.summary: White Fang’s theology is strictly empirical. Men are gods because sticks and stones fly at their bidding, because they make fire, and later because they make steamboats and cable cars; the more power, the higher the god. The scheme lets London describe domination from underneath, as something felt to be in the order of things, and it means that every beating in the book is also an act of worship.
themes.development: First felt as the man-animals’ mastery over dead things in Part 3; ranked, with white men above Indians, at Fort Yukon in Part 4; pushed to the point of terror on the pavement of San Francisco; and domesticated at Sierra Vista, where the gods’ power shows chiefly in what they forbid.

themes.name: Eat or be eaten
themes.summary: The Wild of this novel is a food chain with no outside. Part 1 shows it from the point of view of two men being eaten, Part 2 from that of a cub learning to eat, and the narrator is explicit that the cub lives the law without ever thinking it. What follows in the camps and the fighting pit is the same law with men added, which is London’s reason for starting where he does.
themes.development: The pack runs down the sled team in Part 1; the cub kills ptarmigan chicks and is nearly killed by a weasel in Part 2; the code becomes obey the strong and oppress the weak in the camp; and in California he must unlearn it hen by hen.

themes.name: The covenant: liberty for a god
themes.summary: The central bargain of the book is put in contractual terms: food, fire, protection and companionship on one side; work, obedience and the guarding of property on the other, with liberty as the price. London calls it the ancient covenant of the first wolf that came in from the Wild, and he is honest that it is a relief as well as a loss, since it is easier to lean upon another than to stand alone.
themes.development: Kiche crawls to her name; White Fang comes in to Grey Beaver’s fire of his own choice in Part 3, Chapter 4; the terms are set out in Chapter 5; whisky breaks the contract from the god’s side in Part 4; and under Scott the same service is rendered for love rather than awe.

themes.name: Like replaced by love
themes.summary: For three parts the best feeling available to White Fang is liking, and the book says flatly that his service to Grey Beaver had no love in it because he did not know what love was. Scott’s hand, which comes down and does not hurt, reaches a capacity that had nearly died. The love that results is exclusive, jealous of its dignity, and expressed by a growl with a crooning note in it.
themes.development: Absent in the Indian camp; awakened against every instinct in Part 4, Chapter 6; proved by the broken window and the pining when Scott is away; and tested in the South, where he must extend a grudging tolerance to everyone the master loves.

themes.name: The enemy of his kind
themes.summary: White Fang belongs to no pack after the cave. The puppies reject him as a wolf, the sled team hates him as a leader, the fighting pit makes every dog an opponent, and he learns to want only to be let alone. London treats this solitude as manufactured, not natural, and the measure of his recovery at the end is that he can lie still while another animal’s young climb over him.
